Has to be one of the best games I've played. I don't take to FPS type games easily but Batman is one of the best FPS/beat-em-ups going. The meleé combat system is relatively easy to get to grips with and progresses nicely as the story unfolds; the story is engaging and creates a great Batman-esque (dark) atmosphere; and the voice acting is spot-on.
I have the game running fairly well under Windows 8.1 with a 4GHz Core i5, 8GB RAM, GTX 760 2GB graphics card, and all the graphics options maxed (except for AA on GeForce TXAA Low) - roughly 30fps or above @ full HD. The game is visually stunning, Gotham is beautifully recreated with lots of detail and a fluid system of moving around.
The gameplay is split between action in the cityscape and action in buildings/enclosed areas. There are some nice alternative sections too and a little puzzle solving to obtain certain objects.
I loved Gears of War on the XBox and this is just as easy to get into. I haven't completed the game yet (30%) but there has been plenty to do and there is good replay value in various challenges you can unlock and training modes.
It's not perfect, mind, there are the occasional camera angles issues and the odd glitch that requires a game restart.
If you like Batman and like FPS type games then this is a no-brainer, for everyone else it's close to a no brianer, and for those that hate these types of games you may be surprised at how good it is.
Now, can someone make a Spiderman game with this engine and dynamics?

By far the worst game 'on the market'. It has easily crumbled to ruins after what the current leaders have done to this game. They let it die and they ruined so much behind it. It used to be a fun, great, addicting game. But now it's a struggle just to even attempt to play the game. The issues that are presented are overwhelmingly frustrating. Let's talk about these flaws.
The connection issues that arose as of late making the game unbearable. The server has some serious kind of issues where the game freezes, your ping spikes up anywhere from 1-200 at this exact moment, your FPS drops up to 50% or more, and you start teleporting or 'rubber banding'. I have never, never in my entire life as a gamer, played an online game that had connections issues this bad. These spikes occur a few times throughout the minute, ranging from a couple to maybe 10 or even more.
Next, we get into the development of the game and who's behind it. Basically, the development is non-existant. This game has barley changed over the course of years. The original developers that had heart and care to make this game great and work on have been gone for quite a long time. We are presented with MEDIOCRE updates time and time again. The only updates that do come out take much too long and bring content that is meaningless. The big picture of this game is a complete failure. A new engine upgrade has been in the works for what, close to two years? Where is that development? We get pictures and false promises. False promises is all that this game is made of. The dev team is quite pathetic no matter what the size. I know teenagers that would do a better job with their amateur development skills in less than 3/4 of the then that of APB devs. And those devs that did stay up until recently are leaving to pursue better things.
There is simply no creativity left. There is nothing left. The game has no quality, it isn't fun to play. It's dying and it's been dying.
In game there are so many issues, so many things that need tweaking. The updates that we do get are horrible and frowned upon by the community time and time again. Lots of aspects in the game that are flawed, don't make sense. Bugs, glitches, stuff that has been here for YEARS completely ignored. Lots of cries that were never heard or reached out to. This is negligence at it's finest. The player never had a say in anything.
They attempted to merge the districts together in order to 'better' matchmaking and open more opportunities. However this was the start of all of the connection issues and the real death of this game. Even with the merge, the servers are very much dead. They have less players than the servers had alone before the merge.
This alone paints the picture of how this game has been going downhill.
Time and time again they neglect their fans that have been loyal all this time. And we get nothing at all in return. Customer support has forever been non existant and they really won't care to help you no matter what kind of issues you have. I have been faced with this multiple times. Gamersfirst staff only care about pushing more sales and more 'joker mystery boxes' because they think this is where the appeal lies. They only ever cared about the money. And nothing else. We are all bent over with our knee-pads on and sodomized terribly to this company.

If you were a fan of the original Mad Max movies than this game ISNT FOR YOU. If you want a repetative, unbalanced reminder that you should rewatch the movies than this is for you. The beginning of the game is great. Fair fights, exciting car chases, intriguing characters, AND EXPLOSIONS!!! Then, after 5 story missions the games difficulty just gives up trying.
The fights start becoming unfair as Max is easily outnumbered by 2-3 enemies. Surrounding Enemies will attack you during a parry or counter-attack which becomes a major problem when your defending against a weak enemy as the other(probably stronger tiered) enemy hits you.
Car combat becomes unpredictable as enemies will either drive super slow, leading to anti-climactic battles; or they will just stop dead in their tracks to get behind you and ram you. The latter seems eassily remedied until you get in battles while trying to take out convoys. The lead truck will always get away unless you deal with it first. If you dont, the enemies JUST RESPAWN.
Also with the car combat, you have your own Quasimodo who will constantly talk your ear off with the same dialogue or 'tips'. He is your car's healer as well who does bugger all when it comes to later in the game. You can upgrade the speed of which he repairs your car....but I havent gotten there yet. The upgrades are so unbalanced it makes the game frustratingly unplayable. It is really hard to fight off level 3 armored vehicles when you dont get any decent upgrades until youve completed at least half of the game. Until then, you have to fight enemies with tier 2 upgrades while some have tier 3-4.
Another issue is the fact that ammo is very limited. You'd think that to balance out how unfairly skilled the enemy was you'd get a plethora of ammo. You don't...you dont even get unbreakable melee weapons like the enemy has. With the two stats that helps Max not break the weapon, they break after 3-4 hits.
Controls...the controls are horrible. Ive tried three different keyboards and the way the game mapped out each button was poorly thought out. On top of that, it takes 2 seconds for the game to register the button you pressed leading to easdy deaths because you couldnt counter fast enough. I checked my PC and it was fine. Come to find out EVERYONE has this problem. I also tried remapping but it seems every key is taken for something stupid you'll never use until you change the key.
TL;DR:
Pros:
-Huge map
Cons:
-poorly mapped out keys
-unbalancxed combat
-annoying side kick
-no dog to help you in combat(YOU TEASE A DOG BUT ALL HES USED FOR IS SNIFFING OUT MINES!!!!)
-Upgrades that are poorly given out(That last mission would have been easier if i got the second upgrade but noooo, i have to practically beat the game to get upgrades to beat the game)

The Hitman games were always unique in the sense that they basically created their own subgenre. Where other stealth games expected you to remain unseen while carrying out your mission, Hitman games dropped you off in a neutral environment and demanded that you blend in with the crowd - hiding in plain sight, if you will. Assassinating a target was always the ultimate goal, but Hitman encouraged the player to fulfill this task as quietly and clean as possible while the environment provided several ways of getting close: Spiking the target's food with laxatives to seperate it from armed bodyguards, assuming the identity of an informant or simply using a sniper rifle from afar are only a few of the possibilities to tackle a single mission. Hitman games are notorious for their replayability.
Despite the vicious deeds the player is supposed to perform, the games were not without their own brand of black humor: You could drop a piano on your target like in a classic Roadrunner cartoon, or you could switch a fake gun for a real one and turn the pretend murder during a rehearsal of a stage play into an actual one without pulling the trigger yourself. There was also the main character’s habit of introducing himself as “Tobias Rieper”. Additionally, the games displayed a touch of class, which was reflected in the locations the player visited or even in the way the main character dressed.
In the past, Hitman: Blood Money perfected this formula and is widely regarded as the peak of the series. It was released in 2006 and the 2012 sequel, Hitman Absolution, was supposed to follow up on it, but fell short for several reasons: It was loud, it was vulgar and it offered only a fraction of the options usually found in a Hitman game. IO Interactive took the criticism to heart and promised to do better. And they succeeded for the most part.
Interesting level design has always been the main draw of the series and in that regard, the new Hitman truly is a return to form. The levels released so far are massive and offer so many ways of getting the job done, it will make your head spin. Just in terms of size alone they’re bigger than anything Blood Money offered.
Disguises were a key element of previous Hitman games and one of Absolution's gravest mistakes was devaluing them. If you disguised as a cop, somehow every other cop in the area instantly knew you didn’t belong and it required hitmana to weasel your way past every single one of them. Even though there are hints of this system still present in the latest Hitman, it’s nowhere near as rigid or illogical: Only a few non-player characters in strategic places will get suspicious if you approach them.
There’s a small online portion, too. Like in Absolution, Hitman players are able to create custom contracts with specified targets, victory conditions, leaderboards and everything. While Hitman games are notorious for their replayability, IO Interactive tries a new spin on the established formula: Every other week, there will be a an Elusive Target roaming the levels - a unique target that is only available for a short amount of time. If the timer runs out or if the player dies while carrying out the mission, the target is gone for good. No saves and no second chances. This approach heightens the tension in theory, but in reality it’s not as harsh as advertized. You can retry one Elusive Target as often as you want, as long as you are still in the time frame for completion and you haven’t killed the target or haven’t been killed yourself. Also, it’s quite obvious not the same amount of care went into the Elusive Targets as it did for the main missions. A nice idea, but certainly not a game seller.
Apart from a few optimization issues and a couple of logical inconsistencies, everything about the actual game is peaches and gravy. However, some of the decisions surrounding it sour the taste - most notably the business model and “encouraged” online.
When you think about it, mission-based games like Hitman are perfect for expansions, DLC and post-release support, yet none of the previous ones really approached the idea. Until now. However, the way this game realized the idea couldn’t be more awkward. Essentially, Hitman is an episodic game that drip-feeds the player a level each month until the number of promised levels is complete. Games like The Walking Dead have proven that an episodic model isn’t inherently bad and even Resident Evil: Revelations 2 - a game that isn’t story-driven - managed to make it work somehow. Though the main difference is that REv2 only made you wait for two weeks until a new episode would be released. Making the player wait an entire month between episodes for a mission-based game is not something you want to do as a developer. Hitman’s release model has an interesting side effect, though: Previously, you would reinstall a Hitman game after months and replay it to try out new approaches. While waiting for new levels to drop, you have few other things to do but replay existing levels and tackle them in different ways. The current release model ensures you undertake those future replays now.
The other main problem of Hitman is its “encouraged” online. Technically, it’s not forced online since the game remains playable even when you’re offline, but it locks you out of many options that enhance replayability. Completing different challenges as you replay a level unlocks equipment and starting positions that keep each new attempt fresh. Unfortunately, challenges are only available online. Same goes for user contracts and Elusive Targets. Plus, savegames for offline and online playthroughs are not compatible with each other. If you lose connection while playing or you get booted from the server, you won’t be able to resume where you left off.
While the servers are stable for me, my main concern with this approach is preservation. Let’s say I get the urge to play Hitman in three years, but the devs have pulled the plug on the servers in the meantime. Sure, the game would remain playable as the levels provide plenty opportunities to turn your target’s switch to “off”, but many many interesting approaches would be lost forever. Here’s hoping IO Interactive rethinks this decision.
So if you're a fan of Hitman and Absolution left a lot to be desired, you might be pleased with this one. Yet some of the decisions regarding distribution will make you scratch your head. Also, as high-quality as the levels are that have been released at the time of writing, there's still some room for the developers to drop the ball.

This game is a masterpiece. It's one of the best games I've ever played, and it's one of the rare games that I know I'll still be remembering in 10+ years. I've played it when it came out (2012) and I still shiver whenever I read about it or hear the soundtrack.
A few things to consider just so you're not disappointed :
1) You're buying this for the SP campaign. MP isn't great.
2) The campaign is maybe 7 hours long. It's the perfect length for this kind of game.
3) Since the game is "short", I HIGHLY recommend trying to beat the game in a short period of time. Ideally in 2-3 sessions, unless you're willing to clear it in a single sitting which I'd recommend if you can. The story is intense and can be quite confusing, so waiting weeks between 2 gaming sessions could have a negative impact on your appreciation.
4) Don't read anything / watch anything about the story or pretty much anything about this game before playing (even some reviews). Spoilers would ruin it.
5) Don't give up on it too early because the first hour or so is average at best.
6) Should be obvious but anyway, make sure to play with sound on (music, sound effects, voice acting). It's not a game you want to play while the TV is on or while talking on Skype.
7) Pay attention to the little details. Hints : Title screen, voice acting, flow of the game, etc. This is part of why it's a masterpiece in my opinion.
8) If you're not great at shooters, don't hesitate to play at an easier difficulty. Seriously you're not playing this for the challenge / gameplay. Some parts near the end can be annoying, and there's no real point in playing this at a difficulty where you'll have to restart often. Just make sure you're comfortable for the ride and enjoy it.

I remember playing the first Borderlands on the 360 back in 2009 when it was released. It was some of the most fun I've had playing a video game. To top it off, the atmosphere, story, writing, etc, was all unique enough to keep me drawn in for the entire duration. Gearbox not only does that again with Borderlands 2, but they go above and beyond with the critically acclaimed sequel with the outrageous comedy, numerous open areas, the lengthy overall game time (story + side missions), the amazing soundtrack from Jesper Kyd, stellar RPG system blended into the glorious FPS mechanics. And I've only beaten the main quest line. There's still all the DLC to be played! Brilliant game, and it runs so well on PC.
Brieft synopsis of the story: Five years after the events of the first game, Pandora is flourishing with a mineral called eridium after the defeat of The Destroyer. The original vault hunters have gone their seperate ways. You are a new vault hunter, similar to the four vault hunters from the first game. You have four to choose from, unless you have the GOTY edition, or purchased the DLC after the initial release, then there are two additional options. The vault hunters are riding a train together on Pandora, except the train is a trap, set up by the man who brought them there, Handsome Jack, the president of Hyperion. Surviving, the vault hunters find themselves in a frozen wasteland, only to be greeted by the last Claptrap. Claptrap and "Angel", the mysterious woman from the first game, guides you to bandit locations so you can free Claptrap's boat and make your way to Sanctuary, the safe city in this game. Sanctuary is the main hub where you'll receive missions. From here, you do several tasks for the Crimson Raiders, which includes Roland, one of the original vault hunters. You main mission is to track down Jack and kill him. That's all I'll say on the story without spoiling anything else. Just know that it's a blast.
One other thing, however. If running an AMD card, bring the PhysX option all the way to low. PhysX is an Nvidia component and your game will seriously stutter at certain points if left on high.

I've been playing games since the mid 80's and RPG's have always been my favourite genre and Planescape Torment is easily one of the best RPG I've ever played, and I've played countless rpg's since I first discovered the fantastic world that was gaming when I saw someone play Kings Quest 1.
I had such high hopes for this game, that hope turned into frustration after the very first fight, then into a big "meh" and finaly into one of the biggest dissapointments I've ever had with a game.
The worldbuilding is indeed fascinating and the backstory is both interesting and both well made and fleshed out, some of the characters you meet and choices you are forced to make is as grey as they come, which is a huge plus for me, but at the end of the day, that's all there is to this game unfortunately. The game is dull and extremely boring with way to much uninteresting information thrown in your face, which is the main flaw imo. If the wall of texts was somewhat fun and engaging to read, I could live with the many flaws this game has, but it's more or less the opposite. I love reading, it's one of my hobbies, but reading boring text is never fun, especially in a game that is supposed to be a form of entertainment. This game barely qualifies as a game.
This game can best be described as a grotesque mix between a walking simulator (in a very small world), an old school point and click adventure with one of the worst UI and inventory managment systems I've ever had the misfortune to come across. Last but not least is the greatets part of the game, which is visual novel and takes up a huge part of the game. Theese genres donsn't mix together at all. So what I did the few hours I played was to avoid combat at all cost after the very first one, since it sucked so bad that whoever came up with the system ought to be ashamed. The word "terrible" dosn't justify how bad the combat in this game is, but then again, you can skip combat altogether, something I belive 99.9% of the players does after experiencing it just once. So after making sure to never enter combat again, I started to explore the world, which is the one and only great part of this game, unfortunately then the next problem imiadetly popped up, because as I said, that's all there is. It's an awsome world filled with dull characters than sends you on quests to speak with other npc:s. It goes something like this;
Talk to npc a, read through a wall of text and make sure you click on every single sentence for bonus xp/skills, after exhausting all the possible choices of the conversation with the npc you get a quest if you're lucky, which sends you to another npc where you repeat what you just did with the first one. Does that sound like a fun? Not to me it dosn't and I have nothing against wall of texts, if the text is actually interesting of course, which in this game it unfortunately isn't. So the gameplay can best be described as talking to npc a, goto npc b who sends to to npc c, which sends you back to the first npc, who sends you to pick up and object and talk to more boring and dull npc:s... After a few hours of doing just that, I uninstalled the game in pure disgust. Unfortunately by then, I had played a few hours to much, which made it impossible to get a refund.
The good.
Great worldbuilding and backstory. There is some very interesting and philosophical thought provoking choices you are forced to make, which makes this game stand out from the usual black & white choices you see in rpg:s.
The bad.
Everything else, since the creators failed to build upon what was actually good in the game and hid it beneath millions of words of dull text and boring talking to every npc you find typ of quests. If you're a fan of Planescape Torment, then this game is not the sequel we've been waiting for since that game was first released almost 20 years ago. It's not a bad game though, it just failes to deliver pretty much everything of what it promised, especiallt after the extremely long developement cycle it had.

It's not perfect yet but I have to admire the story design.  It really shines in its reactivity while still offering a strong narrative.  Choices do matter and depending on the order in which you do quests some options may not be available.  The ending less so in its reactivity, it offers options but few are going to be blocked off.  Overall I loved the immersion in the setting (Numenera is one of my favorite table top settings, up there with Planescape and Dark Sun).  I enjoyed most of the companion NPCs but the lack of character portraits for most NPCs was a shame.
The combat and overall mechanics were servicable.  I said Numenera was one of my favorite settings, mechanically it's good  for what it's trying to be but not great.  I get the feeling they originally tried to do a full Numenera mechanics approach, that didn't work so we got some sort of amalgamation of it and d20.  It works fine but isn't exactly fun in most combat situations.  In its defense when facing a more complicated crisis the number of options to procede is great and those are interesting.
I'm hoping for a director's cut so I can give it a second playthrough with fresh content.  It's worth picking it up now but if you can hold off you're likely to save money and get a more fleshed out product.

For those of you whining about the combat system, go play Dungeons and Dragons/Pathfinder/Any tabletop RPG. There's everything from limited movement per turn, and a limited amount of actions, along with various weapon proficiencies.
For those of you whining about the reading, go read a book or something. You clearly don't do that often enough.
Basically, almost every aspect of this game is well done. The combat, the story, the dialogue, etc. Honestly, the only criticism I have with the game is a slow start, but that picks up soon enough.

Foreword: as someone who has never played a dating sim or any kind of visual novel before, I actually had a fun time with this even if my initial purchase was mostly just an impulse buy on my behalf because of how something like this seems like a joke on the surface and not an actual game.
Pros:
• The art is nice to look at, and very consistent in terms of visuals and is very pleasant to look at. My only criticism is that I would say the backgrounds weren't exactly too-eyecatching compared to the characters themselves, but other than that, I like this game's art and character design a lot.
• The choices and freedom regarding how many different people you can date is much appreciated, I like the variety between all the different dads in this game.
• The music and sound quality is easy on the ears, though the soundtrack is a bit limited so it might get a bit repetitive after a while.
• The character development in this game is very good, I like how the game naturally eases you into meeting every single dad at least once without forcing you to date all of them, and the interactions that you can have with your daughter between dates with the other dads and how you can help her with her life outside of home.
• The price isn't too bad for what it is, but I definitely would wait for a sale before purchasing unless you're, for whatever reason, REALLY desperate for this game.
Cons:
• Unfortunately, a single playthrough of the game is way too short for my liking, I managed to
in under two hours of playing, and I get the feeling that's really not a lot of room for replay value here besides changing which dad you wanna date in each subsequent playthrough.
• The character customization is a good feature to have to a degree, but the only time you ever get to see your character is when your speech bubble shows up on screen, and even then, the quality of the art on NPCs does not carry over to your character, making him look a bit bland compared to them.
• I'm not sure if this is a problem that is common in visual novels or not, but effectively having to play as basically a pre-established character makes it feel like the game is putting words into my mouth with the only input I have being dialogue that have little to no effect on the story at all.
• Literally the only way you could possibly 'fail' a date (and I'm saying that word VERY loosely here) is completely just do nothing in the minigames you have to play, there's really no challenge at all and the gameplay itself is for the most part just clicking through text boxes with your mouse or clicking an object on the screen.
• The voice acting in this is limited to the occasional sigh or grunt from NPCs (with full quotes at the end of dates), which does the job to a degree I guess, but still left me a bit unsatisfied, especially with all the dad puns in this and how amazing they would be if fully voiced acted.

I quit this game pretty early on and, I have to say, I want my money back.
The game says that it wants to show you the dark side of war giving you hard choices. Only there are no choices.
Look into the game before you buy. I wish I had. It turns out the main character is delusional. So you aren't being forced into making hard choices, you're being forced to play a madman.
That completely disconnects you from the point.
It's true that war is dark and there are difficult decisions to be made. The fog of war means that on average 3 civilians are killed for every militant in a war. WWII saw 10 civilians killed per militant.
But to show the moral dilemma of this, you need to be presented with a sane character that does the best he can; not an insane one that is responding to delusions. I thought I would be playing a difficult situation where I may very well have to let civilians die or even kill them myself in order to complete my mission. This could have long term consequences for either decision to be made.
Instead, I'm following around a delusional character in a game that claims to give you a choice but then shoehorns you into a predetermined outcome.
Good thing I bought this on sale. I still want my money back.

EDIT:
With Patch 1.02 out, I'm going to take another crack at this and try to give it a bit more fair a review.
If you're looking for a continuation of the previous four(five?) games, it's a bit hard to say whether or not you would enjoy this one. It seems to disregard everything FNaFs 1-4 set up, the murders, the cover-ups, Springtrap, and that's just the tip of the iceberg. While you can find references to past games, they're few and far between, and as far as I can tell, the only thing worth noting that this game makes reference to is the time period of a certain event, one that about half the fanbase already knew about. The 'horror' is also incredibly weak, and while the first couple of nights work with the atmosphere and setup fairly well, it seems to just kind of give up around nights 3 and 4, relying more on difficult puzzles than actual fear-inducing setups. The 'free-roam' isn't free, the mystery(if there is any) is practically spelled out for you, the jokes aren't that funny(not that a horror game should have that many jokes, especially not with this much frequency), and the scares are, well, not scary.
With that being said, Sister Location isn't *bad*, more or less just...unexpected. It's a change of pace from the previous four main titles that nobody was really prepared for, but that's not always a bad thing. The animatronic models look really nice compared to the previous titles(which, in all fairness, weren't slacking either), the voice acting, while it does take some time to get used to, is overall pretty good, and the story, as blunt as it is, is decent.
If you're looking for another FNaF game that builds upon the mysteries and mechanics of the others, you're not going to find it here and would probably be better off saving the money. If you're just looking for a distraction for a few hours, go ahead and pick it up, you might be delightfully surprised.

This game is a refreshing change to the other games. Each night is different and you can tell Scott put alot of time into this game, some nights are argueable ALOT harder than others, night 4 had me for 45 minutes. It's also got some humour in it too at the start of each night. Mechanically the game plays very similar, and has the same look to it. The audio queues are on point too. There is obviously alot of easter eggs too, there's panels and buttons everywhere. The only one I found was the Baby minigame, as well as the standard nose honking ones. The game took me just shy of 4 hours, beating most the nights quickly, so it's a decent size for a FNAF game.
For help on each level, look below. I'll try to avoid spoilers.
Night 1: Easy, did it after 2 tries after I learned you had to pull the door back. Listen to the instructions and you'll be golden.
Night 2: Got it first try. Just listen for movement when pressing the restart buttons. If you do, come out the menu and hit your recording button. Wait until the danger sign is one green bar before you start again.
Night 3: Caught a couple of times, no issue there... Take a few steps, flash, repeat. Stop if you hear footsteps. In the second part, press the buttons in order as instructed. When asked to press the big black button, you'll need to be patient. SLOWLY move your cursor around and you'll spot what you're looking for. Hold the light NEAR it but don't go on it and wait. It'll slowly reveal itself so you can quickly press it. On the way back, just repeat the first instructions.
Night 4: This night is by far the hardest night. It will be down to the wire everytime. Go around in a circle, the more mannequins that crawl up you, the fast the bolts come undone, so start getting faster as you go around and don't tighten them as much. Wait with wiggling to see if you can get 2 of the side ones off at once, saves the bolts loosening more than it needs to.
Night 5: Just follow the instructions and you'll be fine. Easy.

If you were a fan of the original Mad Max movies than this game ISNT FOR YOU. If you want a repetative, unbalanced reminder that you should rewatch the movies than this is for you. The beginning of the game is great. Fair fights, exciting car chases, intriguing characters, AND EXPLOSIONS!!! Then, after 5 story missions the games difficulty just gives up trying.
The fights start becoming unfair as Max is easily outnumbered by 2-3 enemies. Surrounding Enemies will attack you during a parry or counter-attack which becomes a major problem when your defending against a weak enemy as the other(probably stronger tiered) enemy hits you.
Car combat becomes unpredictable as enemies will either drive super slow, leading to anti-climactic battles; or they will just stop dead in their tracks to get behind you and ram you. The latter seems eassily remedied until you get in battles while trying to take out convoys. The lead truck will always get away unless you deal with it first. If you dont, the enemies JUST RESPAWN.
Also with the car combat, you have your own Quasimodo who will constantly talk your ear off with the same dialogue or 'tips'. He is your car's healer as well who does bugger all when it comes to later in the game. You can upgrade the speed of which he repairs your car....but I havent gotten there yet. The upgrades are so unbalanced it makes the game frustratingly unplayable. It is really hard to fight off level 3 armored vehicles when you dont get any decent upgrades until youve completed at least half of the game. Until then, you have to fight enemies with tier 2 upgrades while some have tier 3-4.
Another issue is the fact that ammo is very limited. You'd think that to balance out how unfairly skilled the enemy was you'd get a plethora of ammo. You don't...you dont even get unbreakable melee weapons like the enemy has. With the two stats that helps Max not break the weapon, they break after 3-4 hits.
Controls...the controls are horrible. Ive tried three different keyboards and the way the game mapped out each button was poorly thought out. On top of that, it takes 2 seconds for the game to register the button you pressed leading to easdy deaths because you couldnt counter fast enough. I checked my PC and it was fine. Come to find out EVERYONE has this problem. I also tried remapping but it seems every key is taken for something stupid you'll never use until you change the key.
TL;DR:

Cons:

-unbalancxed combat
-annoying side kick
-no dog to help you in combat(YOU TEASE A DOG BUT ALL HES USED FOR IS SNIFFING OUT MINES!!!!)

I have supported Hitman since the days of Blood Money.  However, the current Hitman, is not quite Hitman Blood Money yet, but it is getting there.
Whilst I enjoy the game at the minute, for what it is, considering that a majority of the content has yet to be delivered into the domains of the mass market, I do not agree with some of the business decisions which have been made by IOI.  Namely, to give the bonus missions to owners of "The Full Experience pack", and "Upgrade Pack", but not to people who have purchased "The Starter Pack", which means that the consumers of "The Starter Pack" either have to refund content, or purchase "The Upgrade Pack", which in turn means that they have to spend even more money in that instance and have to purchase content that they may already own a copy of, in order to unlock the extra content.
Furthermore, this decision has driven a dividing line between the members of the community, which now feels like a hostile environment resulting in community members being at each others throats when we should all be working together, for the common good.  I cannot help but feel that IO Interactive should have focused on solving issues such as equality, on creating a sense of community, and shared values, for the greater good of both the community, the product, and the business rather than putting barriers such as this in place, which is what they have done, however inadvertently or otherwise, by making this decision.
In that sense, I can recommend Hitman, but I cannot recommend IO Interactive, so I am torn between what to do, since, by default, if I support Hitman, I support IO Interactive and their, to be frank, rather idiotic business decisions, since neither entity can be extrapolated from the other.
Finally, I have found that Hitman is a solid product, despite containing DRM, and the game itself performs admirably, for me at least.  The levels are enjoyable, whilst at the same time being quite vibrant and quite large.  However, I feel that the business has made a bad decision in the marketing of this product and how it, and the business, relates to the customer.
Hitman 8 out of 10.
IO Interactive 3 out of 10.

Torment: Tides of Numenera is a narrative-driven RPG with much more focus on the world, the characters, and the story, rather than combat.  Many have described it as a visual novel, just how Planescape: Torment is described as a visual novel for exactly the same reason as this game.  Personally, I'm a huge fan of this.  Planescape: Torment is remembered as such a fantastic game for its incredibly deep world, the themes, the story, and the choices that you can make in the game.  Tides of Numenera seeks to be a successor to Planescape: Torment not just superficially, but it wants to be a deep, fulfilling experience, just like Planescape: Torment was, and I believe it has succeeded.
There's a lot of negative reviews that seem to be largely focused on the game's lack of combat, so let's be clear: if you think RPGs are all about leveling up your characters to make them stronger, get loot, and beat up monsters, then look elsewhere.  You are not going to find this game fun if you can't enjoy a game that focuses on the setting instead of combat.  I've seen people who claim to have enjoyed Planescape: Torment while simultaneously criticize this game for its lack of combat.  I simply cannot understand that.  Planescape: Torment hardly had combat.  What combat was in the game was almost entirely skippable and universally very easy (while also being quite buggy and boring, mostly auto attacking).  Combat is not what made PST remembered as one of the greatest RPGs ever made.  Planescape: Torment is remembered as such a great game, but it did not make a lot of money because a lot of people just couldn't get into it.
This game is the same.  You should only consider buying this game if you like reading and you're ready to jump into a deep narrative experience.  If these things appeal to you, then you should enjoy the game a lot.  That's my two cents.

Being a fan of this dev team and Planescape, I kickstarted Torment: Tides of Numenera with excitement but tapered expectations. When Torment initially released into Early Access, my excitement grew. The writing was good, the characters were intriguing, and skill checks felt like they'd deliver a legitimate roleplaying experience. After finishing the game, I can't say it was bad game per say. But I'm definitely disappointed, and I definitely would suggest a slew of other RPGs ahead of this one. So what went wrong between Early Access and release?
For one, combat never evolved into a strategically challenging system. Several abilities are completely useless, the encounters were generally all uninspired, and before long you'll want to avoid combat purely because of how mundane it all is. It feels like the team started with a good system and then ran out of time to finish it (a pattern you will see repeated in this review).
Combat might be forgiveable if the skill check system were properly balanced, but mid way through the game I was easily passing every check. Torment bills itself as a game where players can embrace their own mistakes. I wouldn't really know because I was flying by without any fear of what might happen on a failed check. Without the fear of failure from combat or roleplaying, all sense of overcoming adversity went out the window.
The characters are generally well written but aren't fully fleshed out. I enjoyed talking with Callistege, Erritis, and Matkina as well as their occasional interactions with one another. Both the dialogue and descriptions were novel-esque, but the game lacked a strong sense of direction. The story starts with a very promising antagonistic introduction but fails to maintain interest during the 20 hour experience. Music/sound was OK but nothing to write home about.
The combat, skill checks, roleplaying, characters, story, and progression options all show tons of promise. Unfortunately, nto a single one of those aspects feel fully realized. For that, I just can't recommend picking this up.

If you prefer fantasy or traditional sci fi, maybe not. Weird nonsensical crazy stuff makes up a lot of the game. It's very Lovecraftian in that respect, tho not so horror focussed. Actually, yknow what, yeah, it's Lovecraft+Torment minus some of the horror aspects.
This game is much like it's predecessor, but with a much beefier story and a lot less combat. This can be good or bad depending on your preferences. The pacing between story/combat is a bit off at times, but it's presented in a far more realistic manner than most games. You will not be accosted by random thugs constantly if you stay in one area too long, for example. Every encounter is relevant to a quest in some manner. Random combat does not exist.
To sum it up.... Story is the focus and combat, when it occurs, is part of that story. If you are here for anything other than story, look elsewhere. If you hate Lovecraftian storytelling, this game might not be for you. That said, if those two things don't bother you, this is a great story focussed game that will suck up well over 60 hours of your time and you should definitely give it a go.

I think this Game doesn't deserve all the bad votes. It is a worthy successor to Planescape:Torment. I'd say, on a mechanical level its even far superior to Planescape. You can finish the whole game without killing anybody, and there is a lot of gameplay even in the dialog, Depending on your skills or your Tides (alignment) you get extra information or even extra dialog options. Also, depending on your Attributes and Skills, you can fail at certain dialog options. Deceiption or persuation for example.
If there is a Conflict, very often, you have the option of interacting with the enviroment or even to talk to the Characters involved. Instead of mindlessly killing everything that moves. This is a huge step up from previous RPGs and i really like it.
Like planscape:torment the world is very strange and hard to understand first, but also very interesting and beleivable. but, like in planescape, you will probably be confused at first and it'll take some time to get familiar. In both games it took a few attempts for me to really get into it.
The story and the varius quests are very well designed, not only is there a massive amount of well written text in the game, a lot (probably even all) the questlines are connected to each other in a very clever way. One will probably notice it in the End of the game.
The game has one unfortunate flaw though, that even planespace had to a lesser degree. And i think lots of the downvotes come from this flaw.
It is a somewhat cold and cerebral game. Even though the quests, and the whole story are very dramatic at times, I missed the emotions, especially from the party members. The fact that there are no romantic options in the game also doesnt help this.
(The End is probably one of the best examples of aformentioned problem...)
Still, I think this is an excellent game, and a must play for any serious RPG fan. To find a better one, you have to go way back (planescape, baldurs gate2, fallout 1+2, and maybe the mass effect trilogy)

Overview: Prison Architect is a game that allows you to construct, manage, and be sentenced to a prison of your own making with a large variety of features.
I typically do a pros/cons section in my reviews, but it's difficult to do that with Prison Architect. The game gives you the freedom to do pretty much everything with the tools it (or modders!) provide you. The AI for the prisoners and staff isn't bad, negatives like contraband, prisoner tension, and needs are fairly balanced with your mitigation options (Which require some thought in implementation!).
This game is everything you'd expect for what it is. The only true downsides that come to mind is that prisoners don't always satisfy their biggest need first (Such as not using the toliet sitting in their cells before going to the shower, then starting a fight over it.)
Vinal Verdict: Solid 9/10. Great game that's constantly being improved!

Let me tell you this little story about a prison in some far off land…
Everything started out nice.  It was a small prison, about 50 cells, and held only those who seemed to be no threat to anyone.  It was the lowest of the low security prisons.  It had a large yard, a great common room, and families had their choice of 8 private visitation rooms.  It was an inmate’s dream!  Then one day, during chow, a couple of inmates threw a few punches.  Nothing major, although they were bleeding all over the place.  The warden immediately put up a medical ward to help them get back to being healthy.  The next day another fight broke out.  But something was different, a couple inmates were now wearing orange and couldn’t return to their cells in the low security block.  The warden now had to make a new cell block for medium security prisoners.  This wasn’t what he had in mind at all…
Time passed, as it always does, and by the end of the first year that small 50 cell prison had become a full blown medium security prison of 150 inmates and having everything from armored guards to security cameras to dog patrols.  Then one day a fight broke out…
10/10 … Would unwillingly build a SuperMax again
Prison Architect is, unquestionably, the best prison management game in existence to this point.  It has a unique minimalistic graphic style that seems to resonate with players, while not losing the fun that this game brings to the table.  There simply isn't anything else that can compare to it, and the slew of similarly styled games popping up all over Steam shows that it's success is well earned.
As mentioned, the graphics of Prison Architect really aren't spectacular.  That said, they aren't supposed to be.  Characters are made up of a simple body and head, with circular hands that occasionally appear when they need to.  The style fits perfectly into a world made up of 3D objects represented in a 2D space.  You're never at a loss to understand what's happening with objects or what characters are up to with their movements, it all plays out extremely well and allows for some seriously huge and busy prisons without slaughtering today's average PC.
The audio of the game is a good representation of what you would expect to find in a prison atmosphere.  There is background chatter which intensifies along with the "heat" of the prison so you not only have visual cues to the prison atmosphere but also audio cues.  Along with that are unmistakable warning noises when things light fights break out or when contraband is discovered.  There's no guessing what's going on in your prison, each sound tells you exactly what's happening even if it's not visible to you in the frame of the screen.  All in all the audio seems extremely well thought out and properly implemented without it becoming annoying or intrusive.
Prison Architect also comes with many different game modes, and Steam Workshop compatibility.  This means not only can you share your prison with others, you can download others prisons to use, improve, or challenge.  Speaking of challenge, Prison Architect takes things one step further here.  Not only can you build and manage a prison, you can also become an inmate and live that prison lifestyle for yourself, or escape it if you dare.
The complexity of Prison Architect leaves nothing to be desired.  Aside from simply building and maintaining your prison, you also have to manage other aspects as well.  You can build classrooms to hold training sessions, have psychiatrists on staff to deal with patient issues, run a fully-functional kitchen, and even build a medical ward to deal with the all but inevitable injuries to both prisoners and staff alike.  You have to manage your staff's welfare as well, providing them with rooms they can store items in, rooms they can take breaks in, and rooms where they can monitor the security of the prison.  To pay for all of this you can institute work prison work programs such as laundry and food prep to cut down on support staff, license plate workshops, and even a lumberyard to output wood for cash.  There's more than enough here to keep you busy for months on end.
All in all I'd have to give some huge props to the developers of Prison Architect.  They had a vision, stuck with it, and produced one hell of an awesome prison management game.  This is certain to be a "must have" in anyone's game collection.

I quit this game pretty early on and, I have to say, I want my money back.
The game says that it wants to show you the dark side of war giving you hard choices. Only there are no choices.
Look into the game before you buy. I wish I had. It turns out the main character is delusional. So you aren't being forced into making hard choices, you're being forced to play a madman.
That completely disconnects you from the point.
It's true that war is dark and there are difficult decisions to be made. The fog of war means that on average 3 civilians are killed for every militant in a war. WWII saw 10 civilians killed per militant.
But to show the moral dilemma of this, you need to be presented with a sane character that does the best he can; not an insane one that is responding to delusions. I thought I would be playing a difficult situation where I may very well have to let civilians die or even kill them myself in order to complete my mission. This could have long term consequences for either decision to be made.
Instead, I'm following around a delusional character in a game that claims to give you a choice but then shoehorns you into a predetermined outcome.
Good thing I bought this on sale. I still want my money back.
It really shows what a war looks like.

I won't recap or try to give any deeper analysis of the game than any of the other deep reviews on here. All I can say is that I've not yet been able to replay this game the way I've replayed othe FPSs such as Operation Flashpoint Red River, COd and etc.
You find yourself getting drawn into the story in albeit subtle, but much deeper ways than you would in most other story driven games.  Most "choices determine outcome" based games allow you to choose between a clearly good option and a clearly bad option. That's mostly designed to provide replay value by way of multiple possible endings. This game puts you in the harsh, and almost nightmarish reality that sometimes there are no good outcomes. In a way I feel that this games is much needed dose of reality in a time popular partiotism, and the glossy marketing veneer that has been placed on war. Over the last 12-13 years we've been conditioned to believe that if you're anti-war then you're simultaneously anti-veteran and anti-american. This games showcases the true cost of war. It reminds us that every soldier who has seen combat comes home wounded, and that not all wounds are visible.
The moment that truly got to me was the white-phosporus scene. One part in particular, which I won't describe so as not to spoil the game, made me put the controller down and walk away from the game for at least 10 minutes to compose myself. The graphic nature of the scene wasn't any more gory than Resident Evil or simular games, but the loss it depicted was horrific to say the least. I've never seen that level of realism in any game of any genre.

It IS a good game, but I just couldnt bring myself to like it.
The real issue for me is that the question, "what does one life matter", asks nothing of those who hear it beyond its answer. It is a "mere" philosophical question. As one of the developers pointed out, the game repeatedly hits you with this question from a variety of different and intetresting angles, but the question dies once it has an answer and, unfortunately, may people already have somthing of an answer walking in. Players are simply actualizing what they already believe into the game world rather than being challenged by it.
In Planescape, the question was "what does it take to change the nature of a man?" From the beginning the question was deeply personal in nature because it's basically saying "there is somthing wrong within you, how can you change that?" When Planescape hits you with the question from a multitude of angles, you are drawn into the suffering of the characters and identify with their struggles WHATEVER it may be because all of their struggles are deeply human (being born to a certain family, being wracked with guilt, being unable to do good like you want, being consumed with ones own trauma, ir simply being unable to rid yourself of the darker aspects of yourself. etc etc etc.)
I guess that's why I can't really recommend the game. It IS a good game, but I went into it expecting to find the same level of humanity its predecessor had and was left wanting. Numenera asked me who I was but Planescape asked me how I could change. For this reason, there is no moment from Numenera that has stuck with me, but Planescape? That game has stuck with me and has captured my imagination for years.
If you have yet to really answer the question this game asks, MAYBE this game is for you. Maybe somthing in it will stick with you and change you in some way. But I for one just can't shake the feeling that Numenera took one step forward in game mechanics to take two steps back in impact.

An excellent game. Don't get this if you're just looking for tactical combat game. However, if you want a story heavy game or are even tangentially interested in the Numenera setting, definitely check this one out!
Let me start this by saying that I bought this game because I'm a big fan of the Numenera Tabletop RPG. I was a bit worried how the system would translate to a computer game and was pleasantly surprised how well it worked out. Some parts were adapted to better fit the new format, but the core features are all there and the game does a good job using the resolution mechanic.
The combat system is up to standards, but nothing to write home about. Tactical combat is definitely not the focus of this game.
I found the main story quite enjoyable, which doesn't really pick up pace until after you finished the first third of the game. It explores some interesting concepts and even though it is a bit heavy handed at times, I found the end very intriguing. However, I feel the game is at least as much - if not more so - about painting a picture of this weird setting. While most of the sidequests and dialog options are not relevant for the main story, they show you a glimpse of this extraordinary world that you find yourself in. In my opinion, this is the part the game excels at - portraying a colorful and weird, but interesting world.
I'm also very happy that the way this game presents the setting fits right in with the rest of the Numenera universe and I would say it is a good starting point for anyone interested in the Ninth World.
I finished my first playthrough in about 28 hours. I did most side quests, but ignored some that didn't interest me and I'm sure there are a few I simply haven't found. There were multiple points where I still wonder what would have happened if I handled things differently - especially with the stories of the companions I picked. I immediately felt inspired to start another game with a character that has a rather different outlook on life and a different choice of party members.

Great game. I was a little worried about the original premise of not focusing on combat, but found that there was enough of it for me. Like the original Torment it has a cool core concept and setting.

Torment: Tides of Numenera is a fascinating, if somewhat flawed, heavily story focused RPG. While I think that the original Planescape: Torment which this is a spiritual successor if is superior (which also has its own flaws), I came away enjoying my time with Numenera as long as one keeps certain expectations and design choices in check.
For starters, this game is not combat focused. While there is combat, it is not the focus of the game, sometimes perhaps to its determent as it is well known that combat can help break up a game's dialog and story. In many RPGs, you'd step into a Baldur's Gate's like city for the first time (after several hours of gameplay) and just talk to everyone and everything and explore it. Once that is done, you'll step out into some dungeon or the overworld and explore the wilderness and the dangers within it. In Numenera it is like that, except once you talk to everyone and explore, you realize that the second part never really happens and you get to talk and explore yet again. If you can not reconcile this, then it may be that this game might not be for you.
The very fact that there is so little combat actually serves to heighten the stakes when there is combat. I certainly felt this a lot during the first Act in Sagus Cliffs where your low level combine with some rather difficult combat encounters serves to make these “Crisis” potent challenges to be overcome through careful preparation and liberal use of ciphers. In its own way, I found this to be a curious statement at the amount of combat that is in “Role Playing” Games.
The chief draw of this game is the amazing world of Numenera. The closest I could describe it is something out of a China Mieville novel. A world full of magic, technology, and fascinating strangeness. This world serves as a vehicle for many great short stories… Perhaps they could had been something of novel instead of a game, yet I enjoyed my time reading them. Whether it was spending hours in a tavern for telepaths seeking quietness from the noises of other minds, talking to the last solider of an empire that once held the world in its hand, or even learning about a cult that takes the preservation of knowledge to a cannibalistic level… and so on. I perhaps enjoyed this more so than anything else.
There are some things which I found annoying, notably related to your companions. You do not have shared party xp with companions that are not in your party, discouraging switching your group up. And while you will be able to get an item that basically lets you change your companions at will, until you realize you have it and/or use it, you might think that once you hit Act 2 that you can't actually change your companions at all.
With such expectations in check as to what kind of game it is, I found Numenera to be an interesting alternative to what an RPG can be; overfilling with many great little stories that it wishes to tell the player. Stories that I was happy to have stayed and listen to.

Undertale is a game that mixes jRPG, shoot 'em up/bullet hell, visual novel and adventure game elements into one weird and exciting package of fun, friendship and death (in quantities chosen by the player from 0 to EVERYONE). It's a game about friendship and game about hard choices done in a cute and entertaining way.
The game presents itself almost like a window to a different world filled with weird monsters, and you roleplay your way through it. You can be just a visiting adventurer who does whatever fits the moment. Someone who befriends everyone they meet. Or KILL EVERYONE. Oh and game will remember your choices even if you reload or quit.
It's not without it's issues. Some jokes aren't let go when they should be. At some points game becomes more moralizing and treating you like a child, although, thankfully, most often it doesn't. And some mechanics and moments just feel a bit off or at least not as good as everything else. But those things stick out just because how much joy you get from the game, how often you smile and laugh. Unless, of course, you want to KILL EVERYONE.
(And here I need to also acknowledge the game's immense popularity and genuinely creepy fandom. It's not "the bestest game ever", no game is, but it's good so just expect it to be what it is. And don't search internet for a lot of fan Undertale-related stuff if you value your psyche. )
Personally, I loved Undertale a lot. I laughed a lot, smiled a lot, cringed a little, had a great time and genuinely felt sad to finally finish it. It's a great virtual world to visit.

So I've put more than 15 hours into each of the episodes released so far, and I reckon that trend will continue on through the second half of the episodes as well. The only game in the series I put much time into before was Blood Money, and this one definitely has the same feel to it.
Sapienza is the best episode so far, but if you're on the fence I'd suggest getting the intro pack and see if you like it and then, if you do like it, get the upgrade pack.
I suppose I'll address some of the bandwagon complaints:
- Yes, I suppose it's always online, but it hasn't affected me very much at all. I've been disconnected once in 46 hours of playing, and even then it was very shortly after an autosave, so I lost no real progress.
- Yes, it's true. But nobody is really missing that much, they're not that much more fleshed out than the tutorial missions were.
- Yeah, if you miss them, they're gone. That was known up-front though since the game was even announced. I don't really see them as that big of a deal, though, I mean, I want to succeed on them, so I usually go for cheap kills instead, which is a shame because there's actually some work put into them. As it is now, it's a tiny incentive for getting the game early, as there are suits you can unlock by succeeding with a number of them, but I'm pretty sure they'll eventually do re-runs of the targets, at which point I'll get to try again for the silent assassins I missed and so on.
Update about 1½ years later:
All episodes were released and while the season did mostly end with a cliffhanger, it was at least very enjoyable up until that end. Apart from that IO continued to support the game with monthly updates with new escalations and featured contracts as well. They've also become independent and released a new mini-campaign as DLC (which I at least found quite good, maybe not quite enough to tide me over until whenever season 2 starts, but enjoyable nonetheless).
Also, the elusive targets are currently on a rerun, so if you feel you missed out the last time, now is your chance.

[Story Spoilers Free Review]
A massive departure from what Scott Cawthon previously established with the original FNaF series. A very intriguing, well built and designed game that becomes too hard for it's own good.
The "sit in a room/office/dumpster until 6am" mechanic was thrown out the window for this one, pretty much nullifying any expectations I had for this game. Instead, Sister Location takes a campaign like approach, with each night being a different level, instead of the same night, but harder. While I'm split on the decision to remove the "sit and survive" gameplay for a more linear story approach, I do think it ended up being a nice change of pace, albeit not what I expected, nor wanted.
Most of what I have to say would be good, so I'll list them off instead.
The game looks good and plays good.
Gameplay is incredibly varied, each new level has it's own trick.
The voice acting is superb, setting the tone nicely.
The humour spliced in through the game is well made and got more than enough chuckles from me, and it doesn't ruin the flow of the otherwise dark storyline of the game.
However there is a decent amount wrong with this game, some of which is merely my preference.
Like I said previously, I'm not sure I liked the change from "sit and survive" to "linear campaign" It's an impressive change that works out incredibly in the end, but isn't exactly what I expected. Personal nitpick.
Each level has it's own trick to beating it, until you get to night 4, which gains a difficulty spike unlike any other in the FNaF series yet. I won't mention what happens, but I will most definitely say that it's brutally unfair, and is almost entirely reliant on luck.
Where I think the linear campaign falls short in is the diversity and screentime dedicated to each animatronic. For the most part, all of them are only interacted with once, except for one of them. The characters who I had the most interest in went just as fast as they came. This is where I wished there was some sort of "sit and survive" mode like the previous games, because you aren't "hunted" or "lingered" by these animatronics anymore, they're showpieces that usually only appear once. The "stars of the show" in Sister Location are given about as much screentime as Freddy in the first FNaF game. It leaves them feeling completely devoid of character to me, and that's a big disappointment, personally.
Kind of ironic that a story driven game with full voice acting gives off less character than the original cast of FNAF, who for the most part only laughed and screamed. You may disagree with me, but hey, this is what I think, not what you think.
Should you buy this game? Most certainly. It's a great, original inclusion to a tired out franchise which really did need a fresh coat of paint. Unfortunately that fresh coat of paint brought with it a difficulty spike that may as well have been a punch in the nuts.

This Five Nights at Freddy's is very unique and fun. Very cool to see how in depth this game is and how it actually tells a story instead of throwing you in a room and dealing with it. It's very neat how you can travel between the rooms and experience the different robots that way too.
However, there are various things that need to be fixed.
First, and foremost, the mouse. When looking around the rooms, the mouse tends to wander wherever it wants to. I know there isn't a problem with my mouse because there have been no other times where my mouse has "drifted". It's especially hard when you have to press the buttons on Freddy because every time I try to press it, the mouse just goes on its own.
Secondly, the controls and directions for certain parts are very tough and vague and I found myself frustrated because I couldn't get past certain parts without watching someone else who was lucky enough to get it right and seeing how they did it. Like back at the part where you press Freddy's buttons, you need to press on Bonnie, who pops up in various spots. I didn't know what to do because I could never see Bonnie's bowtie and I didn't know if I needed to grab Bonnie, so I just randomly clicked around when Bonnie showed up until he jumpscared me.
Overall, I would enjoy this game more if it was easier to control and understand because I could actually progress instead of scratching my head on how to do a stage and not want to throw my mouse at a wall because the camera decides to float in any direction it pleases to. This game seems to have a lot of care put into it and a lot of cool story to add to the lore. I just can't seem to easily and enjoyably continue through with this current version.

Innovative boardgame-esque spin on football.
Lots of positions with passive and active skills to choose from to build your own unique team.
Whereas the campaign offers long-term planning challenges to offset the short-term tactical game planning.
While winning games with your best experienced players and leveling them into godmode might be appealing, the stark contrast of having to consider bringing up the next generation of players to replace the soon-to-be retired current stars is a challenge in and of itself.
Progression itself comes in many forms - be it higher income, better youths, more exp gains, or just better players.
The individual matches themselves are quick and to the point, each player has its positional passives and learned skills together with its stats - you make turn-by-turn decisions based on these options and hope for the best.
Entire seasons can be rushed through fairly easily, as the managorial parts are simple enough to be a "means-to-an-end" for the core match gameplay.
However, the heavy emphasis on RNG (it's boardgame-esque, after all), is starting to become really annoying very quickly.

I have 70 hours in on this game. in a SINGLE playthrough. This game was pure CRPG refinement. This is a masterfully done throwback to the artistic story driven games of legend.
But enough about my opinion.
The facts:
If you don't like reading the game is lost on you. Not saying you cant expedite dialogue choices, but as the sequel to Planescape: Torment the game expands exponentially when you embrace the dialogue. There are even multiple choose your own mini adventures in the form of "merecasters" throughout the game which are, for the most part optional.
Combat is a lot of fun. There are many choices to be made which affect your resolution of "crisis" which can be done through guile or firepower.
The story is extremely well written. Definitely feels like the games of old, as I said. I found myself very enthralled and very engrossed in the story above and beyond the combat. Hungry and curious for exposing all the secrets and mysteies of the Ninth World and beyond.
Be seduced by extra-planar entities. Playing for the paragon? Find yourself mystified and enthralled by a giant fleshy predator that approves or disproves your choices. Slowly corrupting you to more predatory actions.
A completely alien world very unique lore and lots and lots of subtexts to help give you a large and living picture of this world a billion years in the future.
Extremely fun and well worth the read/playthrough.

With the game coming out so many years after I had backed it in on Kickstarter, I was disappointed to see the relatively poor reception it got on Steam. It was with some apprehension that I decided to finally try it out.
I am happy to say my fears were unfounded and Torment: Tides of Numenera is a worthy spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment. The writing is generally deep and evocative, and it works well with the art direction - there are some truly beautiful panoramas and haunting alien landscapes in this game. Some of the companions seem to be of slightly lesser quality when it comes to the writing, but I still thoroughly enjoyed interacting with most of them. The quest design is not groundbreaking by any means, but most quests are quite reactive, with satisfying resolutions, and nearly all of them can be finished in multiple ways.
As for the combat, it wasn't nearly as bad as some people are making it out to be, despite it being quite clunky and unsatisfying at the beginning of the game. I was actually looking forward to getting into fights sometimes. That said, I would not qualify it as 'good', either. For such a relatively complex combat system, it does not accomplish much of note that couldn't have been accomplished by a simpler and/or more satisfying system.
The main negative point of the game for me is its bugginess. There are a number of bizarre bugs and glitches throughout the game, and more importantly, dialog windows will almost inevitably start lagging if a conversation lasts long enough. The automatic scrolling grinds to a halt and you have to fiddle with the scroll bar to be able to click on the next conversation option. This happened in my game at least, whether or not I had V-Sync turned on (running on Win 10/GTX 1070/i6700-k). I have seen others report this issue as well. In such a text-heavy game, this is simply unacceptable and it should have been patched by now.
It is clear that the ending was rushed as well, as evidenced especially by the sudden reliance on the CYOA text adventure format as the game was winding down.
All in all, I still very much enjoyed my time spent playing Torment: Tides of Numenera, and now that I've finished it I think its current score is undeserved. Perhaps it's because the worst bugs had been patched by the time I got around to playing it. I hope that, going forward, its fortunes will improve. As said, despite its flaws, I think it is a worthy successor to Planescape: Torment and I certainly would be interested in a sequel.

I took off really writing Steam reviews for a while, but now that I’m starting to go back at it again I want to review Torment 2. I threw in around $120 for the Kickstarter campaign and played this at launch fyi.
Torment 2 seems to be unfairly ♥♥♥♥♥♥ on here I feel. Is it as good as Planescape? No, but that’s honestly an unfair comparison. Planescape is utterly fantastic and one of my all-time favorite games, but even after nearly twenty years it’s had extremely few rivals and even the RPGs that I also think are fantastic such as Undertale and Witcher 3 excel in their own areas when it comes to writing and roleplaying sort of separate from Planescape. Is Torment 2 a worthy successor though? Yeah, I think it is. Torment 2 is very much a quality RPG on its own merits and while it doesn’t quite capture the full spirit or comes close to the highs of Planescape, its closer than any other RPG to it. (People laud Mask of the Betrayer as this, but I found that game a rather mediocre slog aside from the conversation with Myrkul, Torment 2 is a far better game I think.)
The game does sometimes has the problem of aping Planescape just to do it because it feel likes the crew thought they were expected to. For example like Planescape Torment 2 tries to have its own arc question. Problem is it just feels kind of half-baked compared to Planescape’s, which was a huge theme that encompassed almost the whole game from the main plot to the main party members and who they are. The game can also be kind of overly purple prosey compared to its predecessor, but I never felt that it became a true detriment.
What really makes this game great is its mission design. Torment 2 gives you a good deal of freedom in roleplaying your Castoff and giving you multiple options to complete objectives. You almost never have to fight people if you don’t want to. A facet that makes the mission design super memorable to me is how they tie together a whole bunch of seemingly disparate sidequests into something far larger than you would expect. I have never played an RPG that managed to pull off what Torment 2 does with its sidequests, not even Planescape did something great as this.
As previously stated the writing can be overly flowery at times but it’s overall pretty good and it always kept me engaged. By Planescape standards the party members are rather lacking, but by overall RPG standards they’re all good. Matkina, Erritis, and Rhin are the real notable ones though and you should definitely roll with them over the others. The game’s writing is hurt some though by the protagonist, The Last Castoff, being a mostly blank slate, compared to TNO, who had a lot of history. Because The Castoff is freshly born with little backstory, they lack all the relationships that TNO had with his cast and the world around him. It’s not a major problem, but I feel it’s one of the reasons why Torment 2’s striving for an all encompassing theme and arc question kind of fell flat.
Combat is serviceable and decent, it’s not great, but I feel it’s an improvement over Planescape’s, because let’s be real Planescape had terrible combat and you really weren’t playing it or this game for the combat. At least Torment 2’s combat feels less disparate. The game does fall into the same trap Planescape did of favoring the mage type class far over the others but at least even a diplomacy build can still be competent in combat, my Castoff was.
Overall Torment 2 is a really good RPG on its own merits and while it never rivals its predecessor, it’s still a worthy successor that I really enjoyed and a must play for people that prefer RPGs that are less combat focused.

"The truth, Walker, is... that you are here because you wanted to feel like something you're not: A hero."
Everyone who played and finished the game will probably have that sentence stuck in your head for weeks, I know that I did. This game is in my top 10 favorite games of ALL TIME. I finished the game a while ago, because it's ending, or should I say endings (which I won't spoil, don't worry) was just... mindblowing, to say the least. It still haunts me to this day, and that is very weird for me, as it's only happened a few times in my life. Anyway, if you happen to stumble to my review, here's what I think of it.
So the story starts six months after a huge sandstorm hit Dubai... A ton of people died and American soldiers that were sent to evacuate Dubai also died. However, a mysterious radio signal is being picked up and a Delta Squad (being lead by Walker, the main character) is sent to locate survivors (the most important being Col. John Konrad, who was leading the evacuation before the sandstorm hit) and then radio for evac. So that's basically all you need to know about the game's story when heading into it. Now comes the gameplay...
Okay, so when I first saw this game, it was in the PSN Store back in 2012, back when I had a crappy computer that could barely run an 8-bit game.., I downloaded it's demo and I found the gameplay to be very good. I was sort of more into FPS games at the time, but this game was still awesome. I didn't buy the game, because I have a terrible experience when it comes to playing demos first and then buying the full game... The full game almost always disappoints me, Anyway, back to Spec Ops... I bought it on May this year, after seeing it being on sale. So, I'm not very used to play shooters on the PC, but this game was suprisingly easy to control. I would say it's your standard third-person-shooting games. You have to squadmates with you, and you can give them commands, like target who they should and send them to heal the other squad member if he's done. Also, sometimes you can shoot a glass roof, for example, and sand will drop onto your enemies, stunning them for a bit. Neat feature, it beats the old "shoot a gas tank to blow everything up" which is cool and all, but there's too much of that in the other "war simulator" games. Ammo in Dubai is very limited, so watch where you shoot and how much you shoot. There's your standard pack of weapons in Spec Ops: The Line: pistols, assault rifles, heavy rifles, etc. All are easy to aim and shoot, but you still get the feeling you're the one holding the gun. Some weapons have alternate fire modes, so you can just fire one bullet at a time instead of having a burst. The graphics look great for a game made in 2012, it makes you really feel as you're actually in Dubai with the Delta Squad. There's multiplayer, but it's the standard... Finally, we reach the most important part of Spec Ops: The Line... The story.
Okay... I literally can't explain anything without spoiling it all... So I just have hints for you:  Get some tissue paper if it's easy to make you cry... I didn't do that, but after finishing the game, I just had a moment where I was like in total disbelief. Every emotion that you could feel went through me all at the same time. Yeah, the story is THAT GOOD.
It's not by luck that 94% of the reviews for Spec Ops: The Line are positive... The developers did a fantastic job. The voice acting is excellent. When you head to this game, don't think it's like CoD or Battlefield... This game is a true war simulator, it isn't just shoot, shoot, shoot, kill, kill, kill.... It actually has a story, and I know I said it a lot throughout this review... But it's damn good.
