I think I need to disclose some things before I start talking about why I do not recommend buying Dream Daddy. The first is that I adore Game Grumps (specifically Arin and Dan), and that they've had nothing to do with the development of the game save for some voicing-- which is really just grunts and 'ah!'s, and some marketing on their channel. The fact that the Grumps' name is on this shouldn't really be taken into account. The second is that I bought it pretty much the day of release and had been following it since it'd been announced. Not as actively as some people, but I knew about all the dads.
I'm going to be starting with the negatives-- frankly, the game itself isn't *really* the issue here. It's the developers.
The developers have been a little shady from day one. Originally, I was unsure if this game was meant to be a joke, like a lot of other people first suspected-- I'm a queer man, so I was hesitant at first. I think it's important to note that I DID read several posts online about how someone close to the dev team had played the beta and got the impression that this was a grab at Representation Points(tm) and that it was just a cash grab--
During the release delay, the devs were suspiciously quiet-- they apologized afterwards, but it was still super unprofessional.
I also vaguely remember (EDIT: I should mention that I can't be bothered to dredge up proof of this) the devs promising they'd add other dads and extra content, and a few of my friends remember them saying similar. And these two above points are absolutely tied; we're three months out from DD's release date, and the devs have gone silent. Since release, we've gotten two patches-- two bug patches, despite fans asking for more. There's still a bugged achievement that the devs haven't explained, and the second patch was a patch so small that it isn't even mentioned on the Recent Updates section of steam, nor on any of the twitter accounts.
Which is what a lot of people feared. I feel genuinely ripped off by the developers and the game; if it weren't for the fact that I've got more than 2 hours of this game, which is INCREDIBLY short and lacks any real story arc to tie everyone together, I'd refund it in a heartbeat. This game is almost $20 AUD and yet I wouldn't honestly say it's worth even that much, especially considering a) length and the fact that the game isn't even really complete and b) the devs have abandoned it.
It's a shame, because otherwise, the game is really pretty and has some great characters; Mat's route is my favourite and the game introduced me to PUP, one of my favourite bands now. It's diverse and cute and I love the fact that you can make a trans dad (even if the CC is godawful compared to character art), BUT the fact that you can now tell that it absolutely was a cash grab destroys it all, and
this game to anyone because of it.

I honestly wasn't expecting much of this game when a friend bought it for me. I'd never thought myself one for this kind of genre. Boy, was I wrong. My play far exceeded that initial summer campaign with friends - I'm nearing a thousand hours in this. Terraria is both an adventure game and a sandbox of the most fundamental sort (including the ability to fill boxes with sand.) The adventure portion of this game may be short, but I've found there's a surprising amount of replay value to it - and your ability to build can make every world feel different with just a little effort. The game's tooltips and dialogue are witty, and there's many references to find, some more overt than others. The game isn't that difficult beyond a fairly forgiving learning curve, but offers a harder difficulty that genuinely is challenging when you feel like you've mastered the basics. There are some classes that seem easier or more efficient to use than others, and some weapons are just too dominant to make others viable, but for the most part the game is well-balanced. The building portion is endless, but in the good, optional kind of way. You don't have to build anything more complex than a box with a bed in it, if so you please... but over the months of having this game, I've discovered a penchant for building cities I thought I'd buried with the Sims. The game presents enough customisation options for the only limit to be your own creativity. It lends itself well to both its singleplayer and multiplayer options, and there's always new content being released, even this long after its launch.
I do have some gripes with Terraria - while the spreading mechanics of the Corruption, Crimson, and Hallow that threaten to consume your world provide excellent flavor and a creeping threat, the actual process of dealing with them is annoying, and feels more like a chore than involved gameplay. Expect to spend lots of time digging tunnels before and after the hardmode threshold. It is also very dependent on RNG, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but can lead to long amounts of time spent grinding the same enemy or boss to get the one item you want. Still, I've had enormous fun with this game and will continue well into the future, and can only give it two thumbs up.

The game just isn't up to the standards of Planescape: Torment. It just isn't. It's a good game, hence the recommendation, but it doesn't have the same draw PS:T had. It doesn't have the color and variety. I mean, in PS:T, the first character you interact with is a floating, snarky skull with intact eyeballs. His weapons are teeth and his special abilitiy is to insult enemies so much they go after him. Here you have two passive-aggressive characters who, for some reason, have a fundamental breakdown in their relationship in the moments following your appearance (and yes, I know why, I'm just making a point).
Planscape is just so much more interesting than Tides of Numera. I can't quite put my finger on why, both have interesting pieces to them, but Planescape drew me in while in Tides of Numera, I was always hoping for something of the same level to appear. Maybe it was simply the lack of quality. I came into Planescape with no expectations and ToN was supposed to be the ultimate game, to blow me away. Like I said, it's not bad, it's even good, but it just isn't good enough. I suspect it couldn't be.
Interestingly, to me it reminded me somewhat of the Mordon Dungeon Crawl. Everything just felt like it was there because it was supposed to be there, not because it made things more interesting. Maybe it was a mistake to make the vendor loot unique because I always felt there could be some clever puzzle to be solved with it instead of just forking it over to a vendor for cash. Maybe it lacked the charm of the terms used in Planescape Torment, berk. I don't know.
Perhaps I will come back a year from now, when all kinds of bonus content has been added and it will be the game I hoped for. But I doubt it.

I do recommend it to those friends who I feel would appreciate going exploring and be fascinated by all the small narratives, the real strength of the game. Give it a try!

I remember seeing this game in Early Access and wanting to play it. Once I noticed it was no longer in early access, I quickly grabbed this game at a decent sale price. Good thing I found it on sale, because this game is nowhere close to release quality.
There are tons of bugs you'll encounter that will halt any progress. I've only seen the main menu once, the first time I launched the game. Every launch since then immediately throws me into an empty prison and I have to load whatever I want to play from there. Reinstalling the game didn't help :(

Objectives are often not very clear, and specific details are often left out. I was only able to progress through the first 3 missions before giving up. No matter how many guards I assign to that security room, none of them will operate the CCTV Monitors.
The wiki states that you can have a Shower within a Holding Cell, as long as it has doors to separate them. However, adding a Shower room immediately breaks the Holding Cell.
There is a sandbox mode where you can build your dream prison with unlimited funds, as well as an escape mode where you can attempt to break out of any prison (local or workshop). I'd comment more on these, but I'm too frustrated with the campaign to bother playing this anymore.
All of this could easily be excused if the game were still in Early Access. As an official release, it's extremely buggy and nearly unplayable (campaign mode). I would not recommend buying this game in its current form. Hopefully more updates will come to alleviate these issues. Until then, this game will sit on a shelf in my Library.

This is one of the most broken, poorly coded, bloated, neglected, newbie-unfriendly MMOs I have ever played, yet I can't seem to pull myself away. It's a mess that somehow still manages to provide hours and hours of ridiculous fun. I consistently neglect the mounting hoard of games in my library to play this game. I therefore do recommend it, although I would caution anyone that wants to get started that the game has a rather steep learning curve. The matchmaking is very hit and miss, which means you will likely get curbstomped for a long time before your feet find the bottom of the pool.
The plusses for this game are its impressive array of customizable options, and the intensity of its firefights, which can, at its best, feel relentless and fast-paced. not recommended. Graphic is nice, totally next gen quality, game is very newbie-friendly ( a lot of hand holdings ), however gameplay is just OK, always-online DRM is wayyy over the top, and the way Squeenix/IO Interactive do business is intolerable.
HITMAN is literally a tripe-A early access game, released in episodic fashion. Knowing people would be hesitant to pay 60$ up front for an unfinished product, combined with the fact that the previous Hitman game didn't give fans a lot of faith, SQ/IOI introduced a way to buy the game by piece, each piece equals a released location, and promised additional contents for those locations as the game develops, with no extra DLC planned. Yet 4 months later, they introduced some above-average contents for existing locations, however only allows people who paid 60$ up front to play with it. The rest will have to wait until after the whole game is out to
it, AKA they won't receive these totally-not-a-DLC contents for free. People who chose to buy episodes separately already committed to paying more than the full buy users in the long run ( 65$ vs 60$ ) and now they'll have to pay even more for those
contents. In the end this is an episodic game that punishes episodically buyers, and they did that without any warnings beforehand.
To make up for the lack of fresh locations ( only 6 locations, so about half the amount in previous Hitman games ), IOI made the maps much bigger, with many ways to complete your tasks. As you discover more ways to finish your contracts, more unlocks will be available in that map ( i.e more starting locations, weapons caches,.. ). However all unlocks are tied to your Squeenix account, and as soon as you're offline you'll lose access to all of it. If you're playing and lose connection to SQ server then you're kicked back to main menu. Offline mode means a mission always start the same way.
Moreover, when you're online the game auto saves very often, and randomly. Those auto save are again stored in SQ server, and when it's autosaving ( takes about 1 to 2 minute in my case ), you
trigger a manual save, and have to wait until the game finished uploading to the cloud. Same case for when you want to load a save, there's a long delay for the game to fetch autosaves down. And when it's fetching there's a very high chance to lose connection, then you are kicked back to the main menu. Bye bye progress.
Bigger map, more opportunities, yes, but most of those key events are scripted, you have to approach the location to actually "trigger" it, instead of "mind your own business" attitude in previous games. This creates a linear feeling inside a semi-open environment. Many mechanics seen in previous games are missing here. No bloodstains, no sniper case, no peeking keyholes, just to name a few. More hand holdings are included, and updates that were supposed to improve the mechanics made questionable decisions. For example in episode 2, the town of Sapienza includes a beach, a church, a town square, a mansion, plus many alleys and tunnels. It makes sense to have multiple security camera systems operating in the town, however a recent update "connected" all those systems, which means you only have to tamper one system to have every cameras in the town to be nullified. And did I mention that there are nobody observing those security screens ever? Overall it's still fun and enjoyable, but if you were a fan of Hitman games a decade ago you'd see a lack of depth here.
Graphics seem to be the saving grace here. It looks nice both at low and high settings, and the world can be very vivid with settings cranked up ( not the first map though, it's obvious that a Paris high-fashion event isn't mean to be colorful ). Game supports DX12, and it does look better on DX12 while require less GPU power, however there are still occasional crashes here and there when DX12 is used.
Sound is ok, it's not a big attraction point after all.
Overall, unless you've taken a great interest in this game, wait until 2017 or 2018 to buy it, because IOI is probably disbanded by then, and Squeenix would be willing to sell the game for cheap, because the way they run business with this game isn't looking very promising at the moment ( first location is good, second is awesome, however third one is a huge drop, along with screwing customers along the way ).
Enter a world of DRM.

This game entirely delivers upon what it promises: a turn based strategy take on soccer. While it's not as deep as something like Football Manager, it's involved enough to be interesting and simple enough to be quick and easy to play.
Matches only take five minutes to play through and involve alternating turns wherein each side gets three moves or actions to use upon an individual or groups of players. Players get tired if you use them too much and can be substituted out. Occasionally someone gets a yellow or red card or gets injured.
Players are rated in four attributes (scoring, passing, defending, and holding on to the ball) and improve upon these categories as they gain experience by playing and succeeeding in matches, particularly difficult ones. Everyone improves with time, and stronger prospects merely have higher ratings at lower levels. You can guide players into specific positions or designations at will and experience gained at a position or position group eventually allows for skills and traits to be developed from a moderately sized list.
Winning gets you money with which to buy better players, which come from an-ever shifting small list of options to pick through. You can sign your players to set value extensions or sell them off for a profit in hopes of buying even better ones. It's all very straightforward and not at all time consuming. You also gain prestige points that you can use to upgrade various things like better scouting or better coaching (experience boosters).
A little bit like Blood Bowl, but without the fantasy setting or violence, if you like strategy games and sports management, this is well worth the cost!

Batman: Arkham Origins is a prequel to the critically acclaimed Arkham Asylum and Arkham City. You play as the Dark Knight in his earlier years of crime fighting on Christmas Eve, fighting off assassins trying to collect a $50 million bounty Black Mask put on Batman's head.
The plot of the game is pretty much what I just explained: Batman has a bounty on his head and eight assassins are coming after him all in one night. Lots of familiar characters from the Batman universe are in this game such as Deathstroke, the Joker, Enigma (later known as the Riddler), and Penguin. The story is very interesting and gives you an idea of how hard it was for Batman in his early days because he has to deal with both criminals and the Gotham City Police Department (GCPD), which is after Batman because he is a vigilante at this point.
The gameplay is about the same as the other Arkham games with a few added things, mainly gadgets. The combat of the Arkham games is some of the best I've ever seen. It is very easy to learn but very difficult to master. During combat, you can use Batman's many gadgets such as Batarangs, smoke pellets, the Batclaw, and the concussion grenade. This adds a lot to the already incredible combat. The boss battles are fun and I especially liked the Deathstroke battle. Sure, it takes a little while to get used to but it's fun and looks really cool. Along with combat, there are also many stealth sections to the game like the other Arkham games. These are very fun and can sometimes show how difficult it can be to be Batman. Arkham Origins, like Arkham City, is open world as well. There are two main sections of Gotham City connected by a bridge. People who have played Arkham City will recognize many areas in North Gotham such as the courthouse and the church. There are many sidequests all around the city, from crimes in progress to finding Enigma datapacks.
The game looks pretty good. Batman's default costume is pretty cool as well as the other costumes you can unlock or buy with DLC. The Batsuit in this game is kind of a cross between the classic Batman look from the other Arkham games and the cartoons and the more armor-like suits in Christopher Nolan's "The Dark Knight" film trilogy. Since the game takes place on Christmas Eve, There is snow in the air, along the streets, and on rooftops. The buildings look realistic and look like what you'd see in Gotham. The animations are very well done too. Some boss battles look like something you'd see in a movie, especially the Deathstroke battle.
Arkham Origins is slightly glitchy, but I haven't noticed that many bugs. Pretty much the only one I've encountered was when I went up an elevator and when through the floor making me restart from my last checkpoint. This only happened a couple of times though.
One thing I don't quite understand is how early you get to the Deathstroke boss battle. It's the second or third boss battle in the game which you only get to in the first few hours of gameplay. I feel like it should have been later in the game mainly because Deathstroke was the main focus of the trailers and pre-order bonus. It's not something I really dislke but it just seemed odd.
Batman: Arkham Origins is one of the best superhero games I've ever played (although people say the other Arkham games are better). It has fun combat, a large open world to explore, a great story, and interesting characters. Plus, the final game in the series is coming out this year, which is sad since it's the last game, but it looks like it's going to be incredible too.
This game gets an 8.5/10

APB: All Points Bulletin is a multiplayer online video game for Microsoft Windows based in urban sprawls and featuring two factions, Enforcers and the Criminals. Players can join either the Enforcers or the Criminals, and form sub-groups in either faction. The game design was led by David Jones, who contributed to the original Grand Theft Auto and Crackdown, and was developed by Realtime Worlds. It was released on 6 June 2010 in North America, and Europe.
On 17 August 2010 Realtime Worlds was placed into administration. The administrators intended to keep the company trading whilst they attempted to find a buyer for the firm. If a buyer could not be found then the long-term future for the game was uncertain. On 16 September 2010 Realtime Worlds announced APB servers were to be shut down "soon" with no specific date given. On 11 November 2010 online games company, K2 Network, purchased APB for £1.5 million. No time frame for re-release or reactivation of servers was announced. On 16 November 2010 K2 subsidiary company Reloaded Productions, announced that APB will be relaunched during the first half of 2011 as a free to play game, renamed APB: Reloaded.

As a successor to Planescape: Torment, TToN is naturally narrative and dialogue oriented. This is not limited to conversations, but permeates to the game's combat and mechanics. There are times when, after combat initiates, you will be able to use your actions to speak with enemies instead of attacking. You may also use these actions to hack into a machine and disable enemies. It is worth noting that you will be reading during most of your playtime, in the spirit of PT and other old school cRPGs. If this is not your thing, stay away from TToN. If it is, you are in for a treat.
I found the writing to be beautiful and the narrative fulfilling. Being a spiritual successor to PT, a lot of the themes will be familiar to people who played the original, as well to elements in the game's structure and its narrative. It is a very personal story and delves into interesting philosophical questions similar PT's.
While PT's combat was good at all due to its focus on narrative, I found TToN's combat to be competent and enjoyable though not its strongest suit. Nevertheless, the strongest point in combat was that you could ultimately avoid it or end it through dialogue or, in some cases, stealth.
The actions you make in combat require you to spend points from a pool based on your character's skills, but these points are not limited to combat, but can also be used to succeed on tasks during dialog and other interactions. I found this to be a good way of bringing together all of these mechanics and allowing you to choose which is more important.
I dare say that Torment: Tides of Numenera is a worthy successor of Planescape: Torment and builds upon the main pillars that made the original so beloved. A recent update added a new companion character, which means I will have to play it again, and I will gladly do so.
Great game and awesome writing. Buy now for an old-school cRPG experience.

Side quests are EXCELLENT. You can come up with different unprompted solutions to side quests, track down characters you think could do what you want, find they often ARE able to do it, and then talk to characters in the world you imagine would be impacted by this decision, and find new unique dialogue and consequences. That is GOLDEN. And rare.
If you usually RP a persuasive mage who can read minds and tries to avoid fights, this game is designed for you. The options the game doesn't have won't be deal-breakers (no sneaking outside combat, no stealing, etc.)
If you enjoy taking your time reading about obscure places and people, this game is designed for you. It's about 80% dialogue and 20% point and click moving. Some of the most interesting and dynamic scenes are conveyed in the EXACT style of the King of Dragon's Pass divinations! Love that! Side quests are extensive, well-written, and offer lots of opportunity to RP and immerse yourself in the game atmosphere. The main quest is pretty linear until a quick ending with a press-the-dialogue-line end choice, but that's pretty par for the course. Length is middling (< 30 hrs if you don't have a habit of replaying conversations to try different dialogue options). Combat is fine but rare. Companions vary (some are intriguing, some are OK). Bugs and glitches seem to be much better than on release.
I would NOT compare it to PS:T or Baldur's Gate II (those games will never be replicated for many reasons, including that they are almost 20 years old now.) I think it compares very well to Pillars of Eternity, KOTOR II, and Mask of the Betrayer.  Highly recommend if you enjoy playing a persuasive mage, enjoy lots of reading, and plan to take your time and RP through the side quests.

It is perhaps impossible to review this game without making comparison's to the cRPG's which inspired it.  Torment: Tides of Numenera is the spiritual successor to classic cRPG's such as Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, and (obviously) Planescape: Torment.  If you have never played these games you might want to search them out and give them a shot first.  This will help you in two ways: 1) It will let you know if you are going to like this game without dropping a huge amount of money and 2) It will help you understand some of the in-jokes and references the game makes.
Okay, with that out of the way, I'm going to assume that you have played through the aforementioned games and are poised to purchase this game but are unsure.
For the sake of brevity, I'm going to leave off discussion about many aspects of the game such as graphics, sound, and UI.  Suffice it to say they are alright but not amazing and mostly certainly not the reason why you are looking at playing a cRPG.
Let's address the elephant in the room:  this game is wordy.  The Kickstarter campaign but a lot of emphasis on scoring writers for the game and this is pretty obvious right from the get-go in a couple of ways.  First, words are everywhere.  In fact, you can talk your way out of many of the combat situations.  Second, this game is written at like a 12th grade level which could honestly be a problem for many.  I seriously had to take eye-breaks every so often because they would start blurring and twiching after reading so much on screen text.  The text and dialogue are good and some of it is very good.  It is interesting and it made me want to read the descriptions on all of the little trinkets in the game and talk to most everyone.  It is not without its weaknesses though.  The non-quest townspeople were not interesting and I tended to skip speaking with them if I could they tell had no purpose.  Some of the dialogue with the companions is also lacking the emotional oomph that made the cRPG's of old so fun to play.  This game, in attempting to live up to its spiritual successor in the story department, may have taken it a tad too far.  This is a problem because while words can be immersive,  too much can have the opposite effect in a game because it removes the element of interaction that is integral to what it means to be a video game.  It runs the danger of being a video...book.
Next up is the ruleset/universe.  You can read the synposis on the store page for the gyst of the universe.  I'll start off by saying I think there are some serious issues with the Numenera universe/rulset in terms of its utilization in a cRPG.  The Numenera ruleset, developed by Monte Cook, was intended to be a "lite" RPG meaning it is supposed to prioritize role-playing over rules.  This is a problem for cRPG's because they do not have a GM (Game-Master) who can facilitate role-laying.  The game is ultimately on rails, sure there are little diversions here and there, but the role-playing elements of the Numenera ruleset aren't really applicable in a video game meaning all the game ultimate inheirits is the ruleset and the setting.  As mentioned before, the ruleset is intentionally lightweight and this proves extremely problematic.  Because the player cannot utilize the role-playing strenghts of the ruleset they must fall back on the ruleset which is very thin and not very interesting whatsoever.  What this means is that there is no real strategy to character building or equipment or anything like that.
In addition, the player creation options are boring.  You can be a nano, glaive, or jack which equates into mage, fighter, or thief in the more familiar fantasy terms.  There are descriptors and focuses which allow you to specialize but it doesn't add anything to the game.  These options make the three base classes very different and extremely different if you are role-playing them in the tabletop game but they don't mean anything in this video game.  In addition, I think the developers made a huge mistake by attempting to stay true to the spirit of the Numenera tabletop universe.  The numenera tabletop universe rewards exploration but not combat.  This improves the role-playing strength of the game but, as we've mentioned before, you cannot role-play in a cRPG.  The game needs combat to fill this void and it has barely any whatsoever.  I mean, I was in like 6 encounters in the whole game.  Seriously.  Definitely less than 10.  And the combat system is lack-luster.  Better than say Shadorun Returns but not as good as Pillars of Eternity.
Okay I realize this sounds kinda negative but bear with me, as you can see from the thumbs up, I actually like this game and I'll explain why now.  There are objects in the game called "merecasters" which transports the main character into little text cut-scenes where they, uh, get to experience anothers life.  These cut-scenes are text only with some ambient sounds and mostly gray-scale backgrounds but they illustrate the real strength of the game.  There is one that stands out in my mind.  You are playing a dying man man and you must decide how to give away your assets after your passing.  You get to listen to the stories of all of the parties who are interested in in inheiriting your estate and then ultimately decide who will get it when you die.  I found myself agonizing over this decision.  All of the people were deserving or undeserving in some way but you must decide.  Even then it is essentially a DOS text based game at this point, I found it super engrossing.  More-so than the more graphical normal parts of the game.
You can see how "tormented" I am writing this review which I'm going to close up here.  I enjoyed the game in general.  I really enjoyed some parts of it.  I think in trying to live up to the wordiness of earlier cRPG's it lost some of the theatricality which made them fun.  I think the Numenera universe is super interesting and fun for a cRPG but I think the ruleset is overly simple for the genre.  I think the game is hurt by a lack of combat but that this is okay because the combat is not very fun.  I think I'd love to play a sequel to this game but they didn't set it up for one very well which is shame.  I think if you made it though my wall of text review, you certainly have the mental fortitude to play this game and enjoy it.
If you don't like reading then this is your game.

I've been playing CRPGs for years and I consider Planescape: Torment as one of the best games ever created. Therefore I can't say my review will be completly unbiased but let's give it a shot.
Tides of Numenera (ToN) breaks with a few RPG conventions in the way it is set up. While there are levels, spells and skills,  characters rely on 3 different stats: Strength, Speed and Intellect. These can be used in combat but also (more often) in dialogues. Dialogues choices also determine your alignment and is used to create your character at the start.
Diving into the game it is confusing at first. The world you're in is full of random objects, buildings and artifacts (supposedly left behind by an unknown ancient civilisation). It's an original thought but it doesn't bring cohesion to the game. Futher on in the game you kind of accept that 'thats just the way it is' but it doesn't help building a believable world to delve further into. Speaking to its inhabitants increases this feeling. The game is EXTREMELY lore-heavy and most of it is just background info (even on various worlds and places you will never even travel). While I enjoy reading and discovering things, I found myself scanning or even skipping dialogues after a while, since it felt all that information wasn't going to add to my game experience anyhow. And mostly it didn't afterwards. Especially if you don't play on a regular basis, you won't remember most of that info, anyhow.
On the other hand, the strange world gave the developers the chance to think up new and innovating things. Occasionally I was suprised by the amount of thought and detail that went into creating these objects and places, even stretching my own imagination of time and space.
The same goes for the main story (which I won't spoil too much): very innovating and well written! It's just a bummer that it takes so long to get into it. Only half way the game (when you get to the Bloom) I managed to get into the story (after filtering all that extra lore) and the more exciting stuff started to happen.
Having a good story is one thing but every RPG needs some action! Here is where ToN pulls the short straw. First off, it's all turn-based. Mostly I won't even touch turn-based games but nonetheless I gave it a try. Because of each monster taking its individual turn, the combat is quite slow. And, once you figure out how the system works, the difficulty level is quite low. Many encounters can be solved by dialogues or use of objects (especially if you have a lot of points in Intellect). The game features 'power items', of which I NEVER had to use any in the game. Compared to the battles of Baldurs Gate or Planescape Torment, this is a walk in the park. While I find many RPG's too combat-heavy, ToN could really use some more of it.
Tides of Numenera is not a bad game. If you liked Planescape Torment, chances are you'll enjoy this too. However, it's not as good as its predecessor. I would probably not give ToN another playthrough to see if the game is really different if I made different choices, while I've completed Planescape Torment at least 5 times. If you don't like reading, stay clear of this, but hey.. you probably wouldn't have read this entire review then, right? ;)
Pro's:
- Great back story and interesting characters
- Innovate gameplay ideas
- Nice visuals and sounds
Cons:
- Very lore heavy (lots of 'unnecessay' reading)
- Hard to get immersed into (feels too random/alien at times)
- Combat is not challenging (and turn-based)

This game is seriously awesome given how old it is. I would heavily recommend picking up the Movie Battles II mod, it improves the duelling system heavily and adds quite a bit to the game. In fact I'd argue that the Movie Battles II mod is far more enjoyable than EA's SWBFII. Sure the graphics don't hold up but if you're not one to care for that this game will be perfect for you.
I mostly play the Movie Battles II mod, but I have played the vanilla game pretty heavily before owning the steam copy so I'll review the rest of it from that perspective.
Combat: Arguably the best part of this game. For a game of it's time, the lightsaber mechanics of this game are revolutionary. It isn't too hard too hard to pick up, but the skill ceiling is definetely high. There's an entire community built around duelling eachother in honorable 1v1 battles. I think the closest game to compare this to combat wise would be Mount & Blade, but they're not the same at all.
Story: Not the greatest part of the game, but it follows Luke's jedi Academy after the events of RTJ. Voice acting is alright but the combat is what'll keep you coming back
Graphics: They were amazing at the time, but of course nearly 20 years later they aren't going to hold up too much. Graphical mods can fix this.
All in all, I think it's an amazing game given it's age and I think the active community really shows this game has withstood the test of time.

I don't write many reviews, but for this game I had to. It is defiantly my favorite and most played game in my library. I have almost 200 hours on record and I don't see myself stopping anytime soon. The game has three different modes so even if you don't feel like building a prison, you can try to escape a prison, or playing the campaign. It combines Strategy with Simulation with Roleplay with Action and so many more genres. There is something in the game for everyone. I would highly recommend it to anyone looking for a fun game, and if you don't like the game, it's in early access so the Dev's will take any suggestions you may have. They update often. I have played other games by Introversion and this one is defiantly my favorite. For those of you who like Pro's and Con's heres a little list I made
Pros-
Three gamemodes, Build, Escape, or Campaign
No official ending, so you can continue playing over and over (Except on Campaign where there is an ending)
Constant updates
Lots of different methods for escaping or building, billions of possibilities
Events to keep you always doing someone, there is never a boring moment
Workshop integration for Escape maps or Building mods/maps etc
Dedicated team making the game. (Introversion)

Cons-
Bugs, nothing huge but sometimes workers won't build what you ask them, or hands appear on the weight lifts even if no one is there...
Slow time movent, even on fastest setting. Can be hard to learn game at first. Both of those can be fixed by community mods and guides.
Once again, I highly recommend the game to anyone.

Batman Arkham Origins, created by WB Montreal, is easily the best game of the franchise so far. People had their doubts about this game because it wasn't developed by Rocksteady Studios. Well believe me when i say this, WB Montreal have done the best job so far in the series and should be recognised for their efforts.
Story: The story takes place 2 years into Batmans career when he is still learning and Black Mask sends 8 assassin's to kill him for a huge bounty, Batman is also a bit more brutal as he is still venting is his anger towards the criminals in an extreme way. The good thing about this prequel story is that it doesn't spend the game finding the origin of Bruce Wayne becoming Batman, it's more so the origin of Batman and his villians kind of like Tim Burtons "Batman". The relationship between Aflred and Bruce is also a nice element, as to Aflred just being a butler that talks to occassionally like in the previous game Arkham City. Overall the story is the best of the franchise.
Gameplay: The game introduces some new fighting skills and moves and also refines the same mechanics by making them smoother which is great. The detective mode is a fantastic idea to add to the franchise making feel more like the worlds greatest detective as Batman is by rewind and pausing simulations of the crime scene. The crime in progress was a nice addition to the game allowing to just drop into a crowd of enemies located by GCPD by radio. Side missions like the penguins gun stashes and the toxic or titan canisters and also the riddler trophies are great fun and incease the games length. Boss battles are also a fantastic addition as they are far more challenging and rewarding that in the previous Arkham games.
Voice acting: Now another thing people were worried about when this game was annouced was the new voice actors that were to voice Batman and the Joker, well i can tell you now both actors were amazing and lived up to the standards. Roger Craig Smith was amazing as Batman keeping it just like a younger Kevin Conroy stile voice but adding his own more aggressive spin on to it. Troy Baker also did a fantastic job as the joker sounding just like a younger Mark hamill.
Graphics: The graphic are brilliant and continue to keep the high standards of the franchise.
Overall: WB Montreal had huge expectations to live up to and i can safely say they rised above those expectations and created the best game of the franchise. Thank WB teams for doing this and would love to see you guys make another game in the future.

DO NOT BUY IT ON STEAM. Steam version of Jedi Academy does NOT load up properly (as of 27th Dec 2017). Only one quarter of the screen shows up on my PC. Can I get my money back, Steam? GET A GOG VERSION - WORKS PERFECTLY from the start, with no patching. It is often on sale, I got it for 2€.

-----
THOUGHTS ABOUT JEDI KNIGHT: JEDI ACADEMY, AFTER PLAYING ALMOST HALF OF IT
Locations in Jedi Academy are interesting, but the story, atmosphere and the tension was better in Jedi Outcast (if I remember it correctly from 13 years ago). Normal difficulty in JK:JA is, in gameplay sense, too easy and will suffice for a nice run-through.
Also, while Disney $hit Worth Universe stinks like a rotting corpse of a sewer rat, Lucas' Extended Universe stories don't fully satisfy either. Did Anakin bring the balance to the force or not and why are all these quasi-Sith jumping around if he did? Or does balance mean no Siths, more Jedis, more anti-Jedis? A great myth (like the OT) becomes just a story for story sake if it goes for too long.
After not playing videogames for a few years, I now find it hard to go around and "play" to slice people and people-like aliens with a flash burning sword, or blow them up with explosives. The game does not really encourage playing as a peaceful Jedi who would be sneaking past or mind-tricking enemies without killing them. (PS: I was a bit wrong about that - after playing some more, I see that mind trick is a good and useful force power and it does make the playing less violent) In the beginning, when you arrive at the Academy, there is some talk about Jedi training in diplomacy, but it seems that the lesson never gets past the "kill everybody" . Most maps are just halls filled with clueless, apparently half blind henchmen with subpar weapons; you have to get past them and they will see you. It's possible to run past them to some degree, but the zombie crowd following you becomes too large - and then these people turn out to be no match for a half-god Jedi. This becomes more and more apparent in the middle of the game. "Enemies" scream in pain as you slice them (as the game encourages you to) while the bright flashy visuals and the game's reward system make your body addicted to violence via dopamine.
Do these Stormtroopers know the Emperor is dead? Should they be told again? How good is the New Republic & the Jedi if there are thousands of Stormtroopers, henchmen and dark Jedi fighting against them? How much do the Jedi know about particularities of certain cultures they interfere with - by force and with half-godly powers (for example: in one mission you help Jawas against Tusken Raiders (PS: the mission in which you invade a culture that is supposed to be left alone because of it's backwardsnes gives even more mixed feelings))? You actively kill, one by one, thousands of sentient (yet combat-clumsy) beings - while "just training"! and while getting a very simplistic explanation of the whole situation.
I tried to play the game with minimal conflict at first, but then got used to the violence and saw myself getting number to it as I played. While deep in playing mode, most of the brain thinks that a cow-person alien that I am slicing while he's screaming is real - and I have to accept that and be even more efficient in the killing to "win". I see why older people were against (violent) games when I was playing them as a teenager (and understand politicians like Hillary Clinton who tried to limit their availability to children). People who say "it's just a game" don't know much about the human brain and are deluded in thinking that humans are this "always smart, always on" robots who make rational decisions. We are anything but that.
It's funny, I just wanted to warn people not to waste their money on a Steam version that doesn't work. I still have to finish the game (GOG version, NOT Steam Version), it's one of those I never got around to finish when I played it as a teenager. I played a lot of games as a teenager and I might have also been a bit (quite? very?) numb.
PS: AFTER FINSHING THE GAME
Just finished the game.
It's enjoyable. I started to use mind trick and found that this is probably the most light side way of playing - making enemies shoot each other. Lightsaber fights are cool and a good mixture of chaos and order. They underline the problem of storytelling beyond the myth - the magical force (in this case, The Force) will get inflated. In JK:JA, you meet probably a hundred of dual lightsaber users. Darh Maul suddenly doesn't feel as strong anymore (remember when you first saw him turn on the other side of the saber?).
Locations are my favourite thing here and maybe in games in general. I especially enjoyed the ancient jedi temple - the first time you get to try stage 3 force jump. Gliding through air is well done, especially for a game from that period.
While playing, I couldn't shake of the feeling of milking the Jedi Knight structure to the end - visting OT locations, meeting OT characters (Fett, Chewie, Luke), other winks to the OT, hordes of stromtroopers, and more and more dark "force users". I still liked it, it's much more respectable than Disney's unholy take and it's been more than a decade since I played Jedi Outcast.
The ending is a bit underwhelming. Great build up with going through catacombs, than a strange lift to the Egyptian outside and a mediocre final fight. On the normal difficulty, it took me 3 takes to finish the boss off. Even the final cutscenes felt a bit strange -  Jaden leaving Tavion's body behind, quasi closing the entrance to the tomb with a lightsaber (this was especially strange.)
What is this game about, besides survival?

Also, my thoughts on game violence were an unfiltered introspection of someone who grew up with pop culture and (violent) videogames and decided to give up on most of that in the past five years (starting in mid twenties)  to try to engage with the real world to be more happy (with great results). My shock to the violence was real, and it went away as I played the game more. One of my favorite things about Planescape Torment was that the character was just another wanderer of no particular importance, trying to learn about himself and the past he had forgotten. You were just a guy that dies and gets back up again, a point of interest for some, a nuisance to others, but ultimately not that big of a deal. It gave the impresssion that you were walking in to a wild, living world that existed completely separate from you and that made exploration and interactions very satisfying.
In Tides of Numenara, the entire world seems to revolve around the player. You were god and a bunch of people worship you. Even the Endless Battle is all about you. There are plenty of RPGs where players can be the chosen one that will save/doom us all, but I always loved Planescape for being a story about one person's journey that wasn't about the rest of the world. The character left ripples, sure, but it was a small story in a big universe. Being the chosen one just makes me feel like I am in another stock/standard RPG.
The setting is certainly unique, though it does feel a little disjointed at times. I appreciate the attempts to make non-combat solutions a mechanical element, but it just didn't really click. Dialogue is extensive, but more is not always better and I feel like some editting would have served well here. Maybe the game makes a big turn around in the mid-late game, but I just couldn't motivate to hop back in after getting 15 hours or so under my belt.

This game deserves a lot more credit than it's getting.  Once I started playing, I couldn't stop.  The writing is amazing, as is the setting.  And let's be honest, if you loved the original Planescape: Torment, it's because it had great writing with an insanely immersive world.  Numenera feels shorter because there's very little combat (before this game, I never realized quite how much even the best CRPGs relied on combat to fluff things up), but it's VERY immersive.  If you loved the old '90s RPGs this hails back to, then you will almost definitely enjoy compulsively exploring Numenera.  If you miss RPGs with odd stories and walls of text, you will enjoy Numenera.
An excellent game that would get much better reviews if it was a standalone title rather than being marketed as the spiritual sequel to the best game ever made.
Like many Kickstarter backers, I'm unhappy at the amount of cut content; however, if the worst you can say about a game is that it should have been longer, it must have been good.

This game has done a very good job at being a successor to Planescape: Torment. Looking at it strictly from a Numenera aspect, everything is a little stripped down, but that is to be expected in a video game, but all the core aspects of Numenera are here. The classes, cyphers, artifacts, and the world in general is appropriate for the setting. Your companions are just as diverse as you find in P:T, but it can be tough to find a connection with them unless you really put in the effort. Each has a story to tell if you take the time to find it.
Just like the first game, your actions matter. Everything you do and say, every fight you start or stop, will all have a consequence. Your choices will also shape how the world responds to you, for better or worse. Just like the first game, this one is very dialogue heavy, and there are many instances where you can completely avoid a fight if your crafty. My first run took me 16 hours, though I didn't explore every possibility thrown at me, so expect to get 10-40 hours out of this title. With all the diverse options thrown at you, there is some replay value as well if you want to look at the other options availiable. While I took the peaceful path, I didnt really feel like I was missing anything by not going full rambo. This is a true Black Trenchcoat RPG story, so if your expecting you can just hack and slash your way out of every situation and ignore the intrigue and depth of the world, thats your choice, just like every other choice you can make and just like Planescape, find the answer to a very profound question....
What does one life matter?

Pros-
Three gamemodes, Build, Escape, or Campaign
No official ending, so you can continue playing over and over (Except on Campaign where there is an ending)
Constant updates
Lots of different methods for escaping or building, billions of possibilities
Events to keep you always doing someone, there is never a boring moment

Dedicated team making the game. (Introversion)

Cons-

Once again, I highly recommend the game to anyone.

Star Wars Jedi Knight - Jedi Academy, although developed and released in 2003, still holds it own today as a fun and cool additional to the Star Wars EU. This game has you playing as a young Jedi padawan recieving training at Luke Skywalker's Jedi academy. As the game progresses, you undertake and complete missions centered around taking out Sith and imperial rebels. By completing a mission, you move onto the next one and this is where you get to pick your new ability, be it Jedi, or Sith. My personal favourites where the Jedi absorption, heal, and protection traits, alongside the Sith lightning and choke features.
Nothing is more satisifying in this game than running through and killing people with your own lightsaber, which you later on in the game get to rebuilt and specialise in a particular style (single handed, dual wield, or staff-saber like Darth Maul). The game does spike in difficulty after a while, and led to a few rage-inducing moments, but all in all this game was great fun and I'd happily replay it after finishing another game or two.
The main story took around 14 hours for me to complete (maybe 12 with some idle hours from being AFK).

TL;DR:
Recommended, but I'd say buy the game and try it out, IGNORE THE DEMO.
Full review:
In the game you start with a decent team in the lower ranks (decent for the rank, I mean), and you play against mostly easy teams, with only a couple of them posing any challenge. This allows you to learn the mechanics, try out new tactics, and pretty much have a great time seeing your players progress and doing awesome things.
The demo however, makes the difficulty escalate quicker by moving from 1 (or 2) easy games, one challenging game, and one simply impossible to win match.
I tried the demo a few months ago. End result: super frustrating. There's no way I can win ANYTHING if all games are this difficult.
Now, the full game is nothing like the demo, fortunately. Seems a lot more fun. Will update when I reach the higher ranks - and although I expect them to be more challanging, I trust I'll have the experience and knowledge needed to prepare awesome tactics that might allow me to accomplish something.
Suggestion to Devs: make the demo cover the whole first season. It's a lot more fun and there's no way anyone who was enjoying it thus far will not buy the game at that point.

As a huge fan of Planescape Torment and the Black Isle rpgs in general, I was pretty stoked for this one.
So, what was I looking for:
- Fascinating world to explore
- Interesting storyline
- Sidekick NPCs that bring life to the party
- A DnD game
The problem with Numenera is that while it does the first point very well and the second one acceptably so, it falls flat on the third and completely misses the last by a ridiculous margin.
Sure, very deep lore to explore, interesting premise and good storyline but we play these games because they're DnD: We like exploring worlds and have a nice story but when all is said and done we want to have fun mowing down hordes of goblins and epic fights with dragons, lichs or dragon lichs. And we just don't get that. Even combat-oriented characters don't make the combat fun. The game isn't embarrased about it either: it obviously wants to give you every possible means to get ahead without getting you into a fight.
Interesting worlds are fun to explore but this is DnD and DnD needs combat, good combat to be fun. The game just glosses over this completely.

I have been playing games on computers when all we had was a monochrome, green monitor and we had to load games with cassette decks. I remember when 8 inch floppies were considered "high tech". My first Commodore Amiga back in the 80's made me the envy of every nerd at my school. ("Motorola processor, 512 K RAM, 8 bit sound and  1024 color monitor? Cool!"} Sid Myer's Pirates! on Amiga blew the IBM version out of the water like it was a frigate with 48 cannons. So, obviously, I've played a few games in my life. I have seen technology get better and better and the graphics and sound improve by leaps and bounds.
However, I also love to read, especially a compeling story.
I guess that is why Planescape: Torment is my favorite game of all time. Fallout 2 is a close second. PS:T  was not the prettiest game at the time. Balder's Gate used the same engine but looked much better.  The combat was clunky in Torment and it was buggy. But the story was original and unlike any RPG I had ever played.  It's like a really good fantasy novel that's interactive. So while reviewing Torment: Tides of Numenera, I cannot help but compare it to what came before it.
Torment: Tides of Numenera is a worthy, if flawed, successor. Of course, it's not anywhere close to being as good as PS:T. Is this really a surprise to anyone?  Sequels and spiritual succesors are rarely as good as the original and almost never better. The bar is too high. The story concept for T:ToN is certainly original and the game setting is bizzare enough to rival the Planescape universe. But it seems the developers and writers were too determined to make it a worthy spiritual sequel. The words do not flow natually or organically, the descriptions are, at times, overly verbose and I suspect a thesaurus was used heavily. Sections of it was like reading an long essay from a high school kid trying very hard to impress a literature professor.
Other issues:
- Side quests in PS:T were interesting even if not related to the main story. Side quests in T:ToN are hit or miss.
- The Crisis, used in T:ToN, was tedious and limiting. It could have been better executed with options to include more movement points for actual combat.
- The NPC, at least the one's I have interacted with so far, are not particularly compeling. The exception is the child as she  posed an interesting dilemna for a good character. (I'll say no more to avoid spoilers.)  NPC's in PS:T were not only compeling due to their backstories but brought awesomely cool options to combat. (Morte's Skull Avalanche and Falls-from Grace's Lightning Strike come to mind.)
On the good side, as I said, the story itself was interesting and gradually unfolded. It was occcasionally predictable but I was genuinely surprised once or twice as well. The different settings for Act 1, 2 , 3 ,etc were well fleshed out, especially the Bloom. (pun intended). And it appears that decisions, or indecisions, in game do matter. That is refreshing.
I have played through it once and I intended to play though it again to see how various decisions effect the outcome. To be honest, I did not expect it to be as good as Planescape:Torment but I found it satisfying enough to want to play it again. So that's why, despite the warts, I am recommending T:ToN.

Recommended with caveats.
This game is very cerebral and novelesque. It also seems to go out of its way to be really weird, almost esoteric. It's really more sci-fi than fantasy, thanks to the Numenera setting, and while it has a lot of interesting vignettes, they were all over the place in tone and content (although they tend toward melancholy). Many of them could have almost been the basis of entire games themselves (or at least short stories). It's sort of a writer's game by writers for writers, and I think that needs to be understood and accepted to enjoy it.
I didn't have nearly the problem that other people had with the combat, despite playing an intellect-based skill character (on medium difficulty). The first couple of encounters were a little rough, but once I had leveled up and unlocked equipment through story quests I cruised through any fighting in the back half. The system seems like it might be okay for PnP sessions but is somewhat less successful at a computer translation. In particular, longevity is an issue initially; you use up all your resources just to survive at one fight and are out of gas for any subsequent ones. Later on, you get the ability to succeed at combat tasks without spending any resources (if you spend level-ups properly), and then end up breezing through.
Overall, I think it can be enjoyed if you know what you are getting into, but it will definitely be off-putting to someone who wants a more visceral experience.

I did not get far into Dream Daddy at all so I won't discuss the actual storylines but here's something I figured out very, very quickly: this is not a game for gay/bi/pan men. It is a game for women.
I was super excited for this game when it was announced because I was tired of playing straight dating sims. I knew that some of the people making it was queer in some way, so I was hopeful. But then it came out.
The character creator was the first thing that made me nervous. Making a masculine character was incredibly difficult. Every character I made came out looking femme. (Not necessarily a bad thing, non-masculine men exist, but it was excessively hard.) I did not get the feeling that this was a game for me AT ALL. And I really, really wanted to love this game.
I refunded this game quickly and got my $15 back. And keep in mind THIS IS NOT A FULL GAME. It is the first chapter of a full game, which is not mentioned anywhere. So you aren't buying a full game, only the first part of one.

I really like this game. The characters are very varied and interesting and I really like that they don't all have traditionally good endings. It makes for a unique dating sim experience. The art and music is beautiful and all in all it feels like a really well put together game.
I have a couple of criticisms however.
The way the story's written doesn't allow you to really sculpt your character's personality. You're stuck with a very specific kind of character and it would've been nice to have more control over the personality.
The music volume is inconsistent. Not a massive issue but in some places the sounds are really loud and in others they're very quiet.
There are a lot of typos/grammatical errors in the dialogue. Again, not a massive issue but it just makes it feel a bit rushed as if nobody properly proof read it before releasing the game. It wouldn't bother me but it's more than just one or two minor errors; There are quite a few.
To summarise: It's an excellent game and is worth playing but it's lacking a certain attention to detail, leaving it feeling slightly unfinished.

This is one of the best games I've ever played, mostly because of the narrative. It's a spiral into insanity in all the right ways. While this greatness is masked by it's generic gameplay style, but that in itself is an allegory for modern shooters, and the mindsets of the players. Who are you killing, why, whats your true purpose for being here, because you want to be a hero? The game takes all of your expectations and throws them out the freaking window. It will make you feel like a horrible piece of crap, you feel dirty while also enjoying the killing. That's what hit me the hardest, I felt good killing people while seeing red. When it was all over I felt like I'd spent the entire night getting blackout drunk. It's fun while your partying, youre having fun on your high but the fall down to reality is harder. I've played through this game multiple times and while I did say that the gameplay is generic, it works in its favor. Picking this up and playing is always enjoyable and trying to handle firefights with different weapons and tactics is always rewarding. As well as finding the hidden intel tapes, that also serve to make you feel even worse and provide good expesition. also playing this game on the, "FUBAR", difficulty is extremely difficult but fun, I'm crazy like that. So if youre going to play this game start with the second to hardest for the most rewarding experience. Yager development deserves your money but even if you decide to buy it on sale absolutely get it. They took a huge risk developing this title, and it's wonderful.

1. Always online DRM: Seriously, Io-Interactive have you guys been living under a rock, the world hates this DRM system because it may somewhat protect your game from pirates but it damages in a big way the experience of people who actually pay for your game. People who bought this game by single episodes are getting the middle finger by IOI by not letting them know beforehand what they'd be missing if they didn't buy the full experience or the upgrade.

Do you like "choose your own adventure" novels? If your answer is a resounding "no," then avoid this. If you like or at least are vaguely okay with them,
might work for you, even if you're not really a fan of Shakespeare's
.
Pros:
+ The humor. It's weird and occasionally surreal. There's one route where you briefly become a horse just before the sun explodes, and another one where Ophelia and Hamlet engage in a training montage and become ninjas.
+ Lots of endings, almost every one of which comes with its own piece of artwork, which you can look at again in the game's art gallery. I haven't counted how many pieces of artwork there are, but I know that I've been playing this game for almost 5 hours total and I'm still missing 40 or 50.
+ Ophelia is awesome.
+ It highlights some problems with the original play that I'd never really thought about before. I kind of wish this had been around back when I was studying this play in school.
Cons:
- The game includes "checkpoints," which are basically "save" spots you can return to in order to try out different choices without having to replay everything that came before it. Unfortunately, all you get are the "checkpoints" the game provides you with - you can't create your own. The "Skip" button is nice and all, but I've gotten really tired of skipping through the pirate scene just so I can get to the stuff right after it. The lack of ability to create your own save points is one of the reasons why I don't think I'm ever going to manage to collect all the pieces of artwork. I don't know that I have the patience for it.
- This comes from all the visual novels I've been playing lately, but I really wish there were a "skip 'read' text" option.
- The narrator doesn't appeal to me at all. Thankfully, you can play the game with narration turned on or off. I started with the narration on and turned it off before I'd even selected the character I was going to play as.
All in all, not bad. I don't know that I'll have the willpower to get all the endings and achievements, but this turned out to be way more entertaining than I expected.

Land Doctrine is a great concept and looks fantastic for the first couple of hours of so, but then you run into more and more balance issues and little annoying things that add up. In the end I have to say, no... I wouldn't recommend it.
For example, infantry are OP. I've got a city that is completely surrounded by massive amounts of enemy troops and tanks. They constantly attack it, and I just as constantly send them packing with huge casualties. There are no supply chain rules in this game, so even in a surrounded city, I can reinforce my stranded battalions with no penalties. And since my new infantry are maxed out in all of the training categories and my units are getting experience from each win, and are insanely dug-in... they're Spartans now. I don't think a nuclear missile would dislodge my infantry at this point. All of my infantry-based units are like this.
You can't co-ordinate your attacks. So in the case of my surrounded city, the enemy can attack from 4 different directions and do. But you can't tell units of different speeds to stick together and attack at once - even if they're all attacking from one direction. And co-ordinating attacks from different directions at once is impossible. So attacks with large amounts of material end up being fiascos.
Little bugs and lack of cleanup...
like some of my units can no longer move. They're still there, they presumably would defend themselves if attacked, but they have a speed of 0.
If you've got units that are all in the same place, you often can't select the particular unit that you want to look at.
If you design tanks, you can't delete those designs later. And the dev went with buttons to select tank types instead of a drop down menu, so at the end of a game you have buttons all over the place when you want to select a tank.
All of this is fixable. But the dev has said he's not going to put much effort into fixing the issues with this game unless he finds a publisher, which seems really cavalier to me. He's an indie dev on an indie dev platform selling to people who tend to go for indie games, but he doesn't actually want to be an indie dev.
The point of Steam is that you don't need a publisher anymore. And I paid money for this Steam product just like I'd pay for a title from EA or Sega or anyone else.
If issues get updated and patched, I'll change the review. But what I've read regarding impending updates doesn't make me optimistic.

Land Doctrine is literally a digital board game. The elegant rules create an experience that is epic in scale, intriguing in complexity, and filled with meaningful decisions.
There is no tutorial, but the manual is concise and illustrated. By wargame standards it's a brief and easy read, with the various systems all being simple and intuitive.
The result is a mix of realism and abstraction that is uniquely compelling. Battles offer a rarely seen level of clarity and decisiveness. Combat in other games often becomes a muddle of +/- modifiers; one blob of units ultimately being just as effective as another. Here each battalion has distinct advantages and disadvantages.
Complaints that you can't field a mix of tanks and infantry in each battalion miss the beauty of this system. Limiting each battalion to one type of tank and one infantry loadout doesn't limit you, it defines them. This in turn challenges you to develop and deploy each battalion to its maximum potential.
Your enjoyment of the game will be hampered by its sometimes convoluted user interface. Where operation Market Garden went a bridge too far, Land Doctrine's interface often goes a click too deep. And much like those doomed paratroopers, at times you'll be cut off from what you want, just when you need it most. The game is never unplayable, but accessing info can sometimes become tedious.
With a few interface enhancements, Land Doctrine is the kind of game Slitherine would publish at quadruple the cost. Especially, if each battalion's 3D model represented the actual tank and infantry type.
Keep in mind, this isn't a Civ-style, peacefully build up, and unleash the perfect war machine, kind of game. Instead, you're thrust into the middle of a war, and the odds are stacked against you. Even the Easy difficulty is a tough fight for an inexperienced commander.
Starting out, your T1 Rabbit tank is actually an armored car with delusions of grandeur. The frontline is a mishmash of regulars and reserves armed with a motley assortment of misfit toys. To top it off, there is nothing in the R&D pipeline, and your production lines are impersonating the Titanic as they churn straight into disaster.
With such an intense challenge, there is a lot of fun to be had here. Every action has far reaching consequences. There is no perfect tank, infantry, battalion, weapon, strategy or tactic that always ensures victory. Truly, everything must be done at its right time, and in its right place. In the end, your choices will become the Land Doctrine that your army lives or dies by.

Rule the Waves stuck you into the role of an early 20th century Naval bureaucrat who helped steer the design and future of your nation. Land Doctrine is this, but with tanks. But how does it compare to the venerable WWI Naval Simulator?
Land Doctrine is a game that, for $5, offers a good deal of enjoyment. We’ll break down what it does, and follow that up with what it doesn’t. If you like the thought of managing a land war, and nothing but a land war, and controlling the design philosophy, then this is your game. You are top brass in this game, someone with stars on your shoulders. Watching the fight is beyond you, all you do is see the results.
It’s not a bad looking little game. Instead of hexes and turns we have a WEGO map with little armored units. Each is a battalion, of your design, that holds spaces or attacks them. Terrain matters, as does urban attacks. There can be up to four factions (including yourself) on a map that can be quite ponderous. War is immediate. You load up and go with a basic army and some even more basic tanks.
You’re greeted with a basic “How-To” once you start playing each game. There isn’t a tutorial or the likes, nor does the game really need it.
Research is incremental and lets you choose between armor tech, infantry tech, or industrial tech. Each nation accrues research points as time goes on and then spends that on research. It’s worth note that you also have to wait a period of time. This feels like a redundant mechanic. Give me one or the other.
In addition to picking research you can use what you’ve learned on different tank variants. Early in the game you don’t have many choices beyond just up-armoring or swapping a single gun. Later on your can experiment and see the final impacts with a wide range of variables.
Production is fairly simple. You pick how many companies you’d like, the type, loadout, and support. This makes some interesting trade-offs, more troops gives a harder hitting army but now you might be light on battalions at the front.
ou’ve got three presets to play with for your infantry. Prefer carbines over rifles? Or maybe you’d like more anti-tank components? It does offer some interesting choices. I usually struck the middle road but I can see specialization between army groups for certain situations.
The battle system is fairly simple. Advance your own battalions, set a few variables, and then let it go. It’s worth noting that some battalions move faster than others so you’re fragile reserve battalion might arrive before the meatier regulars.
The resolution is heavy on the details for each phase. This reads rather like a battle report from a Grigsby game. At each phase-range you get to see how your forces performed and what sort of casualties you incurred. The winner remains in position while the loser retreats. If those loser retreats into another hostile army it is destroyed. If your armies can arrive at the next destination before the shattered army, it’s destroyed. This feels like an unintentional blitzkrieg mechanic.
Finally you get a summary from your troops on the ground. In a lot of grog games it’s hard to tell what worked. Even in Rule the Waves you sometimes have no clue if a certain battleship was all that effective. Here at least you get some instant feedback and can use that to gauge the effectiveness of your forces.
One thing that sets Rule the Waves and Children of a Dead Earth apart is a tactical layer build on top of a research layer. Not only do you get to steer the research, perform the design, but you can also play as the Admiral or star marshall. You get a deep down, visceral, in your face, example of the prowess of your forces. (Or lack thereof). You can try a crazy design of just casemate guns on all of your battleships. Or you can tinker with huge engines and just railguns.
In Land Doctrine we get a summary and no visual of what’s going on. I can understand why, but it still makes me yearn for a Rule the Waves type game that let’s me play with crazy designs and watch them get destroyed.
Combat feels a bit off. One engagement will seem like a surefire win and ends up being a total rout, and another battle is the total opposite. Though it seems to be very player dependent as I’ve heard some people spend hours and have a really fair match up.
My biggest issue is lack of a run up. A year long cold war would allow the player to steer research and get a wildly different game without having to survive the initial onslaught. The AI seems either suicidally aggressive or docile. One game I found myself attacked on all fronts while in another everything seemed chill. The chill game let me play with more designs and it was a more satisfying game.
For it’s few flaws it’s a surprisingly solid game. Sure I can complain about it not having a tank-on-tank physics simulator, but it’s not what the game set out to do. For just $5 it’s a damned good deal.

Free demo? Check
Cool Concept? Check
Cheap? Check
This game is rough around the edges, but really is the direction I want to see indie strategy games go.
If anything, I'd like to see a build up phase before the war starts.
