Ok, so I have never reviewed a game before, but this game had me so shook by the end I couldn't not review it.
I downloaded this game because I wanted a fun, gay friendly, dating simulator. I wanted to support a developer making queer friendly games, in an industry where that does not happen much.  Anyways, I did that, and I got that. A fun dating simulator where you can go on dates with handsome dads, make puns, and play odd and fun mini games.  I was surprised when some of the other dads didn't laugh at my dad humour (hello, everyone knows I'm playing Wonderwall on the guitar BECAUSE it's a cliche), delighted when I received eggplant emojis for saying just the right thing to a daddy, and charmed by all of the characters archetypes, (especially the Coffee Shop guy).  But after every date with a daddy, I would look forward to coming home and finding out what my cool kid had been up to while I was away. This game has incredibly well rounded characters for what is essentially a visual novel, and your daughter is no exception. The strong relationship between the daughter and youdaddy, is truly heartwarming and weirdly rewarding. I don't want to make this too personal, but it really had me wishing me and my own dad were that close. I was having flashbacks to the relationship between Dan Akroyd and Anna Chlumski in My Girl, only there's no McCauley Culkin or bees. I was tearing up by the end... But then...
I realized, it was actually I, who was the dream daddy all along.
I GIVE THIS GAME 10/10 GOOD DADS

+ Voice acting is mostly passable, with a few notable exceptions
+ Visuals, animations, and effects are decent for year of release, so it's hard to justify counting them against the game; they didn't necessarily age well, but certainly not to such a degree as to hold it back
+ Movement and platforming feels smooth and organic; this is particularly evident when 'force jumping'
+ Environmental puzzle elements are well-designed, and work well with the use of the player's core 'force abilities'
+ Dark side/ Light side orientation can be chosen, but isn't necessarily influenced by dialogue, as in many other titles
+ Audio design is ripped directly from the films, and does well to complement the final product
+ Melee and FPS transition works seamlessly; both are fun in their own right, and neither serves to detract from the game's enjoyment
+ Combat is both fun and engaging; this, clearly, was the primary focus of the developers, and the combat system is easily that which works best in the title
+ Secret areas are available, offering tangible rewards for one's mission
+ Controls are intuitive and adequately explained in the tutorial missions; however, there is seemingly no controller support to speak of
+ Plot is nothing sensational, but it measures up fairly well to the rest of the franchise, and doesn't divorce itself from the established nuances of the Star Wars universe
- Vehicle controls, notably turning, can prove a bit clunky in practice
- Enemy AI is positively atrocious

Great game with many flaws.
* Fishing should be completely rehauled.
- The fact that I can do 100 Angler quests (40 hours of real time!) and not get a single fishing accessory is dumb.
- The fishing line breaks way too often. This makes fishing VERY frustrating when you consider that, as mentioned before, you could complete an entire playthrough and not get a single High Test Fishing Line (the item that stops the line from breaking). Right now the chance for the fishing line to break is 14% (even if sometimes it feels way higher lol), I would make it slightly lower, around 10%.
- The Angler armor should be made a consumable that gives you the armor's fishing bonus passively. This is mostly a QOL change and not that relevant, but the fact that you have to change your armor each time you want to fish is kind of annoying. I would make it so the Angler gives you a consumable that you can left click to permanently increase your fishing bonus by 5%, kinda like Crystal Hearts, Life Fruits and Mana Crystals.
- Fishing absolutely breaks the game. On your first hour of gameplay you can get a fishing rod, some bait, fish for half an hour on the ocean, and get a Reaver Shark, the equivalent of a Molten Pickaxe. That's the best possible pre-hardmode pickaxe gotten with 0 effort by left clicking every few seconds for a while, and it allows you to mine every single pre-hardmode block, including Crimstone, Meteorite and Hellstone.
- Fishing also completely breaks hardmode. By fishing for crates before defeating the Wall of Flesh, you can get all the hardmode ores that you want right upon entering hardmode. This means that you don't need to destroy altars, you don't need to mine ores, you just open some crates and get a Titanium armor and a Titanium pickaxe.
* Red slimes shouldn't drop lava on expert mode. I can't believe this even exists. The only reason Clowns sucked before the 1.2 update is because they could bomb your house and destroy it, they fixed it and then 2 years later they decided to add slimes that can grief your buildings in the Underworld. This isn't Minecraft, mobs shouldn't grief the world, much less upon death, which makes it unavoidable.
* Playing Mediumcore gets really tiring after a few deaths. When you die in Mediumcore, you drop all your items on the ground, and when you go and retrieve them, your inventory gets all messed up. If you don't know, inventories in Terraria are usually super filled with stuff. You have a couple of weapons, a pickaxe, the grand design, a bug net, a fishing rod, ammo, a money trough, a magic mirror/cellphone, food to get the "Well Fed" buff, torches, health potions, your armor, at least 6 accessories (up to 12 if you use the vanity slots to quickswap them depending on the situation), a light pet, a hook, a minecart, a mount and some dyes if you are into that sort of stuff. And most of this stuff is important, you can choose not to have stuff like the grand design and such, but most stuff is essential. What I'm getting at is, when you die in Mediumcore, it all goes to♥♥♥♥♥♥ You have to spend a good amount of time sorting stuff in your inventory, and as I said, it gets tiring after a few deaths. I propose that the game should "remember" where your stuff is, and when you get back to the place you died and find your items, the game tried to sort your inventory based on the place your items were if you died.
Again, Terraria is a great game, super fun, addictive and you get a lot of play time for the price you pay, but it has many flaws and some of them make the gameplay very frustrating, so take this as you will.

There is a reason why this game has nothing but, positive reviews. However, I am going to focus on the negatives rather then the postives since nearly all of the reviews are nothing but, positivty for the game.
My quick list of things I like about the game:
1. It's cheap for a game that has this amount of content which shows that the developers cares about their game.
2.This game has ALOT of content.Large variation in enemies, Bosses, Events along with more changes to the enemies and bosses in different difficulties.
3. Building system. Make your base/home anywhere.
4. The ability to upload your character and worlds to the steam cloud for safe keeping.
5. The ability to cross play with any character you make with any world you make.
6. Just the insane amount of content is awesome.
7. Creativity is strong in this game. This game has a large variation is furniture and other building resources which allows you to make some very uniqie structures.
8. Nearly what all of the other reviews has to say about the game.
Now for the Negatives that I mentioned that I would focus on:
1. No in game help.Besides your first NPC which the game doesn't tell you that he offers some help. The biggest problem I have/had is the learning curve. There is no tutorial showing you the basics of the crafting system(which is massive btw) which I had to figure out with the help from youtube and it's official wiki. I am sure glad I used youtube and it's official wiki because I found out that once you enter hardmode(hardest difficuly/end game content) your world is then "infected" with contagious blocks(biomes) that will spread across your entire world if not stopped so, I am making preparations to prevent the spread of these biomes before entering hardmode. I don't think that the infectious biomes is a bad thing but, would be nice to know before you invest a lot of time in a world making a fancy house that it can be effected in a potentialy negative way.
2. It's time consuming and/or hard to advance within the game. This isn't necessarly a bad thing but, ive gotten to the point where I lost interest in the game because I didn't know what to do in order to advance. With help from videos and the official wiki.
3. Items are shared when in multiplayer. In multiplayer all items are shared with whomever is connected to your world. They can take your items from you when you die and from your chests. From what I know there is no way around this and items that drop from bosses are public or atleast the items dropped from regular enemies are public. This isn't all that bad when you are playing with people that you trust but, it sucks  for those who didnt know and made their world public and had someone join just to steal items. This is more of an assumption but, I think it's safe to safe that it's true.
4. My biggest issue is the constant threat from monsters when building anything. Trying to build your house and getting hit by an eyeball just to fall and die isn't bad if it happens once and only once but, if it happens non stop than it's no longer a challenge but, only a nuiscene. Bosses are annoying when your chilling in your house and they can phase through your walls to kill you when you can't do anything to stop the bosses or monsters from bothering you in your house early on because your weaker than a bunny and once again it turns from a challenge to a nuiscene.
I think this game is good overall. I would rate a solid 9/10 on price against content. You'll die a lot and you'll be like "WTF!?!" and then you'll give up but, sooner rather than later you'll be back on dying again. In the end you'll be very experiecned in dying so, it shouldn't happen anymore or atleast not as often. Did I mention that Terraria have over 3,000 different items in game? :)

Unfortunately this game makes me sad for what could have been. Being a KS backer, I got to see some of the early development, and as a backer reward I got the Tides pdf for the Monte Cook PnP Numenera game. The PnP version is an open world where the designer wanted to emphasize completing objectives, and using creative solutions over "kill = xp" Obviously a video game will not be able to match Open PnP perfectly but the original versions of TToN came close... matching the PnP mechanics well, then they changed it, coverted the PnP mechanics into more common rpg things "evasion and willpower" or like a single hitpoint bar instead of forcing the player to be cautious with skills and abilities because Damage was taken from the same "resource pools" (and maybe because they wanted bigger, flashier combat numbers which made using the resource pools impractical). Additionally TToN tried to de-emphasize combat according to the KS dev updates. While this is not bad by itself, it does require a balance such as more content to explore and objectives to be done, or more alternate solutions available then "Talk option 1 Talk option 2  Fight" Finally the gakme is supposed to be about the Namesake, the Tides. In this case the Tides are supposed to be a unique and unexplained character ability which is influenced and changed like sea tides and the moon by the character's personality / choices. Unfortunately the character's choices, except for party interactions and a few elements near end-game, seem to have little to no consequence, likewise the character's Tides (Compassion, Impulsiveness, Mysticism etc) are not trackable anywhere in the game even something so vague as "Your Tides are a deep Crimson shot through with small amounts of Gold" which would let the character know or take pleasure in the "shape" of thier character. Further, regardless of the character's Tides / decisions in-game, they seem to have zero affect on the character's (sometimes manditory) use of the Tidal Power which is almost always self-damaging and/or detramental to the target / environment. Perhaps I am wrong in my thinking, but following RPG logic I would have assumed that cultivating "positive" Tidal aspects would modify, mitigate, or at the very least minimize destructive results, however such is not the case. All in all, the game is decent and fun but given the background that it comes from and the resources / talent thrown at it, it COULD have and SHOULD have been MUCH greater.

After playing this game for so long and enjoying it, I really thought about what I was playing. And I don't reccomend it. This review goes for most COD games before MW3.
First of all, the community. Gutter trash. Need I say more? Let me go in detail.
You play well, you are a tryhard/have no life
You play badly, you are a noob
You stay in cover tactically to avoid getting killed, and you are a camper and a "fegit"
You use a sniper rifle properly you are a "hardscoping noob"
Basically, you can't do anything without people complaining. If you are trying to find friends to play with, dont start from the game itself, get into a group or something. Hell, you have to be Indiana Jones to find a good person to play with in-game. Make one little slip-up and your whole team can be hurting your fillings.
The gameplay. Yeah, the graphics look nice. I'm impressed with the optimization for low-end computers. My bad lenovo laptop can run this game 60fps on medium textures, which is really good. It can be action packed at some points. But usually it's just repetetive. Shoot a guy. Run. Shoot the other guy. Run. And so on. Nobody even goes for the objectives in the objective gamemodes. If you're in combat training, (that's the only way you can really get into objective games since nobody really plays the standalone objective modes) don't think people are gonna be capturing any flags in CTF. Not much planting bombs in demolition, either. It can be fun at first, and incredibly satisfying when you can get in a lot of kills and few deaths. But in general, it can be boring. At points playing, you might just think to yourself ; Is this fun?
Graphics: The graphics are probably this game's strong suit. Greatly optimized.
Controls: Easy to get used to.
Singleplayer: Fun. Lots of choices for different endings. If you are getting an FPS for singleplayer, get BO2. For multiplayer, I would reccomend a title like battlefield.
With the regular modes, you can be put with people with totally different skill ranges than you. I believe league play puts you with people in your skill level, but I don't think anyone uses that anymore.
TL;DR, this game is greatly graphically optimized, can be fun for some time, but can be repetetive after some time. The community is gutter trash, but you can't expect much from competetive players trying to get under your skin to gain some edge.

Alright, after completing this game here are my thoughts.
In the beginning I was loving this game, it had the same powerful beat-downs that would put a smile on my face when achieving a cinematic free form fight with a group of thugs.
As I progressed through the game the flaws started to show. I bought this game recently when it had gone on sale, so thankfully most of the bugs that made it to the initial release were not an issue for me. I did read all of the numerous patch notes and the volume of bugs and fixes they list was above average which in my opinion is unacceptable and gives me the feeling that the game was rushed.
I thought the story was well composed and I don't mind the lesser known villains in this game because the origin story calls for them, and that may just be an excuse, but I'd rather they used lesser known villains then try to shoehorn super-villains in the game "just to have them".
It has been a year or so since I played Arkham Asylum and City so I was inevitably comparing this game to its predecessors, but it was mostly from memory. After finishing Origins I was compelled to go back and play the first two and that's where Arkham Origins falls flat. Arkham Asylum was released in 2009 and it is superior to Origins in almost every way. The fighting is a lot tighter and the animations are more fluid when changing directions in free flow. What was the most surprising (or maybe not so because of the trend these days with console ports) was the higher quality of textures, lighting and normal maps in Asylum, the environments are lot more interesting as well. The voice acting is great in Origins and I thought Troy Baker did a excellent Joker, but after hearing Mark Hamill again it's hard to want to go back.
My bottom line, I would recommend this game in its current state if you can get it on sale. In my opinion it serves only as a bridge between Arkham City and Arkham Knight, because Origins was not developed by Rocksteady and unfortunately it shows.

After playing Arkham Assylum and Arkham City, this one wins the prize. Not to mention the storyline wasn't short as hell like Arkham City. I enjoyed the interactions when it comes to fight bosses and stuffs plus the contect was extense just like it's suppose to be.
Now... let's see if Arkham Knight can beat Origins.

How similar to XCOM is this game? Well, I will tackle this topic first.
So is the game similar to XCOM? I'd say yes, to the newer ones. Enemy Unknown and XCOM2. It is actually as close to XCOM as a football game probably can be. The numbers system is a bit different here but the basic idea is the same. The game involves a lot of risk management and evaluations, around said numbers and skills. In XCOM you can use supressing  fire, in Fooball Tactics you can use pressing, which lowers the enemy accuracy, ball control etc, just as a simple example. So yes, the game is very similar to XCOM, biggest difference being that your team can't just go on the field and straight out die. They can get injured though.
So the game is awesome. I haven't encountered any bugs and its absolutely great and playable in it's current state.
They added more advanced classes in a HUGE update and I was wrong, I prefer it this way.
I also found out the default match is just too short for my liking but you can customize that in the league settings. However, I haven't found a way to change it mid-season/career so I'm pretty sure it is impossible. Kind of forced me to start a numerous new games to find the perfect lenght for me. There are also other options you can customize, i.e. no injuries, no fatigue, unlimited cash etc but these do disable achievements.
While there still aren't difficulty options per se, you can enable "hard mode."
My only complaint is that I hope the game would extend the time as long as the ball is in penalty zone. In real Soccer if you're basically still on offense, the perioid won't be whistled over. This would make late-perioid corner kicks way more interesting imo, since defenders need to actually clear the ball or get it to goaltender. But this is just my opinion and not a flaw per se.
I don't often write reviews on steam, in fact this is my second one. I feel like this small developer deserves one, and a positive at that. If you're unsure,
.
TL;DR Amazing. Reminds me of XCOM. After the new update, I'd have to say its even more amazing.

A good example of Early Access games done right. The devs have been actively updating the game and often ask the community for feedback. Taking inspiration from games of other genres (like XCOM with its various skills and classes) could sound like a risky goal, but Football Tactics has achieved it. In some ways it has been so successful at this that players don't need to follow the actual sport to enjoy Football Tactics. Initially I had a flickering graphics issue with some of the in-game screens but was able to fix it (which was straightforward after searching the steam forums for solutions) by opening the config.exe file under SteamApps > common > Football Tactics, going to "Troubleshooting" and just ticking the box called "Fix missing or flickering fonts, buttons etc".

Considering nowadays gaming industry where barely a day passes without another early access or AAA scandal Football Tactics suddenly comes along to remind us of better days where developers created games out of passion and excitement for video games!
The asking price of 15$ for this indie title is in my eyes almost too low, especially when I look at their crazy character creation editor which easily trumps many modern AAA games! In fact, there are so many options that I stopped bothering with getting through them all at some point to finally start playing the freaking game :). Steam Workshop has also alrdy many mods to get around license restrictions or in other words mods which override fantasy names in favor of RL football clubs and players!
Like in XCOM have your protagonists the chance to learn many different special abilities to achieve your goals as a football club.. Your players have besides special abilties attributes like accuracy, defence, passing or ball control and it's up to you to use the right ability & right attribute at the right time, basically like XCOM in soccer jerseys..
There are minor issues here and there like the occasional line of second language type of english or insecure AI. It is, however still an EA indie title which tries to do an honest job and I applaud them for that!
The only thing I should warn you about is that Football Tactics isn't a hardcore sport managament simulation nor a hardcore tactics game! The mix makes this game a decent casual experience!
I'll let you know when I stumble over anything that might interfere with my recommendation in the future.

I first played this as a star-wars loving kid. I keep coming back to it every so often as an adult.
One of the best Star Wars games for gameplay reasons alone: it took the previous game's (Jedi Outcast) revolutionary lightsaber fighting system, refined it and added not only new moves but two entirely new fighting styles (dual lightsabers and staff). It can be enjoyed singleplayer in a decent (read: fun but story light) campaign, multiplayer or even multiplayer by yourself with bots. And if you don't enjoy lightsabers and force powers, there are many other weapons available turning the game into an adequate shooter.
I also need to mention the (still active) modding community which has in the past done crazy feats like recreating the worlds of, for example, Final Fantasy VII and Jurrasic Park as multiplayer maps. By now there are game-overhauling mods like Movie Battles II (which attempts to recreate the battles seen in the movies in balanced multiplayer game modes) or Knights of the Force 2 (which allows you to create your own scenarios and play as almost any Star Wars character you can think of in a singleplayer setting). Content from the new Star Wars movies is also still being added to the game by modders: characters like Kylo Ren, Rey and even Jyn Erso are all available.
If you have ever gotten excited over Star Wars you owe it to yourself to give this game a try: Push past the limitations of it's age and see whether you, like me, consider this an underrated gem.

HITMAN has mixed reviews due to its episodic release schedule, but make no mistake - this is the best game in the series since Blood Money, and one of my favorite games this year. This is the stealth-action-murder-puzzler genre at its finest.
Though the levels are few, each one is packed with detail, events you can set in motion, and tricks to learn. Challenges, Escalation Contracts, Community Contracts, and my favorite - Elusive Targets, give each level tons of replayability. Challenges provide incentive for a variety of playstyles, tasking the player to figure out accidental kills, sniper kills, stealth kills, and the trickiest one: Silent Assassin - Suit Only. Escalation Contracts each have 5 levels of difficulty and have you go after targets with specific instructions like 'kill the Scranton Strangler with fiber wire while dressed as a paper salesman', then up the ante each time you complete it.  Elusive Targets pop up every couple of weeks and provide limited-time only opportunites to scope out and assassinate a brand new target with no saving or retries upon failure. These are tense, well-done and provide great moments of elation or frustration depending on your result.
I think the episodic release fits the game well, though I shudder to think of what the "AAA" gaming industry could do with the idea. In my opinion though, the trickle of content plays into the fantasy of being 47, called upon every so often to take out some trash.

Batman: Arkham Origins is the third installment in the Batman: Arkham series of video games; it serves as a prequel to both Arkham Asylum and Arkham City and provides an insight into the early days of Batman's career. This is the first game in the series I have played extensively, despite owning the other two titles.
This game follows Batman/Bruce Wayne on Christmas Eve in Gotham City; the villain Black Mask places a significant bounty on your head, meaning the best and brightest villains flock to Gotham on Christmas Eve to take down Batman. I thought this was a great way to provide diversity in the villains you'll encounter, each with their own characteristics and different fighting styles; Bane, Copperhead, the Joker, Deadshot, Mad Hatter, Deathstroke, Electrocutioner and the Penguin are all villains that Batman will encounter in one way or another. The voice acting and motion capture of these characters is absolutely brilliant, and it was very enjoyable to face off against them.
This game is a sprawling open world brawler; Batman has a number of tools and gadgets to navigate the vast environments such as grappling hooks, glue grenades, smoke grenades and batarangs, all of which come in useful in a variety of ways. You can glide across the cityscape uninterrupted; this is one of the best features of the game, as the player is allowed to navigate the world as you choose without limitation.
Gameplay in Arkham Origins consists of engaging in fist fights with goons, sneaking around areas, solving puzzles and gliding around Gotham. Like previous entries in the series, Arkham Origins uses the freeflow combat system; as Batman, you can fly around a punch up whilst delivering hits and countering attacks. Different enemies require different fighting styles and techniques, and the enemy diversity as well as the range of tools means the fights are always entertaining and challenging. The stealth sections are equally entertaining, as you can use your tools and the environment to eliminate enemies undetected. You'll also come across challenging puzzles within the game, such as bypassing traps and blocked areas as well as solving puzzles left by Enigma.
Video and sound design in this game is also very good. Excellent attention to detail in combination with a highly appealing graphics engine, this game looks absolutely stunning on high settings. Voice acting and sound design is also fantastic, and feels like a highly authentic Batman experience.
This game was very enjoyable due to its highly polished gameplay and compelling story. Without spoilers, the scenes concerning the Joker and his early meetings with Batman provide a unique take on the story that I found extremely interesting and riveting for the game. If you enjoy action packed brawlers in an open world setting, I highly recommend this game. Loads of replay value and excellent value for money, Batman: Arkham Origins is an epic game for fans of Batman and action games in general. 9 / 10

Arkham Origins is a great game with a very bad launch which makes it underratred. Different studio on an Arkham game means a different aproach, which in this case turned out to be a solid job. The gameplay is now brutal, there are more gadgets, the city is bigger and colder, the story feel more alive and the soundtrack helps making it all epic.
The STORY is well written, has many epic moments and does it job at keeping you entertained and keeping your interest in, which is great considering it's a prequel. In this game, Batman is in his early days, fighting both criminality and law. In the night you're playing, 8 assassins mean to kill, all organized by the man behind a mask. There are characters like Joker, Bane, but new, even unheard ones from the past games, like Deathstroke, Firefly, and Shiva. The main story is great and the sidequests are a joy to do(only there you'll confront some of the assassins)
The GAMEPLAY is brutal, fun and challanging on hard. Having more gadgets and moves keeps things fresh for an Arkahm veteran. There are regular thugs, armored thughs, brutes, martial artists, thughs with shields and armed thughs and there is a gadget, a move for each one of them. You have the dark knight system, which challanges you to do different things and gives you rewards which consists in upgrades and experience. The challange room is fun to play, but it should be approached after most of the upgrades are aquired. There is also a new game plus and new to the series, "I am the night" mode, which is the ultimate challange.
The MULTIPLAYER is totally enjoyable. There are some things that tie in with the singleplayer, but aside from that, you can play as Batman or Robin, or you can be part of Joker or Bane's gang. Being a hero means intimidating both gangs, before they one kills the other and captures every point. You can even play as Joker or Bane, if you are the lucky thug to open the door for them.
GRAPHICS are stunning, the game being the best looking Arkham to date. Also the texture models are a real eyecandy. It has the innovative thing of snow getting deformed at your movement, which is something available for every type of video card.
The BUGS are solved now, haven't experienced any, but a crash while hitting the exit button. Gamebreaking bugs are solved now, but there are still some to report some problems.
All in all, Batman Arkham Origins is a great game that does it's job of making you feel like Batman, a must own for every gamer, since right now it's the great game that you can enjoy. "Welcome, Eggs Benedict!"
I don't know about you, but I didn't even know we were expecting yet, yet another Five Night at Freddy's game, so this was certainly a surprise! No, let's change that to a "pleasant" surprise, as the good news is that this is easily the best Freddy's game since 3, and by far the freshest and funniest entry in the series since the first.
But do we actually want our horror games to be "funny"? Answer: only if they're also scary! Thankfully...this one is.
Now, I know this franchise has an infamously, erm..."young", and somewhat overzealous fan base. Truth be told, the average Freddy's fan is (correctly, as best as I can surmise) stereotyped as being about ten to fourteen years old, quite possibly female, and not someone who is usually a fan of horror games. It's my opinion that this isn't necessarily the first game's fault: it was clever, full of character, fairly original, and actually one of the "scariest" games which I, as a fortysomething year-old horror-obsessed adult male, have ever played.
The key to this scare factor was suspense, plain and simple. I've actually gotten quite tired of late with explaining to people that the much-loathed "jump scare" only works if it's preceded by suspense. The suspense in this instance is intact, if not quite at the pressure-cooker level of the first Freddy's. This is partly due to the fact that, instead of a lengthy, sustained single location situation with consistent mechanics, this Freddy's is more like a series of shorter mini-games with slightly differing mechanics, moving between different locations as different "technical problems" arise within the game's more futuristic setting.
Obviously, this new approach has both its benefits and shortcomings. On the plus side, the gameplay is certainly more varied. On the downside, the suspense comes in short bursts, and that old feeling of "♥♥♥♥ me, five minutes in, if I don't survive the next two minutes it's all the way back to the start of the level" is evidently lost. But the suspense is still pretty thick, and the jump scares as effective as ever.
Unfortunately, the difficulty factor is as ruthless as it ever was, and while the first two Nights are pretty easy-going, by the third I managed to reach a point where the game decides to "compensate" for the abovementioned lack of lengthy waits between checkpoints by making you do multiple mini-games in a row, each at least a couple of minutes long in its own right.
If there's one thing which ♥♥♥♥♥ me in the gaming world, it's having to re-do "bits" which I've already conquered. So yet again, it's looking questionable whether I'm going to have the patience to see this one through to the end. I have a sneaking suspicion, however, that the die-hard Freddy-philes won't have that same problem, seeing what a relentlessly loyal bunch they are.
An easy recommendation, then, for hardcore FNAF fans. For everyone else, well, if you didn't enjoy any earlier games you might enjoy this one, but I wouldn't fancy the chances. To me, it's yet another quality game from Scott Cawthon - and a huge improvement over the massively disappointing Freddy's 4 - but he's yet to top the first one in my humble opinion. Full points, though, for changing it up quite a bit, while still maintaining at least most of the elements which have made the franchise so stupendously popular.
Verdict: 8.5/10.

There are stories out there (be it movies, books, or in this case, video games) where it is highly encouraged to experience with 0 prior knowledge.  I would suggest doing so with this game, but let's be honest, you most likely know that this game leaves you with some heavy emotional baggage.  With that said, I will do my best to avoid any plot-specific details, and instead, mention their presence.
This falls into shooter subgenre, the 'Modern Military Shooter'.  The subgenre is classified by solely focusing on Multiplayer, with short, linear campaigns, because making a game that's multiplayer only isn't worth 60$ (though the Single Player isn't valuable). The gameplay itself relies on hitscan weapons (weapons where bullet travel is instant, and explosives travel about as fast), very low damage threshold, and regenerating health.  I bring this up because Spec Ops dumps their eggs into single player, and only added multiplayer because 2K requested it.  Without getting into finer details, the gameplay doesn't derive itself very far.
The story is more than serviceable; it's good.  The story is based around the special operatives Walker, Lugo, and Adams going into a post-apocalyptic Dubai to find signs of life, and if so, leave and signal for a rescue team.  It takes you less than a tutorial level to find out a bunch of anti-American zealots  have taken a marine trooper hostage and plan to execute him.  So, instead of finding out about survivors and leaving, you go after the hostage.  Along the way of killing survivors in self defense, you run into a splinter group of marines who you trade bullets with.  So now, you are killing marines who survived the apocalyptic sandstorms, and the citizens of Dubai.  This is counter-intuitive to saving the city and its people.  The events that transpire end up getting to our three generic grumps, who end up going crazy and stricken with PTSD the more the game goes on.  The descent into trauma is the best part of this game.  At the start of the game, you're talking with your squad using terms like "tango down" or "target down", and as the game goes along, slowly degrades into Nolan North shouting incoherently.
The problem is that the whole game, you're told that you're responsible for all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ problems that you experience, while the player is disempowered from being responsible for the situation.  The developers say that your power as the player is to whether or not you quit the game or keep playing, and even incited this mid-way through the game.  I don't think I need to point out how juvenile of an excuse that is.  The only option is option A, I took option A, and now the game is telling me I'm a monster for taking option A.  I don't mind that the characters start to slowly lose their sanity, because they are empowered as human beings, and do debatably evil things.  I, as a player, am coerced into doing debatably evil things.  There's a plot twist at the end which I'm not going to spoil, because, you know, you're reading this to debate whether or not to buy this game, but do know that it almost ruined the entire experience, because it was so bad.
The gameplay is vanilla with a cherry on top; a bland, but competent formula with a topping that is in and of itself bland.  You have a cover shooting system, weapons that do a lot of damage, recoil, but are samey.  You have a heavy assault partner, and a sniper.  You can make them focus on killing certain people, and, if you're pinned, they can throw a flashbang grenade to save your♥♥♥♥♥  Between Elizabeth in Bioshock Infite and Ashley in Resident Evil 4, their AI is closer to Elizabeth, while not being absolute game breakers.  I played on Hard, and it definitely kicked my♥♥♥♥♥  I'd recommend playing on Hard because you're supposed to be playing a game that makes you feel like♥♥♥♥♥♥ and making it difficult on top of that helps.  The game does get more difficult as it goes on, because your cover options become less and less suitable, though they do throw a meat shield or two your way, and your only option is to kill them before they kill you.
For a game with the words "Spec Ops", I don't really feel like a special forces agent.  If I were a heavily trained soldier, with a focus on saving lives, I would imagine being more like Naked Snake or Adam Jensen where, while I can fight in open combat, prefer to not be caught.  You're given silencers on your base guns, but those silencers don't matter when the level designs don't permit this gameplay.  Instead, the levels cater to set piece battles (a real problem with cover shooters, sadly).  I do think that the game's story would have been damaged though, if you managed to get through almost all of the game without getting caught, and are then told by the game that you're a horrible dude because you killed all those guys.
I do have legitimate problems with this game.  It does have a good story that does throw some legitimate sucker punches at the players, with what is most likely the best story of any modern military shooter in a superb environment.  However, the gameplay detracts from the whole experience, because you have no choice (or illusion of choice at points), and are treated like you did.  I leave it with a recommendation, because I can tell people to play this game comfortably, but you might find the game's hollow gameplay and disgusting plot twist detract too far from the game.

It's been a year since I picked up the game, and I still cannot bear to play it again when I think of what overcame me when I finished the game.
As my playtime indicates, I finished this in a massive rush. I played from 11pm to 4am, expecting that the game was some sort of quick-play game that I could put down easily at any time, like, say, call of duty (oh good grief, even the comparison makes me cringe). I was so driven to finish the game
. This revelation made me hate myself beyond belief, as I realized the very same determination, the self-same urge to commit to a goal made me ignore warning signs all over the place. This game makes you truly explore yourself, the deepest darkest recesses of your psyche where the hidden threads of psychopathy lie.
When I finally finished the game at 4am, I was unable to sleep. I stayed awake, tormented by what I had done
. I kept telling myself: "This is a game. Get over it and get to sleep.", but I just couldn't get over the fact that at the heart of every human is the capability to take things to an extreme in order to pursue a perceived greater good. It is the very thing that drives the best of humanity and the worst of humanity. Medical scientists pursuing a cure, versus the extremists ♥♥♥♥ing up Syria as I type this. This game revealed an inner heart of darkness that needs to be understood, addressed and controlled. If only every one of us could think about it with the due weight and clarity that is needed in such a discussion.
Play the game, and finish it, please. Do yourself a favour and finish it. Understand how dangerous it is to be unaware of your own actions, and bloody well learn from it.

"...that is the question." Everyone knows the line, and mostly everyone who hears it know that it's from Hamlet, arguably Shakespeare's greatest play, and undoubtedly his longest. But when most people think "Shakespeare," they don't automatically think "Shakespearian-based-Visual-Novel/Choose-Your-Own-Adventure-Game" as an actual, plausible way to make Hamlet understandable and, indeed, relatable to those unfamiliar with the Bard. As both an avid gamer and someone with a few years of professional training in performing Shakespeare (including a few actual performance credits under my belt), I was surprised to learn of this little gem's existance, and eagerly dove in.
Having completed the "Main" Storyline, I am entirely satisfied with my purchase...and now look forward to going back through it again and discovering all the crazy tangents and unbeaten paths.
For those who've never seen or read Hamlet, the game helpfully marks the choices that take you down the course of the plot with little skulls. To those scared of being overwhelmed with confusing text, fear not, as the game only dips into the play's text for two or three of the more well known speeches. The rest is told in a humorously critical analysis of just what the characters were saying to each other, and just how insulting and coarse the Bard's characters can be sometimes.
And that's just the path that follows the Bard's version of the tale. Every choice you make could put you into the shoes of      Hamlet himself, his girlfriend Ophelia, and even the Ghost of King Hamlet Sr. without warning. One of my favorite moments so far came from a sidepath of the Ghost King that took me completely by surprise. I won't spoil it, but that moment alone has made me determined to unlock every possible ending just to see what crazy misadventure happens next.
While not the most orthodox way to introduce newcomers to Shakespeare, this game is a treat that should not be passed up by anyone. I give it a 10/10.
I picked this up on a whim and have found it immensely enjoyable and well worth the $12 I paid for it.

To Be or Not To Be is the best sort of parody - one that goes over every line in Shakespeare's original with a magnifying glass and mocks it mercilessly while still showing an appreciation or fondness of the play. See any edition of 'Dinosaur Comics' for an idea of the kind of thorough analysis, smart♥♥♥♥♥and righteously PC commentary and gleefully silly fourth-wall jokes you can expect. In the prologue, Ophelia is described as having 'a -1 weakness against water'.
Also be aware that this is an ebook rather than a game in the strictest sense - though it's very much an interactive 'choose your own adventure'. North takes the time to get as much as he can from the premise ('make fun of Hamlet'), sometimes allowing the player's choices to explore wild tangents that have less to do with the original play but are there as options for those who would rather help Claudius battle skeletons than pick apart another soliloquy. Throughout, though, the book goes to the trouble of adding multiple, widely-varied paths and alternate 'playable characters'.
The presentation for the Steam edition is a little awkward (you'll want to switch that music off very soon and probably also the voice-over) but the layout - following the printed version - is very solid and doesn't skimp on quality illustrations from numerous respected webcomic authors.
At one point I had Hamlet make up for his caution by turning into the Incredible Hulk over Ophelia's grave. I loved it.

HITMAN has mixed reviews due to its episodic release schedule, but make no mistake - this is the best game in the series since Blood Money, and one of my favorite games this year. This is the stealth-action-murder-puzzler genre at its finest.
Though the levels are few, each one is packed with detail, events you can set in motion, and tricks to learn. Challenges, Escalation Contracts, Community Contracts, and my favorite - Elusive Targets, give each level tons of replayability. Challenges provide incentive for a variety of playstyles, tasking the player to figure out accidental kills, sniper kills, stealth kills, and the trickiest one: Silent Assassin - Suit Only. Escalation Contracts each have 5 levels of difficulty and have you go after targets with specific instructions like 'kill the Scranton Strangler with fiber wire while dressed as a paper salesman', then up the ante each time you complete it.  Elusive Targets pop up every couple of weeks and provide limited-time only opportunites to scope out and assassinate a brand new target with no saving or retries upon failure. These are tense, well-done and provide great moments of elation or frustration depending on your result.
I think the episodic release fits the game well, though I shudder to think of what the "AAA" gaming industry could do with the idea. In my opinion though, the trickle of content plays into the fantasy of being 47, called upon every so often to take out some trash.

Even with all the BS surrounding this game, you just can't deny that this is the ultimate return to form...with scenarios that are (almost) as good as Blood Money and with so much stuff to discover and do, Thanks IO for listening to your fans and for putting so much love into this game.
It's a pure delight and even at this moment with only 3 of the 7 episodes released totally worth it's asking price.
P.S: Disable all hints and maybe even the minimap for a better experience.
P.P.S: ♥♥♥♥ Squeenix.

Torment: Tides of Numenera really is one of those games that make me wish Steam had a review option somewhere between "Thumbs Up" and "Thumbs Down".
On the good side, its story and world design often are gorgeous. You hold conversations with cultists who eat corpses to gain their knowledge, crawl through the memories of other people, and fulfill various quests that merrily laugh into the face of dimensional barriers. As you make your way through the mainquest, you see all the little seemingly unrelated tidbits from various side quests pulling together like pieces in a puzzle until you finally get to face the Changing God himself.
It could, for all intents and purposes, be an excellent story-driven RPG. But then the bad parts kick in.
The entire combat system with its effort mechanics is tedious at best and frustrating at worst. While you can mercifully avoid combat in almost all situations via dialogue options or skillchecks, even those few situations in which combat is inevitable make you roll your eyes and wish to get it over with as quickly as possible. But fair enough, Torment's spiritual successor Planescape:Torment was not exactly known for its enjoyable combat system. You play this kind of game for the story!
And indeed, the story of Tides of Numenara, isn't half-bad, quite on the contrary. Problem is: As fantastic as the writing often is, as bloated can it be. Information and dialogue that could be presented in a single paragraph instead is stretched across five because the writer couldn't help but stuff it with lovingly written but ultimately pointless details. A sizeable portion of informaton you gather in the game is stuff that you read once and never remember afterwards. Particularly during longer play sessions, you often reach the point where you simply want to ask someone for the location of this or that, only to groan and click your way through walls of text because the NPC in question needs to tell you its whole life story. The merecaster sequences - essentially glorified text adventures - do not help.
Another issue with the writing is that the fantasti aspect of it at times can be overkill. Meeting one transdimensional entity surely is interesting. But when literally everyone and their mother either come from a different age, a different dimension, or a different multiverse, it plainly loses its charm. A defender of the game might argue that the entire Numenera setting is built around this, but still, the occasional 'normal' fellow could really have helped in terms of variety.
Add to this some few (thankfully minor) bugs that still are in despite of four years of development, a considerable amount of cut content promised to Kickstarter backers that never made it (or at least currently is not) in the game, and you get a rather flawed gem - Torment: Tides of Numenara is still enjoyable, but can be terribly exhausting at times. My recommendation hence is a cautious one.

This is my first try of doing a legit review of game, so bear with me, and my english isn't great.
Tides Of numenera is a spiritual successor to Planescape, and its important to remember that sentence throughout the review. It really tries to capture that nostalgic feeling from its previous predecessor, and to some extent it does, but it also copies a lot and specially the story.
Like for example you do not have any memories, you revive after dying, though you do spawn in the laboratory mind, before you enter the physical world. You have the endless war instead of the blood war. It only different is the world, we are in the ninth world, which has a large population of humans with some cults in the beginning and very few strange creatures. In the start you have a large city where you can travel between its territory , but as you progress to new areas, you're very limited, it is as you're set on linear quest, where you don't actually has any opportunity to travel back, only to follow where the game demands you to go. Luckily there isn't a arrow to point where to go, so you still have to figure things out, and you can use the "Tab" button to see what you can interact with, so you always have someone to hold your hand.
One important thing to remember, when you're playing, is to take it slow and read the whole dialogue, and have patience, it is one of great thing they really capture from Planescape, so if you like to read, you're in the right place, because you'll need to read before making a choice and there is a lot of choices to make, most of them is to avoid conflict, which brings me to combat, a lot of times you don't want to fight, you rather escape the situation, so I like that they changed the combat to be turn-based, it makes it a challenge to retrieve quest object and escape. The combat itself wasn't anything to brag about, because first of all, four companions wasn't enough, I felt overwhelmed most of times, hence why I choose to avoid fighting, even though they mention that you could use the environment to your advantage, either I missed some of it or I never bothered to notice them.
Which brings me to classes isn't quite as balanced as hoped, I choose the nano class, because I want to complete the game with using conversation, and at no point did I feel that I wanted to continue the game with jack or glaives. And many of the important fights wasn't about defeating the enemies, there was a few side quests in the beginning, where eliminating could be done, but I didn't really care. The nano class is just more attractive, but even then the spells available wasn't interesting, they were kind of disappointing.
Now companions, there wasn't anything special of those I recruited except Matkina, their introduction starts very dull, but their backstory and how you involve yourself into their story gets expositional better throughout the game. But it wasn't really mixed as in Planescape, there wasn't that much excitement, when the only companions you can get are humans, but still it something I need to check more on in the strategic book, so I could be wrong.
Now when you're progressing in the game, and talking to a lot of NPC, you'll notice that you're going to make a lot of choices and at no point did I feel that I was cornered, that I was set up with a ultimatum, something the simulated a real situation where the outcome would have a real life consequence. The tides did have a lot affect and I liked the idea with three pools, but somehow I didn't felt as free, I was just put on a path to follow, which return to the point of the linear story plot. I felt like joining a cult should determine how to process to the next area, it should limit the choice you have, because of the choice you made, there wasn't at any time I felt punished for the choice I made.
The last thing, Tides of Numenera does restore a lot of things I missed in CRPG like no arrows, use your brain and having patience to explore, taking the time to understand the qualities in the game, and more importantly the philosophical aspect creates a whole new level of depth and nuance, it makes the player think unlike many other games today. Their universe is still great and fun, but in the end the story could've been longer and combat made the game feel a little bit rushed. I would still give it 6,5 / 10, Inxile still did a lot for the genre, and they still did a good job, and I had still had the nostalgic feeling when I read through the text like I had in Planescape. So I believe from this point, it'll keep getting better, it was hard job to recreate something like Planescape.
Unfortunetaly I would not recommend this game for people, who hasn't tried this kind of genre, and it's not worth 45 euros, I would wait to summer sale to see if the game got a 30% discount.

When Arkham Origins came out, it got a lot of bad press for being derivative and buggy. I mean, it's not all that different from Arkham City, but is that a bad thing? Arkham City was pretty great.
Arkham Origins is pretty good. I think it revisits too many of the villains from Asylum and City, and some of the gadgets are inexplicably similar to gadgets in City but not Asylum (despite being a prequel), but it's still a fun game. If you liked Batman: Arkham Asylum and Arkham City, you're going to like Arkham Origins.
If you've never played either of those games, start with Arkham Asylum! It does a great job of making you feel like you're Batman within the frame of a 3D Metroidvania with an excellent combat system. And if you're still into it after you get through Asylum and City, then by all means, get Origins. But I wouldn't recommend making Origins your first Arkham game.

I'll update this more as I play but Here's what I think so far.
FNAF SL is the biggest improvement Scott cawthon has made to this franchise, It's not without issues, but it's one of the more unique horror games out there right now.
The original 4 games were sort of like these episodic games, each one having mostly the same kind of gameplay style with minor variations. In a sense, 4 was the end of the saga, and SL is the start of a new one.
Gameplay-Wise, It's less of a horror time management sim,  and more of a horror point and click adventure. Each night you're given new tasks to carry out, which act as mini puzzles. They can range from rebooting the power while Freddy is right in front of you, to trying to make it to one end of a room to the other without an animatronic noticing you.
While a few of them have a similar gameplay style, it's the atomsphere and aesthetics that differentiate them.
My favorite part of the first game was just how well the sound design was, something that I don't think the rest got down right. SL nails the sound design perfectly, with subtle ambient noise and pretty damn good voice acting to boot. Each of the Animatronics have a dsitinct voice, with some of my favorites being the eeriely threatening yet playful voice of Freddy, the graceful and but emotionless voice of Ballora, and Baby's innocently sinister banter. Each Animatronic feels distinct in this sense, unlike previous games where they all kind of blended together.
This game isn't without fault however. For starters, since each night is now longer and based not around time, but activity, the game utilizes checkpoints for whenever you fail. For the most part they're alright, but some of them are a little weird. For example on night 2, you have to make it through Ballora's room to get to the power room. This includes a minigame for getting through the room that's pretty easy, if not drags on for a lil long, and then a minigame with Freddy that can be a bit challenging the first few times. If you die to freddy however, you need to restart at Ballora's minigame. It's not too big of an issue, but it is annoying. That, and checkpoints don't save your game, so if you quit before finishing a night, you'll have to go through all the night introductions all over again. I'd prefer it if the checkpoints also counted as savepoints, but that's minor.
My Big issue with the game is how unclear some of the objectives for the minigames/puzzles can be. While you are given instructions, they're not always clear. The very first challenge has you barricading yourself behind a desk while you're attacked by these little clown things. You're told not to look them in the eye through the holes in the baricade, but eventually, they'll start to open the baricade. What you're supposed to do is grab the door and hold it to slow them down, but you're not given any indication you can do that unless you click on the edge (When I was playing, I was trying to look as far away from them as possible). And that's just one, other's like funtime foxy or the bonnie puppet aren't always clear on what to do. Once you do know, it's easy, and there's of course online guides and such (I figured things out by looking at discussions), but it is annoying.
And lastly, While scott continues to work Clickteam fusion to do some cool things, I do think that this would have benefitted greatly from a new engine. Clickteam does hinder the game both graphically and gameplay-wise.
But to go back to the positive, the story in this one is pretty good. It feels a bit more self contained than the others, so if you haven't gone and played 1-4, then I'd say you could probably play this one. There are some minor references to the novel that came out a while back, but it'll be a while before we can say how much the story refers back to it. It's got a nice amount of mystery and intrigue, as well as some charming humor as well (Between night you go back home and watch this tv soap opera thing that's just so ♥♥♥♥ing ridiculous, I don't even wanna get into detail. It's narmy but it's got a lot of charm.)
I might update this review more as secrets are found and such, but for now, I'd say FNAF SL is worth $8. After the past few FNAF's, I've said that I didn't want him to keep the franchise going, that it was time to pack it in. But After SL, I'd honestly be open to another game. Not any time soon really, the quartly releases is what I think really harmed the previous games, but I think the format of this game has room to really grow and do some cool things.
If you didn't like FNAF before, this may change your mind, or it might not. But if you're in the least bit interested, check it out!
Worst comes to worst, you can always refund it.

To Be or Not to Be feels like being told the story of Hamlet by a really good friend -- one with whom you share a goofy sense of humor and a lot of off-kilter inside jokes -- but there are a few issues I'm hoping to see fixed.
First, let me be direct here: I love To Be or Not To Be. I like that I can play a storyline in the 10-minute breaks between my classes; the writing style, humor, and references work for me; and the game singlehandedly convinced me to nickname my car Ophelia (+1 to science, -1 to water, and +10,000 to badassery). This is also a game where it is really fun to achievement hunt -- achievements tip you off to lots of silly but non-required moments, and chasing them down is a good way to structure your playtime.
That said, the humor relies a lot on the inherent silliness of juxtaposing Hamlet with modernity and may not hit the mark for everyone. Additionally, a lot of humor is milked from the narrator being exasperated with and/or railroading you, a la The Stanley Parable. I found this funny, but given the way To Be or Not To Be is checkpointed, I understand why others might find it frustrating.
And that brings me to my biggest problem with To Be or Not To Be: the checkpointing. Checkpoints are infrequent, and while they mostly come at sensible points (at any major scene/plot turn), you'll still end up skipping a lot of text to get back to that one spot where you didn't take the other branching path. It's a minor annoyance, but it's still an annoyance.
Additionally, for whatever reason, only some of my checkpoints (and ending art!) ever persist after exiting the game -- this is a known bug, and I'm hoping it'll be patched soon. [Edit: This has since been remedied!]
A lesser problem is the sound controls. Although the music and narration volumes have been adjusted since release so the former no longer totally drowns out the latter, there's still no sliders; you can only turn things on or off. My advice: Skip the narration and leave the music on. It's more fun to read the story in your own voice and give the words your own emphasis anyway, and the music really adds to the scenes and the humor in a way that the narration doesn't.

Batman: Arkham Origins is pretty okay.  Unfortunately, it still appears that it has some game-breaking glitches, despite the patches put out when the major ones were made a known issue in Nov. 2013.
The gameplay itself is pretty much the same as the last two installments in the batman series (Arkham: Asylum and City).   Bats glides, beats-up to string combos and special beatdowns, sneaks around in predator encounters (vent, grate, hanging takedowns are the same)  etc etc.
Personally I found it different in the overall feel of the game.  The previous installements seemed to pay much more homage to the comic book character's canon and story, with little touches  such as references to classic or obscure batman villains.  Arkham Origins is the beginning of Batman's career, so granted he hasn't encountered as many in this story line, but I would have preferred some of that love of the actual comic flavor as in the previous (for example: Bane is rocking what sounds to be an attempt at some Eastern European accent, despite being from Santa Presca).  Instead with Origins, we are given a storyline that only barely jives with the continuity of the previous games and gameplay that feels much more   of a beat 'em up and less of a love-letter to the batman franchise.
As to the glitches, about 56hrs into the game (and gathering every collectible possible) I experienced a clipping glitch where batman fell through the map.  Because the game has auto-save and it unfortunately saved during this, I could not load to before that. Unfortunately, it looks like I will have to restart the game.

The bad :

Here, you are forced to upgrade the earlier upgrades just to move up this dumb tree system.
I give arkham origins a 7/10.

The idea of a spiritual successor to PS:T created a ton of hype.
Some of this hype was warranted, some of it was not.
I didn't follow the Kickstarter campaign and I didn't contribute (I often don't due to past KS dissapointments that I managed to sidestep with my general laziness towards contributing). My perspective comes from not having time to develop ridiculous amounts of hope only to be slapped with disappointment in the end (which is what I've taken away from a bunch of the reviews here).
All I know - being a HUGE, HUGE fan of PS:T - is that when T:ToN was announced, I got a warm, fuzzy feeling.
With that said, the game ain't perfect. It took 15 hours of slow enjoyment for it to grow on me. That's where I am now, roughly, but instead of coming home from work tonight and going "Let's see if this gets any better," I came home going, "Let's see how much better it can get from here." A small shift, but a notable one.
On the Writing:
I'm the kind of CRPG player that devours lore. I've gotta be in the mood for it, but when I am, I inhale as much of it as possible. I've seen complaints that a lot of the writing in T:ToN was unnecessary and didn't serve the plot... this is true, but I don't see a problem with it. They're building a complex atmosphere that goes far beyond the plot. I have no prior familiarity with the whole Numenera setting, but every paragraph I read, I like it a little more. It's a slow, steady build-up. A large undertaking for a setting with such a massive background. As of right now, the main plot (as it's revealed itself to me so far) is not terribly interesting and frankly feels kinda tropey ("Ooo look at me, son of <POWERFUL♥♥♥♥♥KING/DEITY/ETC> and I'm all confused and have to learn about my powers and my place in the world - blah blah blah"), but it works for what it is. It was way less interesting 12 hours in. More so 9 hours in. Even more so 5 hours in. At hour 3, I was basically calling the game a disappointment. Give it all time to grow on you and try to actually read and visualize the sometimes-long-winded descriptions. Yeah, it's wordy. Yeah, it feels like they went a little too hard after writing, but it's ultimately pretty decent.
On the Choice of the Numenera Tabletop System:
Again, no background with the setting or the tabletop system but they seriously could've done without it. I absolutely hate the Might/Speed/Intellect stat pool concept. It's kind of cool in certain scenarios, but it feels weak in general. I haven't had any issues with running my stat pools empty before I can safely rest up to regain the points like I've read in some reviews, but stat pools make the game feel a bit more like a chore. Somewhere out there was a more graceful way to handle stuff like this... but that would involve dumping the Numenera system and I guess they married themselves to it.
On the Combat:
The combat is pretty terrible (hey, just like in PS:T!), but not wholly unenjoyable. It takes a bit of getting used to and there isn't much of it, so I suppose that's a plus. The concept of cyphers is virtually useless. So far I've acquired plenty more than I've been able, or had the need, to use and every time I get a new one, I groan because my main PC gets it and he immediately gets cypher sickness, so I have to figure out who I can give it to avoid the penalties... what's worse is that combat is rare enough that I don't want to put points into cypher-related skills because I'd rather dump them into stuff like Persuasion and Perception to allow me to further dialogue in more interesting ways.
On Character Progression:
Leveling characters was so-so. In other CRPGs, distributing points and choosing skills was always  something that made the pleasure center in my brain go off everytime my party members flashed on a level up. In T:ToN, it just felt incredibly limited. Starting with only 3 classes and kind of ending up pigeonholed into 4 party members sharing 3 roles, trying to divvy up dialogue-related skills among them while also trying to keep them combat ready with more useful skills feels a bit tedious.
On Available Party Members:
The size of the cast of party members is pretty standard fare for a CRPG. Party size is 4 (including the main character) and you have a choice of 6 different characters you can use to make up your Last Castoff's team. The characters themselves are interesting in their own ways, but ultimately underwhelming. My current party makeup consists of Aligern, Erritis, and Matkina. Mainly because I wanted to hava decent spread and 2 jacks, a nano with decent combat abilities, and a glaive have been a good mix for me so far (I recently traded Tybir out for Matkina because I liker her backstory more and my Last Castoff is built with Intellect/dialogue checks in mind so Tybir was kind of redundant).
Some of the people who have managed to scale this far down this wall of text might be thinking, "Man, this guy is not making this game seem like it's worth much," but I have to say that at this point, T:ToN's whole is actually much greater than the sum of it's parts. At some point, the feeling I was chasing after from PS:T clicked in and I realized that this really IS a spiritual successor to PS:T.
For all of it's faults, my initial disappointment turned to disinterest which has now ultimately turned into a simmering appreciation. I'm now hoping that it'll turn at least to a low boil before I see the credits roll.
Pesonally, I would have much preferred a PS:T successor that took place in the original game's setting with a much wider scope than just running around Sigil and getting a peek at a a few alternate dimensions. Hell, I would have accepted just another romp through Sigil (the city is constantly changing - they could have done a LOT with that concept, frankly).
What we got instead was T:ToN and you know what? I'll take it.
-----
TL;DR
This♥♥♥♥♥♥ain't your granddaddy's CRPG - Numenera flies in the face of everything you know from D&D-based CRPGs... you'll have to be open-minded and allow for the paradigm shift if you want to actually enjoy it.
For PS:T Fans - It's definitely worth playing. The art and general weirdness are actually quite reminiscent of PS:T if you allow yourself to see it. It takes its sweet♥♥♥♥♥time getting good, but eventually you'll start to get those flashes of PS:T that you're looking for. Don't let the completely different setting and system fool you into writing it off immediately.
For general CRPG Fans -  If you like dialogue/lore/reading heavy games with incredibly weird settings, you might wanna look T:ToN up and give it an honest spin.
For combat-heavy CRPG fans - Move along. Nothing to see here.

When a game that starts as a kickstarter to one of the more beloved RPGs of its time, Planescape: Torment, is announced, a certain amount of hype is created. That hype becomes bolstered by a wildly successful kickstarter campaign in which numerous additional funding goals are completed and a slew of content is promised as a result. When the dust settled, reality set in. Clearly the developer faced a series of unexpected issues when it came to realizing the vision of the Numenara setting and Monty Cook's Cypher system for the gameplay. Changes were made, content was removed and the game was released to much clamor and outcry, both from detractors and supporters. So the question is, how is the game?
My playthrough of Torment last 36 hours and involved a ton of reading, talking my way out of fights and finally, learning how to fight. I found the setting to be engrossing and interesting and completely bizarre. They really managed to capture the insanity of the Numenara setting and in doing so, at least evoked some fond memories that I had for the Planescape setting and even the few novels that were written.
The story itself is a fairly common one, the search for one's self. This is brought about through exploration, conversationa and the recalling of memories. Certainly the amnesia trope is a somewhat common one and it was mostly utilized here to good effect. While not anywhere near as engaging as the Nameless in Planescape, your character was still an interesting blank slate.
Like most RPGs, this game contains a series of main story quests, side quests and even some companion quests. While the game does manage to avoid the "go kill me 5 monsters and bring me their parts", most of them are still fairly standard. I must admit I did enjoy moving about the various locales and seeing hot spots that could be manipulated. The sheer amount of strange creatures and entities available made for an enjoyable journey.
The combat, as has been pointed out elsewhere is not the strongest. It was not really until well until the game that I started to come into my own in terms of fighting. Part of this is because I chose to talk my way out of nearly every enocunter I could find. The downside to this was that I never really had the opportunity to learn fighting strategies early on and it took me a long while to get past the first few mandatory battles. I also did not realize until well into the game that during a battle (or Crisis as they are called here" you can sometimes speak to your enemies and in some cases actually talk them out of fighting. There are also a number of enocunters that include parts of the terrain, traps, devices, etc that can help turn the tide of your battles. I just wish there had been more exposure to the combat, since it wasn't all avoidable.
The stat pools mechanic was also a bit of a strange thing to get used to. These stat pools covered things like trying to persuade or intimdate somebody, to snatching an item off of an unsuspecting NPC, to actually being required for us with combat and combat abilities. Much of this information is just not really properly explained all that well. I think a more extended intro with more tutorials would have been highly beneficial. Still by the end of the game, your stat pools should be so high that you are able to easily make your ability checks.
There has been much talk about the length of the game and as always, your mileage may vary based on your indivudal play style. I know that I missed out on some content, including one companion that had their own quests. I also missed out on talking to a certain beast in a tank that I look forward to doing next time. I also played the game and talked my way out of so much, that I intend to try it a different style next time. Having said that, many may be expecting the kind of enormous, epic sprawling adventures of Baldur's Gate 1 and 2. This game is a smaller game, featuring perhaps 5 different areas to explore and aside from the first one, they begin to feel confined after a while. Another issue will be the exclusion of promised materail from kickstarter stretch goals and I can only hope that the developers add as much of that content post release as they are able to.
I found a few bugs here and there, but thankfully none of the game enders that others have reported. There has been a little patching activity from the develoeprs since release, although the month of April has been relatively quiet for them. If they continue to support the game, then this should help remove many of the issues that others have described.
Ultimately, this game is my type of game. I like the sometimes absurd setting, the ability to talk my way out of battles and at least the illusion of choice in this game. I would have liked to see more useful loot in the game, as I found I had to buy my best weapons for the most part. I also would have liked far more encounters and combat opportunities. Perhaps my play style led to that outcome, I guess I will find out next time. While I would have liked to see more of all the content on offer, I did find what was there to be compelling and worth playing from start to finish. While this game may never end up reaching the heights of its spiritual prdecessor, I think many will find it to be enjoyable. Maybe wait until it goes on sale.

Love this game.  It's a well designed and well executed foray into designing and running your own prison. The mechanics are deeper than one might guess at first glance, and there's lots of tools at your disposal with which to either build your dream reform-based prison, or your dream complex of human-rights violations (or somewhere in the middle).
I only played for the tail end of Alpha (the last 6-8 months or so); but I can safely say Introversion has been active and engaged with this game, even after making the final push from Early Access to full release. Their monthly Alpha development videos can still be seen on Youtube (along with their funny, self-depricating early alpha trailer that was initially what attracted me to the game).
Now delightfully bug-free (or bug-minimal), the full release includes a campaign in addition to the core sandbox-style prison builder we've come to know and love.  The campaign serves as a tutorial to the game's mechanics, as well as giving an overall frame to the "world" of prison architect.   While much of the campagin's gameplay is a bit same-y for people who have been extensively building their own prisons, the story itself is compelling and keeps you treking towards the next snippet of story. Having said that, one chapter included gameplay I hadn't actually experienced due to my play style, which was a nice change of pace. For newcomers it is an excellent addition to give some scope of what the game can do.
No game AI is without its issues, but the rate at which I find myself cursing my prison staff or wishing something had been designed differently is pretty minimal. The vast majority of issues my prisons have experienced have had something to do with something I've personally overlooked, which is exactly the experience you want to be having.
TL;DR -- Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes contruction/management sims. An excellent experience. Well designed. Engaged development team.
