Following the critical acclaim of Hitman: Blood Money, Absolution didn’t really hit the mark for most people. Diverting away from the previous formula in the Hitman franchise, Absolution focused on more linear levels with a problematic disguise system to boot. Luckily however after much confusion around the release structure, the new Hitman is back to form with the largest levels in the franchise and countless amounts of ways to deal with your targets, and with a seemingly weekly content drop, this game will surely take you for a ride.
The new Hitman is split into 4 different modes. Firstly is the main story missions which generally task you with completing a hit on one or more targets and or completing a secondary objective like the second mission Sapienza’s bio lab sequence where you have to instead destroy a piece of evidence as well as your normal assassination targets. The second mode is called an “Ascension” where you have to do a mission 5 times, each consecutive completion however introduces a new objective or modifier such as only using a certain disguise or hiding all bodies in 90 seconds. Thirdly are the “elusive targets” these are limited time missions where you only have one chance to take out a target and are ranked against your friends, these also have new lines of dialogue to keep things fresh. Lastly is a mode returning from Absolution where users can make their own missions, they set parameters such as disguise and weapon, they then have to complete the hit themself.You then attempt to beat the creators own score and time, which is then also added to the leaderboard of that contract. What all this means is that Hitman has plenty of content to keep you going as long as you don’t mind that it all occurs on the same maps, but learning as much as you can about each of these intricately designed maps is what Hitman is all about.
The release schedule for Hitman is centered around the idea of monthly “Episodes”, there are to be 7 in total with six featuring full new locations, however the next one is a strange mid-season break where they are instead introducing new ideas into 2 of the pre-existing levels. For the space in between these episodes the developers scatter a couple new missions, either being elusive targets or the ascension mission to keep you going if the user generated content isn't enough. When the game was originally released you were given 2 training missions and one main mission Paris which involves a large multi-story fashion show, which can currently be bought alone as a starter pack if you’re unsure about committing to the full game, but now with the release of Sapienza, a full italian town. And finally Marrakesh which is a moroccan city where a political uprising is occurring outside a swiss embassy.
This means that Hitman is feeling more and more like a complete product, and as a fan of the series I feel safe in knowing that my purchase has been smart so far, and knowing that more maps are coming in the future only gets me excited. Because in the new Hitman each map feels distinct, paris is a very tightly packed affair dense with opportunities, Sapienza is sprawling with many interesting locations and assassination opportunities, and Marrakesh which falls in between, as it is more horizontal like Sapienza but features a dense population in its crowded marketplace.
Each map is impressive in its own way, the designers have obviously had a ball trying to stuff in as many interesting assassination opportunities as they could. On paris I dropped a lighting rig on the main target as he walked down the fashion strip, Sapienza featured me placing an explosive golf ball on my targets tee that he then proceeded to hit with a significant amount of force, leading to his unfortunate “accidental” demise. And Marrakesh where i killed my target by cutting the wire on a light which was touching a handlebar which my target then grabbed onto, electrifying himself. Each level is full of stuff like this, and it’s always fun completing them, because you have the option when you start the game to have “opportunities” turned on, I would recommend turning this to “minimal” where the game will notify you of what assassination opportunities there are, but won’t tell you how to complete them like it will in the “full” mode.
The core progression of a Hitman mission begins with you deciding on where you are going to spawn in, and what gear you will bring with you. This involves a concealed weapon, generally a pistol, and two pieces of gear like a coin to distract people, or a lockpick to get you past the occasional locked door. You are also then able to select a secret drop location where you can receive a large weapon such as a sniper, however these can be seen on your character, meaning you can be recognised in most disguises. You then set off on your way, scoping out your target, where they go, what opportunities await you, generally you will want to look for a new disguise which will allow you access into higher security areas. The new disguise system works much better than that of Absolution as well, you will now only be able to be detected wearing a disguise by those either of very high rank such as the target, or some highlighted senior workers of your own disguise. For example you can dress as a chef but the head chef can detect you whilst the other workers cannot, different to how it worked in Absolution. These new mechanics are in reference to the older games, but modernising and improving on them, fixing the ones that didn't work in Absolution.
Some things that don’t sit well with me however, one thing is that perhaps the arrangement of these levels should have been thought out a little more before launch, Hitman’s first real level is Paris, which is a very dense level both horizontally and vertically, requiring you to have quite a lot of knowledge about how the disguise system works and some of the quirks in the AI to successfully complete, which seems rough if you are new to the series, giving you Sapienza instead which is a lot more spread out but still challenging, in the sense that it is more focused on you getting creative in your decisions instead of which uniform you are wearing to not get patted down by guards.
Ultimately however Hitman is a surprise, it's wishy washy marketing leading up to the game's release in terms of its final episodic form hurt it somewhat. But the game has proven to be worth the wait, every time a new piece of content is added to this game, I have no problems jumping back into it, just to see where it will take me next.

A fascinating game with some issues that can possibily reduce/kill the experience.
Pros
-An Amazing and to be truthful educational experience.  For example,the mission in Paris shows a slither of the amount of corruption that spawns from the desire of power and wealth.

- To be honest, its fun just to listen to listen to the NPC's and enjoy the scenery.
-Lots of ways to terminate the targets and send them to ever-lasting oblivion.
Cons
-It seems to be un-optimized for many people even with high end machines however this is indeed a very demanding game with complex architecture and scenery. The maps are also filled with important and unimportant(civilians) NPC's
-Episodic release. Many people hate this however some people like it. I do not prefer this at all. The game should of been released with everything ready to go.
-Always online DRM. This can be a pain obviously. No need for explinations.
-Lack of highly realistic blood loss and splatters. It kills the realism somewhat. I HIGHLY suggest an update comes to address this.
Conclusion

Early Access on Steam has a notorious reputation for being a haven for dodgy developers and half-finished alpha prototypes that never make it into a Beta stage of play. Let me assure you: Football Tactics does
fall into this category. This is a game and development team that are doing EA right. But why listen to me? Take a look at the up-to-date demo provided here on the store page; visit the discussion forum to see how often the devs visit, respond and take in feedback; and look at the highly active workshop community - which the devs enjoy highlighting in announcements.
This is a game community to rival any AAA title community.
The game itself (as of Dec 30, 2016) is a highly polished turn-based strategy game. The demo lets you play a full season with all the bells and whistles, and if you do purchase the game, you can continue your saved game. As of writing I have started season 2 of my NCAA-mod game and I couldn't be happier with the state of play. The mod is brilliant in of itself, and the developers are looking at ways to incorporate even more community ideas based.
It may seem like a turn-based strategy and a usually fast-paced sport like football shouldn't go hand-in-hand, but something just works. Somehow it blends well together and provides a challenging and unique take on not one but two genres. Players have unique stats for their positions which can be improved on through training and game-play, there are plenty of leagues incorporated into the game itself, and the newly implemented league editor encourages you to include leagues that may otherwise not be in the base game (like the NCAA).
The UI is easy to navigate and lends itself to a simple to read yet still detailed enough management side of the game where you can build your strategy for match day via a formations menu. You can either be hands-on during match day, simulate or watch (and then intervene at your leisure). The AI, in my opinion, is well adjusted for each level of team and league I've played so far. Teams with good defense won't suddenly let you score goals, and you have to change up your tactics to suit your opponent. Gameplay is rewarding in its challenge.
Football Tactics, as it stands, is a complete game that offers a refreshing take on the hundreds of other football titles out there. Fancy on building a team that resembles your favourite players, well you can, with the current build featuring a face editor. New features are promised as they come to light, and I think even when this game has left Early Access, we can look forward to many more features and content from the developers and the active community.
This is a title that could change the landscape of a rather stagnant sports genre. RTS NFL? Yes please.

Played as Ophelia, totally made out with Hamlet, NICE.
If you need anymore than that, watch (more like listen) to me make out with Hamlet:

In all of English literature, is there any work whose protagonist's choices are more lamented than those of Shakespeare's Hamlet? Seriously, the Prince of Denmark is a colossal dumbass. He spends most of the play in a state of crippling indecision, talking to himself, talking to the ghost of his father and on one occasion even talking to the skull of some dude he used to know. When he does choose to do something, it is in almost every instance the worst possible thing he could have done. No man of action is Hamlet, instead he's an emo manbaby whose most famous speech is basically him debating whether or not to off himself. Pretty much anyone could do a better job of being Hamlet than Hamlet did, am I right?
Well, good news! In To Be or Not To Be, you can find out just how well you'd do in Hamlet's shoes! You needn't limit yourself to being Hamlet, either. You can also choose to play as the beautiful, brilliant, emotionally unstable Ophelia or Hamlet's dad! Yes that's right, the dead dude, but remember, the whole reason the play even happens is because his ghost is hanging out in the castle! If you want, you can skip getting your idiot son involved and carry out your own ghostly revenge. Pretty kick♥♥♥♥♥ eh?
I couldn't reccomend this game more highly. It is clever, funny and highly irreverent. To Be or Not To Be is an awesome and hilarious interactive novel with dozens of story paths and over 100 endings, each one beautifully and humorously illustrated by a wide variety of artists.

Amazing! If you're a fan of Choose Your Own Adventures, Text based games, or Homestuck than you HAVE TO play this!  I loved the meta humour, and am a big fan of North's and Hussie's works. CONS:

To Be or Not to Be is a really good concept of a game. I happen to be a fan of "Choose Your Own Adventure" books and this game was trying to emulate that. What made me buy this game was the Kickstarter page, where it raised more than $500,000 for an originally $20,000 budget game. It clearly had devoted fans and excited developers (especially the writer), so I had to try it out with the expectation that this would be a witty and fresh take on the Hamlet story.
My biggest criticism is that the pacing is rushed. There was too much summary, like the writer is assuming we don't want to read certain bits or want to know how we got from Point A to Point B. In one playthrough, I played Ophelia and I got a choice of who was at the door: Hamlet, her father, or her best friend. I chose her best friend, but the narration declared that it was Hamlet and Ophelia can't "CONTROL reality with her MIND. Sheesh!" Then why would you give me the choice? Unless that was supposed to be funny, which leads me to my next criticism: The humor. There was no subtlety. Imagine someone paraphrasing Hamlet for you in a parodied slang, and then whenever a joke is coming they only get LOUDER and LOUDER to emphasize their point. That is the humor of this game.
Another playthrough, I played Hamlet Sr. and I had a choice of how to kill Claudius, his brother: Enlist your son to do it, or do it yourself. I chose to enlist his son, Hamlet, to do it only to be met with judgments and grief from the narrator claiming that the choice was "awful, dude". So they emphasize I have to live with this choice and then attempt to save me by saying I should pick an "afterlife career" (to which they needlessly list a bunch of mundane careers) or I can continue with my choice. I chose to go through with my choice only to be yelled at more and the narrator refusing to cooperate with me. So they just changed my character into Hamlet instead of my original choice, Hamlet Sr., because if I was going to "induce a man to murder", I had to go through with the murder myself. If I refused this change of events, they gave me an abrupt ending. In Shakespeare's play, Hamlet Sr.'s ghost form appears to Hamlet and tells him about the murder, planting the seed of revenge in Hamlet's mind. Judgmental narrators can work, but not when they don't allow you to make the choice at all.
As for the art (one piece for every ending), there wasn't too much of it and I don't think it was redeeming enough to make up for the writing, which is the dominant force of the game. So if you're buying the game to see the art, I suggest waiting for the game to go on sale.
I went in expecting a coherent, branching storyline where "your choices matter" and you develop relationships with the characters in a way that was more in-depth than Shakespeare. This game is very casual and rushed, a playthrough possibly taking no more than a minute. While the "canon" playthrough is accurate and developed, I would suggest reading a Sparknotes version of Hamlet if you don't want to read Shakespeare's version. If you're still interested in the game, pick it up when it's on sale. However, if you share my criticisms, there are many games that do this style of game better.
EDIT: A commenter pointed out that the Kickstarter was for the print book, not the game. Which in that case, I understand the rushed pace and perhaps lack of funding for the game. But my points still stand, since most of it was for the writing.
If you enjoy shakespeare, this is great. If you don't enjoy shakespeare, you can go on a revenge fueled vigilantism spree as a ghost exploding people from inside.

This is an interesting game, both from the standpoint of building a prison in your own way, as in the depth of various systems that have been implemented.
It has, however, many, many flaws. I have bought into this game when it was still in beta. I have seen the game evolve over time, systems get added, bugs get fixed, but the game is broken even in the release version.
From the outset, the game looks reasonable, and plays reasonable in the beginning stages. If you play this game for longer, there are a lot of little bugs. To name a few:
- Decent sized prisons, even as low as 300 inmates, run very very badly. FPS drops to the low tens, and the game simulation speed is lowered. Building things already took a fair amount of time, but with the reduced simulation speed, building a cell block can take up to an hour REAL time. My GPU is mostly idle, and even my cpu is not utilized completely. The worst part is that performance-related bugs in the official bug tracker are closed as "they are no longer considered a bug". Most people blame the pathfinding, but I can't confirm or deny that. Performance gets worse when there is more staff/prisoners, but even at in-game night the performance does not seem to improve all that much.
- When fps is low, the game experiences input lag. Dragging a wall or foundation usually ends up in the wrong place. Buttons need to be clicked several times before the click registers.
- Some objects can be placed over other objects, but not the other way around.
- Objects are displayed in a random order, causing flickering textures
- Objects are not displayed in the right order, causing guards to sit *on top* of filing cabinets.
- The Mail Room system seems to be completely broken, causing mail bags to pile up in the delivery area's, while mail is sorted but never delivered
- Shakedown (searching every item in your prison) causes all items that were stored in inventories to be displaced out of the corresponding inventory. This has "funny" consequences, such as sorted mail piling up in quantities of hundreds! inside a mail room, the game spawning in new clean plates, because your serving table does not contain any serving plates. It prioritizes that over puting the 100's of clean plates next to it back into the serving table. Alternatively, over time 100's of clean plates will pile up next to the sink as they are displaced out of the "clean plates" inventory slot of the sink. If those clean plates are not displaced once in a while, dirty plates will stack up all through the prison, because all sinks are already full, and the clean plates can't be placed in the corresponding serving table either.
- Areas sometimes get marked as "too dangerous", causing your workers, janitors and gardeners to get stuck. The only solution is to save and reload the game, because this status does not get reset.
- Outside-facing cells do not get clean uniforms, even though there is a laundry room associated with it and it has way more capacity than it currently has.
- Guards and other personel cannot possibly look through outside-facing doors, even though the same doors indoors have no problems whatsoever.
- Items only work when placed in a room. Any room. Prisoners will not use a telephone booth in the hallway outside their cell *unless* you mark that hallway as a common room. This hallway will now show up as a room in the "programs" menu to clutter things up more. Chairs placed in your parole room? In your execution room? In your class room? If your prisoner has access to it, they will happily walk into someone else's parole meeting to sit down. Meanwhile, the common room is empty.
- Kitchen rooms that do not serve any prisoners or canteens attract most of your cooks and food, causing the rest of the prison to starve. Why? We have no clue. Effect gets enlarged when you do a shakedown, causing the food in these kitchens to get displaced outside their inventory, causing more food to be brought to that kitchen.
- Sleeping death row prisoners happily eat food that is placed a few squares from them on the ground.
- Food can be spilled under locked doors, causing one or more workman to just sit there, looking at a locked door, hoping that it will ever open.
- Guards abandon their stations for reasons unknown. A prison that uses "remote doors", which can only be opened from such stations can run into serious problems when a guard abandons such a station that links to a key door. A large crowd will now attempt to get through that door, but no guard can open it. Even having up to 4 stations that can open such doors will not guarantee this from happening.
- Random events will require you to remove tv's from common rooms, and weight-press benches from yards. This will cause those needs to not get fullfilled. The obvious solution is to put weight benches in your common rooms, and tv's in your yard. Because logic.
- Pathfinding is wonky. Entities in the game eventually get where they need to go, but they don't use the faster path, and will usually deviate their path in the absolute direction their end point is, rather than in the direction of the next door. They seem to be re-inventing the wheel (finding the shortest path) every time they go somewhere, in a mostly static prison.
- Entities can get stuck on certain edges. This is particularly annoying when trying to execute a death row prisoner, where you are stuck in a certain view and cannot solve the issue other than cancelling this execution.
- The game is obsessed with puting items in random inventories. This is most noticable in the laundry system, where clean and dirty clothes are put in random laundry baskets. Clean clothes are also *bought* automatically. Eventually, all baskets get filled up with clean clothes, causing it to no longer be able to gather dirty clothes.
- Another bug is visible in the reception area, where laundry baskets get moved back and forth between the laundry room and the reception area, apparently not meeting any criteria to stay in those rooms.
- During shakedowns, objects on trucks need to be searched, even if they are exported. This causes the truck to not be able to leave. The earlier mentioned "placed out of inventory" bug causes the searched items to eventually be placed visually on the truck, but technically outside the truck, causing the truck to leave empty.
- Cars spawn on the second square from the top of the road, causing them to drive on top of a road gate if you placed one, instead of through it.
So why in hell would I recommend buying this game? It is fun to create your own prison, and you are not likely to spend as much time in this game as I have. Buy it when it is 66% or 80% off and have some fun with it.

REVISED REVIEW:
I feel it's only fair towards the devs behind Hitman to revise my review of the game.
The main flaw, bugs (bodies getting stuck and NPCs seeing through walls) and random crashes have completely disappeared (at least for me personally). The game overall runs brilliantly apart from very rare random frame drops (running on 2x GTX 970).
Full Season One now boasts a handful of levels which do open world just right. The levels are large enough to allow you nice bit of exploration and lots of ways to kill your targets, as well as lots of ways to screw up hilariously. But at the same time, they aren't too big so there's no vast empty areas to just wander through or meaningless trinkets or chest to collect. Every place has a meaning and a purpose. All levels are also sprawling with NPCs making them feel like truly living breathing places.
Between main storyline targets, various pre-planned ways to kill them, bunch of additional side objectives/achievments/tasks/whateveryoudcallthem, player made extra missions and elusive targets, HITMAN offers a ton of stuff to do. Granted, lots of it is wandering around the same levels doing stuff in different ways, so if repetition isn't your thing, look elsewhere. Personally, once the game started working flawlessly, I found perfecting my runthrough of levels and doing all tasks in them to be lots of fun.
I get why Elusive Targets are frowned upon by many, and I admit I personally don't like that I can't play them whenever I want. Nowadays I have much less time to play so I miss most of them. But I do understand the idea behind them and do think that it's pretty cool. Only being available for a short window of time and only getting one attempt at each of them makes you feel like a real assassin. You need to use all the tricks in your sleeve and your knowledge and mastery of the levels to do it right on the first try. Or you could just shoot the target in the head and run away. It's up to you.
HITMAN is definitely one of the best releases of 2016. I still think that Blood Money is the best in the series, but now only by very narrow margin.
If you like Hitman series, this should be a definite buy.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Gives promise of a great and proper Hitman game with large levels that have tons of ways to assassinate your targets.
Sadly however, it's a broken mess. Not necessarily completely unplayable but will constantly screw up your mission with various game breaking bugs and glitches:
Crashes randomly without any clear reason.
Bodies get stuck on floor, walls, and furniture effectively preventing hiding them.
NPCs randomly see bodies and crimes through walls and from impossibly far away.
Edit: Hitman Blood Money is still easily the best in series. I highly recommend that instead if you haven't played it and want to pull off some assassinations.

I would agree with others, in that the game suffers by comparison to PS:T.  Taken on its own, I'd give it a solid B+.  With reference to PS:T, probably not higher than a B-.  I thought there were a lot of missed opportunities.
With the companions, I didn't like the arbitrary limits on how many and who could be in your party, when combat is so minimal.  And even if they're not "in" your party for combat/skill purposes, they could have been hovering unseen for social interaction purposes.  There was rarely any point to talking to them regularly, and they did not evolve for better or for worse during the game (sometimes the text implied they did, but not in a mechanical sense, with a few exceptions).  As others have said, they were all pretty boring, despite hints of intrigue.
I didn't understand the character development options being so limited and combat-focused when the game is so combat-light.  Likewise the inventory management, especially the cyphers, which were almost all combat-oriented.  The few non-combat cyphers generally weren't needed, because skill checks in conversation got very trivial very fast.  The Last Castoff's character options were especially bland.
I thought they handwaved away the most interesting locales, like the Necropolis.  When I think of Curst Gone/Carceri in PS:T, and how you could literally sway the fabric of the setting through interesting interactions ... there was nothing like that in T:ToN.  For that matter, the Tides didn't even matter, they should have been fundamentally reshaping the world by the end of the game.
Is it worth playing?  I think so.  I didn't have problems with bugs or glitches and found the game pleasant.  The Numenera setting is beautiful and compelling.  But it would have been better to plan a trilogy and done the first part of the game in more depth.

I can't get myself to finish this game. I suppose I'm about halfway through, but everytime I try and play it again I quit within 10 minutes due to boredom. I love RPGs and have played many of the classic ones, including Planescape Torment. I'm not averse to reading, but what I read has to at least mean something. Much of the dialogue in this game is lengthy descriptions that ultimately don't say anything, they are just words for words' sake. I'd much rather read a good book than have to wade through Tides' wordy dialogues.
What else is there to the game? There's a bit of combat which is neither interesting nor difficult. There's a plot which is not very engaging, in my opinion; It's revealed to you in the beginning who and why you are, so there's hardly any mystery left in the game.
Also, while you do level up in the game, it doesn't feel like you are getting any stronger; dialogue skill checks are absurdly easy to pass even in the beginning, and combat is so rare and far between and easy that it doesn't seem necessary to level up.
I guess it comes down to the lack of anything to look forward to in the game. I can't look forward to trying my new cool high-level skills in a difficult boss fight, can't look forward to the reveal of the mystery of the story, can't even look forward to saving the world. Just wade through the dialogue and wait for the game to finish.
A shame really, as I was really looking forward to this game. It's just not engaging at all. It'll probably be the first RPG I own that I'll never finish.

I did a strange thing because I have bought WRC 5 title after playing WRC 6. Reason was simple - I wanted to enjoy official WRC licenses on my dated PC. While WRC 6 was quite good and improved in terms of graphics and physics, the system requirements also rised, and I struggled with really low FPS on some stages (almost all Super Special Stages) while others ran fine. But this isn't the point, you can read my review on WRC 6 if you wish.
This is the first WRC title from Kylotonn games studio after incheriting the license from Milestone. I can say this is good game.  I mean graphics are really nice, game have its own nice colorful style. I like it, but it mess up fotorealism (some sunrise/afternoon atmosfperics and awesome effects) with childish colorfulness and not really realistic stage and road design.
What you get is simple: tutorial lessons, quick stage and career mode. Career ofcourse starts from slowest cars (Junior WRC) through WRC3, WRC 2 to the most thrilling one which is of course Word Rally Championsip. You can adjust setup on the car, you will need to repair it, because damage model is quite nice.
You can destroy the engine, break gearbox and make it stuck on 3rd gear, break steering which result on car turning itself etc. And you get whole WRC calendar, so 13 countries, around 7 stages long each (2 stages in every coutry are often repeated, just other conditions). In terms of weather conditions this is what is reallywell done here. Awesome graphic effects, in rain roads are wet, they reflect enviroment, there is nice mist effect etc.
In conclusion: it is not bad, however, I would recommend it only for players who like official content and licensing, because if you are looking for decent graphics or enjoable physics I think you will not be satisfied. But if you really wish for official content, I am not sure if you are looking for 2014 specification cars; to be honest you can get better product buying WRC 6 unless you have dated PC, for me WRC 5 is working fine. If you are good on rig, buy WRC 6 or WRC 7 which is about 3 months to be realeased as I am writing this reccomendation.

Borderlands 2 is an action role playing first person shooter, developed by Gearbox Software and published by 2k Games in September 2012. It is the second game in the Borderlands series and the sequel to the popular 2009 hit Borderlands 1.
As with the first game, you are able to complete a campaign with the main story quest and optional side missions as one of the four Vault hunters. All of the key gameplay features are all present, such as online co-op, randomly generated loot and character building elements such as talent trees are all found in Borderlands 2. There has been a game of the year edition released last year which includes all the DLC apart from one.
The gameplay at it's core is the same as Borderlands 1. The focus on randomly generated loot plays a huge part. Each of the characters you have the option to play as have their own specialty, and will bring a feel of originality to each playthrough on either of them. We also see a new elemental effect in BL2, Slag, this is a substance that increases the damage a target takes if they are covered in it. You will also find Eridium bars as you play the game, these can be used to purchase storage upgrades and increase the amount of ammo you can carry.
We also see an element of customizing how your character looks as well, you can unlock different skins, head designs, colour schemes and vehicle paint jobs. Another major addition to BL2 is the "Badd@ss rank" system; points are awarded for completing certain in-game challenges, that in turn award tokens that will allow you to increase your base stats. These stat increases also take effect on all of your other single player characters too. Also similar to the the original, we also see the return of a New Game Plus mode, in the form of "True Vault Hunter Mode", which increases the difficulty, and gives you a higher chance at even better loot drops. You are also able to level up to 50 in this mode too.
The graphics in Borderlands 2 are virtually the same as the original, but with just a more enhanced look to them. We see the vibrant colour schemes in each zone come to life. Along with better quality textures too. The style of graphics in Borderlands has always been a huge drawing point for me as there are hardly any other games which pull this style off as well as this.
Your first playthrough Borderlands 2 will have a number of difficult encounters, but these can easily be overpowered by returning to the same bad guy, mission or zone after leveling up one or two more times, or getting a bigger better gun. If you stay on top of all of the side missions as you progress through the story mission, you will stay at the right level so that you won't just hit a brick wall of impossible monsters/enemies. To make matters easier when it comes to deciding how tough a mission will be, each one also has a recommended level - so you can easily see how hard a single mission will be without actually having to test the waters first.
A full playthrough on single player of Borderlands 2 took me just under thirty hours. That is a pretty decent amount of content on offer, with the side missions and a decent amount of loot farming involved too. I have put almost 140 hours into Borderlands 2, as I have played various different characters through the story a number of times. This is a game where you can easily spend 300 hours and still be having the same amount of fun.
I had zero amount of technical issues throughout BL2; the game is perfectly optimized, will run at 60 fps, and the cloud save feature makes it even better technically.
Borderlands 2 is easily in my top 5 favorite games of all time. Just like the original, Borderlands 2 is a perfect game with no flaws in it at all. I cannot recommend this game enough. Most people will already have it since it goes on sale so much, but PLEASE play it. You will NOT be disappointed.

Mad Max is an open world, third person action game.
The player steps in the role of Max and has to progress through the wasteland to seek revenge on a gang of raiders, led by Scrotus, who robbed him of his possessions. Max gets help from Chumbucket, a blackfinger (a mechanic) and together they aim to build the ultimate battle car: the Magnum Opus.
While not doing the main quests you can explore areas on foot, discovering collectibles and scrap metal. You will need alot of the scrap to pay for upgrades which are more or less necessary over time.
Also you can clear areas from Scrotus influence by destroying Scarecrows, disarming minefields and by taking over enemy camps. Unfortunately, you have to repeat those things over and over again if you want to clear all areas.
It takes approximately something between 30 and 40 hours to finish the main story, for finishing all which has the game to offer it takes something around up to 60 hours.
If you are an achievement hunter, and want to achieve 100% it will become pretty repetitive during the grinding process you have to go through.
Overall, Mad Max is a good game besides of the repetitive aspect, also it is not necessary to know the movies before playing this game.

Mad Max has given me many hours of entertainment, for it to be a console game it's really good. I do find it frustrating sometimes that they didn't go the extra mile to make it an amazing PC game, the potential is there. Another aspect of the game that I really appreciated is the open world and sidequests. For me, the sidequest was better than the main story. The fact that an anti-COD even exists makes this game somewhat interesting. As a story and as a videogame, however, it comes off pretentious and a bit juvenile. That said, you may appreciate your time with Spec Ops if you're a bonafide fan of military shooters. This is because the stinger at the end will have a positive effect on you.
Gameplay is fine. Shooting is inaccurate, it's really hard to score grenade kills, and you die extremely quickly. You can carry only very limited amounts of ammo, so you'll be swapping your empty weapon for a new one on the ground very often (I earnestly found that bit interesting). You have squad commands, but they're limited to "shoot that guy" and, when the game prompts you, "flashbang those guys."
The story is where a clever idea suffers from pretentious, juvenile storytelling. A literal read is impossible, because it's complete nonsense. For example, progress always moves in a downward direction, even when the laws of physics would normally prevent it (you drop through the sand, then fight through a hotel, then drop through the floor, then end up on a terrace overlooking the entire city of Dubai, then you drop down to a lower level...). Presumably that downward progress is symbolic.
Your mission never really makes sense, but that's to make a point that the game spells out for you right before it ends.
And on and on. That this game is nonsense when read literally is what makes this story pretentious. The story wants to be clever food for thought, but the ony way the writers knew how to tell it is a nonsensical sequence of metaphors and other symbols.
Then, at the end, it chastises you for playing a military shooter. But, if you're not the type who normally plays military shooters, it'll sound like a boss at work making you go to a training about something you learned at your last company, all the while acting like he or she is really giving you an important learning opportunity.
Play everything you want to play, then, if you still want to play a video game, give this one a go. 5-6 hours turns out to be just the right length, and the brevity actually makes the story a little less pretentious than it otherwise would be.

Finding a game that has a sole focus on LGBT themes can be hard, which is part of the reason this game is so great, after having playing through all of the routes I can say I absolutely recommend this game, and to keep this review as spoiler free as possible I'll cover the basic positives and negatives of the game!
•Negatives: (I'll cover this first to get them out of the way)
- The mini games honestly feel very bland, while each time they appear they manage to grab the point of the date you're on they don't have a lot of replay ability and get boring and repetitive after a while (this is most present in one of the Brian dates, once you get to it you'll know what I mean, the achievement for his route is a total pain).
- Options feel... limited, once you get the hang of what each Dad likes it's easy to plow right through the game, which again can make it VERY boring.
- Some of the voice lines for the dateable Dad's at the end of each date can be hard to hear, this can easily be fixed with an update but it can sometimes be hard to hear what some of them are saying I found this a big issue specifically with Craig.
• Mixed: (Both Positive & Negative)
- The game is short. There's not much else to say I've completed all dates and I was surprised by how little time I had actually spent on the game, this can be both bad and blessing being short helps with replayabiltiy, but on the other hand the game is well- short.
• Positives:
- For a game with heavy gay themes this game absolutely nails a lot of the characters, they for one reason or another feel very real, and you want to know more about them as your Dadsona (and you slowly fall for each Dad)
- Building off the last point the dialogue in this game is excellent, aside from the few moments where some grammar is off the game manages to put together strong and believable dialogue between characters and has both it's deep and serious moments and moments that'll make you howl with laughter
- While most mini games feel rather bland, the ones on Brian's route are rather creative (aside from the one that's admittedly infuriating)
- The Dadsona's daughter Amanda, is a very strong character that's written excellently, she's probably one of the best highlights of the game
- I must give the game props for allowing your Dadsona to be transgender and/or have been in a relationship with a man or a woman previously it gives more depth to he game and recognition for whomever is playing the game
- This game will speak to you if your gay, it's amazing to see gay characters written so well when TV Shows and Movies continue to add them in as one dimensional or in the background, being able to have and play a main character whom is LGBT is simply amazing
- I'd you're LGBT you'll love this game, you just will it'll just make you happy 😂
- It's cute? Idk
Final Score: 7.8/10, too much Dads (Yes this is the actual final score)
Hope you enjoyed my review and I hope you check the game out! It's worth it! 😁

This game is full of amazing ideas and insane concepts, all packed into a condensed space. Though you probably know by now, only play this if you really are in the mood to read!
It's one of those things that throws so much overlapping content at you that you'll feel overwhelmed until you realize you only really have to pay attention to the stuff that interests you (ala William Gibson or Cloud Atlas). The game emulates the world it creates: everything feels old (it is really retro) and confusing; like layers upon layers of unknown culture, you are often lost, but find ways of sorting out the problems by exploring.
Gameplay wise, you mostly LISTEN in this game: talk to NPCs, learn about the world, solve quests. The combat is fine thanks to it being turn-based. Inventory management is minimal, as are most systems not related to dialogue (though it can be odd that, when you level up, you are often making precise decisions about things you will never use in the game at all). The "pools" system, like RPG stats that deplete based on checks that determine if you fail or succede, is novel.
It's telling that many people's favorite part of of this game are what's called "meres." Essentially when the game strips everything else away and become a simple choose-your-own-adventure. At its heart, this game is a graphical representation of a very inventive paper & pencil RPG sourcebook, which a cool story running through it.
Also: If you are a fan at all of Jack Vance, you should definitely pick this up!

For excellent writing that conveys meaning and evokes a response I look to Pillars of Eternity. The writing in Torment: Tides feels too clunky, forced, as if it might be trying too hard to impress, whereas in Pillars of Eternity, the writing is crisp, concise, and utterly effective. Also, Baulder's Gate series is a good example of excellent writing.
So, unfortunately, I cannot recommend this game.

Most people either love or hate the FNAF franchise but Sister Location should be looked at differently.
First of all, before I start, the graphics are not a main focus in the review. I don't care if a game has bad graphics as long as it plays well.
This game is good. It's unlike the other FNAF games because instead of being stuck in one room, looking left and right checking cameras, it's free roam! Most people might think it's more of the same just, you can move but the game is more like a scripted story. Many people enjoyed the phone guy dialogue in FNAF 1-3 and here, there is similar funny dialogue with more dark humor than what we got from phone guy in 1-2. The free roam feature is all scripted and there are few moments where you can actually explore the facility but over the 5 nights you will see everything this game has to offer.
The way the game works is that you must do certain things to either help the robots, help the facility or save your life but they are usually actions that seem like mini games. You will die on one section because you don't know what to do before going back again and doing it right. You take a deep breath as you turn a corner and enter a chamber teeming with hostiles of both organic and artificial descent. As you begin to react all of them make a sinister growl to signal their awakening and they begin their assault. You fire two quick shots taking out an imp and a turret. You fall back and slash the remaining two wasps with your knife but not before taking a few hits. You slowly creep back around the corner making sure the coast is clear. You pick up the bullets you shot and reload your gun, a large pistol capable of putting down even the greatest of enemies in only a single shot. Just as you wipe the sweat from your brow a snakeworm lunges from a nearby bush and siezes you of your last bit of health. You start a new game but now know to be wary of the purple bushes. This is the cycle of
.
There is no tutorial, the controls, the items, the enviroment, all are a mystery for you to uncover. In
you're expected to learn fast or else you'll be brawling in the first few levels for the duration of your time spent playing. Each game opens with the same dialogue between two suits working at Highrise Hunting Grounds, an enclosed hunting zone dressed up like a jungle presumably atop a tall building. In their conversation they state that the hunting ground's security mainframe is malfunctioning and attacking customers instead of the dangerous beasts contained within. They offer a bounty of $5000 to any of the company's janitors if they can reset the mainframe and secure the facility. You play as a janitor, or actually multiple janitors assuming you don't beat the game on your first attempt. To achieve your goal you must traverse through eight levels of techno jungle, encountering two bosses and a plethora of other enemies along the way.
There's enough variation in
levels to make the game interesting for many playthroughs. You'll see different types of plants and after the first boss the sun falls and darkness rises atop the artificial jungle canopy over your head. The mostly black or yellow enemies are very distinct from the purple/blue gradient of the walls allowing you to see all your enemies clearly as soon as you enter a room. The world is more interactive then you would think upon first look. Bombs can be used to destroy boulders thus revealing hidden areas containg items like extra bullets, more bombs, a keycard, or maybe a knife. Speaking of knives they can be used to chop tall grass revealing enemies lurking on the other side.
Knives and bombs are only a small selection of the many items available. A bullet magnet causes your shot bullets to fly back into your pocket after you shoot them. Repellent will protect you from those pesky snakeworms. A gold potion will refill your health completely. There are quite a few items in
some of which can only be found behind hidden walls like the snake boots allowing you to kill snakeworms on contact.
Hiden walls aren't the only feature that harks back to the classic FPS games of the nineties. This game provides the same  twitch shooting gameplay as
,
, and
. Like those game
can be played as fast or as slow as you want. One is obviously more challenging than the other but both are very satisfying. The difficulty can only be described as unforgiving. When you die it is because you slipped and made a mistake. I didn't make mistakes often, but when I did the game would punish me adamantly and bring about my death with no remorse. In that regard
is a love letter to FPS games of old refitted in an interesting aesthetic and rogue-like gameplay.
Unfortunately
has been known to perform poorly on machines is has no right to lag on. Occasional stutters are common and ruin your run in a matter of a few seconds. The only known fix to this unacceptable problem is to enable VSync but that only improves performance instead of fixing it all together.
Wrapping up this otherwise great game is some of the most intriguing sound design I've seen in a game. All sound for the game was made by DOSEONE who have truly outdone themselves. The ambient music fits the claustrophobic jugnle perfectly but that's not even the best part. The screeching sound of imps, the lound thunks of shooting a crawlers shield-like legs, and the various beeps and boops of the automated turrets all combine to create a truly unique audible experience. Not to mention my personal love for the character's monstrous burps when drinking a potion.
It's amazing how
is able to create a believable world outside of the levels you play in simply through sound and visuals alone. There is no lore given to the player and there is little in the means of story yet the small amount of information the game does tell you allows your mind to fill in the gaps and create your own vision of what it's like in the world of
. I don't even think humans exist in the game due to the main character growling in pain like a wild beast whenever he or she or it is damaged.
When you get down to it
is a great indie shooter that remembers the old while embracing the new. I'm excited to see what developer Terri Vellmann chooses to do next. If you're interested, Vellman and DOSEONE have since created another shooter similar to
called
.

This is a twitchy shooter with an ironic low movement acceleration.
Gameplay loop is boiled down to two actions repeated over and over. Most items are useless. Enemy variety are practically reskins. And the "visual style" causes eye strain for me. Movement
heavy/slow. Bosses are unfairly overwhelming. Sound and music sucked.
Early game: Kite the enemies to pick one by one, snipe sentry batteries, step on worm mines to get damaged for free.
Endgame: Consists of flying garbage rushing you, and now there are sentries that walk towards you and giant ones that shoots explosive missiles and their battery can't be shot, it is turned off by going up to it and pressing "E".
Boss fights happen in a room full of clusterfudge that you can't retreat from. (double door closes behind you and a slowdown sentry holds you in place as soon as you open the next door)
(the level 8 boss I barely saw but looked like the same but with 3 times the enemy density, spammed over twenty bullets everywhere killed everything visible and got safe distance to analyse the situation, during the same second, a Suicide Bomb enemy killed me through the corner of the pillar I was hiding.
Most items are useless, pills lasts the time you get to leave the room where you found it, just carry a Last Will or golden potions (or both with a backpack).
Level design is garbage, just a bunch of preset corridors procedurally mashed together in a straight line, many many dead ends happen in junctions between corridor blocks.
The "artstyle" is just lack of talent and investment, spacial awareness suffers from that, constantly going back and forth making sure I wasn't forgetting anything, levels were tiny enough and previous gates lock behind you so, not much backtrack is possible but navigating is a pain in the behind. Slight eye strain from playing this.
I even stopped using the bank after my third playthrough, and got to the end boss. The first playthrough I died at the second level, getting the hang of the sensitivity and hitboxes. The second time I got to floor 5 and died to a snake mine right outside the start since I defeated the boss first try but lost heath figuring out where to shoot.
So the third time it was a cakewalk, got full coin magnet early on, a backpack and stockpiled 3 golden potions and 26 bullets total, never used anything else just blazed the entire game easy. damage was mostly garbage jumping at me through corners, Snake mines and failing to dodge turrets when the movement is awkward.
At level 7 I got bored and decided to rush in and oh boy, circlestrafing turrets makes them useless, but gets difficult to dodge normal rushing enemies, having quick fingers was not a problem but snake mines chip away health in this playstyle. When I ended up using one of the golden potions I went back to the boring "kiting rushers and poking turret batteries" default playstyle.
The enemy idle sound cues were the only thing design-wise they did right, but most sound effects I can do it myself better by pressing Randomize in BFXR (a free 8-bit sound generator), they all sucked along with the music, it was just background noise made in some trial version talentless wannabe artist, that I even forgot to put in the review and editing this in now.
Every time I got to the next level it "rewarded" me with the most jarring sound effect I ever heard for a level ending.
By the way, it's been 45 minutes since I stopped playing and the eye strain still hurts, I knew it was possible but not this quick and as bad as "Dying Light chromatic aberration" bad.

Although the title might lead one to believe that this game is a joke, this game is definitely worth playing. Once the player gives the game a real chance, it will not disappoint you. In fact, I was pleasantly surprised by the emotional bond I had formed with the characters from the first playthrough. They grew on me, and the player's daughter, Amanda, has an interesting story which gives you a lot of chances to create your personality as a dad, but also to explore the lore of Dream Daddy. Later on in the game, DadBook is introduced, and as the name suggests, it is a lot like FaceBook. The idea was smart, and the game lets you save and load the game any time you want and as much as you want, there are no "checkpoints" or "save stations", which lets you come back to DadBook if you want to re-do a date or  if you want to try to date another dad.
A minor complaint I have with the game is that the minigames you have to play on some dates are hard. Like genuinely hard to pass. Some are really easy and some are really hard. It's nice to vary the difficulty of a minigame, as one isn't equally good at everything, but the problem is that there is no medium difficulty, so you will either complete it in 0.1 seconds or re-do it 10 times.
The story is good and consistent, the characters have good dialogue and they are likeable, which boosts positivity towards the story. Even the less likeable characters have a deeper story than they let on, which makes them interesting and adds complexity to the game.
All in all, I would recommend this game to people who want to play something light, but also with a good story to it. You can spend from 1h to 100 in this game, and you can either play quickly through it to see what the fuss is about or dive deep into every character's background and read everything about them.

First off, disclaimer: I purchased this on itch.io some time ago. Recently the developer announced that he could give Steam keys to those who bought it over there, and thus I got a Steam copy. So I did not receive the original for free, but I did recieve the Steam copy for free.
I promised I'd review this sucker, so I gave it a fair shake tonight, and...mmf.  I actually really want to like this game; it's clear there's a lot of mechanics and depth to this experience, but I just couldn't enjoy it.
It's rough around the edges, to start; and a lot of that roughness cracks right through the middle of core game mechanics.  Some of it is harmless; bad spelling, oddly-alligned visual elements, rough graphics here and there.  Some of it ruins the game, such as the numerous crashes I experienced (accessing crafting, accessing my equipment, and trying to turn on a stove all crashed my game for unguessable reasons), lighting issues (one area I was brought to was entirely pitch black, ruining a run), and beyond.
I tried to work around the problems, but on top of all this bugginess...the game's hard.  You can choose from Normal or Expert difficulty at the start, and I merely chose Normal...  It's a survival-based game, you have food, water, health meters...but everything drains far too quickly right from the bat for you to get a foothold in the game.
Here's my best example: Due to all the complexity, I started by doing the optional multi-part tutorial, but I honestly could not complete it...as my character would die of one stat zeroing out or another before I could!
A combination of difficulty plus bugginess makes this one impenetrable for me.  After about 5 crashes, a 'soft-lock' due to the lighting bug making me blind, and a few game overs from death before I did anything of import...yeah, I had to call it a day.  I'm not the best gamer out there, but I'm hardly the worst; it would take some real effort and luck to actually make progress in this.
Here's hoping it gets better. A less-buggy experience, with the difficulty toned down (at LEAST for the start of the game; meters really shouldn't be so quick to decrease but hard to increase), would make this a lot more interesting to jump into I feel. For all I've said here, there is clearly something fun to be had in this game; the dev has some great ideas. He just really needs to make it all more accessible to the rest of us.

A 90's game in 2016? It's more likely than you think!
"Survive Me Miolhr" is an RPG based game with a zombie theme. When I first played the game, it reminded me a lot of the old 90's Pokémon. Not only does the gameplay remind me of Pokémon, but the main character looks similar to Ash. At first, I had a great nostalgic feeling. However, I was very disappointed when I encountered one of the many bugs in this game. Despite the crashes and bugs, the similarities to Pokémon kept me motivated. I continued to play, and I recommend it even with those errors.
Pros:
Any non-ancient PC can handle the game. If you want to check if you can handle the game, go to
.
Good choice of sound, it is a little repetitive but it does fit the game very well.
Very nice graphics, I love the nostalgic feeling this game gives you.
I appreciate the storyline in this game. The first few hours are a bit confusing, but after this short struggle, it makes sense and is a positive addition.
Motivating achievements, very easy to unlock.
Training mode which gives you a taste of the game and teaches you how to play it.
Awesome developer, who takes suggestions into account.
This game is great for experienced players. It starts out tough, which is nice for a good challenge.
Cons:
The keyboard controls could use some fine-tuning. It would be more user-friendly to have one row of controls, instead of what it is right now.
While I like the sounds overall, there is a barking noise that is irritating. I would prefer if it was removed.
There are several bugs and crashes due to the game still being in Early Access. They are being looked at by the developer and should be fixed by the time it is fully released, so I can forgive this.
The tutorial could provide some more information on certain items, including details about keys.
There are typos in the game and on the store page. A proofreader would be helpful.
The character controls a bit stiffly, and is slower than needed. I would like the movements to be smoother.
Overall experience:
The concept of "Survive Me Miolhr" is good. Its unique flare and compelling story makes it worth playing. It has a lot to improve on, but as an Early Access game, this is to be expected. I recommend giving it a try, either in Early Access or when it is fully developed. Certainly Pokémon lovers would find something in common with it, but it has other appealing elements too.
Rating:
I rate this game 6/10 for its Early Access score. When it has been fixed up, I will bump that number up accordingly!"

First game I'm reviewing on Steam.
My favorite all-time game is Baldur's Gate 2 and I loved Planescape Torment.  I was stoked for this game and backed it when it was first made public.
I am not very happy with what I ended up with.  The ending (in particular) was very poorly done and felt incredibly rushed and disjointed.  A lot of times I felt like the designers challenged themselves to come up with as many outlandish characters and dialogue as they could without worrying about whether things would actually work.  And there was no depth.  The locations presented with shallow with barely any interactivity.
Basically, this is a short, somewhat poorly written illustrated interactive fiction story.
Connections between situations were tenuous and I barely cared about what was happening.  I thought there were some interesting points to the background story but the bit of good material was squandered in a rush to make the situations work.
And, again, the ending.  The ending was a mess.  And the antagonist!  I don't want to spoil anything but it would've worked better if it had stayed silent and menacing.  Instead, I felt like a kid at a cheap magic show:  excited at the idea until the table and poorly made boxes fall apart to reveal the trick.
Not recommended.  The designers felt like they were trying to be too clever in order to replicate PT without any depth or satisfying conclusion.

Disclaimer: I backed the game on Kickstarter and played it on GOG rather than Steam.
The first thing anyone should know about this game is that it is very heavy on text and could almost be thought of as an interactive novel rather than as a game. I've you have never played any games like that (such as Planescape: Torment) I would not reccommend buying this game yet, as the price is quite steep. Wait until you know for sure whether you like this style of game or until the price drops.
With that out of the way, I can say that this game is in my opinion a more than worthy spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment. There are significant differences between both games, but they clearly fall within the same niche subgenre withing RPGs. However, as much as some people seem to have fond memories of Planescape, I never liked it all that much. Its setting and characters did not feel relatable to me. This made it hard for me to care about the story or the world, altough it must be said that some of the characters definitely had their moments.
In comparison, Numenera offers a setting that is an interesting blend of fantasy with science fiction and a bit of post-apocalypse. In many ways, it feels familiar and therefore is often much more relatable. But this familiarity is constantly broken up by strange and mysterious elements, giving the setting the weirdness that also defined Planescape's setting. In my opinion, the better setting also leads to ToN having a better story. In contrast to Planescape, ToN managed to make care about the world, the story and characters and kept me engaged and from beginning to end. I feel this is the most important aspect of any RPG and would therefore greatly reccommend this game. Of course, whether you like a story or not is heavily subjective as it depends entirely on individual preferences, but I had the best time playing an RPG since I played Baldur's Gate.
That being said, the game is not without flaws. Its is relatively short and the combat system feels like an afterthought. Even though this game focusses on story rather than combat, I do feel that combat is essential to any RPG. A better combat system and more content would have greatly improved this game.

Story heavy with lots of options more avoiding combat. The engine itself leaves much to be desired, but the game overall certainly follows in Planescape: Torment's footsteps, IE: lots of text reading.

However, I also didn't keep up with the updates, and looking back at what was promised (and what was delivered) I can definitely understand why people feel frustrated with the game. One companion I was really looking forward to, the Toy, was cut out of the final release. The Ruins of Ossiphagan only appear in a flashback sequence that is entirely text. The "Labyrinth" is more of a two-bedroom house. I only ever opened 3 fathoms and they didn't introduce anything new upon revisiting (though maybe I just didn't explore enough).
What I don't understand are the poor comparisons to PST. It's called a spiritual sequel so it makes sense to draw a comparison, but the things people claim PST did better are not really there at all. Nostalgia is a very powerful thing. Taking on some of the complaints I read in the other reviews:
Now, to discuss the game on it's own:
The setting is gorgeous. I loved the unexplained weirdness of the numenera, and how you'd come across ancient technology that people just shrugged off as everyday. The giant, immobile robots that have been in the same place for thousands of years and are the architects of the entire city? Yeah, that's just my factory boss. The cannibals that live underground? They're just creepy archivists, and sometimes they help the authorities solve crimes.
All the companions are human, which is a shame when you live in a world with people from different planets and even different dimensions. None of them, except for Erritus and Callistege, have anything immediately eyecatching about their characters. But they eventually grew on me, through their interactions with you and each other. Take Aligern, for example. I thought he was a real buzzkill, and needlessly suspicious of Callistege. I only took him with me because I wanted to see the Cult of the Changing God first.
But then I started calling myself the Changing God. Philosophically, I'm not entirely wrong (I have his body, his memories, and his experiences--I might as well have been the Changing God just with amnesia). And it was so fascinating to watch Aligern trying to decide whether or not I actually was the Changing God, and if he could still trust me if I was. THE Changing God, the one famed for being an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and that he blames for the destruction of his village--is suddenly at his side and telling him that she will help in his search for answers. That's when I really started to feel for him, when I wanted the answers just as badly as he did.
Rhin annoyed me at first because she had to go everywhere with me, and couldn't even be temporarily swapped out. This poor kid is getting mauled, shot at, burned, psychically punched, and more, and she still won't wait outside until I'm done with this fight. I had to take her into a hell dimension infested with insane murder cultists (Bad Parenting 101). But through it all she remained so, so sweet. She also gets better mechanically (as a healer and cypher user) and seeing her finally being useful in a fight made me feel like a proud parent.
The game feels way too easy after the first 30 minutes. I rarely had trouble passing any ability checks, especially when I could just have a party member do it instead. By the midpoint of the game, the combination of my accumulated skills, bonuses, and edge made it so I could pass any intelligence check...without expending any effort. That feels like it should be a good thing, but it made the Bloom's challenges trivial. There's a portion of the game where you can get bonuses on checks if you convince your companions to go with you, and I didn't need to take any of them because my bonuses were already so high. I also had thousands of shins that went unspent--you can only buy armor for yourself and upgrade your companions gear once for less than 100 shins.
They took an interesting direction by trying to replace mundane dungeon junk with unique items classified as "Oddities". I definitely feel like that design choice added to the mystique of the game world, but I'm not sure if it worked entirely because some of the descriptions had me wanting to hold on to everything
it would be useful.
I will admit that combat felt more fun in the end game, after I had enough stats and equipment to be able to do what I wanted. Wiping out 4 murdens at once with a powered up Flash was nice. There's just something about it that feels very clunky. Maybe it's the character animations, maybe it's the slight delay after selecting an action, I don't know. I dislike that you can't buff NPC's that are helping you out (aren't they also allies?) and in the early game it feels almost impossible to hit anything without spending all your effort on a single attack. I rarely ever used cyphers--in the early game you're low on shins, and in the late game you can one-shot a lot of things as a nano.
The Tide system is an interesting take on morality meters. Apparently it only affects the game in very subtle ways, so I never really noticed if it had any affect on the game world. Honestly, I'm fine with that. I liked it because I could treat it like a Myers-Briggs type of personality quiz. I still feel like the game is very skewed towards Blue though, especially if you want to piece together what's going on. I tried my best to follow my Idealist path, but in the end there were just so many more opportunities to gain Blue Tide affinity.
On a final note, although inExile is getting some heat from unfulfilled promises, it really felt like they were listening to their backers during development and trying to incorporate their ideas. It might be just a coincidence, but most of the issues I raised when reviewing the beta were addressed in the final version. Nice!

I was a backer of this game. PS:T is one of my favorite game experiences. My emotional attachment to the original is very high. So high in fact that this game inspired me to take up game design and writing as a hobby. Without PS:T I would not be the human being that I am today. When the Kickstarter was announced I never expected the game to recapture what PS:T meant for me during my youth. I just wanted to have another game like this and to reward some of the principal people behind PS:T.
Miraculously Tides of Numenera delivered much more than I expected. The game is great, a worthy successor and one of the most thoughtful cRPGs of this decade (granted, it's not exactly a crowded genre...)
Much like the original Tides of Numenera has a unique and wonderful world where the deeply unsettling coexists harmoniously with the joyfully bizzare. This fantastic world bridges the gap between the impactful short fiction in the form of side-quests and memorable minor characters and the overarching story.
There are a lot of throwbacks to the original, but it rarely feels forced. The writing of this game is very well paced and so polished that you sometimes wish there was a bit more of an individual tone behind it. The writing is consistently great and delivers on all the complex themes it touches upon but could have been improved even further. For example it would have been great if the narrative voice of the descriptions matched up with the players dominating tide.
The gameplay is an improvement over the original. It is cleaner, streamlined in places where it needed to be and more complex in the areas that are the focus of the game and its story, namely its dialogue with the introduction of the Effort and the Tides systems. By forcing you to manage a stat pool for conversational skills the game gives you much more opportunities for roleplaying than similar titles. While the system will probably not blow mind your mind it is a huge step in the right direction and a milestone for the genre.
Character development, while not very complex, also gives you a lot of freedom. You can roleplay a machine-expert and smooth-talking warrior just as well as an intimidating rogue that is tougher than he looks and falls over his feet during his first step into combat. While historically the genre's roleplaying capabilities of minor subspecialization is characteristically weak it is rather well done here.
As an aside, the combat system could be improved, the animation speed is painfully slow and mysteriously non-skippable, but each fight is a meticulously crafted narrative experience that often but not always offer multiple solutions.
While the story shares a lot of thematic and emotional similarities with PS:T the general tone of the narrative is different. PS:T was broody and tragic, Tides of Numenera is cautiously optimistic and embracing. It is technically possible to play PS:T from a different perspective, but the story of the Nameless One and his influence on the world around him implicitly suggests the route of atonement. Tides of Numenera is more open in this regard, thereby allowing the player more agency to define him- or herself. But on the flip-side, this does make the game feel less like a novel and more like a collection of philosophically inspired short stories in the guise of science fantasy.
Unlike PS:T this game does not focus much on the player's party. Here the world is at center stage and your party takes a backseat, which gives you more freedom to express yourself but also limits what to many might have been the essential and outstanding quality of the original. But ultimately both games deal heavily with the human condition and in that sense both are equally rewarding.
Tides of Numenera is a journey to a world very unlike our own but more intimately human than any other game from the recent past that I can remember. This is not a game to rush through. Every hour of gameplay offers material that is rewarding to reflect upon. Enjoying Tides of Numenera is largely a cerebral experience; it lacks some of the heavy tragic punches of its inspiration but makes up for that in streamlined design and a tighter experience. It is one of those rare pieces of art that gets better the more you think about it. If you enjoy fantasy fiction because they are awesome page turners then this is probably not the right game for you, if you on the other hand love fantasy as allegorical tales about the human condition in an otherworldly beautiful veneer then this is the perfect tale.

All I expected it to be. It`s a true spiritual sequel to PS:T; Strange, alien worlds, oddities aplenty that you can take interest in or leave by the side, truly unique and interesting companions and several novels worth of dialogue, both optional and main quest related.
The effort system is quite innovative and well done, if surprisingly easy to game, and the Tides system is, possibly, the best way a game has ever quantified your alignment and how that influences how the world around you reacts to you.
It IS quite a short game for its genre, which many seem to consider a negative, but I would heartily disagree. Tides keeps a very tight narrative focus, which would be impossible for a game of much greater length, and allows for a much easier replay to explore choices not taken the first time. It does not meander endlessly through sidequests, sideplots, base building and what have you; it`s a game about one man/woman, the choices they make, the emotions they feel, and their impact on the world around them, and it is better for that than a thousand epic fantasies of chosen ones and dark forces.
And let us not forget that PS:T itself was quite a short game, and it too was better for it.
A hearty reccomendation for what may well be the best Roleplaying game of 2017.

Purely judged on its merits as a shooter and on gameplay, SO:TL is mediocre. It's a little cumbersome and a touch sluggish, as though your character is tired; the graphics are more than a little last-generation, but it skirts that okay by sticking to environments that are easy to render realistically.
What it lacks in technical perfection, however, it more than makes up for in humanity.
If you haven't figured out by now, SO:TL is a very clever interperetation of Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness", as well as a very biting commentary on shooters in general. It begins as strikingly generic, and then becomes strikingly meta. It's a little hard to describe.
If you enjoy good, well-paced, energizing gameplay that makes you feel like a hero, then maybe skip this one, or wait for it to go on sale.
If you're a fan of literature or psychology and want to try something very distinctly different, grab this right away and pay close attention.

Spec Ops wants very badly to be the thinking man's Gears of War (or Binary Domain), and now you know exactly where I'm going with this review. I can't really talk my way around it, this game lives and dies on its story because everything else it does has been done before, and spoiler alert, the story ain't gonna save it. You and your two gruff, snarky squadmates trek into Dubai after a biblical sandstorm annihilates the city on the lookout for survivors. What you find are rebels and remnants of the US Army regiment sent to aid the populace engaged in an endless shootout, which you of course join. It's third person action with sticky cover, two weapon slots, and thankfully enough guns to give variety to the 6 hours or so (I guess, I think I'm like 2/3 of the way through) of shooting hundreds and hundreds of dudes. Levels are pretty short and fights are pretty challenging on the upper difficulty levels. The graphics are pretty good but it really just looks like a very sandy over-saturated Divide from Fallout: New Vegas to me.
So that's it, it plays like Binary Domain, but with none of the clever characters or entertaining story to prop it up. It's very much Apocalypse Now with an extra dose of "no YOU are the monsters", and honestly that's where the whole thing falls apart for me. I've never liked this trend in shooters to make the player character question the morality of their actions, because that moment of self-doubt always comes after murdering like a hundred other people. The whole thing hinges on clear good guy/bad guy labels to conveniently absolve the player of inconvenient guilt, and it's honestly pretty gross. In Spec Ops you get a few chapters of grizzled "This is ♥♥♥♥ed" as you mow down rebels and fellow US soldiers, and then the thing happens and all of a sudden you're supposed to feel like a REAL murderer. ♥♥♥♥ing really? No game has really pulled this off well; the best example I can think of is Modern Warfare 2 and that was because it came very early in the game and they dialed the atrocity up to 11 for shock factor.
Before THE TWIST it was a mostly unremarkable third person shooter, afterwards it was an unremarkable third person shooter with the albatross of MORAL CHOICE EXCEPT WE MADE IT FOR YOU hanging around its neck. I wanted to see it through in the hopes that the story would eventually redeem itself somehow, but the bland gameplay was the final nail in the coffin. I won't fault anyone who got invested in the story, but I was expecting better.
