In Avenged Sevenfold's (well, really just M. Shadows) break into the gaming medium, we are given Hail to the King: Deathbat.
In HttK: Deathbat you play as a fallen king, Andronikos, hellbent on returning to his throne after the god of evil killed and replaced him with an evil twin.
The story, while laden with dark fantasy tropes and cliche's, is interesting enough, and while I never became bored with it, I don't feel that it is all that memorable.
The main character is supposed to come off as a cool and care-free badass, with cheesy one-liners included, which almost directly conflicts with the story, and makes him completely one-dimensional.
Combat is simple as you only have two attacks; melee and magic, and your magic is based off of whatever your melee weapon happens to be at the time. Melee will be your main form of attack, but each weapon uses the same animations, no matter what style weapon it may be. The animation is fine for a sword, but it looks silly with anything that isn't a sword. It just looks weird when Andronikos is bashing the enemies with the handle side of the scythe. Magic, on the other hand, is ranged and very powerful, especially with some of the later weapons. You can charge the magic to do a more powerful attack, each charge attack is different, and the effects accompanying them are nice. While your magic meter runs out somewhat quickly if you spam the attack, your mana is easily recovered by simply standing near a mana fountain. However, the combat is too simple; each enemy is either affected by hitstun, knockback, or must pause for a moment to line up their attacks, and almost every fight plays out the exact same, no matter what enemy you're fighting: poke the enemy with a melee attack, run a circle, poke, run, poke. This strategy works on most of the bosses as well.
Controls are responsive and simple; they could easily be translated to an NES controller, as you only ever move around and have two buttons to worry about, melee and magic. On that note, you'll want to play with a joystick; I used a 3rd party (Rockcandy by PDP) Xbox 360 controller, as I found mouse and keyboard controls to be clunky, because all movement is assigned to WASD. There is the option to change the movement to different keys, but a point and click option similar to Diablo (which this game tries model itself after) would be nice. However, with a joystick, you have no menu control. You can pause the game, but you're still required to use a mouse to navigate the menus or use your equipped potion or item. I played on a touch screen monitor, so this wasn't as big of an issue for me, but it's still annoying and wasteful to drop one hand off the controller to do anything. You can switch melee weapons mid-fight, but you need to click on the icon with a mouse to do so, as there is no way to map these options to a joystick. It would be nice to have this option assigned to a face button, or even SELECT/BACK. But you won't want to use a keyboard as the game plays so much smoother with a joystick. It's an annoying and detrimental Catch 22.
The art style and graphics are well-done, but the Avenged Sevenfold logo of the Deathbat is EVERYWHERE. I know this is their game and all, but it's just too much. However, each level design is different, unique, and very well paced. All the levels with the exception of the starting area and world hub are based off of a song, and that song has been remixed to fit a neo-classical Castlevania style. More on that in a bit. There's plenty to find and do in each level, and while veteran adventure gamers won't find any of this to be completely new, I always wanted to explore every bit of it to find the games many different collectibles. But there are some parts where your path is obscured because of the environment, and these areas are very frustrating if there happens to be an enemy hiding where you can see. I hardly felt like my deaths were unfair or cheap while fighting an enemy, but a few of the many traps and obstacles contained within each level did. (I'm looking at you, falling rocks and rolling spike barrels.)
The soundtrack is very solid, but those who aren't a fan of Avenged Sevenfold's music probably won't find much to enjoy. Every level theme is a remix of one of A7x's songs, many to the point that it's almost a new song entirely. As I mentioned earlier, the songs are redone to fit a game, and they're done very well. They never become annoying or repetitive, and are almost nostalgic for those who enjoyed Castlevania. That being said, the music for the level bosses is whatever song the level is themed after, minus the vocals. The level bosses always have a little introduction with The Wicked End's interlude and bridge, followed by the level's theme for the fight. The mini-bosses are where I ran into a problem. The music behind every miniboss fight is always Unholy Confessions, and while I enjoy the song on its own, it quickly became repetitive the more I played, as every level has at least two mini-bosses.
Enemies and bosses are plentiful, and there are unique mobs for every level, which make for a good variety of things to fight. Each enemy and each level lasts just long enough to enjoy, without ever feeling like they've overstayed their welcome. While the strategy to fight them never varies much, they're still enjoyable thanks to the different way each of them attacks. Once you learn the pattern though, each fight plays out the same way I mentioned above: poke, run, poke, and run. I didn't notice much variety to the mini-bosses, as it seems there are only two varieties: One that summons a bunch of adds and attacks directly, or one that puts up a shield, summons a bunch of adds you must defeat to lower the shield, and then attacks directly. You'll know when you find a mini-boss area, too. It's always in a large, empyty clearing that you can't walk out of once you enter, thanks to a barrier that erects behind you as you enter. Fortunately, each level boss is challenging and very unique, and each one must be fought in a new way.
I hardly encountered any glitches or hiccups, except for one almost game-breaking glitch during the level, Babylon. I exited the game mid-fight against the first mini boss to return to The Crypt to buy some health potions, and upon my return found that the barrier that erects for each mini-boss fight had not disappered. I could not re-enter the arena to fight the mini-boss, therefore could not complete the level. I tried exiting and re-entering the game multiple times, and eventually had to lose all of the lives I had so the level would reset, and I could continue.
All in all, for a game ported from a mobile platform to play on PC, Hail to the King: Deathbat is a decent first game from Avenged Sevenfold. Avenged sevenfold fans will enjoy the soundtrack and art, and adventure fans will enjoy the gameplay. I can honestly say I'd buy a sequel if they were to ever make one. It gets a solid 6.5-7/10, and if the above issues with the controls, environment, and combat were addressed, the game would easily be an 8/10. Being a fan of Avenged Sevenfold will make or break the experince, but if you're indifferent about the band behind it, this could be a good budget adventure game for you.

This game is good, but needs to be reviewed objectively from two sides.
As a fan of A7X: The game is great. It's all about atmosphere, there are several references to the band that a seasoned fan understands, and even though the game play is linear its still easy to understand and the over all vibe makes up for it. It was on sale when I got it for for a buck ninety-seven, so very worth it.
As a casual gamer, there several things wrong with the game; the gameplay is linear and the combat gets repetitive, there could be much more variety for the "RPG" it's passed off as, and the story is decent but pretty generic.
Aside from combat being repetitive, it is often very difficult too. I've heard several interviews, and have the understanding that the game is supposed to be as hard as a classic dungeon crawlers, and it is, but the combat is fundementally broken. The magic, for example, has no reticle and I hardly hit anything. There are a couple good weapons to start with but there's no heavy RPG elements, like armour or character customization that make the game dynamic and replayable.
On the good side, I love the games atmosphere, it's everything I could ever want in a fantasy game. If you are a fan of Divine mythology type stuff, it's perfect. I also spent a lot of time on the mobile version, and I can safely say that this version is miles better, because of things like the character weapons being purchasable without real money, and dynamics of using a PC. So if you're not an A7X fan, but you like a dark, divine type of fantasy dungeon crawler, AND it's on sale for dirt cheap, buy it.

The graphics for this game are fine and I actually like them. However the graphics are hindered significantly by a cluttered HUD (Heads-up Display) and side menus that just take up the whole screen. It’s to the point where the user cannot even see the graphics, let alone enjoy them.
The sound is decent, it’s nothing special. The only issue I really had with the sound is that there was this an annoying barking noise that seemed to be part of the soundtrack and it only served to irritate me to the highest degree.
The gameplay is the weakest part of this game. It’s absolutely horrendous and atrocious to put it mildly. Basically, the game throws a storyline and gameplay information at you that is so hard to make sense of. It tries to stuff two hours of plot and gameplay tutorials into two minutes and it just does not work.
•	The graphics are really cool and brought back nostalgia of Pokemon HeartGold and SoulSilver on the Nintendo DS.
•	The soundtrack isn’t too bad apart from the barking noise I described earlier.
•	The story has a lot of potential.
•	The screen is too cluttered by text and menus.
•	The barking noise is extremely annoying.
•	The gameplay is near non-existent because it’s so hard to understand.
This game is a disaster, just don’t even mess with it right now. However, in fairness, it is in Early Access and is self-admitting when it comes to the fact that it is far from a complete product. It has a ton of potential, it’s just up to the Developers on whether they want to make a proper foundation for that potential to flourish and blossom. As of right now, that potential is not being utilized properly.

I don't do speed runs, I don't ignore side quests yet the first run through took only thirteen hours to complete this game. (I have no wish for a 2nd run through)  I'd like to say this was down to my brilliant RPG skills cutting through the Gordian Knot but given it took me 23 hours to complete Tyranny (not known for it's length); no, this game is short and I'm feeling short changed.
I'd make some combat about how weak the combat system was, but I really didn't see enough of it to be qualified to comment.  I think I had a grand total of 5 fights (or crisis) all game, what little I saw did not impress me.  In most RPG's you see more fights before getting out of the tutorial.  All that really sticks in my mind was how slow it was, if there was an option to speed up the enemy animation I didn't find it, those few fights I did have really dragged.
Without combat, what was there?  Puzzles?  What was there was so simple I'm not sure they were meant to be a puzzle or not.  The game was mostly running back and forth, clicking on NPC's and ploughing through the turgid dialogue.  I think the writers used every word in the dictionary except brevity, very little of it was useful to completing the plot.  At no point did I need to engage my brain in this game.  Humour?  Nope.  I got more laughs from watching Clockwork Orange.
The real killer though wasn't it only took 13 hours to complete.  No, the clincher is; at no point in those 13 hours do I remember enjoying the game.

What can change the reception of a game?
In my mind the game here falls short of its predecessor. That is not to say it is unworthy of your time, which is why it gets a thumbs up. Merely that it does not reach the heights of PS:T.
The writing is quite good, but weirdly truncated and towards the end it certainly feels like the narrative was abruptly cut-off. No doubt victim to real life realities of a project for which we can only speculate the reasons. Its ending is perfunctory and cauterised and all the elements which were being woven together abruptly resolve. Surely another longer closing act was needed to bed down all the story elements and really deliver the pay-off it had been building.
On the writing as well, I believe the story seemed to suffer from the "mystery" of the setting. With a sort of pick and mix approach to differing magics and technology. There was no consistency or explanation of much of anything. Everything you come across is a new and wonderous technology from a far-forgotten age. All of them apparently from different ones. Which in some ways begins to dampen your excitement as you realise you will never be able to put any sort of coherent lore in your head. Whilst i understand that this is the whole point of the setting, I think that it could have been reduced somewhat by the writers if they though
It's full screen narrative sections are beautiful and feel wondrous, Giving the sensation of being a handcrafted tabletop experience and the outcomes of which certainly seemed to have quite a bit of depth (Though minimal impact outside of them usually)
The companions, whilst interesting also seem to lack any real input on alot of what's going on. Only ever interjecting (from memory) on main plot moments or there own set PLOT MOMENTS. Whilst I did develop a soft spot for them, i felt there was little opportunity to demonstrate it. The opening section of the game sets up the idea that your companions will have disagreements and there will be consequences and though notably all of the banter in the game is usually the companions sniping at each other (very little friendliness), there is rarely an opportunity to interject or any real consequences for the group dynamic.
Finally, the inventory items were a great opportunity that seemd to fall flat. You get all these marvellous oddities which just scream to be used in quests or interactions but never have the opportunity to do so. I kept most of my items in order to find if any items could be used in obscure ways. But I was only ever able to do so on one occassion where I didn't pick the item up right next to its point of use. - For a game with a supposed emphasis on reactivity and conversations , I feel like this would have been an excellent opportunity to reward players who kept certain items because they liked them, because as I said all the items seem cool and interesting and are just BEGGING to be used. Of course this sort of reactivity takes time and as I said earlier it does seem like they ran out of it on even finishing the main storyline.
A flawed game but an interesting one.
If there is anything I have learned in my gaming across the platforms, it is that many things can change the calibre of a game.

What does one promise matter? Deception.
A tragic tale of modern CRPG where all the dreams about a true successor of the greatest CRPG of all time shattered like broken glass. Torment: Tides of Numenera has everything going for it to be the definitive modern CRPG to remind people that this genre doesn't lack behemoths. And what a disappointment it is, 4 years in development, having collaboration from Mask of the Betrayer's original designers, PS:T's Colin McComb and Chris Avellone, over 4 million dollars funded on Kickstarter, comes a video game proved that inXile Entertainment forgot what made PS:T a true masterpiece.
For a game that boasted itself as "having more words than Bible", T:ToN surprisingly has very few memorable moments and characters, its writing relies on unnecessarily long and flowery descriptions that seems to try too hard to shout "look at me, appreciate all these Pulitzer-inspired writing prompts" to readers. There's no fault in bringing a lot of text in CRPG, because it's one of the definitive features of the genre, but the problem is T:ToN has very few interesting things to say, and one thing won't get more interesting no matter how you keep describing it. It's a wordy game for the sake of being wordy, it sometimes feels like a very long pretentious short book that was made for people who don't have a huge vocabulary. As someone whose native language isn't English, I can read the translated version of Witcher saga from Andrej Sapkowski which has arguably equal amount of vocab but way more comprehensive than T:ToN.
You have a lot of questions, NPCs have a lot of answers and descriptions, but only a few of them is worth listening to. The story itself doesn't have any real climax or tension, one plot twist revealed near the end of act 2 is way too predictable, none of the companions is memorable or relatable in any mean except Shin, and the story only gets somewhat interesting when you reach The Bloom. It's 2017 and we're comparing role-playing games through words count? Why is the successor of Planescape: Torment is more boring, forgettable and lack any suspense when compared to Tyranny - a side project from Obsidian? Morte blew all of the companions in this game out of the water which is incredibly stupid because important character arcs is the trend of writing in modern video game yet T:ToN failed short in it. It's too proud of its pretentous messages and forgot that there are confusing readers being left behind in its mess of a narrative, a dumbfounded hollow of writing in CRPG that missed all the marks, lacked any emotion and didn't give us anything worth remembering.
Everything else about Torment: Tides of Numenera screams lack of professional game design. The UI is stupidly designed, NPCs don't have portraits (yet several important ones have it in battles?), available portraits span from terrible to horrible, crisis has a decent concept yet in reality, is tedious because inXile has no idea how to make compelling combat sections, so they throw roaming/respawning/a huge number of enemies into your way as obstacle. Effort mechanic leans to Intellect skill checks too much, there's no reason not to play Nano unless you tend to fight your way (which is not a great idea since all battles in this game are crap) or you want to cripple yourself. The Tides' impact is incredibly hard to notice. The Cyphers span from being completely useless to overpowered. Mark Morgan's 50-track OST doesn't have any remotely memorable tune. The Meres get old quick with more and more overexposition.
Torment: Tides of Numenera was supposed to be the "dream game" for CRPG followers, instead, it's a game where hipsters try to pluck through the narrative then come back and ♥♥♥♥♥ slap people "because you don't like reading in video games". T:ToN is a badly made video game and a mediocre book with millions of unheard words that better stayed silent.

I was an early backer for this game after hearing about it in conjuction with the Numenera tabletop RPG, and I have to say it lived up to its expectations well. The story is very solid with lots of decision points and tidbits to uncover.

I was not a backer of Torment: Tides of Numenera, however I am a great fan of original Planescape: Torment and text-heavy RPGs. I waited for TTOM (I'll use this abbreviation) for a long, long time and it is one of the worst disappointments I have ever faced in gaming.
So now, dear friend, let me shortly summarize how incompetent InXile was while creating this mess.
1) Writing. Many people here complain on terrible combat (that's true) or broken promises (that's true), or at best complain on awful companions (also true) but whitewashing the writing of this game. As I have written above, I am a fan of original Torment and text-heavy RPGs in general. But if TTOM is what devs nowadays understand as "deep, high quality writing" then I'd prefer to play hack n slash, because surviving the writing style of this game was... torment.
Planescape: Torment had a lot of wonderfully written, moving, wise, meaningful text. Torment: Tides of Numenera looked at this and the only thing it understood is "a lot of ANY text is good". The final result: the game is filled to the brim with verbose, overdescriptive, exhausting, pretentious, and worst of all - completely redundant, meaningless, non-engaging writing. TTOM is proud of describing the most trivial **** in the most bloated, pseudo-intellectual way possible, and breaking rules of "show, don't tell" in every way. And trust me - I read a lot of books, so I'm not averse to a lot of reading - I simply hate meaningless writing which confuses quantity with quality.
Maybe I would be less angry on writing in TTOM if next to this nonsense it actually bothered to be emotional in some aspects. But it has completely failed to move my heart and soul. In this game you will get 100 000 words describing how characters look, yet very very few words which even attempt to make you feel what those characters feel.
2) Story.
Another catastrophic failure, on a level completely separate from the horrible writing style.
Planescape: Torment had story which was simultaneously personal, moving, emotional, philosophical and coherent.
In this game, you spend 90% of it to "find x to get information on artifact y", waiting for hours for your questions to be answered - for some kind of reveal - only for this reveal to be super disappointing. Within first 15 minutes of  the game, you ask yourselves a lot of plot questions ("What is Sorrow" etc) - none of them are really answered in a ridiculously rushed, chaotic mess of an ending. Main story of TTOM is hilariously desperate to be "philosophical" but it doesn't have anything genuine to say, so it indulges into pseudo-intellectual babble about Tides, while failing to build empathy towards any of its characters.
3) Companions and characters
InXile originally promised us 9 party companions, then delivered only 6 while saying "we needed to cut out those three to make remaining ones really good". I have no idea how bad those characters were before, then, because the final result is party of completely bland, uninteresting NPCs you don't give a **** about... with one exception - hilariously, that exceptional character was written by an outsider "guest" writer, not devs themselves. Other than this one character, I failed to care about anybody in TTOM universe, including main character.
4) Nonlinearity, morality and endings
My character was follower of compassionate, Golden Tide, so he got two extra lines of description on one of the static, ugly ending slides.
5) Difficulty level
I don't really wanna to indulge in mechanics of this game here, let me just say that it is so "brilliantly" balanced and designed that after first few hours you will be capable of passing almost every single skill check with 100% success rate - at least that's how it worked for me, although I am not alone and others had similar problem. No tension or difficulty at all.
6) Awful combat
Combat mechanics in TTOM are quite probably the worst I have ever experienced in any RPG, with the possible exception of Arcanum. Combat here is rare, but when it happens it is incredibly slow, bugged, frustrating, non-strategic mess. Encounters you face are absurdly designed - for example, the moment you begin combat your enemy insta-kills your weakest character and cripples three other party members. Generally 90% of enemies you face have higher initiative than your party, so good luck with strategy when everybody you encounter jumps on you from all sides.
7) Nonexistant soundtrack
I can't honestly say TTOM's music was "bad" because I have barely heard anything of it over the course of game. For some reason 90% of it is quiet, bland ambient.
8) Broken promises
InXile has promised us: few more locations (especially Oasis M'Ra Jolios and Ruins of Ossiphagan), three more companions, crafting, player's stronghold, lacunae, separate Labyrinth mechanics, dozens of Focuses and many other things. It not only failed to deliver them, it failed to inform us of them.
So, that's my opinion on Torment: Tides of Numenera.
Enjoyed it but wanted more.

As others have said, "Meh" is kind of what this game left me feeling. The overarching story is decent, but the entire package didn't work. I would recommend solely for the story, which is interesting and takes place in an interesting world.
Game length - Kind of short for this style of game. I would have liked perhaps a side quest or two for each companion, and at least one more story arc. Overall there are basically 3 open maps to explore, locked from one another. In a single playthrough of Wasteland 2, I had 5x the playtime.
Camera - Locked in viewing angle makes precise movement very difficult/impossible in some areas, especially during combat. You had a great system in Wasteland 2, why change it?
Replayability - Very few options impact the greater story, only minor plotlines and the end-of-game summary slides. I can tell they put alot of effort in this, but they seemed to lose the forest for the trees. I will say it definitely makes your experience "technically" unique, but not disguisably so.

The most important question, apart from expectations set or disappointments given, is:
Is it a good game? Is this worth playing?
Yes. It is both of those. Regardless of what was envisioned, but not delivered; was promised, but then changed; sounded cool, but didn't work out; was underdeveloped, over-cooked or simply not to ones liking.
For what it went out to do (succeed Planescape: Torment), it is not only as close as we can get to it today, but a very good game, indeed. It has, however, inherited the very same problems:
It is a complete game, but has unfinished parts.
The combat is atrocious, maybe even worse than the original.
The alignment system doesn't always result in what you would reasonably expect.
The story can be highfalutin and narcissistic at times. (It's very good, overall, though.)
Recommended for anyone waiting a long time for anything like Planescape: Torment.

What is there to say about Undertale that hasn't been said a thousand times already?
Spot-on gameplay, engaging story, absolutely lovable characters, and an atmosphere of coziness that I haven't felt in any single other game. Sure there are better games, games with more refined mechanics, bigger games, games that consume you whole for weeks or months - but none of them,
, gave such a warm, fuzzy feeling, that this game does.
What really differentiates this game, however, is that, in this game, the way you play it matters. Not in the way of multiple options for reaching your goal, not in the way of having influential choices - although this is all true for Undertale. No, this has been done many times, but in Undertale it
matters. It's not just about replayability - the way you play Undertale, and whether you replay it at all or not, says something about you as a person.
My second playthrough was a Genocide run. I regret completing it. But it was my choice. My morbid curiosity. I accept it. This game makes you think of your choices differently, instead of simply providing branching content. That is truly unique about Undertale.
Will I play Undertale again? Never, probably. Will I advice you to play it? Hell, I wish I could
you play it, because you must. It's a once in a lifetime experience. A masterpiece.

Spec Ops wants very badly to be the thinking man's Gears of War (or Binary Domain), and now you know exactly where I'm going with this review. I can't really talk my way around it, this game lives and dies on its story because everything else it does has been done before, and spoiler alert, the story ain't gonna save it. You and your two gruff, snarky squadmates trek into Dubai after a biblical sandstorm annihilates the city on the lookout for survivors. What you find are rebels and remnants of the US Army regiment sent to aid the populace engaged in an endless shootout, which you of course join. It's third person action with sticky cover, two weapon slots, and thankfully enough guns to give variety to the 6 hours or so (I guess, I think I'm like 2/3 of the way through) of shooting hundreds and hundreds of dudes. Levels are pretty short and fights are pretty challenging on the upper difficulty levels. The graphics are pretty good but it really just looks like a very sandy over-saturated Divide from Fallout: New Vegas to me.
So that's it, it plays like Binary Domain, but with none of the clever characters or entertaining story to prop it up. It's very much Apocalypse Now with an extra dose of "no YOU are the monsters", and honestly that's where the whole thing falls apart for me. I've never liked this trend in shooters to make the player character question the morality of their actions, because that moment of self-doubt always comes after murdering like a hundred other people. The whole thing hinges on clear good guy/bad guy labels to conveniently absolve the player of inconvenient guilt, and it's honestly pretty gross. In Spec Ops you get a few chapters of grizzled "This is ♥♥♥♥ed" as you mow down rebels and fellow US soldiers, and then the thing happens and all of a sudden you're supposed to feel like a REAL murderer. ♥♥♥♥ing really? No game has really pulled this off well; the best example I can think of is Modern Warfare 2 and that was because it came very early in the game and they dialed the atrocity up to 11 for shock factor.
Before THE TWIST it was a mostly unremarkable third person shooter, afterwards it was an unremarkable third person shooter with the albatross of MORAL CHOICE EXCEPT WE MADE IT FOR YOU hanging around its neck. I wanted to see it through in the hopes that the story would eventually redeem itself somehow, but the bland gameplay was the final nail in the coffin. I won't fault anyone who got invested in the story, but I was expecting better.

If you like Avenged Sevenfold, get this game.
However, if you don't like unforgiving and challenging dungeon crawlers, I'd avoid this, even if you like their music. I won't bother going into the story of how this game was made, but it draws inspiration from such games as Legend of Zelda and Diablo. If you enjoyed those games, you will like this one. If you are a casual gamer, there's not much here for you besides the music. But I'll get to that.
The story has been called "generic" in reviews I have read, and I can see where those complaints come from, yet I did enjoy it myself.
The gameplay is not amazing for a PC game, but it was initially a mobile game, and from my experience I have no idea how anyone would play this on a mobile device. It requires too much precision that would be difficult to get on a small or even medium device. But, gameplay is smooth on its PC port, and it's easy to control.
The port itself is not what most people look for in a good port, but it did surprise me in some ways. First, it has no graphics options menu. In my opinion, though, I don't think it needs one. I could most likely play it smoothly on my old Windows XP with little incident. It does not try to be hi-def or realistic. You play as ♥♥♥♥ing deathbat, it's not going to be realistic. But it has the graphical style of some of the games it draws inspiration from, which is actually really well done. Second, it runs well. It does not feel like they rushed the port to make a deadline, because it is well optimized. Third, the options menu it does have is extremely extensive...for one thing. Controls. You can fully rebind the entire set, to anything you like, and you can bind a set of controls for a gamepad. All included. Granted, there aren't many controls for the game on its own, so this may not come as a surprise to many, but I was impressed by it.
Now, more about gameplay. The map allows the travelling to several different areas (All named after A7X songs, which is awesome) that include different visuals and music, as well as music related to the theme of the area. Each level includes several boss fights, and each boss has a different fighting style and attack patterns that you will need to get used to in order to kill. It's obvious much time was put into this, although not enough to make it a triple-A title.
The Rev also makes several appearances, which are amazing.
Okay, so if you want my final opinion, this game is amazing. The music is amazing. Everything about it is great. I have some small problems with some areas, like how some boss patterns are hard to avoid and some are hard to find out how to kill, but these all add to the overall difficulty of the game, and that tends to be a good thing. I haven't found any glitches or bugs that break the game, and I enjoy seeing that for once as well. In the end, I'd buy it again.
Just not for a phone. Don't do that.

First of all, if you are looking for a rally sim, this game is not for you. I really wonder why Kylotonn Racing Games says that this game is a simulator, because it's not. Not even close, to be honest. And it's not a bad thing. Not for me, at least. Of course that it's a very negative aspect of the game, given the fact that the fans were waiting for an officially-licensed WRC simulator for ages. Unfortunately, they will need to wait a bit more. Even if it's not realistic, playing it is quite enjoyable: it makes you feel like a professional rally driver, nailing all the corners and flying through the straights. It's one of the most rewarding feelings while playing a rally game, of course. And you do not even need to practice a lot to be able to reach that level of "skill", which makes it suitable for rally lovers without too much spare time. And, even if pretty easy, nailing the stages is rewarding. Just like it would be at a simulator, but effortlessly.
"Why are all the reviews negative, then?". That's something worth questioning. And it's clearly noticeable after 30 minutes into it: it's a massive step back from WRC 4, graphically, content-wise and physically. And it wasn't even a great rally game back in the days, because Milestone (old developer) wasn't able to leave the comfort zone and make something different. From WRC "1" (2010) to WRC 4 (2013), nothing changed at all, with a few exceptions (career mode was slightly improved after WRC 3, bringing classic cars and new categories). Anyway, small changes end up equalling to nothing. Mostly when pretty much everything looks the same. This is exactly why Kylotonn ended up holding the license, with a simple mission: develop the best WRC game ever made. I don't even need to mention that they failed miserably.
WRC 5 is not bad. It's far away from it. The negative results are simply the reflex of disappointing the WRC fans. They were expecting a simulator, with great graphics, close to real-life stages, realistic engine sounds, convincing physics and top-notch content overall. What they got, though, was "more of the same": the only thing that they could consider as new were the updated cars, drivers and stages. Everything else, from gameplay to career mode, was the same. Nothing innovative, nothing exceptional. Just the usual. How could they expect their fans to react nicely?
The cars are considerably beautiful (given the limitations), and so are the stages. It's really fun to drive fast through every country, nailing every single piece of it and feeling like the ultimate king of WRC. It's more than fun, honestly. It's amazing. That's where WRC 5 shines. The career mode is great, extremely immersive and rewarding but kinda empty at the same time. Maybe because it's exactly like every single career mode that the franchise had before. Innovations could and would be great. Why not to make something different like character customization, press conferences, etc...? Is it that hard to do? I don't think so. Kylotonn had to dig deeper and bring something jaw-dropping, but they decided to not take any risks and brought something that the players were used to. It's an arrow in the knee, considering that career mode is usually what most of the players are looking for (and multiplayer, of course).
If you are a huge fan of the onboard cam, this game is going to disappoint you a little bit. It felt just like being shot from behind when I took the Lancer Evolution X to a ride through Mexico and noticed something quite unusual about the interior: believe it or not, it was the Impreza's. Yes, a Mitsubishi with a Subaru interior. This evidences how much research were done in order to bring the best WRC experience that you could ever ask for.
There are lots of positive aspects, though. The cars have different liveries for each and every rally, with the respective logo (ADAC, RACC, Neste Oil Finland, etc). It's a small detail that makes a lot of difference. DiRT Rally, on the other hand, has the same sticker for each and every stage. Would be even better if it was actually an innovation, but the old Milestone titles had it as well. Same for the custom name on the window (which is incredibly immersive and extremely cool, and I am glad that Kylotonn "copied" this). Two little details that end up counting a lot.
Regarding wheel support, this game is a joke. The actual list of supported wheels has less than 7 different models if I am not wrong. It's unacceptable for a 2015 game, and the devs promised a fix one year ago. Nothing yet. Continuous support is really important if you actually want your game to be popular and loved by the players.
If you are just a casual looking for fun, dust and high speeds, this game is definitely worth a try. Do not pay full-price for it, though. Kylotonn is asking way too much for what the game actually offers. Wait for a sale and then buy it, download it and play it. If you are a rally lover like me, you are going to enjoy this game a lot (as long as you do not expect it to be a simulator, and also ignore the negative aspects).

At first glance, Mad Max is a fantastic open-world adventure teeming with things to do. The excitement can give way to boredom because the short story can’t hide the required grind to advance. Still, there is a plethora of different dusty environments and strongholds / outposts, while the detailed landscape is full of things to do and discover.
Total size on my hard drive: 32.8 GB
++ Optimization is stunning. One of the best optimized games of the past year or two.
+ Graphics are great. Light, dust, haze is a great icing on a highly detailed cake.  Clouds look a little low-res at times, but the skybox looks fantastic in general (if you like sunsets / sunrises, there are some great screenshot opportunities).
+ Punchy sound design. Explosions have great impact.
+ Great story - gritty and grim - but it’s short. Do yourself a favor and complete the Wasteland side-missions in addition to the main campaign. You’ll get to know the factions a bit better and the game feels more complete.
+ The wasteland is wonderfully detailed. Rocks, caves, forts, pumping stations, strongholds, outposts – even though it is a dusty wasteland, there is plenty of visual variety.
+ Customizing the car. From the body style, to the suspension, engine, armor, and more, you can really make the car you want to play the way you want.
+ All the unfinished missions and quests return after finishing the main story campaign so you can take your time, explore the wasteland, and 100% the game if you want.
+/- The hand-to-hand combat is a riff on the Batman Arkham combat system with fancy finishers but without gadgets. It works well enough, but nothing outstanding about it.  (If keyboard & mouse is your preference, be sure to have a 3-button mouse.)
+/- The game is a grind for scrap, which is used for much-needed upgrades. If you hate grinding, walk away. If you enjoy exploration and looting, then Mad Max is an amazing experience.
+/- Child slavery content warning. There isn’t much, but it is there.
- Checkpoint saving is the primary method of storing progress. Awkward in a sandbox game. You can save the game from the menu, but it does not hard-save the last checkpoint; it saves Max to the nearest fast-travel location. Not very useful.
- Driving mechanics are sub-par; floaty and imprecise, the smallest bump can send the car flying, leaving Max facing the wrong way in seconds as the enemy speeds off into the distance. Not good in a game that focuses so much on driving. The Gastown race almost made me rage-quit the game.
- Enemies are endlessly re-used.
- Grinding is required. Upgrades are sometimes hidden behind completely clearing a region of threats.
- Glitchy menus. Hitting Escape to view a new log entry would frequently result in seeing the menu headings, but no images or text. Switching to another menu then switching back would usually fix the issue.
- Messed up mission progression. Need to build the “Jack”, a special class of car referred to as an Archangel. Well, the next part of the mission wouldn’t trigger, no matter what I did. Checked online. As it happens, I had parts on the car that were a level HIGHER than what was required to progress. First and foremost, DDADDS is absolutely hilarious. I don't think I've ever played/read something that has made me laugh as hard and as frequently as Dream Daddy has. The dialogue is wonderfully ludicrous, and witty, with so many puns, it'll make your head spin, not to mention the ridiculous made up shows and double entendre.
That being said, I have quite a few issues with DDADDS; mainly the advertising for it. Number one, it says a dad dating simulator, but in all honesty, it's really not. Most of the time, you're spending time with a Dad, not calling it a date, having one or two lines of internal dialogue that goes something along the lines of -- "Oh no, he's hawwwwt!!!! Wait! Don't think that!!", a quick "romantic", "heartfelt" moment, and then, suddenly, you're at Amanda's graduation party, and the game's over. There's really no dating involved. Most of the "dates" are pure happenstance, because most of the time, the dads need you to do something for them; whether it's chaperoning a dance or a trip to the aquarium, or watching a game that a dad is coaching. There's no romantic undertones either, save for an awkwardly inserted comment about their physical attractiveness, and no tension. It's just two hangouts, and then one more hangout, with a wham, bam, thank you, Pam, and boom, you're "dating" them....I guess. I don't know...I was just thoroughly disappointed, because this didn't FEEL like a dating game. It just felt like the writers spent more time trying to make it as funny and meta as possible with a very thin plot thrown in.
My second problem with the advertising, is that it was being sold as this warm, heartfelt game, and honestly? It really wasn't. Again, it focused much more on being funny and quirky than it did on character development and actual feelings. Your relationship with Amanda was the most fleshed out relationship, which makes sense, since she's your daughter, but all of your romantic prospects are really kind of bland in terms of relationships. None of the men really seem to break out of their stereotypes, and if they do, it's SO cliché and overt, that it's kind of terrible.
And the sweet, heartfelt moments last a paragraph or two tops. Really. They finally address the "problem" with your love interest, and when things get interesting, they immediately cut it off and it's just so frustrating. Another problem I had with the relationships is the relationship your Dadsona was in before he came to the other side of Maple Bay. Your partner is mentioned in the very beginning of the game, which you reflect on them for a very brief moment, and then again in the middle, where we start to get a little bit of a backstory about them, but, then it's cut too short again, and we're left with nothing. How long ago did they pass? How do we feel about it? Are we even ready to date again? I'd really like to know more about that, and I was angry that we didn't get to know more. And Amanda doesn't seem to be affected by their death much, either. She gets sad when they're mentioned, but that's it. How does she feel about Dadsona dating again? In the game, she seems fine with it, but I feel like, realistically, it should bother her in a way, since one of her parents died, but whatever.
Speaking of Amanda, this might be nit-picky, but toward the end of the game, she reveals that she got into a fight/betrayal thing with her two best friends and she was extremely upset about it. Her friends seemed to be cruel to her for absolutely no reason, and then, suddenly, they're back to being friends again at Amanda's graduation. Why? How? It just threw me for a loop, I guess. If you're going to include a conflict like that into the game, and then resolve it, give us a reason for how it was resolved!!
Finally, the CGs. You get one CG per Dad, and honestly, they're not even CGs really pertaining to the game, they're just little photographs. What bothered me about this, is that they're all in varying art forms, which is extremely distracting. Not to mention that, in a project such as this, they couldn't swing to get more than one CG per Dad? Really? I've seen FREE visual novels with more routes come out with seven or eight CGs per character, instead of just one. And yes, I understand CGs would be hard to do with a customizable dad, but honestly, Magical Diary did it, so why can't DDADDS?
In the end, I wish there was a "Meh" button, because that's how I feel. I'll recommend this game only because it's hilarious, and despite how much I ragged on the dads, I will always love Damien from the bottom of my heart

Overall, I really enjoyed this game. The art had a consistent style which I sometimes find is an issue in dating simulators. Great diversity in the dads that you can date, which is more than I can say for other dating sims of late. I enjoyed the music and found it to be simple but not too repetitive. I was disappointed that some of the dads reject you in the end of their route, but it's understandable, and my disappointment is not a criticism. The stories were original and cute, and the jokes were honestly hilarious most of the time. One thing that I found tedious is that every time one plays a new dad, the story with Amanda stays the same, so I found myself mashing the space bar through the common dialogue. I understand why it isn't changed from dad to dad, as each route isn't separate from the others, and one can date every dad before choosing their 'Dream Daddy' for the third date, but for people who want to 100% the game it's really boring. Another thing that I didn't like is how short the game was. I'm disappointed that the relationship with each dad isn't expanded upon, and each story seems a little stunted. In my opinion, there should be more dates for each dad, as the player doesn't get to really experience each storyline with the limited 'three date' system. In comparison to other games in the genre, this game is very short, and I would like to have played it for longer than I did. I didn't feel it got the story across in the time allotted. All in all, I really enjoyed the game and it's unique, if not campy, concept. I wish I could have played more of it, but the time I spent inside the games universe was well worth it. If a sequel was to be made, I would certainly buy it.

Well worth the money if you like old-style RPGs and pulp sci-fi novels. If you're some kind of game-mechanics-production connoisseur, then maybe it ain't. I'm the first sort.
Upsides: I liked the story and the idea of the main character, and how the character interacts with the game world, lots of interesting ideas and thoughtful psychology. The writers are obviously fascinated with objects and artifacts and how we interact with them; everything you interact with is described in Proustian detail, it's great fun if you like to read (if you don't, it's probably infuriating). The world was strange and intriguing, enough to make you wish there were more of it. And little to no fighting! Which, as a contrast to something like Pillars of Eternity (also great but in a different way), was refreshing.
Downsides: The scale was smaller than I expected, and it ended strangely, abruptly (though one could argue the real story had ended already a few minutes before the "game" ending). The companions (except for Rhin and Matkina) were pretty dull, I'm thinking that next time through I'll try just not having any at all, see how that feels... Kind of a low-budget feel overall, but still a top-notch story and main character.

A worthy successor to my favourite game of all time, and I great game in its own right. TToN has wonderful worldbuilding that drew me in and always interested me. You need to be in the mood for reading a lot, but if you are, you'll be rewarded with some excellent storytelling and quests. The world feels so well fleshed out, there are no filler NPCs, everyone has their own story.
Meres act as choose your own adventure experiences, which are a standout in the game. It's like a tabletop d&d game without the dice or needing to remember all the rules. Every item you find has an interesting story, each person has a tale to tell. I also really like that not everyone is honest with you - characters have their own motivations, though you obviously play the protagonist the world doesn't revolve around you.
I've heard complaints about the combat taking too long. For me, it's not a factor of poor combat mechanics but too many enemies and characters taking part in each battle. It can take a while to go through all the turns. But there's always a way to avoid combat with conversation or other means and I really love that. I felt like I could play the game as I wanted and the game systems supported that. My biggest complaint is that the character modesl aren't that defined or attractive, but the backgrounds are very nice.

All in all, I really enjoyed the game and it's unique, if not campy, concept. I wish I could have played more of it, but the time I spent inside the games universe was well worth it. If a sequel was to be made, I would certainly buy it.

Hail to the King: Deathbat is a PC title that kind of surprised a lot of music lovers. The reason being? Subscience Studios had entered into a partnership with the Alternative/Hard Rock group Avenged Sevenfold to put out a game based on the Deathbat. The band also acts as the publisher of this title. Released the day before Halloween of 2014, it has quickly become one of the more talked about games available for purchase within the marketplace. But is this really a good game, or is it a better marketing piece that requires users to pay to experience?
The story to Hail to the King: Deathbat all stems from the legend of the group’s poor excuse of an Overkill knock-off mascot, The Deathbat. Well, at least that’s what they say. The game follows a king by the name of Andronikos, who banished the darkness from the land and kept his people safe until he was assassinated. He has awakened as a zombie, who is out for revenge against the one referred to as Dark Andronikos, the “new” ruler who appears as the original king in disguise that allows the monsters to roam freely within the kingdom. When you sit down and look at the game, this would make for a good stand alone title, makinh the fact that this is in association with the band Avenged Sevenfold really feelslike something tacked on for notoriety.
Hail to the King: Deathbat handles much like many PlayStation 1 and 2 titles, most notably games like Legacy of Kain with a top-down dungeon crawler vibe a la Diablo II on PC. You start off in one spot and make your way along the linear path to the end of the stage, sometimes having to solve small puzzles like standing on the proper pedestal in a certain order, or perform some kind of fetch quests like recovering certain gems to open up the next doorway and continue along towards the boss of the stage. For the most part it’s fairly simple, though some later levels can be pretty expansive, making the simple obstacle of the stage to advance far more time consuming than it ever needed to be.
And, much like any Action title along these lines, there ‘s to be a certain pattern to attacking, but one that seems to be a bit delayed. Regardless of the weapon you are using, even with magic spells, your foe will be knocked back but require an extra second or two before another hit will do so again. If you’re not privy to this knowledge, you will end up having your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you more times than you want to admit to. Really, it seems more like an odd delay in queing damage than something deliberately installed in the coding for the sake of difficulty. Sometimes any additional swipes won’t even count, forcing you to have to pace yourself, or run around in circles like an idiot to avoid being hit while spacing out your attacks for optimal damage.
There are ways to help get yourself through the few stages that exist though, which requires a great deal of grinding. Coins are just as important to you in this adventure as health and mana end up being. Within the crypt, which is the game’s introductory stage, you can buy health and mana potions, expand how much of each you can have at one time, as well as buy new weapons. The costs don’t seem much at the time, but for one of the better swords that will maximize how much life and magic at your disposal, not to mention do a little extra damage, you’ll end up shelling out over four thousand coins. Considered the norm is one coin, once in a while finding chests or breakable caskets filled with gold coins valued at ten, you’re better off just hanging out in the early stages grinding away, not to mention exploiting the bonus stages that feature a treasure goblin you can take down for more money aside the lines of free cash in this levels.
You can also change who you play as within the game through the aforementioned crypt. As you progress and complete levels, you will unlock “friends” who are meant to aid you in the quest. These individuals are actually the zombie versions of the members of Avenged Sevenfold. Even if you’re not the biggest fan of the band, some of them do actually seem to have benefits you can use, such as quicker attack times, not to mention a change to the random one or two line voice overs like Andronikos’s constant “Wait, don’t I know you?” inquiry to random foes over and over.
What’s more, there’s plenty of references to the band as far as the overall game design goes. The most obvious are the stages, which are all based around specific song names, such as “Bat Country”. There’s also song references in the bosses found throughout the quest as well, such as The Harlot, which comes from the song “The Beast and The Harlot”. Even the music is taken from Avenged Sevenfold‘s discography, touted as an original eight-bit score that actually just sounds more like a modern computerized version instead of that signature .midi format. Either way, fans of the group will definitely get a kick out of hearing these songs brought to interactive life.
Hail to the King: Deathbat is also a fairly short title. With grinding time included, you’re looking at maybe ten to twelve hours for a complete run through, making this a game you can hammer out over the course of the weekend. But, if you want some additional fun, there is a New Game + mode available upon completion. You keep everything you have already acquired as you go through the world with a different color scheme, fighting against enemies that have a little more life than they did in your first time through. With the right sword, health and mana maxed out, nt to mention remembering the proper attack patterns, and grinding for extra coins when necessary for additional potions and extra lives in the case you die, this new mode is still an easy run through. Of course there’s bonus stages you can unlock and pages to The Book of Mortals to be found, though neither seem to carry over if you take on the additional task.
Overall, Hail to the King: Deathbat isn’t a bad game, but it’s not a great game either. There’s not a lot of levels, though some seem to go on longer than any real need, the hit detection seems a bit delayed, and a good couple hours of game play seem dedicated solely to grinding for gold in order to get what you need to reach Dark Andronikos. There’s very little challenge once you do get enough for a better weapon, not to mention maximize how much health you can have at one time. But, for a six dollar (US) purchase from the Steam marketplace, or less on other mobile device stores like Google Play, you get what you pay for: A good title you can plough through over the course of the weekend and have no regrets about.
Overall score: 6.5/10

Update: Since I wrote this review a few months ago, I finished the game, so I'm updating this and mention a few things that changed.
I bought Hitman, after watching the guys at Giant Bomb play through the first 3 episodes and it looked really good.
I've never really played a Hitman game and while I like stealth games, I don't remember playing a game like it in the past where I can use disguises, different tools, so many methods to kill, etc.
I've finished the main story, the Summer Bonus Episode, a few Elusive Targets and started dabbling with the Escalations.
I usually try to do as much as possible in my first playthrough, because I don't replay many games. Since Hitman is supposed to played repeatedly I was a bit skeptical at first if I'll get my money's worth. These worries have since been put to rest. I'm enjoying the levels and have replayed the first three a few times and would still like to play around on them some more.
I think the first few levels are better that the later ones, but that might just be because they get more difficult (the later levels) and you can't ♥♥♥♥ around on them as much. Once I get more familiar on those, learn about the details, I'll might enjoy them more.
While I like the Opportunities to create chances to kill your targets, some make it really easy and almost impossible to fail and are pretty fast. A few are really fun though and I laughed more than once when I completed them and killed my target.
The Elusive Targets got better for me, once I stopped caring about getting a Silent Assassin rating for those. I currently don't have the patience to sit at these for hours to create chances to kill my targets unnoticed, especially since you can't save during these. I did that with the first few and had some fun but it was also really frustrating at times.
I can't say too much about the Escalations yet, I've only finished one and started a second one, but they seem to fall in the same category as Elusive Targets for me. I'll probably have more fun when when I don't obsess about getting the perfect rating.
The fact that the game requires a constant internet connection to get the most out of it sucks but hasn't been a problem for me apart from the time I played the game for the very first time and the servers were down. I still hope they remove this in the future though.
I encountered a few bugs when I started playing this game a few months ago, one or two even game breaking but it definitely got better over time. The AI still seemingly stops working here and there, though not very often. This really improved over time.
The developer did a fantastic job with this game, the constant release of new content and improvements of the existing stuff. I hope they continue to do so in the future and I have high hopes for Season 2 and I'm really looking forward to the Christmas themed content that's supposed to be released over the next few weeks.

To be clear, this game is fun. And it is possible to beat stronger teams with good tactics. I like the fact that if you study your opposition, look at their players and abilities, you can formulate a strategy to neutralize and even win, even against good teams. If you like strategy games, and football, you will probably enjoy this. Real life concepts, like using players to pull the defensive shape apart and then following on with players moving into the vacated space, work well.
But I also feel that the RNG in terms of special abilities favors the AI. My players special skills fail routinely, even at full energy and against weak opposition, while the AI players seem to somehow manage to beat my rolls consistently, even when they have no business doing so. I'm not opposed to challenge, and I understand that it's not supposed to be a walk in the park in the higher divisions. But I do feel like even with perfect tactics, the AI sometimes decides their abilities are going to work, and mine will fail.
Matches take between 10 and 20 minutes, which is great for just popping in and out. The tactics setup can be tedious, with lots of clicking through menus to line up your squad properly, but it's not a crippling feature.
After a couple seasons, the difficulty ramps up considerably, and you will probably need to grind a couple campaigns just to bring the overall quality of your squad up to par. If you are enjoying the game, this probably won't bother you. But it can be frustrating to consistently run up against teams you simply cannot match up with, no matter your tactical brilliance. Like most games, the more time you put into it, the better you (and your squad) will get.
All in all, I definitely recommend this game to football fans, or anyone who likes a simple (yet deeply challenging) strategy game. It's easy to learn, but there is a decent amount of depth in terms of lining up your squad to match up and defeat the oppostion. The devs seem to still be engaged, so perhaps the true 1.0 will be even better. Considering the price (I got it on sale for 11.99 US), this is a good investment.

While I have never been a big fan of CRPGs, mostly because of their boring combat and often slow and uninspired character creators...one thing that is almost always on display with CRPGs is superb writing. inXile returns to form with their kickstarted spiritual successor to what many people consider the greatest RPG of all time... Planescape Torment.
Torment: Tides of Numenera is a spiritual successor in just about everyway...well...I think it falls short in pacing, as the game can certainly drag on at times. But it does a good job going away from the boring Paragon/Renegade or Good/Evil moralities. You can find yourself having a number of different tides, which help shape your character. The character sheet/customization is pretty lacking, especially with almost no ability to customize your looks.
But if you like strong lore, strong story-telling, and a well written (but not too long) story I would certainly purchase this game.

People have basically said it all, so I won't say much except that were there many disappointments and some shady business/model advertisments....including early videos of neat things like portraits for ALL characters involved in dialogue, and more voice over work than ended up in the game...much revealed to only be in early "test" versions of the game which were not revealed as only test versions till a good time after official launch?  Yes to all of that....unfortunately, BUT...is the game still worthwhile, entertaining as all hell, and unqiue with an existential, Søren Kierkegaard, and even Kabalistic/Flower of Life...ish...kinda philosophical mash up/theme?  Hell yeah, and done well and not corny...imho.  A lot of negative reviews could possibly be butt-hurt kickstarter backers and people with legimate gripes like...promised Italian localization which was never implemented...etc, but all n all...great game that is somewhat light on combat, but if you WANT to engage in more combat the option is definately there.  For example, people might state that there are only 5-6 possible combat situations in Sagus (the first area in the game), but during my play through of Sagus, with determination of finding all the combat I possibly could, found well over or around about 12-15 combat scenarios.  Do you have to take a certain dialogue path to reach some combat?  Yes.  Can you avoid much of the combat in the game?  Apparently, according the the devs...noted post launch mind you, you are ABLE to avoid ALL combat if you try hard...they stated it would not be easy to do so, but that they intentionally designed the game so that this is a possibility.
I have over 40 hours post launch in the game right now and am only in the second area of the game, but I am slow and enjoy taking my time exploring every nook and conversation.  Even clicking the NPC's without branching dialogues has some reward to it, so I do so.  Also, future updates will apparently clean up combat in some unidentified respects, AND add a kickstarter promised companion called something like "The Toy," or some such that tinkers more with the whole "Tides" aspect of the game which sounds interesting.  I know I said I wouldn't ramble, but there you have it, hard not to praise what IS present and good about this game.

I like this a lot more than public opinion seems to hold! It's probably overpriced, the combat is mostly terrible, and as an RPG it's not really as complete or as generous as Original Sin and will probably be handily outdone by Original Sin 2.
BUT! I think this has been really underrated as a spiritual successor to Planescape Torment. The original game's visuals and combat (of which there is way too much, compared to this) have not aged well at all, and its writing, however beloved, is very "90s D&D."
By comparison, the writing in this is very enjoyable in a broader SF context -- the biggest complaint I could leverage is that they occasionally run out of ways to describe Dune-like interactions with otherworldly devices -- and there's less conspicuous philosophizing, which is more to my tastes. The worldbuilding in general is very nice; the graphics are only good enough, but the visual design of every area is distinct and memorable (lots of great blues and purples), and it's really to the benefit of the game's narrative thrust. The scope is relatively narrow and linear, and the side quests are basically typical CRPG fare in that you can play for completion and try to get the best outcome from everyone, but the game stays interesting from start to finish and there's a lot of creativity from one minute to the next. Individual NPC's are regularly more interesting and three-dimensional than major characters in the average BioWare game. It's also pretty bug-free and polished on the whole, although the balancing is pretty weak by the end.
Torment 2017 is also pretty affectionate towards the source material of Torment  1999 and manages to be thus without seeming derivative -- the bar in the first main hub town, the references to the "endless battle," and so on are all distinctly P:T-esque.
Definitely play any of the newer Divinity games first, but this is great and unique and deserves better than the response it's gotten.

I can't reccomend this and I can't willingly motivate myself to keep playing this game. There is more than enough well written reviews of this game so I won't bother repeating a great deal of what has already been said about the short falls and issues.
*Have since played another 3 hours on a friends account and its only reinforced my initial perspective...
The main reason I'm dropping this game already, less than 5 hours of play in, is because it just doesn't hit the mark to stand with the legacy of Planescape Torment. The atmosphere and asthetic elements are just not right, too much flashy sci fi styles spilling into the gameworld of TTON (lasers, facial augmentation machines etc). The asthetics are just off; there are points in the city which will feel similar to the city of Sigil from Planescape Torment but there is too many other graphics and designs that just don't fit. The combat is horrible; slow, contrived and a constant feeling of playing through scripted battles (removing real rpg aspects we enjoy; grinding, leveling, stats, looting). The Tides/Skill interface is clanky and slow; bringing nothing really significant to the game that I felt validated a need for this system at all. From the start onwards the dialogue is just dull and fails to immerse me into this world. I found no vested interests in my characters plight or the party members who joined me, besides Rhin. The character creation system is interesting but felt like it makes next to no difference in general with how events and quests play out (and come on, no option to chose a potrait - stuck with some bland face that looks like it came from a 1970's Sci Fi novel cover). I think that by focussing on being a dialogue/text heavy game too much the developers have ultimately failed to incorporate typical RPG elements that made the original game so good - we've got this unbalanced result of a game that has turned into a very linear. almost point and click adventure game. Big dissapointment.
There is moments, glimmers of good writing and creativity, where this game shows some potential I found in a few of the side quests. But these moments are over shadowed by the points I made above.
Look forward to modders ripping this game apart and rebuilding it into something the Torment community wants. I feel for the backers who got screwed over here but hopefully update patches can fix some of these issues. Save your cash and buy the Enchanced Edition of Planescape Torment or check out many of the other recent RPG's like Tyranny, Pillars etc

It's not often I feel compelled to write up a review of a game but some games such as Torment: Tides of Numenera deserve it, partly because of quality but also because of the anticipation of waiting so many years for it to be released.  I was a massive fan of the original Planescape game  (which at the time was underrated by a number of prominent gaming magazines), and is my favourite RPG of all time.  With regards to Tides of Numenera I feel that it has the potential to be nearly as good as the original Planescape but falls someway short.  That does not mean that it is a bad game, only that it is a good game that has a number of flaws that prevent greatness.
First the good:
Setting - originally I was disappointed that the Planescape campaign was not being used but having seen the decline of Dungeons & Dragons over the past couple of decades (which Planescape is a part of) in the end I was glad that they went with the Numenera campaign setting.   As a reader of Jack Vance and a fan of the blend of sci-fi/fantasy that influences Numenera, I found the Ninth World instantly engrossing, and, just like with Planescape, felt I wanted to explore it further.  I particularly enjoyed the less linear sections of the game including Sagus Cliffs and the incredible Bloom, one of the best game worlds ever.
Story/characters - I enjoyed the story, which kept me engrossed towards the end of the game, and appreciate the amount of text used to flesh it out, which I believe was over 1.2 million lines of dialogue.  I enjoyed in particular the back-story of the world's inhabitants and the games subplots perhaps more than the main story itself, and felt that this area started to approach that of Planescape.   Some people were complaining about the amount of reading involved so this game is not for everyone but for myself I thought it was well written, comparable with Planescape.  I also liked that you could basically complete the game with almost no battles if you chose to, relying on other skills such as guile or stealth.  Other reviews were not happy with the lack of spoken dialogue.  Whether this lack of dialogue was a design choice or because they ran out of money I am not sure, but I do personally find spoken dialogue too slow and distracting and much prefer reading at my own speed.   In term of characters they were generally very interesting and I felt that the personalities of the companions that accompany you were well thought out and each one intrigued me, particularly Rhin.  The downside to characters was that there were not enough of them but I will bring this up later on.
Loading screens - when I heard this game used the same engine as Pillars of Eternity I was immediately apprehensive as my experience of that game had been ruined by loading screens.  Thankfully, Torment load screens were not a problem on my computer and the game was structured so there were not dozens of rooms to be entered (probably because of the game engine).
Stats/Skills - I found the use of Might, Speed and Intelligence an interesting system and how you could put points into tasks.  I particularly liked how failing a task could actually open up new options in the game world, which offers potential new playthroughs.   I also enjoyed the types of skills on offer and levelling up characters, although I felt the level cap was a little low (see not so good).
Combat - there were a few complaints about the turn-based combat (which Planescape did not use unless you count pressing the spacebar to pause the action) but I have to say that I am a fan of this as it allows me time to think and strategise.  I thought Tides had much better combat than Tryanny (which seemed to be mostly AI and confused the hell out of me), but not as good as Divinity which had some very interesting spell combinations.
Now the not so good:
Length - this for me was the biggest weaknesses, partly due because of the games strengths.  Around 40 hours into the game, and really starting to enjoy myself, all of a sudden I found myself levelled up to tier 4, and the game was starting to draw to a close.  40 hours seems reasonable but this was after completing every quest and having already played a large section of the game with a different character type before restarting, so it is feasible you could complete the game in much less time. I feel that the world setting was so good, particularly the Bloom, that I just wanted more, and it was very disappointing that it suddenly nosedived to a conclusion.  From what I am reading online it appears that the developers cut a whole game world and it certainly feels so from the flow.  You really feel that you are building up to something fantastic only for the carpet to be pulled from your feet as you are steered towards the end.  Hopefully, they can allay some of these issues by releasing additional downloadable content.
Transition Linearity/Maps - although there are a couple of hub areas which give a degree of choice of how to approach quests there were a couple of linearity issues with the game.  For example, once you complete a certain stage you cannot go back.  There are a couple of points I would have liked the option to return to Sagus Cliffs to see if choices I had made elsewhere have influenced events in the city but this never happened.  This is possibly linked to the length of the game but there was a point on one map where it looks like you had a choice of portals to different locations but in the end you are shuttled through due to the approach of the Sorrow, which I found a little disappointing.  I also felt that more dungeon areas should have been introduced, particularly during the Valley of the Dead Heroes level which is more a sequence of rooms.
Tiers (levelling up) - this is related to the shortness of the game.  The maximum tiers you can reach is 4 (which is about 16 levels) and when I levelled up and could go no further, I had the sinking feeling that the game was starting to end.  Ideally, I would have liked a bigger game world and the opportunity to reach tier 5 - downloadable content please!
Bugs - there were a number of bugs in the game that I noticed including one that actually prevented me from taking a certain action to complete a quest resulting in the game freezing.  I also encountered a couple of freezes during battles.  With so much time spent developing the game this is something they should have got right.  Thankfully, unlike certain Atari RPGs (Greyhawk - which when patched is fantastic btw) at least they did not hinder my enjoyment of the game.
Merecaster Sections - I grew up on Fighting Fantasy gamebooks so I am not put up with interactive text but I found these sections incredibly dull.  The problem was that they contained massive amounts of text and I was not clear what (if any) effects my choices were having.  I will have another run through the game to see if this improves.
Minor gripes:
Extras - while not a major issue I would have liked some form of overall world map to have been available.  Planescape also had a codex/bestiary which I found interesting and I feel that Numenera missed out on this, although there may be some plans to introduce this via updates/downloads.
Overall I would say this is a good game that just misses out on great due to missing one major game location which leaves it feeling slightly unfinished.  I think expectations hindered it, and the fact I was not a Kickstarter Backer mean I am not as disappointed as I could have been, but it is worth purchasing if you are not put off by reading and turn based combat.  The characters, story and gameplay options mean that it is interesting enough for a second run through using different character companions and the Bloom is one of the great game locations of all time.  I would definitely be interested in more updates and games involving the Numenera game setting.
