This is a difficult game to recommend or not recommend.  I'll start off by prefacing: don't buy the game if you expect something on the level of PS:T or BG1-2. It doesn't compare to those favorably at all.
As for the actual review, there are a lot of good things going for the game. The world is extremely well developed and rich in lore. I greatly enjoyed just reading all the flavor text spread liberally throughout the game. The story, while nothing unique, is sufficient as a vehicle to get the player through the game. Best of all, the game actually means it when it says you can build any type of character and be successful at clearing the game. I fought a total of four times in the entire game. Then there are the characters, most of which have interesting back stories and designs.
Unfortunately, there's a lot to dislike too. While the characters ARE interesting, they're also extremely flat. They never truly progress anywhere with the exception of one, and you only see that development at the very end for a brief moment. Then there's all the lore text: it's ♥♥♥♥ing massive, the equivalent of a hefty novel all on it's own. The combat system is hit or miss, as well, though credit is due to the game as it does allow you to talk your way through even combats. The ending is also unbelievably boring, just a brief conversation at the very end with a generic "This is what happened after..." slideshow for the epilogue.
I think the worst of it all, however, is just how short the game is. I read through all the flavor text and took my time doing all the quests available and I still finished the game in less than 25 hours. Admittedly, I'm a quick reader, but that's pretty pathetic for a 45 dollar RPG. There's not much replay value to it either, as despite what it says your choices don't actually affect much throughout the game outside of maybe some flavor things.
Overall, I'd recommend it if you can get it on sale for about 20 dollars. Otherwise, just wait for it to go on sale or see if inXile  is releasing some amazing DLC or a modding system or something.

I actualy had to take a several weeks break from the game before writing this review. Also I fell like I need to be honest, that I did NOT finish the game. The reasons will be described.
I cant do the usual +/- scheme review because this game is... different. So I'll just write my thoughts down.
First of all, I am a huge fan of PS:T and BG games. I also played all other games from Bioware but they didnt left such a deep mark like the first two.
When they announced the successor (I know ''spiritual''...) to my all time favourite PS:T I was rejoiced. I remember spending my teenage years, not playing, but living the Nameless One's story in front of my computer screen. The feelings and emotions of despair and decay the game could invoke vere first and only I ever felt from a computer game. The writing was amazing, the design was perfect, the atmosphere cant be described, you, who played it know what I am talking about here.
But I was sceptical. I knew that PS:T 2 is impossible to make, so I waited with backing and preorders until the very release. I gave it a try... and liked it. No in the hindsight, I regret buying it.
- First of all as non native english speaker I had trouble with the VAST ammount of extremely long text that has NO purpose other than being long and to fill up the blank and boring gameplay. I dare to say that my english is on a good level, but I had trouble focusing and remembering all those vast lines of non-important text that was thrown at me at every step.
Stick with me here, I am not by any chance some barbarian who doesnt like to read and just want to hack-and-slash through the game. I am a huge fan of all fluff and trivia in games and always read them. But this is just TOO MUCH. Also you may notice varying quality of texts, like if multiple authors were put together on one book
- The atmosphere and setting is something I hated from the first minutes ingame. I couldnt get into the world and feel like a part of it even though I very much tried to. It is all just so flashy, shiny, colorful and bright compared to PS:T. Everyone in the world seem to be desperate and tortured to some degree, yet the world doesnt feel tortured and grim. It is all like a huge carnival, only the clowns were missing.
- In comparison to games like Baldurs Gate 2 and PS:T the NPCs are absolutely boring, flat and if they dissapeared I wouldnt notice. You dont make any connection to them and few days after finishing the game you dont even remember their names. Jaheira, Morte, Dakkon, Minsc. Those childhood companions of mine, I'll never forget. I didnt play this game for several weeks and I recall only boring albino, some dark haired pirate and glowing imbecil.
This review is VERY personal that is why I dont talk about gameplay mechanics at all. They were mentioned by others.

Gunplay is almost non-existing, because in most cases (except for turrets) we can see enemies from long distance and the best strategy is to stand still, and wait until they are so close, you can't miss. You have limited amount of bullets, but it rearly does happen to run out of them in a fight, moreover, you can pick up fired bullets, which makes this mechanism just redundant.
And there is an upgrade system. Unfortunatelly, you can carry only one item at the time, there are no separated slots for passive and active upgrades. In fact, you can't upgrade your charactem much more, than increasing life points and number of bullets (which in fact doesn't matter).
It's not a bad game. It's just not good.

My favorite in the series.
As much as I love 3089 and 5089, nothing quite captures the surrealist atmosphere and intricate cities like 3079.
When I first played 3079, I was dropped straight into a dystopian Scifi world, literally! You fall from the sky and get attacked by demons who have taken over the heavens! You can either die and wake up inside someone's house nursed to health (which is what happened to me) or you can evade the demonic forces and use your wits and your jetpack to land safely on the ground, while the face of the world is being altered by constant faction warfare.
Call me nostalgic, but 3089 and 5089 just don't capture the same vibe for me, and as much as I enjoy 3089 and 5089, they are very "Arcade" in comparison to 3079, which has cities that light up at night, giants that patrol the streets, with giant walls preventing anything from getting in or out, which of course you overcome with your trusty grappling hook.
3079 also features bases in the sky you can raid and take control of, and you can also change faction relations depending on who you are attacking! Want to switch sides? Shoot humanoid Humoids and start working for the arachnid Neanders.
Bases are distincted by the colors used on specific lights, which gets the job done, but a lot more could have been done. Buildings overall have much more interesting layout than in 3089 or 5089 which are based more around outdoor combat with hoverboards and attack ships.
While there are Attack Ships in 3079, the controls are not as polished as in 3089 or 5089 from what I've experienced, though I don't fly much, because I usually crash.
While the visuals for 3079 aren't much to look at, they really drive home the rather alienating and surreal atmosphere, and the voxel-based environments allow for destructible environments and terrain, akin to Minecraft and the like.
I have yet to blow holes in buildings, but I've certainly dug a few holes with high-powered explosives, something I have not done in 3089 or 5089.

For those who've played the mobile version and are wanting to know what to expect from the Steam version, the answer is nothing more, nothing less. It's the exact same game in every way. There are no graphical options, the resolution defaults to your desktop resolution. The UI is still decidedly touch oriented, and gamepad support is lackluster requiring you to reach for the mouse every time a menu or pop-up box appears. You won't be playing this on your couch undisturbed. But it is a fairly smooth port that looks and runs about the same as its mobile counterpart. You won't be impressed, nor will you be disappointed.
For those who have yet to play it and want to know what the fuss is all about, the answer is not much. Hail to the King: Deathbat claims to draw inspiration from games like Diablo and Legend of Zelda, yet it sheds some of the most enjoyable elements of those games. All that awaits you here is a linear hack and slash with one button to slash, one button to shoot magic and movement keys. That's it. Equipment is limited to a weapon and items are limited to barely more than health and magic potions. Most of the levels share a similar design, typically a dark gothic appearance and consist of decent textures slapped on low-poly models and maps. The games story is decidedly lackluster and the only time the games music gets good are when an instrumental version of Unholy Confessions plays during the boss battles. Outside of that, it's Psuedo-Retro sounding tunes with Arin occasionally bashing his drums over the top. Hardly a terrible soundtrack, but a waste of what could have been a memorable one.
A rebuttal to the common prasing of the games difficulty: The game gives you five lifes and makes you restart the level should you lose them all. Aside from that, there's no other real consequence. The game isn't hard by any stretch of imagination and offers but a gentle slap of the wrist for repeated failures.
All things considered, the games price reflects the game itself. It's only a few bucks. Feel free to dive in if you're curious, but be forewarned: there's nothing to call home about.

While not as good as the other Arkham games, it is still a great game. The story is interesting, and the dialogue is well written. It is very straight to the point, and the story makes it clear that this game is all about the boss fights, and in that regard, it doesn't dissapoint. The boss fights are varied, and very fun. From the hand-to-hand fight with Deathstroke, demanding split second timing and reflexes, to the surreal brawl with Copperhead, and the tactical stealth ancounter with Deadshot, this game will keep you busy with each passing boss fight.
Sadly, I can not say the same for the side missions. It is the same thing we've been doing since Asylum. Scan this, collect that, go there. Not much variety at all. It doesn't help that you're doing this on the same map as Arkham City. Sure, they have added new areas, but it doesn't offer much in terms of variety. It is hard to know your way around the map, when everything looks the same. They say in the game that you have to go to the industrial district, but the entire city looks like an industrial district! In fact, like Arkham City, the entire city looks like a war zone in an industrial district. It makes sence in City, being a cut off part of the city for prisoners, but in Origins, that is not the case. Things are on fire, the bridge is covered with piles of crates, broken cars and criminal activity. And navigating it has gotten harder. I swear they have reduced the amount of grapple points in the city. Even in places where there is no logical reason why I wouldn't be able to grapple, I can't. It gets very frustrating. And there are fewer things you can climb up on. Sometimes you can clumb up on objects that are, maybe, 3 and a half meters tall. At other times, you can't even climb up on something waste high.
Then there's the gadgets. You won't find much in terms of variety here either. Most of the gadgets are just altered versions of the old ones, or the exact same ones. But they do the job. If I have one major criticism of the gadgets, it is one that applies for all of the Arkham games. The gadgets are a bit far fetched. They feel out of place. It feels like they belong in a sci-fi game. They explosive gel has no reason to be a gel. In the comics and other media, Batman frequently carries explosive charges. Why does it have to be gel here? It feels a bit contrived. And why does he have to spray it in the shape of a bat symbol? Wouldn't that just take more time? And the disruptor looks like some sort of plasma rifle. I don't mind what the gadgets do, I just think they look a bit to futuristic. But that is just preference on my part.
All in all, I think it is a really good game. Its charm doesn't lie in its open world, or the side activities. It lies in the boss fights,, the the different levels and the characters. If that is what you're looking for, then I wholeheartedly recommend Arkham Origins. But if you are looking for a great open world game, with a lot of things to do, I recommend waiting for Arkham Knight, or pick up Arkham city which, while not very good at side activities either, does at least offer more grapple points, and climbable ledges, making the city easier, and more enjoyable to navigate.

I don't play a lot of old school RPGs. I couldn't get through Pillars of Eternity because I got bored by the story. I never properly played Planescape: Torment.
I couldn't stop playing this game. Yeah, the combat kinda sucks, but the story is great. The writing is great. The side quests are great and meaningful.
I'm glad it only took me around 20 hours to get through it as I usually lose interest if games go on too long.
I usually don't post reviews, but I just can't stand idly by when the game has so many negative reviews on here. I don't care about what happened with the Kickstarter or whatever. This is a good game and I thoroughly enjoyed it!

First off, this is one of the only games that I have played recently that I have been motivated to complete.
It's a fantastic game that should be experienced slowly and thoroughly. The writing is the standout feature - it's easily some of the most engaging and imaginative I've seen in a game. Most of your playtime will be spent reading. Plenty of choice with clear consequences.
Constructing/defining your character (your character’s CHARATER, not just your stats) is central to the game, which is unfortunately refreshing given the current state of roleplaying games.
Combat system is solid, but it's possible to avoid most fights if that's how you want to roleplay.
Your companions are interesting, and you will become invested in them if you give them the time. Although, I do think that each character could use one more quest to strengthen the investment. Experience is not gained by characters outside your party, so you are encouraged to choose three and stick with them.
Overall, if you are willing to invest in the game, like you would with a good novel, it offers a very rewarding experience.

Okay, here's the thing: in order to like this game, you have to like visual novels.  If you don't like VNs or dating sims, you won't enjoy this game.  It'll probably have nothing for you (even if you love the Grumps).  If you don't like VNs, I wouldn't get this game at all, despite the hype.
Now: if you do like VNs, this game is great.  It's very well written, laugh out loud funny in parts, and made my stone cold heart warm at times.  (I got teary-eyed.  I only cry once a year, what is this trickery?)  The artwork is gorgeous, and varied enough where you won't mind staring at it through each dating arc.  Because really, that's what visual novels and dating sims boil down to - am I taken in by the story?  Is the art good?  If you've checked yes and yes, then it's for you.
There are a couple of things that I would improve.  I'd love the option to turn the music down or off entirely.  It's charming and cute, but after playing for an hour or so, it does bore into the skull.  I'd love to be able to adjust the text speed.  And (sorry, Vernon) there's still a few typos.
Did this game reinvent the wheel?  No.  Is it deserving of all the hype it got?  Yes and no.  Of course, a ♥♥♥♥♥on of the hype is coming from the fact it's produced by the Grumps.  I love them as much as the next person, but if you don't like the genre of the game, having the grumps do voices isn't going to make you love the game.  Some of the hype I've seen comes from the fact that it's an inclusive game and handles LGBTQ themes with a lot of heart.  That is where I'd say it lives up to the hype.  I'm an Old Person on the internet, and I'm also an Old Person in the LGBTQ community, and I can say I legitimately never thought I'd see the day where a game like this would come out.  Thanks, game creators.
TL;DR: This is a great first outing that has a lot of charm and heart.  This is a game for people who a) like VNs and/or dating sims, b) are aware there's LGBTQ themes in it and are okay with that (although I'd hope you would be from the title, but hey, reading comprehension can be difficult), and c) people who are obsessed with puns.

I'm a huge fan of the Mad Max movies, so I knew I'd eventually play this game. Unfortunately, having played The Witcher 3 and MGS V: TPP, I automatically compared this game to those two. Sure they're not entirely the same, but being open world games and how they offer entertainment is what I mostly had in mind.
Mad Max was fun, but most of what was offered in its vast wasteland was repetitive, and at times I didn't bother to pay attention to these sidequests. Despite ignoring these sidequests, there were moments where they were necessary to advance in the main storyline. Honestly, that bothered me a little. I'm the type of player that's playing for the main storyline, not to collect special items or discover all the locations on a map. Most of the times, these types of additions to a game are included to beef up the amount of gameplay time, but that's a weak way of doing so. I'd rather play a medium/long game that involves a well written storyline or gameplay, much like The Witcher 3.
Despite this complaint, I enjoyed Mad Max. The game's setting was well created and the storyline was decent, along with being an interesting way to expand the Mad Max lore.
One thing I've heard others complain about is the combat system. The combat system in this game is similar to the latest Batman games. Honestly, it didn't bother me because it can be upgraded and this allows some variety and I genuinely enjoy that combat system.
Overall, I enjoyed the game and I recommend that you play it, even if you haven't seen the movies. I give this game a 3.5/5.

Mad Max is an outstanding open world action/adventure masterpiece which takes some of the best parts of it's genre siblings and mixes them with a fantastic theme to create an unprecedented stand alone experience.
Step into Max's boots, a man who just wants to get his car back, driven solely by survival instincts. You take to the road in a freshly built and decently customisable new set of wheels to topple a fiendish bloodlusty raider boss named Scrotus and reclaim the Interceptor, the black on black.
With fantastic driving combat built from the ground up coupled with the acclaimed hand to hand combat/counter system made popular by the Batman: Arkham series (as well as Shadow of Mordor), there is a lot to see and find out in the wastes as long as you don't mind a little bit of repetition. Mad Max is also a beautifully example of how good Photo mode in these games can be (I've a couple of nice shots on my profile, bit of a photographer in games) and you can get some truly stunning shots.
For a game no one saw coming and didn't have much expectation on, Mad Max rallies with the release of Fury Road to bring this post-apo universe back from the dust with fire and nitro and madness for all

I'm so so torn.  I spent about 44 hours playing this game through to completion.   There were parts I really enjoyed...like wandering around Sagus Cliffs, the first main city of the game.   Exploring, talking (great writing BTW), etc.    But there was much more that I felt was rushed, not fully fleshed out, etc.  It's clear they spent a lot of time coming up with a weird, quirky story with lots of characters to talk to.  But the game just wasn't "fun".  What I enjoy about a CRPG is a great story, plus great exploration, plus a little strategy in a tough combat.  There's no point in leveling up if things aren't progressively difficult, require some strategy, planning, luck, etc.  Things were NEVER difficult or tense.  The while "spend as many points as you want on a check, and just refill by sleeping" was only annoying at the beginning before you found a place to sleep.  Leveling up is really kind of pointless...all you 'really' need is more points in your talent pool of choice.  I so so wanted this game to be great, and from a weird story perspective, it IS great....like a good pick a path book.  But everything else about it is lacking from leveling, to exploration to combat, to acquiring gear, etc. all felt like RPG lite lite.  I remember people complaining that the strategy and leveling of the Shadowrun Kickstarters as being a little "RPG lite"....this is too.  Before anybody says "well if you just want combat, this game isn't for you", remember, I don't "just want combat".  I want good combat, challenges, leveling, story, companions, etc.......like you got in the original Torment, Baldur's gate, etc.   This got the story and companions right but missed on everything else.  This would have made a great book.   For those reasons, I can't recommend this game like I would PoE, Wasteland 2, Divinity Original Sin, etc.

I backed the kickstarter and waited patiently for the release, I didn't actually realise how much it was delayed but well, here it is and now I've completed it. Others have spoken about InExile and the kickstarter promises and so on, I will just speak about the game.
This game is all about the lore and world-building, and everywhere you go in the game there is something to poke and prod at and uncover secrets and memories. Even the loot is mostly unique, giving you little snippets of lost cultures and mysteries to ponder. I love that, and I spent a lot of time pouring over every bit of text I could find. The characters are varied and interesting, pulling from the lore to create a fascinating cast of original characters, which was definitely remiscent of Planescape: Torment. I found the companions a little lacking, though they each stand out they perhaps didn't have as much to say as I would have hoped, and they didn't react to events very often and didn't have much of a part in the final scenes as the companions did in PS:T.
The story is obviously the main focus and I'd say it's interesting enough to recommend. It's very much a personal journey and while you do have an effect on the world, it's not your generic world-in-peril kind of stuff which is refreshing. There are some twists and turns and in the end your choices feel meaningful, and present a moral challenge that makes you think beyond "what is the right choice?"
The combat is garbage, what else can I say. Planescape: Torment is probably my favourite game and I feel like it was a massive departure from the spirit of the original game to go with turn-based. In PS:T, the combat was criticised for being too simple and chaotic, but I liked that, and even where it failed to impress it at least went by
. The same cannot be said of T:ToN. There is no hurry-up or skip turn button for AI characters, and so in big fights you have to sit and watch them derpily stagger around turn by turn, and if they all decide to gang up on the main character, then too bad load a save or start again with less items. In PS:T you could pause the combat and use a healing item, but in T:ToN if it isn't your turn, too bad you can't do anything. There are at least a couple of fights in the game with an enemy that can one-shot anyone on the screen and if it targets the main character... yeah you guessed it. There are non-combat options to get out of crises or have them not start at all, but due to the turn based nature it can often be frustrating to achieve them when your character is standing right next to the thing but can't interract with it because they have to let themselves get wailed on for ten more turns because that makes sense. In case it isn't obvious I don't like turn based combat, I'll stop ranting about it now. It's not the draw of the game, and I only point out how bad it is so that people don't have any expectations that this game has any kind of decent tactical combat - it doesn't.
All in all I think it's a decent shot at a spiritual successor to PS:T, and I'm glad I backed it and played it, and I will play it again in the future to try the different classes and companions. I don't agree with others that the game is too short, I feel the story warranted the length and it feels like value for money to me, especially as it does have some replay value. I don't think it's going to be making my favourite games of all time list, but if you want an interesting story-based RPG then I'd say this is worth your time.

The mouse cursor is on the screen at all times as well, but that's not a big deal really.
What is a big deal, is the fact that to actually hit an enemy, you need to walk towards it first.
This doesn't sound that bad, but when the only possible way to dodge attacks is to walk AWAY from enemies, this makes it practically impossible to avoid damage a lot of the time, unless you play the game as though you were a manual balloon pump, taking a single swing, moving backwards, and then moving in again to take another single swing, for however long it takes to kill a single enemy, which judging by the enemies in the first level, is about 5 seconds per enemy. With quite a decent number of enemies, combat becomes very boring, very quickly. If it was fun to kill enemies, this wouldn't be a problem. But it's not fun. There's hardly any feedback to your blows, and it just doesn't feel good smacking things around with your sword.
Why is it like this? Why is this game so utterly mind numbingly simple? Well, probably because this is a mobile port.
Yeah, a mobile port. Hopefully this made some of you turn away already, because you know how badly this usually ends up. Mobile ports of games don't really change the gameplay, and since they were made for mobile devices, they are generally VERY simplistic in terms of gameplay. Oh, and it used to have microtransactions, though those are not in here any more. Take that as you will.
So, what exactly does this game offer? It has fantastic visuals, that I can't deny, it has pretty good music from what I can tell, though not all of it really sounds like what Avenged Sevenfold would make. And the voice acting is... non existant. Punishment for death is pretty much non existant as well, as every time you die, you just respawn at a frequent checkpoint with no consequence. Seriously, not even more effort, as enemies do not respawn. Except for the bossses of course. And with no way to dodge attacks other then just... moving slowly... bosses can be somewhat annoying to a degree. As like I said before, you need to move towards an enemy to attack them, and cannot attack while dodging in pretty much any way.
The incredibly simple and obvious mobile port type gameplay is not something that can be overlooked, and leaves this as a very boring and occasionally frusterating game. It's a shame really. I did not have high hopes for this, but it looked good from the screenshots. It ends up being more of a chore than a fun game. If only it was a bit more complex, or at least made it fun to kill things, this could have been good... but alas, it is not.

Heavy Bullets is a great rogue-like fps that has two unique features that sets it apart from the rest.
The gameplay is mostly the standard run and gun style that most games in the genre have. What makes it unique is the fact that the player has to reuse the bullets. After a bullet is fired the player will need to pick it up again. Thats a good thing because the player will have 6-8 bullets on average.
This makes for fun and frenetic action as a player needs to rush past enemies to get his ammo back.
The level design are good most of the time, although there will be a unfair level since the levels are randomly generated. The levels also lacks any verticality since every level is on one floor. There are no stairs, dips or inclines.
The other unique aspect of the game is the presentation. The graphics are low-fi. The levels are low texture and low poly. The enemies are also low poly and kind of ugly. This style actually benefits the game since they are appealing to a certain degree and help the game stand out. The sound is also mostly a series of beeps and boops.
The rest are all standard fair. Perma-death. Items. Banking money for the next run. High difficulty. The game is still worth a try since it will give a player a unique gameplay experience.

According to my stats, I've played this for over 118 hours.  It remains one of my go-to games even though I've been killed a great great many times!  It's high energy.  It's high action.  But it's also very stratigic and engages all your thought processes.  I'm not sure just what keeps me coming back.  Somewhere it's about outgunning monsters, outwitting them and surviving to tell the tail that holds the fascination.

As a disclaimer, I haven't put much time into this game nor have I come anywhere close to beating it, but I figured I'd recommend it since I do enjoy it.
Heavy Bullets is a rogue-lite game where you progress through floors while killing monsters and trying not to die. The gimmick is that you can pick up your bullets after you fire them. This makes it so you go into each fight with a very limited amount of ammo, so you need to place your shots well. This can be hard when you get jumped by something hiding in a bush and start to panic fire. It's difficult, but very well designed and feels fair. When I die I know that it was because I messed up or wasn't paying attention. There is permadeath, but you can save some of the money you get in each run in your bank. I also love the atheistic of the game with all the neon colors.
I feel like I've only scratched the surface of the game, and would say that it's worth the $10 they're asking for. But do keep a look out for the game going on sale as it seems to do that quite often.

So... this is a good game when You have just a little time and You want an escalating challenge where the fast reflex and precision is the key.

This game was really fun and entertaining to play, if as others have pointed out, a little short. The art throughout the game is lovely and makes a change to a lot of dating sim/visual novel games which I often feel suffer due to unappealing art. It also benefits from a great concept, I love that you have to manage taking care of your daughter alongside your dating life and the relationship with Amanda is well thought out. That being said some of the dad's routes aren't especially well done, I particularly didn't like how the relationship with Brian developed as it felt silly in a not fun way at times. It's also annoying that you can't get a more satisfying ending with Joseph and develop a better relationship with Mary who is a great character.
The minigames can be quite frustrating and are a little basic, especially the golf one which I just found aggravating. However there are some really fun mechanics like 'build a dad', the pokemon brag battle and of course dad book, although it would be nice if 'dad book' and 'build a dad' had more influence on your dating life. I think the game could definitely benefit from an unlockable story once you've completed all routes in order to fully flesh out the characters and throw in that air of mystery visual novels love.
All in all this was a fun game and worth the money for the clear thought and effort put into it which made it so enjoyable to play. It's in no way a revolution within the dating sim/visual novel genre, but it is different and offers some really sweet relationships between LGBT+ couples. I know I'm going to find it difficult to find another game which portrays romantic LGBT+ relationships in such a well thought out and non fetishised way. Dream daddy has definitely found a gap in the market which will hopefully fill with this games success.
So I recommend for fun, wholesome dad dating with a side of raising a rad daughter while enjoying an uholy amount of puns.

The most recent Elusive Target, #4 'The Sensation' is my example for this:
See Target at party.
Target is drinking a Vodka, all other drinks are Wine.
Walk up and Taint Targets Drink to lure him away.
Spend 30 Real Time Minutes watching said Target NPC complete his scripted path over and over again....
And Never Once Touch His Drink AGAIN!
Why offer all these 'choices' to complete the mission when in this one simple instance you fail to test to ensure it would complete as designed.

Never mind, not waiting until the Elusive target ends on Monday - this company has screwed this game completely, no further episodes... the remainder to be released in late 2016?

The improvements started around Episode 3: A Gilded Cage (Marrakesh), with the latest two: Episode 4: Club 27 (Bangkok) and Episode 5: Freedom Fighters (Colorado), finally having that polished feel.

The story is where this is going to be key, as in Episode 5 we got some hints of where this is all going.

Dustforce truly is a work of art. I don't mean that lightly. The way it's animated plus its music gives it that title in my book. I can find myself playing one level for an hour, maybe even hours at a time. The frustration of losing levels is filled with relaxation and calmness because of the ambient music. The way the levels are crafted is truly mindblowing. They had a system in which you had to perfect a level to earn a key, and you would use that key to earn more levels. In layman's terms, to earn more levels, you had to perfect current levels. They ditched that and added an XP system in which you gain more XP to earn a key the more levels you play and perfect. I'm very glad they added this system and was skeptical about buying it. But now that I did buy it, I do not regret it even for a second. One thing I really love about this game is how you don't have to unlock base levels. In a sense, this game is open world. That sense is that many levels are available to you, and you can choose whether you want to advance into more challenging levels, or stay where you're at. To get an S in completion, you have to sweep up EVERY leaf, and to get an S in Finesse, you have to maintain your combo throughout an entire level.
Another thing I absolutely enjoy about Dustforce is its expasive community. There are lots of Community Workshop maps for you to sharpen your skills on, and lots of people who can set a good example. I'm sure most of the people who get best times on all the levels have a Youtube channel, so you can probably catch them there. The community may or not be active, but it sure is good and friendly.
Overall, in terms of gameplay, music, artstyle, animation, and difficulty (it's not an easy game, but it's not that hard of a game either. It just depends on how much you want to play it), I rate this game:
10/10

This game was a lot of fun. The stories are very humorous and touching. I very much liked the game's theme song and the transitions between the different character portraits. The squash and stretch effects where a nice subtle touch added to character art transitions.
There are a few moments where the audio feels very unbalanced with the rest of the game. It seemed like 50% of the character Damien's audio clipped and it was clear that not everyone was working with the same equipment. This isn't a knock against  the game but it did distract from the game and I wouldn't recommend playing the game with headphones on.
However I do wish that the developers had implemented a different kind of save game menu. Currently the game saves are all in one big list with the most recent at the top and the only way of telling what you were doing is a time stamp and a screen shot of the background. For a game with multiple endings I find that a numbered save system works much better. That way you can save the game at points in the story to easily remembered slots. I wouldn't say that this is game breaking in any way but it is frustrating when I have completed a route and want to go back to just after the character introductions.
tl;dr: Great game! Minor audio complaints. Wish the save game menu were numbered slots.

I was a backer of this Kickstarter, and now that I've finally had a chance to play it, did it live up to my expectations?  Well, it's not quite up there with Planescape, but I was enthralled by the world.  I actually recommend reading the Tides of Numenera Novellas first, because they added an extra layer of familiarity to the world and locations (finding a certain skeleton and the weapon beside it actually made my jaw drop as I realized who it was, but only because I had read the novellas). The world is fascinating, the characters I traveled with a little less so (although there were definitely touching moments with some of them). The final conflict was a little underwhelming, and I may go back to try it differently.  But the whole concept of effort and finding alternatives to fighting in the Crises was intriguing and well implemented. But there were so many interesting stories, and the central plot, once unveiled, will leave me thinking for a long time.  It may not stand up with the classics like Baldur's Gate and Planescape, but it's only a small step down from them, and still definitely worth the time of Isometric Role playing games (and interactive fiction fans who don't mind dealing with some of the trappings of traditional RPGs).

I backed this game on Kickstarter and had high hopes for it, and I did play it all the way through, so that's saying quite a lot.
However, I feel like it missed the mark, or else, our hopes were all set too high.
First, the game is buggy. Very buggy. Freezes are not uncommon. Graphic corruption is not uncommon. Freezes are often persistent, such that you have to just skip that chunk of the game to get around them. (For example, if entering a certain area causes the game to freeze, it will generally do so every time, so the only workaround is just to not go there.) The 1.0.2 patch didn't help that for me -- if anything, it made it worse. Also, there are little "bugs" like the wrong gender in dialogue and things like that, but there are a fair number of them, so it does interfere with your immersion.
Second, the game is surprisingly short. That's likely why I actually got around to finishing it. It just didn't take all that long. For a game of its type, for what I paid for it, and for the reputation of its franchise, that was a bit disappointing. [Steam tells me that I played for 38 hours, and that includes restarting areas multiple times due to freezes, and walking away from the computer for hours at least once.]
Also, there's a lot of dialogue, but it's not very fluid and doesn't evolve much. Conversations feel pretty "gamey", and you can generally explore every conversational thread -- none will get cut off because of another thread you followed. It feels ... old school in that respect, and not in a good way.
And then, there are just a lot of bad UI choices. For example, when you use an ability, it plays a sound effect if you succeed and labels a button "Continue", but if you actually click that, which I kept forgetting to not do, you'll actually skip over the screen that tells you the results of your action. (It's surprising how often that happened and how much I didn't really care.) As another action, on a complex battlefield, if you want to use an attack or ability on an ally or enemy, you must pick them out on the battlefield, even if other characters occluding them make that nearly impossible to do. The game is *aware* of who you select using the character portraits in the initiative list, but won't use that information. Why not? Also, many items have a "Use Item" button that does nothing because instead the game wants you to click back to the main game screen, click on the little backpack on the left side, and then select them there to use them. Why not make both work? If the button doesn't work, why display it?
I didn't hate the game. I did enjoy parts of it a fair bit. But the tone is often grim-just-to-be-grim and the fact that it didn't really draw me in made that feel less "adult" and more just egregious, or even childish. Also, I would have liked to see not only more content and a larger adventure, but more locations. There are hardly any in the game.
Oh, and this probably matters to very few people, but I largely backed this game because I'm a huge fan of the Numenera role-playing game, and the system implemented in the video game is *not* the same at all. It barely qualifies as "inspired by". They should have made more effort to stick to the actual system where possible if they were going to market it the way they did.
In the end, I think people who own the game will enjoy it, but I'm not likely to recommend people run out and buy it. I'm going to go tackle Pillars of Eternity next, and I'm expecting to get more out of it.

Mad Max is a great game, the graphics, driving around in the wastes, working on your car, the survival elements, they all work beautifully. The best part being the car combat, the handling also feels very nice and the weapons available on the cars are also fun to use.
The game however loses all that in the sections where you leave your car, the melee combat is similar to that of the Arkham games or Shadow of Mordor but lacks the depth that these had. You will spend most of your time doing simple combos and parries. The bossfights were also a big letdown, they are all identical, they share the same model and moveset only difference being that they have different weaknesses.
I would have liked they focused more on the driving aspect, maybe have the bosses drive unique cars on the road similar to the convoys that are in the game but with more depth and special mechanics. Even simple exploration would work just fine if not better whilst driving the car as seen in the missions taking place in the underdune where you have to avoid traps or in the tunnels where you salvage a train carriage with your car.
The car customization could have used some more options but its enough to keep you busy in a casual playthrough and the plot will not win any awards but it will keep your attention and has some memorable characters and moments.
The passing years have given us a lot of great open world games. Mad Max is one of them, It's a treat to explore the world for the first time, the vistas are amazing and the world itself is filled with tons of interesting locations and side activities.
The game is totally worth the €20 and even more when its on discount.

Yea yea, gameplay and story is good and all, but what about using the console?
I have spent more hours using console commands than actually playing the story.  My younger brother also did the same thing, experimenting what we could accomplish and manipulate.  Some stuff we did:
Put about 10 Luke Skywalkers next to each other, then keep spawing a tusken raider until they end up killing another Luke.  This makes them all attack each other out of confusion.
Have a wampa pick up someone, then have a rancor pick up the wampa.  The wampa walks around cut in half with it's victim still attached to it.
If you noclip to a part in the level where a cutscene will happen, spawn some NPCs.  Since the game uses a character's entity for both gameplay and the cutscenes, they have a side (good/evil) and even have health.  Spawning some jedis will have them attack any villains that make an appearance.  If they end up killing them, the cutscene breaks and you have to restart the game.
If you change your playermodel, you also inherit the propeties that character has.  For example, did you know Kyle has 125 force points rather than the default 100?
Changing your playermodel to the ATST gives you it's cannon weapon.  If you change back, the cannon is still in your inventory and you can use it as a regular weapon.
15 cultists that only use lightning can take down the mutant rancor.

This initially appears to be a minecraft ripoff because it basically is.   There's a few notable differences in gameplay and theme, but the guts of what's going on here is still deep in minecraft territory.
While Minecraft is a notable success in part because of it being part of the now flooded survival genre, 3079 eschews survival for a more traditional RPG which, if it was any other game, might have worked out well.
Gameplay: You generally have to figure out the game yourself or watch youtube videos/walkthroughs to get started on questing.  The plot is hammy and slapped together and none of it really makes a lot of sense.  Thematically it just misses every mark and fails to hook you into the RPG side of things.  You do collect a bunch of different items and instead of wandering around in procedurally generated hell, you run around in half finished lazy developer hell.
Graphics: Terrible... the game does run in 4K but it's still very amateur.   Minecraft mods show that voxel based games don't have to look ugly, so the ugliness here is because the developer was lazy, unskilled, or deliberately wanted to make the game look bad.  What sticks out even if you want to humor the developer being "artsy" is poor design language - some textures are great (so probably stolen from someone) and others are hideous.   Fonts and interface styling is all over the place.
Technical - controls are clunky, but it does work okay with mouse and keyboard.  Graphics options are limited, which is a shame because that would have been some easy marks for the developer to try hide his lazy effort on the quality of the artwork.
Just buy Minecraft and mod it if you want a voxel game.  Play Ark if you want a survival game.  Play Skyrim if you want an RPG.   Those are just examples - there's so many games better than this.

The building is kind of finicky, but once I got the hang of it, it was EZ. GGWP.

Sheesh, this is one hell of a game.  I'm an old gamer that has been around before PCs used DOS, and I still can't get over this game.  I got this game on sale this week at $0.49 and it is worth a whole lot more than that.
I've been strafed by two planes at a time.  I've been fired upon by a Flying Fortress in the heat of multi-squad battles, exploded the Fortress with my AI buddies while it was doing a bombing run over us and it crashed into us with a huge explosion, forming a real time crater beneath us while doing so ... and lived.  Now, I don't know about you, but that's about as good as it gets.  Who needs a combat MMO when you can play this with AI and no internet connection?
Do the game's graphics look a bit like something out of the Stone Age?  Sure.  But this game takes Combined Arms to the limit.  You were told there was a violent war going on, well they weren't kidding.   The whole terrain is littered with pits, craters, used by some as fox holes and others seem to be having moments of extreme war fatigue in them, and you'll join them soon enough.
The first couple of hours you'll be wondering what the heck is this thing called 3079.  You'll feel like a poor rube who somehow got caught up with the resistance, but you don't even know what a war is.   When you land, night and day changeover quickly.  The nights even from the starting town, have not only the sounds of flak and gunfire in the distance, but you can actually see the tracers and explosions of vehicles and men out there beyond the town's fortified walls and above the tree tops.  And those tracers and explosions are the real deal, that's actually happening out there.  They are not canned ambience tracks or graphics for effect, it's the news come to life. Yep, this is one wild ride.  It may sometimes look like a throwback, but few games give you an experience like this of war.  You'll be confused, out-flanked, cowering in fear -- and then slowly but surely you'll get your bearings, start looking for battle and heading out to the action, using buildings and terrain as best you can.
The game has things which annoy.  The lifts are easy to get momentarily stuck on, just back into them and adjust so your back is fully to the lift blocks and away from the edges and you'll be fine.  You'll be bumping into the roof on the highest level, but you'll figure that out.  The "Demons" in the game are a pain to deal with, pulling you towards them with some unknown telekinetic power and attacking everyone, friend or foe.  But once you get some Demon Smiting Swords via Quests, you will have a solution.  There are a few too many buttons and nothing is that well explained, but that's why I wrote a basic tips guide for newbies in the forums, in case the videos on the game, which are really terrible, don't get you over the hump.  You can also talk to npcs that aren't giving quests or aren't merchants for a random tip or two.
Ever wanted to be an astronaut/soldier/special forces guy sent to investigate war on a planet and try and stop the war and bring peace?  Neither have I?  But that's what you are up to here, but good luck getting there in one piece. Do yourself a favor, on the launcher menus, choose Easy Mode, it's still exciting as heck, and you'll still die enough to learn to respect the game.  Also, up the FOV to 115 or so, in this game the camera positioning really needs it and you still we be caught broadside from your flanks easily enough.
For those of you looking into this game, I've posted a basic starting guide to help on the forums.  I'll probably move it into the 3079 Guide section later on.
All I can tell you is that most of the YouTube videos are made by people who have no idea of how to play a game and on early beta versions.  You can catch some of the early excitement, but good luck getting any tips on playing the game.  For example the following things said in some videos are wrong.  The game can't kill steal, you up your stats by overloading any action of that stat.  Test your limits to improve, it's not that confusing. So overload and empty your energy in your batteries, you may up your total energy.   Overload your inventory so that the weight is too high, barely walk that way and soon you get extra strength, and by soon I mean in a matter of 10s of seconds.  Think of overloading a skill as leveling and improving by necessity. The game is cool like that as it wants to promote the way you decide to play.
I actually enjoy this game more, so far, that 3089, even though 3089 has more polish and a lot less seemingly irritating things in its GUI.  They are similar.  But the gravity of the situation in 3079 is a lot more tense, you are a lot more confused from the start, and combat is almost visceral in that weird alien way.  Just forget the graphics and experience what is going on, and you'll probably end up enjoying it as much as I do.  3079 is more raw and brutal than 3089 and on sale for $0.49 it's worth taking for a test drive.  Learn to survive, because if you think simple graphics makes for an easy game, you don't know Phroot.  To get past the initial confusion, however, is going to take at least 2 hours.  So, if you wish to be protected by the Steam Refund Policy, I suggest you read a basic guide and maybe look at a couple of videos before you play.  Or just buy it on sale next time and stomach the two bits you paid. If you can get past the graphics, you are in for one hell of a ride.
On top of that, the game has night vision goggles, allows you to build fortifications, you can use a grappling gun to climb buildings, ride and jack into airplanes.  It has suspended flying cities in the atmosphere.  You can teleport, you can cast effects on your enemies or yourself using Transfer Effect guns.  You can capture towers via hacking the enemy computer in enemy towers if on a quest.  That's just what I've learned and experienced so far.  It has a ton of different weaponry, heavy guns, assault rifles, pistols, shotguns, sniper rifles, explosives, grenade launchers, jeez.  All of them have the potential to have additional modifiers on them to stats.  A lot of them don't really make sense, since when you equip your weapon you can't mine for example, you need the mining tool on you, but still it's like Diablo 2 met Battlefield on a crucial Hill 49.
Highly recommended, if you can get past the graphics and first 2 hours. If you can't get past the graphics, I recommend you take a look at 3089 and 5089.  Those games have a better user interface, much fewer irritating issues, and look better.  They are easier to get into since more info is available in game as tips and help.  It's not as wild a ride, but it covers the same type of gameplay.
(This game runs fine on an Intel HD 2500 Integrated GPU.  So if you have that or later on a laptop, it should work.  I can't speak for the AMD Integrated Chips, it may work just as well.)

Don't turn away this game because it "looks like a Minecraft rip off" because it isn't. Surprisingly, the only similarties are the blocks, and the building system, which you rarely ever use. I'd compare it to games like Strife instead.
The game isn't very friendly to newcomers. You start out in this giant space with lots of broken, chipped astroids. Only after watching a video, do I realize you have to float downwards in order to get to the planet. The game still isn't easy after that. Enemies take a lot of hits, and guns don't seem to be accurate. And waiting for guns to recharge after shooting takes a long time.
One of the complaints I have with this game is that you move way too damn slow. Thankfully, this can be fixed by purchasing speed generators and speed upgraders with in-game credits you earn by either selling loot found from carcasses of your enemies, or completing quests. This is thankfully, improved in the later games where you can now sprint at the cost of not being able to shoot your weapon.
This game is also surprisingly well balanced. Hell, even the difficulties are balanced. Easy mode makes you dish out more damage, at the cost of your energy replenishing slower than normal mode. A quip I had with most AAA games (Looking at you, Halo.) is that if they have some sort of cloaking device, you can only use it for around 30 seconds before you're uncloaked, which is annoying. Stealth is about patience, waiting for the enemies to move in a certain spot so you can take them out without alerting others. When you're forced to panic kill an enemy because your cloak ran out, it's not fun, and just feels tedious. In this game, however, the cloaking is balanced well; Cloaking makes you move slower, and you cannot regenerate energy while cloaked. However, you can cloak for as long as you want. This is what cloaking in games should be.
The graphics are pretty bad, but it IS an indie game made in 2011, so you do have to give it some rest. Graphics don't make a great game, evidently, shown by here. I have had a few graphical glitches (invisible textures) but they rarely occured, and didn't ruin the game experience much.
The steam run does not start up the game itself, but rather a bat file that loads up the options menu. This means that the game cannot use steam overlay. I suppose it's easier to run the game this way, I guess.
Pros:
+Fun gameplay
+Randomly generated; It's different each time you start.
+Game is quite challenging.
+Grappling hook is great.
+Trading cards
+It's cheaper than beer.
+Can run on a toaster.
Neutral:
*The game is not forgiving to newcomers. This may make it more challenging to others, but it's not exactly for the casual players.
Cons:
-Guns are incredibly inaccurate. I believe this depends on the gun itself you pick up.
-Graphics are poor, but it is an indie developer making this.
-Graphical glitches.
-No steam overlay.
-Only a few songs in the game. One of them sounds pretty good, but the others are royalty free songs.
Would recommend? Yes.
I do recommend this game if you want to see what 5089 is like. Keep in mind, there are still some improvements in 5089, including graphics and menu system.

When I first bought this, I thought it was going to be Minecraft with guns. That couldn't have been further from the truth.
3079 is a procedurally-generated voxel-based world, much like Minecraft, but aside from occasionally breaking down blocks, that's where the similarities end. Everything else is just as the title says -- "Block Action RPG."
The majority of the game is spent acquiring new quests, obtaining and equipping/selling items, fighting enemies, and retrieving objects -- all of which are fully randomly generated. Everything in the game (and I mean EVERYTHING) is generated procedurally, and while this never creates any particularly memorable characters or items, it does mean that on occasion you might stumble upon some pretty great rewards, interesting landscapes, or intense quests completely by accident.
I'll just come out and say it.... Graphically, this game is ugly, and by that I mean most other games I've played suddenly become eye candy. That being said, something about the horrible ugliness is genuinely charming. These two-legged "humoids," four-legged "neanders" and bright red demons are all wonderfully childlike in their portrayal, with simple dollar signs and stars on the bellies of vendors and commanders, respectively. I thought the simplicity of the graphics would put me off, but after about fifteen minutes of gameplay I fell in love with the world.
And gameplay is really the redeeming factor here. No, the stat system doesn't make sense (and is mostly based on failures rather than successes), the leveling system doesn't make sense (your level is determined by the highest-level creature you've killed), and the vehicles are merely a switch from walking to flying with the image of a ship HUD plastered across the screen. But damn, is it fun; I had more outright fun with this game than a lot of the AAA games I've played in the past year. In one particularly exciting moment I was charging into the skies after a demon ship, blasting away (weakly) with the ship guns, when a nearby demon annihilated my ship. I started falling through the sky and in a state of panic pulled out my grappling hook, aiming at the nearest thing -- the demon ship. As I flew forward I let go of the grapple and switched to a rifle, sending the ship into an explosive oblivion as I soared through the debris, curving downward toward the planet. "This," I thought, "is fun." Just pure and simple fun; it doesn't take a 1000-person team and a $60 million budget to create fun.... Just a developer named phr00t and the patience to give his game a chance.
This is one of those rare games where the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. On the surface it looks like what you might expect from a one-man indie game (an ambitious one, at that), but if you give it a serious chance and try to beat the game at least one time (a two or three hour venture at most), you'll find yourself enthralled with this creative rendition of the future.

I've been in love with football management sims since the days of
. That's 1992, my friends.
I've never enjoyed one as much as this one.
This game is simple enough to play that you can jump right in and start playing. And if you want a casual experience, you can play this game like that. Don't think too much about your decisions, just pick what feels right. You can do that and have fun.
Or, if you want a more analytical experience, you can take your time over each decision.
You can put your roster into a spreadsheet, plan out which players you will develop and which ones you will sell, and when.
You can crunch the numbers over the tactical decisions in the match. Do I take a shot from long range with my ACC 52 midfielder against his DEF 67 keeper, or is it better if I try a layoff pass through his center back to my forward, who can then try to score with a rainbow feint? You can do the math and figure out which one has a better chance at a goal--and also think about what position you leave the opponent with if you do not get a goal.
In other words, you can play this game hardcore, and try to make the best decisions all the time (even though many of the decisions will defy exhaustive analysis), or you can play by the seat of your pants, and try to win by instincts. It is a remarkable acheivement to have created a game that can satisfy both types of play styles.
As of the date of this writing (April 29 2016), the game still has the Early Access tag, but it is really a complete game.
The developers are adding additional features, but there isn't anything missing.

T: ToN is a great game and a worthy successor to the Torment name. The strengths and flaws of the two games are pretty similar, so if you're looking for an immersive, story (text) heavy game to explore and think your way through, here it is.
+ The world and characters within it are fantastic, it's easy to immerse yourself in a place that feels alien setting-wise but familiar mechanics-wise. This is the thing I love most that both Torment games share.
+ The writing and quests are overall very good. The quests react pleasingly to the different ways you can solve them and the descriptions and dialogue are often thought-provoking and fun. There are times when a little too much text is dumped on screen without much other interaction, but if you don't enjoy reading you wouldn't be playing a writing-heavy RPG in the first place. People who are complaining about "reading a book"... what the hell did you expect?
~ The combat is solid, but not wonderful. I did run into a couple of bugs in combat (I didn't encounter any outside of it) which was annoying, but eh. I expect a few bugs in a game this size. I actually enjoyed the turn-based combat here more than the Real-Time-with-Pause of Pillars of Eternity, which surprised me a bit, being a big oldschool IE fan (BG, BG2 etc).
- It's quite easy. The combat and skill checks are at least reasonably challenging to begin with if you avoid sleeping while you do all the first town quests like I did, but after that there's not anything that took more than an attempt or two to ace. I don't really play narrative games for a heavy skill test though, I play for the story and setting. Making the moral and investigative choices in dialogue is where the "difficulty" lies in my mind.
- Yes, the final act ends a bit abruptly and the game is a little shorter than I'd like, but it's not worth getting bent out of shape about. 64 hours for a methodical runthrough of an RPG seems decent enough to me. I don't care what budget the game had or where that came from, I care if the game is fun and (in my mind) worth the money, and this one is.
If you're the sort of person who likes investigating all the nooks of a game before moving on, this one has plenty of fun to discover. People wanting a more mechanics-heavy challenge or who get bored reading long chains of dialogue, then yeah, stay away.

Mad Max is a great game, the graphics, driving around in the wastes, working on your car, the survival elements, they all work beautifully. The best part being the car combat, the handling also feels very nice and the weapons available on the cars are also fun to use.

You will spend most of your time doing simple combos and parries. The bossfights were also a big letdown, they are all identical, they share the same model and moveset only difference being that they have different weaknesses.
I would have liked they focused more on the driving aspect, maybe have the bosses drive unique cars on the road similar to the convoys that are in the game but with more depth and special mechanics. Even simple exploration would work just fine if not better whilst driving the car as seen in the missions taking place in the underdune where you have to avoid traps or in the tunnels where you salvage a train carriage with your car.
The car customization could have used some more options but its enough to keep you busy in a casual playthrough and the plot will not win any awards but it will keep your attention and has some memorable characters and moments.
The passing years have given us a lot of great open world games. Mad Max is one of them, It's a treat to explore the world for the first time, the vistas are amazing and the world itself is filled with tons of interesting locations and side activities.
The game is totally worth the €20 and even more when its on discount.

*** Yes, but set your expectations accordingly ***
I'll adress this review in particular to fans of this game's spritual predecessor, Planescape Torment.
While it would be unfair to call this a bad game, it does feel like a shadow of what it could have been, to say nothing of how it stacks up against the masterpiece whose legacy it was trying to live up to, Planescape Torment.
While the writing is mostly good throughout, I felt a distinct lack of the humour, quirkiness, and freshness of the title that this game is trying to imitate. It seems like this game is trying to hit many of the same keynotes that PST hit, but done without the same sense of confidence and originality. For as much as the game boasts about the word count in its script, I never felt as connected to any of my companions as I did to Morte or Fall from Grace. That's not to say that the characters your meet aren't interesting at all, but it seemed like the devs were more focued on breadth rather than depth as far as your interactions with other characters. This extends to the antagonists of the story, which felt drawn similiar yet less compelling than the antagonists of Planescape Torment.
I think what the devs missed about Planescape Torment is that for all that game's (excellent) philisophical musings, they lost sight of the fact that some of the most memorable moments of that game were the humourous banter between your companions, the bizarre and quixotic situations you found yourself in. Remember getting sucked into a Modron Maze, or engaging in philosphical debates with a reformed succubbi in a brothel for quenching intellectual lusts? None of that here, I felt as if the game takes itself too seriously ( or more likely didn't have the dev time) for such interesting diversions.
There is a distinct lack of polish throughout. While the digitally painted backgrounds for the most part are creative with a wonderful sense of art direction, I wish I could say the same for the character models and sound design. I also find it odd that there's no option to customize the look of your character aside from choosing a gender, and the lack of character portraits for the people you're talking to in dialogue seems a strange omission.

A great game to pick up and spend a weekend playing, Heavy Bullets is what every roguelike FPS should try to be: a game that rewards many playstyles in interesting ways. From the slow methodical approach to the quake-like run and gun, every playstyle has items that back it up, but aren't powerful enough to do anything but support you. There aren't any items in this game that could be considered a 'crutch' or a 'run-winner' in contrast to other roguelikes such as The Binding of Isaac where runs are heavily affected by what items you find. In Heavy Bullets it's largely up to you to conserve your health and hit your shots accurately. This game rewards skill quite heavily, allowing you to attempt to make skillful decisions to get yourself out of a rough situation, such as shooting enemy rockets or grenades out of the air. All of this sounds great on paper, however the way the camera moves in this game can sometimes be rather sluggish and other times seem a bit too fast, and the game itself is rather poorly optimized, I often get dips in FPS in the later levels which can greatly interfere with my aim when it happens. Other than that, I believe the pros of this game greatly outweigh the cons.

The gameplay itself is a typical third person shooter affair, with just enough variation to not get boring. It plays very much like the action scenes in Mass Effect, without the 'magic' parts ofcourse (ME also has a longer and better story). But ofcourse to make it feel like a movie the game also very much feels like a on-rails shooter, you do have freedom to move where you want yourself, you're just playing out parts of the movie, what you do or how you do it has little effect on the story, and although there are choices to be made along your path of destruction, i don't think they matter much in the end. You will get to the menu screen and hear music playing and then the screen appears to be hanging. This can last for several minutes, just be patient and wait, once it gets through everything will work just fine. This is the only slowdown/hang i ever had in the game.
Buy this game if you like playing interactive movies, but paying full price may not be worth it.

I Think you either love or hate this game, everyone's different. This game will either infuriate you to an unnatural level, or be the most fun fast paced side scrolling platformer you've ever played. For me, i absolutely love this game. Team Meat! Really hit it out of the park with this one, this game definitely has brilliant reviews and awards for a reason.
For starters, it is you're average "save the damsel in distress" game, but with unique and amazing gameplay.
You have short little cut scenes that expand the situation after every stage, and then you're thrown straight into this fast paced side scrolling platformer. You can race against the clock to see how good of a rating you can get or leisurely bounce throughout the level at your own pace. For every "A+" rating you get, you unlock that level in the "dark world" which is essentially hard mode. I felt that in each level, to get that A+ rating, every jump and every move you make has to be precise and timed perfectly. A hell of a lot of the times, you're life depends on it. you can expect to die in this game many many times, but the respawn is quick as lightning, usually in games if i die and i have to sit around to respawn again I’ll get agitated, but you're back up as quickly as you were taken down, ready to try that level again. Some levels are complicated and only having one life to complete it really gets your heart rate going, for me the pressure makes it all that much more fun, dodging blades, saws, missiles, monsters, lava and much more as the game progresses, it starts to become a real challenge.
There’s also a fun little system of collectables you can use to unlock new characters and “retro” levels. Each of the characters have different abilities that can help you in harder levels.
You are meat boy, a boy made of meat, and your girlfriend is bandage girl. It’s gross but weirdly sweet, as I’ve heard before in an interview the developer did, that meat boy’s skinless body makes him vulnerable and bandage girl protects him. (Even though he's doing the rescuing) meat boy fights to get that back.
Anyone familiar with Edmund Mcmillens work will recognise the brilliant art style a mile off, his games really take you into the mind of the developer, the crazy ideas he comes up with could only be a work of Edmunds.
The Music in this game is amazing, and the way it plays so smoothly throughout your stay is great, when you die, it doesn’t stop or restart, it’s not painfully repetitive and it fits well with the setting. It really adds to the experience, hectic fast paced music for a hectic fast paced game, it’s great. I even went as far as to add the soundtrack to my collection of music.
I could talk forever about how highly I think of this game, but hopefully I’ve said enough for it to be something people would consider trying, all in all, it’s a great game, and if you don’t want to pay full price, buy it when it’s on sale. It’s worth the time and money put into it, but again… if you are someone with a short fuse, and can see this game getting on your nerves, maybe it isn’t for you. You will either love it or hate it.

Let's start by comparing this game to a "lightweight Bloodbowl with better AI" and say I don't usually play heavy simulation games like Football Manager. So far, the gameplay is fun but lacks in depth for a strategy title. I would normally give a positive review for this game in early access, but I want to counter balance the very positive reviews it has so far, since I believe this game to be worth 80% positive votes instead of 94% (at time of this writing) with its current "depth". It does the job well as a soccer team simulation, my review focuses more on the "strategy" aspect of its categorization. If you like simulating games and managing a team, then I would bet this game is perfect for you. If you like levelling up your goons and playing deeply strategic games, especially turn based ones then keep reading.
I enjoy playing it casually so far and after 7 hours I can say the difficulty curve increases with advancement. But not in a "strategies become more important" kind of way. It's all about my forward's accuracy vs the defenders defense. Wish me luck ! To be honest, I still have to fully realize the depth of strategical option, since I did about 4 seasons (with 3 different teams), so I haven't tried all the skills yet ... but right now I can only say, strategy in this game is very streamlined and the one best option is easy to identify with no reason I would stop spamming it in hopes of getting more goals. Basically, there's no real "setting up for the goal" since it comes down to getting the ball to the forward, get him as close as possible to the goal and shoot: from there, it's a skill throw for the shot and it's always boiled down to probabilities. I can score through 3 defenders on the other team if they are amateurs ... or it is impossible to score in season 2 against 3rd league teams until I have taken enough losses that my players have leveled up (which isn't the problem for me but a reality in this game).
By changing a few mecanics, this title could become a very, very good turn based strategy title with light RPGs elements. But then it would become a lot more time consuming I guess, since they would have to give more actions, make actions harder, passes shorter, having other adjacent allies provide support automatically while having adjacent opposing players provide pressure automatically making actions harder, provide appropirate skills for all new concepts, etc. which would make games longer through the system AND mking you think about each move, to set the best probabilities for your actions.
Conclusion: a negative review due to lack of depth in actual match gameplay. A good simulation title. Will play it casually and adjust review to a positive one if more depth is added to playing the game vs simulating it and making it more about team development.

Football Tactics is quite a decent casual game that you can pick up anytime and/or get addicted to.
The game mechanics work on a simple duelling premise between two players across 4 player stats (Accuracy, Passing, Defence, Control), with the addition of several skills/abilities which can turn the game in your favour.
Being an indie title, obviously there is no licencing for official team/player names, which isn't an issue for me or likely anybody that spent their childhood playing Pro Evolution Soccer. There are a number of things you can upgrade for your club (stadium, scouts, coaches, etc.) to help improve the players you have and club finances. However, it becomes a bit of a grind and there is a lack of variety to the gameplay beyond this.
Overall, it's likely to keep you entertained for a little while, or a bit longer if you multi-task like me and play the game sporadically in addition to doing other things. There's a lot of potential with this title and I would expect "Football Tactics 2" at some point, with development of the current gameplay and a load of additional features.
