3079 is an Open World FPS set on an alien planet where you are sent in to stop a never ending war between two species. At least that's what you’re told to do but upon landing you instantly pick a side of the conflict and work as a mercenary for hire. The species friendly to you at the beginning are the humanoid looking aliens but you can switch sides by killing enough of them to please the other side. It may seem like a good idea to immediately head out of the city and hunt some aliens but as you will soon find out they are soldiers that only know war while you on the other hand are the space equivalent of some random dude running off to the battlefield with a Nerf gun. You will immediately realize how useless you are at fighting at the beginning and it is an important lesson to learn since dying means losing a random item. I say random but most of the times they seem to take away your grappling hook or your most used weapon.

It is a really rough introduction to the game and even if you manage to knick a weapon off of an enemy killed by someone else you will not be able to use it. There is no ammo in this game, instead everything relies on your energy meter and the more powerful a weapon is, the more it uses. At first you may as well be carrying a broken gun as you will not be able to fire off a single round without it overdrawing your energy and harming your health. This game features skills like stealth, energy and charisma to name a few, which get more effective as you use them in a certain manner. Unfortunately the way to improve them are usually insanely tedious. You'd think that by using energy its stat will go up but the way it works in this game is that by using more energy than you have and harming your own health it will eventually increase. Since in the beginning you can barely fire off any rounds at all that means you will spend most of your early adventures staring at a wall and repeatedly firing just to get your energy up. Enemies regenerate health so by the time you have enough to fire again they will be mostly healed meaning you must use the better weapons with heavy energy usage.

Honestly, this energy thing is what harms the game the most and will be a problem for the entire game as you need more and more energy. Stealing is pure RNG and requires you to get caught in order to increase its stats while being hit when you are camouflaged makes you better at Stealth. The progression system is a complete, nonsensical mess sadly and by that logic I'll become a mathematician by failing my math tests. Seems like a petty thing to complain about it but it is honestly no fun and means you only get better by either doing tedious things or getting shot in the face. The only thing you really get for killing enemies is their weapons to sell to a vendor later on. Vendors are the same as any other alien but with a ”$” symbol on their shirt. You could buy useful objects from them like grappling hooks, armor or generators that increase your stats while active. These generators can have some rather cool effects such as increasing your jump height enough to be able to jump houses and walls which makes you feel pretty awesome as you take down several enemies midair.

You can tell any none busy ally to follow you around and gather up your own posse to hunt down the enemy if you so please. It is a really handy feature, especially early in the game when you are pathetically weak. The AI is not all that great so they are only useful in open fields, don't expect to be rescued while in buildings. AI is embarrassingly bad for the spacecraft that fight like if you had a giant magnet to your face and will stick right on you until one of you is dead. You can attempt to hijack which is a pretty cool feature and lets you zoom around the skies though it is rather weak and likely to get you killed if used in a fight. It's also a bad idea to go too far out as the further you go the stronger the enemies are. Along with the two species at war there are also demons that look like red gummy bears out to kill everything. These are a very annoying as they will pull you in near them no matter the distance between you two. They are not rare and it is not unusual that you have to fight with the controls just to escape their gravitational pull any time you want to go somewhere.

Demons can only be killed by a very specific kind of sword which brings me with another issue. You can only equip 4 weapons or items to the hot-keys at any one time. The rest of your number keys are useless and you will always want to have the demon sword and grappling hook equipped so you only have two hotkeys to work with. This adds completely unnecessary micromanagement whenever you need something else like a satchel charge, your drill or your construction tool. You can mine the randomly generated world for gems though they offer very little money compared to simply scavenging guns from a battlefield. This game does feature destructible environments but only with the satchel charge unfortunately. Building your own base is possible but ultimately pointless as the point of the game is to move further and further out into the map while staying in a low level area is useless.

Grappling hooks in this game are a ton of fun to use and have a pretty long range making you feel like a mix of Spider Man and Rambo as you quickly navigate the environments. There is an anti-gravity device that allows you to float around at the cost of not being able to recharge your energy. It is really useful for reaching the floating buildings and did lead to an insanely awesome moment where I was near death & surrounded at the edge of a cliff, jumped off and managed to activate it a few feet from the ground. 3079 does have its moments and incredible potential but seems to sabotage itself at every turn. Like the previously mentioned grappling hooks an anti-gravity device can only support a certain amount of weight from your inventory. It sounds reasonable enough but as you head to a higher level area which happens quite often, everything starts weighing more and more. That's not anything unusual in video games but it feels so artificial here where even the health packs start weight over 30 pounds. One area will have a grappling being sold with up to 400lbs usability and the next one will have one with 440lbs. You don't think “Wow, I can carry more now!” instead you're feel the need to facepalm as everything suddenly gets heavier in order to make your gear obsolete  time and time again.

You receive missions from allies with stars on their chest but they are rarely worth the price. There are main missions that revolve around the fight against demons and you will need to do at least one of those to get yourself a demon slaying sword. At the end of the day 3079 implements a ton of ideas into one package but fails to make the overall product fun. As an example you turn on your night vision and grapple onto the top of a tall tree with a sniper rifle to take down some enemies. Multiple things keep this from being fun. For one your night vision goggles only pick up enemies of a certain level so you will have to keep buying new ones every time you enter another area until you can't be bothered. Second your sniper uses up a ton more energy while using the scope yet has no added damage, so you may as well use it without the scope which defeats the purpose of a sniper. And finally, it is not unlikely there will be a demon in sight that will cause you to fight with the controls just to keep your footing in the tree even if it is far away and unaware of you. 3079 has a ton of ideas and a ton of heart no doubt but I'm afraid its progression system, annoying mechanics and combat heavily hampered by energy make this a game I simply can't recommend.

Playing this is both very enjoyable and incredibely frustrating. It's a somewhat difficult first person shooter with a bunch of RPG elements. Procedural generation and randomized aspects, such as algorithmic quests and unscripted faction battles that will certainly change the topography of the map, give the game a majestic feeling and some replay value. At that appraisal, I should have nothing but love for this game, but unfortunately it frequently dips into the realm of taking otherwise good ideas and implementing them in the most extreme, unenjoyable ways.
For example, simply starting a new game is a matter of chance, as the starting equipment you receive may not match your play style, and it is very easy to die in the beginning of the game even with desirable inventory, often due to low-damage, low-accuracy weapons. Meanwhile, enemies get very accurate weapons that are often scaled far better than your own. 99% of better weapons can be found on dead enemies.
If you survive your first several hours, you will discover that the difficulty and shop scaling is based on how far away you go from the initial spawn point. This makes some sense, to keep the player from constantly being bombarded by overpowered baddies, but it also turns the beaten paths into a tedious slog with little reason to ever backtrack, except maybe for a quest.
The difficulty is the most noticeable problem, however. Apart from inaccurate guns, there is also the constant issue of rules that just don't apply to enemies, but do apply to the player. Enemies don't get hurt by their own explosions. Their ships never crash. Friendly fire is off for them.
The biggest problem is the punishment for dying. Upon death, the player loses one random item, and this can absolutely cripple a character build if the item in question is particularly useful. For example, if I die and lose a powerful antigrav pack, which allows the player to fly, then replacing it with an equally strong pack requires a trip back to the intense enemy territory where can be found the only stores which sell items that useful. In the worst case I had, it was a 20 minute round trip. Long story short, the punishment for dying is really just that, punishment, not really fun or interesting at all. I did find a bit of a way to circumvent this, by filling my inventory with crap that I don't mind using, but, surprise surprise, I can't fly like that either.
As much as I've complained about it here, this game is actually quite worth the money. It's addicting, and it provides a decent level of depth. There are the parts that make me want to tear my hair out, but that's balanced out by fun.

The game is fun but gets stale too quickly. I gave up on the story after it asked me to take down a borg cube-lookalike demon ship with a flying vehicle that explodes after just one hit and me trying that for an hour. The demon ship requires like I-don't-know-how-many hits as it keeps healing back up and I can't avoid not get hit long enough while I evade enemy fire from multiple sources at the same time. I assume this is likely me doing it just wrong.
I kept walking West instead as I noticed earlier enemies become stronger if you keep walking, hoping to find a vessel that lasts more than one hit, but nope. I bought armor instead, did some of the neverending skirmishes around town, sold all loot I didn't need, walked West again, more skirmishes, shiny new weapon... and so on and so on, until... till after everything was around level 80 and capable of killing me in like two hits - that's because of the way your character improves: it gets better as stats and abilities are frequented. So, if you don't take damage from enemies as you move up in levels your max life won't increase. This requires you to stay in an area, work on your skills (as in take damage on purpose, for example) and only then move on.
It doesn't help when you think, you could just travel far for a shopping tour, come back and enjoy the game that way. Yes, you can do that but the progress remaining is the progress itself. If you can make it far and survive somehow in higher areas there's no point in going back as everything from back there is also right where you are - always. Except the little Minecraft-ish things you can build, like /home, chests, lamps and a few blocks. THAT does not move with you.
Then it came to me: This isn't going to stop, it keeps on rising, so yeah, 3079 is incremental!? I bet, someone already made a Youtube video of how far he could make it and end up in like level 3400 with 12400 stamina, or something. It wouldn't surprise me. As someone who's played Planescape: Torment many times over the years, I've been excited about this game since I first heard about it.  In general I can recommend it on its own terms, and I think that, for the most part, though it does not quite live up to its ancestor's greatness, it does solidly fulfill expectations of existing PS:T fans.
Pros:
- The degree to which the Ninth World and its denizens are fleshed out and given life is marvelous.  The writing is mostly very good, and occasionally even better than that.  Some of the descriptions manage to find novel ways of conveying impressions and events, which reflects not only on the skill of the writing team but their dedication, in whole or in part, to truly evoking the gameworld.
- Several of the companions are highly memorable.  I've only done one playthrough so far, so I haven't been able to fully explore all of the companion interactions (I only used 4 of the 6 extensively).
- The visuals are great.  The backgrounds are static and pre-drawn, but the detail, variety and outright strangeness on display bring a heavy dose of the weird to the proceedings.  In many ways, graphics such as these, done right, are more evocative, more creative and more detailed than ultra-realistic, 3D graphics.
- Lots of quests, some big, some quite small.  All of them display an attention to detail and self-contained emotional impact that makes them worth completing.  The general story and arc of the game is also compelling and evokes many of the same issues and tropes that made its antecedent so wonderful.
- The game system is easy to learn, flexible and, unusually for an RPG, gave me no headaches with regard to the UI or its implementation.
- The music is mostly electronic and ambient in nature, but does an excellent job of setting the mood in the various locations in which you find yourself throughout the game.
Cons:
- I didn't run into a ridiculous amount of bugs, but I did experience crashes every so often; 6 or 7 times if I'm remembering correctly.  All required a forced closure and restart of the game.  Most of the crashes happened only shortly after I'd saved, but a couple happened several minutes into extended combat/crisis situations, resulting in my having to replay a fair bit of dialogue and fighting/evasion afterward.  It's not gamebreaking, but its definitely frustrating.
- The game is, as RPS noted, slightly artificial in its feel.  It was definitely designed with a specific audience in mind, and while this can lend a game focus, it also constrains the margins and limits of what the game will or will not be.  PS: T felt organic - Black Isle made the game they wanted to make, and they hoped there would be an audience for it.  This game feels a bit more like a product crafted to meet demand.  As such it doesn't leap out at you with new and fresh insights and experiences the way its predecessor did.
- The story while multi-threaded and satisfying, is still essentially about how you try to defeat the menacing bad guy.  This makes it feel a bit more traditional than PS:T.  Likewise, much of the mystery lies in determining the motivations of others, rather than in self-discovery.
- Not enough combat.  And before you say, "But it's not about mindless fights!  And neither was PS:T!", I'l go ahead and make clear that I know that.  But where PS:T was ~65% story, 35% fighting, T:ToN is, if you avoid unnecessary violence, 85% combat free.  These are rough %, but the point is the same.  I'm glad it focuses on story, interactions, quests, puzzles, etc.  But the game plays this virtue almost to a fault.  I had so many cyphers and awesome weapons and armor, and only got sparing use out of it.  It is possible to play a bloodier playstyle, but it still doesn't seem that it would shift the ratio that dramatically.
- Too easy.  Once your main character has enough edge and stat pool boosts, you're basically going to succeed at almost eveyrthing.  Since your companions can also use their stats to help, by the time you're 40% through with the game, or so, barring failure to rest or bring refresh items with you, you're not going to fail many, if any, skill checks.  It's a testament to the story, world and lore that despite this the game remains compelling, but some additional difficulty would have been nice.
Conclusion:
In a game like this, story and characters are king, so those elements win out over concerns about difficulty and lack of combat.  That said, you can't just ignore the flaws.  There are some things that may turn some folks off and, potentially because it tries so consciously to ape its forebear, it falls short of the greatness of PS:T.  That said, after completing it today, I felt that pang of regret and sadness at knowing the journey was over, the one you feel when you finish a particularly great book or game, and I'm already thinking over when I'll play through it again.  I think T:ToN is a very good to great game that falls short of true excellence, and would recommend it to those who loved PS:T (despite the noted differences), and those who love CRPGs in general, especially if story is of critical importance.

I keep finding myself in disagreement with the "majority" of RPG fans, so maybe I'm not as much an RPG gamer as I thought to be.
This game feels like that part of an RPG, for which the developers didn't get funding, but re-e-eally wanted to squeeze in. The obvious drawback here is that it doesn't contain any other compelling parts... The writers worked real hard trying to bind the storylines to one another and cross-reference everything with everything, but I feel that it cost them that much more effort for barely any benefits - looking back, I still would describe most of my time in the game as dull, even if I acknowledge the craftsmanship.
The major "plot twists" were nothing but obvious, and the ending brings back memories of Mass Effect 3. I shiver at the thought of ever attempting a second playthrough, and from now on will be even more suspicious of any review hype-train that claims a game "earned its place in the old-school pantheon"...
P.S. The sporadic and therefore tediously long combat sequences regularly froze on enemy movements; exchanging items between your companions lead to duplicates, cyphers placed in inventory slots, inability to sell items etc. As is tradition, the closer I got to the ending, the more bugs surfaced when attempting anything but the "most predictable path". So, I guess if you're sensitive to that sort of thing, I'd probably hold off on the purchase.
It's been a long time since Planescape, and maybe my perception is clouded by those wonderful memories, but nothing in here is even close to as good.  Read a book, it's more satisfying and cheaper.

I recommend this game, because overall I did like it, but there is no escaping the fact that it was a big let-down.  Planescape: Torment was one of my favorite games of all time, so when I learned that it was getting a sort of sequel-in-spirit, made by many of the same people, I was very excited.  Then came the waiting.  I have no information about what was going on behind the scenes, but it seems obvious that there must have been serious development troubles, because this game was announced in March 2013 with a scheduled release date of December 2014, but didn't come out until February 2017.  I started and finished law school, passed the bar exam, and started working at a law firm in that same interval.  If I had not had to wait so long, I would not have been so disappointed.
The other problem is that this game is inferior to Planescape: Torment in most respects.  P:T had a more interesting story with more interesting characters.  I really cared about my companions in P:T.  They were traveling with me for a reason.  My companions in T:ToN were just sort of there.  With the exception of Matkina, none of them had particularly good reasons to follow me around.  And none of them, except Rhin, had interesting stories or personal quests.  I also found the main character's story to be much less interesting.  In P:T, TNO had this gripping personal saga, and it was just that: personal.  TNO was confronting his own mortality.  He had to learn from his past mistakes.  In T:ToN, the LCO was just being chased by this poorly thought-out monster for not much reason (once you find out what it is and where it came from, it becomes clear that the Sorrow is little more than a weak imitation of a Mass Effect Reaper).  Again, though, what hurt this game for me was the high expectations I had for it.  I was expecting another experience like P:T, and I didn't get it.
Why then, if I was so disappointed, am I giving this game a thumbs-up?  Because it was actually a fairly solid journeyman effort.  As long as you go into it with moderate expectations, this is a reasonably enjoyable game.  Far from greatness, but still decent.  It has an interesting setting and competent storytelling.  It is definitely on the easy side, although there are a few serious challenges.  I had hoped for a lot more, but it's still an enjoyable game.

Despite it's many flaws, I still recommend this game... but if you get it on sale.
This game will draw comparisons to two games: Planescape Torment, and Pillars or Eternity. The former is in terms of spiritual succession & writing whilst the latter is in terms of technological performance & gameplay.
Compared to P:T - it's not as spolished, feels a bit incoherent at times, and I think the companions aren't that interesting. The story is more of an interactive novel with not much impact on the world and quests that can be solved quite easily (a few just by going to the next map and talking to someone).
Compared to PoE - I hate the "crises" combat in this game. It's awful and makes me realise why Obsidian went with pausable real time combat, rather than with turn based. But luckily most of the compbat in this game can be avoided which is nice. The maps in TToN feel a lot smaller, but on the plus side have a lot more 3D assets with things actually happening (i.e. light arks, water dripping, light pulsating, etc) whilst PoE felt like playing on a painting.
So I seem to have been quite negative compared to both P:T and PoE, so why the recommendation? I feel that I got enough enjoyment out of this game to warrant buying it on a sale. Some of the quests were quite interesting, the world artwork / 2D assets were very qurky, and (very) few times it made me laugh.
FYI: even thought it says Ive played it for 2 hours, I've played it offline for 47 hours and done every quest I could find.

It was a flawed, but ultimately enjoyable experience. The world is strange and beautiful, the characters all have a quirk to them. There's a lot of high-fantasy/absurd stuff going on around you. The dialogue and writing are generally enjoyable.
The core system is extremely hackable. This tends to be balanced by combat scenarios throwing "more of them" at you. It's kinda laden with philosophy: the core theme is kinda bland, but there are more than a few interesting peripheral themes.
I enjoyed this game because of its details; the world was just constrained enough to direct my exploration in a way that felt organic. I may play it agin?

I played this game after going back and completing Planescape: Torment and, honestly, it's very very loosely attached to it. The only things that a taken from that are a few vague themes. I'm not complaining about that at all because this game stands up on its own.
As with every game like this, the main upsides are going to be the story and the characters. The characters and their development were done very well. Each person has their own unique feel and you do genuinely get drawn into their own stories, none moreso (for me) that Rhin.
The story, on the other hand, was pretty bare bones but I feel it was more a vehicle for the characters and it was interesting to a point.
The look of the game is also great, lending a lot to the themes and the different ages of history that you're told about. The cyphers and esoteries (spells) are also quite cool and well animated.
Now for a few gripes I had. Firstly, the voice acting. The quality itself was fine, as you would expect from a higher budget indie game but the amount was quite disappointing. You expect to have voice acting all along the main storyline in games like this but, even when you would expect it, it wasn't there. For example, the last encounter of the game had no voice acting.
Secondly, there is A LOT of text. I feel like these 2 points are linked but I feel this would turn off a lot of people.
Finally, the combat mechanics were a bit poor. I feel like it would have benefited from a system with disengaging strikes and other things from the game Tyranny.
Overall, it's a great, interesting game with a hell of a lot of character and you can just tell the devs loved making it.
If you like story, grab it. If you like old school CRPGs, why haven't you already got it?

As an early backer, it ends up this is not my kind of game, it plays more like an interactive novel than an RPG.  So far other than a single battle (in addition to the tutorial one), all I've done is walk around the same 2 areas and spoken with a ridiculously large number of NPCs.  They've given me a good number of quests, which are also solved by walking around and talking to the same NPCs over and over until you get new dialogue options.  Not to mention with skills linked to persuasion/deception you can simply talk your way out of any situation.

pro:
* great storytelling
* mind-blowing setting
* great quests, with many different possible endings
* no good/bad morality system, rather an five-different-affinities system, which allows also for mixed affinities (are you e.g. more the knowledge-seeker, or more the narcissist, ...)
* good-looking and good-sounding game (for my taste)
con:
* combat can feel a bit clunky, in particular since there are chances to miss attacks.
All in all, this is a great rpg in the spirit of Baldurs Gate. If you are into that sort of thing (including reading a *lot* of text), then this is your game. I love it! It is rather slowly paced, though, so if you get bored easily, then this might be not for you. I don't like the combat, but then again you can talk (or sneak) your way around many encounters, without missing too much, in particular it is not the killing of enemies which gives XP, but the resolution of problems (and acquisition of knowledge).

Let me preface this by saying I'm not an absolute hardcore sim-racer - I don't have a wheel or a racing rig, I just play driving games using an XBOX One controller. PCARS, DiRT Rally, Race 07, etc, etc - I own and play them all.
WRC 5 is rough around the edges, but with some TLC I think the game could go from good to great. It's not DiRT Rally, but it's also not awful. It's not another Milestone travesty, so we don't have to worry about garbage like the sound dropping out after two stages.
I'll start with the bad:
- Robotic co-driver: You do get the option of a woman co-driver, but both male and female options are spliced from sound clips rather than smooth pace notes like DiRT Rally or Dirt 2 / 3. It's not bad (and the pace notes are effective), but it's something to note.
- Poor engine sounds: The cars sound like toys.
- No actual routes: The courses are approximations of the real locations. It's close, but it's not the actual course.
- Wheel support: There's a limited set of supported wheels.
And now for the pros:
+ Classes: Junior WRC, WRC 2 and WRC. You get a good selection of classes and cars, plus all the licensed drivers and gear.
+ Career mode: The team stats are slightly randomized so you get a good selection of goals to choose from.
+ Stages: 5 unique stages and a repeat per rally, usually in a 2-2-2 format. The stages aren't terribly long, but they are fun to drive. Finland's scary at night.
+ Challenge mode: The MP challenge mode is pretty fun. Time trials on a specific stage using a specific team.
Reasonably, hard-core sim racers aren't going to like this. It's a balance of arcade racing and sim racing, using a real-world license. If you want a nice introduction to rally racing, this is a good place to start. It's better than WRC 4 (which isn't saying much, admittedly, but it's a marked improvement and is a decent little racing game).
7/10 - needs some work, but is playable and fun.
EDIT 2015-10-14: Patch 1.03 helped with the variable framerate and set DX11 as the primary launch mode, rather than DX9. I adjusted the cons to remove the framerate issues and upped my score to 7/10. The game still needs work, but it's not bad.

For me, this game doesn't live up to its praise.
What I will praise the developers for, however, is the interesting art direction. I like the color choices made; they successfully captured the clashing beauty and chaos of the war-torn desert environment. Although I appreciated the visuals and great voice acting, the campaign is short and lacks replay value other than going back to collect achievements. Gameplay is average and mostly involves blasting enemies head-on.
Most importantly, the actual story wasn't as gripping, guilt-inducing, and thought provoking as the developers had purported. They wanted to show players that their actions had consequences, but... they really didn't. The game was linear, and pivotal choices simply amounted to earning an achievement whether you went with Option A or B. I was expecting to be forced to make decisions between different, but equally horrible, options.  In my opinion, this would have been more impactful in providing a tacit explanation of Walker's psychological breakdown than the cliche representation that was later revealed. To be fair, I did feel horrible at two points in the game after some "bad" decisions you are forced to take.
Consequently, the reveal of Walker's downward spiral seemed stereotypical and unnecesarily "artsy" to me. It severely detracted from my understanding of the chronological events of the game and made me impatient to get to the end. I knew what angle they were going for, but it gave me an unsatisfactory grasp of what actually happened in the time I invested into this game.

Plot

Gameplay
In this game, you need to have quick reactions to flick to your enemies, tiny black balls with ferocious teeth that sprint at you at Mach 10 speed. You also need to pay attention to detail, there are tiny worms that blend into the bushes that can quickly kill you and have ended all of my runs so far. There are also turrets, which you have to strafe to avoid, while getting close enough to drop a bomb to disable them. You can also save money in the bank for other runs, which allows you to have more money later to purchase things like health, life insurance, bullets, mines, all the good stuff.
Graphics
Very nice graphics, neon vibe. I have a 8192MB ATI Radeon RX 480 Graphics (XFX Pine Group), so I don't really experience any lag playing this game. Very nice art style, can't get enough of it.
Should I Buy the Game?
yes. oh my gosh yes. This game is absolutely lovely. The graphics, the gameplay, all of it really comes down to replayability. This is the type of game that you can replay over and over, without getting discouraged, hoping to get to the next floor. I recommend this game to anyone who likes fast paced, neon, unforgiving, punishing, insanely difficult games that have an extremely high replayability factor.

An indoor hunting grounds complex has been hacked, and the turrets are now as hostile as the weird wildlife. As one of many disposable janitors, you've been assigned to go through the eight floors and clear them until you reach the mainframe and reset it.
Your giant revolver shoots oversized bullets that you then go and pick up and use again. That means each shot has to count. It also means if you shoot an enemy far away, you have to walk over there to pick up the bullet.
You'll be dying a lot. Being the dedicated employee that you are, you can collect the gold coins that enemies drop and stash them in ATMs  so the next poor sucker has a better chance of purchasing upgrades and clearing more floors.
Taken at face value, Heavy Bullets is a simplistic roguelike FPS. But once you've played a few lives, you start seeing the depth of the gameplay. I'm not experienced with roguelikes and usually I don't like them much, but it's all about playing the long game. Giving each run your best shot, but also planning ahead in case you don't make it all the way.
You'll be finding or purchasing upgrades such as a coin or bullet vacuumer, spare bullets, rockets, an Aliens-style motion detector, speed boots, health potions and much more. You have to decide whether to hoard your gold or go all out. Maybe you'll do a few "farming" runs where you just stash as much gold as possible, and then do a proper run to clear the game. And since you can only carry one special item with you at a time (unless you get the Backpack upgrade), you have to decide what to keep and what to dump.
One negative is performance. Mostly the game runs butter smooth, but despite the simple graphics I get a random stutter every now and then, on my GTX 980. Doesn't make sense, and can ruin an entire run in game like this that relies on split-second reflexes.
Also, watch out for the snakes in the bushes. Those ♥♥♥♥ing snakes.

I cannot stress enough how incredible this game is.
Pros:
-simple gameplay that almost anyone can pick up
-Instantly lovable characters
-Reminiscient of classic games, like Pokemon and Earthbound
-An engaging story
-CHOICE; not a single person has to die in this game. Which means every time you DO kill someone, that blood is on your hands
-CONSEQUENCES: choosing to murder without care can lead to permanent consequences, especially on Steam. ANY action you take in this game has an effect on the story. Your actions have consequences, and not all of them can be taken away by deleting your save file... be warned. If you murder everyone, and then restart the game, you may find that not everyone's forgotten what you did...
-Depth, and attention to detail. This game has SO MUCH hidden within it that it's virtually impossible to find every secret without either sinking hundreds of hours into it, or joining the online community and watching videos about it. The game really forces you to go off the beaten path. And speaking of...
-Sparing enemies isn't always easy. The game makes a point of the fact that mercy often isn't the easiest road to take. The game will set up rules, and then you will later have to BREAK those rules in order to remain a pacifist.
-Beautiful art, in some areas. Every so often, you enter a certain area of the game that is just stunningly gorgeous. It's amazing how much Toby Fox achieved with pixel art.
-An active fan community. If you enjoy fan content, this game has a TON of it. Sure some of it's terrible, but some of it's also amazing. This game has inspired people to talk, theorise, come together and become artists in their own rights.
-The music is incredible. Seriously, I can't stop listening to the soundtrack.
-Toby Fox has designed this game with multiple endings. In the spirit of that, he has recognised that people won't want to replay the entire game over and over, and made it as EASY as possible to get all endings with minimal replays. He's also made backtracking as easy and fast as possible, given that getting the good ending requires a bit of this.
Of course, no game is without sin. In that spirit, here are my perceived cons:
-The puzzles can be a bit underwhelming. This isn't really a puzzle game; the puzzles are seemingly just there to add extra gameplay that isn't combat based.
-If you don't like classic RPGs, you won't like this. As mentioned earlier, it takes heavy inspiration from Earthbound.
-The fanbase can be annoying, if you let them. It's just because they're REALLY passionate about the game, but it CAN get to you.
-One of the main bosses can get slightly tedious, as you're forced to face them multiple times. However, Toby does try to make each encounter different and interesting.
-There's a harsh difficulty spike between the second and third boss battles. All of a sudden it goes from being very easy to being a LOT harder.
-Some parts of the game are TOO well hidden, and can go completely over your head. I first played this with my partner, and there's a part towards the end where the game closes on you. You have to reopen it, which initially looks exactly the same as every time you open it normally. At that time, we both literally thought that was how the game ended. It took ages for us to realise there was more.
-This game involves a LOT of replaying, especially if you mess up. In order to get the "good" ending, you have to first get the "neutral" ending. Granted, you don't have to replay the entire game - IF you played the game perfectly the first time, you can just reload your save. But that requires knowing in advance how you have to play the first time.
-If you go for the bad ending FIRST, you can permanently lock yourself out of the good ending. And I mean it. PERMANENTLY. Uninstalling your game will not fix it. You can mess with the files to remove the data that causes this change, but from what I've heard if you have the Steam version all that data just gets re added. You basically have to get the good ending FIRST if you ever want it.
All in all, I didn't LOVE the idea of playing this at first; mostly because of the hype train pushing me away from it. But once I gave it a chance, I fell in love. I strongly recommend at least trying it, especially with Steam's generous refund policy. You have very little to lose, as it's a short game, and a LOT to gain.

I thought this would be a case of 'give it some time and it will grow on you' but alas it doesn't seem possible. The description of this game describes it as "THE racing simulation standard". Well, if that is the case, I'm not so sure how someone came to that opinion.
Here is what I PERSONALLY like and don't like.
Pros - WRC Licensing. I love seeing the pros and their cars. Though, I'm not certain the sound effects are spot on. Also, It would be great if there was a better viewpoint inside the car.
Cons - Nothing online worked for me. I'd get errors connecting to the server. Another mode told me there were over 100 days till I could play it online. Well, alright, fair enough. I guess you need a following to promote an e-sport. Sadly I'm not sure there will be one.
Controller Support -
This game is limited in what you can  and can't use. Some of the most popular logitech wheels aren't supported, and you can't use multiple inputs in your setup. It doesn't support clutch pedals, so no manual override.
My current rallying setup includes a shifter, a wheel, a pro 3 pedal setup, and a separate handbrake. It would not read the input from my handbrake at all - only my wheel as a game controller.
Audio - You'll end up wanting to turn off the co-driver voice - which is about the worst thing I can think to do in a rallying game. It's like a robot that doesn't understand word structure or inflection, just belting out words over and over. It's hard to follow and doesn't sound realistic at all.
This game is planted firmly in contemporary rally, which is great if you are into it. however, after playing the game with multiple cars and setups I wasn't able to find anything interesting in trying different cars. There were differences, but not anything noteworthy enough to make the game seem fun.
So that's the big thing for me. If it's not a sim, it should at least be fun. I'd have kept it if it were good at at least one of those things.
Yeah... No support for Logitech G25. Says it all!

For the price and current state of the game, I would strongly suggest keeping your money or buying other rally games such as Dirt Rally. If the game gets patched in the future, this has the potential to be a decent game, but it's not worth the price right now.
The game is an arcade game (which is fine) but it has VERY limited wheel support and the FFB is far from perfect. Car handling and physics just feel awful, while the graphics aren't great considering I have a GTX 780 ti and  i7 4770k.
The game does have some positives, with the full list of WRC rallies/cars included and car damage has been done pretty well. The stages are also decent. But unfortunately the other deficiencies of the game outweight the positives in the current build.

I'll take a bit of a contrarian stance on here to most of the people commenting: I never played PS:T, and I have no familiarity with anything else regarding the game's world or the developer other my experience playing this game. I can respect the people that come in with their expectations and biases, but I'm evaluating the game based entirely on its own merits.
First off, T:ToN is an exceptionally-written game. As many have stated, it's much more an interactive visual novel than it is a classic game -- something, to my understanding, that made PS:T such a cult hit. It is a great surprise to me, then, that there is so much egregious focus in other reviews on the combat mechanics not being this or that. I was recommended the game by a friend who was a big fan of PS:T and backed this game on kickstarter, and he was very upfront about what I should expect based on the developers' history. Nowhere did he mention "damn man, PS:T's real time combat system really sold me the game!" No, it was "hey, you should check this game out, PS:T had an exceptional story and narrative and this game is its spiritual successor."
It should be understood, certainly, that T:ToN is not a conventional game, but I don't think it ever promised itself to be. The entire game is intended to lay out a very detailed world, and build up a compelling story based on very subtle and sequential revelation. Many people complaining about the pacing, I imagine, were expecting to plow through the game with a bunch of combat as you chase down the mystery of the Changing God, and were broadsided by the fact that the game is far more reading than it is fighting. But that's where T:ToN really shines: the developers clearly never intended to make this a fast-paced experience, and you can definitely tell they placed their efforts entirely on developing the strongest narrative possible. The story is central and key -- and yes, that means there are a bunch of characters who are small and irrelevant from a gameplay perspective. But these characters add to the overall depth of the story. NPCs in this game aren't NPCs in the traditional sense: they're narrative delivery devices, and laid out in such a way to add bits of depth to the player who is willing to spend time and effort to explore. You're not going to get Bioware little romance plots or a Beach Scene with the Team, or really detailed Friendship Time Scenes with your companions. Your companions feel extremely real in that regard: they're aren't your friends or pals, they're people who incidentally end up traveling with you for personal reasons.
I won't talk to any points regarding the story in terms of content, as the story is the entire reason you'd play the game. In terms of replayability, though, some have said there is none; to a certain extent this is true, but I think the writing is interesting enough that you a 2nd playthrough is certainly possible and would be enjoyable by making very different decisions from your first playthrough. It was about 25 hours for me to beat the game on a full playthrough doing as much as possible, and I could see another 15-20 on a replay. But, as with most RPGs, this is something I'd do down the line in a couple years' time and not right away.
Does this game have some flaws? Absolutely. I think the stories with the side characters could have been fleshed out a bit more, and I think more effort could have been made to develop a world map to tie in visually tie story events in with the narrative. I really enjoyed the Meres from a storytelling perspective, but felt some of them were a little too abstract tying things in with present time. But most complaints of this nature are minor.
Play this game if you enjoy reading books with good stories. But if you're looking for a gameplay-driven real time action RPG, steer clear. The devs made a niche game that is not going to have a lot of widespread appeal, but they really nailed the niche well. I'll definitely keep my eyes on this company in the future.

Hey Folks,
First of all I would like to give a shoutout to all the wonderful developers over at InXile who made a bold attempt at bringing a true spiritual successor to one of the best RPGs of all time - Planescape Torment.
The road to hell is paved by good intentions...
I have been psyching myself up to do this review for some time now, it's been around a week or so since I finished Torment. Also, I would like to note that I have not been an original backer, though I did pledge around mid 2015 directly on the site. I am highlighting this to mark that I have not been emotionally involved in the Kickstarter process and have no idea about the stretch goals and the subsequent delivery on those.
I have thoroughly enjoyed PS:T back in the days and loved Wasteland 2 even before the directors cut came out, which made all the better.
Pre-game:
I know it sounds a bit stupid, but the Main Menu screen looks like it has been done by High School student. It threw me off whenever I booted up the game. I very much enjoyed the way the game preselected a character type for you based on a series of answers and I actually ended up playing the proposed one. But the lack of appearance customization just plain killed me. I couldn't even choose a portrait!!!
Graphics:
I played on my work laptop with built-in Intel Graphics so I definitely did not have the chance to experience the full power of T:ToN. The backgrounds and environment looked gorgeous, though all of the characters - much less so. And for some strange reason the vast majority of NPCs are actually missing any kind of portrait. Combine this with poorly detailed models, zoomed out screen and literally walls of text you end up feeling like reading a book rather than playing a game. Imagination has to run wild, otherwise there is simply no connection.
General Gameplay:
I actually very much enjoyed the stat pool mechanic, it felt like an interesting and fresh approach. That said the balance is completely off, nanos rule supreme, majority of stat checks are Intelligence and you can actually brute force the rest just by having enough stat pool points available.
I made my playthrough opting for a non violent route and I could I mostly got away with it safe for a few hard coded battles where I could actually resolve them in a nonviolent matter within the Crisis itself. But make no mistake, I did not like those moments or solutions as they felt forced and breaking the pace of the game.
Combat:
Speaking about the pace - any combat is just horribly slow. Every enemy turn took at least 4-5 seconds just to get them moving!!! Having a mage-like characters I never felt underpowered but I was dissapointed with the variety of spells and weapons at my disposal. And the cyphers were just plain dumb - I haven't used a single one during the game. Overall the combat felt like a last minute add-on on top of the game just for the sale of having it without any proper mechanic or item support.
Story:
The overall plot while not a revelation by any stretch of the imagination is decent with a nice twist or two. The companions however are a complete disgrace. There is no romantic interest, the dialogues do not get further than 2 levels down. There is only 1 quest per companion and even those are just solved almost automatically as you clear out the game areas.
The dying mechanic - a cornerstone of PS:T is completely tagged on just for show. It's a struggle even just to get killed, but when you do - it's a small
Labyrinth area with nothing to do there safe for a couple of 10min sidequests of kill/stun them all
The overarching plot itself is far too short, progressing in leaps as you move from one area to the other. I absolutely loved the depth of the world hinted at but T:ToN failed miserably in exploring it. All information is given in walls and walls of text. And don't even get me started on the Meres.
They are just lazy game development. On one hand they require you to do tons of reading and tough choices, without hinting on what is a better/worse one and absolutely NO RETURN. That's right, you need to spend up to half-hour reading, hoping the stat pool check pan out, etc just to have zero impact back in the game. No perks or loot or anything. Initially I thought that after  you finish a mere the respective castoff would appear in the labyrinth. Nope.
Interface:
Is just plain horrible. The text is prevalent up to occupying almost half of the screen when in dialog. The inventory screen is dominated by the cypher section, which almost is useless. The amount of equippable slots on the characters is akin to an action/rpg and the inventory itself is showing no more than 2 rows at a time. Also, during the game you come upon a lot of items, called oddities, which are very confusing as what to do with them. Some you are able to use and even get a permanent bonus, others you can transform to artifacts, some you can actually use in quests.  So it's difficult to tell what you can safely sell. Which in the end is not that much of a problem since anyway there is little interesting to buy.
Summary:
However much I wanted to love it I was very much dissapointed with T:ToN. And it was made even worse because I saw that with just a few shifts in priorities in presentation and story it could've been so much better. The sheer amount of writing has come before everything else. Walls and walls of text meet you everywhere. If some of that effort was spent on expanding the item list, the skills and abilities, the companion quests, the portraits and overall locations  - it would have been a much more enjoyable experience.

I've never been a fan of dating sims because it's so easy to get the result you want. My first two play throughs ended with the guys ditching me for other options. At the time I thought oh, they just don't have happy endings, but it was because I hadn't earned a happy ending. My Dad wasn't a good match. The Dads are written more deeply than their surface appearance and that's why people have developed such a love for them.
I absolutely love that diverse sexuality is made completely normal in this game. No one is surprised about the characters orientation, least of all any of their children. Aside from that, it also puts a very human face on issues that come up in everyday life. After playing through my favourite Daddy's story line and turning to the internet for more content, I learned that the character was designed as trans. At no point did the game ever lead me to believe it (or maybe I just missed it) but I just thought, "Oh cool, that's fine. That doesn't change how I feel, I still love him." Which is kind of the point, isn't it? To know or not know, but to love that friend/colleague/lover anyways, since we're all simply complex people.
Mechanics wise, there's not much to say. Select option, proceed. It's a dating sim, not WoW. The characters are well developed and the story is engaging. The mini games serve to break up any repetition.
In the future I hope for more Daddy building options, like facial hair, a colour selection wheel and some more "serious" clothing options. More Dads would add more content. More mini games, especially references like the Pokemon style one. Part of me wants a "life after epilogue" type deal, but maybe no. Give me more of anything, I'll play it.

Repetitive game that brings little to no innovation to the table, satisfying driving, great performance, but the overall experience is very dull.
You might have noticed that my playtime is still somewhat smaller than the average players, that's because I got burned out on the game very quickly. The last few hours I was just pushing through the main story to see if it goes anywhere it the end. Spoiler, it doesn't. I will admit that one part of the narrative that was enjoyable were Chumbuckets lines during gameplay, that were often funny and told you a bit about the world around.
I didn't find in too enjoyable, or interesting would perhaps be a better word to describe it. The combat is repetitive and basically slower Batman, so it should feel pretty familiar to you. One thing that I very much liked is that your HP doesn'T replenish, instead you need to find water in the wasteland in order to heal up, playing nicely with the survival theme of Mad Max.
The open-world sandbox is what you'd come to expect in most of today's triple A games: replacing quality with quantity. There are colectibles and "side-quests" everywhere, but these are rarely interesting or different from one another. It's nothing but filler.
The driving, which is probably the biggest draw of the game, feels pretty good. Although I dislike the scaling of enemy HP , progression taking way too long and being clearly catered to the massive world filled with collectibles. Another issue is it's very easy to find the optimal approach to vehicle combat (after earning certain upgrades), so it quickly becomes almost a chore and loses the variety that can be found in the early stages of the game.
The game is really stunning, especially during the vehicular combat where you see flaming cars barel-rolling past you in slow motion, it really shines through. It's a great PC port, so you should be able to get it running pretty well even on lower end PCs. With a GTX 1070 and an i5 6600K I was getting easily 60fps in 4K will plenty of breathing space.

The below review I wrote for Tasta.me and can be fully read
.
Hitman has always been a special game for me. The kind of game you have a love/hate relationship with. I absolutely love the idea and the concept behind the Hitman games, it’s brilliant. The stealthiness was core to the series, but the dozen potential ways to eliminate a target was the thing that made it special. But for some reason I always burned out on Hitman after a couple of hours. Why? Even though it’s supposed to be a difficult game, not being able to pull off all the crazy (also, funny) assassinations time after time becomes tiresome and frustrating.
While the last two games (Blood Money & Absolution) were more accessible, I was still failing my mission too many times. Purists probably love the steep difficulty but for a more mainstream audience, the developer needed to up the accessibility while also staying true to their biggest fans. And they did exactly that. But let me take a few steps back first…
When the new Hitman got announced, Square Enix reported that this game would be episodic. No mission packed game at launch, but every month a new big area/mission to be launched to the masses. This allows new players to try Hitman at a lower price since there’s an ‘Intro Pack’ for about 18 bucks with the training, prologue and the first mission included. You can then buy the following episodes separately to your liking. Fans of the first hour were and are still able of course to buy Hitman as a regular game. The new episodes will be downloaded & installed automatically as updates.
People were sceptical when they first announced this system, but we’ve all been proven wrong. It’s working great for this game. At the time of writing, two episodes got released. The first being Paris and the second called Sapienza. The areas are huge and there’s a lot of gameplay to be found in each of the two levels. Being able to come back every month with a fresh area really helps this game. It’s an interesting way to stay relevant across a wider time span.
As mentioned before, the love/hate relationship I had with Hitman has finally been settled. The new Hitman is what I always wanted from a Hitman game. It offers me all the options (and then some) but guides me along the way so I can feel awesome and less frustrated. Don’t worry though, the developer struck the balance between guiding and being too hand-holdy perfectly. Having all the potential opportunities being pointed out when you encounter them in combination with ‘Hitman vision’ to detect enemies & targets, really helps conquer the learning curve. Hardcore Hitman players don’t need to be disturbed though. They can tweak all these systems to their heart’s content, leaving them in control on how difficult the game should be.
It’s not only the gameplay that excells this time around. The game looks magnificent. The first episode in Paris was already a nice looking environment but it’s Sapienza, the second episode that really blew my mind. The area is huge, it looks beautiful and runs great. It’s safe to say that the second episode is a step up from the first one so if you’re not fully convinced after episode one I would recommend giving the second one a try. It’s great on all levels: gameplay, technical and visual.
The one major negative I can say for this game, is the narrative between episodes. There’s a story tying the prologue, episode one and episode two together but it’s conveyed in a very loose manner making it hard to care about it at all. A missed opportunity since the episodic nature of the game could have made story telling in Hitman even more interesting.
Hitman is back in its finest form ever. The game plays great, looks great and has struck the perfect balance between fun, accessibility and challenge. For me it’s by far the best Hitman game to date and one of the best games so far in 2016. Pick up the intro pack for a small price. You won’t regret it.

Although I do not have enough hours on the current iteration of the game to give it a proper review, I will say that I am pleased with the developers and their efforts to dominate the survival game genre. Rust is an unforgiving survival with a focus on PvP and extremely restricted solo play. Some may find that the game lacks in opportunities for solo gamers to thrive and I find this to be a true point. I would not reccommend playing the game if you are a lone player unless you decided to inhabit one of the servers with less of a population. PvE is extremely lackluster, there isn't much of an environmental factor and NPCs are not a difficult challenge to overcome. Gunplay is enjoyable, however, there is room for improvement. Clans dominate servers and are an overwhelming force for many players to overcome. Building is not an aesthetic aspect of the game, the current style allows players to construct some unsightly bases. Overall, I would say that the legacy version of the game was much more enjoyable and immersive. Although the environment is considerably attractive, the game could definitely use some improvement. I would reccommend this game for players that want to engage in intense combat with their friends. I would not reccomend this game for solo players.

First off, I must say that my opinion of this game is severely swayed by my undying love for the past two games. I was really hoping this game could match them, or get close. I can say that this game is absolutely beautiful, well optimized, and definitely worth a playthrough.
However, it absolutely does not live up to the other Arkham games. For some reason the main story feels way too rushed, not to mention short (6 Hours Tops), and the game as a whole seems to rely on the majority of the content being challenge maps. I can enjoy challenge maps, but after playing so much of two other games with the same combat, Im kind of burnt out of just fighting dudes after dudes for no reason.
There were many parts of the game in which I thought were very well done including environmental design, especially inside the buildings, although the city area as a whole seemed dull. Seeing as this is my review, Im am going to tell you why I was upset about this game because of lacking portrayals of two characters:
JOKER: I think troy baker did some good work, but honestly, it was noticeably off, and with the joker I need him to be perfect or I get really sad. His appearance reminded me of a small elf that grew some legs and put on facepaint, but the joker is the joker and I love it just the same.
HARLEEN QUINZEL: This game made me think it would deliver the gripping Harley/Joker backstory in which I love so much, and it even had a build up in the character development, but then it seems they forgot about the whole situation and left it alone. I am still upset that they didnt finish what they started, especially when it comes to my 2 favorite Batman characters.
Overall, the game is enjoyable, but certainly does not live up to its predecessors. If you are playing this game for the story, go ahead, but you may just end up feeling like something is missing. I’m such a big fan of Sports Interactive‘s Football Manager that when Creoteam approached me to cover their Football Tactics game rather than another game that I was hoping to feature developed by them that I was more than a little skeptical. Nothing is as in depth, serious and addictive in regards to football management games as good old FM. I’ve played many hours in a number of other management games that attempt to push FM off of its porch but nothing has ever come close. I feared that Creoteam’s game was just going to end up being just another game that tried its best but fell woefully short. Thankfully I was quickly alleviated of my fears when I realized that that wasn’t what they were attempting to do at all. What their intention to create was a football management game that was much more accessible to all gamers – not just football super fans – as well as a game that was much more casual and nature and just an overall fun gaming experience.
In many ways Football Tactics reminded me of a few of the older shareware football management games that I played in my teenage years. These were games that were nowhere close to the uber tight management games that FM and Out of the Park Baseball are producing today but they were games that I vividly remember sinking tens or even hundreds of hours into.  For a gamer and a sports nut this game has the potential, and already is for its stage of early access, to be a lot of fun. You don’t need everything to uber serious all of the time so the game is going to fit a very nice niche.
The game plays out similarly to turn based combat games do on a grid with the obvious difference being that its football rather than an action-strategy game. Players have various different skills that are what you would expect from a football player with special skills such as shot cannon, lob passes, etc. giving the game some spice and flavor. Games are relatively quick affairs with some players feeling that they’re a little too short so perhaps an option to extend the game’s length – which many sports titles currently allow – perhaps being a nice option to appease them. I’d also like to see some more options within the game – a few more moves added. However, I’ve just been promoted out of the first league so more advanced techniques and skill may start becoming available as I progress during the game.
I like the amount of options that have been developed outside of matches themselves. The full gamut of options for a football fan are present. You can play the transfer market – buying better players and selling those that have been made redundant. You can also upgrade your club in a number of different ways. You can increase your seating capacity which will in turn increase the amount of money that you take at the gate. Improving your youth academy allows you to get better young footballers into the club. The first scout assistant decreases the age of players on the transfer list while the second scout assistant increases the number of players on the transfer list. Improving your major assistant enables substitutes to get experience after a match and finally positional coaches increase the amount of experience players get following matches.
The game is already heavily Steamified with 51 achievements giving hunters something to aim for and there are eleven trading cards to get to collect a full set. Steam Workshop integration has already been added to the game so that players can create mods, leagues and other things to improve the game. Finally, leagues can be played by both a single player or multi player to add a more competitive spirit to the game. In all, I’m very impressed with the amount of work that has already been completed on the game. I've been playing Rally games since I got a DOS version of Lombard RAC Rally in the late 80's and Championship Rally for the Nintendo back in the early 90's (my sons), and later  Rally Championship 2000,  RalliSport Challenge, all of the Colin McRae rally games through to Dirt 2  as well as the  later Dirt games, and  although not classed as rally games the early  road  racing Need for Speed games, Richard Burns Rally , Sega Rally,  Xpand Rally   plus a few others I've forgotten the names of.   I've   loved most of  them for various reasons and  WRC 5 is no exception.
The latest iteration of World Rally Championship  v5 is IMO perhaps the best  in the WRC  franchise so far, with decent physics when driving on the various surfaces   such as gravel, snow dirt sand etc.  the sounds, including external  environmental sounds,  hitting various obstacles, the various  'tame' expletives your co driver  shouts  when you  crash or   have a near miss, are not the best, but all go to making  a decent  rally game experience.   For newcomers to rally games there's  a  useful  Rally School  mode and an easy driving styles  mode when playing  solo.
:
:
There are two main  modes of play, Solo and Multiplayer. Solo is divided into four more modes, 'Quick Stage', where you play just one stage of a rally, or   'Quick Rally' where you can choose to play any one of the rally  meets, including all of the stages. The third  solo mode  is   Career mode, where you play all of the championships  rally meets in a particular order; you can't  select   any rally, you have to play them in order according to the real World Championships, starting with the Monte Carlo Rally, then, you move to the next, i.e. Vodaphone Rally de Portugal etc etc.  Some stages in each rally are repeated but  with different road or environmental  conditions, such as day  and night, clear or icy etc.
If you wish to start a new career,  you can do so, but it will wipe all progress  from the career you've already started.
The final solo mode is the  Rally School, a useful tool if you are a novice, or not very confident rallying.    This is divided into five different   sections that initially cover the basics  such as pace notes, detailed angles, different kinds of turns and surfaces, accelerating and stopping on tarmac (the easiest surface to negociate), using the hand brakes etc.  Then there's coping with 2 wheel drive  4 wheel drive (two separate sections for this) and advanced techniques.  at the end of each section you have to put all you've learnt in that section together.  You are not able to skip any part of the  Rally School tutorials and you need to pass a certain standard in each  part to progress to the next.
:
The multiplayer options include online and offline multiplayer, quick match, online invitation and creating a private or public game.  These modes basically speak for themselves so there's  no need to go into detail.  The offline multiplayer  is  almost like playing single player, in that you race  singly between up to 8 players, each one  playing in turn, whereas with  the online multiplayer option, all players  race together, but  do not interact with each other (i.e, you can see them as Ghosts.  As I'm not primarily a multiplayer enthusiast, I can't expand on this area at this time.  I only like playing  vehicle based games online  with good friends as I'm embarrasingly  dire when it comes to technique and racing in general;  for example, looking at the world rankings for this game  20 hours into  the game being released  I stood at 377th out of 450  players, with a 45 second gap between my times and the leader and that was  just for one complete rally and championship type.  There are   three or four of these included in the game  (JWRC, WRC etc).  I felt like I was going as fast as the road conditions and my vehicle allowed,  yet being beaten by 45 seconds makes me wonder what I'm doing wrong.  Hopefully as I work through the rally school I'll improve somewhat. (fingers crossed). For those who are competitive, there are leader boards that show  overall  rankings for all players,  as well as  friends leader boards.
:
There are three configurable modes of control; Keyboard, Steering Wheel and Controller.  For any rally game enthusiast, the   Steering Wheel is the  best choice as you have more  'configurable' control over the keyboard,   and is the  most immersive control option;  for example you can  configure acceleration, brake and steering sensitivity with dead zones, whereas the  keyboard has no dead zones. The  Steering Wheel option also includes force feedback, (as does the Controller option) which gives a much greater feel and immersivness to the game, plus  your vehicle is much easier to control  compared to if you used a keyboard.  Unfortunately I've  still not unpacked my Logitech steering wheel, pedals and shifter since we moved house  (must do that soon). I've read that others have been having problems  with their  wheels not being supported.  Hopefully  this will be  addressed  in an update soon.  I found using the X-Box controller was  easier than the keyboard and included basic force feedback. There appears to be six degrees of freedom with this game, at least in some of the camera modes, for example, you can look from side to side, upwards and behind in  chase mode and in  cockpit mode  left and right and upwards.  Unfortunately the track IR hasn't been configured for any of the WTC games, so it's unlikely that we will be seeing  WRC5  Track IR enhanced, Maybe   Naturalpoint (the developers of the track IR system) may be considering  the latest title. The first 3 Dirt titles and some of the earlier Colin McRae as well as most of the other titles I mention at the beginning of this review   all have Track IR enhancements.  If this game gets it, it will add even more immersivness.
The game also works with the Novint Falcon a force feedback device that gives excellent force feedback, but as the   device was primarily designed for mouse based games and  games with guns, it's not  as easy to control your driving unless you use it in conjuction with the keyboard.
:
There are four driving styles to choose from  starting with easy, through to medium, hard and  expert.  I've only played it on easy so far so can't  expand on the differences yet.  I will be updating this  review as and when I continue to play the game as I'm only on the second rally  at the moment.
:
You can configure/tune you car  (in the motor home) for various conditions  to ensure optimal driving.  Skill alone  won't  see you winning every race because if you  haven't set up your car for the right conditions for the stage you are about to enter, you'll find your  vehicle will  damage more readily.  You can only  repair your vehicle between  the main stages in any  rally and   depending on how much damage you have   you are likely  not going to be able to repair everything  because you are only allowed   an amount of time that represents the  time allowed  in the real WRC  championship;  i.e. 45 minutes,  so you need to prioritise  which areas you  repair, for example geras, engine, body work,  brakes, electronics, steering etc.  for those less experienced with   the  more recent rally games (the  last WRC   game and I think the  later dirt games have a similar  repair  process) you can  set repairs to automatic. If you select this the A.I. will repair what it considers the  most urgent  repairs. However, don't  ignore the manual process entirely because   damage can also be dependant on the players  style.

Hitman has always been a special game for me. The kind of game you have a love/hate relationship with. I absolutely love the idea and the concept behind the Hitman games, it’s brilliant. The stealthiness was core to the series, but the dozen potential ways to eliminate a target was the thing that made it special. But for some reason I always burned out on Hitman after a couple of hours. Why? Even though it’s supposed to be a difficult game, not being able to pull off all the crazy (also, funny) assassinations time after time becomes tiresome and frustrating.
While the last two games (Blood Money & Absolution) were more accessible, I was still failing my mission too many times. Purists probably love the steep difficulty but for a more mainstream audience, the developer needed to up the accessibility while also staying true to their biggest fans. And they did exactly that. But let me take a few steps back first…
When the new Hitman got announced, Square Enix reported that this game would be episodic. No mission packed game at launch, but every month a new big area/mission to be launched to the masses. This allows new players to try Hitman at a lower price since there’s an ‘Intro Pack’ for about 18 bucks with the training, prologue and the first mission included. You can then buy the following episodes separately to your liking. Fans of the first hour were and are still able of course to buy Hitman as a regular game. The new episodes will be downloaded & installed automatically as updates.
People were sceptical when they first announced this system, but we’ve all been proven wrong. It’s working great for this game. At the time of writing, two episodes got released. The first being Paris and the second called Sapienza. The areas are huge and there’s a lot of gameplay to be found in each of the two levels. Being able to come back every month with a fresh area really helps this game. It’s an interesting way to stay relevant across a wider time span.
As mentioned before, the love/hate relationship I had with Hitman has finally been settled. The new Hitman is what I always wanted from a Hitman game. It offers me all the options (and then some) but guides me along the way so I can feel awesome and less frustrated. Don’t worry though, the developer struck the balance between guiding and being too hand-holdy perfectly. Having all the potential opportunities being pointed out when you encounter them in combination with ‘Hitman vision’ to detect enemies & targets, really helps conquer the learning curve. Hardcore Hitman players don’t need to be disturbed though. They can tweak all these systems to their heart’s content, leaving them in control on how difficult the game should be.
It’s not only the gameplay that excells this time around. The game looks magnificent. The first episode in Paris was already a nice looking environment but it’s Sapienza, the second episode that really blew my mind. The area is huge, it looks beautiful and runs great. It’s safe to say that the second episode is a step up from the first one so if you’re not fully convinced after episode one I would recommend giving the second one a try. It’s great on all levels: gameplay, technical and visual.
The one major negative I can say for this game, is the narrative between episodes. There’s a story tying the prologue, episode one and episode two together but it’s conveyed in a very loose manner making it hard to care about it at all. A missed opportunity since the episodic nature of the game could have made story telling in Hitman even more interesting.
Hitman is back in its finest form ever. The game plays great, looks great and has struck the perfect balance between fun, accessibility and challenge. For me it’s by far the best Hitman game to date and one of the best games so far in 2016. Pick up the intro pack for a small price. You won’t regret it.

HITMAN 2016 is a flawed game at present, but fans of the series will find it incredibly refreshing.
I've been playing the Hitman series since Codename 47. Countless hours put into my favorite missions on Blood Money, Contracts, and Silent Assassin. In particular, played A Murder of Crows and A New Life to death. And then came Absolution, which I couldn't even finish. Hated the mechanics, hated the story, didn't feel like a Hitman title at all.
In many ways, HITMAN 2016 is an apology from Io Interactive for Absolution, I think. Some of the Absolution mechanics are still there, but the game is much truer to Blood Money than any other Hitman. I've had a ton of fun playing the extremely detailed locales in Paris and Italy and Morocco. Io shows that they remain one of the greats of globe-trotting gameplay, at least as far as the visuals are concerned.
It's not all good, however. The DRM/Always-Online requirement and its justification is lame. Although I don't have a huge problem with episodic gameplay, many do, and there is a certain incompleteness to the whole game at the moment that accentuates the lack of polish in certain areas. Voice acting, in particular, is moribund, with the same bro-tier American English being overheard in Paris, in the streets of Italy, and finally in the souks of Morocco, where I have lived and can assure you there is little English to be found. It's silly, and detracts majorly from the "spy novel" feel of this Hitman. Jesper Kyd is also no longer making the Hitman soundtracks, which is a huge blow, immediately evident with the cliched "action music" present in all levels. To top it all off, the system requirements for this Hitman are steep, and performance seems to fluctuate a great deal between patches.
Perhaps - as with many video games - the worst feature of this Hitman are the fanboys. I consider myself a pretty big Hitman fan, but I'm not above telling Io when they're making a mistake, i.e. the voices in HITMAN. This opinion - that Moroccans should sound like Moroccans - recently got me banned from HitmanForum, which was the only Hitman-themed forum I could find to discuss this game, other than Steam. I copped a cool 30-year ban for telling one of the admins that Moroccans speak Arabic and French, not English. Lol. What are you going to do? Fanboys gonna fanboy.
At the end of the day, HITMAN 2016 is for Hitman fans. New players will find it hard to pick up, I imagine, though not impossible. It has flashes of brilliance, and if Io listens to constructive feedback, I believe it could be the Blood Money for the 2010s. If not, it'll remain a flawed experience, but still very playable.
In short, buy it if you like Hitman, wait for the finished product if you're not sure.
