As a big fan of first two parts I've got really disappointed with the feedback this game has got. And probably even more about the fact that this part wasn't developed by original Rocksteady team who made a gigantic input to the genre, while I didn't know much about the new team. Then I watched a couple of videos of it and I was just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off by the facial animations, also graphics didn't look so well on these videos (as it turned out later on these videos were either made on consoles or weren't the highest settings)... So I decided to wait for a discount.
And here I am, got it yesterday and played for just a few hours, but it feels like I already have a strong opinion (by strong I mean that it probably won't change much later on) on this game. This game in fact is not so bad, I would actually say it's pretty good for those who finished the first 2 parts. It doesn't have much new to offer, but it's still fresh enough.
Graphics in fact are slightly better. Cutscenes look too polished, I think there was some post processing on it, but I don't really mind - the difference is not too big and it's cool to have these nicely done cinematic scenes. There's again a good use of PhysX, which was amazing in previous games, but here there are some improvements. For example, you're making deep footsteps in the snow which won't disappear 2 seconds after. DX11 is used widely so the level of detail is good (although I still have a feeling that if it would be made by Rocksteady, they'd manage to get even better results, considering how awesome graphics are even in the rather old Arkham Asylum). As for facial animations, or if to be more exact, lips animation - it really sucks. It's just so choppy, even though lips movement is somewhat improved (you probably could read what they're saying by lips, if they would move smooth). Sometimes it looks so silly that you can't pay attention to what characters say and laughing instead. I wish they would leave it as it was in the first 2 parts.
Combat. That's the main part and they didn't fail with that. It got quite harder than the previous parts (and I was playing the second part a few days ago, so it's not me getting old... even though I do). On Hard though, not sure how it is on lower difficulties. Enemies attack more often and Batman is not as fast as in the previous parts, where you often could just ignore incoming attack and hit. Here if you're 1 millisecond too late you gonna get punched. I really like this, I always was a fan of the combat system in Batman though, so as long as it's not worse than in the 1 and 2 parts I'm happy. However they missed something what Rocksteady did: before, if you die in a combat which happened after a cutscene you could continue straight from the beginning of the fight, without a need to watch the cutscene. Here you have to watch it all over again. And you can't skip it because it's either loading or saving (which is silly, because it overwrites the exact same save file). So when you get really stuck you have to rewatch the cutscene for like 10+ times and that completely ruins characters' charisma. Why? Because you start to hate them just because they're repeating same crap again and again... So, for example, take Tracey - I loved her pronunciation (can't call it an accent, can I?) and scummy type of speech, but after listening the same replicas for half an hour (yeah, I was terrible at this fight on a ship), I started to hate her. I mean, really, the ability to pause or skip ANY cutscene is a must in my opinion.
Overall I'd rate the game positively. And you should really get it if it happens that right now there's a sale on it - it's probably worth even a full price.

5 Hours to Complete
TL;DR - As a game it’s quite weak. As an experience, I know how generic that sounds, it’s a surprise. Having a more realistic and dark view on the effects of war is missed in games. Never before did I waste bullets to stop the screams of an NPC.
In depth:
Performance - Some dips but otherwise decent. Many of the scripted cut scenes is when it dipped and which is annoying but better than in gameplay.
Graphics - Actually quite good. Considering the game is desert environments look the same a lot of the time, which is any game I would scrutinise but this its work as it fits in with the theme of a “never ending“ theme.
Gameplay - You are not going to like the game. And you’re not meant to. The game is designed to be generic to get a point across. The story is dark and shows what can and does happen in war. Never in a game have I executed an enemy or shot them to put them out of their misery despite their horrible actions over letting them surfer. This game is an experience and a good one. The ending (message) is really good which I refuse to hint at. It also gives tough decisions which can blur the lines between right and wrong. Will you sacrifice a few people to help a guy critical to your mission to save more people OR help the people but in the long run more may in fact die?
In terms of a game it’s as generic as can be with♥♥♥♥♥♥poor enemy design and AI. From sound, to look and to feel of weapons it’s a game you are familiar with as you have probably played it before a lot. Coop and multiplayer is dead. Not the focus of the game by any means. Coop is somewhat un-playable as it’s balanced for another.
Replayability - As coop and multiplayer is dead not to mention gameplay being generic does not offer a lot to replay. The different endings and the psychological trip of events kind of justify it enough however.
Conclusion - A great experience but not game. I would suggest playing it at least once when on sale as it’s an experience you can’t get in any other game.

Overall, I really enjoyed this game.
The good:  The story was well written and I really liked the companions I chose to bring along.  It had a very Planescape: Torment feel to it, as befits a spiritual successor.  There were a lot of quests but none of them felt like chores.  The ability to not just interactively "remember" the past but actually change it is quite a cool concept.
The neutral: The game does strip down much of the staples of the classic RPG genre.  Combat is infrequent (and mostly voluntary), gear upgrades are few, there's no such thing as grinding and even character progression feels somewhat unimportant.  Most of the game revolves around dialog and your choices there, and there's basically no truly "trash" encounters.  These could go either way - I found them a refreshing departure from combat-heavy games, but if you enjoy killing a lot of stuff and getting a lot of gear / XP then you may find this game lacking.
The bad: Tidal surge is a mechanic that both seems fascinating and woefully underutilized.  In fact the entire Tides system had no obvious impact upon the game, in spite of being a key focus to the plot.

1. the game is SHORT, even doing all the side quests it took me about 20 hours to complete in total.
2. the game itself is very linear in progression, you lack much of the flexability PS:T allowed you.
3. the combat system is very very unresponsive and slow, this is very problematic when you have at least three points during the game where you cannot avoid it.
I actually enjoyed it. The puzzle elements are well made, the story is good and the plot twist is even good-er-ish. The only thing I didn't like was that there was too much comic relief.

First impressions:
Graphics:  With a 4670k O/C'd to 4.3 ghz and a GTX 970 I'm getting very low frame rates (less than 60), even with all graphic settings set to LOW or OFF.  This is just at 1080p.  Very few options to change as well.
Sound:  Watch some vids, it's pretty awful.  Co-driver sounds like a robot, car sounds are very poor.
HUD and Camera Views: Standard camera views, but when you switch to cockpit view, you have NO tachometer, no speedometer, and no idea what gear you are in.  This could just be a bug for the car that I was using.  If you shift views in the middle of the race it will reset your current gear to 1.  Why on earth would this happen?  The tach is nearly impossible to see what RPM you are actually at, as the colors of the green/red only get slightly darker as you progress.  You really only know when to shift if you hit the redline.
Wheel Support and Force Feedback:  Just atrocious....  No clutch pedal support whatsoever (don't think H shifter either, but haven't tried yet).  There are some adjustments for sensitivity and deadzones, but only a bar to move with no numerical values.  FFB is quite awful, but it is there.  There are 2 sliders in which you can change the strength and vibraton (?).  If you completely lower the sliders to 0 then the wheel suddenly becomes a vibrating mess.  In short, this game is probably best played with a controller...
Physics:  About what you would expect.   More arcade like but you do need to use the brakes in this game at least....
Rally school:  A complete joke.  Not even worth discussing.  You have to do the same courses for Basics, 2wd, and 4wd.  Honestly just a huge waste of time.
Overall:  With only an hour of playtime so far, I'm giving this game a 2/10.  This may change with further playtime, but currently its a buggy, laggy mess.  Stay far away from it.

I'm flipping my review from negative to positive. It's time.
Guys, this game is really good. Good enough that I believe it's worth putting up with the minor-to-moderate technical issues that haven't quite been fixed yet: DX12 is still buggy, 8GB of RAM isn't quite enough all of the time despite it being the recommended spec, and the always/only online thing is still a back-of-the-mind concern even though it's never been an issue for me at all.
But oh boy, what a game! I've long fallen out of favor with first-person shooters, or even true third-person action shooters. But Hitman has always been different. More composed, more cerebral. You need to be smart to do well at this game, and it rewards you handsomely for finding things out on your own. Moreso for finding new things that fall within the game's rules, but not necessarily its intended design. Many times I don't bring a gun into a level with me. There are so many other options at your disposal, you don't even need to shoot anyone to get things done efficiently.
Still, you can also be dumb, often on purpose, and still have a lot of fun with things. It's really nice to play a thoughtful assassination-puzzle game and then switch gears to a slaughterhouse murder simulator whenever I bloody well feel like it. Tote that new shotgun around or find a new sniping location and go to town. It's your world, all those poor NPCs are just living in it. However so briefly you desire.
If the episodic nature of the game is giving you concerns, consider that I put 35+ hours into the first part of the game (the training levels and Paris), and that only cost me $15. I'm still working through Sapienza (Episode 2) to finish all the challenges and contracts. I've barely scratched the surface of Marrakesh (Episode 3). I'm buying the game as I go, so I have no right to complain I'm not getting what I'm paying for. I'm getting more than what I'm paying for.
There are people out there that want to wait for the game to be "finished" before buying it, and that's fine. As for me, I prefer to play this game NOW, and enjoy the ride, and the constant updates and improvements along the way. After feeling the rush of playing the limited-window, one-time only Elusive Contracts, I believe I made the right decision in doing that.

Most of my time spent in Hitman was mining Paris for everything it had. The challenges are achievements done right, as each requires problem solving and or/execution and some will surprise and delight you. As maps to play through once, each mission is also believable and dense in a chewy way.
I was very excited for this game but I expected much more from it. It's VERY short and it's not worth its price.

The minigames need work, and for the love of God, 'gay' or 'bisexual' is not a bad word - the total dearth of those terms made me feel like they went out of their way to avoid them, and that was disconcerting. But it's a really cute, enjoyable game with really solid writing and nice art. I might wait until it's slightly less expensive - $15 is a bit much - but it's still worth the time.

Though it’s not afraid to lore dump on people who seek such things, the adventure occupies a world that’s bigger than your unnamed protagonist and will just carry on around you with or without your understanding. Ignore some quests for too long and they will progress without your input, eventually resolving themselves at times and leaving you without reward and experience. Or perhaps you’ll undertake an action that seemed to be for the best and suffer the consequences when forced to view your solution from another angle. There’s talk of a mole-like monster hiding in the dumps that keeps burrowing under people’s houses, prompting them to fatally collapse on their occupants. Surely just killing off that pest would benefit everyone, so why not gather up the flaming torches and pitchforks?
Because there’s rarely just black and white in Torment; there are varied shades of grey. And there is always another solution available for people who look for them. Though the game has a reasonable combat engine, you can avoid the vast majority of conflicts by charming, lying, bluffing or threatening your way out of most situations. Even when a battle does break out, you often have more options than just putting everything to sword. A relic left by an advanced civilisation long dead has its basement filled with hostile AI drones you could probably bash to bits if you wanted. Or, you could try creeping around the sides and purging command consoles to restore them to default setting. Because even in the realms of high fantasy, the answer to almost any IT issue is to turn it off and on again.
I appreciate moments like these, because if Torment has one big failing, it’s the hopelessly drawn out and somewhat clumsy battles that always seem to take three times longer than they should. In the combat system's defence, there’s a lot to fit in; each character has a healthy range of battle options, and the equipping of ciphers which act like (often) one-shot special attacks. Effects range from the commonplace, like blasts and stuns, to the more remarkable, such as when a target is forced to walk around muttering randomly to itself for six turns while it drops a trail of money. Some characters can hide from sight to escape the enemy’s attention, or to set up devastating ambush attacks. Others have skill sets involving grappling hooks, short-range teleportation or especially harsh words.
But the world itself is Torment big star, shuffling in alien creatures from different dimensions or sentient beings of gleaming liquid metal as the norm because why shouldn’t they be? Why shouldn’t that fountain shoot gibbering eel-fish instead of water? Why shouldn’t there be a centuries-old would-be warlord, cursed with immortality and now forced to stand in a corner as punishment for a war waged so long ago, it’s faded from memory? Why shouldn’t some of the artifices you find be ridiculously useless knick-knacks from a race of people history insists never existed? Why shouldn’t someone’s half-remembered guilt of an age-old atrocity be manifested in your own mind to offer slight stat buffs?

This game was early backed for me as a gift.  I tinkered with the early-release for a while but was never really wowed by it.  Once release came, I decided to devote some real effort to the game.  I ran through with different options and different NPC's in group.  Ultimately I have to say, it was really a pretty big let down.  When you compare it to the RPG's its supposed to harken back to, it lacks depth, it lacks immersion, it lacks complexity.  Sure, there are lots of ways to 'handle' the various situations that arise.  But it almost always comes down to either having a skill or rolling a skill.  Which can be influenced by effort.  Honestly, I had more fun going back and replaying Dark Sun: Shattered Lands than I did playing this game.  And the excuse of not including certain milestones in the final product because it would have 'taken away' from the game?  Yeah... no.  This came across as a 'take the money and run' endeavor.  Save your money and get something else.

I Picked this up being a fan of Planescape: Torment and the Numenera tabletop RPG. I will approach this review from that angle.
The Numenera system works wonderfully in a video game format with minimal modification, and at least for me is much more approachable than the tabletop version, given that it can be hard to visualize a world so alien.   I was a bit disappointed with the lack of character customization, given that the game would lend itself to it better than most.
As far as a Planscape: Torment successor goes, it is acceptable.  Not the highest praise, sure, but when you're trying to make a successor to the best written game of all time, it's hard to eclipse the original.  The writing is solid, the world building is excellent, and the combat is mediocre at best (Still better than Planescape).
Much like the original, it's a great game if you want a story.  If you want a combat centric RPG, Tyranny, POE, or any of the classic CRPGs would be a better option.

Ever since I learned about this game from the Game Grumps I've been following the process step-by-step.  I was a tad skeptical about how exactly the creators of the game, Vernon Shaw and Leighton Gray, were going to pull off a dad dating game... but the team really knocked it out of the park.  It's much better than I could have ever expected!  From the story to the artwork to the (sometimes infuriating) mini-games... it's just all so awesome!  I LOVE all the dad puns!!!
There is such an excellent cast of characters, and not just the dads.  I mean, the Dream Daddies are obviously the most important part, but the side characters provide a lot of insight into not only the dads but the story as well.  It was fascinating to see the impact the other characters had on the dads.  And I love the dads!  Each one was completely unique.  I mean, it's typical for dating simulators to have unique characters, but there usually seem to be some overlapping in character design or something of the sort in the dateable characters.  Not the case with DDADDS.  Each dad's story and character is entirely unique.  And I was surprised at just how in-depth the story went into each character.  Each dad had a powerful story, full of feels and squeals and love.  It was just all so perfect.
There's so much in this game that I don't even know how to include it all in a proper review.  All I can say is you just have to play it to truly see it.  You can read as many reviews as you like, but until you actually try it, you won't be able to get a proper understanding of just how awesome this game is.  I highly, highly recommend it!

Although I do not have enough hours on the current iteration of the game to give it a proper review, I will say that I am pleased with the developers and their efforts to dominate the survival game genre. Rust is an unforgiving survival with a focus on PvP and extremely restricted solo play. Some may find that the game lacks in opportunities for solo gamers to thrive and I find this to be a true point. I would not reccommend playing the game if you are a lone player unless you decided to inhabit one of the servers with less of a population. PvE is extremely lackluster, there isn't much of an environmental factor and NPCs are not a difficult challenge to overcome. Gunplay is enjoyable, however, there is room for improvement. Clans dominate servers and are an overwhelming force for many players to overcome. Building is not an aesthetic aspect of the game, the current style allows players to construct some unsightly bases. Overall, I would say that the legacy version of the game was much more enjoyable and immersive. Although the environment is considerably attractive, the game could definitely use some improvement. I would reccommend this game for players that want to engage in intense combat with their friends. I would not reccomend this game for solo players.

I'm flipping my review from negative to positive. It's time.
Guys, this game is really good. Good enough that I believe it's worth putting up with the minor-to-moderate technical issues that haven't quite been fixed yet: DX12 is still buggy, 8GB of RAM isn't quite enough all of the time despite it being the recommended spec, and the always/only online thing is still a back-of-the-mind concern even though it's never been an issue for me at all.
But oh boy, what a game! I've long fallen out of favor with first-person shooters, or even true third-person action shooters. But Hitman has always been different. More composed, more cerebral. You need to be smart to do well at this game, and it rewards you handsomely for finding things out on your own. Moreso for finding new things that fall within the game's rules, but not necessarily its intended design. Many times I don't bring a gun into a level with me. There are so many other options at your disposal, you don't even need to shoot anyone to get things done efficiently.
Still, you can also be dumb, often on purpose, and still have a lot of fun with things. It's really nice to play a thoughtful assassination-puzzle game and then switch gears to a slaughterhouse murder simulator whenever I bloody well feel like it. Tote that new shotgun around or find a new sniping location and go to town. It's your world, all those poor NPCs are just living in it. However so briefly you desire.
If the episodic nature of the game is giving you concerns, consider that I put 35+ hours into the first part of the game (the training levels and Paris), and that only cost me $15. I'm still working through Sapienza (Episode 2) to finish all the challenges and contracts. I've barely scratched the surface of Marrakesh (Episode 3). I'm buying the game as I go, so I have no right to complain I'm not getting what I'm paying for. I'm getting more than what I'm paying for.
There are people out there that want to wait for the game to be "finished" before buying it, and that's fine. As for me, I prefer to play this game NOW, and enjoy the ride, and the constant updates and improvements along the way. After feeling the rush of playing the limited-window, one-time only Elusive Contracts, I believe I made the right decision in doing that.

Well, I'd never thought I'd be writing an UnderTale review in 2017, BUT HERE I AM!
Before anyone starts reading, there are some spoilers here and there, so if you haven't yet played Undertale and DON'T WANT SPOILERS, then stop reading now.
UnderTale has been an absolute BLAST for me, mainly because when it first came out it caught me by surpsrise. As a KickStarter backer, I knew the sinopsis of the game, yet I found really heartwarming the way Toby Fox managed to develop it into 3 different playstyles: Pacifist, Neutral and Genocide, also known as the "Sans is gonna knock you out countless times" run. The way these 3 playstyles develop during the game is pretty simple: Pacifist implies that you spare every single monster you meet, no matter how unintuitive it may be (I'm looking at you, Undyne!). Neutral is the classic RPG playstyle: kill whoever you want just enough to proceed without too much trouble. Lastly, there's the Genocide. Now things start getting interesting, since you have to kill every single monster there is in the Underground (duh). Each ending  gives you more insight on the world, and also gives you a hint on how to obtain one of the other endings, breaking the 4th wall. However, it isn't just a simple "Deus ex Machina" to help the player: breaking the 4th wall is often used in the game as a sort of comic relief, or to give an extremely powerful message to the player (The Genocide ending is a clear example of the latter option). The gameplay itself isn't all that difficult, but still feels quite rewarding when you finish sparing (or fighting, I don't judge). However, Bullet-hell players will find it quite easy to just speedrun through most of the game. The game is, in fact, quite short in terms of the actual time needed to finish it. However, UnderTale isn't just about the gameplay, but rather the story it unfolds while playing. It is an incredibly good story, which I'll try not to spoil. I'll only say that it involves themes going from murder and loss to peace, forgiveness and acceptance.
UnderTale has been a moving experience for me, making me look at the world in a different view, and as stupid as it may sound, I started to see the beautiful things I'd never notice, and met many great people while at it, and I'm sure this game will probably have the same effect on you.

Just finished the game. Overall impressions are very postive, mostly thanks to the Numenera setting and pretty good writing.
The world of the game is pretty bizzare to say the least and in some parts feels like it came straight out from the creepiest pages of some P.K. D i c k novel. Of course while some quests are great, the others are pretty generic, but I wouldn't call any of them dull. The main questline is pretty good too, I found it involving and interesting with all its transhumanistic ideas and moral issues being the highlights. Now that I think about it, the game's plot also has some pretty depressing and would-be shocking moments, but unfurtunetely they are obscured by the overall otherworldliness of the setting.
On a bad side, the story is somewhat unevenly paced with the Sagus Cliffs and Bloom parts being intense and content heavy while the middle and the final parts of the game feel mostly like linear fillers or story propellers.
Character writing is okay, it's not stellar, but definetely not a failure as many reviewers on Steam suggest. But I must admit I felt the characters to be more of a gateway to understanding the Ninth World rather than some "very interesting" personalities you're supposed to run around and pester for the duration of the whole game.
Now let's talk about the GAMEPLAY itself. That's where Numenera actually fails in a pretty bad way. While I like the Cypher System and think that it has been implemented pretty well within the game, I can't help but admit that the balance between stat pools is clearly off with Intellect being by far the most superior stat and Might being by far the most inferior, especially considering that the game is short on combat sequences.
Another downside is that apart from the game's early stages you never feel threatened to run out of your stats resources, the pools are simply too big and, even more importantly, there's way too much possibilities for resting and refilling those pools. Most of the tasks are also too easy to complete, rendering the whole Effort system almost useless.
Cyphers are another interesting part of the game, but just as with the stat pools you rarely feel any need for them because of how easy the game is how rare the fights are.
Same goes for the abilities, there's simply too many of them for the absolutely tiny amout of combat within the game. That makes them feel unimpactful and redundant. But that's kind of a problem for the absolute majority of RPGs out there, too much useless and meaningless  junk, especially when it comes to skills and abilities.
Tides are a good moral (viewpoint) indicator, but the problem with it again is that they change so slowly that no one decision feel very impactful when it comes to the Tides. It kind of makes sense when you think about it from the ideological point of view, but absolutely fails as a gameplay element.
Overall I can recommend this game to anyone who isn't afraid of reading and is looking for an RPG that can offer you more than 10 romance options and 100 craftable items out of 1000 types of resources. It's a rough gem that could benifit a lot from proper play testing and tuning, but even as it is now, it can give you a lot if you bother to read and reflect.

Okay, here's the deal. This game has been the target of so much free hate that I cannot give it a bad mark, seriously. It has its flaws yes, the voices (everyone speaks English) or the fact that there are still a lots of bugs (even though I encountered none) but ffs it does not deserve this hate.
Some people will complain about the episodic content but I have to admit, that, even if I was sceptical at first, I start to find it extremely interesting and well thought. It gives you time to have fun in the levels, do it again, try new things etc. Besides, the fact of waiting makes you eager to have the new episodes. It's like waiting for a new episode of your favourite tv-show. It's pleasant in a torturous way.
Concerning the gameplay, well, it's Hitman. Blood-money-like Hitman, not the one we had in Absolution. So this is good news. You will find new/interesting/surprising ways to kill your target everytime with or without help (you can deactivate the minimap, the instinct etc..). The levels are huge, there are a lot of costumes, weapons, improvised weapons etc plus a lot of things to unlock by completing the levels.
The graphics are pretty good and the game runs more smoothly after every patch (in my case at least). The music is great, the ambiance is okay but could be better. The only problem, as mentionned before, is the fact that everyone speaks English even in foreign countries (France, Italy..). It's a big turn-off but I have hope that this will change in the future (fingers crossed).

This game has a lot of negative reviews, but I think most of them stem from the always online-bit. Which I guess can be abit of a nuisance.
I purchased the first episode a little while after its initial release and have yet to experience any issues in that regard.
I really liked it. I've always heard about the Hitman-games, but never got around to actually play them. This game is what made me buy and play through Absolution as well.
The levels are huge and sandboxy. Open World and free to explore (under the right circumstances/disguises). There are a multitude of ways and places to assassinate your targets, and if you should so choose, the game offers to guide you through a few of them. Hints and ingame assistance can be turned on/off at the players own discretion.
I was sceptic to the episodic release at first, but if it hadn't been, I probably wouldn't have bought it in the first place either, so it is a good way to give a teaser of the game and fully try and see whether or not this is a game for you. On the other hand, having to wait a month for the next episode is also incentive to fully explore the destination(s) you already have and master them.
Unlike Absolution, you are able to save at any time while playing the main mission which makes it quick to load if you should mess up. Some may not like that bit, but I really liked not having to play through what could have been 10-15 minutes of preparation again when/if I mess up royally. If you forget to do that, you may also take use of an autosave instead.
In addition to the main mission, there are also escalations released pretty often (usually 5 stages) which aren't mandatory but gives you something to do. If that still isn't enough to keep you busy, there are also player-created contracts you can do or create for that matter.
Agent 47 has an array of tools at his disposal, and as you progress you will keep unlocking more and more. Tools earned in later destinations can be brought back to the first ones, making for even more variation.

Agent 47 is my favorite character of all time, I bought this game because I like the feeling about being a hitman like 47, as it turned out, it didn't disappoint me overall.

As far as I'm concerned, I don't mind the "episode released"thing, this is no rush to finish the mission, every episode is well-designed and there are numerous details to be found out . The best thing I like about this game is it doesn't have a linear story line, which is better in comparison to Hitman Absolution, you don't have to follow the story line anymore, the freedom it gives you is the best part of experience this game has to offer. Like previous hitman games, there are many ways to kill a target and there are many accomplishments attached to them, try a challenging way to assassinate a target, infiltrating with different costume, etc, that's the way you will have fun in this game.

As for the downsides of this game, terrible optimization definitely ruins my game experience, and making a single-player game rely so heavily on internet connection sounds weird, I encountered connection issues sometimes and it took a long time to get me back online, but you can dismiss it if you have a stable network.

The one thing that matters most is that this game is getting better, keeps it that way, this game is gonna be back in the spotlight.

First things first: I gotta hand it to the devs for including American teams that are either close or spot on in terms of names of the MLS teams.  With a mod you can even get the real names and logos. The game is fun in a sort of "mindless" way and the games go by quickly so it can be addicting to just keep playing one more over and over.
Now I have to list the negetives. THIS IS STILL WHEN IT'S IN EARLY ACCESS:
1. MY overall experience so far is that the RNG is missing the "random" part. There have been way too many times where I'll have a range of 1-50 and the CPU will have a range of 1-9 and I end up with 8 and CPU gets 9. The RNG is tipped so much in favor of the CPU that I rarely ever try to cause these. Whenever I'm on offense I play it safe and do short passes through open space. This can easily be fixed throughout the Early Access so this might change.
2. As great as it is to see the team I follow in MLS in this game, I wish the players that were on the team in real life were in this game. I completely understand that this game doesn't have the license from MLS but they could still put similar names and similar attributes to the players. Small issue in the end but it'd be a nice addition.
3. The game gives you three turns to move but I rarely find that it's enough. Occasionally you'll get lucky and the stars will allign or the CPU does something dumb and turns the ball over at midfield but most of the time they'll bring the ball to your box, miss and then youll spend three turns passing it up tp your forward when your turn ends. I understand that this could be to emulate how soccer games can be: two teams running the ball back and forth but the way it is now makes the game feel choppy instead of realistic. I think the best way to handle this since soccer is a game that's very much about movement is to borrow the turn based mode from XCOM: EU and have two actions per "turn" for the three players you choose. For example, using a through ball isn't possible unless your player has a certain trait learned which can take up to a full season to learn and it can only be used once a game. If the XCOM turn based mode was introduced you could have one guy run ad midfield and pass while  a striker ran to meet the ball and one time it at goal.
The RNG really kills it for me bcause I haven't experience some of the one on one combat due to the high chance that my team will lose and concede a goal.
As it stands, I can't reccommend the game right now. It feels like the goal was to make a simpler Football Manager 16 while also being more nuanced than the FIFA 16 Manager mode but IMO the game is an acrade game that relies too much on chance. I hope some of my issues are fixed because this has the potential to suck days of my life if I feel like my preperation of my team has an effect on the one on one duals.

Here's a question: did you like Blitzball in Final Fantasy X? No? Would you have liked it if it were... better?
If so, Football Tactics may just be the game for you. It's a super addictive management sim that's leagues simpler than Football Manager.
Grain of salt warning: At the time of this review, Football Tactics is an early access game, so stuff's still being balanced.
Pros:
-The unique player abilities definitely add a bit of spice to the RNG.
-The interface is super clean and easy to read
-Actual matches are fun. I also enjoy the AI mode for when I get burned out and want to play while I'm doing something else. It's nice that you can take control if you think your AI are being stupid, too.
-I like the versatility of being able to use players in non-native positions, like using a Defender as a Midfielder. It really allows you to mix up your team and tactics.
-Hot Seat multiplayer?! I don't think I'll ever get a chance to use it, but I'm pretty excited about it anyway.
-Like a billion real countires and teams to pick from. You can also customize your club's logo and uniforms.
Cons:
-The difficulty curve is a little wacky. You start out in the noobie league, so it's understandably easy. If you do some smart team management, the next league is ok too. Once you hit Second League, you're likely to have a 1.5-star team regularly going up against 2-3 star teams, both in the tournament and the cup. When you tie or lose, your players get fewer XP. Fewer XP means you don't level as quickly. Not leveling means you're grinding in autopilot way longer than you need to be. To my knowledge, there's no way to move backward to lower leagues to train your players. As it is, It kind of feels like an intentinal time sink.
-Addendum: As you move to higher leagues, you get more XP for losing, but your players have time limits on their careers. You can get starting players as young as 16 or 17, but they retire at 35-40.
-CORNER KICKS. I don't know if it's the load time as players get into position, or having to manually move each defender for coverage, or the fact that high-powered teams have a habit of getting 3-5 of them in a row, even with my roided out goalie. Corner kicks are my #1 motivator to spectate matches.
-Also, it'd be cool to swap BACK to spectator mode after taking control. Sometimes I only want to play Offense, or to avoid a Corner Kick or whatever.
But really, this game is super fun. Also, it's cheap, and worth sinking a good 5-10 hours into, at least.

Of sedentary football technicians there are many, sitting amidst the plush comforts of their immovable habits, while boomingly piping up to the gaffer for that long awaited change. Yet, for ludophiles and enthusiasts, little remains other than to play "Football manager," the lacklustre manager-mode in any reflex-based title, or simply have a go at some 2-bit "Fantasy Football" league somewhere in the dusty corners of the net.
But lo-and-behold, when choices seem as meagre as empty mist-wrapped stands, when a hot soup-flask is not enough to warm your cockles, Creoteam come to the rescue with a more than interesting, even palatable, offer. "Football Tactics" is born, underrated hidden gem like Matthew Le Tissier, seemingly casual, at times unexpectedly difficult, always overwhelmingly addictive.
"Football Tactics" is worthy of attention, and not only for fans of the game. The game plays out with familiar turn-based mechanics, a system encompassing rules seen in well known titles like Civilisation, X-Com or the recent Wastelands 2, but also adding some specials seen in systems employing the "Active Time Battle" combat. Yes, those are JRPGs more often than not, and this game makes use of abilities and talents in a similar manner.
The all-too-familiar compulsion mechanics are there; win games, gain XP, level your footballers. Train one of four stats (Accuracy, Passing, Defense, Control) and mould the style of play which suits you. Play the Guardiola game by controlling the football with high "Control" and "Passing" stats. Or simply hoof the ball upfront with the "Long Pass" skill, and hope your lanky centre forward latches onto it. Want to keep possession? You can "fortify" your striker in the same way you fortify units in Civ, getting a "Control" bonus. Want to dribble past the whole back-four, like Diego did against Belgium? Use "Raibow feint," one of the talents gained by levelling up your footballers.
Granted there is still room for improvement here, like additional modes and a beefier, more-complex ruleset. As it stands, the game is breakable simply by upgrading your youth coach, waiting out promotion, farming XP, and building an all-star team which will waltz through the first two or three leagues, like a vintage Omar Sivori. But improvements are being made, and it really does look promising.
Overall, amply recommended; among the big rubbish pile that is Early Access, there is a sparkle which gives us hope.

This is an old-school RPG with all of the pros of 90s gaming - high on ideas and low on fluff.
Some of the complaints here are totally unjustified, money-driven and give you a huge sense of how entitled gamers have become. For the record, Planescape: Torment was also 40 Euros/Pounds/Dollars back in the '90s.
Torment: Tides of Numenera is an immersive experience that expands your mind, confronts you with hundreds of philosophical questions and makes you look at morality in a completely different way. InXile should be applauded because this is the first RPG I actually could stomach for a long time. There have been a lot of saccharine, stupid games in the genre over the last 15 years and the imagination that went into this game is a feat in itself.
If you want epilepsy inducing 4k graphics, non-stop killing and brainless clicking, look elsewhere. This is a game that demands your absolute attention, logic and abstract imagination. Torment: Tides of Numenera has the same undeniable quality, weirdness and presence that PS:T had... except it's not Planescape, the combat is turn-based and it's a bit short.
Pros:
- Some of the best game writing in a long time.
- You can think or talk your way out of any situation.
- The Crisis system is an inventive take on turn-based combat.
- The graphics are a great nod to the original Torment.
- Excellent soundtrack. Dark, atmospheric, ambient.
- The meres: mini-stories that allow you to influence the game.
- Forces you to think critically.
- Numenera's Tides System is a new take on morality - all of it is relative.
- Beautiful, weird and downright disgusting locations.
- The visuals and animation breathe new life into the isometric RPG format.
- Items can help or harm you and all of them are odd.
- The sheer number of options and outcomes make it very replayable.
- Totally alien and dystopian: free of shouty 21st century politics.
(potential) Cons:
- Shorter than expected.
- No faction system.
- Very text heavy. If you don't like reading, don't buy it.
- Not for zombies. Requires imagination.
- There are some minor bugs in the current version.
- Some very blatant re-hashes of the original Torment.
- Small choice of characters.
$4,188,927 'nuff said.

I am one of the exceptions here in that I enjoyed the lengthy dialogue, despite its sometimes tedious verbosity. I enjoyed my experience, although, as other reviewers have mentioned, this game is not without its flaws. Predominantly, I didn't find myself particularly drawn to any party members, as their characterization seemed a bit tepid and lacked that distinctive allure that party members in similar game offerings feature.
The conclusion was disappointingly, but expectedly, abrupt. I was pleased, however, that my dominant tides were at least referenced at the end, even if I didn't feel that they had a significant impact. The later sections in the game felt somewhat rushed in comparison to earlier sections.
Again, I'll place myself in the minority by stating that the dearth of combat options didn't irk me. Plenty of alternatives exist, new and old, in terms of other RPGs if combat is a must. I enjoyed actually being able to think outside of the box to some extent, even if sometimes the presented options seemed a bit contrived or unimpactful. I really thought the "Tides" system, while admittedly simply another version of various RPG attribute systems, was nonetheless interesting in its own right, and characters throughout the game commonly remark on your dominant tides or when you behave in a manner inconsistent with previous choices.
This game does take place in a futuristic setting riddled with anachronisms, and it feels like a setting straight out of a Jules Verne or H.G. Wells novel.
The soundtrack is pleasant but largely forgettable, and voiceovers are sparse, which is probably a good thing since the quality of the voices, when present, leaves something to be desired.
Ultimately, if you're looking for an epic that keeps you on the edge of the seat, I advise you to look elsewhere. This isn't Star Wars or Mass Effect (and I have a great admiration for these), but I can appreciate it for what it is: an enigmatic, intruiguingly bizarre, and beautifully rendered creation with sometimes engaging and sometimes tedious prose that will wholly absorb you if you allow it. It's not going to be in my top five RPGs, but it was an enjoyably unique experience nonetheless.

I'll update if I find anything else, but I think I've explored most of the games mechanics by now.
Pros:
Boss fights: Bossfights are fantastic, infinitely better than rocksteady's to be honest, well, a few of them. (poison ivy anyone?) I've had a few so far, but the Deathstroke and Shiva fights were fantastic. Copperhead as well, can't wait to see what comes next. I loved the challenge, and getting the perfect completion trophies was a great was to test my skills. Few generic fights that every game has, but overall they've been great.
Open world: lots of enemies, plenty to explore. Alot of the side missions are unlocked by story progression, so expect to be locked into that. If you liked the design of City, it carries into here.
Crimes in Progress: I love these. Usually a tough group of enemies, nice difficulty, just don't expect to wrack up good combos without mashing dodge 24/7 (see below)
Cons: (so far)
Combat: I wish they had copy and pasted it. I wish. Enemies are extremely aggressive, and youll often find yourself being punched in the face while trying to perform a simple strike, and since batman moves in slow mo you cant hit and counter in time. If you played Arkham City to death like I did, youll notice. It's not obvious, but any veteran of those series will feel the slight change. Its ridiculously frustrating how hard it is to maintain any sort of combo without mashing dodge and striking once. The thugs will teleport punch to you, so even if you use freeflow to move 10 feet away, he'll somehow still hit you. I cant even batclaw slam without being punched in the middle of the slam and they weren't anywhere nearby. Really?
EDIT: i tried out the combat challenge mode, and the combat feels totally different. Very quick and responsive, felt even faster than it was in previous Arkham iterations. (Deathstroke is so fast i can barely follow how fast he strikes in focus flow) Not sure why its so different.
Collectibles: Scan tags, collect data packs, batarang network relays, interrogate informers. All a copy of different systems used in Arkham City and Harley Quinn DLC. I wouldnt mind but its all so mindless, I've yet to encounter a single challenging puzzle like I did in City. Got all the collectibles in City and had a blast. Here it feels like a chore.
Flying: I often find it really difficult to simply shoot to the top of a building and boost past. It likes to select the fire escape on the side of the building and makes it incredibly frustrating to get anywhere quickly. And expect alot of flying around, since you cant unlock all the fast travel points from the get go and the drop points can be rather far from the edge of district.
Upgrade Trees: I hate these. I hate these with a passion. I get it, its Batman starting out, he has to learn. Anyone who has experience with poorly designed upgrade trees knows what I'm talking about. Oh yeah, by the way, you HAVE to complete challenges in game to get some of the gagdets. They aren't too hard, but it took too long to get my damn sonic batarang.
It's a great game, if you loved Asylum and City you'll enjoy it, just don't expect anything too amazing. Hopefully Knight will remedy all the mistakes here.

This game is the definition of quality over quantity. Absolutely a classic.
It's not a long game, nor a complex one, but every little detail it has was well thought out. It's amazing how it can continually surprise you. It delivers memorable moments rather than flashy ones that drown in the sea of "cinematic experiences" that AAA studios brag about year after year. If you can make an iconic game with "Microsoft paint" level visuals in 2015 you are doing something right.
This game is about story and characters. Gameplay is very simple, there are only a few extra minigames. Pace is slow and not forced. You are free to explore. Key moments are well built up to. There isn't much replayability once you complete the few different "routes" (trying not to spoil too much), but the game doesn't strive for that either. The endings are satisfying and rewarding enough.
Music is a strong point of this title. The retro style soundtrack gives you the feeling of playing a classic Nintendo title, but it doesn't force itself to be "authentic" and modern instruments and sounds are fittingly present. You will find yourself listening to this games soundtrack after beating it.
Overall this game is a complete package. Nothing is missing here. Only complaints I have are minor quality of life improvements. With the game being as short as it is, they won't bother you.
If you want to smile, laugh and then almost cry, and have fond memories of the whole ride, get this game!

Spec Ops the line is a third-person modern military set in a ruined version of Dubai, now wait a moment before typing "Uuuuuggh, another modern shooter?" in the comments or what have you, because unlike other shooters this game focuses more on the story and still keeps some good gameplay elements.
Pros:
A fantastic story filled with moments that question your morality and the true consequences of war.
Good sound design and graphics, making it look and feel like you're actually shooting a gun when pressing fire.
Unique mechanics of using sand to your advantage and commanding two specially trained squad members.
Difficulty scales with how far you get into the game, making you feel exhausted after long battles near the end, and so do the three protaganists in the game.
Great characters with their own personalities and moral standpoints that make you question your own.
Said characters (especially the Walker and his squad) get more and more mentally scarred as the game goes on, an example being Walker changing his "Tango down" to "GOT THAT MOTHER*beep*ER!"
It makes you feel like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ person and hate yourself.
Cons:
It's short, only took me 6 hours to complete my first playthrough, though it does have some replay value with it's multiple choices throughout the story and an extra unlockable difficulty setting.
Multiplayer seems pretty dead, but this game didn't really focus on it to begin with.
It makes you feel like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ person and hate yourself.
But besides those three(ish) cons, the game is well worth the 20 Euro (at time of writting) price tag, buy it for yourself (or for a friend if you already have it and need to spend some money quickly), play it to the end.
Once you've done that, stop for a moment and ask yourself: Do you feel like a hero yet?

I just beat this game, and I replayed the last chapter to get all endings and hear a single line that when I first heard it, hit me like a cannon shooting bricks.  And it hit that way each subsequent time, never losing its impact when I thought about the events that had transpired.  Anyone who has finished this game probably knows which line I refer to, and if you play this game after reading this review, you probably will too.
This is not a game you play for enjoyment.  The gameplay itself is generally perfectly mechanically functional, though sometimes it seemed that taking cover was a bit delayed, resulting in quite a few deaths.  But is also mundane and doesn't change much through the campaign.  Fortunately, the single player is fairly short, so from that standpoint, Spec Ops doesn't overstay its welcome.  The other plus with the length is that it is the perfect length to tell the story it is trying to tell without dragging itself out with nothing to show.  There is one event where it all begins to spiral out of control, and neither you nor the characters can get it back under control.
This is a game you play for the narrative and for character arcs driving the events.  And if you reach a point and find yourself unable to press on, you may be a better person than the character you play as, or players who do press on.  I'm not quite sure.  I'm still not sure what I should be thinking or feeling, but right now, as I write this, I feel slightly physically ill and emotionally dead inside.  The player and the character will share in a declining mental and emotional state, gradually unable to quite tell what's real and what isn't.
A tiring, grueling, exhausting experience, but one well worth playing to remind you that war is far more about absolute horror than it is about glory.

Let me start by saying this: there are a lot of Steam reviews that give the game a thumbs down because it doesn't live up to the venerable Planescape: Torment. This is true, but the game can still easily be recommended. It's by no means a bad game. If recommending a game hinges on whether it lives up to one of the greatest games ever made, then you might be setting too high a bar.
So no, this is not Planescape: Torment. On that note, let's get the negatives out of the way first. The plot is not as interesting, nor as personal as Planescape. The characters are not as fascinating and deeply wrought. The dialogue isn't as clever or as unique. It's also not as funny. On top of that, the animations are often janky, there aren't that many party members, the game isn't all that long (in cRPG terms), combat is a bit of a mess, character abilities and progression feel limited, you can't return to major hubs after you leave them, and the oft-mentioned Tides system has almost no impact on anything.
All that would make the game sound pretty awful out of context. However, here is what you do get:  gorgeous and fascinating areas to explore, an interesting and well-written story, deep and satisfying conversation options with interesting NPCs, difficult moral judgments, lots of branching choices, and numerous fascinating little side quests and miniature stories to experience.
Ultimately, it's the discovery in this game that makes everything worthwhile. While I never felt pushed forward by the plot, I was always interested in the characters and the world around me. Numenera is a great and fantastic world with tons of variety and wierdness. The developers have really explored this and used it to its fullest. The numenera you get, and even the useless oddities you acquire for sale all have their own little stories or quirks. Exploring a city inside the body of a living transdimensional monster is awesome, as are the wonderful people that live there. I wanted to keep playing because I wanted to know what was up with this immortal dimension-hopping guy over here, or what would happen if I told this kid he was adopted from a family in another time.
So no, it doesn't do everything we might want from a Torment game, but it does enough to recommend it. I enjoyed my playthrough of it. I think, if you like cRPGs, you will too.

Damn this game! I can't stop playing. I thought it was going to be just a simple turn-based football romp. As I continued to play, I realized how much depth there was to this game. There is so much to think about trying to match up players, picking offenses and defenses, hiring coaches, and those agonizing decisions like whether or not to sell off that star vet for the money and trust that new 19 year-old kid you just contracted. Then, should I use the money for better players or that new stadium? Decisions, decisions...

The problem with Football Tactics, simply put, is that it lacks depth. At its core this is supposed to be a turn based strategy game, yet it also tries to be as casual as possible. The movement is limited by the small pitch size and the relatively small choice of actions means that you'll be doing the same things over and over again. Since the game is heavily reliant on RNG you will usually have to play the numbers to have a shot at a consistently succesful season, which further limits your influence on the proceedings. Your players will, for large parts of the game, have only one skill and most situations are dictated by a singular attribute, so your decisions usually get simplified even further.
Progress mostly comes from player stats, which give the game an RPG~ish touch, yet also seem to be mostly random. You can buy and sell players, but due to the way finances are set up you'll want to grow your own, which mostly means getting decent young players and leveling them up. Upon level up the player gets a semi random set of stat upgrades. Level ups come quite regularly but are usually pretty meager on their own (+1 to your primary stat seems to be the average), which means building up a team to take on the best opposition is a lengthy undertaking.
On the plus side these may be things some players look for. There's minimal input on your end and yet, through unnecessarily grindy upgrades, there's some sense of progress (which you will attribute to your skill, even though you know better). I've put quite a few hours into the game while watching Netflix on my primary screen and I have to admit it's a great fit for that. The UI/graphics are simple yet pleasant and while the audio is laughable it's fortunately entirely irrelevant. It isn't punishing at all, there is no fail state and it will reward you just for being there, which I personally fail to appreciate but can still potentially see other people enjoying.
Maybe I went in expecting the wrong thing. I read the name as if there was an emphasis on tactics, I thought of great games like Frozen Cortex or even Blood Bowl and while I never expected the game to have that kind of quality, this was stilll a huge let-down. I spent more than ten hours with it hoping for the game to improve towards the late game, but its inherently simple design stops it from ever becoming more than a casual side activity. I'd expect this kind of game to be on a mobile platform for around five bucks and I'd recommend it to the crowd that goes for those. For people looking for anything more than a time-killer I'd suggest staying away.

*EARLY ACCESS REVIEW*
I really like the idea of turn-based football - it brings back the tactical part to the game, instead of rewarding skilled players as other football games do. I really enjoy the aesthetics, the system and the advancement rate.
The game could definitely do better with a bit more depth: maybe recording all statistics for players regardless of their position, or allowing to change their roles (DF into MF, for example). I would really love to be able to review my club's historical players and data.
What I think could really improve the game, is reducing the RNG's weight, especially for the use of skills/special techniques, which completely ignore the relative level of the players involved.
Overall, I liked the game but it needs a lot more work, and I think it's headed in the right direction. At list in my personal experience, the Devs have promptly replied and guided me, and I feel my feedback may help improve the final product :)

Football Tactics is a simple game of football team management and coaching. The goal, pun intended, is to move your club into the premier league of your nation to compete for the top championship. It will appeal to players who are fans of football and players whose time is limited to 30 minute play sessions. That’s about all the time you need to set your line, make a few improvements to your club, and play a match or two in Football Tactics.

Compared to other football management sims, this game is simpler. For example, the footballers who populate your club’s lines have only four rated skills:  accuracy for shooting goals, passing to other teammates, defense for taking the ball from your opponents, and control for mainlining possession during an opponent’s defensive action. However, these four skills, tactics cards, tactics formations, and your players’ age and energy level create on field challenges that are deeper than expected.
The matches are turn-based with each team alternating through 3 actions per side for a set number of actions per half. During one cycle you might have a mid-fielder pass to a forward, the forward dribble to get  a better shot angle, and then the forward make a precision shot on goal. Of course, the opposing team will try to counter your moves each step of the way.
Off the field, club mangers can shop the transfer market, direct player training and development, and oversee expansion of the team’s fan base, coaching staff, and facility upgrades. The business model is easy to understand. The better players perform on the field the higher their price and trade value rises.  Put together a string of victories and your club’s fan base will grow helping you earn more from ticket sales for home games. In addition to money, your team will also earn prestige points that you can spend on team management decisions.
Football Tactics includes stock leagues from around the world in addition to a growing number of national and international leagues that users are adding on Steam Workshop. If you don’t like your club’s name, kit, or logo, then you’re free to modify them in the in-game editor. Also, you can edit the names of team members, too.

The Skinny: Good polish to an interesting concept tagged and labeled as a genre bending tactical/strategy/rpg/sports simulation game. Confusing design decisions caused this title to suffer an identiy crisis deciding if it was going to be a casual or hardcore. Worse still the developers failed to circumvent some of the pitfalls that come with combining so many concepts together.
Even More Skinny: This game feels alot like a very polished mobile phone freemium game without the microtransactions.
I do of course approve of the developers excluding the microtransactions and the care they have taken in refining their product to be presented in a a concise and easy-to-use package.
The Longer View:
Tough game to pin down and fit into a Box but I will give it a shot...
I would say this game is a Sports Simulation first and then a Strategy game consisting of some Turn-based RPG elements with a strong Tactical component. Conceptually it seems like an excellent foundation from which you could start building a very unique and deep game but I did not find there to be much complexity to any of the mechanics that were built on top of that great foundation. To me the concept of the game suggests and hints that this is going to be a hardcore crowd pleaser. However, from a presentation standpoint the UI, graphic design, and simplistic text descriptions of events/outcomes/etc. are all much more in line with a casual gaming experience usually found on a mobile phone or facebook game.  I can honestly say that I enjoy both casual phone games (the higher quality ones at least) and hardcore pc games. I will also say that all of the genre's I mentioned earlier are favorites of mine. but I feel that this game comes up short in the areas that usually make each of those genres fun and appealing.
I Liked:
Unique Concept
Player agency in chosing between a few different methods to build your squad
Tactics (I personally am going to buy your game if this is in the title and the screenshots/playthroughs/video is anything short of atrocious)
RPG Elements blended with the Sports Simulator
UI and controls are streamlined perfectly (really well done)
No Microtransactions
AC/DC:
Predomintly a Casual Game
Medium-to-High RNG elements
Grindy
Sound Effects/Music - I would say this aspect was OK but also somewhat sparse and repetitive (I play most sim games listening to a soundtrack of my own choosing anyway)
But awwwwww C'mon:
4 attributes are just not enough.....unless you have an excellent system of Special Abilites to compliment them...
Special Abilities are a bit vanilla and many of the defensive ones pointless
No real storyline feel and very limited options for customizations to "create your own"
Small size of the playing field grid limits options
Very Limited Defensive Options
Feels like a Hardcore Gaming Input is required b/c....
Progression is slow and incrimental
Difficutly/Balancing Staggered Resulting in Long Periods of cruising followed by getting your face crushed once you've hit a (non-pay) wall
Juxtaposition of the two points immediately above this one
That last point was the real fun killer for me. Football Tactics fails in this regard by setting itself up with a freemium game structure in that you are either struggling to progress because you have not inserted enough currency (in this case time spent grinding) or blowing the competition out of the water because you have. The tactical aspects of games will occasionally allow for you to beat a superior opponent and it is at the moment Football Tactics shines brightest. This too comes with a pitfall unfortunately because of the limited amount of diversity offered in your player builds and to a lesser degree limited number of spaces and therefore movement on the field. The result is that there are a limited number of choices to your strategies and many of them will come down to attempting a similiar set of actions that rely more on maximizing your best chance at a good roll (RNG haters beware) than careful planning. I really felt like I was being punished by the game for succeeding with these tactics early on as it caused my squad to advance up the divisions twice in concurent seasons and left my underfunded squad facing more difficult odds (literally rng odds not tactical difficulties)
than any tactical approach would be able to sufficiently overcome.
Two comparision points I would like to bring up are the statistical heavy Football Manager Series and Tactical Aspects of Blood Bowl.  In a way I feel like Football Tactics is alot like playing a toned down version of the Football Manager series when your simulating games managing your squad, improving through the transfer windows, or youth player discoveries or in-squad development. The depth of the systems for Football Manager is really what makes it a game worth playing in the first place and again the lack of options present in Football Tactics prevents it from succeeding in the same way. As a Tactical Game Blood Bowl succeeds in the importance of placing your units in the correct spot is crucial because you are making a choice of influencing some control over a large amount of space (by spreading your characters out) or influencing a greater amount of control over a smaller area (keeping your units closer together). Football Tactics gives your units VERY limited influence over space and gives you a very limited field with which to work. When your opponent has the ball most of your units can only influence the space they occupy by being giving a chance to steal the ball if your opponent chooses to challenge that space by dribbling through it or passing almost directly through it. Most of the time this will not factor in as your opponent will choose to forgoe any chance of an interception by making a very safe pass (when a more direct approach is necessary in terms of scoreline/time managment) or simply dribbling past your player. Defenders have the ability to influence shots that cross the spot next to them which is a good start but why do they allow the ball carrier to dribble into that same space without interference? It just does not work for me to have a game labeled as TACTICS and have such a limited number of tactical options.
Casual FM with a Turn-based Tactics similiar to Blood Bowl sounded like a sure-fire winning column title in my book but the pace of progression/balancing aspects and strange design choices really drag this one down in the mud. This is still early access stage so things could improve but baring some momnumental shift in the game design and direction I can not see my opinion changing at this point. Would love to be proved wrong here btw. I am really hoping to see a sequel/reboot/clone that adds depth pop up and deliver on the substantial amount of promise I see unfufilled here. Points for UI streamlining and original concept though....

Heavy Bullets is a really unique take on the Rogue-lite genre, and one that I feel anyone can thoroughly enjoy. It has the unique distinction as being one of the only Rogue-lite FPS games I've ever encountered, and it really milks that label for all its worth. With a colorful, neon design and blocky 3-D graphics, it's a pleasant break from all of the "retro" pixel games that have been coming out recently, so it's visually appealing as well.
In Heavy Bullets, you are given a revolver with six slots. You can fire these six bullets and then pick them back up to reload into your gun. Sounds simple, but when enemies begin swarming you, you can quickly find yourself separated from your bullets, which are now all the way accross the room. The game itself is extremely challenging, though as you get accustomed to the controls and gameplay you can feel yourself improving. The gunplay is responsive, if a little finnicky at times and killing enemies is satisfying, as they explode into a cloud of coins and bullets. Secret rooms and locked doors make exploration a pleasure, and a unique banking system allows you to store money and items for future runs, a feature that I really appreciate.
However, I must say that the control is a bit of a mixed bag. You move extremely fast in this game, far faster than any other FPS I've ever played, and this means positioning yourself for strafing kills or aiming can be a challenge until you acclimate to the lightning speed you move at. Items are also a part of the game, but they too suffer from some flaws. Certain items are more useful than others, and some are even detrimental. (why would I want running shoes if I already have trouble controlling my character?) Bombs are extremely difficult to use without hurting yourself in the process, and the in game text is a little bit vague and hard to understand. Carry Item+ does NOT let you carry an additional item, it just lets you carry more of the one you already have
All in All

I just beat this game, and I replayed the last chapter to get all endings and hear a single line that when I first heard it, hit me like a cannon shooting bricks.  And it hit that way each subsequent time, never losing its impact when I thought about the events that had transpired.  Anyone who has finished this game probably knows which line I refer to, and if you play this game after reading this review, you probably will too.
This is not a game you play for enjoyment.  The gameplay itself is generally perfectly mechanically functional, though sometimes it seemed that taking cover was a bit delayed, resulting in quite a few deaths.  But is also mundane and doesn't change much through the campaign.  Fortunately, the single player is fairly short, so from that standpoint, Spec Ops doesn't overstay its welcome.  The other plus with the length is that it is the perfect length to tell the story it is trying to tell without dragging itself out with nothing to show.  There is one event where it all begins to spiral out of control, and neither you nor the characters can get it back under control.
This is a game you play for the narrative and for character arcs driving the events.  And if you reach a point and find yourself unable to press on, you may be a better person than the character you play as, or players who do press on.  I'm not quite sure.  I'm still not sure what I should be thinking or feeling, but right now, as I write this, I feel slightly physically ill and emotionally dead inside.  The player and the character will share in a declining mental and emotional state, gradually unable to quite tell what's real and what isn't.
A tiring, grueling, exhausting experience, but one well worth playing to remind you that war is far more about absolute horror than it is about glory.

After completing the main story in one, non-stop playsthrough, here's what I think (and it's only my humble opinion).
- The graphics are not ugly, if not exceptionnally good or revolutionnary.
- The gameplay mechanics are smooth, easy to get used to (especially with a controller, but I had no trouble whatsoever with my mouse and keyboard), if again far from a revolutionnary new concept.
- The sound effects, soundtrack, acting and voice acting are all spot on, backing up the story and general tone of the game just as they should.
- It all felt a bit short for me, but a few choices along the way can make for alternate endings (and I strongly believe it is worth replaying), and I'm guessing the hardest difficulty settings can be a bit of a challenge.
- And now for the only reason anyone needs to try this game : the story. Try picturing playing a 3rd person version of what I would call "Call of the Apocalypse Now : Post-apocalyptic Dubaï Warfare". When I got through only the first stages of the game, it was obvious it wasn't to be a generic, seen-it-all-before patriotic shooter filled with bad guys and good guys. In this game, everyone is a monster, or becomes one eventually. When I got to the ending, with the video game equivalent of PTSD, all I could think of was the last line of "Apocalypse Now". It's like the game, more than entertaining me, wanted me to reflect on warfare, violence, the dire consequences of it, and my own desire to indugle in virtual violence ("You like violence ? We'll cure you of that !").
"The horror"...
To keep it in a nutshell : seemingly average third person shooter, but with a storyline and a tone you cannot forget, and is well worth the money I spent. And you'll never use white phosphorous in game ever again. Ever.

This is quite possibly the best hitman game to date.   Hitman 2016 makes a return to open ended maps with tons of replay and exploration value. a new feature is Opportunities, which remove a lot of the blind running around older Hitman games suffered from.  This also serves to make the game much more newbie friendly.  Contracts mode makes a return and is fun as ever, however there isn't a way to search for friends' contracts at the moment.  There are also even more challenges, even some tough ones for experienced players like my current addiction: Silent Assassin Suit Only challenge.
The game is unfinished, which makes it a hard buy not knowing if it will keep it's quality up in coming missions. The always online component is annoying and a huge barrier, and I had to reduce settings so the game would run well on my PC.
Despite it's issues this is an amazing edition to the series with potential to be even better than Blood Money.  New players will find the system easy to learn, yet hard to master, and old fans will be happy with a return to form.
Pros:
Return to classic Hitman gameplay
Massive maps
Hours of replay value
New player friendly yet
Challenging for series veterans
Return of Contracts mode
Cons:
Poor Optimization
Online connection required for most features
Cannot search for friends' contracts
Epsodic release of missions makes current quality unguaranteed.

This game feels almost like a halfway house between the Football Manager series and games like FIFA and PES. You get to create your own team (or mod in famous teams and players) and fight your way up your country's ladder in a turn-based football combat game.
Sometimes, the lack of control from the turn-based nature of the game is frustrating, as it leaves you powerless when RNG-based intercept plays fail and you concede a goal, but on the whole the idea works and is well executed.
Outside of matches there's also a fairly light team management sim going on, where you use "fame", "fans" and "money", basically 3 forms of currency, to expand your team and stadium and get better players. You also have the option to sign sponsorship agreements each season, which will dictate certain conditions to fulfill in order to get extra money. I feel this part of the game still needs more work, but it fits in fairly well overall
This review is from Early Access, so of course your mileage may vary, and the game is still subject to change.
