Warning: This Review of mine will be really long, but i suggest you read it completely. You will be informed and entertained!
First of all:
Wow! Definetly worth the Price for this Early Access (!) Game, if you´re into Soccer Management and tactical Gameplay and want to see a well rounded Game for the asked Price!
The Game:
This Games Base is solid and working, both performance and mechanic-wise. I fell in love with what this Game is already and even more so with what this Game can definetly be in the Future.
Football Tactics has, as i mentioned before, a good working and fun to play mechanic for the Games and the right Options on what to extend your Club on the management Side. There are real Choices to make, depending on your Play-Style, that make a Difference:
Need stronger Defense to hold the stronger League you got promoted to? You can do that!
Want even more dangerous Strikers to aim for the Title? You can do that!
This Game is so solid Gameplay and Fun-wise, that i have to admit i feel flattered to see a Game that doesn´t claim to be or tries to be more than it is.
It´s fun. It´s engaging to see your Club develop. And you feel the Difference of stronger enemy Teams and Teams that you are supposed to win against.
There is always a Chance to get behind when playing a supposedly weaker Enemy and always a minimal Chance to get a good Result against the overwhelming odds of a higher Class Opposition, if you have the right Idea and a bit of Luck. It´s Soccer after all.
All this without losing the importance of your Team Tactic and your Formation. In my first Season i made it to the second Round of the League Cup against all Odds, because i played with a 6-Man Defense and just tried to have as much Ball Posession as possbile. It was a boring 0-0 and i won in the Penalty Shootout. I´m not a big Fan of this Tactic, but i won and got a big Load of Prestige, Experience and Money to invest into my Infrastrcture and my personal favorite: My Youth Team.
So what are the Cons and what needs to be implemented to reach the maximal Potantial of this Game?
Cons:
As i mentioned: The game works perfectly and has a very solid and working Base + Fun-Experience, so it doesn´t need any Fixes. Which bring me to the "real" Cons of this Game, which is Content and Multiplayer.
Implementations (Cons 2):
This Game needs Multiplayer! It just does! It´s a shame to keep this Experience from the Multiplaying-Community! We Football/Soccer-Fanatics NEED to be able to measure our Skill against other non AI Opponents. Make it happen! It´ll eventually make this Game way bigger than it is atm! Seriously!
My Second Complaint is, that there isn´t more of this Game. With this solid and well developed Gameplay-Base there just needs to be more Content.
Examples:
More active Skills for the Players than the few we have, even when this few are very nicely done. Also make the Skill a little deeper and not just dependend on Player Skill or his Stamina. Make (mainly for Multiplayer Reasons) Rock-Paper-Scissors like Skills, like a certain Striker Dribble-Skill is weak to certain defensive Skill, which will result in +50% Bonus on the Defenders Throw. That would make it a real mind Game on what to choose in a Situation for the Players and it would even influence tactical Choices, like in reality where a certain Player who normally isn´t in the Starting Team gets thrown in, because he´s good against a certain Player from the Enemy Team. Also, implement more Passive Skills, maybe to make certain Players able to move even 3 Fields in 1-Turn. That way you would get so much more tactical Variations and each Team would really have a unique Face and Style.
In Short:
- Make Multiplayer happen
- More Content: More Active Skills, More Passive Skills, Deeper mechanics for SOME (!) of them
If you make this happen, this Game could really achieve more than anyone would think. At the Moment it´s a good Game for a fair Price.
It can be more though.

It's a interesting idea, but it just doesn't really come together as a tactical game. The team building elements are solid, and if that type of game (manager game) is your thing, you might really like this. But, if you're looking for Blood Bowl Soccer without the blood, you're going to be disappointed. This just doesn't have that level of complexity, at least not yet. Maybe with some tweaking and fixing, this could be solid. As is, you only have three moves to make per turn, and you're supposed to be able to get more by executing skills, but rarely does this work, and there's really no explanation why. It basically ends being a matter of which team has better stats. The team with the better players can score easily with no real tactics, and the weaker team has few tools availble to stop them, or even slow them down.
I'd like to recommend this game, and spent a fair amount of time playing it, but it's just not real good, yet....

I loved the game. It made full use of the Dying Earth setting to deliver a slew of strange concepts, which I found extremely stimulating. The writing was generally of a very high calibre, and even the descriptive text I found to be a cut above almost anything else in the RPG genre (c f Pillars of Eternity where a lot of the descriptive text and worldbuilding is awwwwwfffuuullly boring and should never have made it into a finished game - though it's a good game for other reasons). I liked the reactivity built into the interactions. I replayed Planescape Torment recently and something that bothered me was how there'd often be no recognition that you'd done or learnt something. For example, I'd be well into the Clerk's Ward, having done every quest I could, and still have the exact same conversation with Pox outside the Mortuary, asking who the Dustmen are and what they believe. From what McComb said in one of the streams, this may have been a casualty of technical problems with the engine. Numenera had excellent reactivity - if I'd learnt something related to one character or which might be relevant to a quest, I'd usually have an option to bring it up in conversation in NPC interactions. Consequently, it was very easy for me to look at the situation the Last Castoff was in, think 'How would I deal with this?' or 'What would I want to know if I were in the Castoff's position?' and explore the resultant avenues of inquiry.
It's probably fair to say I was most interested in the setting and writing behind the individual quests, which is where the game was strongest. Gene Wolfe's The Book of the New Sun is one of my favourite literary works of all time, and Jack Vance's Dying Earth isn't far off (honourable mention to Michael John Harrison's Viriconium - Harrison is, much like Wolfe, a technical writer par excellence). The thing I most would've wanted that the game didn't give? More! And by that, I don't mean that the game is short - I don't know exactly how long it took me; my recorded gameplay time is just under 43 hours, but I spent quite a bit of time with the game open in the background while I was doing other stuff, so I'd estimate I'm in the mid-30s for game time, which is not short. What I mean is I loved the world and quest writing so much, I'd love to have played a sprawling, Baldur's Gate 2 length game, seeing all of the weirdness that the Ninth World has to offer. But I understand this would be beyond budget and not worth the return on sales. Anyway, the game's flaws don't feel so significant to me.
I can see how they would turn someone else off the game, however. Combat was flawed, for example - not irredeemably bad, but with faults in execution such as the time taken for turns, and poor encounter design. The central storyline was also not great. It didn't feel like the game's primary antagonist related particularly well to the game's purported theme, nor was it well-developed. I think the inadequate attention paid to the Sorrow is probably the biggest failing of the game's writing. An additional area to the game, in which you explore a location related to the Sorrow's origins, would have done a lot to remedy this, even if it wouldn't have fixed the direct role of the Sorrow in the story's central conflict.
The Changing God was interesting and I thought dealt with well. Possibly more could have been done with him, but he's a concept which could be pushed in so many directions, and there's so much that could be done, that it'd be very hard to look at any particular use of him and say that that use exhausted his concept or executed it perfectly.
Some of the flaws other people experienced I did not find - for example, I liked the companions. Again, more could have been done with them, but what is there is not bad. The only one I did not care for too much was Tybir, who was simply too generic. He wasn't done badly, so that failing is no real knock on the game. I also liked the visuals. Sure, more animations would have been nice, particularly combat animations, but I thought the art style and colouring were vivid and evocative.
To summarise my view on Numenera, considered alone: I liked it a hell of a lot, and it's probably my favourite RPG since the Witcher 3, and before that... Vampire Bloodlines? Arcanum? I'd put it comfortably above other relatively recent high quality RPGs like Pillars of Eternity and Fallout New Vegas, which I also enjoyed but didn't resonate on a deep level. The writing with respect to the individual characters and the setting are top-notch, even if the central story lacks in some respects, and earns the game a place in my pantheon of great videogame storytelling experiences.
How do I think it compares to Planescape Torment? Having replayed that game recently: quite well! PST is a more coherent game, from a storytelling perspective, and that gives a good argument that it is better from a literary view, but I didn't think the setting was as fascinatingly varied and exotic, and the quests aside from the central storyline weren't as consistently engaging. Combat in PST was also, rather than being deeply flawed, fundamentally bad and odious. Character wise, PST has an edge, because each companion related thematically to the central storyline, though I found that the common thread of the binding nature of torment and suffering was a little relentlessly dour.
On the whole, I'd say they're closely comparable in the level of enjoyment I derived from them. I suspect my view that they are comparable in terms of overall merit is premised on my affinity for Dying earth science fantasy settings over straight fantasy settings, even ones as strange as Planescape, so take that for what its worth.

I would recommend this game but with some reservations. It might be best to get the game when the price drops or after future patches and added/re-added content. I enjoyed playing the game, with three different playthroughs, but not without some criticism. The very nature of this being hyped up as a spiritual sucessor to Planescape: Torment already set expectations too high and caused them to over-promise, which ended up coming back to bite them. But taken for what it is, it is a decent game. It just could have been more.
World/Story - The setting is imaginative and intrigueing and the story is pretty good. The plot is a bit linear and, unfortunately, it feels a little rushed in the 2nd half of the game. Relative to my expectations for an RPG, the game's playtime is dissapointingly short and the areas are small. You get a strong sense that they had earlier iterations that were much more epic and had twice as many locations, but they ended up cutting out half of it. That's probably the biggest dissapointment for me. It's all over too quickly.
Character Progression - On a related note, the level cap comes a little too quickly, at least if you play as a completionist and do all side quests. This is a feel bad thing in any RPG. In all three of my playthroughs, my main character reached the cap with about 1/4 of the game left. There was 1600+ experience past that which I couldn't use. That's easily enough XP for another 2 Tiers. If they added abilities for 2 more tiers, they could easily raise the cap to 7.
Choice and Consequence - This is probably one of the aspects that they nailed pretty good. There are usually at least 2 or 3 ways to resolve most quests, sometimes with vastly different results. There are also lots of variable dialogue options that affect your tides. That said, in the long term plot, there isn't as much of a sense that your choices matter as there could be. It's all sort of foisted upon you as you're rushed to the ending.
Graphics/Art/Music - The area backgrounds look beautiful and are well done. The character/NPC avatars are much more simplistic and clunky in comparison. The background music is pretty good for setting atmosphere, though maybe a bit empty at some points. You do get a sense sometimes that there was extra graphical/animation polish that existed in earlier iterations that they took out. This aspect is not that big of a deal to me though.
Dialogue - It should be expected for this type of game that there is a lot of dialogue. This isn't a bad thing in and of itself. Anyone who wants a hack and slash dungeon crawl doesn't get what a game like this is supposed to be about. That said, sometimes they got overly verbose for details that didn't matter. 90% of the game is reading text and it could have been paced out better with a little more combat and exploration. Even Planescape: Torment wasn't as heavy on the text-adventure aspect as this is.
Combat - Combat isn't quite as bad as some people are saying. It isn't a great though and the Crisis system can get buggy. With the relatively few combat encounters there are, and the fact that you can talk your way out of most of them, players may feel like they rarely get to use their combat abilities and thus character progression feels a bit empty. Much the same goes for all of the Cyphers, which are unique one-time use items, but you don't get enough of a chance to actually use them.
Skill System - The general idea of the skill system is pretty good. The way they implimented it, however, probably makes the game a bit too easy. With investment in Intellect based skills, Edge points, plus the ability to use your companions to help with skills, it is easy to pretty quickly get to a point where skill checks are no longer a challenge. With a few exceptions, after the beginning it's possible to breeze through most of the game's skill checks regardless of your character build. Needs to be rebalanced with more risk and limitation.
Tides - This is one of the most interesting and flavorful aspects of the game. The way that your choices determine your tides and the world subtly reacts is pretty well done. My one complaint about the tides is that I wish there were more explicit ways you can use them in gameplay. With a few exceptions, the tides are just a display of the morality of your actions and are not as reactive as they sold it to be, within a given playthrough. The subtle effects of the tides do show more across multiple playthroughs though.
Companions/NPCs - Aside from Rhin and maybe Castillege, the companions don't feel as fleshed out as they could be. There is a significant lack of companion interaction, party banter, and voice acting in general. The game also pretty much encourages you to choose a team in the first area and stick with it, and there's no going back to the first area once you leave. There are no mid or late game companions. The lack of NPC portraits also takes away from immersion. Also, unlike Planescape: Torment, most non-quest-related NPCs can't truly be interacted with, they just show one liners above their head if you click them.
Basically, I think the game has a lot of cool ideas and potential, but they just didn't flesh it out as much as they could have, or they gutted their own ideas a little too much to a point where quite a few features that were either promised or that actually existed in earlier iterations of the game ended up being left out entirely (including: NPC portraits, more voice acting, more companions, two or three more game areas that could have easily added 10-20 more hours of content, and so on). That makes the game feel a little empty or over streamlined.
With all of that criticism, I still would recommend the game because it is still a unique experience, it has a unique setting and story, and it has its share of flavor. In some basic ways, they did capture the feel of Torment, they just could have refined it more instead of putting time and money into making it a console port and over streamlining content. I also am holding out hope that there will be future patches and add-ons that make up for at least some of the criticism.

I was an early backer of the game, I usually back each and every CRPG that resembles old school RPGs. But TTON was my first big disappointment. My main problem is one of the selling points of the game, that you can beat it without killing anyone. I expected some sophisticated dialogue and skill system, but in reality, it is simply using Tide points to "solve" dialogue options that come up in every situation. Tide points are divided into 3 sections. Might, Speed and Intellect. The more Tide point you spend in an interaction, the higher chance you will succeed. The problem is, that Tide points can be used individually by any party member, so even a dumb brute can easily convince a fanatical deth acolyte to stand bck from his plan. For a brute, the options should not even pop up in my opinion. But like this, basically you can talk yourself through the game without ANY effort, in case you run out of points, you just need to rest and continue.
Pros:
-Interesting setting
-Unique environment
-Okay graphics
Cons:
-Tide system; you just talk yourself through the game in literally ANY situation
-Combat is clunky and pointless
-Main character is blank, you cannot even customize its look
-Almost non-existent and bad voice acting
-Uninteresting cliche companions with zero motive
-Dull soundtrack
-Tiny, cramped maps
-Cyphers (so far) are more annoyance than use
-Writing is tedious and overcomplicated
All in all, given its hype and huge funding, the game underdelivers in almost every aspect for me. I keep going as long as I can, maybe I find the fun part of it, but so far it is more like a tedious graphic novel from a conceited literature student. For full price I definitely do not recommend it, on sale only if you are up to tons of reading and ONLY reading. (And by too much reading I mean compared to any other, enjoyable CRPG.)

(Full disclosure: Kickstarter backer)
I aboslutely loved the original PS:T, and consider this a worthy successor.  As good as the original?  Well, no.  But I consider that the greatest CRPG ever made, so nothing else compares that well either.  Nonetheless, this game has faithfully recreated a similarly mysterious world in which you can spend hours unravelling its mysteries.  It's fantastic fun to dig around numerous NPCs and interactables for little bits of knowledge or small rewards.  If you liked Planescape:Torment, or NeverWinter Nights 2's Mask of the Betrayer, then you'll definitely enjoy this.
As far as downsides go, the game definitely isn't perfect.  First off, the combat is not terribly enjoyable.  PS:T's was bad too, but this is worse.  On the upside, your choices can avoid almost all of them.  The companions also don't hold up as well as the original -- several of them are not nearly as quirky, interesting, or interactive.  Lastly, there's a _LOT_ of reading.  Even compared to PS:T.  Plenty of the language is used is...overly complicated.  Esoteric words, etc.  Not necessarily a downside, but I can't recall another game that made me consult a dictionary as often -- and that's from an avid CRPG fan and book reader.
There's also plenty of Kickstarter drama surrounding this game, but don't let that concern you.  TToN was funded at the height of Kickstarter's popularity, yet before developers got good with managing promises and rewards.  Combined with poor communication on their part, and it resulted in some upset backers.  But the game stands on its own, and is still worth playing.
I would hands down recommend this to any fan of the original PS:T or NWN2: MotB.  If you like CRPGs, and don't mind a word-heavy low-combat game, then you'll probably enjoy this as well.

-----------------------------------------Introduction--------------------------------------------
I am glad that I can finally recommend this game. It is an unique treat for FPS lovers. The game is riddled with issues but it has no competition in areas where it shines. Besides, the issues only become unbearable on high difficulty. I have tried my best to circumvent the issues even on high difficulty and can assure that it is possible.
----------------------------------------------AI-----------------------------------------------------
I have never seen AI like this in any other game. It not only dodges very unpredictably and uses cover well, but each enemy type also plays to its strengths and weaknesses. The AI is very good at using group tactics. If you are behind a cover with two open sides, then often enemies will attack you from both sides, provided such units are available. Rats continuously move their heads at awkward angle. Stalkers can cloak are very good at dodging hits from even point blank range. Pestisilent stalkers keep running away and jumping from distance. Enemies often wait behind cover and regenerate their health before attacking again.
However, some enemies are simply overpowered. They just combined insane speed and melee damage with insane health. Lazy design.
------------------------------------ This game is challenging-------------------------------------
Many enemies deal insane damage. They also respawn quickly, making backtracking difficult. On high difficulty, enemies constantly regen health to discourage camping. There are enemies with metal shields that repel all bullets. There are locked doors that make pacifist run impossible. Health injections can't be carried. There is damage over time (DoT) that can kill even after you take cover. Gun crosshairs keep moving. Displayed gun stats are often false. The game only saves the current nearest fast travel point, inventory, and mission progress. Each time you reload, you go back to the starting position of the dungeon and all enemies respawn (excluding mission-specific enemies).
------------------Introduction to finer points of BL gameplay and terminology-----------------
(Skip it if you find such info useless in a review)
Enemies have massive health, player not so much. The game has a huge variety of enemy and gear types. TVHM is mid difficulty, UVHM is high, OP levels are higher. Completing the story in normal unlocks TVHM, & completing again in TVHM unlocks UVHM. After that, each completion of Digistruct Peak unlocks one OP level. Chests and killed enemies drop loot. Bosses respawn, and can be farmed. There are raid instances. There are skill tree & leveling for players and enemies. Enemies scale with player. No friendly fire, no bullet drop. Critical hit does massive damage. In TVHM everything is locked at level 50, but player can level up if UVHM pack is installed. This can be deadly because if the player does not switch to UVHM at 50, they have to face high level enemies with L50 gear. Not getting the UVHM pack until you get all the legendary drops is called playthrough 2.5. Most gears are randomly generated, some are unique, but even the uniques have variations that get decided randomly. There is no armor for player, but there are energy shields. There is no crafting or potion. One player character can use magic, but I am not sure how that plays out. There is infighting among factions. There are elements like fire (useless against armor) & shock (destroys energy shields), but no frost. Corrossion destroys armor. Slag increases all other damages thrice (in UVHM). These elements are chemical, not magical. Creatures with elemental abilities resist damage from their element. Explosion is average against everything and goes through metal shields. Some energy shields boast immunity from one element, but only from DoT, not base damage. Invisibility and teleportation are used in combat, but not all characters and enemies can use those. No character cutomisation. There are six character types, and there are extreme differences between their play styles. Grenade mods change the behaviour of grenades, & relics just provide buffs. Bee is an energy shield that adds huge DPS buff while the shield is full. DPUH is a pistol that some claim to be the only gun that works on OP levels. Rubi is a pistol that heals the player by leeching a certain percentage of damage done to enemies (even with another weapon) as long as it is held, & one of the player characters can dual weild (hint). Fight for your life refers to a mode where you get few seconds of invulnerability before dying and if you manage to get a kill, you get second wind. You can't use sniper scope, can reload, but can't open inventory in this mode.
There is some vehicle combat in this game. Mediocre.
-----------------------------------------------Cons-----------------------------------------------
Everything falls apartonce you reach UVHM. On UVHM and upwards you will only be using a few tried and tested weapons, gears, and techniques for all characters and on all enemy types. Melee Zer0 looks awesome in the trailer, but is a letdown in actual game. There are certain gameplay aspects that make sniper builds quite underwhelming. In every difficulty, enemies do not spawn unless you are a few meters from them and most of the badass variants rush you. There are many winding hallways and combat arenas that are impractical for sniping, & health regen makes any sniper gun useless that can't kill in one or two hits. On the other hand, the combo of Bee, slag and a SMG of proper elemental type kills so fast that I have no incentive to try anything else. Also, fight for your life is not for sniping. The only advantage of ranged build: blackhole threshers.
Any character works if you play properly. There are people who claim to solo OP raid bosses with Sniper or melee Zer0, but I suspect that it requires many sacrifices and a solid bout of luck. After enjoying the huge liberty upto TVHM, UVHM is a big letdown. If you are just trying to have fun, forget UVHM.
Prime source of my headache is lack of enough active weapon slots. There are only four. Every other fault would have been more bearable if there were more slots. Slag is mandatory on UVHM, & demands fine muscle memory to switch to and from. So one slot is reserved for slag, another for rocket launcher (second wind). Just two slots remain. I have to open the inventory mid-combat to switch to appropriate weapon for current enemy, & even in SP I often lose Bee while doing so because it hinders my fluidity. What about co-op where the game does not pause?
Why just four slots? For comsoles? They have eight corners on those POV hats.
------------------------------------------------Bugs----------------------------------------------
Lets talk bugs. Environment design is horrible and sometimes the player abruptly gets stuck on slight elevation changes or can't jump properly. Rocket ammo is rare, only 33 can be carried, and it hurts to see rockets just clipping through enemies instead of hitting, especially while fighting for second wind. Speaking of FFYL, sometimes FFYL mode is skipped, abruptly ends, or passes very quickly, I am not sure if it is a bug or a feature. There are some other bugs like messed up hitboxes, but you can adapt to those.

My feelings toward Torment: Tides of Numenera are mixed. While much love and dedication was obviously put into this CRPG, its hard to ignore it's weak points.
I chose to recommend this game because at the moment of writing the game's overall score deserves some positive correction upward. I think people should be encouraged to play this game, and games like this in general (such as PoE and Tyranny), though when it comes to this title they would be served best by curbing their expectations.
Pros:
* A fascinating world full of wonders to explore and discover.
* Interesting questlines and characters, for the most part.
* Well written narrative, for the most part.
Cons:
* An incredibly frustrating combat system with long waiting time between rounds. (Although you can choose to avoid combat most of the time).
* Banal and unsatisfying asnwers to some of the game's most intriguing mysteries.
* Rushed ending that fails to meet the expectations.
Verdict: Play this game to enjoy the ride and don't expect a mind blowing closure, just try to avoid the combat.

Hardly an heir to Planescape Torment; and certainly no Baldur's Gate.  It doesn't get the gameplay basics right and its writing isn't enough to redeem that.
Torment's writing is passable, though often much too long and complicated.  Few of the characters are compelling or memorable, and the setting doesn't in any way feel like a real place.  The issue here is that Torment's game mechanics are terrible, and the game has nothing but the writing to recommend it; that writing isn't good enough to do so.
All of the game mechanics are BORING.  What difficulty exists largely comes from a lack of communication to the player about how certain systems work (what does this ability/skill do?  will it be useful?) and frankly antiquated and thoughtless design choices (you can't re-pick abilities; aren't you glad we didn't explain them very well?)
It's 2017 and I'm really not very tolerant of long load times in order to read a paragraph of dialogue that should have been a sentence.  It's less about your money; don't waste your time.

8/10 - Very Good
Here's why:
I have read other people's impressions of this game and find myself wanting to weigh in on my own review.
This game was treading dangerously from the get-go.
Planescape: Torment was a game-changer for storytelling in computer games imo. A lot of people for the first time found themselves engaged to the point of violently lashing out at family members for interrupting them during a particularly interesting spool of text. So when I see negative reviews where people are screaming out "NOT a worthy successor to PS:Torment!" I cant help but feel like that's an unfair assessment.
This game captures the spirit of Planescape: Torment very well. It definately has the writing skill and deep mystery element of it's predecessor. The world feels vast in the sense that nothing that you see ever fully comprehends the complexity of it.
A wall may seem like a wall, but in reality it's name is Fred and like's the taste of human flesh at midnight.
A particular NPC you are talking to may seem like a run of the mill human, but in reality it's a transdimentional traveller who exists in many dimensions at the same time.
The very land you walk seems to tremor, but that's only because it's got an itch that it so desperately wants to scratch.
This is what I enjoyed most from both games. That feeling of being in a world that is almost uncomprehensible. A world that makes you think beyond the bounds and rules of reality.
Of course it doesnt mean I think this game is perfect, otherwise why would I give it an 8.
There are bugs, but let's be honest, it's got ties with Obsidian so I cant help but expect it.
Character's bug out at times, text boxes get stuck on screen, characters freeze and wont move from their positions. Hopefully these things will be fixed in later updates but I tend to deal with it as long as it's not game-breaking.
The characters are not as interesting as the ones from PS:Torment. They lack the personality depth that the originals did by a fair margin.
The character models are ugly. The fact that you are unable to customise your castoff was a disappointment for me, but then again you werent given that same freedom in PS:Torment either.
However there are so many things to like as well.
The dialogue is rich and engaging. I never felt reading it was tedious. NPCs always had something interesting to say that pulled me in. And some of the meta themes being discussed really blew my mind at times.
The many choices you are presented in dealing with people and situations in the world was also really well done. There are always 3+ ways to deal with most things.
The main character and his followers all had some interesting nuance to them that made me want to go that extra mile in learning more about them. My favourite follower was Rhin :).
I have already gushed about the world so I wont restate it.
I found the combat to be OK. It got the job done. It wasnt anything amazing but that isnt what I was playing the game for to begin with.
So tying this up. Do I think this game is a worthy successor to PS:Torment. Yes!.
Do I think this game is better than PS:Torment. No. But when you think about it, does it really need to be? Would we rather this game never existed?
I for one am glad it exists and had a blast playing it.
For all it's worth I am excited for the future. I look forward to seeing what other games are made in the Numenera multi-verse ;)

First off I just want to preface this review with saying that I am fascinated with procedural generation in games. The univerese is a unpredictable place with random chance occurrences happening everywhere. It is unpredictability which makes life so diverse and interesing.
In this game all chatacters, weapons and the world itself are randomly or procedurally generated. This creates a unique experience everytime you play. It also creates hilarious moments where unexpected things happen.
Procedural or random generation is a two sided sword. Because of the random generation, the game experience is not always balanced. Sometimes you will get your *ss handed to you by powerful enemies, sometimes you will find a item which gives you an enormous advantage. The random god giveth and the random god taketh away.
I think a good way to judge a game is similar to judging good music. Does it make you experience emotion? In 3079 you will experience every emotion in the spectrum. Happiness when you take out a huge enemy capital ship or find a very good unique weapon. Anger when you see a demon hacking up your fellow humoids, Fear when a demon is pulling you in and you don't have a demon smiter sword and you are over your weight limit on your grappling hook, Exiliration as you fly from mountaintop to mountaintop with a combination of grappling hook and antigravity pack. Pride when you build a inpenetrable underground fortress or capture an enemy building and see your fellow humoids come to inhabit it.
My suggestion is to not rush through the game and see how fast you can beat it but to take the time to learn the different styles of gameplay and explore the emmense world created for you.

This is quite possibly the best hitman game to date.   Hitman 2016 makes a return to open ended maps with tons of replay and exploration value. a new feature is Opportunities, which remove a lot of the blind running around older Hitman games suffered from.  This also serves to make the game much more newbie friendly.  Contracts mode makes a return and is fun as ever, however there isn't a way to search for friends' contracts at the moment.  There are also even more challenges, even some tough ones for experienced players like my current addiction: Silent Assassin Suit Only challenge.
The game is unfinished, which makes it a hard buy not knowing if it will keep it's quality up in coming missions. The always online component is annoying and a huge barrier, and I had to reduce settings so the game would run well on my PC.
Despite it's issues this is an amazing edition to the series with potential to be even better than Blood Money.  New players will find the system easy to learn, yet hard to master, and old fans will be happy with a return to form.
Pros:
Return to classic Hitman gameplay
Massive maps
Hours of replay value
New player friendly yet
Challenging for series veterans

Cons:
Poor Optimization
Online connection required for most features
Cannot search for friends' contracts
Epsodic release of missions makes current quality unguaranteed.

HITMAN is definitely the classiest of stealth games, from the suits to the combat to the locations everything is (almost) as clean cut as agent 47 hair (pun intended),
the controls are easy to use and square enix has thought of everything to give you the ability to shoot, stab, blow up and generally end your targets and still walk out undetected.
the problem with other assassination and stealth games is that they either only allow one style of play (e.g contract killer is 90% sniper) or they involve you getting shot at more than sneaking (mgs or warframe) but hitman allows you to find your own style, do you kill everyone in the country or discretely poison your targets drink and be gone ages before they even drink it (a.k.a really stealthy) the choice is yours.
of course there are downsides, the mastery rank system is good and unloking that sweet new suit is rewarding but at the same time, when you start a new location (e.g marrakesh) you can't really do much to start off with and may have to do the same thing or complete insanely difficult challenges over and over to be able to get the most fun result.
the other thing is that if you want a reaistic game, this is really not for you, apart from the incredible graphics and the fact that shooting someone in the leg causes them to limp (y'know, like real life), being able to dress yourself at a speed that makes the flash feel faint kind of loses the imersion (thats not saying that i WANT to see agent 47 strip himself and a dead person before putting on said dead person's clothes) not to mention the rediculousness of distracting someone by throwing a coin (they kind of just look at the coin for a bit before going back to whatever it was they were doing.
obviously there are others but i'm not writing a book here.
so in conclusion HITMAN is an experience that i would recommend to anyone who wants a fun, challenging, classy and violent experience that'll definataly keep you satified for hours (and also wanting that next location)

So the best summary I can come up with: it's short and sweet.
Visual novels/dating sims are definitely not my thing, but the game has gotten such good buzz that I had to pick it up (and let's face it, there are some hot dads in it). Calling it a Dad Dating Simulator is really only half the story, as it's just as much a Single Dad Raising An 18 Year Old Daughter Simulator. The writing and characterization are really superb, and as a fan of awful dadjokes, the amount of puns in this game really brought a smile to my face.
PROS:
-Great writing and art style
-Sweet, but not too sweet
-Touches on a wide array of modern issues in a thoughtful way.
-Good amount of replayability, but you'll have to speed through Act One until you can unlock Dadbook and start seeing the personalities of the various dads.
NEUTRAL:
-Like I said, it's just as much Daughter Simulator as it is anything else. This may or may not be your cup of tea -- however, the character and dialogue with your daughter are REALLY well written, and it is a really sweet story about a single dad. I didn't really expect it from this game going in, though.
CONS:
-Very short. Assuming you beeline toward romancing a specific dad, you'll finish it in around 2 hours.
-You get three "dates" with each dad, which makes it feel a bit short. In the storyline that I picked (Craig), it was a very slow burn. The first two dates didn't feel terribly date-y, which is made worse by the fact that Craig is also your former roommate, and you continue to call each other "bro" until the end. Makes it feel a bit less like you're dating Craig and more like he's just a hot buddy.
All in all, I'm looking forward to playing through the other storylines just to see what the other dads' personalities and backstories are like. It is what I expected it to be. Grab it if you want to date some interesting dads or if you're already used to visual novel type stuff, otherwise wait until it's on sale.

Just finished this game, Steam says I have 66 hours on it. It's awesome until about a quarter of the way through (which is SUPER fast if you follow the story and don't waste your time like I did being a completionist for no real reason).
The thing is, less than halfway through the game you have already maxed out your abilities and bought everything you can, yet ALL rewards (from everything) are either MORE ability tokens or money (scrap) that you can't even use. Plus looting is pointless... you get like 300 scrap for turning in a scrap truck or 500 for looting scrap boxes after a storm, but you get literally 1 to 9 scrap for looting bodies and locations.
Of course here I am complaining about paying $4.59 for 66 hours of gameplay, but I feel it's warranted since I was ready for the game to be over looooong ago, and other people only seem to be going on about how amazing it is and nothing else.
That being said, the first bit of the game is pretty impressive and brutal - and it does feel like it fits nicely in the Mad Max universe, but again, it doesn't take long before you've seen all the game has to offer. This game is basically a Mad Max version of Shadow of Mordor, but somehow less satisfying. I feel like they spent a lot of time making some aspects of the game really awesome, but leaving many others feeling incomplete and shallow.
On a final note, some in-game achievements seem to still be broken. Many people are stuck at 76/77 insignias. Poor form, since this problem has been around for a long time.
I'm marking this game as "recommended" - You'll enjoy it if you take the above into account and don't expect more.

Many people got this game because they liked Planescape Torment. I got this game for one reason: Pat Rothfuss. This review is thus aimed at people who are doing the same.
He wrote an NPC called Rhin who is designed from the ground up to be more or less worthless. For most of the game, she deals 0 damage, dies in 1-2 hits and her only redeeming function is that she can use special consumable items and hide. I can't help but feel that this is a deliberate bit of trolling on Mr. Rothfuss' part, but the game isn't so terribly difficult as to make her presence in the party a terribly big deal. Besides, having Rhin in your party probably means that you're generally going to take the non-violent and sneaky options instead of chopping your way through everything.
In any case, Rhin will be instantly familiar to a Rothfuss fan. She tosses out lines like "He's not a rock. He's a stone." and all that goodness. Unfortunately however, I have to report that there isn't really much there. Rhin is very interesting, but her full story is at the periphery and much is left to the player's imagination. This is a really text heavy game, but I don't think you would have a very thick booklet if you were to print out all of her dialogue.
The rest of the game is cool and imaginative. I liked the story (which is probably one of the most high-concept bits of science fiction I've encountered in a video game) and I liked the other characters for the most part. You can definitely feel that Pat Rothfuss had some creative influence on the overall direction. But this isn't the Name of the Wind by any stretch of the imagination.
Overall: Don't buy this expecting to find a huge amount of Rothfuss inside, but it is still worth exploring nevertheless.

Torment: Tides of Numenera is a decent execution of the heavily-story focused old-school Isometric RPG type game.
The setting and little side stories of Numenera are by far its strongest aspect, with the 1-billion old world filled with strange stories and technological wonders from ages gone by. Considering a majority of your time is spent learning and interacting with this world, it being so interesting and fleshed out alone makes the game worth playing. It is, and this cannot be overstated, absurdly varied, imaginative, weird (in a good way), and unlike any other setting I have seen in other fiction. I will not soon forget it, and it is easy to see the vast amount of writing, design, and other work that it took to craft this detailed a realization of this world.
And then there is the rest. I found almost everything - the main story, companion interactions, combat, navigation - middling in quality. The main story is focused on an interesting concept of a 'Changing God' who lives forever and spawns endless immortal castoffs who are powerful and do much to shape the world. This leads to some interesting lore, but is undercut by the antagonist being 'The Sorrow' (seriously? a generic unstoppable evil force?) and the crux of the conflict being highly abstract and removed from real-world moral concerns. The story is also undercut by spotty pacing, big intermittent info dumps, and mixed quality of writing. The same is true for companions' stories; some or better than others, and the writing of the characters is actually quite good, but all suffer from how they are delivered. Don't get me wrong; the story is not bad, on the whole I found it pretty interesting and worth going through, but it feels like it could be told much, much, better. Likewise, the world-building dialogue is often delivered in uninspired ways, much as it was in Wasteland 2 - you can ask for backstory on everything, to the point that it becomes tiresome.
As to the gameplay - my biggest complaint for the game may be that the combat feels terrible, and there is not much else of interest. The combat system itself is actually pretty cool, but the degree to which actual combat moves slowly and clumsily is ridicolous - in the age of the recent X-COM revival and other far superior turn based combat games, it is strange that this one is so badly executed. This is not a huge deal due to how little combat there is (the vast majority of it is avoidable, which is cool), but sadly the dialogue-based solutions around violence are rarely very interesting. In the vast majority of cases I could simply use my 'Persuasion' skill, which made it seem ridicolously overpowered and the actual act of pulling of dialogue solutions unimpressive.
The game looks good insofar as the worlds are detailed and imaginative, but is otherwise underwhelming as far as graphics go; all characters are only ever low-poly models which you see from the usual isometric perspective (there are portraits for you and your companions, but they doo little to help things). It could really benefit from less stilted dialogue, some cutscenes (such as the story trailer), or really anything to make it less of a choose-your-own-adventure book. The audio is barely worth mentioning, except that something started making a constant sound effect in the latter half of the game that was maddening.
So... yeah, a narrative-driven game with a flawed narrative but a fantastic setting/premise and many memorable details. I do recommend it, if only because there is very little like it out there, but with the caveat that the execution is rough and going through it will involve far more reading than playing.

some people mistake the question steam reviews try to answer. it is: "do you recommend this game?" and while an objective recommendation -very much like an objective 'review'- is not reasonable to expect nor necessary to have anyway, i believe it's at least good sport to recommend or not based on what you have at hand, and not on what you expected.
(long story short: i believe lots of people that're disappointed with their KS investment are blinded to what this game offers, making a disservice to both parties.)
so here i am, recommending a game that i actually backed during KS and then didn't follow development progress at all. (i'm kind of busy anyway, no time to worry about games that are not out yet.) so i installed the game, a bit surprised that it's out already (turns out it was 2 years late. oh well), and curious to find out if they could convert me back to numenera (played some tabletop rpg of it, wasn't exactly our cup of tea) but wait! why did i even back it on KS in the first place, you should ask! was it because of my everlasting love for planescape torment? or did i want to go back to isometric cRPGs like it was 90's again? or did i simply buy into hype? (well, my complete disinterest in development tells otherwise) turns out there are more reasons: back then i was getting back into tabletop RPG scene, was curious to find out what monte cook was doing, hence my interest in numenera. i also might have been interested in a modern take in isometric RPGs, taken in by nostalgia of things that never was. you see, i was not much of a gamer when originals (baldur's gate's, planecape and others) shook the market. so i have secondhand memories of those times, and wanted to try it for myself, i suppose.
Eventhough I gave a "thumbs up", the most I can do is try to convey what this game offers (to the best of my understanding. keep in mind that i'm nowhere near close to completing the game, even with 23 hours played) and let you decide, since you alone know what you expect from any game.
this game is some sort of a tour guide in a science-fantasy museum that we call the ninth world. visiting a museum makes you feel wonder towards the cultural excellence at display (and you can go deeper and marvel at technical excellence that makes it possible for such a collection to be available to you to admire) but once you visit every hall and some hidden corridors, ogle every painting and sculpture, and read their history, ponder what the artist tried to convey... then you leave, and museum does not stay with you. writing this review, i'm now fully expecting to not have a lasting impact once i'm done playing the game. (not impression. my impression will remain) of course this is a beautiful game the way i see it, and i expect to 'visit the museum' a couple of times in the future, to try and experience it from a different angle. but this is not a captivating novel. we don't follow story of some interesting character in interesting times, we won't turn the last page and say "this will stay with me for a life time, and i'm different person for it" (going back to museum analogy: yes, museums change people too, but not on a personal level)
now, i will not try to make excuses for inXile. first, being a museum and not a novel is not a bad thing. second, they chose it and i'm just trying to show you what this game is offering. i will, however, try to offer explanations to as why this may be the case:
1) cRPGs face a difficult dilemma: you have a singular software, but true to its name, you want every single player to "role play", and experience their own story. isometric cRPGs, where you control a party of 4 characters, have it even further: you now need your player to have emotional connection with every one of those 4 characters! unlikely, if not impossible
2) developers could have had lots of stories to tell, so instead of making main character deeply connected to the setting, they could have chosen a more middle-ground approach.
whatever the reason, that is the case: main character, the last castoff, is not a real character, but just our avatar walking through the museum. honestly, first explanation i offered is also why i didn't expect to get connected to the last castoff anyway (geralt from witcher, for example, also starts as a blank slate, but quickly gets filled as a character, hence is easier to connect to)
in other words, this game is a walking simulator. if this term unnerves you, my guess is you wouldn't have liked it in the first place.
these complaints are about numenera system than its implementation in the game.
but the combat is simply not good. anyone familiar enough with D&D rules can get the general feeling: combat is good, because there are lots of options for player expression and creativity. hell, it's even possible to consider it as its own board game. this game, on the other hand, tries to change things a little bit, by giving you an expandable pool of resources that you choose to spend or not before the dice is rolled
(traditional D&D method was this: roll the dice, add your [static] bonuses, check if you've crossed the boundary or not. modern numenera method is this: add your [variable] bonuses, roll the dice, check if you've crossed the boundary or not. however, this seemingly small change ends up frustrating, because a missed roll makes player regret his choice of not spending more resources, and a succesful roll  wondering if spending was necessary in the first place. and resource management gets more troublesome. well, at least T:ToN managed to implement a "classical" hit point system)
still, not enough combat options. i'm curious to see how a more aggressive playstyle will play out, because from what i've seen so far it may end up disappointing.
also, this is not my complaint but may be for others: combat is far and few between. told you, this is a walking (and more than that, reading) simulator. i am okay with it, considering how i'm not particularly happy with combat in the first place, but more because i love walking and talking and reading in this big museum.
overall, i am happy with this game and what it's trying to do. it presents a world full of wonders, interesting characters (just not
) and curious sidequests. surely a pleasent experience, with surely some room for improvement, but let's continue our analogy to say that it's like having terrible cafeteria in a otherwise great museum.

Heavy Bullets is a rogue-lite FPS with pretty high difficulty. Like most Rougue-ish games you only get one life (although you can inherit goodies from your last go-though) and of course the levels are randomly generated. There is a pretty good selection of goodies to pick up and use such as knives, bombs, speed pills, sniper shots and more and not all of them are good for you. There is SOME character  development as you can also be upgraded with more hit-points, the ability to carry (oh boy!) 2 items!  (by default you can only carry one item at a time), increased pickup range and more. I really enjoy the banking system that allows you to store away money and items for your next playthough, or trade unused items for cash. It's just a small thing, but really helps flesh out Heavy Bullets into a more deep experience.  Play-wise it is a pretty sparse corridor shooter that focuses on short skirmishes with a small amount of enemies at a time. A couple small mistakes will generally lead to your demise as pretty much any of your foes will kill you easily given the chance. Oh, and watch out for the grass: they just love to hide in the freakin' grass. I warned You. The presentation is pretty simple: Atari 2600-meets-3d Playstation One graphics, with sound consisting of bleeps and bloops reminiscent of the 8 bit era.  It's a unique look and I like it quite a bit although I realize it may not be to eveyone's tastes.
All and all I like Heavy Bullets: It's great to play in small bursts and has just enough depth to keep me coming back for more. Good stuff indeed.

Also there's only 1 gun, and its a pistol. Also, if collecting coins isn't tedious enough, you also have to collect your bullets every time, and just like coins, standing almost on top of them doesn't even work unless you have bought collector upgrade, making it extra annoying. There's tons of cheap damage. You open door get immediately hurt. There's turrets that shoot every 1 second but you have to aim at this small bos with your TINY crosshairs so you often get hurt with more than 1. Enemies are much faster than you, meaning you can't run backwards if they're chasing you and kite them. Some cheap enemies like bombs that are right around the corner and you can't do anything before they are on your and explode if killed and hurt you. There's snakes that blend into grass and are impossible to see if not looking for, but there's grass everywhere, so you can get hurt by not always looking for them 100% of the time. Then there are cheap deaths like me fighting a boss, then I throw a bomb at it, it blows up immediately right in my face killing me instantly and I lost 30-45 min of progress for some inexplicable reason.....no want to try again. This is also because you fight the same 3 enemies in the exact same corridors with the exact same 1 gun the entire game. Then there's terrible design decisions like the fact you can only carry 1 single item at a time, and increased health, or backpack to carry 1 more item are super expensive or super rare to find, causing you to never get much stronger or change over the course of the level. So with repetitive play, lack of character strength and progression during play, and no carrying over to next life there's no incentive for this game.

The first time I played this game, it seemed interesting and quirky. I got some gear and a quest to bring an item to another NPC. To do so I had to shoot the NPC just so he'd come low enough for me to give him the item, as he was a flying guard. I should have known that this would be one of the less aggrivating parts of this game.
I started a new game and played for about half an hour. During this time I died five times. I never completed a single quest, and so I made no progress whatsoever. I would explore the different buildings, breaking wooden crates to sell the material right back to the vendors in the same buildings. I would finally have enough to buy an item or two, or sometimes found items while exploring, but none of them seemed to make a difference.
The quests I tried to complete are as follows.
"Destroy the capital ship." The small pistol I had bought seemed to have no effect until I got close enough for the ship to open fire on me and reduce me to a fine red paste.
"Protect this Humoid for X seconds." I made it over to the target fine, and things seemed to be all right. Until a hostile flying ship flew over and hammered him into the ground before I could even pull my weapon out. And then it killed me.
"Kill X Neanders in X seconds." This wouldn't be so bad if I wasn't standing in the middle of the Humoid city, and there's no sprint mechanic. With a little abuse of the grapling hook, I was able to quickly hop the nearest wall and went to fight a Neander. This one, the only one in the area, happened to be considered a 'giant' and so was doing ridiculous damage to me. I had previously lost my pistol to a death, so all I had on me was my melee sword.
The only time I maybe killed an enemy? When I was on one of the floating buildings, apparently owned by Neanders, and used stealth to hit a guy. The knockback tossing him off the edge of the platform; I have no idea if he actually died or not, because a shopkeeper in the same building quickly killed me again.
I'm sure the game might be worth $6.99 to some people, but it's just too tough for me, and I played on the 'normal' difficulty. After the time spent to make zero progress today, though, I don't really see myself playing it again. All in all this game seems like an interesting idea, but it feels like the ideas they put forth - RPG elements, material harvesting and crafting, science fiction storyline - are all handled much better in other games.

3079 -- Block Action RPG is an interesting title.  First off, I don't know if I would call it a role-playing game at all, it's more of an adventure FPS that has quests, equipable items, and skill increases...well, maybe that's enough to be an RPG.  Either way, the engine and music in this game are very good.  It's a very fun, sandboxy experience; however, as far as it being a game goes, it needs some work.  The game is in desperate need of a tutorial, and it takes quite a lot of trial and error to figure out what you're supposed to do.  Even after reading all the help menus and tips it took me three new game instances before I figured out to go into my inventory and turn of my jetpack to land instead of flying around aimlessly until I got killed by demons.  The quests are also recycled a lot and it's pretty difficult to get anything done without dying.
That said, if we don't look at this title as a game and instead look at it as a sandbox engine and tech demo I'm pretty impressed.  As stated above the music is *really* nice, and it's fun to play around in the engine for an hour or so (the grappling hook is my favorite).  There's also a boatload of settings to go through (anti-aliasing, field of view, completely customizable controls - always a big bonus!) and a pretty simple multiplayer feature that hosts a local server with the basic game client.
Although I'd pass on recommending this game (unless you're looking for a well put-together sandbox game engine) I'm impressed with what the developer has created so far and am looking forward to future, more gameplay polished releases.

**Revised review March 5, 2016**
The latest version of
, as of this review, has converted my original vote of no to a yes. However, the part that swayed me is an optional setting, so please note that the default game still seems too random. So long as you go into it with reasonable expectations,
can be quite charming.
For one thing, it features slick design and UI. Information is easily accessible with a few clicks, and managing positions and rosters is straightforward.  This ties into the streamlined managerial experience. People who want a lot of number crunching and projections can play
.  This game is more arcade-like, with a simplified simulation.  You still get the whole experience (signing, training, budgeting, seasons, tournaments, etc.), but it's bite-sized.
The matches play in a similar fashion to blitzball in
: players have four stats that determine their passing, shooting, defensive, and positional abilities.  There are also "skills" that allow them to make harder shots, longer passes, etc. It is turn based, and each game consists of 48 actions taken in threes.  Success is determined by rolling one's players stat versus the opposition's stat.  For example, a player with a Pass rating of 24 is attempting to pass through an opponent with a Defense stat of 12.  Both players generate a random number from 1 to x, where x is their stat; the higher number prevails (ties go to the active team).
In the default settings, the RNG has too much variability for my taste, and they can significantly reduce the effectiveness of your tactics.  Some games devolve into a matter of who rolls better, you or the computer.  Training players takes a lot of time, and acquiring better players is expensive.  Tournaments happen each year, and if you get to enter, you will likely be facing teams from much higher leagues.  Their stats will be significantly higher than yours, and you will only be able to hope for a tie.
There is a new, optional setting when creating a new game that gives players a skill floor of 30% of their rating.  This means that high-skilled players can more consistently outclass weaker opponents, although they can still be beaten.  Although I would prefer that this setting be integrated into the core game, its presence makes it easier to execute tactics consistently rather than gambling on a lucky roll.

Highly addictive, definitely feels like a "easy to learn, hard to master" title. Matches can be as quick or long as you decide, interesting mechanical depth regarding skills, offense vs defense contests and all the different options you have in terms of positioning, formation and mitigating bad luck on the dice rolls.
Team management is done pretty well, with training, transfers, player age, match exposure, contracts, sponsors, and more. For an Early Access title, it feels like a complete game and the devs are proving that they have confidence in the future direction.
If you like Club Football, tactical games and management sims, pick it up.

This game is like good play off chess.
To simply describe it:
You start with bunch of amateur players on some public park, getting new young members from watcher - pals, choosing what to train and getting skills.
Every match means exp for your playing players, some money and "fame" while nothing of it is in the game just for effect.
You'll find yourself thinking how could someone balance the game so simply and exactly together. Why cant i stop playing this?
Every player is basically characterized only by 4 attributes: accuracy (shot), control, defense, passing
Every turn on field is counted on opposite attributes which are relevant to current action.
For instance tackle is counted as defense of tackling player versus control of player with the ball. Then dice are rolled and result is counted by probability (difference of opposite attributes)
Then you have passing, shooting, dribbling turn actions, or just control the ball to prepare your possession for opponent's turn.
Then you can train certain skills (like perks) which you can use as extra (like special move, or special shot), you can specify players by this skill for certain things in the game, build whole team tactics.
You can even use weather to alter your match tactic!
I have to admit i didn't expect so addictive gameplay, i simply cannot stop playing it.
Would recommend game like this again..

The new Hitman is a true return to form of what Blood Money accomplished. While it has yet to feature a level as memorable as the suburban one (you know what I'm talking about) in Blood Money, it features expansive levels with a multitude of routes and ways to take out your target. Sure some of them seem more... puzzle-like in nature. Such as finding a specific way to find an object you've found to kill the targets but overall, the game shines. The Elusive Targets are also a great feature that lead to tense, nail-biting scenarios. While I missed the second one (moving :( ), they add great value between episodes. Also, I find this is one of the few games where the episodic rollout works. Let's just hope by the end we haven't paid $80 to play the full game if you buy them piecemeal like I have.
All in all, slick, modern day graphics. Serviceable AI. Massive, detailed levels that make you feel like you're on vacation.. as the world's best assassin and solid gameplay. The servers are a crapshoot at this point which is a downfall that irks but overall, it's an experience not worth missing if you appreciate feeling like a true badass.
On an ending note, I would HIGHLY recommend plugging in your PS4 controller using InputMapper to emulate an Xbox controller and play it that way. It controls much, much better via controller as some of the keymapping are very awkward. And on that note, I rarely keymap games as that's the developers job to figure out what feels right while playing.
After the first 3 episodes and 5 hours in, this game will be getting a LOT more playtime in my vast library of games.

Ever since the release of Arkham Asylum, I have been a diehard Batman video game fan. I had doubts for Asylum that were quickly disproven and from that point, I went to the midnight release of Arkham City. That being said, as soon as I saw that WB Montreal was developing a prequel game, I began to worry. Now, some of those worries were founded, others not so much.
Arkham Origins is a mixed bag. It brings both good and bad things to the Arkham franchise. I'll start with the negatives.
Deja-vu. You'll play this game wondering what is different about it than Arkham City. You have almost the same gadgets, combat upgrades, grappel abilities, etc. It's not bad; it's just really familiar. Mission types are similar, if not the same, and a good portion of the map is the Arkham City map covered in snow. Granted it's in greater detail with a graphical overhaul, but it's the same map.
The good: Story. It's not as good as Arkham City's story with all the twists and great care and attention that were given it, but it's decent. It introduces many of Batman's familiar villains in a plotline that isn't disappointing. That's something that isn't easy to pull off.  The voice acting is good, with Troy Baker stealing the show with an excellent Joker presentation. (especially considering that he isn't Mark Hammill) The graphics can be excellent, but can also disappoint. Some areas have great details and effects, but even those aren't jaw-dropping. I run this on a 1GB GTX 650ti and get around 45FPS average, which is decent for the settings I run it at. The sound editing could use some work, as it was difficult to hear voices over SFX sometimes, even after altering the levels.
I haven't tried multiplayer much yet, to be honest I probably won't do it at all. I didn't buy this game for the multiplayer and I'd be surprised if anyone did. The single player doesn't disappoint, but it really doesn't exceed any expectations either. It's a good entry in the series, but it's not as excellent as we've come to expect from an Arkham title. If you're a fan, it's worth getting, but you may want to wait for a sale to purchase this game.

Lastly, if I have a Last Will, which SHOULD save my items upon death, and is in the backpack when I die, it becomes useless and I lose my 15+ keycards and bullets.  I'm perfectly fine with passive items not working in the backpack, but I think that this is just nitpicking right here.

A fantastically sculpted adventure.  Beautifully drawn landscapes are populated with interesting characters, and the world has a spectacular back-story.  Gameplay itself is fresh, and the story is not combat driven, although the player has many opportunities to engage in violence if it is sought.  Read the first page of the manual, then learn the rest through experience.
It's an excellent game in the same vein as Planescape: Torment.  This is definitely worth playing, and inXile should be supported in their efforts to make great rpgs.  In all those millions of words, I didn't find a single typo.
---Spoilers follow---
The narrative is compelling at first, but falters after the first act, and the game is ultimately over just as my interest peaked.  Maybe I'm a jaded fogey, but I feel like the game needed two more acts, and several more hours of gameplay and interaction in order to bring the narrative to a satisfying close.
Overall, the story feels rushed.  Many revelations don't even have time to sink in before the player is forced to make game-ending decisions.  The big, scary antagonist's motives are never fully explained to my satisfaction (they are revealed in a database in a memory-- come on!), and the human antagonist's motivations are ultimately boring.
I enjoyed the meres, but felt they needed more impact on long-term gameplay.  I like the memory referencing oolatek and the Heavy Metal movie!!!

Having played Planescape: Torment many times, and with all the information I had about Torment: Tides of Numenera prior to the game released, I had the highest expectations when I bought this.
Although not as great as Planescape: Torment I still think it's a good game with a good story. One of the main differences is the main character, the last castoff, that - unlike Planescape: Torment - isn't the main focus of the story and is more of a tool/vessel whom the story unfold around. The game is more 'a' journey than 'my' journey. The roleplaying game is toned down and the emphasis is on the narrative.
The companions, with a few exceptions, feels less likable and interesting compared to those in Planescape: Torment. I wish the developers had dared to go further with their imagination in the creating process.
Very nice graphics. I loved it. Sagus Cliff, the Bloom...beautiful, fascinating. Characters, for example the last castoff, is unfortunately quite "robotic" and the visual effects of spells/effects on characters a bit annoying after a while.
Music is great, especially in the beginning - ambient - though there were an overall lack of songs that stood out, like "Fortress of Regrets" in Planescape: Torment. Sound effects are sometimes too prominent.
Many of the quests and sidequests are even better than those in Planescape: Torment. Lots of different ways to solve them with lots of different results.
New system for skills, abilities and fighting. I like it and I think it's promising. The biggest problem is that it's too easy. In the beginning of the game it's ok but quickly the challenge disappears. You fail a skillcheck because you choose to (can sometimes give interesting results), not because you run out of skillpoints.
8/10
Knowing what I know now, do I regret buying it at full price? No.
Will I buy any expansion in the future? Yes.

The new Hitman is a true return to form of what Blood Money accomplished. While it has yet to feature a level as memorable as the suburban one (you know what I'm talking about) in Blood Money, it features expansive levels with a multitude of routes and ways to take out your target. Sure some of them seem more... puzzle-like in nature. Such as finding a specific way to find an object you've found to kill the targets but overall, the game shines. The Elusive Targets are also a great feature that lead to tense, nail-biting scenarios. While I missed the second one (moving :( ), they add great value between episodes. Also, I find this is one of the few games where the episodic rollout works. Let's just hope by the end we haven't paid $80 to play the full game if you buy them piecemeal like I have.
All in all, slick, modern day graphics. Serviceable AI. Massive, detailed levels that make you feel like you're on vacation.. as the world's best assassin and solid gameplay. The servers are a crapshoot at this point which is a downfall that irks but overall, it's an experience not worth missing if you appreciate feeling like a true badass.
On an ending note, I would HIGHLY recommend plugging in your PS4 controller using InputMapper to emulate an Xbox controller and play it that way. It controls much, much better via controller as some of the keymapping are very awkward. And on that note, I rarely keymap games as that's the developers job to figure out what feels right while playing.
After the first 3 episodes and 5 hours in, this game will be getting a LOT more playtime in my vast library of games.

Turn-based football. You have time to think about your every move and feel the full control over your players. I am not FIFA fan, I don't even like football. But the way developers made the game totally won me over - it is a lot like chess (my favorite board game) but with elements of RPG like gaining levels of footballers and gaining skills and tallents for them. Moreover the developers are constantly improving the game to suit player's tastes (players can pick match duration in turns, will players playing on different position get a penalty for it, will there be injuries, how fast footballer's stamina will recover and more) and provide new options and additional content. And if there happens to be a bug from what I've seen they are fast to release a fix for it - usually within hours.
I don't know if all the FIFA fans would like this a bit slower and more tactical version but I recommend it to all who like turn-based strategies and RPG-type of games, at least for me it was a fun new experience that may not have as many resource types like in other strategies (fame, money in this case) but is just as fun.

Wanting to know more about the game, I checked out the Community forums. The top post is "NOT a ripoff of Minecraft."
The whole post is wasted on just the graphics. 3079 is a minecraft clone in that it moves, feels, and acts like Minecraft. Being a Minecraft clone is not a dirty word. In the 90s, if you were a FPS, you were a Doom-clone. If you were a 1vs1 fighter, you were a Street Fighter-clone. Tetris-clones were everywhere. But then there was Dr. Mario, and Tetris Attack, and the block-puzzle genre was born.
Now that we got that out of the way, let's review 3079. It's a big open world with a randomly generated properties. There's a lot of the same. Once you've seen one building, you've seen them all. You're exploring and doing quests that surrmount to basic fetch quests. This is a game where you get out there, and shoot stuff and watch your numbers get bigger. I spent the next few hours scratching my head, wondering, "What am I supposed to do?"
3079 is sparse. With a better tutorial and more interesting 'ah-ha moments', there could be something here. But not right now.
It's a good game and it's not minecraft, so shut up.

Spent a little over 30 hours on that game and i just finish the main story. Here is my toughts on this.
At the begginning of the game, i had mixed feeling. It felt like a cheap knock of version of Shadow of modor (which i loved). I have no problem for it to have the same core gameplay, but at first, it didn't had it's own flavor that made me love the game.
The more the game progress, the better it gets. The combat get more intense and a bit more diversified (althought, one would argue that they are still very repetitive, but it didnt bother me much in the case). The story is getting also a bit more ingaging as your car (which is a center piece of the game) gets better in every aspect - at first, the car handling are just awful, but don't worry, it get better much faster.
Car chases and combat are always fun (for me anyway) and the explosions never gets old.
The story is fine and the caracter too. Some are just there for their function but it didn't bother me much. There are a few plot twist that suprised me (especially close to the end) so it's all good in that regard for me. It is not a scenario that will be remember for ever but it get the job done.

In conclusion, i did like this game, more than i thought i would. I'm probably never gonna play it again because i fell like i'm done with it. So that's pretty much it. Grab it in sale if you like Batman Arkam series and Shadow of Mordor type of combat and want to have a good time. But don,t expect to enjoy it more than a single playthrough.
