Having came from many a shooter, third-person, first-person and genre mutts alike, I found myself forcefully thrusting myself into what I had expected to be just another typical "white knight," heroic power fantasy such as Call of Duty, Medal of Honor or Battlefield.  With all of the derivative shooters you'll find on the market these days, I really try to play more unique titles and stray away from any shooter games when craving some single-player campaign with a entralling story or something to at least mildly interest me for any amount of time.
I was dead wrong.
Spec Ops: The Line is something of a highly underrated masterpiece that, I don't believe, was ever given the recognition it deserved.  The multiplayer is pretty bad, but from multiple sources, the games developers originally were against the idea and 2K (the publishers) forced the concept to push sales and stick with the multiplayer trend in the market.  But in terms of single-player story, this game is a marvel, something I honestly never expected from any military video game.
Firstly, I'll address the issues people have with the actual gameplay.  I personally find nothing wrong with the gameplay at all really.  The actual firefights and action sequences are what we've come to expect from shooters these days and is therefore nothing special, but it's what fills the moments between these action-filled firefights that really make this game.  The controls and mechanics are smooth and feel great, damn me for saying, they are comparable to Gears of War in feel.  The shooting is superb and the movement is a bit sluggish at times, but overall, still a good shooter from this perspective.
Where Spec Ops: The Line really shines is it's absolutely shameless telling of the truths and atrocities of war in the modern age.  Nothing about it is good, nothing about it will make you a hero, no one really is in those situations, and this game will really make you realize that.  This game takes the stereotypical shooters "heroic" stories, and tosses them in the trash.  Then burns the can.  Then shoots it into space where a black hole swallows it.  This game does away with Hollywoods interpretation of modern age warfare and digs deep and dark, where many are too scared to go.  This game will completely destroy the image of war that most games would have you believe in and instead deals with depression, self-loathing, Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, and the grittiness of war that no game has mentioned.
Buy this game.  Experience the story.  I'll meet you on the other side of The Line.
Oh....and Welcome to Dubai.

The game is so good because the story is absolutely brilliant. It doesn't glorify war, or America, or anything really. It is something I have never seen in a video game before, and to describe it in words is to do it a cruel injustice. The ability to choose which ending based on your actions is brilliant. I've done four endings so far, but I know the developers talked about a fifth one, which is simply for the player to put down the controller and stop playing the game. Once you have experienced the story, you'll truly be able to understand just how powerful that last ending is. I can't stress it enough: BUY THIS GAME!

This is an amazing game in an interesting world.  It's probably the most complete approach to non-combat oriented videogame RPGs.  I'm only listing shortcomings here due to the plane fact that anything I enjoyed about the game couldn't really be improved.
That said, it won't be for everyone.  There is quite a bit to read and remember, and while it won't really slow play if you forget something, it seems quite easy to forget enough to render an experience confusing or meaningless.  The game is pretty empty if you don't like reading.  Also, failure is a common tool in the game.  It occasionally provides bonuses and typically gives an alternate solution to a problem.  The shortcomming of failure is that it is random, you can't chose to fail a roll if you think your character wouldn't succeed at something.  So while it offers more freedom of experience by rarely making failure absolute, it doesn't let you wield failure as a narrative option.
There are also a few places where gameplay isn't smooth.  You can't always click certain objects that are clickable which leads to your characters moving over the object and, since your characters are clickable for some reason, they end up getting interacted with.  It would probably be a good idea to move most follower interactions to the character portrait rather than the game window.  Also, the flourish on creature names takes up a large amount of the game play window often obscuring the creature names when you click tab to show all interactable objects.  Maybe there's a way to shrink them that I don't know about.
A minor quibble I have is with the hard follower limit.  While it's fair that certain party members want nothing to do with one another, it seems that restricting the party size to 4 encourages a player to often swap characters in the middle of stories to ensure that they don't miss anything.  It would make much more sense to include all available characters as desired.  You also end up cycling through unused characters to get at their resources during contests, this creates a weird dynamic that doesn't play very smoothly.  I would expect some better method of accessing the other character's insights and abilities without swapping through characters regularly.
One weird narrative issue I've come across is the primacy of intellect.  Maybe my personal bias is manifesting as an in game bias, but it seems solving things through intellect is always a more rewarding path, particularly in a game where lore is the reward for many interactions.  Beyond that though, you will occasionally be faced with social interactions that could be solved with violence, that never present violence as an option.  I realize that this is the norm for RPGs but choosing a more peaceful path when there isn't an alternative makes that choice less meaningful.

Torment: Numenera HISHE (How it Should Have Ended) Review
Torment: Numenera is a true sucessor of the Planescape formula. A rich and deep story on an interesting world bordering on a literary adventure of the surrealist fantasy genre. While it is certainly worth playing, it falls short from it's goal of achieving the same level or even surpassing it's predecessor. Not surprisingly, this has far more to do with the narrative aspects than the gameplay or technical aspects, simply because of the fact that, a true roleplaying game worthy of such a label has to be focused first and foremost on storytelling, it's characters, the choices made and their effects on the world. Numenera's story isn't told as well as Planescape had been, even with the advantage of being made 20 years later, after much experimentation and innovative narrative mechanics have been developed. Even if we take into account that surpassing Planescape Torment is essentially the tallest possible order for any Roleplaying Game, and Numenera is much better written than most recent triple A RPG games, its shortcomings are so glaring that they cannot be ignored.
Planescape Torment had a similar Main Character, one who started life suffering from an accute case of amnesia and immortality. However, if we take a closer look, the similarities become evidently superficial. The Nameless One was a character who could indeed become any class, and voice many different opinions at any point, he could be a bully or a hero, kind or aggressive, but unlike the Last Castoff, he always did so with style. The Nameless One was always his own character, never a clean slate, a tabula rasa. The western industry standard of writing for video games, especially RPGs, is the idea that the character must be written is such a way that the player will feel to be the one fully in control to be properly "immersed" in the story, free to do as they please. Instead of creating immersion, what this actually does is create an awkward dynamic where your Dovahkins, Wardens and Vault Dwellers are template characters instead of having a mind of their own. The only effect this game theory has on storytelling games is creating a disconnect of the narrative and it's central character.
The Interrogator
The worst part, however, is the way how the Last Castoff interacts with the world, or more accurately, how the world interacts with her. Go out and ask the first person you see the following question "Tell me your story". The last thing that person will do, is to answer what you asked. Not only it is invasive and even creepy, people will often not reply to questions with objective, direct and concise answers, especially when they have ulterior motives and well rounded personalities. The only explanation for the way people talk to the Last Castoff is if they are being forced to speak in such an open and unusual manner by some kind of influence from the Tides. This would be a way to justify it in game, but even then it would simply be an excuse to spare the writers the trouble of coming up with realistic interactions and explaining away the bullet point, excel table, conversation style of Numenera's NPCS.
Torment: Tides of MacGuffin
Numeneras are MacGuffins, the definition of a Numera is exactly what a MacGuffin is. MacGuffins are useful storytelling tools, but they often create Deus Ex Machina situations. The Tides themselves are Lacanian/Campbellian archetypical forces, and can only have such a powerful effect on reality when we accept the premise of existence being a construct of the mind, human or otherwise. It's an interesting premise that would be especially easy to accept when taking the 4th wall into account. Unfortunately, even when it is the very center of the story, since the nature of the Sorrow is to be the actual representation of Campbell's Shadow, it's not properly developed, well explained, or interestingly delved into. Even the Changing God's personal quest falls flat and uninspiring by the end. Especially since it's revealed to us at a point where it was simply way way... past the time to sympathize with the character, and there was no bond at all formed between the player's character and the Mysterious Girl. It's a shallow and hollow sideshow, instead of an emotional reveal.
Railroad Ending
The game ends with yet another interrogation type conversation, where the Sorrow delivers a heavy dose of plot exposition, in a similar way to the Architect's Monologue in Matrix: Reloaded. It isn't as bad, and allows a window into the mind of a being that couldn't have been understood, according to the story, except for the fact that it totally could. It would be far better to discover all about the Sorrow during the story, exploring the past, learning about it's origins from other sources than simply "asking for exposition". Too much exposition is awful by itself, direct exposition from the main villain? I shouldn't even have to say anything about it.
If the idea was to show that the Sorrow isn't truly the villain, but the hero. That Castoffs are in the wrong, selfishly destroying the world to achieve their own ends, and the only option to destoy the Sorrow would be the ultimate act of selfishness on their part... then it falls flat on its♥♥♥♥♥completely.
HISHE (How It Should Have Ended)
After the main villain makes its whole spiel about how the Last Castoff has to choose options A through Z: Kill the Castoffs by subsuming them into 1 person, Kill the Sorrow to let Castoffs Live but condemn hundreds of thousands in the present and potential millions in the future to a horrible death, allowing the Sorrow to persist, thus condeming the Castoffs to extinction by it's Grim Reaper hands, etc...
The Last Castoff finally decides to take an active role and confronts the narrative of the Sorrow, showing the flaws in its reasoning and taking it down from its high horse forcing it to accept the moral low ground on which it stands. Then, with the power of the Tides, the Last Castoff makes it see the horror of it's existence and kill itself, letting Castoffs and humans free to choose their own destiny, accepting the consequences of their choices.
The Sorrow is a World Killer. It has killed millions if not Billions before and deprived other tens of billions, if not trillions, from being born. It is a genocidal force that wiped out civilizations, allowing such a thing to live would be a far greater crime, even at the cost of hundreds of thousands of lives. Because at some point in the future, it would be inevitable that technology would once again discover the power of the Tides, conscience transfer or whatever, and after the Sorrow managed to prevent access to the Resonance, it would be far more difficult if not impossible to stop it.
The effect of Castoffs bodies self-sustaining with Tide energies is a potential problem, but only when they actively decide to use the Tides, every other subliminal effect implied is either too subtle to be perceived or just hasn't been properly represented in the story to be relevant. We live in a world where our emotions and self-image is constantly manipulated by chemistry, propaganda, marketing, and even the temperature or hardness of where we sit can change the way we look at things and how we feel about the world.
This is a very poor excuse to condemn Castoffs to death, especially in a world where people constantly use Numenera to influence each other and the world around them. Where telepaths and empaths, Machine Intelligences and Ctonic Ctullhian transdimensional entities move around the world unchecked and unfettered.
As it is, the moral of the story is that The Last Castoff is simply not smart enough to debate against the Sorrow, "technology is too dangerous", "the price of Immortality is too high" and "It is more moral to embrace mortality and live a short happy life in ignorance than to pursue the understanding of fundamental forces in the universe"

Its more than 2 years later. Time for a small update to my review! I'll keep the old one below, as a reminder to myself some game developers actually know what they're doing when improving a title beyond its initial promise.
First off, the turn based tactics is still key to the enjoyment. Somehow they've made it really work for a title like this, and I re-iterate how fresh it feels to the stale and frustrating 3D animations of other series. The fact that you get to play out your formation and choice tactically through the game day is so much fun, and this game has all other game beat when it comes to depth. You'll get the actual calculations, you'll understand why you concede and score goal, and you'll probably not feel like the game is unfairly punishing you without explanation when you suddenly trip out in a 1-5 defeat after a series of wins.
It's just sooooo much better than a certain other title. If you enjoy chess or X-Com or Civilization or just any form of turn based tactics you can't go wrong with this. I would even say you don't even need to enjoy "soccer". The abstraction of the match day into pieces on a chess board with limitations to actions and movement, is enjoyable for anyone with heart for tactics. This title gets two thumbs up from this "PC-masterrace guy" and I hereby lift the "embargo" on it as being a mobile phone title. It really isn't anymore. 2 years of improvements and the inclusion of more tactical choices and speciality classes, have brought the match engine to a state of near perfection.
Updated con/pro list:
Pros:
-Game expands its mechanics as you play, so it will never feel overwhelming for a new player
-Rewarding skill progression on players
-Surprisingly decent animations and overall aestethics
-2017: match engine depth. Tactics feel really rewarding, and you can go full Magnus Carlsen on the game and be rewarded for it. You'll start losing "easy" matches if you think you'll cakewalk thru' anyone.
-2017: Its actually as fun to be struggling as it is to be a top team.
-2017: The RNG factor is on the money.(its minimal) I've never felt arbitrarily punished in this game after the latest updates.
-Has that "just one more turn" feeling which all good turn-based games need.
-2017: The AI is tough to the point of perfection. Its hard to make it trip up.
Cons:
-Lack PC-gaming masterrace depth. (the 20+ years of headstart from the CM/Football Manager series when it comes to Transfer Market, Player Database, Stats, News, Random events, etc... Basically this game has all that CM/Football Manager does wrong right, and vice versa. Often to no fault of their own.)
2017 update: Still applies, there's some basic functions, but this game is still all about match day. But at least you can finish a season in one sitting.
-Matches feel a bit "short" or like your managing a little league game.
2017 update: No longer applies. There's a setting now to increase length. I'm at the point where I wish that was even longer, but thats just me being greedy. They've managed to get the game to a point where even with extra turns for each half, that doesn't mean you'll get insane results. I still wind up in 2-1 wins and 0-1 defeats.
-Tactics might feel gimmicky if you are looking for realism.
2017: They do indeed. But this is just a con if you despise chess or turn based gaming.
-2017 con: Hard mode isn't balanced yet.
-2017 con: Game still looks like a mobile phone game in its presentation. Which is fine for now, but if they want a sequel, they need to rework the UI.

In all honesty, I never review anything on Steam. But I felt compelled to write one for this title. I followed this game's progress since I first heard about it on Tumblr, and can say that I was not disappointed in the least when I bought and played it for myself. I don't regret a single dollar I spent on it, and I gladly would have paid more for the quality I received in return.
Dream Daddy has some of the best representation I've seen in a game outside of Bioware titles. Not only can your main character be gay, bisexual, or transgender, there are NPCs in the game who fall under those categories, too. Each dad's story and personality are unique, which is amazing considering just how many of them there are. Their romances are written in thoughtful, considerate, and often downright hilarious ways and it has been a delight for me to go through and play each and every one I've chosen so far. I even liked all their children; how is this possible?!
Speaking of children, your own daughter Amanda is one of the best written characters in the game. She's extremely relatable, realistic, and fun and I adored each and every one of our interactions. The banter between her and your main character is equal parts hilarious and emotional and I loved it. I kind of wish she interacted with your intended romances more often, though, or at least talked to you more about them like she did during Damien's route. That's my only complaint and it's a miniscule one.
Other than that, I'll try to keep it short. The sountrack was catchy, the dogs were adorable as all hell, and the mini games didn't make me want to bash my head against a wall. 10/10 Best Game of the Year for me!
TLDR:
[PROS]
- Fantastic LGBT+ Representation
- Phenomenal Art Style
- Fleshed out, Three-Dimensional Characters
- Entertaining and Witty Dialogue that Remains Realistic
- Mini Games That DON'T Make Me Wanna Die
- That Music Tho...Dude...So GOOD
- Manda Panda, Daughter of the Year
- The Best Bro to End All Bros
- Doggy Butt Pats
- Knife Dad. He's my favorite.
[CONS]
- Too short, man! I'd adore some extra Date or Holiday DLC.
- Joseph exists (he's a great character, this is not an actual complaint about his story, I just hate him as a person).
- I didn't get to adopt a dog. Or cat. Who was responsible for this oversight? Was it Giacomo? I trusted Giacomo!!
[SUGGESTIONS]
- Pet DLC; let me have my Dog/Cat!!
- College DLC; lemme visit my baby at school!
- Holiday DLCs; Halloween at least. So many possiblities...
- Extra Date(s) DLC; I want more time with my Dream Daddy!

The Campaign (which also serves as the tutorial) opens with a prison that isn't quite finished yet. And you are told by your boss, the CEO of the "For Profit" Prison, that you have been given the task of executing a murderer. And this order comes from the state itself.
The game then turns towards teaching you how to work the basic construction tools, explaining power, water, foundations, interior walls, and room basics in a straightforward and clean manner.
Then the game shows you exactly why your prisoner is guilty.
It is not a pleasant experience to watch as a tiny cartoon man walk into his home, find his tiny cartoon wife ♥♥♥♥ing a tiny cartoon stranger in his bed, and then tearfully shoot them both in the head.
This gives us the biggest lesson of all: Prison Architect is not a happy game.
Prison Architect is a top down management game where you run your prison company exactly how you want it. As far as the state is concerned, it doesn't matter how high your rehabilitation rate is, all that matters is that you have no escapes, keep the deaths to an acceptable low, and you keep the prisoners in line by any means you deem fit.
Once you finish your campaign, which takes you through the systems of the game, explaining core concepts quite happily while also telling you tales of loss, pain, murder, ambition, hope, and sheer murderous rage. Of course, the problem is that the game ONLY explains the core mechanics and leaves more complicated ones for you to figure out yourself. That said, while there is a Wiki and many a guide for you, the point of the core game in sandbox mode is mostly to see what works best. To adapt to problems and overcome even of it must be done through trail, error and blood.
The game provides security measures such as cameras, remote doors opened by a button or a timer, stab vests and tazers for your guards, and even heavily armed maximum force response teams kept on site with shotguns, full body armor, and the will and means to paint your prison red with blood at your command. Along with this the game will provide schedules, assignments, patrols, and even resticted acess zoning, all of which is designed to keep your prisoners under control so they do not kill each other.
Along with this is provided many means to turn your prisoners into peaceful members of society if you so choose. You may provide basic education, as many prisoners lack even a child's reading and writing skills. And some of them cannot even read at all, let alone write. Give your prisoners trade skills as carpenters or metal workers. Teach them how to be cleaners or work a laundry. And then set up security systems to prevent prisoners stealing hammers or making crude knives.
Prisoners may come with medical issues such as addiction, alchoholism or violent pshycological instability. Build a common room for AA meetings, an office for one on one meetings for professional mental help, an infirmary for chemical treatmeants to help with addiction and minor surgery when the prisoners try to kill, and a mourge when they do kill.
Your prisoners are humans, with desires and needs, thoughts and feelings, and intelligence. Prisoners need to be fed, and you may give them things to do. Build a common room with tables, television sets, and phones. Provide meals at preset times, as many times as you want, in large quantaties and variety if you want, or a simple bowl of vegetable soup once a day if you don't. Prisoners with many things to do are less likey to cause trouble, and giving them these things may make them very happy indeed.
This does not mean you may treat them like sane members of society. You are running a prison. They are prisoners. And Prisoners are not in the habit of obeying the rules. Prisoners steal, fight, and even kill in your walls. Make no mistake, you and your officers are the only order inside the prison. Without your constant watchful gaze and omnipresent guards the prisoners will fall upon each other like wild animals; killing, fighting, and breaking.
If your prisoners are exceptionally angry, and if your prison is weak enough, the prisoners may decide that they can do whatever thy want and there is nothing you can do about it. They may decide to riot. Or you may subdue them, show them that any antisocial behaviour will not be tolerated, and make them docile through fear.
Problems may arise in your prison, and of course these are optional. Make it so that he game throws problems your way at random. Maybe a highly contagious disease is rampaging through your prison and killing your prisoners. Perhaps a water main has burst. Maybe a generator has overloaded, causing a fire and a blackout. Or maybe the mayor has bowed to political pressure and decided to implement reform without consulting you.
If you feel particularly brave, allow the game to generate gangs, and watch as your prison becomes split by three gangs into territories, and attempt to usurp your authority. And then spiral into gang wars, burn your prison down, kill your guards, and extort prisoners.
Prison Architect, ultimately, is exactly what it says it is, with a remarkable and well made game that most will like.  BUt do not expect to laugh because of the cutesy graphics.
They mitigate the horror, but only make it bearable.

It's clear that Avalanche spent a lot of time building the world in Mad Max.  It's a phenomenal game world that’s perfectly reminiscent of the film universe.  It’s a shame that Avalanche learned from the Ubisoft school of open-world design in how best to fill their map with “content.”  You will do the same three things, with zero variation, hundreds of times, if you allow it.  Of the thirty-seven camps I liberated, only one was memorable.  The majority of this game is spent clearing little dots off of the map.  This is repetition to a mind-numbing degree.
I’d forgive all this if the game were fun to play.  Driving around the wasteland is awesome.  Getting ambushed by enemy cars, is not.  The car combat is not exciting thanks to how poor your car controls and the few options you have in destroying them.  This extends to the on-foot combat.  Imagine a vastly simplified Batman: Arkham Asylum fight system with unresponsive controls and an awful camera.  There will be instances where you will get hit or stuck in a damage loop swearing you hit the block button on time.
I held out hope that the story, which starts of well, would finish strong regardless of its short stay.  By the end of the game, Max is neigh unrecognizable from his film persona.  He’s closer to Kratos from God of War.
In less than two hours, you will do everything this game has to offer.  Staying for the story isn’t worth it as I don’t consider it true to the Mad Max character.  It’s a bad game full of repetition matched with poor gameplay.

I haven't finished the game and I'm writing this review now because I'm not sure that I will. It's a decent game, but when you set yourself up as the successor to Planescape: Torment, you have to live up to high expectations, and Tides of Numenera just doesn't. The concept and world are amazing, but the implementation is just unfinished, making the experience feel like you're just scratching the sruface.
First, here's what the game does right. I really liked the original story. It's a bit of a slow burn, but most of the writing is good, and they included all the interesting and bizarre little details, side-stories, and dark humor that really nailed the same narrative feel as PS:T. Also, the promise of being able to take multiple approaches to situations has been delivered. They also definitely brought it with the art. The various game locations I've seen so far are varied and exciting, and in the era of 3D dominance, they still manage to make an isometric game look attractive and visually engaging.
However, the flaws really prevent this game from coming together into an immersive experience. The idea of the tides affecting how everyone in the world reacts to you was barely there, really just adding up to a few throwaway dialogue lines of, "I had heard you were that type of person..." It never seemed to actually affect outcomes. Also, there are no real factions like the ones you could interact with and even join in Torment. I "joined" one of the groups in the game through dialogue, but it has had no effect at all as far as I can tell. No one treated me any differently, I got no stat bonuses or penalties, it didn't seem to help or hurt the group's standing in the world, and I later I even met people who were members of that same group and they had no idea who I even was. Again, there was a lame line about how the various branches of the group didn't have much contact with each other.
The skills, abilities, and effort setup felt needlessly complex, and some of the mechanics were never fully explained. I never figured out how to tell the difference between a one-handed and a two-handed weapon except by equipping it, and I'm still not sure why weapons were divided up into heavy and light. I don't need a lot of hand-holding or a huge tutorial, but as far I can tell, this info wasn't available for me to see anywhere at all. It sucks having to buy a weapon just to see if my character can use it with his shield, then having to sell it back at a loss when it turns out it's two-handed. Maybe I missed something. Finally, I encountered a bug that would cause combat to freeze periodcially. It didn't happen every combat, but several of the bigger ones I had to keep reloading and replaying, which was really tedious. It's a known issue, but a fix doesn't seem to be forthcoming.
I really, really, wish they had fleshed this game out a little more. There was so much promise and if they could have polished it a bit more and made sure that the player's choices had more of an impact on the game world, it would have equaled or even surpassed its "spiritual" predecessor.

Having came from many a shooter, third-person, first-person and genre mutts alike, I found myself forcefully thrusting myself into what I had expected to be just another typical "white knight," heroic power fantasy such as Call of Duty, Medal of Honor or Battlefield.  With all of the derivative shooters you'll find on the market these days, I really try to play more unique titles and stray away from any shooter games when craving some single-player campaign with a entralling story or something to at least mildly interest me for any amount of time.
I was dead wrong.
Spec Ops: The Line is something of a highly underrated masterpiece that, I don't believe, was ever given the recognition it deserved.  The multiplayer is pretty bad, but from multiple sources, the games developers originally were against the idea and 2K (the publishers) forced the concept to push sales and stick with the multiplayer trend in the market.  But in terms of single-player story, this game is a marvel, something I honestly never expected from any military video game.
Firstly, I'll address the issues people have with the actual gameplay.  I personally find nothing wrong with the gameplay at all really.  The actual firefights and action sequences are what we've come to expect from shooters these days and is therefore nothing special, but it's what fills the moments between these action-filled firefights that really make this game.  The controls and mechanics are smooth and feel great, damn me for saying, they are comparable to Gears of War in feel.  The shooting is superb and the movement is a bit sluggish at times, but overall, still a good shooter from this perspective.
Where Spec Ops: The Line really shines is it's absolutely shameless telling of the truths and atrocities of war in the modern age.  Nothing about it is good, nothing about it will make you a hero, no one really is in those situations, and this game will really make you realize that.  This game takes the stereotypical shooters "heroic" stories, and tosses them in the trash.  Then burns the can.  Then shoots it into space where a black hole swallows it.  This game does away with Hollywoods interpretation of modern age warfare and digs deep and dark, where many are too scared to go.  This game will completely destroy the image of war that most games would have you believe in and instead deals with depression, self-loathing, Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, and the grittiness of war that no game has mentioned.
Buy this game.  Experience the story.  I'll meet you on the other side of The Line.
Oh....and Welcome to Dubai.

This game is a true hidden gem. Reviewers are right when they say the game doesn't add anything new in terms of gameplay, but that's not why the game was created. The clichés and repetitive cover-shoot-kill-run cycle are there partially to mock every other war game that follows the same formula, and when placed alongside the story those negatives in effect show the player how ridiculous they are to believe that wars are fought using that system. The game is so good because the story is absolutely brilliant. It doesn't glorify war, or America, or anything really. It is something I have never seen in a video game before, and to describe it in words is to do it a cruel injustice. The ability to choose which ending based on your actions is brilliant. I've done four endings so far, but I know the developers talked about a fifth one, which is simply for the player to put down the controller and stop playing the game. Once you have experienced the story, you'll truly be able to understand just how powerful that last ending is. I can't stress it enough: BUY THIS GAME!
10/10 Would question my actions and sacrifice my morals again

Origins was solid although not as broad as the previous two Batman games. The story was fun to follow although brief, and I was definitely done with punching people way before it was completed. The side quests added some variety although it wasn't long before I had to punch someone. The casefile recreations were very cool, mainly because I got to recreate someone punching someone else.
There were some standout parts, including being the Joker for a bit, and solving the Riddler's many puzzles. The Mad Hatter mission was both unusual and interesting.  The stalking was still great fun- taking out 7 armed guards without any of them seeing you never got old. You also get to play through many of Batman's first encounters with most of the canon's characters.
There were some negatives. Some of the missions didn't work, and the boss battles were fun usually until they add a hundred henchmen to it that you have to punch. It was also tough to 'fly' around the map because the grapnel options were more limited. The area seemed bigger here than in Arkham City, but I had to leg much of it.
The final plus to note is the art. The buildings and the character visually of the city were simply amazing. It would have been fun to be able to explore some of these striking skyscrapers, but only mission oriented ones were open. The weather effects were also impressive-the snowy, gusty setting was immersive.
This is defintely on par with the other games, but the shortest and weakest. The characters were fun to meet as a younger Batman, the missions were engaging and well connected. If you enjoyed the Asylum and City you will get into this. It was just a little tiring by the end, running the streets of a gorgeous landscape in a game that knows how to pull and pull it's punches.

I bought this game primarily because I want to support the GameGrumps/Youtubers in general making or producing games. If that's what you want the game for, I say go for it.
If you want this for an enjoyable game or because you love dating sims, I don't recommend buying it. At least not unless you wait until it's on a pretty decent sale.
The writing is pleasant, absolutely. If you can look past the continuity errors, it's a well written game with enjoyable characters and great art... which seems like a decent game, right? However, I cannot support a game that sells itself as a dating simulator that
allow you to get a "good" ending with all Dads. Meaning, yes, there's a character in this dating simulator, while set up exactly like all the others... you
One of the devs straight up called people sociopaths for wanting to get with said character, too. Maybe don't choose a dating sim if you think people are creeps for wanting one fictional character with another?
There's various other, smaller things that add up as well that make the $15 price tag seem a little much:
-Not a satisfying amount of time with the other Dads. It's mostly a sim about being a father yourself (which is still enjoyable, but not what I thought I was getting!).
-Not enough variation in endings. There's multiple endings - but every ending is set up and presented the same way every time, so replayability feels limited.
-Your options don't usually feel like they make much of a difference in the story, yet another can ruin an entire playthrough with a certain character if you choose wrong... which feels unfair, and you won't even realize unless you replay. (Yup - happened to me)
-Those continuity errors I mentioned before: they're aplenty.
-Your Dadsona has poor art compared to the rest of the game (that sticks out like a sore thumb), and not a satisfying amount of options to choose from to make up for it.
-No CGs like most other sims have, just each character's base art (if you don't know what this is, you probably won't care).
So, overall? No, I will not be recommending this game in its current state.

It's not like at the end of a playthrough you would need time to get over your crush before you could ever think to date an other dad. Say you want to complete the game. You will have to read through the boring main storyline 14 times and more if you want to get all the acheivements. The differences in dialogue goes from minimal to none. But beware of FFW throught it because it won't stop for new dialogue that might appear.   You will easily go from date to date has you will have an unavoidable visual indicator for good and bad choices, you'll just have to reload the last (realy frequent) autosave to redo your choices. And when all is said and done, you'll always end up in your backyard, celebrating Amanda with mostly all of your neighbors, who will mostly say the same boring thing to you, until all the guest are gone and your chosen dad waits for you on a bench either wanting to just stay friends ( bad endings) or lovingly holding your hand (good endings) unless you romance one of those dads who do not have a good ending at all. I'm going to review this game as a newcomer to the series and hopefully address why I recommend it. Bear with me.
tl;dr I'd totally recommend it for newcomers (which is what I'm gearing most of this review for).
I'm a fan of Giant Bomb, and loved to see how much fun Brad and Dan had with this game on some of the UPF's as of late. I'm usually the type of person who jumps feet first into gaming and buys all DLC available. Not sure where I picked that up, but there you have it. So when I saw how much fun they were having, you can only imagine my surprise to see all the negative reviews. I took the time to read through them and there were a few common themes. I decided to pull the trigger (pun entirely intended), but went for the Intro Pack, since I can stand losing $14 on a game I won't play much. So, after my brief run with with, I have to say...it's pretty fun.
The first thing I noticed was how this game was broken up into episodes, and truth be told I approve. I like that I can just buy the intro package to get a feel for the game and, should I sink enough time into to warrant the purchase, buy the next episode, or even buy the rest at once. I understand why, on the surface, that looks bad. It's easy to say "Well, that's because they don't have a full game and are looking to get more money from us!" Some DLC may be like that, sure, but I don't see that being the case here. If they sold each episode as a near full price AAA game, yeah, you've definitely got a case to make. However, here the intro game is the price of some (if not most) indie titles, and the full DLC (at $9 a piece) brings it up to the typical $60 price we're accustomed to. Why I love this method is it allows more freedom in what you want. Even the intro package still has a fair amount of replay-ability (which I'll get in to in a second), so the base package is well worth the price.
Graphically, this game looks great. I have a GeForce 970, 16 gb of RAM, core i5 box and can play this at near the highest settings. The environments look terrific, though I have noticed some broken animations, like a chief using the Force to stir a wooden spoon 15 away from him. Those haven't been too apparent and haven't really detracted from the game, although I do wonder how bad they'll get the further into the game I go.
The gameplay is fun, but with a few minor quirks. I've been noticed through walls on occasion, and I wish the option to be able to drag a dead or unconscious body appeared right after the animation. Too often I've been in a situation where I have to knock someone out and have only a few seconds to store the body before a passing patrol. I played a lot of Splinter Cell: Conviction, and I had the most fun with the single player missions and finding new ways to kill people and clear levels. Ultimately, that open ended play was my biggest draw to this game. Aside from the elusive contracts, Allowing me to go back and try to kill someone with an explosive toilet seat will definitely trigger something in me to want to keep playing.
I've read the reviews from the hardcore fans of this series, and I see exactly where they're coming from. If you've played every Hitman game in the series, the complaints given here are well within their right to exist. However, if you're like me, you may not need to be interesting in pay for a ton of content you may never see, and just want a game with decent stealth and puzzle mechanics, and the freedom to find new and exciting ways to murder bad guys (and anyone else unlucky enough to wander into wrong bathroom). If that sounds like you, I highly recommend the Intro Pack for starters.

I doubt anyone's going to read this, but I gotta say.
I have 148 hours on Undertale (at the time of this review) and the game is, at most, about maybe seven or eight hours on the route with no special endings, on your FIRST playthrough. The game is so enjoyable for me that I've played it several times, over and over again. I've searched for fangames, looked at fanart, and listened to the soundtrack more times that I can count. But what makes this game special?
Well, I don't want to go into anything really in-depth because of spoilers, but I will say this game is super unique. You of course already know of the unique battle system - "sparing". But what is sparing? In most RPGs, when you come across an enemy, you have to fight. People don't even think about the alternatives because that's the norm - we're expected to fight, to have only one possible outcome.
But Toby Fox did something else with this game. You can fight, like in a normal RPG, but you can also interact with every monster you come across. You can befriend them, convince them not to fight you. Every monster in this game is so unique - you have special options for each of them when you interact with them. You might come across a Loox, who doesn't like being picked on, or Vulkin, who thinks it's helping you out by attacking you.
What's better is that the game has special endings prepped for you depending on what you do. You can try to spare - or, you can try to fight, What do you want to do? It's your choice. Just remember - you'll have to accept the consequences of what you do. And if you go down the wrong path, well, know that...
y o u ' r e   g o n n a   h a v e   a   b a d   t i m e  .
Anyway, I usually don't write reviews, but this game is one of a kind, and I highly recommend it.

Football Tactics:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Always wanted to find out how the top coaches made it all the way to the Premier League? Well, don’t look further, they are all playing Football Tactics!!
Football Tactics is a football manager game using a turn-based system during match day which gives this game its originality.
First you will have to choose which team and in which country you will be playing. Then, the Amateur League will start. This league is realistically a tutorial and will help you to understand how to play the game and you will probably find it quite easy. As soon as you move up to the next league, the difficulty will increase straight away and you will be facing tougher opponents. In total, you have 5 leagues and 2 cups to play in and the aim is to reach and win the Premier League and the Cups, of course.
The management aspect of the game has good depth but it is easy to use and understand. I really like it that way. You can . . . upgrade your stadium to get more attendance and revenue, upgrade your youth academy so you can find better young talents, purchase new players during the transfer window, get specific coaches and assistants so your players improve their skills (but you will need prestige points). How do you get prestige points, you may ask? Really simple, if the goal difference is  1 in your favour then you will get 1 prestige point. If you manage to finish the season in the top 3 teams, you will be rewarded with additional prestige points.
Match day – Each half will consist of 24 action moves to be used between each team, with a total of 48 moves per match. Remember, you and your opponent will use 3 action moves per turn. They are plenty of moves to make your mark and score goals. At the end of each match, your player will get experience points which in turn will help them to reach a higher level. If you win, you’ll get higher experience points.
The graphics are smooth and polished and the game runs well. This game is an early access and it is very impressive so far. Please bring on the full version, I can’t wait!
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good and easy Football Management
-	Turn-based match day
-	Really fun to play
-	Addictive and challenging
-	Plenty of achievements
Negative:
~~~~~~~
-	No trading cards
9/10

Stormworm+ is the evolution of the classic snake that people will remember from brick phones back in the day. It builds on top of the classic game by most notably adding an extra dimension, but the ability to jump also shakes up the classic gameplay and gives a player with fast enough reflexes an out when they would have otherwise died. The leaderboards make it easy to compete against players from all around the world or claim the top spot among friends and the multitude of game modes and maps will give you plenty of opportunities to prove your skills and reflexes.
The devs have publically stated that even though this is version 1.0 it will certainly not be the end of development for this game and that hopefully with fan feedback they can introduce new features and keep the game feeling fresh.

Colourful and addictive, Stormworm+ oozes polish and captures that "just one more try" feeling.
It clearly builds on top of the classic Snake mobile/arcade game, but the elements it adds makes it a unique experience, not the least of which is jumping, which is ultra-responsive and adds a lot of tangible skill and choice to the game.
The core of the game is working your way up the leaderboards, and there's a different one for each combination of map and mode, so plenty of chances to beat your friends' scores, or rank on the global leaderboards.
PROS
- Jumping feels great
- Controls are tight
- Automatic camera is never punishing, always points in the right direction
- Meditative, easy to zone out
- Performance is slick
CONS
- Music is lower energy than the rest of the game, but you can mute it and blast your own.
- Using a controller takes a while to get used to as it uses non-analog input, but it means an even playing field for high scores, and the rumble adds a lot.

I have finally played through all of the routes and got all of the endings possible, so I wanted to leave a review to give my opinion after completion.
I went into this worried I wouldn't like it and I ended up LOVING it. I wanted it to be good so badly and it delivered. There are a lot of deep and insightful messages and life lessons hidden within the different routes, which I appreciated. One struck a little too true with me, but in a good way (Craig's route, man). I also enjoyed the mini games and the parts where you had to really use your brain (I won't give it away). All in all, this was a dating sim that is really unlike any other while being similar at the same time.
The fact that you can make transmen/nonbinary characters is amazing and I applaud that effort, as well as the choices in the beginning (your mother; your father) (when you were born; when you were adopted). Inclusivity for the win, always! As a transman who loves dating sims, especially dating sims with other dudes, it is almost impossible to find a dating sim without the main character being a female protagonist dating men. So this game ultimately attracted me for that reason, but not that reason alone. That was a surprising bonus. Not to mention the awesome fact that all body types are treated as equally attractive and being gay is normalized and not made into a joke.
***LIGHT SPOILER AFTER THIS. SKIP THIS PARAGRAPH IF YOU DO NOT WANT POSSIBLE SPOILERS***
One of my main gripes was Joseph's route. He was the character I thought I would like LEAST, but he ended up being my second favorite next to Damien, who is my first. I do have to say also, though, in the same vein, that imperfect endings were also necessary in a game like this. We spend a lot of time playing these games and they all are predictable at the end: Person gets romance with other person and they ride off into the sunset. Not enough dating sims have a plot twist like that, where things DON'T turn out like you want them to. That said, I am still emotionally compromised at Joseph's ending.
***END SPOILER WARNING***
I really hope there will be more to this in the future. A sequel of some sort, or DLC or some sort of add ons to experience more of the story with the dads, maybe even more bits to add on like extra dates, random one-off stories with the dads, etc. I did feel like I was left wanting for more as the third date, at least for Brian alone, felt like too much was crammed into a small limit of text. Brian's definitely felt like it didn't connect, but although the others settled well with me (save for Joseph), I wanted more out of it. More story and more time. I'd say Robert's story, in my opinion, was probably the most fulfilling and in-depth out of them all.
I fell in love with all of the characters and their stories, which is something I don't normally do with dating sims. So bravo for the Dream Daddy Team for making loveable and memorable characters!
Summary:
Pros: Awesome insightful life lessons/advice, A+ Dad jokes, Brilliant humor, beautiful art, and awesome characters.
Cons: The three date limit made things feel a bit rushed and some more content/stories with the dads would be nice.
My rating: Definitely an A. I love this game.

From the get go I was against the very idea of this game. Hitman is one of my favorite franchises and having it be episodic sounded downright horrendous. Yet I heard from multiple places that the episodic structure worked well, the game was good and everything was fine. I decided to give Sqeenix yet another chance and buy the full game.
Despite terrible performance I had a good time with this game after knocking it down to medium/high (on my 100% WC, 980SLI, DDR4, SSD, Intel x99 build). They have nailed the basic Hitman part of this game. The combat is fun and challenging, there are plenty of weird stuff to do, everything is very well made. There are some unfortunate things missing from the good old Blood Money days, like customizable weapons and loadouts (other than picking few basic items), the newspaper report after each mission and the game can get pretty grindy if you want to unlock all the different weapons. But dammit if this isn't just a whole lot of fun.
Then the shoe drops. The performance seemed to get worse for me after an update, even with others reporting improvements. Servers go down making it apparant how incompetent the developer and publisher is at managing a server infrastructure and WAY more importantly how they handle what to do once that infrastructure fails to work.
Hitman is a singleplayer game with essentially zero multiplayer aspects to it apart from some custom mission sharing, yet without the online server you can't progress, use your unlocked items, unlock new items or even access most of the things you have, even when you have your save locally on your own computer.
But wait, thats not all! They even manage to mess things up more than that. Sometimes when the servers go down you can't even enter or quit the game, it just loads and loads forever telling you it finds the online server, but then can't get your information or something.
On top of all of this the recent release of Episode 3 tells people who pre-ordrered all the episodes that they have to buy the next mission in order to play it and redirects you to the Steam store, where it will actually let you buy it. I was wondering if I hadn't actually bought the full game and had to check my purchase history. This is simply inexcusable, you just cannot do something like this. The game not working properly is one thing, but potentially tricking people into buying the game a second time is just above and beyond, even from Square Enix.
My guess is that they fail to check for the full version and that the people who werent stupid enoughs to pre-order the episodes like I was are happily playing the game right now.

This is a great game.
So, are we going back to roots or into something immature-new? Neither. Don't get fooled by the good-old "HITMAN" sign. It is a whole lot of a different game. Old IOI is now Reto-Moto. New IOI team consists of new professionals. This is how Absolution should be. GIGANTIC open levels, ASTONISHING, MARVELOUS level of detail of everything (exterior and interior), HI-End design, every part of the levels feels alive and breathing. A believable representation of what life of rich and powerful is like. Sadly without razor-sharp/stereotypical satire the good-old-IOI-Hitman had and without soul-crushing tracks from Jesper Kyd. The game now has real AAA+ game feel, unlike demo scene/underground-art vibe of before-reboot-Hitman. And here come the flaws. Poor performance on non-hi-end systems (and bugs related to. SSD is strongly advised), big bunch of oversimplifying gameplay features (casualization), shallow soundtrack, poor and illogical rating system, linear approach to special assassinations.. All of these things take away the little bits of immersion.
Only one issue is left standing in the middle - the episodic release policy. On the one hand very affordable prices starting from 5 USD for intro pack (don't get started with paid demos. Free demos are done for, we have youtube now), 19 USD for a full experience. This system encouraging one to play on and wait for the next episode (Episodes are coming every month, and you don't have to pay for them) thus extending the game's lifespan. On the other.. some players want it all in one take.
The sum is: this is a total reboot, a new game with no connection with an old franchise. The game with reasonable demands for processing power of player's PC. The honest episodic approach, and some casual gameplay-elements. The eye candy level-design and an average soundtrack. Interesting, fun objectives and challenges and linear approach for completion.

With a neat, minimalistic and highly stylized environment, Splice has you down at the cellular level solving puzzles. You must re-arrange the cells to match the outline given in a certain number of moves. The catch is that each cell can only have 1 or 2 child cells attached. Also added in each Sequence is a new type of cell. They are introduced in an easy level so you can understand what they do.
You are able to scrub your timeline of moves (move forwards and backwards) so quick trial and error is easy to control
Splice can get mighty difficult. I went through the game only consulting a guide for a small handful of puzzles. The epilogue is brutal and I was burned out at that point…so I finished the rest with a guide.
The music is great and very soothing. It blends in and never got old to me.
It does get pretty repetitive but I understand it’s a puzzle game with a single concept.
This is locked at 30fps, which is a shame as it’s very pretty to look at and I would have loved to play it in 60fps.
I couldn’t find a way to re-play the normal puzzles after the epilogue was done. Maybe I missed something?
+Fantastic visuals
+Great music
+Puzzle concept is neat
+30fps
+Can get stale after a while
+Can’t re-play normal puzzles?
+Can be brutally difficult (mostly in Epilogue)

This game is pretty fun but I'd only recommend buying it durring a sale like I did. I don't think it's worth 10 bucks but thats subject to each person's opinion. It has some replay value and even if it doesn't particularly grab me I find myself loading it up every so often.
Pros:
It's got some pretty interesting mechanics what with the bullets being reusable and causing you to retrieve them due to the fact that you have nothing to defend yourself if you run out of bullets. The whole rougelike mechanics are pretty heavy in this game as well. You don't really make a lot of money off of enemies so with the prices going up the deeper you go it becomes really important to balance what you want to spend your money on. Potions, healing, bombs, the discount (which should be top priority), your life insurance, etc. With money being so important it both makes sense and sucks that almost everything in the game only sells for 5 dollars, with a few exceptions.
Cons:
Although it can be fun I can't really recommend it to people, as interesting and unique as it is. As many have said there is an unsolved sutter issue that happens every so often. Its pretty random when it happens. You can go a whole game without it and sometimes you cant get it to stop. On top of that I feel like theres some balance issues with hitboxes and such. I've been attacked through a wall from around the corner by one of the imps as well as a crawler. Turret placement can be a real pain to deal with when its only weakpoint is behind it and it shoots two times per second. The turrets are deadly accurate as well, forcing you to constantly move in order to dodge them which can really put you at a disadvantage if theres more than one or other enemies in the same room. I've also had it on more than one occasion where a turret's bullet clipped a corner and still damaged me even though I was out of the line of fire/line of sight.
On top of all that the developer has given up on the game so there won't be any updates in the future. It's a pretty barebones game that has the potential to be better but sadly wont be. I wouldn't mind seeing some more balances, bug fixes, and additonal items and enemies.

Every decision matters in Heavy Bulllets, which is strange for a game with a 2-sentence story and maybe as much dialogue.  This game could be called a management sim: You're always keeping track of money, items, and the titular bullets, which you need to pick up after firing. At least then I wouldn't be making purists angry by calling it a roguelike.
Heavy Bullets is a hard game, but you won't know that until you've already gotten through one or two levels. It has a really nice learning curve that punishes mistakes just hard enough for you to not make them again in 5 minutes. You may be frustrated, but there are almost no moments in the game where you can call ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
I may be the odd one out on this, but I feel like the music takes away from the game. It plays at intervals, and then only for a short period of time. The music is good, sure. But the atmosphere I get when it's not playing feels a lot more tense. Pick up this game if you want dungeon crawling with a gun. And you don't mind the vaporwave color pallete they use (which I love)
Heavy Bullets is a great game. It plays perfect for me and has awesome replay value. I love the level design and the the sound effects. Everything is simple yet effective.

**Edit: After some progress, I have to say that unfortunately, the stutter 'lag' massively increases in the last few levels. I would still recommend this game, because the first 4 levels were fine for me and gave me a lot of enjoyment, but you might want to wait for a sale. The lag on the last few stages makes it hard to enjoy, especially for a game that is heavily reliant on fast reactions and twitch shooting. However, I would say that the first 4-5 stages are a lot of fun, and I would say it is still probably worth buying if you get the game on sale.**
If you enjoy twitch shooters, difficult indie games, roguelikes or dungeon crawlers, I can't recommend Heavy Bullets more.
I have not experienced any of the extreme lag others have said, but I do get the occasional stutter (maybe once or twice a floor) but that generally doesn't happen in combat and barely effects gameplay. **Edit: In the last few stages it rapidly increases makes the game almost unplayable. Be warned**
Even if lag might be an issue, it's well worth buying it. You can see if you experience the lag and if you do you can easily refund it.
Now, to the game:
The gameplay is addictive and fun. For games like this, a lot of the time I find myself getting bored and just being careless/running through quickly (looking at BOI). With this game, I find myself much more invested in each playthough,
There is a sense of progression - upgrades make a noticable effect and the further you get, the harder the enemies get, but also the more equipped you are to deal with them. There are 8 stages (it shows you every time you load the next stage) and I have only got to 4 so far, but I already feel determined to beat the game. It might take a while though.
There isn't much to learn in terms of items and enemies (again, not like BOI), so you generally don't feel cheated after you get used to the pacing of the game (and learn about the three main types of enemies - charging enemies, worms and turrets). None of the items you pick up can effect you negatively and most are pretty descriptive as to what they are, so you are never left thinking 'What does this item do?'
The randomly generated aspect of the game can be annoying at times (I'm assuming that is what causes the occasional stuttering?) with some places being out of reach, but it also gives the game insane replayability.
The biggest gripe I have with this game is the explosives. You start with three grenades, but you only do a tiny throw when you use them. This makes them basically useless. There are several explosive items in the game and I barely find myself using them. There is an item that lets you throw them further but it is fairly rare and when I find it I am normally carrying more useful items anyway.
In summary, if you are interested in this game and think you might like it, get it. I don't know about full price but it is definitely worth it on sale. If it tags too much, get a refund.

Amazing narrative and pacing, though the controls were often sticky and could be frustrating at times throughout the game.  I found the gameplay to be quite enjoyable and much less of a slog than what others have claimed it to be, though admittedly I haven't had much experience with third-person shooters in the past.  The story is truly where it's at though, and if more mainstream shooters could introduce this level of immersion to their campaigns, I'd be all over them.  It pretty much felt like I was playing an interactive version of Apocalypse Now, and the frustration and challenge of playing on Suicide Mission difficulty really made it that much easier to "become" Walker and put yourself in his shoes.  Traversing the roads, tunnels, and rooftops of a post-apocalyptic Dubai was absolutely gorgeous too--hauntingly so--and it reminded me of the breathtaking beauty of games like Mirror's Edge at times.
That being said, I did have issues with certain areas of the game such as the Ride of the Valkyries helicopter sequence, which honestly should have been a cutscene and in which I had to pray to RNG Jesus to survive.  Raiding the yacht in Chapter 13 was incredibly frustrating as well as you were swarmed with enemies from all sides, had limited cover to utilize (and which you frequently had to abandon with all the grenade and RPG-happy assailants), and when the storm sets in you seriously have no idea what's going on or from which direction enemies will be attacking.  I think I died at least 20 times in that segment alone.  The other issue I had was with the sprinting system that was unusually sticky and which caused me to run past cover and get killed on numerous occasions.  Still an enjoyable experience overall--I didn't buy into the whole thing with the game trying to guilt you over your characters' choices or criticizing the conventions of the genre--was fun to think about though!

One of the best stories I've ever experienced in an RPG, a truly memorable adventure from the beginning till the end. The writing is top-notch, there is no artificial padding of gametime, no grindy bits of any kind, the pacing of the story is constant and flows well. Sadly, there is not much actual challenge, but I didn't get bored at all. Yep, it's around 40 hours of almost pure storytelling.
Just don't expect it to be some sort of tactical simulator with lots of micromanagement and strategizing, it's a type of an RPG more similar to visual novel-ish choose-your-own-adventure-ish Shadowrun Returns style games (yet I felt there was still less reading than I had to endure in Shadowrun: Hong Kong!). So if you find the premise and the setting appealing and you're ready to read a lot - definitely give this one a shot.
And don't listen to those who fanatically worship Planescape: Torment and other Infinity Engine games in the reviews around here, because more often than not they're out of their minds.

I wasn't a kickstarter and though I've been looking forward to this game as someone who loved Planescape: Torment, I subjected myself to as little hype or foreknowledge as possible.
THE SETTING: It's a bit like a cross between Fallout and Planescape. The premise of a Sci-Fi/Fantasy world filled with gadgets that might do something cool or blow your face off is very appealing and could possibly lend itself to all sorts of great stories. Absolutely loved it, I hope they'll make more games that use it in the future.
GAMEPLAY: I really like the Crisis system and the idea that you can, and indeed sometimes have to, resolve them without combat. In fact, I experienced so little combat I can't even properly comment on it.
STORY: WARNING, SLIGHT SPOILERS. This is where the game lets itself down a bit for me. Of course, I still compare it to Planescape: Torment (which I rate as the best video game of all time, storywise), so it's still not BAD. Just, could be better.
I liked the party characters, none of them felt flat or one-dimensional (with the exception of Erritis but perhaps that was intentional). I just wish game developers stopped enforcing arbitrary headcount limits.
The foreshadowing you can get with Anamnesis gets a bit spoiler-y at times; I guessed several major plot twists (like the importance of the Ghostly Woman) before I even left the first city.
The abrupt ending feels more than a bit rushed and the central question "What does one life matter?" gets a bit flimsy at times, where Planescape: Torment's "What can change the nature of a man?" never dropped out of focus.
Also the final end sequence I hated, for the same reasons I hated Mass Effect 3's ending. Throughout the game, the primary antagonist (The Sorrow) is represented as a hateful force that tries to kill you through no fault of your own and cannot be reasoned with. At the last moment it basically goes "Turns out trying to kill was really hard, maybe I should just talk to you instead" and offers the same insane troll logic the Reapers in ME3 used as justification for trying to kill you. And then the game forces you to agree to play along with the Sorrow's one-sided offers for compromise; The only ending where you don't is shown to be a bad one.
So far it is great game very much like Planescape.

Basically a sequel to Jedi Outcast, this game tells a story of a student, which is subordinate to a previous entry's protagonist. But frankly, story is so bland, it's not even worth mentioning. Writing is as run-of-the-mill Star Wars shtick as it could be, and it is delivered mostly through unskippable cutscenes. Oh, my... Level design isn't brilliant at all, and some of the single player levels are examples of "so bad it's not even funny" game design(that level with hoverbikes comes to mind).
But it still delivers where it matters - combat is more varied, sporting new game-changing saber styles and movement abilities, multiplayer is still alive and mod scene delivers to this day(google "jedi academy movie battles"). And even not-so-spectacular single-player campaign lets you scratch that nostalgic itch. Basically, if you want a game that features jedi duels, there is no better place to go.
The amount of fiddling to make it run properly on modern systems is very reasonable - several .cfg file edits and maybe a fix or two installed will grant you a mostly smooth experience.

I like the premise and setting of the game, and I'd be lying if I said there wasn't some fun to be had, but it simply isn't worth its price. One curator named it as "retro-version of Hitman," but don't be fooled; this is nowhere near the Hitman games especially in terms of depth. The only thing that factors in is whether you get seen while shooting someone, and then whether or not you decide to hide the body. The former isn't much of an option since being seen will almost certainly get you killed, while the latter is highly risky but rewards only pocket-change.
It's a stealth game, so it's very slowly paced. Your objective is to hunt down and kill targets for money, but there are no indoor environments and the targets never seem to go into alleyways, which means there are few opportunities to kill your targets discretely. In addition, your starting weapon is always a terrible little pistol with bad range and a long charge up time that makes stealth kills even more difficult. You can upgrade to new weapons that fix these problems, but they are expensive, and you don't get very much money from each job.  This is fine, but this game also wants to be a roguelike, which is a genre notable for high difficulty and permanent death. Both of these are gameplay aspects, but neither of them are optional. So you might spend 10-20 minutes waiting to kill a single target due to not having proper resources or opportunity only to make a single mistake which results in being killed by near invincible police helicopters. At which point you're out of luck, and now have to spend another half hour trying to get enough money to be where you were before you died. What this ultimately leads to is frustrating and hipocritical gameplay that contradicts itself by requiring extreme patience for little reward while also sparing no patience for the player themselves. If more skill were involved this would be somewhat forgivable, but as it stands you have little say in whether or not a previously unseen witness will enter the scene right at the excessively long time it takes to manually unholster your weapon, aim it at the target, get within range and wait for your weapon to charge up enough to actually fire, and thus result in you becoming wanted by the police, who then hunt you down and kill you resulting in you having to start all over again.
The controls are also pretty awkward. It's top down perspective, and your character always faces where the mouse is pointing, but the WASD controls move relative to the cursor. So, if the mouse is at the top screen, the W key will move you there, but if its at the bottom of the screen it will move you there instead. In a better game this would be forgivable, but as it stands its just another factor that worsens the experience.

I dislike Call of Duty for a lot of reasons, but I've always enjoyed the campaigns, if for no other reason then they are impressive strings of scripted events. Carl on Duty: Black Cops II breaks the mold a bit by offering a branching story with at least three outcomes, and the possiblity to miss some events in one playthrough. I expected the much-discussed Strikeforce missions to cause me a lot of trouble, but they were in fact the easiest parts of the campaign, as most of your losses are replaced and you're not penalized for losing guys, which is kind of sad if you think about it. I also counted only two unecessary celebrity voice actors this time, so I guess more money went into actually developing the campaign. All that said, it suffers from the same problems that plague the entire series: stupid deaths, tiny health pool, marmalade-vision when damaged, limited variety of weapons, depressingly short vehicle segments and a sense of moral myopia that typically comes when trying desperately to portray America as the good guy while we go about policing the world and shooting Russians/Arabs/Latinos/(Insert non-American whites here). That said, Two Black ♥♥♥♥♥ manages to make its central characters seem equally morally justifiable, which is no small feat. Overall, it's a solid single-player experience, though I'm one of those weirdos who actually gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥about CoD's singleplayer. Treyarch proves themselves the superior CoD developer once again. On the other hand, it's Call of Duty. It's stock, it's short, it's overpriced and you could do a hell of a lot better. I enjoyed it, but those of a more refined palette may wish to look elsewhere.

Batman: Arkham Origins is the third installment in the legendary Arkham series, and a lot of skeptisism surrounded the release of Origins, as it was being developed by WB Games, rather than Rocksteady, the creators of the series. I have to say, given the time and resources they had, it's not all that bad. Now, for the long-time fans of the series, this game was a bit of a letdown, but as I said before, it's not a big surprise. Origins is essentially a copy of Arkham City, with a slightly bigger world and some altered mechanics. The boss fights were reduced to combinations of punching and countering, and were basically upgraded thugs. The Most Wanted system for side missions took all of the mystery and continuous searching out of the game, and basically handed you a location and a group of enemies. Now, for the first-time player of the Arkham series, the game is great. It's well optimized, it has great graphics, and an okay story. Now, story. The most important part of a Batman game. WB Games decided yet again to make the main villain someone who, (without giving spoilers) has appeared in all previous games, and is getting a little stale. It's understandable, because WB Games was trying to more continue the series, rather than innovate it. All in all, Arkham Origins is okay, but I would highly reccomend Arkham City, as the boss fights and side missions are much better. I would rate Batman: Arkham Origins a 6/10.

Undertale is a fantastic game and one that you won't soon forget. If its unique RPG gameplay and retro-style graphics don't win you over than its colorful cast of quirky characters certainly will. In fact this game is worth playing just for its Characters ad story alone. Beautifully written and full of hilarious and even heartbreaking moments.
The gameplay itself is simple and easy to pick up. Blending together traditional RPG mechanics with elements more commonly found in bullet hell action games. If your looking for a decent challenge
than you'll find it here and for those looking to really push themselves to the limits of controller breaking insanity, well...there's always genocide.
As far as controls go, they are a bit different than what you'd expect. The game opts to using the arrow keys instead of the more common W,A,S, and D. However, this isn't terrible and you adjust pretty quickly. Really the controls just boil down to personal preference and while there is no way to customize the controls you can always use a gamepad for a much smoother experience.
Of course I have to mention the soundtrack which is just gorgeous. Each track is unique and instantly memorable and you'll find yourself humming along long after you've stopped playing. Level themes are soothing and ambient and the boss battle themes are, in my opinion, among the best in gaming.  I highly recommend picking up the soundtrack if you can.
Overall I could not recommend this game any higher and if you haven't experienced Undertale yet than you are missing out on a true gem of a gaming experience.

For all it's faults it's a really enjoyable game in classic hitman style. It has the humor, the core mechanics, and the level design that made those games great.

The latest Hitman has to be the first time that I've been genuinely impressed and excited when playing a modern videogame in an incredibly long time. The semi-open sandbox puzzles of previous hitman titles such as Contracts and Blood Money return with a mixture of certain gameplay elements from Absolution (sans the obnoxious disguise system or level design of Absolution). In fact, the changes to the disguise system in this iteration give it a nice balance between the useless disguises of Absolution and the lack of any challenge that occurred with the disguise system of Blood Money. And, this is further reinforced with the expansive level design of the currently available episodes.
I've gotten nearly 100 hours played in this game with most of that time being spent in Paris and Sapiezna. Both are  incredible levels boasting tons of various ways to go about eliminating your targets and the little touches such as conversations revealing the background story behind your targets and their motivations. Sapienza especially has tons of small conversations and small easter eggs that make the level a lot of fun to replay and explore.
The game isn't without its problems of course. The always online DRM and the finicky servers for the game can make it incredibly frustrating to play at times when you're kicked out mid-mission after setting up the perfect solution in a level. Fortunately, I haven't had this happen personally that often but the issue is certainly there and you should be wary of it if your internet isn't all that great. And, a lot of the patches end up adding in issues that were never their to begin with (such as the 'subdue kill' bug) which only results in more patches that continue the cycle.
Regardless, these issues haven't outright ruind the game for me as I end just having an absolute blast playing through the current levels and trying out different ideas and routes.
