Spec Ops: The Line, where do I even begin? I love this game. I love it more than Portal, more than Half Life and more than CS GO. This game is underrated and didn't get the attention that it deserved.
Graphics and Audio- This game looks really good for 2012. The environments are rich and have so much detail. You can even use your surroundings to your advantage. The models look great for both characters and weapons. The only thing that I don't like about the graphics is that some cutscenes look worse than the actual game and they seem poorly rendered. The audio is also great and has a lot of depth to it, but the audio design seems simple. What I mean is that the stronger guns sound more powerful than the weaker guns, but this doesn't bother me.
93/100
Gameplay-This game plays kinda like Gears-of-War and shares some similar mechanics. For example, when you sprint your camera gets lower and your character is slouching. Also, you can vault over cover while behind it and you can switch cover if you are looking at it. But, the gunplay is different. Each gun is designed for a different situation. For example: most shotguns are ment for close range, the ARs are ment for medium range, the SMGs are ment for close-medium range and shooting while on the move and so on. The gameplay can get annoying at time since sometimes, while your character slides into cover, he can get riddled with bullets and even get killed. This gets really annoying and even frustrating at times.
84/100
Story- I'm not going to spoil you the story because it is just amazing. Once you play through it, you might leave with some unanswered questions. This is good becuase that means that this is a game that makes you think about what happened, what you did and if you really are the Walker you think you are. Also, there is a lot of character development. First you start off with three cocky Delta operatives and through out the story, they change and by the end, they are completely different characters. The story is the best I have ever seen in a video game.
100/100
Multiplayer- The multiplayer doesn't use the story so you don't really care if you loose or not and the game modes aren't even that great. It's just gunplay here.
65/100
Final Verdict-I highly recommend this game to anyone that is tired of CoD campaigns going over the top and making you think about what you are doing. Right now this game is $30 and I think that is a fair price. The Final score is an 85.5/100, but that is with the multiplayer. If you take it out than this game becomes a 92.33./100. The second score is more accurate and if multiplayer wasn't in the game, I think $30 is still a good price. If you don't want to pay $30, you can wait a bit since I see this game on sale a lot or you can get for a great price online. The story will blow you away and make you want to play more, so give this game a try.

Mad Max was an absolutely superb game. I highly recommend it to those who like Batman Arkham, Shadows of Mordor and even Assassin's Creed. All of these games share similar styles in combat and exploration. I played way to long on this game sadly, but it was well worth it. I have all but 1 achievement (it is sadly bugged in a few locations), but it was really worth it regardless.
You have a completely open world with a few required quests to show you the way to the 2nd portion of the game. You can upgrade your character and vehicle on the fly which I think is very well done and easy to manuever in the UI.
The only bugs that I had in this game were around challenges that are required for the hardest achievement *Up to the Task*.
Combat is very tight and strong. You learn a few different reversals, increase your strength and begin to completely drive the hordes of Scrotus' minions into the ground.
Driving around can be a little frustrating with low grade tires and suspension, but once you unlock more upgrades through destroying the enemy fortresses and lowering the hold on the area it can start to pick up and you can build yourself the ultimate Mad Max road warrior.
Tons of content to play like blowing up large fortresses, taking on boss fights, blowing up towers and scarecrows, finding minefields. I personally love to go around and get 100% on these types of games, because having an open world from the start means no limits. I was almost a completely decked out road warrior by the time I had completed the first two large zones (Gutgash and Jeet). The missions are pretty good with mainly killing enemies and doing small little explorative missions. You meet very interesting characters along the way (I love chumbucket!) and the story takes such a dark, painful twist towards the very end. Superb ending to a very painful start.

Mad Max is...
1) Fun ( just sit back and enjoy... RPG aspects shouldn't be taken too seriously e.g. the Witcher series)
2) Worth the really low price (regardless of a discount)
3) Currently running on "Very High" settings ( no performance issues experienced so far)

You're a contract killer in Metrocide. Not much is explained, but that's fine: the contracts early on are fun, and it's interesting to plan out if hiding the body will be an option or not every time. The starting blaster requires charging, and it's really ♥♥♥♥♥♥. Honestly, a gun with ammo that only held one bullet before reloading would be more fun and strategic. Every time you die or start a new level you are given this god awful gun, and it sucks a lot of the joy out of the game. Once you get 350ish credits and unlock it, you can whip out a shotgun instead, which is pretty fun. The objective is to get enough credits to get out of the area, which is 2000, 4000 and 8000, respectively. If a camera, cop or civilian see you kill someone or whip out a gun, expect to be chased and dealt with. Leaving bodies increases police presence, and bodies can be dumped in sewers, which are single use, or rivers, which have multiple spots. Contracts unlock as you progress, starting with people that just run away, to armed, paranoid targets with escorts. The problem though, is that the AI is so bad that you can exploit armed and paranoid targets.
When anyone, including NPCs, draws a weapon and fires, the cops are on them. Even if the cop is escorting that target. When NPCs pull a weapon, they tend to stand still, even if you duck behind cover, shooting their rounds into the side of a building until the cops or someone deals with them. Vigilantes roam the streets, so if the cops don't kill them, they will. This means that completing your contracts is as simple as aggroing, running behind cover, and waiting. It's a shame this is so easy to do, but at the same time the last zone is almost unplayable otherwise. The player is unable to follow targets in buildings, so the massive network of cameras and cops makes regular contract killing a chore and extremely unenjoyable. The AI and balance needs a LOT of work for this to be more fun, but the masochist in me wants to complete this game. Beating the game is much easier than doing some of these ridiculous achievements which rely on luck. The only semblance of progression is when you unlock new items to buy, which are all expensive and can be seized during a scan, including the guns that aren't supposed to be illegal.
In the event the developers don't revisit this game and retool it, I hope someone is inspired enough by Metrocide to remake it with more of a focus on environment design and introducing other ways to kill targets.

I really wanted to like that game. The reduced graphic style looked rather interesting and the promise of something Hitman-like without the slag of some detailled graphic engine with all its problems seemed tempting. However this game does not really deliver on those. The pixel look makes it unnecessarily difficult to find out in which direction targets and witnesses are looking, which often is a death sentence.
Also while stalking a victim migh be fun, there is the mechanic missing which would make the way of the victim forseeable, like it is possible in Hitman. Instead it seems like entirely erratic movement, with random direction changes, which don't go well with the previous lack of clarity. The whole stalking part gets boring quickly.
The player gets thrown in all of this without an introduction. There is no beginner level which allows to learn the game mechanics. The player has to find out everything on his/her own. As some features need money to unlock, this leads to hours of playing just to find out the effect of those features. You wasted all your money on a shotgun just to get killed before you were able to use it the first time? Try again. Invest another hour of tedious stalking. To avoid the player having any fun, the designers combined this with the absence of a save function, which results in replaying of the same beginning, which does not change a bit.
These days there are too many games trying to play the roguelike-gameplay-card to cover their flaws. The gaming world has moved on and as tempting as the initial concept might seem, Metrocide did not move along.

I got this out of this week's Humble Bundle, so I ended up paying less than a dollar for the game. Game is totally worth more than that though. I think I would have paid about $5 or $7 for it comfortably.
For as simple as the game is, it forces you to pay close attention to your surroundings. You have to use the city against your targets, and come up with a few different plans about what to do if things go south, or there's a witness you didn't account for. You do always have the option of just killing everyone and bailing before the cops arrive, but there is eventually repercussions to being careless...
I've even managed some pretty smart stuff, like killed a guy in front of a vigilante, who accidentally killed another civilian, and the cops showed up and neutralized him as the suspect for both crimes.
It can be tricky sometimes to tell which civilians are going to turn vigilante early on though. Later, it seems like everybody is packing.
I completely recommend this though to anybody that's a fan of stealth and assassination games, especially with a touch of gritty Bladerunner style cyberpunk. Personally, I can't wait til these guys make a sequel or DLC or something to expand upon the game.

Ever wondered if you could play a game that would give you a "Super Mario Bros." vibe, introduce some of the best platformer video game features, and still have new things to offer you?  Well if I had to say it, that game would be Super Meat Boy!  It recycles the common storyline of some retro video games: main character's girl gets kidnapped by some big bad guy, and you got to save her!  There are PLENTY of levels to explore, the difficulty quickly changes after you learn the basics, and many secrets and unlockables are to be discovered.  You get to constantly run around and wall-jump, while avoiding obstacles and pitfalls that would result in your death.  Of course every time you make a mistake it pisses you off, but the gameplay is so much fun that you WANT to keep trying just so you can get to the end.
All I can say is that the game is much better than it sounds and contains humor, so it is one you can enjoy either way!  If you like platformers, then you must play this!

HITMAN™ is a great game, it's a refreshing take on the Hitman franchise after the mediocre disappointment Absolution was, and it definitely brought back the feeling of sandbox assassinations that Blood Money captured so perfectly into the year of 2016; while still feeling like a graphical and technical upgrade to the franchise. It makes me feel giddy just seeing the mission planning  feature making a return after so long, and performing various methods assassinations really feels satisfying, and playing it feels amazing overall, although not perfect, it's definitely one of the better ones out there compared to other games in 2016.
Personally, I've not really paid mind to this entire episodic thing people's been ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ their pants on, I was sceptical, but Sapienza and Sanguine feels like a genuine Hitman level; It gives you targets, puts you in the map, go figure it out; and both are really good in my opinion, vibrant with life and chatter, without feeling too excessive, and eavesdropping on npcs gives you a greater intrigue and general knowledge on what is really going on behind the scenes without needing to shove it forward to your face (or just throw a coin and shoot them in the back).
However, it's undeniable that the game is ridden with bugs and glitches, both ranging from silly to frustrating ones, and the game seems to break its own immersion for players at every turn (Not neccessarily making it a horrible game), like moments where the AI seems to fail at understanding the concept of mirrors.
AI in the game seems very straightforward, they ignore explosions and prefer investigating the sound of coins in a giant ballroom full of chatter and noise, and makes it fairly easy to exploit given enough patience (Just throw a coin behind a corner until everyone in the map is subdued). Most of them don't seem to have any awareness that someone's been murdered and acts very unnaturally if you'd bother to follow them, guards stare at the corpse for a whooping 10 seconds, and then bags the body to the garage never to be spoken of ever again, while other npcs suffer from momentary ptsd before returning to cleaning the walls, and life proceeds as normal (wtf); however to give credit where credit is due, the targets do have extra interactions if one is killed after or before another, and seeing that was kinda cool, although I don't get why no one gives a ♥♥♥♥ or concern that a killer is loose after the phonecall.
Bugs and glitches range from subdues resulting in killing npcs, and npcs being able to see me through walls (bathroom walls in specific for some reasons ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)), resulting in me having to reload over and over again only to meet the same issue everytime.
Elusive targets are weirdly scarce but enjoyable, having more than one in each map/locations would definitely be a treat for players, to justify the punishing permadeath mechanics it has, and so far it's been something worth going back to check out for with the extra lines of dialogue and challenge.
It's also very concerning that HITMAN™ opts for an always online DRM system, where I assume is used to combat piracy and the sorts, but then I also figured denuvo should've already had that covered, so why have it? It isn't fun to waste a couple minutes spamming that refresh button just because a connection couldn't be established to the Hitman servers, and I've noticed that going offline means that you're literally cut off from Contracts, Mission Planning, and features that really shouldn't need an online connection, and this is where my concern comes in, purely speculatively, as of current, I've been able to enjoy Blood Money until to this moment to its full extent without having to deal with any online restrictions, what about Hitman™ say, 20 years to the future? Will the servers be shut down? Will we be left with an empty husk that is the 'Offline Mode' of HITMAN™?
All in all, if you're not a super-fan of the franchise, don't get it unless it's on a sale or something while the episodes are still in the making, buy it once it's fully out (all seven episodes).
Also, its episodic, so who knows if I'll change the review once the hitman season is done ayy

The way that Call of Duty has been going these days, I was not expecting much with this game. However, I was pleasantly surprised by this Call of Duty outing.
Call of Duty games of late have not been very variable. The campaigns have been basically mission after mission of shooting into huge crowds of enemies while trying not to be killed, and the multiplayer's just been the same over and over again, but with minor changes. With Black Ops 2, however, this has changed slightly, and for the better. The campaign does have its fair share of shooting and running and craziness, but there's also some stealth elements mixed in there, as well as some interesting new mechanics, for example the Millimeter Scanner which can detect cloaked enemies, and the real-time strategy-esque"Strike Force" missions. This, on top of a surprisingly good storyline, helps to breathe a little new life into the ageing Call of Duty series.
The multiplayer's had some changes as well - Whilst retaining the gameplay of previous games, new weapons and attachments make the game just a bit more interesting. In addition, the Create-a-Class menu has been completely reworked, now allowing players to select more than one attachment by default, as well as the new Wildcards, taking some of the Perks from previous games and reworking them.
All of this makes Call of Duty: Black Ops 2 one of the better Call of Duty games, up there with Modern Warfare. If you're going to play any Call of Duty game, this game is not a bad choice.

Max Payne is perhaps one of the greatest third person shooters of all time if not the best. The game plays just as perfectly as it did when it came out and has a stellar story told through something like a comic strip and through the enviroment. I can confidently say there is not a dull moment through the entire campaign, and wholeheartedly reccomend playing this all the way through.

Make no mistake about
, this classic from 2001 allows you to jump around in slow-motion dodging mobster, mercenary, and secret agent bullets.
follows the story of, well, Max Payne - your New York cop framed for murder by the higher-ups. His story is told through noir-style comic strips with chilling narration from Max himself (which i love, his metaphors and way of narration is awesome. Hell, for some reason, my brain keeps repeating his first line in the introduction ala
). The game atmosphere also fits well with Max's story - cold, quiet, weather fit to unleash wrath as he's got nothing to lose. Sure you can say the graphics are bad, the levels are lackluster and too closed, but once you play it the story will help you forget about those and you'll have a fun experience.
What's more awesome is that it looked like the developers had fun making it; just look at the enemy's faces and remarks, some faces in the comic, hell, even Max's face himself (Who can say no to that face?). There's even this
part that i found funny in such a seriously-themed game.
Nonetheless, all games have their own cons. The biggest problem with this game is its age and compatibility. It won't run well in modern operating systems as expected with old games (Vista and above), but thankfully there are experienced people who have provided fixes for it when the developers never bothered to release any.
In conclusion, if you like a nice noir-themed story taking place in a cold winter night driven by slow-motion action.
is the game for you.

There are PLENTY of levels to explore, the difficulty quickly changes after you learn the basics, and many secrets and unlockables are to be discovered.  You get to constantly run around and wall-jump, while avoiding obstacles and pitfalls that would result in your death.  Of course every time you make a mistake it pisses you off, but the gameplay is so much fun that you WANT to keep trying just so you can get to the end.
All I can say is that the game is much better than it sounds and contains humor, so it is one you can enjoy either way!  If you like platformers, then you must play this!

I was sold from the video, it looks great. Minecraft with guns and a grappling hook! Like Just Cause 2 in Minecraft. What's not to love?
It is like Minecraft with guns made in Java. Before the developer was done with this game, he was already hyping up the sequil. This is great for a first time developer. It is a simple Minecraft with guns. The guns work well enough, the enemies are giant and easy to hit. When you die, that's it. You crash back to the launcher. Speaking of the launcher, that's the only way to adjust the settings. Including controls. This is probably the 2nd worst button configuration I've ever seen. You select what the key does, then you find the key from a drop down list. When you set a key, chances are it unsets another key that has nothing to do with the key you just set. Such as if I set something to use the 'Right Key' then I set something to the 'Enter Key' it will set the previous 'Right Key' to the 'F2 Key.' Huh? Again, this is clearly someone's first game.
With all that being said, the game generates a random world and yet always starts you suspended high above the ground in orbit, suspended. When you find out the gravity button to drop you from the sky you might die on impact. It is quite unforgiving. If you survive the fall through the use of the gravity button, you're immediately in hostile territory. Sometimes the floating red monsters will murder you before you even land. From the start, the guns are underpowered. When you run out of ammo, you start losing health when you shoot. An understanding of enemy levels would have been nice, such as a beginner enemy should take one or two bullets. Then as you progress they take more bullets and then you find better guns or upgrade so they take less bullets.
The only redeeming factor about this game is multi-player, but really, if you're playing with friends any game will be fun, because you and your friends will always have fun. That's why they're your friends.
There are far better FPS games, which this is a FPS. I can't even call it Minecraft, since there's not much crafting or world craftability as there is with Minecraft. I just can't recommend this game. It is also very telling when a game took so long to be Greenlit.

Having played the first two games to death, I looked forward to another Arkham game, even though I'd already heard this game was inferior to the first two.
Pros:
*It's the goddamn Batman!
*Game combat is basically as good as previous games (less the cons I'll describe later).
*New enemy types
*Interesting cinematic fights - especially Deathstroke
*Decent, albeit standard Batman storyline
*Detective mode got a major upgrade, making it a lot more interesting
Cons:
* Glitchy - and I mean annoyingly glitchy! From menu glitches that took me a while to get rid of, combat glitches (counter signs that don't do anything, this mainly happens with the new enemy types), flight glitches (random mid air spasms that require falling and reactivating glide to continue), grappling glitches (randomly not being able to grapple to obviously usable spots)
* Annoying camera - okay, in some of the fights the camera actually comes through, offering a different feel than the previous games. However, in some circumstances, it is far from appealing (the Mad Hatter level is supposed to slightly replicate the Scarecrow levels of the previous games, but the camera and movement controls are absolutely horrible).
*Barely any new animations - some of the animations have quite literally been copied from previous games, and it feels like there haven't been any noteworthy, new animations added to the mix. Add in the fact that some of them glitch when they never did in the previous games, and you can see why it is a bad thing...
So in the end, a decent game, but if you've already played the first two, this one is worth a skip. At least until they fully correct the glitching (which I do not see happening any time soon)

Heart of Crown is probably most easily compared to Dominion, and you will grasp the basic concepts easily if you've played that beforehand. It is however not fair to say that it's just a copy, HoC does enough original stuff to stand on it's own two legs, and DBG's are a genre I would love to see more of on steam.
The artwork is nice and bright, the music is serviceable and it's one of those "Gotta like the genre to like the game" type of things. The biggest surprise is that the AI actually performs nicely. Most games like this barely provide "Drooling Moron-Bot" for their CPU Matches, HoC actually put some work into their Bots, and I still consistently enjoy playing against them. They play about ten times quicker than your average player, for starters.
As far as Bang for your Buck goes, card variety could def. be bigger. Counting my time played Offline I got about 10 hours in and I think the game could profit massively from some Expansions and greater variety. Playing with a random Lineup is still fun, but I wont be for long for anyone looking to really sink his teeth into it.
The Tutorial is also implemented badly, in my opinion. I've played a good few DBG's in my time, and thus adjusted quickly. But any new player unfamiliar with the genre is liable to get completely lost. Especially because the Setup is set to "Beginner" instead of "First Game" the first time you boot it up. Devs should probably take a look at that, maybe make it accessible without having to play on the side.
Another gripe, the "Campaign", which you will have to be generous to accept as such, consists of drawing random Scenarios presented Visual Novel-Style. That by itself is cute, and I was actually curious on getting some more background-Lore. But for some reason you are limited to drawing a card per day, even tough I usually get enough points for buying 4-5 just from playing an hour or two. There is zero reason to do that, unless it's just blatant padding of conent, in which case: Don't do that please.

HITMAN™ is a great game, it's a refreshing take on the Hitman franchise after the mediocre disappointment Absolution was, and it definitely brought back the feeling of sandbox assassinations that Blood Money captured so perfectly into the year of 2016; while still feeling like a graphical and technical upgrade to the franchise. It makes me feel giddy just seeing the mission planning  feature making a return after so long, and performing various methods assassinations really feels satisfying, and playing it feels amazing overall, although not perfect, it's definitely one of the better ones out there compared to other games in 2016.
Personally, I've not really paid mind to this entire episodic thing people's been ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ their pants on, I was sceptical, but Sapienza and Sanguine feels like a genuine Hitman level; It gives you targets, puts you in the map, go figure it out; and both are really good in my opinion, vibrant with life and chatter, without feeling too excessive, and eavesdropping on npcs gives you a greater intrigue and general knowledge on what is really going on behind the scenes without needing to shove it forward to your face (or just throw a coin and shoot them in the back).
However, it's undeniable that the game is ridden with bugs and glitches, both ranging from silly to frustrating ones, and the game seems to break its own immersion for players at every turn (Not neccessarily making it a horrible game), like moments where the AI seems to fail at understanding the concept of mirrors.
AI in the game seems very straightforward, they ignore explosions and prefer investigating the sound of coins in a giant ballroom full of chatter and noise, and makes it fairly easy to exploit given enough patience (Just throw a coin behind a corner until everyone in the map is subdued). Most of them don't seem to have any awareness that someone's been murdered and acts very unnaturally if you'd bother to follow them, guards stare at the corpse for a whooping 10 seconds, and then bags the body to the garage never to be spoken of ever again, while other npcs suffer from momentary ptsd before returning to cleaning the walls, and life proceeds as normal (wtf); however to give credit where credit is due, the targets do have extra interactions if one is killed after or before another, and seeing that was kinda cool, although I don't get why no one gives a ♥♥♥♥ or concern that a killer is loose after the phonecall.
Bugs and glitches range from subdues resulting in killing npcs, and npcs being able to see me through walls (bathroom walls in specific for some reasons ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)), resulting in me having to reload over and over again only to meet the same issue everytime.
Elusive targets are weirdly scarce but enjoyable, having more than one in each map/locations would definitely be a treat for players, to justify the punishing permadeath mechanics it has, and so far it's been something worth going back to check out for with the extra lines of dialogue and challenge.
It's also very concerning that HITMAN™ opts for an always online DRM system, where I assume is used to combat piracy and the sorts, but then I also figured denuvo should've already had that covered, so why have it? It isn't fun to waste a couple minutes spamming that refresh button just because a connection couldn't be established to the Hitman servers, and I've noticed that going offline means that you're literally cut off from Contracts, Mission Planning, and features that really shouldn't need an online connection, and this is where my concern comes in, purely speculatively, as of current, I've been able to enjoy Blood Money until to this moment to its full extent without having to deal with any online restrictions, what about Hitman™ say, 20 years to the future? Will the servers be shut down? Will we be left with an empty husk that is the 'Offline Mode' of HITMAN™?
All in all, if you're not a super-fan of the franchise, don't get it unless it's on a sale or something while the episodes are still in the making, buy it once it's fully out (all seven episodes).
Also, its episodic, so who knows if I'll change the review once the hitman season is done ayy

If this review had a title, it would probably be "I liked it BUT".
What actually is in the game is good or great. The storyline is great, the companions are decent (except Erritis who's great), the fights are few but each of them has at least a little quirk (and at least they don't suffer from the RTWP plague), the setting is interesting, the choices are enough to keep things interesting but not so many that they lose weight.

Are you expecting something as wide, deep and revolutionary as the first Torment game? You're going to be sorely disappointed. There *are* things in this game that wouldn't feel out of place in its predecessor, they're just too few.
Are you just expecting a good small-ish RPG, with above-average writing and mechanics that at least don't get in the way of the story (looking at you, Pillars of Eternity, I love you but your battles are made of annoyance and boredom)? Then you might enjoy this.

Easily the best game I've played so far this year, but I have those opinions you get when you like something recognizably flawed.
For a 'spiritual sequel', this game is actually at its best when it forgets to be the distant progeny of Planescape: Torment and explores its own vast, colorful world. The Last Castoff's personal conflict with their past was a dim shadow of the Nameless One's, but the potential conflict with the world, lingering at the edges of the game, was by far the greater.
I feel like the Ninth World was meant for a game that truly fits the word 'epic'. I'd really like to see this setting in particular, and the loving way in which it saturated the gameplay, on a grander scale.
Like, I get what it was trying to do, with the whole quest of self-discovery, that's all very 'Torment'. I liked it for that, but I wasn't surprised when it didn't quite capture the intimate, personal feel that PS:T had. It had one-off NPC's that were more interesting than half the major characters. Vendor trash that was more interesting than artifacts. The game was flavorful to the extreme, but that flavor itself was often at cross-purposes with its stated narrative goal.
This was mainly a game about people dealing with a precursor, a history, that was innately unsympathetic, even hostile, to them, and trying to find a way to make that harmful past serve their future. It was a good metaphor for the Ninth World itself, what with folks poking through the garbage of great ancient civilizations for useful junk, but the whole feel of that was sort of muddled by the end, because, well, spoilers, but also because the devs themselves seemed to forget that treating the characters like set pieces defies the message they were ham-handedly trying to send.
tldr: Beautifully-written, organic world. Rich characters. Slightly stilted 'themes'. Play it.

Torment: Tides of Numenera is the long awaited spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment. After a successful kickstarter campaign, and several delays, the game is finally out. But how well does it hold up?
What sets Torment apart from most other CRPGs is the amount of reading you have to do. There's not a whole lot of combat in this game, and what is in there can usually be avoided through dialogue or skillchecks.
Torment tries to emulate the look of the old infinity engine games, but with a more modern coat of paint. The result are some beautiful, and very imaginative looking environments, that look both familiar, and unlike anything I've seen in another game. The art style is consistently strong, and the environments are varied. From the sky docks of the city, that evokes a fantasy/steampunk feeling, to the fleshy interior of the Bloom, there's a lot to like about the environments.
Sadly the character models don't fare as well. While they are not hideous, they do look dated, with a low polygon count, and relatively stiff poses. It's not something that really distracts from the game, but they could still have been done better. The humanoid models are also visually uninteresting, with little that really stands out about them. Where the game that inspired this had a large cast of very distinct looking characters, here they mostly look the same. Non-humanoid characters do fare better, and there are a couple of interesting looking creatures in this game, but once again, the quality of the character models do disappoint a bit.
There's not a whole lot to say about the sound in Torment. The music works as background music, and often feels directly inspired by that of Planescape, but after having played the game, there are no tracks that really stick out in my mind. The voice acting is overall not bad, but not spectacular either. Most of the dialogue is not voiced, but what is voiced does the job well enough.
This is where Torment shines. The game is, as previously mentioned, set in the Numenera setting. The setting offers a mix between fantasy & sci-fi, but in a more coherent and logical way than games like Wizardry or Might & Magic. There are remains of ancient high-standing civilizations everywhere, with younger civilizations building on top of older. This means that during play, you run into both fantastical beasts, and robots, ancient constructs, and modern architecture. It's an interesting setting, one I wish to explore further after having played through the game.
In terms of story, you start the game falling from the sky. You're not sure why, who you are, or where you've landed. Unlike classic amnesia stories, there's a reason for this that makes perfect sense in setting. You're the creation of a god, or are you the god reborn in a new body? You're not sure, but as you move through the world you find out more about this god, about the struggle it faces, and about its conflict with its children. I'm not going to spoil it further, but it's a mostly well told story, although it ends up feeling rushed towards the end. The main story also ends up feeling a bit too linear, and once you've left an area, you can never go back. The way the progression is structured, the game world actually ends up feeling really small.
Like many other CRPGs of this type, there are also plenty of side quests to be done, many smaller stories that are being told around you, and that you can influence. There are no rats in the basement quests in this game, or go and deliver this box of cupcakes to that person, all the quests have their own stories, that are generally well written and interesting. There are also several different ways to solve most quests. You might talk your way through them, fight your way, use specific objects in the world, or a combination of the above. And they often have different outcomes that sometimes end up haunting you further into the game.
Each of your companions also have their own quests, and a large amount of dialogue, that lets you learn more about them. This is against quite well written, but I do feel that some companions are far more interesting than others. None of the ones I've used have been boring, but some could have used a bit more work. Still, if you're the kind of person who loves to get to know your party members, Torment has you covered. Sadly Planescape does trounce Torment: Tides of Numenera quite soundly when it comes to party members. There are more of them, and they are also more interesting.
There's a lively debate surrounding this game's predecessor, about what counts as gameplay. Just the combat, or does the dialogue choices you make also count as gameplay? Depending on which side of the line you fall on, Torment either has very little gameplay, or still a fare amount of it. There are a lot of dialogue choices to be made in Torment, and they can have wide-ranging consequences.
One system that I really liked from Torment is the "efforts" system. When you're performing a task that requires a skillcheck, you've got a base chance based on your skills & stats, and then you can spend "efforts" into improving your odds of success. These efforts are treated like a resource that replenishes  when you rest, and it's a really nice system, which allows you to be the judge of what skill checks you think it's important to succeed in. Efforts come in 3 categories, might, speed & intelligence, and each character has its own pool of efforts to spend from these categories. I did find intelligence to be the far superior category to build my character around though, as there are more skill checks that requires intelligence than there are from the other categories.
As you level up you can also gain "edge" which gives you free efforts to spend in each skillcheck. So basically if you were to make an intelligence skill check and have 2 in edge for intelligence, you've already got 2 free efforts spent in each skill check  using intelligence. This is both a nice idea, allowing you to become noticeably better through the game, and almost gamebreaking, as you've got so much edge towards the late game that running out of efforts becomes a non-issue.
Combat is the game's weakest point. It uses a turnbased system that feels like something out of a pen & paper RPG. The efforts/edge system is in use here as well, and it works well enough, but sadly none of the combat encounters feel very well designed, and the slow animation speed makes them drag on for longer than they should. You're also never given enough options for it to feel really tactical.
I'm a bit torn on Torment. On the one hand, the writing is great, the story is interesting, the setting hints at something amazing, I like the dialogue system and the effort system but on the other hand, the game feels too linear and towards the end rushed. The combat system also feels underdeveloped, though luckily you can easily avoid most combat. Despite numerous delays, the game still feels like it could have used some more time in development.
Do I recommend Torment? Yes, I do, if you enjoy dialogue heavy CRPGs, but it's not a glowing recommendation. The game has some very strong point, but also some weaker points that holds it back from greatness. But if you've already played Planescape: Torment & Pillars of Eternity, and want to play another party-baed CRPG, Torment: Tides of Numenera is not a bad choice. Just don't expect it to be as good as Planescape: Torment.

Max Payne is an interesting mix of action, shooting, and Film Noir. It's these three components that I'd say are most obvious about the game, and they make it a joy to play even to this day.
The gameplay is pretty barebones. You can move, jump, roll, dive, heal, crouch (I guess), and shoot. But there is a decent selection of weaponry to choose from that are unlocked as you progress. They can all be boiled down into main classes: Melee, Pistols, Fully-Auto, Shotguns, Explosives, and Sniper; pretty standard stuff. They all have their uses, so you will likely be switching between them during combat which keeps things hectic. It's executed quite well all things considered, and it's certainly still a lot of fun to mow down enemies despite its simplicity.
Also, the game has bullet-time, a mechanic where when you dive the game slows down and allows you to shoot enemies before they can properly react. It was probably a unique addition back when this game came out, and it is of course really useful, but it does feel a bit clunky when you land and have to wait for Max to pick himself back up. You will likely die if there is still an enemy left during this, but thankfully any deaths can be quickly forgotten by quick-saving (which I
recommend you use at all points as you will die a lot).
The story was pretty enjoyable. It's ultimately a revenge ploy for Max, but the way it is presented through these comic book-style cutscenes along with some great voice-acting definitely works in its favour. It never feels intrusive, rather it feels complementary as they are nice breaks in-between the shooting. That and the derelict atmosphere the game has --
a dangerous snow-ridden NYC that only gets covered in more snow, turning the city into a cold, black-and-white warzone -- really adds to the Film Noir aspect of it, too. There are some nightmare sequences as well, which while they did not have that much of an effect on me can still be disturbing to some.
I did really enjoy this game, and I did only beat it in 2017 so it certainly passes the test of time there. I can only imagine how great this game must have been at the time it came out, it was an early third-person shooter that potentially popularised the bullet-time mechanic and delivered a perfect mix of story and action. If I were to point something out with the PC version however, there was an audio issue on Windows 7 (and presumably any other OS past that) that required an unofficial patch to fix. But yeah, this one is worth playing.

The only problem is that there's a sound bug that cuts the sound from every cutscenes in the game and distorts every other sound like gunshots and footsteps
There's a sound fix, but you'll have to find it if you want to enjoy this otherwise great game.

After a couple of hours I feel like I can write a decent initial review.
I really like the concept of this game. Starting naked with a rock and torch is a cool idea. I like the idea of having to find (or make) food and clothes, gather resources, hunt, make fire, and fight off other people. The progression seems intuitive and it doesn't take ages (most of the time) to get anything done.
I still haven't figured out for sure if there are different settings in different servers, but it seems like there are (i.e. amount of "gatherable" materials, number of players allowed in the server, maybe the size of the map). The graphics are very good and I haven't seen too many graphical anomalies.
I do have some criticisms, though. The game feels too focused on fighting other players for all of the other things one can do. It seems a bit unbalanced. I expected more crafting, gathering, surviving, and exploring than i did fighting other players, but it seems that player vs. player is the focus. If that is nor the intended focus then I think they have more work to do. If it is the intended focus, then it is still unbalanced; A player who just starts (naked with a rock) can immediately die if a person with a gun and armor decides to hunt them down. Granted, the person with the gun and armor has been alive long enough to craft those items, however it still feels quite unbalanced and, at times, not fun.
Overall, I like this game. Personally, I feel that they should pull back slightly on the player vs. player. I understand this is part of the game and it's fine, but it feels too forced considering everything else that can be done in the game.

If you've played the likes of Dominion, Ascension or Star Realms you'll feel right at home with this game. If you've played/own Tanto Cuore, you'll be right at home with the mix of aesthetics and gameplay. If you aren't familiar with any of that... well good luck to you, the tutorial is pretty rubbish. However the game is pretty easy to pick up, just a little confusing to look at. 'Campaign' isn't any sort of gameplay, just a way to unlock cards. There's no story or development here, just a core game with an anime artstyle.
Dominion is very much what I'd compare it to, not only for the deckbuilding, but for the slightly flavourless feel to it... it's neither good or bad as such, and the more advanced cards add a bit more to it. Star Realms is a bit more fun. Ascension has more randomness, which makes the games more interesting.
But there's a reason that Dominion is the most widely played deck building game, and that's because it's easy to both pick up with the easier cards, and develop through to the more complicated ones, there's strategy in picking the right combinations, of knowing when to focus on building your engine, when to mess with other players, and when it's worth switching to going for the victory condition, and the princesses are a nice little touch with their special effects.
So all in all, I like the game well enough, but don't love it.

Recommended for those are into deck- building card game, waifus and multiplayer challenges.

1. Game Mechanics : using only mouse in this game making this easy to control. About the gameplay, many fellow HoC gamers said it resembles Dominion so if you're familiar with it, this game might have the same system. As for me, these kind of games is pretty fresh and new, so the learning curve is quite gradual (practice makes faster to understand). The game offers 15-30 minutes of game each session (assumed the CPU think is set to fast and we as a player think as fast the CPU).
2. Visuals : anime- style waifus are pretty much eye candy. Too bad there are only 7 (yet) to choose with. The interface and layout of the game is neat and beginner- friendly. There is also a downside, that the game is better in windowed mode (not in fullscreen as it will be blurred by a bit).
3. Sounds : while yes, a digitalized version of a card game will be enhanced by matching sound effect, it's nothing too special. There is a less- known feature that is we could add custom BGM in the game local folder. Is there any possibilities for voice acting of the princesses? That will add up some fun.
4. Story : the only "story" you could get is via obtaining random card in Campaign Mode. Basically, we must earn points to unlock each random card. This system either makes me motivated to play more and sometimes makes me disappointed for the "story" unlocked content after trying so hard to obtain points is so brief.
5. Replayability Value : you could replay the game until you're bored. So good luck with achieving all the Steam Achievements before you got bored ^^.
6. Fun Factor : the fresh game mechanics of the game is still amuse me until now (even with so much losses to the Weak CPU). The nice graphic is very much entertaining all the time.
7. Value for Full Price : to support the great developers out there, why not? I buy this game because it was ranked pretty good for a card game but I have a hard time playing board game irl so digital version is the compensation for that. Imagine that you don't have to spend extra time to shuffle card nor to place each card based on their layout and especially not to have calculate the points ourselves. While yes, that's the charm of board game but I prefer something easier to have fun.
8. Others : This game will be pretty stressing if you expect for victory each time you play. Instead try to discover ways to obtain Succession Points with different card or different princesses.

The story for me was "meh", The Joker took over the plot ,as he always does, and most of the other villans are the minor ones who aren't popular. I'm not saying lesser known villans are a bad thing, but most of them aren't popular for a reason. Then the fact the game is a prequel. BMAC lost all it's momentum when they made a prequel, they could have easily brought a strong sequel instead, they didn't need to bring the Joker back, what about Hush and Scarecrow they had instances in BMAC that forshadowed them coming back. The only thing that stuck out for me was "I am the Night" mode, because of the tension of knowing that your save is lost when you die. Outside the obvious differences the the game is a copy of BMAC, that being said, the game is still good and fun, but i can only recommend if you played the heck out of the games before it and want more Arkham. This game is sweet, funny, charming and generally lovely. It's not, however, a flawless experience. (Although I haven't experienced the masses of bugs some reviews speak of, thankfully!)
I can't claim to be the most experienced with dating sims and I don't know how many of my likes and dislikes of the game are common to the genre, but I liked that you could design your "dadsona"- although it felt like a lot of the options for certain features were jarring and stylistically didn't fit at all with the rest of the game. (Especially the eyes!) It's still far preferable, in my opinion, to having a player character who looks like Mr Blandity Blandness- and despite giving you that freedom in appearance, the player's character isn't a blank slate, so his personality comes across, which I also like. It does give you a lot less control in how he reacts, but the result is a more interesting character in my opinion.
The characters are varied and compelling. The "dates" are often more about getting to know them- which does make it feel like a more mature relationship forming rather than a helter-skelter hormone-fuelled lust frenzy, but at the same time it sometimes results in the relationship feeling a little underdeveloped. An additional date for each character would go a long way towards helping with that.
It's also a little disappointing that you can't really get any sort of more interesting ending with any character other than the one you pursue, other than a line or two of recognition (if that!) that you've spent more time with them.
Overall, I consider it well worth the time and money- but I can't blame others for disagreeing, if they consider those flaws to be too much of a drawback.
Plus, I got to play as a dad! Dating other dads! That alone made it more compelling to me.

Let me preface this by saying I have been playing tycoon style games for a long time and rarely do game in this style reach epic level, but I'm happy to add this game to the list.
When you first look at this game the graphics might turn you off, but don't be fooled. This game is in the top 3 of this style of game play. For me it doesn't get much better. So let's get real and talk about this game.
For starters this game was in early access for a long time. The early version was plagued by lots of little quirky bugs, some of which still happen once in a while. But this has always been part of its charm. The game has a campaign mode whichacts as kind of a tutorial as you play and learn the mechanics of the game. You don't really need to play it as you can go right in and build a prison from scratch but the campaign is loads of fun.
What sets this game apart from other tycoon games is that very often in this game you get attached to all your prisoners, watching them do their thing, wanting them to better themselves, learn a skill, maybe get their diploma, or kick drugs and alcohol for good. You genuinely want to build something that your prisoners enjoy.
Don't get me wrong, its still a prison, but at times it feels like doing the right thing and giving your prisoners the amenities will get them that much closer to being a useful part of society when they get out.
And of course if you want to be a hardass you can do that too, building smaller cells, adding an electric chair, forcing them into making you money via license plates.
Let's talk about the things I love:
+ Graphics, although not perfect, its all part of the charm.
+ Tons of management options. You have the ability to decide every aspect of how your prison runs, whether its a supermax or a prison paradise, its all up to you.
+ Super easy to learn: Although anyone can start playing this game and do fairly well there is nothing boring about it. The sheer volume of content available allows you to build multiple systems across many different saves, or even within the same prison. And it never becomes tedious, it remains enjoyable 5+ hours in, 20+ hours in, 60+ hours in.
+ The steam workshop ability to mod this game adds even more to an already complete experience.
A few of the things I do not like:
- The game still has a few bugs that make it annoying at times. For example during the campaign when you are ready to complete a scenario you click on a polaroid to end it, however in the last scenario of the campaign I found a bug where if you expand your prison the location of the polaroid moves. Depending on the size of your prison it can be very hard to find meaning you cannot end it. As of the time of writing this review, I still have not been able to find the polaroid.
- The remote door/servo system is a little weak and complicated which means in any prison I make I never use it. Also there are weird issues with debris that actually really anger me a little. You will find that when you destroy a wall or something that debris can be left behind and if its near a door, you are screwed.
I could probably list a lot of bugs as the primary reasons I dislike it, but even with all of those things its a pretty solid game. As I said with the amount of content built into this game you expect there are going to be some things that still do not work. I just wish the developers would find all these little things and zap them. For that reason alone I could never give this game a perfect score, but it comes close.
If you can get past these types of annoyances you have a solid game here with endless replay value. I find myself playing this game and losing all track of time. It's not uncommon to be playing for 10+ hours at a time.
My final score on this game is a 8/10. I wanted to give it a 9 or 10 score but because of the few really almost game breaking bugs like debris doors which would let any prisoner escape with no way to fix it, or the inability to even finish the campaign mode, in good conscience I cant give this a higher score. Provided these bugs get fixed, there is no reason why this game cant get a perfect 10/10 for me.
Even with the few problems I listed I still wholehearedly recommend you buy this game, especially if its on sale, that's a no-brainer.

Splice is a small, fun, unique puzzle game.

Splice is a wonderful, serene puzzler that resembles many of the same aspects from game flOw. The DoF driven visuals, to the level progression using interior depth, and more. Now this isn't a bad thing I would humbly say, and for a game like Splice, it works out perfectly.
The mechanics in Splice revolve around splitting various molecule/DNA strands to fit certain outlined patterns. The concept is simple, but the execution becomes quite the challenge during the mid-late game levels for sure.
I found gameplay to be quite intuitive for the most part, however a few of the mechanics for splitting became a bit confusing, and I often forgot how to do a specific splice. This led to some levels feeling extra challenging when maybe they shouldn't have.
Splice is a great game to bounce back and forth in. Jump in and tackle a few levels and then go about your day, revisiting it at a later period. It's a game that will hook you, but given the challenging nature, won't often persuade you for a marathon session (unless puzzle games are your weakness of course!)

Splice is an interesting puzzle game. It isn't groundbreaking; however, everything about it screams original. Without giving too much away (there is not an instruction manual - part of the joy is discovering how it works), the game is to arrange cell parts (?) into a set orientation by moving the pieces. Each puzzle has a set number of moves (splices) that you can make. Then to top it off, there are some puzzles that have "angelic" solutions. These are denoted by a "jingle" playing when you open them and the "Splice" logo flashing in the corner. These puzzles can be solved in less than the given number of moves for an "angelic" solution.
The first part of the game has seven sequences, with each sequence having seven strands. Forty-nine puzzles; twenty-five have angelic solutions. Then the fun really begins. There are four epilogue sequences with seven strands each. Twenty-eight more puzzles; eighteen of them angelic. These are much more complex and almost seemingly not possible. But they all can be done, and all the angelic solutions do exist.
As I said, the game is not groundbreaking but screams originality. The interface is extremely elegant and functional. It does yell out for a tablet conversion. The ambient music is fantastic. This is a great game to check out if you love puzzle games.
A very simple game with enough scientific rigor and visual beauty to bring me back in, this game is a fantastic palate cleanser and, for the microbiology fans, quite an evolutionary ride.

Metrocide is an interesting, yet simple to learn game set in a dystopian world with plenty of flavour to it. The player takes on the role of a contract killer who needs to earn money to skip town. To do so, as his or her job title implies, they take contracts to end the lives of their targets without being shot by cops, vigilantes, gang members, paranoid targets or their bodygaurds. While at this, they will need to hide the bodies to prevent the police from increasing the priority coverage of the zone they are in and they will need to kill without leaving witnesses - Or risk being hunted by police drones which eliminate criminals without any remorse or trial. This leaves oppertunities, however. Should you pull out your gun and show it to a paranoid target, the target may open fire at you first. Vigilantes will do the dirty work for you, and citizens will give your target's description to the police instead of yours. Then when they all ran, nobody will be around to identify you as the killer when you shoot back.
The mood it sets is excellent, with districts small enough that you will be able to learn the layout of them without too much time wasted going into dead ends, while being large enough that it feels like you're actually moving around and doing things. One thing I found slightly disappointing was that none of the roads and paths lead out of the districts, and it seems buildings block off every side of the map. While I understand wanting to keep the area contained, this makes it feel more game-like rather than a large city in a big world. A similar effect could have been made by police checkpoints which would not allow you to pass without travel papers - The thing you need to move on to the next zone anyway.
While I was at first worried about the top down camera not showing enough to really see what's going on, I've found it to be positioned well enough to allow you to play the game without having to worry about not being able to see enough, or seeing too much and being overwhelmed. It has something of the first few GTA games, which used a similar top-down camera, and movement feels like it handles in a similar way. The one thing that is not explained very well and needs you to look in the help files are the keys and methods to use things aside from guns and movement - I still have no idea how to properly use explosives or the hololure, and their relatively high price makes it feel like it may not be worth buying them except for extreme cases where the target has a bodyguard and does not go to quiet places for a stealthy takedown.
You start with a small pistol which needs to charge to shoot. This takes long enough that anyone with a gun can pull it out and shoot you before you can shoot them. All other items need to be unlocked over time. While this unlocking felt slow, it does help you learn to use your items one at a time. Sadly, most of these items are very expensive compared to your goal in a level, so you may just get a single gun early on and then never try the others as they are a significant investment - The unlocked pistol is 950 credits while your goal for the first zone is 2000 credits. There is simply no way to justify spending half of your goal worth in credits on a gun, and it remains a huge investment in the other zones. Only in the third zone does this seem like it may be worth buying. Prices, or maybe just the goals and your income feels like it can use a little more attention and polish.
There is apparently memory leak which leads to crashes that effect some players more than others. The developper appears to be aware of the issue and has posted that they are attempting to fix the issue. (Edit: This has been fixed, devs are pretty good)
Other small things I've found to be mild negatives were the lack of cars (Large open streets, plenty of people, no moving vehicles except the ones that fly around with minimal interaction), though it appears the third zone's large open roads are being build upon, so perhaps all cars just disappeared overnight. And the music(Fitting for the dystopian feel) in the area near some buildings being maybe a bit too loud
In the end, however, it is an interesting game with good interactions, good gameplay, and a great mood. The only thing I am worried about is the replayability. While it is interesting to be the sneaky assasin, and there are plenty of challenges and achievements to be had, I do not see much to do once you have finished the storyline and done the achievements.
My judgement on it is positive, it doesn't have the content to sell for AAA game pricing of 50 dollaridoos - but it isn't asking for that either.
It's a fair price for a good game, and has enough replay value to keep you coming back to try it again

The streets are brutal and lives seem disposable in a bleak metropolis of the future, and the only ticket out of this town is a high commodity with an even higher price. Armed at first with only a slow blaster only slightly more useful than a toaster and your wits, you'll seek out each contracted kill amongst the likes of paranoid vigilantes, loose cannon gangsters, and the buzzing drones of a totalitarian police state from above.
Metrocide is a gritty top-down trip into the dystopic streets of an open cyberpunk world of stylish minimal visuals with pulp noir flair, the city around you living and breathing with its own unique population. All of the residents of this drab environment have their own personality, their owns faults, and their own routines they carry out and you never know which of these unsuspecting people will be your next paid hit.
Contractors can be found throughout the open map each offering different hits on personalities of the city in exchange for cash, with armed and timed targets earning you more money. Money earned can then either be saved for your ticket into the next area or used on arsenal and tools that will make or break your attempted assassinations. Weapons come in a variety of shotguns, SMGs, and pistols with tools ranging from lures to distract pedestrians, jammers to disrupt police drones, and explosives to remotely cause havoc.
The action of Metrocide is steady paced and calculated, requiring a keen eye and a bit of patience. You'll watch your target carefully, following stealthily and strike at only the most opportune moments, and when you take your shot you have to take it quick. The frantic action and split-second tactical decision making here is often compared to Hotline Miami, but I feel this is done in a much more deliberately drawn out and subtle manner of stalking your prey from the undetected shadows of city alleys.
Death comes swiftly and without warning, and once you're gone you're gone for good being forced to restart as a broke hitman yet again. Jumpy vigilantes and gangsters won't hesitate to blow you away at the first sign of aggression and civilians will be quick to report you to deadly authorities who'll quickly have you on the run. This is not an easy game whatsoever, the eyes of the city constantly have the upper hand on you and through a rigorous routine of learning the streets as well as the arsenal available to you will you survive long enough to earn your blood money.
After what feels like hours of repeated deaths and failed hits on my well prepared targets I've finally survived a run long enough to scrounge up the cash to get myself a ticket out of the Downtown area. Before even meeting my first quota and leaving this first area I had earned 10 achievements, all of them related to myself dying in some horrific and unique way.
It's an extremely tough and failure ridden road getting there with loads of patience required, but in the end an incredibly satisfying feeling and an experience you'll take new skills away from for your future endeavors on the mean streets of MetroCity. Metrocide is top-down stealth action at its hardest and finest.

"Don't think, feel." These are the words one should keep in mind should they journey into the ooey-gooey meaty depths of Super Meat Boy. The challenges the game presents will seem daunting and maybe even insurmountable at first, but it's a game that is entirely about feeling as if the gamepad is an extension of your body. You don't think about those daring wall jumps between saw blades and over wide chasms, you just "feel" them. It's a game that can really only be truly enjoyed when you shut your brain off and just go with it.
You're given near-effortless control of Meat Boy to tackle the challenges in this game. It may feel foreign at first because, save for a few rare older exceptions, games don't usually provide this much precision in control and then present you with obstacles that ask you to utilize that precision. This is absolutely not a game you can blame the controls for when you die, so don't even try. You pansy.
Super Meat Boy's difficulty curve and level design are probably some of the smoothest I've seen in years. There's never any weird random spikes in difficulty or what the game is asking of you, and it flawlessly communicates new mechanics without ever resorting boring tutorials. You just always know what you need to do because the game is telling you.
It's pretty hard not to recommend a game that can feel so rewarding, satisfying, and brilliantly designed, while at the same time being packed to the brim with content. Get it.

Many reviews (and the game's marketing) focus on its credibility as a spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment, or lack thereof. For people wondering how it compares: overall, it doesn't quite reach the same level of storytelling as its ancestor. It's also significantly shorter, with my first full playthrough clocking in at about 25 hours with almost all of the sidequests completed. I completed the entire game with only two combat encounters, and, although the combat system is uniquely designed and fun when it works (it's certainly much better than the endless waves of enemies in PS:T's Baator), its frequent bugs and the very, very slow turn-based movement eventually take the fun away. Because there are so few unique locations in the game, the world also feels much smaller and somehow less memorable than that of PS:T.
Despite all this, you'll notice that I've still recommended this game. That's because, if you move away from the gigantic shadow of nostalgia that PS:T casts over it, this game is still incredibly fun, presenting a great array of dialogue options and possible actions to resolve situations. Many encounters, despite seeming linear, can actually be replayed in a vast variety of ways which have small impacts on subsequent situations in the game. I also enjoyed the stat-based system, which, although simple, fits with the overall feel of the game. Picture Baldur's Gate 2's Athkala, with all the combat replaced by stat checks and RNG, except with more depth to the NPCs and more nuanced dialogue choices and ways to resolve conflicts. If that sounds like something you'd enjoy, buy this game.
I've also seen a lot of comments about the companions. If we're comparing them to PS:T - they're more interesting than Falls-From-Grace, but none of them manage to beat Morte. Companions have many interjections and their own story arcs, although the most fleshed out companions are Erritis, Rhin, and Matkina by far. The former two are particularly memorable, and resolving their quests actually felt like it had far-reaching consequences. Their character arcs are incredibly satisfying. While the other companions also have multiple resolutions (or none) to their quests, they feel more "standard" and less reactive than the others, who actually have evolving dialogue as you discover more about them (like Dak'kon).
In conclusion, even though it was short and not as memorable as its predecessor, the overall package makes for a very good game. It suffers because it's not "great", like PS:T was. But if you play with an open mind and don't expect it to be exactly the same, you've still got a solid RPG with storyline branching, interactive companions, excellent NPCs, and very interesting and unique quests. Recommended for RPG fans.

A previous reviewer really summed it up perfectly when they suggested that if Planescape: Torment had never existed, than this game would be considered remarkable on it's own. Tides of Numenera would not exist without the original obviously, but I think it's an important point to make. This game falls in the shadow of one of the most beloved CRPG stories of all time, AND raised huge expectations from fans with the Kickstarter. So there's some baggage.
I think it's good, and you should try it if you liked it's predecessor, or if you think you otherwise fit the target audience (old-school RPG's, lots of text and story fluff). It's not as good as Planescape: Torment, but that
in my opinion. Also, let's remember that P:T wasn't exactly perfect either. Some parts of the original game were rushed and not fully fleshed out, and the combat (which is the main criticism for this game) was also not that great. Tides of Numenera does plenty of things well, and a few things that I liked even better than the original -
Things I liked-
There wasn't really anything I hated, but I have to acknowledge some flaws for the sake of creating an accurate picture. Think of these as more of a "mixed bag" list-
I hope over time people can appreciate this game more. It's not a masterpiece, but it's something different, maybe even unique. Personally, that's all I really wanted.

Less like a traditional cRPG to me and more like an isometric choose your own adventure game which happens to have pretty decent writing overall (there is a lot of a reading in this game) so if you like choose your own adventure books you will probably like this but if you go in expecting something like some of the newer cRPG's released of late like Divinity Original Sin, Wasteland 2 or Pillars of Eternity as examples then you may be slightly disappointed.
There is a lot of content the developers cut from the game which annoyed me as a backer on Kickstarter but they have promised to work on bringing as much of those things as possible with few exceptions later through free content patches so I have not dwelled on that aspect in this review. Since I have also not yet completed the game I did not delve deep into the mechanics or too much of the gameplay specifics in this review, I will update this review with that sort of information once completed it but until then this is more a general review about the game format/style, value and issues I have with it so far in my playthrough.
Combat in the game happens rarely and way to easy to avoid with little to no effort in my opinion, the stat/skill checks are very easy which makes the world feel less threatening in the sense of not on edge worrying about game over screens much and less rewarding because the game is heavily weighted in favor of you passing checks and balances to avoid most conflicts so avoiding them does not feel like much of a challenge. Normally in past cRPG's avoiding conflict was harder so when did manage to wriggle your way out of getting into fights it felt more rewarding.
It does not feel like you are in much danger most of the time and also feels like hardly anyone poses much of a threat because of how easy it is to talk your way out of most conflicts plus you tend to ressurect in your mind in most cases when die anyways with very few perma death situations. Investing in combat abilities feel somewhat redundant for most of the game so I found picking things that boost worldly knowledge and things to help pass dialogue checks a better choice overall.
I have seen others calling this game akin to a 'visual novel' but that is not an accurate description of this game and to call it that is a bit misleading since there is enough actual gameplay and action to counter that perception. The writing is good in general, the companions are interesting enough even though there is not much in the way of quests for them, the world setting/lore is very interesting plus the music is also fairly decent at times but it is not the game I hoped it would be when backed it on Kickstarter if being honest. I was expecting a high quality traditional cRPG but this is pretty much a choose your own adventure book in isometric game format.
I am pretty far into it I think but have yet to finish it so do not know if it drastically changes between now and then though I doubt it will to a large degree. Overall I would give it a 7/10 so far of which the score I give it may go up or down slightly by time I finish it. I like Wasteland 2, Divinity Original Sin and Pillars of Eternity more than this overall even if each of those have their own flaws, this one I put on par with Tyranny as it stands currently. I will likely update this review when finish it.
If you are unsure whether will like it because of how expensive it is you might want to wait till on either 33% or 50% off sale, I think it is worth at least 50% of it's current price personally so around 20-25 GBP, I do think it is a bit expensive at 35 GBP for specifically people unsure about whether will like it or not and if you are one of those people then you shold definatley avoid buying the 50 or 70 GBP versions. Obviously also take into account my valuation on things might not match how you value things but I stand by what I said for those who remain unsure about picking this game up.

It's kinda like Dominion, but a lot cuter and fun. Reminder that this is a deck-building card game, not a collectible card game. You don't have to buy packs, you already start with all the cards needed to play. You build your deck during the match.
Gameplay: Everyone starts with the same 10 cards in their deck, a couple of useless maids and some land cards. Lands give you gold which's used to buy more land or other stuff that can also give you gold or have a nice effect to annoy other people. New stuff you buy get added to your discard pile. Once your deck runs out of card, your discard pile containing the stuff you bought is shuffled and becomes your deck, this way you build your deck in-game by recycling cards, unless you banish them. Once you have enough money in your hand, you can back a princess, each with different skills, and then start giving her succession points with the backers you buy off the market (lol). You win the game by reaching 20 succession points, unless other people get to reach 20 points before your next turn. If that happens the first one to get to 30 wins.
Pros:
+ Simple and extremely fun game.
+ Short games, around 10 to 20 minutes.
+ Nice and cute, family-friendly, art.
+ Klam-Klam.
+ You can NTR other players.
Neutral: (mostly quality of life issues, nothing that makes the game bad imo)
. Can't (re)join a game after it's started (replacing cpu).
. There's no time out for turns (yet. it's being implemented), so you'll have to restart the match if someone dies while playing.
. You get immediately thrown back to the title menu after a match ends, so you can't easily replay with the same group.
Cons:
- No chat.
- It's easy to get addicted to HoC...
- You will get NTR'd by other players.

It's Dominion with the Etrian Odyssey artist drawing cute young maidens for it.
Actually, not quite. It's a deck builder (If you are unfamiliar with the term, a card game with no collectible aspect. You all start with terrible decks and use the powers on your cards to buy more cards that get shuffled into your deck to give you more abilities.). Dominion is still the grandpappy but this isn't too bad, going a more Euro direction than Ascension, Puzzle Strike, or Star Realms, its competition on Steam.
You still get cash to buy big point scoring cards, but you must buy a princess candidate first. She will take the cash cards you used to buy her. With her at your table, you have access to her special ability, you can store cards on the cash cards she took to get them out of your deck and play them on one massive turn, and you can (really, you MUST) drop off your scoring cards with her to actually get your victory points.
This is very different from the elegance of Dominion, in both good ways and bad, but above all else it is an interesting twist and deserves play. It is closer to Dominion's elegance than the other games of this type on Steam. It requires more strategy than Star Realms and Ascension (Though it lacks Ascension's sometimes crazy combos) and is much less of an intense knife fight than Puzzle Strike.
All those VN segments you see in the screenshots? Those are bonuses. A side game. There's no story campaign here. Just vs AI or Online vs. The AI is decent from a couple of plays. The segments are part of the "Campaign" which is not a story so much as a tracker to see who is winning with each princess candidate, rolled up with the ability to buy skit scenes with the characters in the game using points you accumulate from playing.
The game is solid. The variety of cards is on point (But not as incredibly generous as Ascension). The english translation is strong. It has a neat art style. I recommend it if you like card games.
EDIT: I will add online takes FOREVER because the cards are more complex than Ascension or Star Realms, and there is no asynchronous play option and absolutely no compromise is made within game logic for async options (Any time you have to involve the other players, the game comes to a halt even when it does not impact your turn until that effect is resolved. Thbe game does not do ANYTHING automatically, even a brain dead "show this so bad thing doesn't happen" requires manual input.), so you're looking at a card game that can easily take twice as long as a PUBG match with ALMOST as much boring thumb twiddling. So if you're buying this and don't want to do vs AI play or play with close friends, you may want to reconsider.
EDIT2: I'm serious I can do entire 20xx levels in the downtime between turns it's stupid.
