I just finished my first play through of Tides of Numenara. (I didn't play it during early access, seemed silly to play a partly complete story based game before it was finished)
Overall, I liked the game.
It's certainly a niche game. You have to like reading, as in full length novels type reading. Combat and character building took a massive back seat. If you play these games to level up, collect loot, and test your characters in combat, pass this game. You won't like it.
It kept the original Torment "feel". Everything is strange, weird and alien. It takes some time to get the "feel" of this strange universe. The game eases you into it by taking a page out of the original Torment, your character starts with no memory. Everything is just as strange and new to your character as it is to the player. The universe is complex, and I actually caught the game breaking it's own internal consistency at least twice. For example your character is pretty much immortal (not much of a spoiler, you find this out 2 minutes into the game), as well as other characters who belong to your characters "race", only extreme things can actually kill them, however, the game forgets about this fact at least once. (not to the main character)
One page it didn't take from the original was the lack of wacky party members. You got some crazy extreme ones in the original, (a floating scull, a succubus, a man who burns forever..) Nothing like this here. In fact I found them to be "ok". The exception to this would be Rhin. Though she is a normal human, her character differs enough the she breaks the mold from the rest. Not that the other characters you take on are all boring and dull. They all have backstories and little mysteries attached to them.
The game can be progressed in various ways. You can avoid 75% of the combat with your choices, character skills, and some luck. When you are actually in combat the in game system is passible for certain. One thing that bothered me with combat was there was no in game explanation as to what all the damage types did.  Combat was also very buggy. Certain functions just stop working and cannot be access for no in game reason and random times. This bringing me to my next point...
BUGS!!! Combat had the most of them, (stealth for example, sometimes I would not be able to select it, sometimes the menu would come up, I would have a good percentage of success, but the "ok" button would not work) If there was an in game reason for this I had no idea why it didn't work. Other abilities seemed to be prone to this. Twice the game got "stuck" on the enemies turn.  A couple times I would somehow break the combat rules and do something not allowed that usually got my character stuck and unable to end their turn. Outside of combat the game gave me issues saving, sometimes it just would not allow me to create a new save file. (thankfully "quick save" always seemed to work) Sometimes I would be unable to select anything for some reason. The only way to fix this was to save and reload. Another frustrating bug was if you look at something then shortly afterwards move to a new area, the window giving feedback gets stuck on your screen. The only way to fix this is to go back and look at the same object and allow the window to close on it's own. Had the game lock up randomly at least 5 times.
One thing I have to bring up, the game creators have a video showing a slice of the game. In this slice they show pretty much every NPC spoken to using actual spoken lines. The game has hardly any spoken lines at all when you actually play it. Worse still, once you arrive at the same slice of the game, none of the characters who spoke in the video speak any of the same lines, (it's all just text reading). I'm not sure what's up with that. I don't mind reading everything, but I don't like being tricked into thinking the game has certain features it does not.
To summarize; if you liked the original Torment, you will like this. If you like reading/story heavy RPGs, you will like this.

A really solid stealth game. The maps are significantly larger than Absolution, and other previous games. Definitely makes the game entertaining to play many times, since you can take a different approach everytime. Some approaches can become very challenging, which is also nice.
My only complaint would be the graphics, which are average yet manage to put your computer under tremendous amounts of load. I can only get about 40 FPS on a high setting, even though I can run other more demanding games on higher settings at a constant 60. There are also occasional glitches (in lighting effects), but I haven't experienced anything game-breaking e.g. light going under walls.
Last but not least, I want to address the "episodic" release of the game. Many people were complaining about it, although Square Enix announced this decision MONTHS before the game's initial release. Plus, it barely even affects gameplay and pleasure since the maps are so expansive. But I guess people will complain about anything.
In conclusion, this is a good game in need of patching and optimization.

This game was originally an iOS title, normally when you see that on a Steam review it's synonymous with a bad port and terrible gameplay, not this time. I'm not sure under what circumstances the first iteration of this game folded but I'm glad it's back and that the developers seem to be really trying to make it work this time around.
GAMEPLAY: Take chess, take football, take a little from strategy games like Blood Bowl and that's what this game is. I've been trying to get into Blood Bowl for quite some time but I find it too obscure and complicated. This has potentially a very rich tactical depth but is at the same time super easy to understand and after a couple matches you'll realize what the best strategies are (once PvP is introduce that depth will turn into a black hole of infinite posibilities). Also, it's nice because it feels like a full fledged turn based experience but every match can be played in a very short amount of time.
INTERFACE: It's super obvious this is a port from a tablet game, but the developer has said they'll eventually introduce widescreen support. Other than that, I'm not bothered at all by the app feel of the interface, it would be awesome if they launched on iOS again and you could continue your league play on the go.
OTHER: In its previous model, this game had a pay mechanic to grant you access to the best players, I never entered the PvP scene because the app crashed all the time and it was super annoying so I didn't inverst into it but that mechanic has been removed (at least until version 0.2). Oh and apparently they are working on Workshop support to personalize the content even further.
To improve until final release:
-Widescreen support
-PvP as soon as possible
-Certain minor bugs here and there (the developers seem active in correcting them though)
My wishlist:
-Local hotseat support
-The ability to play with selected teams already at the top
-Multiple save slots
TL;DR: If you like strategy games and you like football this game is the real deal. Best case scenario, you invest 13 bucks for a game that will eventually become a monster in strategy and sports gaming (the core gameplay certainly has the potential for that). Worst case scenario, the developers give up tomorrow and you invest 13 bucks in an amazing single player experience that even right now is very polished and very addicting.
It's a very fun football tactics game. I'll be very happy once they add the planned Multiplayer. It's going to be a blast. :D

It's a long review, so if you are discouraged by it - let me start with a SHORT STATEMENT ON WHY IT'S WORTH TO BUY THIS GAME:
It's fun, it's engaging, it pulls you in from the first moment, not to mention the fact that the community and devs are really great. If you like football games, if you like tactical games, if you like games that take a cool new approach to stuff we know and love: buy it! You won't regret it! :)

This game is really impressive. For the last two hours I experience a heavy case of "just... one... more... game...". Brilliant.

A beautifully crafted Puzzle game with an organic twist.
The goal of Splice is to reshape a strand of bacteria either through "splicing" = rearranging (hence the name of the game) or special feature bacteria into its ideal form (provided by the game). You go through strands in various sequences, starting from forgivingly easy to mindwreckingly hard.
Secrets inclusive! Do you have what it takes to push the boundaries even more? Angelic splicing is the key!
The visual design of the game is surprisingly astonishing with awesome animations and an overall beautiful visual design.
The piano soundtrack of the game fittingly underlines the beauty of the game, even if it can get repetitive, if you play for too long (which you will, this is a puzzle game, duh).
I deemed some of the puzzles way harder than others, some are simple realignments, some felt like thinking around 4 corners ahead (given the same difficulty level). Mixed difficulty is ok, but some puzzles who were not far away from each other, in terms of sequence, really made my head spin.
No Options within the game. You cannot turn down the volume in the game.
The tutorial section of the game falls really short and is pretty shallow, I got the hang of the game after the first sequence. If you still need help even after trying everything you could, seek help in the forums.
Beautiful game, both visually and auditory. Mixed difficulty on puzzles. Secrets and extra content inclusive. Garanteed Content for over 6 hours.
Modern DNA-Testing? 149€.  A centrifuge? 200€.
Finding out, that you can splice a strand bacteria in a Videogame without any additional tools? Priceless.
There are certain things you can buy. For everything else, there is Splice.

After a couple of hours I feel like I can write a decent initial review.
I really like the concept of this game. Starting naked with a rock and torch is a cool idea. I like the idea of having to find (or make) food and clothes, gather resources, hunt, make fire, and fight off other people. The progression seems intuitive and it doesn't take ages (most of the time) to get anything done.
I still haven't figured out for sure if there are different settings in different servers, but it seems like there are (i.e. amount of "gatherable" materials, number of players allowed in the server, maybe the size of the map). The graphics are very good and I haven't seen too many graphical anomalies.
I do have some criticisms, though. The game feels too focused on fighting other players for all of the other things one can do. It seems a bit unbalanced. I expected more crafting, gathering, surviving, and exploring than i did fighting other players, but it seems that player vs. player is the focus. If that is nor the intended focus then I think they have more work to do. If it is the intended focus, then it is still unbalanced; A player who just starts (naked with a rock) can immediately die if a person with a gun and armor decides to hunt them down. Granted, the person with the gun and armor has been alive long enough to craft those items, however it still feels quite unbalanced and, at times, not fun.
Overall, I like this game. Personally, I feel that they should pull back slightly on the player vs. player. I understand this is part of the game and it's fine, but it feels too forced considering everything else that can be done in the game.

Reviewers have compared this game to Myst, which can be misleading. This is not a modern game that is
of Myst. It is adventure game that would fit literally into in the 90's - complete with 90's technology, UI design and philosophy, and technological limitations of the era.
All games follow tropes, because they'd be incomprehensible otherwise. But Catyph uses a few fascinating themes that I like - an eerie, uncanny world with a secret to discover, and an environment to match the mood. The style is classic deep sci-fi, and it's not surprising that it's compared to Myst for these reasons. It reminds me of Arthur C. Clarke's works.
Catyph is remarkably fresh in this way - the way only small developers seem to be these days. That should be commended.
Catyph's UI is worse than early Flash-based games. The videos seem to show the character walking around the world in real-time, but it's actually a point-and-click game of still images with grainy, compressed animations between them - just like you'd find in the 90's.
The geometry of the world is impossible to figure out given the way you travel. You can click on an arrow that teleports you to another scene, but you can't tell what direction you're now facing. This makes the world feel unreal, and more like a collection of network nodes than an actual place.
Besides the fact that the designers ignored everything we've learned in the last 20 years about UX (User eXperience), they also failed to advance the genre even by 90's standards. The puzzles seems logically disconnected from the world, and while some of them are interesting, they also seem pointless. It's as if one game designer created a world and backstory, and then another came in afterward and just distributed puzzles through it without knowing anything else about it.
I've never been very tolerant of nostalgia trips, because they are almost universally disappointing. The experience you had in the 90's -- when you were 20 years younger -- cannot be duplicated. You were a different person, and lived in a world with a different set of limitations that you accepted at the time. And more importantly, you hadn't already seen it once, so you didn't have expectations.
Nevertheless, I decided to give Catyph a try, partly because the reviews seemed good overall, and partly because the premise sounded interesting.
Unfortunately, what I got was similar to grabbing an emulator and picking up an original copy of Myst, which isn't the experience I wanted.

An amazing puzzle game with a complex storyline!
But first of all, Catyph is not a game for everyone. As a sequel to ASA: a space adventure, it is a classic Myst-like or Rhem-like in terms of gameplay, but it is way much more difficult.
Clues are not directly apparent and require some very good observation skills and intuition (you need to figure out if something you see is a clue or simply just part of the surrounding world). Puzzles are very diverse as in the previous opus ASA, but are more difficult. Curiosity and perseverance are a requirement. But even then, it will still be sometimes necessary to take a look into the walkthrough...
I quite enjoyed the wide diversity offered by the exploration in the game. While exploring 6 beautiful worlds in completely different environments, you will be able to use different modes of teleportation, experience time travel, pilot a submarine robot while dodging some prehistoric creature, explore the inside of some beautiful painting…
I really had a lot of fun solving the puzzles. In fact, I became so engrossed in trying to solve them, that I completely lost track of the storyline and forgot about reading the database… After spending hours grinding my teeth on the puzzles, I realized that the storyline videos were kind of messed up since I had moved back and forth between worlds when I was stuck. Since I had not followed at all the storyline, I decided to start over, and this time, exploring each world one at a time (which I recommend), watching and reading everything.
About the storyline, the game starts with a video that was, I have to admit, kind of confusing on the first view. Watching it again later while knowing more about the game world helped.
The story takes place in a parallel world of our solar system.
You play as an astronaut who is equipped with a (super-) suit that can be controlled by a (very knowledgeable) AI named MAIDEN. A database storing all informations about the storyline and the game world, as well as a system producing blue energy (some new energy discovered after the events that occured in ASA) are integrated in the suit. This blue matter system can be used to create a shield to protect you, increase your strength, or simply emit blue energy particles to interact with objects made of dark matter. It can be recharged using blue matter wells located a bit everywhere or by playing some minigames (one located in your database and one that is found later in one of the worlds).
As part of an exploration team of planet Catyph and its moons, you travel and land by yourself on the 6th moon of Catyph where an alien construction with a huge black cube has been sighted. Approching the cube, you accidently activate a mine field surrounding it. Protected by the shield of your suit, you find yourself projected towards the cube which then teleports both of you on the 5th moon of Catyph, Tytaah, using a technology, you learned later, called the Kunci. There, you discover more alien constructions and start to investigate. After fixing a teleporter, you will be tasked to collect black dices in order to save your own planet Terra. To do this, you will have to explore the 6 differents continents (worlds) of Tytaah.
The storyline is very rich with a lot of details, but might be somewhat technically too complex for some people.
But contrary to ASA where we had to use a lot of the astronaut diary content to solve puzzles, the disappointing part here was that most of the reading content is useless to play the game. I think only three puzzles use some little information from the database. So I would say that the database is mostly destined to people who like reading and are curious to learn more about the black cube series world.
To continue the comparison to ASA, Catyph offers better graphics and a greatly improved AI. In ASA, the AI made me feel like a small kid. In Catyph, it made me feel like a scientist, telling me all kind of scientific informations about the environment. I found that kind of cool.
I would recommend playing the previous opus ASA first. Puzzles are mostly easier and it starts as a good introduction to the black cube serie and helps understand Catyph storyline better as it refers a lot to facts and characters previously introduced in ASA.
In all, I found that Catyph was an amazing game, all the more impressive as it was achieved by only one person. There are sadly so few challenging puzzle games nowadays that it really was a pleasure to play this game.
So big thanks to the developper to have brought us such a wonderful game. I am looking forward to the next opus!

Must-Have for Fans

There's a certain art in rebooting something. There's always the risk of alienating existing fans, with the potential payoff of enticing new ones. This is particularly true in franchises, and, really, financially, what are superheroes other than franchises?
It's no coincidence that the first steps of a fledgling superhero are the most memorable ones in a comic book or film. That's when the hero, upon which sometimes we project ourselves, overcomes adversity, fear, obstacles, to become what we already know he'll become by the end: a symbol. A champion. But during those first few steps, he's still, at least partly, us. And wish fulfillment of sorts makes these first few steps cathartic, not just enjoyable. That's why so many superheroes have had so many reboots over the years. At the same time, though, you risk alienating the ones already emotionally invested in it, breaking their own bonds with the character by changing their past.
Besides, that really doesn't work in video games, as a few examples showed. You don't want to take those steps for the character, you want to be able to do what he does after he's taken them. You don't to become, you want to be.
It's a good thing, then, that Arkham Origins, the newest installation on the Batman: Arkham franchise, doesn't reboot. It rewinds.
Chronologically, Origins is set roughly at the same time as 1989's Burton film, albeit in a different universe; The Batman is out there already, more of an urban legend than a staple. There's no Bat signal lore-wise, though it does double as an objective marker. Crooks are still uncertain if he even exists, and clever (but scripted) lighting tricks terrify them. The police isn't on his side either; you'll have to beat sense into dirty cops more often than not in the Pre-Commisioner Gordon GCPD. Most of the elements that make up the Batman mythos are there, though. Perhaps a more accurate name would have been Batman: Arkham Early Days rather than Origins.
This Burton/Nolan amalgam of Gotham, set on Christmas Eve, creates a rather unique and beautiful Gotham that's a pleasure to play in, though the actual game area is still relatively small, but this time so much more believable than City's rendition. Speaking of City, you'll recognize some of the areas reused in Origins, however this time the same areas mesh together better. City tried the militarized/derelict look on the same areas, but somehow the snowy, part art deco, part goth and part industrial depression look makes them feel that much fresher. This is one of the most believable urban environments you could get in a game like this. Don't be tricked, though; the story experience is as linear as it gets, but it's good enough and tricks you just the right way for you not to really pay attention to it unless you want to.
The Christmas Eve/snowstorm excuse for the practically non-existant non-hostile NPCs out in the world is something the original Max Payne used as well, but Origins doesn't just use it as an excuse, but rather as a narrative sledgehammer. It's used to emphasize the loneliness of what the Batman is doing, the isolation, the withdrawal from normality. When everyone is huddled up inside with their loved ones, the Batman doesn't rest. When you're out there solving the case and the clocks of Gotham strike twelve, a stoic but melancholic Alfred comes on your radio to wish you a Merry Christmas and all Batman can reply is a “You Too” that holds within it all the gratitude and tenderness the Dark Knight can muster for his butler, replacement father and more, you'll know what I'm talking about. The game keeps focusing on the emotional side of things throughout, presenting for the first time alternate viewpoints on events. The feels are strong in this one.
The story goes: it's the early days of Batman, and there's not that many power players in Gotham yet. The GCPD is mostly corrupt. The gangs are ruling the streets. The main gangsters are the Penguin and Black Mask, gangsters that are quickly forcing the more traditional mobsters out of the picture in favor for the masked/monickered criminal. Batman is in the middle of their turf war when the Black Mask puts a hit out on the Bat, a hit that different assassins try to make good on: Electrocutioner, Deathstroke, Copperhead, Deadshot, Bane, Firefly and Shiva (which, oddly enough, doesn't actually appear in the game). These are, as you would expect, no ordinary scraps. They all create the illusion that you really are Batman fighting these villains, not just an average protagonist. For example, the Electrocutioner, Deathstroke and Copperhead encounters are a stroke of genious. Some, however, can get annoying due to the mechanics of the encounter and the checkpoint system which reloads you again and again from the beginning of the encounter. It makes beating the encounters that much sweeter, but not 100% of gamepads will survive it.
I'm not going to spoil the story more than what the trailer already gave away, so here's my summary in words of one syllable: oh em gee. The twists, while telegraphed from early on, are nevertheless delivered pitch-perfect and with a cinematic flair that's become a staple of the Arkham games. There's quite a few characters that make their appearance, though people only aware of the game lore rather than the comic book lore might miss it, such as Barbara Gordon, aka Batgirl, aka Oracle, Vicki Vale, Harlan Quinzel aka Harleyquin, the Mad Hatter, or Edward Nigma, aka, Enigma (eventually Riddler), as well as good ol' Killer Kroc.
Gameplay-wise, though, the game doesn't “rewind”, which might annoy purists. All the gadgets from the previous games return, and there's a couple of new ones too. Batman is just as powerful as he was by the end of City, though he's supposed to be much younger and inexperienced. What you do as the Batman though is pretty much the same as you were doing before, and hey, if it works, why fix it? The game doesn't bank on gameplay innovations rather than the story and the atmosphere, and the good thing is that it works. A new -and awesome- feature is the Crime Investigation. That's every bit as sci-fi CSI as you'd expect, and study of a crime scene is where Batman finally shines as the World's Greatest Detective. Also randomly within the world gang scraps will occur that Batman can choose to resolve forcefully, which serve as random crimes other open world superhero games have introduced in the past. A new gadget is the shock gloves upgrade, which adds an electric element to your fists as a momentary powerup during fights and can also be used to power panels in the world. Also redesigned is the Line Launcher, now Remote Batclaw, which can now also tether enemies to other enemies or objects in the world.
Graphics-wise, the game is what you'd expect. The Unreal engine isn't really showing its age just yet, and the audio...oh the audio. The music fits the game perfectly, and the voice acting remains stellar throughout.
Overall, Origins is the crown jewel of the Arkham games, and considering just how good Asylum was, that's saying something. Batman fan or not, no gamer should give this a miss.

I really enjoyed this classic point-and-click game. Although it's a sequel, I don't think you need to have played ASA before this, although it certainly wouldn't hurt. The storyline is very good, with a great deal of well-conceived background, and the game's flow fits the story well. The puzzles fit nicely into the overall story; the majority are challenging, with some really tricky ones, which makes solving them particularly satisfying (although I did have to get help on occasions!). In-game help is available in easy mode and a walkthrough is now available, so there's the option of that for people who want to play in the harder modes. The artwork is great and there are some very lovely mini movies, especially at the start and end of the game. As others have said, overall it's very Myst-like, but to me that's a real compliment.
The game ran well; I had no problems with any of the features. Save worked fine and the game autosaves regularly. I did hit a problem when I missed something in one of the regions which prevented me from seeing one of the game endings. However, the developer was great and very procactive, and helped me figure it out. Having just completed that ending, I'm glad he did! I think the developer's estimated 15 hours of gameplay is a bit short if you're going to try and crack the puzzles without help (but I may just be slower than most!).
Overall, if you want huge 3D graphics, timed puzzles and/or things to fight with/kill/run away from, and hate reading, then you'd probably want to look elsewhere (although you'd be missing out!). But if you want the satisfaction of figuring out tricky puzzles within very nicely rendered environments following a detailed and interesting storyline, and especially if you're a lover of classic Myst-style games, I'd certainly recommend Catyph.

I'm going to try and elaborate on what this game is and what it delivers upon and I will not be short in my review.
In summary, the game is a beautiful stealth/infiltration game that manages to maintain the ballance between fun and frustrating. It is very well designed and offer numerous opportunities for replayability in a multitude of new ways.
The player mechanics have been greatly improved and even though, at times, it might feel slugish, the game provides a very easy way to maneuver around and do what you want to do. On behalf of the game-world, it provides an insane amount of detail with opportunities at every step to change a route and try something new.
Because of its episodic nature (which I will talk of later), every map has numerous Challenges and various 'tricks' that you must complete to unlock all assets available to 47; these make sure the player is still engaged for the duration of the whole month, before the next episode releases.
And if that weren't enough a multitude of Contracts and side missions provided by both the community and the developers are available for you to really refine your skills in the art of killing NPCs. In my opinioin these are good but are not quite as enjoyable as they should be, one of the main reasons for their unenjoyability I will speak of later.
As the missions progress, each episode reveals more of the story. It reveals a nice story that is definately going to continue in their second season. I'm really curious about the pricing, however.
The game looks astonishing. The level of detail and the precision of that detail are both unbelievable. Now. granted, you will need quite the horsepower to run this, I am running it on a GTX 760 with a Quad i5 and it runs smoothly on High graphics. Hitman has never looked so good. However, the optimisation is♥♥♥♥♥♥poor. Compared to other games having come out in the late 2016 it can also improve, as well.
Overall this game provides what it says it provides: a Hitman game. Granted it came out in this 'episodic nature' but I don't mind. It's not DLC, you can buy it all for full price. The fact that it comes out each month feels appropriate to me since it can keep you engaged for longer.
The game requires quite the skill and finesse and proves a challenge for experienced Hitman players. It is not really a gateway for new people to enter the franchise.
[update] Also the Elusive Targets can be quite an annoyance for people who have a job but really want to get that perfection out of the game...

HITMAN No Subtitle is a great game!
Season One:
Pros:
1. The gameplay is great. Brings back the open-world feel like the old games
2. Soundtrack is great!
3. Graphics are Good!
4. The maps are well designed!
5. Love the new "Opportunities" system.
6. The episodic system. I didn't like the idea of it when it first came out but when more missions and content got pushed out, I did not regret my decision. The amount of content IOI pushed out makes up for it.
Cons:
1. IOI sometimes messes up with releases of missions or updates.
Showstopper (Paris) :
The map is well designed and there are tons of ways to eliminate your targets. Your goal is to eliminate Darlia Margolis, Supermodel turned Spymaster and the mind behind IAGO, and Viktor Novikov, Ringleader of IAGO. The two are a power couple, and could potentially be one of the most dangerous people in the world. Meanwhile, an IAGO auction is going on above the fashion show. Eliminate the power couple before people get hold of a list of MI6 agents.
A World Of Tommorow (Sapienza, Italy) : The map is alright, but a bit too big for my liking, but definitely bigger than Showstopper. Your goal is to eliminate Silvio Caruso, worker for Ether, and Francesca De Santis, Scientist in charge of a project. The two are in charge of a virus being made by Ether. Destroy the virus and the two targets.
A Gilded Cage (Marrakesh, Morroco) : The map is good, but feels a little claustrophobic. Your goal is to eliminate Claus Strandberg, a banker who stole 7 billion from people of morroco and escaped from a convoy transporting him to prison. Your second target is General Zaydan, the man who was the mastermind behind the escape for Strandberg. Eliminate the two targets.
Holiday Hoarders (Paris): The map is the same but with christmas decorations. And the two targets are references to Home Alone. You might even see someone special who wears red...
Summer Bonus Missions:
The Icon (Sapienza, Italy) : It's horrible. Honestly it's very bad. The map is messy and the mansion and beach is totally BLOCKED OFF, and it requires you to keep changing outfits to enter areas. It's very annoying.
A House Built On Sand (Marrakesh, Morroco) : It's slightly better than the previous one, but it just shows that they did not put in effort. It's in night time, and has very good opportunites unlike The Icon. This was better than The Icon.
Landslide (Sapienza, Italy): Another one Sapienza... But it's better than The Icon. The Icon was very restricting, but this map is beautiful. The whole map is kept but with more decorations. Except the mansion. This has to be the best out of the three Summer Bonus Missions.
Club 27 (Bangkok) : 47 visits a hotel in Bangkok. The 2 targets are Jordan Cross and Ken Morgan. It's a fun lil map but gets boring after a while. Too small for my liking, but it has multiple storeys.
Freedom Fighters (Colorado, USA) : ONE OF THE BEST MAPS AVAILABLE. 47 heads to an abandoned farm in Colorado. I've heard many say that it gives a Blood Money vibe. I have not played BM but I'm taking their word for it. You have four targets. Sean Rose, bomb-maker. Ezra Berg, chemical interrogator. Penelope Graves, former interpol terror analyst. Lastly, Maya Parvati, former Tamil tiger turned insurgent. Eliminate the four targets and enter the tornado shelter to have an idea of who the Shadow Client is. The story really starts to pick up from here. Multiple ways to kill your targets. Poison them, snipe them, fiber wire them. Although there are 6 opportunities only (3 for Sean Rose, 3 for the each of the other 3 targets), it is still an incredible map. Once you're in, you are on enemy grounds. Watch out 47, this is a hard one. But nothing you cannot handle. The soundtrack in this map and Situs Inversus are the same, but it's amazing. Some people hate that it's a "all hostile" map, which I don't blame them. But this map is my favourite.
Situs Inversus (Hokkaido, Japan) : My second favourite map. 47 heads to a highly advanced hospital in Hokkaido. Your targets are Erich Soders and Yuki Yamakazi. The opportunites in this mission are very fun yet challenging. Most areas are restricted which forces you to change your disguise and avoiding the staff. Eliminate the targets. And that's Season 1 for you.
Professional Difficulty: If you have completed all missions and reached mastery level 20, you can switch to professional difficulty. This means, cameras, bodyguards and civilians are much more observant and agressive. Initially, I was terrified because I found the normal difficulty quite fun and challenging at the same time. But the more I played it, the more I realised that it is really fun. Well done IOI.
Soundtrack: 2 words. Bloody amazing.
Season 1 (Overall) : I enjoyed it. Most of the missions were just growing the story. I am very excited for Season 2. 8/10

Prison Architect is a very addicting sandbox game with varying levels of complexity. It is simple to build, place items and put together a simple facility. The Grants system will give you in game money for continuing to improve your prison, first with simple, necessary things like building the necessary buildings to start off, to harder ones like getting prisoners to pass education programs. I played it when it was more in early access, and now it's even more fun with the full systems. While it can seem confusing at first, it doesn't take long until you're building prisons like a pro, and the wiki that's accessible through the pause menu is VERY useful.
It's also an interesting kind of social experiment. What happens when you're put in charge of a virtual prison? Do you view the prisoners as uncontrollable animals and lock them up as much as possible, or do you do everything you can to make them comfortable and happy?
Very fun game, could probably play forver. And now, you can even try to escape from the prisons you make, which can be harder than it sounds sometimes!

Pros:
+ Good writing with interesting characters and lore.
+ Open-ended quests with lots of roleplaying opportunities.
+ Really rewards you for being thorough and gaining as much information as possible.
+ Lots of skill checks.
+ Weird and wondrous sci-fantasy setting.
+ Combat is mostly avoidable.
+ Almost every piece of loot is unique.
Cons:
- Combat, while better than PST's, is mediocre.
- Inventory is as bad as the one in PST.
- Some bugs.
- No codex (may be implemented later).
- RNG-based skill checks are and have always been inherently pointless.
- By the halfway point, you (or your party) can successfully complete any skill check, making your character build somewhat irrelevant.
If you're looking for an RPG with deep, strategic combat, look elsewhere. If you're looking for a hardcore RPG where you're forced to specialize or else end up with unviable character, look elsewhere (i.e. Age of Decadence). If you're looking for an RPG that is less about what you can do and more about what you choose to do, Torment should be right up your alley. It successfully recaptures the strengths of Planescape: Torment in providing you with plenty of interesting characters to talk to, exotic locations to explore and deep, open-ended quests to complete. As a fan of PST and interesting content in general, I'm very satisfied with Torment.

Overall a good game but nowhere close to the original "Plancescape: Torment".
The game desipite it´s only roughly 30-40 hours long campaign still a good match for the original in aspects of general playtrough (focus on story not on battles) and unfortunatly companions (P:T as combat aid, T:ToN as combat aids (minor) and skill mules (major). Aside from that they are glorified NPC´s)
The new mechanics work and fit into the story.
The overall story is also good (if short)
Despite the overall matches sofar there is however one, or rather three, big part/s that invalides the game as a successor instead of a standalone: It has nothing to do with the charactes, places or story of the first game.
Places:
As the name of the original suggest it takes place on the "Planes" more specificly the first 2/3 take place in Sigil, a place called the City of Gates (to other planes) and is filled with creatures of said planes. T:ToN on the other hands play on the "ninth world" and among other things you see at least 2 spaceships and in "flashback" one space station.
Characters:
The only character that comes from the first game is Adahn. First Game he was a fictional character that could be brought to some sort of live by telling people that it´s your name. T:TON makes it the name of the previous host of our body in the game.
Story:
The only elements of the original story that makes it into this one is that the Protagonist can´t die (with exceptions). The reasons in P:T was that we underwent a ritual to seperrate us from our mortality. The reason in T:ToN is that we were made this way as a vessel for the changing god.
Summary: Would buy again (even the Immortal Edition but that one only in a Steam Sale) but take down the "Successor of Planescape: Torment" Award. That one is undeserved. Even as a "spiritual successor".

Early Access Version 0.2 review:
Let me start by saying I am not much of a football fan at all. I mean I'll follow the world cup highlights, but that's about as far as I go. As far as gaming goes, I last seriously played Footbal Manager on Commodore 64, as later PC versions turned out just too tedious for me.
But then I came across this. And *boom*, I love football again. Well done Creoteam, really well done. Why is it so good? Because it is simple, yet deep. Easy to grasp, but will take cunning and skill to master.
First I spent an hour deciding on my club's name, fiddling with the colours and jerseys, then it plunges you straight into the competition. Only a few tabs, like the team roster with the basic pitch layout and who you want to play where, the training menu with just a couple options for each player, the buying/selling transfers one, the upgrade one and the league table and calendar. Nothing to get lost in, easy to keep all your players in mind and how to best use them in a game.
And the game? A brilliantly simple concept.  3 actions per turn when you can try to take the ball from the other team, pass it, dribble or shoot. The skill of your player vs. the skill of the opposing player will determine if you will be successful. But whenever you score a goal, you're genuinely happy, because you executed a tactic perfectly.
Even at version 0.2 the game is perfectly playable, the looks and animations are excellent for a simple-graphics game, you'll probably want to turn off the repetitive music after a half an hour, but otherwise it's great fun.

Football + Chess = Football Tactics. Played for few hours and I really enjoyed it. The depth in the game is quite good. Really makes you think twice before making a move and still can go wrong. Easy to get a grip of the game mechanices.
Deploying the right players in the right position before starting the match is crucial. Can't change tactics during the match. Also have 3 type of training; attributes, skills and talent. During the match, skills will come handy and gives bonus when the skill performed perfectly. At the same time, players need to have good attributes to pull it off perfectly and even good players make mistakes in late game since their stamina gets low and it affects their attributes. And also after the match, they only recover a bit of their stamina lost each day till the next match and at the same training uses stamina. So its up to you whether you gonna rest the player or play for the next match. Tired player = poor performance. Players also gain experience after a match and level up. Levelling up unlocks skills and talents to be trained. Also have upgrade section; stadium capacity, coaches, assistant, scouts. Like I said, the depth in the game is quite good.
The developers provided a lot features and in-depth game mechanics for an early access game. Will update my review after few more hours of gameplay. Just wanna see how the game progress.
Verdict: Highly recommended
UPDATE - 9/6/2015
-------------
After playing about 9 hours, I feel the game has a lot of potential. You can make changes to your tactics in the match but the changes will happen only after an event. Ex: after goal scored. It resets to your new tactic. As the game progress, it gets tough and feels more challenging. I like how the developers let lowest league to be easy. It give players some time to understand how things work and manage things. There are few things need tweaking. Like the chances of getting injured player (went a full season without injury), distribution of "Fame" points after match, expensive players and contract renewals. Developers has been helpful in the community, engaging with the players. Just few bugs here and there, developers promised to fix it in the next update release.
Verdict: Highly recommended
UPDATE - 11/9/2015
-------------
Playing the game back after the update v0.3. So much improvements to the game mechanics. Addition of weather effects which increases probability of fouls and decreases passing ability, is a an excellent update. Make players to choose proper players for different matches. Injury mechanism is been improved. Players get injured and slowly recovers full stamina. Reward (money and fame points) has been improved. Youth Academy is been added which gives a youth player depending on the current club Youth Academy level, every half season. Better Youth Academy level = Better youth player levels. Now players are cheap to buy and cheap to renew contracts. Stadiums been updated too. Game feels more balanced now. Tiny bits of bugs and errors here and there, nothing major, still an excellent game.
Verdict: Highly rcommended

Unfortunately, I think that most of the negative reviews are coming from people who may not enjoy visual novels? Or from people who don't play them often? Speaking from the point of view as someone whose PC gaming is pretty much limited to visual novels and otome games, Dream Daddy holds up. It's got a nice, cute story. What a game, oh what a LOVELY game!
This must be one of the greatest games based on a movie EVER. For one, it's not based on one particular installment, but simply set in the Mad Max universe (which never really gave much of a damn about continuity), so it's free of any plot constraints and is able just take the best of it to both do its own thing and expand on the films' world. And BOY does it do it well!
The missions are pretty hectic and interesting, and it's all supported by some truly fantastic game mechanics. The graphics are absolutely gorgeous (you'd think a desert might get boring, but the different types of terrains, the beautiful sky effects and even the different times of the day make everything look absolutely stunning), the game controls great (the cars do take some getting used to, but they do the job), the fighting system (a less flashy and far more brutal variant of the Batman: Arkham combat mechanics) is as violent and guttural as you'd expect from Max and feels absolutely satisfying, and there's a TON of stuff to do.
As in any sandbox game, you can follow the story missions, but you can also freely explore the wasteland and take to uncovering many of its secrets, as well as doing the loads and loads of sidequests available. Off the top of my head, there's loot locations (to get scrap, basically the game's currency), minefields to clear with your dog (once you rescue him and the buggy), several types of races you can participate in, many different enemy camps (some of them with bosses) you can raid for your allies to take and give you resources, convoy routes where you must destroy groups of enemy cars to get accesories, and lots of mini wasteland missions you get from "civilians".
You can basicallly spend HOURS doing things, which yields some juicy rewards for Max and his Magnum Opus. Starting as little more than a skeleton with wheels, the Opus is your main mode of transportation. As you and your unlikely ally Chumbucket (a deformed crazy hunchback) spend the game finding scrap and upgradeable parts (which go from engines to armors and even weapons), this rusty heap soon becomes a murderous beast soaring through the wasteland and leaving heaps of scrap and flesh in its path.
Simply put, even if you're not a particular fan of the movies, GET this game, and, if you are, prepare for the ultimate Mad Max experience. (There really is little that you see in the films that you don't get to do here, and everything feels totally authentic, even up to unlocky Max's classic uniform jacket and the famous V8 Interceptor)
Totally recommended!

TLDR: If you like crpgs or want to try and dip your toe into the genre, this is a good place to start.  There isn't too much combat to worry about and slow your enjoyment of the story.  Great replayability, if you like reading and want something different from typical scifi or fantasy play this game you won't be disappointed.
As a gamer that has never played the original Planescape: Torment and having limited experience with crpgs, I went into this a little intimidated.  The ones I've played were daunting in terms of gameplay, while they were all rich with deep storytelling the pacing of the game would often be hampered with the endless amount of creatures which  you would have to fight between story sections.  Some of which could be a frustrating wall until you grind even more weaker monsters to progress yourself.
That is not the case with Torment: Tides of Numenera.  I completed the game on my first playthrough in 40 hours, throughout that time I had very limited combat encounters and instead got to enjoy and immerse myself with the well written story and side lore that each environment you cross paths with uninterrupted by needless combat.  The developers weren't kidding when they say they have a books worth of story packed into this game.
I enjoyed this game, on the second playthrough you'll likely skip a few dialogue here and there but not in the same manner as other rpg games where you'll make a few different choices but be lead the same way.  In this game, there's a lot of replayability.  There is no way you can see everything in a single playthrough even if you save-scum.
What a treat this is. Are you bored of Dungeons and Dragons? Goblins and elves? All that usual fantasy guff? Well look no further than Tides of Numenera for a flawed but thoroughly refreshing RPG.

I've been waiting for this game since it was announced, and it was well worth the wait.
The world is astoundingly detailed: everyone and everything has a meticulously crafted story.  In many places, those stories will intertwine with eachother, both on a short time-scale, and across chapters. The end result is that almost every decision you make feels important at some point or anothers.
From a mechanics perspective, the Tides are a refreshing change from black and white morality that has become so common in the past 15 years.  It leads to some interesting conversation paths, though there are times when it feels as if it was designed to have a bigger impact than it did.  The crisis system is also a novel new approach to combat.  The wide array of options in handling conflicts is incredibly unique, and led to interesting challenges.  It probably could have been featured more heavily, but the lack of  conflicts may have been due to my conversation-based playstyle in my first game.
The game does suffer a few minor issues, however.  I was absorbed in the game, but not as the player character.  So much of the game is about the world that the central character can slip your mind.  Another flaw is closely linked with the crisis sytem.  By focusing on alternate methods of conflict resolution, the violent approach feels less developed than similar RPGs. With the focus of this game being so far from combat, this doesn't feel too out of place.  Finally, the character models feel bland.  With one or two exceptions, your eyes slip away from the cast, and to the gorgous backgrounds.  The disparity between character and background visuals feels odd.
All in all, this game was successful everywhere it needed to be to feel like an appropriate successor to Planescape: Torment.  The game could still use development in a few areas, and I expect that content updates in the future will help to improve on some of the problems.  It would be a real shame if the team doesn't create a follow up to fully marry the storytelling at which they've excelled with improvements to their core game.

An inmate is attempting to escape my prison. He's running along a path between two cell blocks, with a baton wielding guard in pursuit. As I pan the camera to follow the prisoner, I notice some activity at the front gate. A couple of workmen are carrying building materials for my latest construction project. The guard closest to the gate opens it to allow the workmen to enter, and I watch with a mixture of horror and embarrassment as the prisoner times his run perfectly to pass through the open gate, and out to freedom.
This anecdote perfectly illustrates everything you need to know about Prison Architect, the simulation game where the player has to build a prison and manage its day to day operations. The main sandbox game mode doesn't have a scripted story (there is a basic story in the tutorial mode), but there's lots of potential for each player to talk about unique events that happened to them. You'll spend alot of time discovering problems and figuring out how to fix them (I solved the above hole in my security by extending the outer fence and adding a second "inner" gate so that anyone coming in or out has to go through both gates). And unlike other management games, there's a constant feeling that your "customers" are actively trying to ruin all your hard work, and at any moment it could all burn down around you - literally.
Each prisoner has a list of needs, such as sleep, food, hygiene, exercise, family and recreation. If you don't fulfil these needs, the prisoners will get angry and eventually start a riot. So you have to make sure you've got a big enough kitchen to keep everyone fed, build showers, hire janitors, give prisoners some yard time, let them meet family in a visitation room, and relax by playing pool or watching TV.
As you would expect, inmates will sometimes attack and kill each other, smuggle contraband and try to dig tunnels to escape. To combat this you can hire normal guards (equipped with batons, upgradeable to tazers) and armed guards (guns) and select which areas of the prison to deploy them. Guard dogs are good at sniffing out contraband and detecting tunnels. You can place CCTV cameras and metal detectors. In the event of a riot you can call in special riot police and firemen. Prisoners caught breaking the rules can be punished with solitary confinement.
If you choose to try to improve the lives of your prisoners, you can give them training so they can work in the kitchen, workshop, library or laundry. You can give them treatment for drugs and alcohol addiction in the infirmary, let them seek religion in a chapel or give them an education in a classroom. This all contributes to "reform" which influences the chance that they commit another crime after being released from prison. This "reoffend rate" is the closest thing the game has to an overall goal. The lower the rate, the better your prison is performing. Or you could just ignore the prisoners' well being and try to make as much profit as possible. The player has complete freedom to design their prison how they want.
I do have some complaints. The tutorial campaign is quite basic, and there's alot of stuff that isn't explained. Once I started building my own prison from scratch in the sandbox I had to find answers to lots of questions on the forums. And the framerate starts to die when your prison gets quite large. My framerate was a constant 60 fps until I reached around 300 inmates, but now I've got 500 its just barely staying above 30 fps. Its still playable (framerate isn't as important for this kind of game as it is for a fast paced action game) but I'm not sure I want to go for the 1000 inmates achievement because I expect it would get even worse.
Overall Prison Architect is a really fun, extremely deep game. There's a ton of more complex systems I've not even mentioned here, but at the same time its not overwhelmingly difficult to learn how to play. I definitely give a strong recommendation to Prison Architect. I've played almost 30 hours just doing the tutorial and building one prison, so there's easily enough playing time to justify a full price purchase.

Well I always really liked the idea of a Football game (soccer in America) and I actually own quite a few of those games.
But the problem I always had is the management was more of a headache and a bit too complex, and the actual football game (where you watch/play the game) was a bit too boring and drawn out.
This game seems to have found a perfect 'level' of things, at least for me.
The management is just the right amount of complexity where you feel like you are managing your team, but not so much complexity that you're too overwhelmed.
And the games are engaging as you have to manage your 'tactics' ;) to move the ball around and get a goal, and controlling each player in a turn-based fashion and stuff like this is just satisfying all around.
I really look forward to seeing the game grow and develop just a little bit more.
(in particular the multiplayer as well as a few little tweaks to the game that are being mentioned on the forums already)
For those curious how the actual matches work, there are a number of features and things that make it quite nicely complex, without being overwhelming.
Every 'turn' in game is 2 minutes of time that goes by, out of the 45 minutes x2 halves.
Each team gets 3 turns in a row, before passing control to the opposing team, you can end your 3-turn segment early
if you wish.
Each player has different skills, accuracy, control, defense, etc.. and these skills come into play, for example, when 'crossing' an opposing player in a match.
So for example the opponent player has control of the ball.. and you want to take it from him.
So you move your player up adjacent to the opposing player with the ball, using one of your three actions.
Then you attempt to 'wrestle' the ball from him.
Depending on each of your skill in Control, a dice will be rolled for each player, with a maximum possible roll depending on skill.
So for example say the opponent with the ball has a maximum 'potential' roll of 30.
Your 'attacking' player has a maximum potential roll of 25.
You attempt to wrestle the ball, the dice is rolled (in the background, doesn't actually show the dice) then you roll a 25 (lucky) bu the opponent only rolls a 20.. you are successful at wrestling the ball from him, despite having lower skill.
But it was still risky.
With your third and last action you kick the ball towards the goal.
There are several defense men and the goalie in the way.
Each one has a maximum potential to block, and you have your potential to successfully kick.
You roll a 20.. then the first defense player rolls a 15, then the second a 7, then the goalie a 17.
Then that's it, the ball goes through and YOU SCORE!!!
The matches are  engaging, the management is deep but not overly so.
The game is just fun, and I can't wait for MP to be added, cause if done right, will make this game just great.
Dev's are listening to minor issues, and improvements suggestions on the forums, and are very active.
I highly recommend this game if you're looking for a good Football/Soccer experience that's fun and easy to get into,
and possibly have been burned by other Football/Soccer games that were just too boring and un-engaging.

I got this game for 99 cents at Humble Bundle. I'd say it's at least worth that, but not nearly worth the $9.99 full price it has. If I had disposable income, I'd happily pay five bucks for it, mostly because of the fact that making video games isn't as easy as some people think, and it IS a gorgeous game, it's just... lacking. The concept behind it was what got it onto my wishlist, and while I appreciate minimal user interfaces and no instructions being shoved in my face, Splice took it a little too far. I spent most of Sequence 1 just clicking on things until other things happened, with a quick check of the simplistic help to make sure that was ALL I was supposed to be doing. The addition of mutations after Sequence 1 only complicated things.
I haven't beaten it yet; I'm wading through Sequence 5 with some saintly person's guide videos open next to it, but thusfar the whole game has been trial and error, clicking stuff until something correct happens. I still don't really understand how anything works. What do the changes in the reticle mean? Why does the circle around the starting segement expand after mutations, and what controls the order of the mutation executions? Is there a set order of operations here or is it based on proximity or what? What does ANY of it mean? (I feel like the double rainbows guy.)
It's a lovely game, don't get me wrong. The music is great (though I wouldn't buy the soundtrack at the full $4.99 either), the visuals are smooth and relaxing (although some sequences had me focusing extra hard on not looking at the background, because I have a phobia of deep water and sometimes the colors gradients and floating particles were close enough to that to give me the heebie jeebies), and again, the concept is great. It just needs a tiny bit more in the way of direction; single floating words in the first level with a new mutation (duplicate, add, delete), drifting text telling the player to grab and pull, to balance the sides out to make it work, or to give some hint about the order of steps after you've reset X number of times. I figured out most of the levels up to this point on my own, with a little ping of satisfaction for each one (especially when my first Angelic was without guidance), but there were definitely a few that I absolutely couldn't figure out. Maybe my brain just doesn't work that way, who knows.

Spec-Ops: The Line is highly regarded for its unconventional narrative that attempts to criticize other games in similarly-themed games for the "power fantasy" that they give players by having them act as a gung-ho hero with no question for the actions they take. It is largely inspired by the Joseph Conrad novel "Heart of Darkness", most well-known as also being the inspiration for the Francis F. Coppola magnum opus "Apocalypse Now"; the story of how prolonged exposure to war and violence can warp anyone, a theme that holds true in this game as well.
I personally found the lofty narrative to be less impresive than I was expecting going in. Yes, the game does attempt to chastise the player by having them perform objectives then showing them the consequences of it but a problem lies with the fact the game is trying to be bleak anyway. Seldom do you get a chance to choose your route and no matter what you do, it ends up being really crummy anyway. The protagonist is torn between his objectives and what is right yet you can never lead him down a positive road. The game's linear structure basically demands you do what other games such as Call of Duty have asked but then admonishes you for doing it, despite the fact it never let you have your say in the first place.
However, that considered, the rest of the game, I thought, was better than most critics had to say. A common complaint is the game is wholly generic and any reason to play is primarily held up by its unique plot but I personally found the gameplay solid and uncompromising. It's definitely rote but as a third-person shooter, it checks all the boxes and does them well. Your team members are also not of the braindead A.I. that you have to be joined to the hip to like most shooting games. They will actively help position you if you use them right and have helpful skills like flashbangs and sniping. The only real complaint I have about the gameplay is some of the animations are too stiff-looking (enemies just pop up from behind cover with no semblance of finesse or human-like movement).
So, ultimately, while the narrative fails to deliver on its intended message for me, I still say play Spec-Ops if you're looking for a fun, albeit by-the-books third-person shooter. And, hey, if you're not as jaded as me then you might even see the message the game was intending to leave too.

I would refund it if I didn't spend the first two hours in it trying to get the game not to crash upon startup and at almost every loading screen.
I understand it is an early access game, but I've played few other early access games this poorly optimized and unplayable, and honestly after spending what was almost an entire week to get it to work so I could play with a friend that recommended it, it didn't feel worth it at all.
So lets get down to the two main points I have to talk about, performance and gameplay.
Peformance:
This is obviously my main issue with the game. Not only is it riddled with problems simply getting it to run, when you finally find a way over all of those hurdles through what honestly seems to be just pure esoteric sorcery nobody on any forum suffering from the same issues can understand or recreate properly, the game itself has a high chance to just run like pure garbage even on a powerful PC. I say chance because honestly there seems to be no clear answer on how to get it to run properly for everyone, for some it runs great on a god damn laptop that costs barely 500 dollars. For others, they might crash on start up or it might tank their desktop PC even if it's worth three times that. My own experience can play anecdote here, as can the experience of people all over the internet who suffer the same problems with the same or even more powerful builds, as can the experience of another friend who bought it alongside me and couldn't even play it at all while I could despite him having a tower that would blow mine out of the park.
The general answer you'll find if you run into any problems will probably be either "it works on my PC" or "just wait till they patch it", and you'll probably find these answers dating back since the game first came out many years ago. Well all these years later, despite numerous supposed "performance updates" and so on, they never patched all the holes and these people still aren't worth listening to.
Gameplay:
Gameplay in rust is interesting, assuming this is your first ever open world survival multiplayer early access game and it's still 2013. First you knock down trees, pretty original, right? Then you mine some stone, you make some tools, you build a hut and you upgrade and defend your hut while your armor/weapon progression slowly turns you into what can best be described as a side character from mad max. All the while you'll be trying to manage hunger, thirst and even battle the elements to a small degree by dressing appropriately. But that obviously isn't the only draw of this game, another draw is that it's multiplayer on top of it all, you can play with friends you can make enemies start little wars and enjoy some very basic PvP action. Unfortunately it takes a bit of time to fully experience this outside of naked rock/torch fights, and even then it usually devolves into that because nobody really wants to take too many important goodies out of their base on the chance they could lose them. I won't lie, I had some fun with the gameplay once I'd grown used to suffering the endless optimization flaws, but if people didn't enjoy these types of games there wouldn't be so many of them.
And thats part of the problem, there are so many of them, and the gameplay doesn't really compare superbly well to many of them. Content wise there may be more to do but that's because the game has been in development forever and even then you'll still run out of things to do inevitably if the PvP doesn't really interest you.
Sadly in the end I can't recommend it at all in it's current state and given how long it's been in the state it's in I don't believe I'll ever be able to in this lifetime. Another early access game that will never ever leave alpha I guess. Perhaps one of the trendsetters for this plague on steam.

Like so many superheroes, Batman as a real life crime fighter would be ludicrous. In comic books, movies and games, Batman works when the darkness is turned all the way up to 11 and the drama is dialled right up. And it's amid this inky blackness and relentless peril that WB Games Montreal has taken the Bat once again, following in the intimidating footsteps of Rocksteady, and the incredibly lofty bar it set with Batman: Arkham Asylum and Arkham City.
Batman: Arkham Origins takes Bruce Wayne back to his roots with a story set prior to the events of the first two games. On paper it sounds like a foolhardy idea to make a prequel, with a whole new voice cast no less, and it begged the question, could WB Montreal match Rocksteady in the execution? In short, the answer is a resounding yes. Batman: Arkham Origins is more of the same in the Arkham City mould, but in the best way imaginable.
"Boom! Power stance, baby!"
Origins' narrative is pretty meaty stuff too, set in the heart of a Gotham City that's tearing itself apart as villains rip through its decaying streets on the search for the Dark Knight, in the vain hope that they'll score Black Mask's $50 million bounty. The game could have quite easily been a romp from A to B, dispatching the assassins out to kill Batman in sequence, but instead there's a strong story laden with twists and turns, and the odd unexpected surprise for the fans.
Bats himself is relatively new to a life of fighting crime in Arkham Origins, a myth on the streets of Gotham, largely unknown by Captain Jim Gordon and the GCPD, and written off as a freak; a bizarre sideshow, a menace. Chatter among thugs roaming the gloomy alleyways reveals talk of sightings, conjecture and hearsay about the Bat, with most dismissing his existence as ghost stories and spooky hokum. Until you show up on the scene and prove that you are in fact all too real, that is. This particular version of Batman is also one who's self-involved, determined to go it alone and fuelled by anger. He's younger, more brash, raw and reckless.
Like Asylum and City before it, Arkham Origins is about instilling fear in your enemies, although essentially the series' core gameplay mechanics remain untouched, with a few tweaked gadgets like the glue grenade, the odd new one like the concussion detonator, and a couple of fresh moves in Bats' repertoire. Though is has to be said, turning the tables on enemies with the shock gloves is an exceptionally empowering thrill.
A game still largely comprised of exploration, free flow combat and predator sections, if you've played Rocksteady's previous two Batman games you'll feel right at home with this one. Arkham Origins doesn't set out to break the mould or reinvent the rules, and yet it still seems like a bold game, and one that proves relentlessly entertaining as you breathlessly freewheel from one set-piece to the next.
"Get that thing out of my face."
Instead of familiarity breeding contempt, Batman: Arkham Origins somehow feels fresh. Even when you bump into a building you're sure you've seen in Arkham City a million times before, it's from a different Gotham years in the past, indistinguishable enough from its future counterpart. Indeed, the city itself is in an entirely different state, with none of the flooding that claimed a chunk Gotham in the previous game, and some taller and more imposing architecture to scale.
Arkham City's locked down Gotham was an urban nightmare caked in rust and decay, ruled by feral gangs running amok. Origins' version is a city on a steep downward spiral, but one where there's still a shred of hope buried beneath its seething cauldron of corruption. Knowing that glimmer of hope amounts to nothing doesn't make the atmosphere and tension any less palpable.
If anything there are more criminal gangs and crooked cops on the streets, and when you're not punching their faces to burger, you'll be foiling another one of The Riddler's plots, tracking down Anarky, Shiva, Deadshot and a host of other villains that you could ignore altogether if you chose to. There's a whole raft of optional tasks to complete in addition to what is a solid 10-15 hours of story. Collectibles are just the tip of a very big iceberg.
"Shocking."
On top of all of this is an improved and more involving Detective Mode, in which Batman gets to prove his credentials as the great and much-vaunted sleuth that he's supposed to be. You now set about reconstructing a crime, piecing together the components of what transpired, before Bats comes to his own conclusion. It's not exactly LA Noire, but it beats the previous games' efforts.
Arkham Origins is not without its frustrations however, and some of the Predator encounters and boss battles can prove trying at certain junctures. Predator areas aren't quite so clearly defined in some cases, and controlling Bats can prove fiddly when there's no obvious place to hide. There's a fight with Deathstroke too where the game attempts to explain that you need to look for an opening to strike and time your counter moves accordingly, but the result is messy and the ultimate outcome – at least in our personal experience – feels arbitrary.
On top of a generously proportioned campaign is an entirely separate multiplayer component, assigned to its own disc and outsourced to UK Brink studio Splash Damage. Multiplayer takes nothing away from the fantastic single-player, and has a few neat ideas of its own. Is it a unique enough proposition to stand out? Not really. A rather shoddy Gears of War clone, multiplayer pits two criminal gangs against one another in a straight-up shootout, then throws randomly selected players into the mix who assume control of Batman and Robin. It's playing as the dynamic duo that proves the most fun, filling your Intimidation Meter and swooping down upon unsuspecting enemies.
The batarang. Don't leave home without it.
Conversely, playing as a bog standard thug is typical tacked-on multiplayer fare with a decent cover system and solid shooter mechanic. It clearly sets out what it aims to do, and Splash Damage has done a fine job in creating a multiplayer mode that slots neatly into the Batman Arkhamverse, but it's hard to imagine it'll have legs amid a slew of better multiplayer options already available and just on the horizon. Multiplayer isn't bad by any stretch of the imagination, but its long-term appeal is questionable.
If you want to complete the entire achievement list, you'll have to put some time in with the multiplayer however. That means reaching Prestige level and achieving maximum rank with both the Bane and Joker gang factions, which will take a good few hours and then some. The story campaign is where it's at of course, and this time there's not only New Game Plus to beat, but there's also the 'I Am The Night' mode. Chuck in achievements attached to the Challenge Rooms, and the wealth of content and replay value on offer is simply staggering.
A triumphant third outing for the Dark Knight, Batman: Arkham Origins is proof positive that the series is in safe hands with WB Games Montreal. Building upon the strong foundations of the first two Arkham titles, Origins boasts the same marriage of compelling storytelling, uncompromising gameplay, killer combat and faithfulness to the source material. Batman: Arkham Origins is an empowering rollercoaster ride and a more than worthy successor to the cowl and cape. Another dark heroic fantasy that demands to be played.

The Max Payne series was a massive hit at its time and managed to create a plethora of wonderful things such as Poets of The Fall, a popular Finnish rockband who started their career by composing the ending track for Max Payne 2.
Extra laugh factors:
- They used the face of the creative writer of the game. Sam Lake or (Sami Järvi) to create the classic cringing Max Payne grin.
- They used their relatives and friends to get the models into the game.
For example, one of the lighter haired thugs in the game which you can see already on the first level "Roscoe-Street Station" was modeled after the guy who filled up Remedy's sodamachine back in the day.
Sam Lake's mother eventually played the main antagonist in the graphic novels.
The singer of "Poets of the Fall" ended up as "Vladimir Lem" in the first game. etc. etc.
- Many many brilliant easter-eggs when easter-eggs in games weren't too common. My personal favorite probably being when you shoot the loudspeakers in elevators that play elevatormusic, Max thanks you :)

I think the Steam community had it right with this one, with 19,000 reviews as “Very Positive.” I wanted to buy this game right away when it came out in 2015, but I didn’t have the graphics card to handle the experience at max resolution (the way it truly should be experienced). It was on my ‘Wishlist’ for quite some time, and once I finally managed to do some PC upgrades, I went for it. Boy was I in for a treat.
At the time, one of my games of the year was Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor. Mad Max has a lot of similarities in the vast expanses of the open world, various options for combat engagement, and character animations. The Mad Max store page describes the game as an, “action-packed, open world, third person action game, you must fight to stay alive in The Wasteland, using brutal on-ground and vehicular against vicious gangs of bandits.” I’d say this is pretty accurate. I truly enjoyed driving around the wasteland, completing main & side missions along the way.
My only (small) grievance was the limited character movement/exploration capability (compared to other titles like Shadow of Mordor or Assassins Creed). A small rock or fence was enough to completely immobilize your route... not really ideal for exploration. Combat could also be a tad repetitive with the constant timed clicks (attack & block), but you could certainly mix it up with evades, rolls, shotguns, etc. Not a deal breaker at all. If the Mad Max & Shadow of Mordor games somehow merged, it would result the perfect open world, 3rd person RPG.
Main story line + most of the side quests took around 31 hours of gameplay. Cut out a good 5 - 10 hours if you like to fast travel instead of driving around. And add loads of time to that if you’re an achievement hunter.
A+, worth the wait for a better graphics card.

This game is probably the worst I've ever played. It seems that the devs really had no idea what they were doing.
Gameplay
The gameplay is medicore at best, and for a game who's selling point is gameplay, that's pretty bad. At worst, the gameplay is a broken mess. For example, there's something called "Second Wind" in which, if you kill an enemy in time, you don't die. That's a great idea. But, I can't tell you how many times I killed an enemy just as I got killed, and there were no enemies nearby to kill. No health packs that you can carry, so I'm basically screwed. Or, I'm in a boss fight, where it's only me and the boss, so what am I to do when I get knocked down? Also, I'd like to comment on how hard this game is. I'm not knocking it because it's hard, I'm knocking it because it's hard just by how badly it's designed. The only way to get adequate gear is to do the side quests. But the side quests are all monotonous fetch quests, so it can't keep my interest.
Graphics
Now, this game does not have bad graphics at all. If I didn't know any better, I'd say they spent all their time on graphics. The game looks nice. If you crouch and look at the ground, you start to see the pixels in the texture, but that's to be expected. The lighting and natural cloth movement is beautiful, it looks very nice. The art style is not really my taste, but other people like it. No one can knock this game for it's graphics. Hell, just the look of acid on the floor is amazing.
Story/Writing
Calling this games story a story is an insult to stories. This games story is so cookie cutter, it makes me want to scream. No, Handsome Jack is not a good villain, no, Pandora is not interesting, and no, the writing is not funny. Yes, I'll be the first to say it, since everyone else in this section seems to be kissing this games♥♥♥♥♥ The writing didn't make me even crack a smile. It's not funny at all. That is, unless you're in between the ages of 7-10 years old. Spongebob is legitimately way better written than this game.
Music/World
Pandora has to be one of the dullest worlds I've ever explored. There is so little going on, it hurts. A radio in the car would be nice, but no, that is not found. There's tons of different areas, like Tundra Area, Desert Area, and Urban Area. And the music is just as bad. It's like one guy got his banjo and recorded everything in an afternoon. It's bad. Very, very bad.
Summary
This game is not fun, it is not interesting, the only thing is has going for it is graphics, IF you like the art style. I give this game a 2/10, complete waste of money. I'm never buying another Gearbox game again, because this was an absolute MESS. And it makes me worry for the future of gaming when THIS has so many fans. Be sure to mark my review as Helpful if it swayed you, and with that, thank you for reading this
