An inmate is attempting to escape my prison. He's running along a path between two cell blocks, with a baton wielding guard in pursuit. As I pan the camera to follow the prisoner, I notice some activity at the front gate. A couple of workmen are carrying building materials for my latest construction project. The guard closest to the gate opens it to allow the workmen to enter, and I watch with a mixture of horror and embarrassment as the prisoner times his run perfectly to pass through the open gate, and out to freedom.
This anecdote perfectly illustrates everything you need to know about Prison Architect, the simulation game where the player has to build a prison and manage its day to day operations. The main sandbox game mode doesn't have a scripted story (there is a basic story in the tutorial mode), but there's lots of potential for each player to talk about unique events that happened to them. You'll spend alot of time discovering problems and figuring out how to fix them (I solved the above hole in my security by extending the outer fence and adding a second "inner" gate so that anyone coming in or out has to go through both gates). And unlike other management games, there's a constant feeling that your "customers" are actively trying to ruin all your hard work, and at any moment it could all burn down around you - literally.
Each prisoner has a list of needs, such as sleep, food, hygiene, exercise, family and recreation. If you don't fulfil these needs, the prisoners will get angry and eventually start a riot. So you have to make sure you've got a big enough kitchen to keep everyone fed, build showers, hire janitors, give prisoners some yard time, let them meet family in a visitation room, and relax by playing pool or watching TV.
As you would expect, inmates will sometimes attack and kill each other, smuggle contraband and try to dig tunnels to escape. To combat this you can hire normal guards (equipped with batons, upgradeable to tazers) and armed guards (guns) and select which areas of the prison to deploy them. Guard dogs are good at sniffing out contraband and detecting tunnels. You can place CCTV cameras and metal detectors. In the event of a riot you can call in special riot police and firemen. Prisoners caught breaking the rules can be punished with solitary confinement.
If you choose to try to improve the lives of your prisoners, you can give them training so they can work in the kitchen, workshop, library or laundry. You can give them treatment for drugs and alcohol addiction in the infirmary, let them seek religion in a chapel or give them an education in a classroom. This all contributes to "reform" which influences the chance that they commit another crime after being released from prison. This "reoffend rate" is the closest thing the game has to an overall goal. The lower the rate, the better your prison is performing. Or you could just ignore the prisoners' well being and try to make as much profit as possible. The player has complete freedom to design their prison how they want.
I do have some complaints. The tutorial campaign is quite basic, and there's alot of stuff that isn't explained. Once I started building my own prison from scratch in the sandbox I had to find answers to lots of questions on the forums. And the framerate starts to die when your prison gets quite large. My framerate was a constant 60 fps until I reached around 300 inmates, but now I've got 500 its just barely staying above 30 fps. Its still playable (framerate isn't as important for this kind of game as it is for a fast paced action game) but I'm not sure I want to go for the 1000 inmates achievement because I expect it would get even worse.
Overall Prison Architect is a really fun, extremely deep game. There's a ton of more complex systems I've not even mentioned here, but at the same time its not overwhelmingly difficult to learn how to play. I definitely give a strong recommendation to Prison Architect. I've played almost 30 hours just doing the tutorial and building one prison, so there's easily enough playing time to justify a full price purchase.

This is one VN that I really enjoyed.
I prefer detective/crime/mystery/horror novels rather than the ones that focus solely on romance [they bore me].
The Adventures of Fei Duanmu 端木斐异闻录 is a detective/crime novel. You play as Fei, a student of criminal investigation.
The game has 2 chapters/cases so far. The 1st one is short and basically an introduction to the mainly characters and the game style. The 2nd is longer and very interesting. You have a few puzzles/deductions plus you get to choose how to conduct some conversations based on questions/topics you can talk about.
Loved the characters in general. There wasn't even one that I disliked. And the art style is awesome too. It's very well made and the characters are beautiful and pleasant to look at.
The menu is clean and beautiful as well [loved the color choices]. The PDA function is easy and add a nice touch to the game.
Glad it was translated to English and the few grammar/spelling errors didn't bother me at all. I got so caught up in the game that I didn't even care.
More chapters will be released according to the dev [as DLC apparently]. I will buy them for sure. Eager to see what's gonna happen and hoping for a romance between my 2 favorite characters. ^^
Even though it's only 2 chapters, the game is worth it's full price. It's not expensive and for the amount of content and entertainment you get, it's definitely fair.
*9.5/10*
Note: You can only save the game when the PDA function becomes available and even then, it's only when experiencing the story as Fei.

-Good art, characters and backgrounds alike look excellent. Character animations are nice too.
-Believable characters
-Interesting story/mystery without any romantic side stuff
-Fully voice acted (in Chinese), sounds good even if I can't understand it
-Puzzles and interrogations are unique and enjoyable, as well as challenging without being too difficult
-Good price for a decent length VN
-The English translation is spotty at best*. In casual conversations there are many grammar issues ("He are" etc;), but it is generally understandable. However, in certain story scenes where the language gets complex it becomes almost unreadable. I had to reread entire paragraphs several times to understand the meaning of a particular passage, which was made more difficult by the fact there is no backlog available to reread past events.
-It's rather difficult to tell which decisions you make influence the ending without a guide.

蛋挞起源于广州，五六十年代渐渐在港式茶餐厅流行。新鲜出炉的蛋挞香味四溢，外层松脆，内馅香甜，无论是在中餐馆或面包店，都是一款非常受欢迎的点心。中式蛋挞的皮不像一般的西点派皮，蛋挞皮一层一层的，非常酥松，配上嫩滑的奶香浓郁的馅，口感好极了。
我们家每次去中餐馆饮茶都要点上一碟酥皮蛋挞，餐馆里卖的蛋挞挞皮比较油腻，毛毛一直期待我给他做这个蛋挞。毛毛妈厨房的中式蛋挞方子经过多次改良，挞皮酥松而且不油腻，吃了还想吃哦。
【酥皮蛋挞】
用料:
水皮：
1：中筋面粉（All-purpose flour）3/4杯（120克），白糖1.5大匙（21克），固态猪油（Lard）4大匙（60克）；
2：蛋黄1个，加水2大匙（共45克）打均匀；
油皮
3：低筋面粉（Pastry & Cake flour）1/3杯（55克），固态猪油（Lard）3大匙（45克）；
奶蛋馅：
4：牛奶1杯+1大匙（250克），糖1/4杯（60克）；
5：鸡蛋2个，打散备用。
注：1大匙Tablespoon =15毫升，1茶匙Teaspoon =5毫升，1杯Cup=240毫升。以上的材料可以做12个中号蛋挞。
做法：
1、水皮：将1料里的面粉和糖放入盆里拌匀，将猪油切小方块放入面粉里（图1），用Pastry blender或用手将面粉抓捏到猪油里成肉馅样。然后倒入2料，用叉子兜匀成较大块。手上撒点面粉，将水皮在撒了稍许面粉的案板上揉几下成面团（图2左），然后保湿静置15分钟。
2、油皮：3料里的猪油同样切小方块，用Pastry blender或用手将面粉抓捏成成肉馅样，然后手上稍微沾点面粉揉成软面团（图2右），保湿静置15分钟。
【酥皮蛋挞】
3、挞皮：案板上撒少许面粉，将水皮面团揉成直径2厘米的圆条，再揪成12等份。油皮面团也分成12等份，做的过程要用保鲜膜盖住其他的皮料保湿。取一份水皮擀成长圆形薄饼，再取一份油皮均匀抹在擀开的水皮上（图3）。折叠两次成3折（图4），旋转90度后沿纵向擀开，然后再叠两次成3折（图4）。接着尽量擀开成长方形的薄皮（图5），叠三次成4折（图6），旋转90度后沿长轴再叠三次成4折（图7、8），稍压一下，保湿静置松弛10分钟。这种叠法会有总共144层。
4、取一份挞皮压扁，将四角往中间推推，然后擀成直径7.5厘米的圆饼（图10）。用7厘米的Cookie Cutter切去边（图11），再稍擀成8厘米的圆饼，放入中号的 Muffin烤盘里（如果有波浪纹的蛋塔烤模的话，成品会更漂亮）。手上沾点面粉，用手指把饼皮捏成蛋挞模的形状，依次做好其余11个。做好的蛋挞皮静置松弛20分钟。
5、利用这个空档来做蛋挞奶液：小号锅放入所有4料，用小火加热至糖溶解后离火，然后边搅拌边倒入打散的鸡蛋（图9），将奶液过筛。
6、将奶液均匀注入12个蛋挞皮中，只要6、7分满的样子（图12）。将烤盘放入预热至400oF/205oC的烤箱内，烤18-20分钟即可。
【酥皮蛋挞】
爱心分享：
1：挞皮成功的关键是：擀皮与叠层时要手法轻柔，不要漏出油皮。
2：挞皮烤熟后会膨胀，所以蛋挞奶液只需要装到6、7分满。
3：剩余的蛋挞可放入密闭容器，在冰箱里储存。吃的时候放入预热至350oF/175oC烤箱中烤8分钟，同样又酥又香。
4：挞皮分开做熟练后，可以不用分开，直接水皮包油皮，两次3折两次4折完成，节省时间。

Surprised that given the Rogue-Lite craze in indie games this title isn't more talked about, especially after being played and promoted by many popular individuals.
Is a low poly FPS with an abstract but appealing visual style, the neon colors have a good contrast so they never feel like an eyesore, and the style has a neat early 3D vibe, the sound design having a glitchy vibe to it.
The gameplay reminds me of the original Wolfestein 3D; there’s no jumping, you walk through semi Labyrinthic corridors killing enemies and finding secrets, but that’s where the similarities end. The random generation is really good; I never encountered myself stuck or in unfair situations that can’t be solved by your own skill. It has some heart pounding moments which makes this game memorable at times, but going through random adversity never gets old.
It has an interesting item variety, which can help you or ruin you over. However, while some items make for different and interesting play styles, I wish the game had more to offer.  Many of the items are only there to be used for the achievements or feel arbitrary, meaning you’ll be selling those or ignoring them altogether. An update that expands the item pool would be greatly appreciated, but I also appreciate that the game is mostly skill focused and you don’t need to rely on the items in order to make it to the end, but they help.
Don’t expect a deep plot or story in this tittle, it constantly contradicts itself (In purpose) and anything regarding the ‘plot’ is told via flavor text and some small things within the game. Its main focus its gameplay with very minor plot elements.
Overall, the execution is original and really fun. The idea of having to recollect your bullets in this manner is something I’ve never seen before, and it’s well executed. Being able to play the game at your own pace is a great addition too. Go slow or go fast, is a blast.
There are people suffering with stuttering while playing, there are many theories for this issue and you can read up more about it on the forums. I play this game on a very out dated toaster and barely noticed issues regarding this, for me it’s rare to say the least. But the stuttering can prove unforgiving or to ruin the game entirely given its nature, if you suffer from it and can’t find a way to fix it, a refund is recommendable. As much as I enjoy this game, no one should go through that, and the creator should make a better effort to fix this problem.

A timeless experience, a masterpiece... Just a beautiful work of art, and probably one of the very few titles that in my "view" demonstrate the true potential of this medium.
Regarding the gameplay, it's fantastic, Max Payne allows you to slow down time, whilst at the same time "lunging" while shooting, similarly to the types of actions movies from the time, or from John Woo, if you ever seen one.
The entire thing plays like an action film, and that's the feeling that it gives you, it is violent, fast, and risky, all of this while still being fair, balanced, and easy to get into.
The story, the world, and the characters, however... It's where the game really shines, it's not only the way it's written, because there are times in which the writing its laughable at that.
It's related much more to the way the game's universe its presented.
Everything its told in a concise, and simple way.
But the game, just oozes this feel of actual creativity, of actual risks, and of actual vision.
The characters are incredibly charming, and hilarious at times even in the midst of an incredibly dark story, and in return, those moments actually "transcend" the genuine feel that they're trying to present.
This is the type of game that serves as a demonstration of what happens when  the developers, writers, painters, and generally, "artists" get control over THEIR creation, and as an end result, even in those moments that might not be particularly too well developed, or presented, in all of their amazing chaotic, and superflous fashion, get, instead, humor, passion, and heart in return.
And they do MAKE you feel that way.
To me, in this medium, in that time, or even now, and even taken as a general story of what the process of creativity demands from truly passionate creators that push foward through all of the social, economical, and even political blockades, demonstrates a deeply beautiful emotion that can't be replicated by marketing, graphical fidelity, or general objective quality.
All of those things that this game already carries, but to have heart.
That is what makes it the emblematic game, and one of the best games ever made...

Origins is not as great as Asylum or City. With that ouf the way - It's still a very, very good game with a good story (yes, it has a bunch of inconsistencies, like the damn shock gloves and the advanced grapple gun that didn't even exist before Arkham City and this is supposed to be before that), lots of content, great familiar game mechanics from the previous games and a few of its own additions (not all of which are good (looking at you, shock gloves)). I had a lot of fun playing through the campaign and the newly added multiplayer addition is suprisingly fun and interesting. The main issues that plague the game are bugs (unfortuneatly I've encountered game breaking bugs more than once which forced me to restart the game) and severe connection problems while playing MP (it can be REALLY hard just to get in a match without everything falling appart). I've seen a lot of negative reviews for this game and don't really see the reason - like I've said, sure, It's not exactly great as the previous titles and has its problems but it's still better than 90% of action adventure titles out there and that's not exactly a small thing. I think a lot of people have written the game off just because it wasn't made by Rocksteady and that's not really fair to this title. I give this game a strong recommendation to any Batman fan or anyone even remotely interested in action adventure games. I would give this game 8/10.

Hello friends this is my somewhat short, but hopefully somewhat useful review of tides of numenera. I'm going to break this review down into four separate categories followed by my closing thoughts.
-----------------
Graphics
So let me be honest with you this games graphics isn't anything special, It's a crpg and I feel graphics isn't one of the major factors you should judge this genre of game on. That being said character models weren't all that impressive but they weren't by any stretch terrible. Some world environments actually looked pretty interesting and had a beautiful tone to it. I feel like the special effects of this game was its strong point in the graphics department but also it's most frustrating part.
For instance there are certain parts of the game when you meet the sorrow and witness its grandstand this is amazing looking and creates a moment of awe, as well as some other maps you encounter look incredibly vibrant and colorful. While others look very plain and unimaginative. The most frustrating part is getting special passives later on in the game. These passives create a colorful shine effect around your character, near end game my guy looked like a walking Christmas tree about to give me a seizure.
Overall the graphics where solid and did its job well that job being able to support the story and help tell it.
Graphics : 7/10
-----------------
Sound
So let me start of by saying the soundtrack in this game was good mixed with a feeling of who gives an S***. There were times where the sound matched the mood correctly and gave me a sense of emotion and feeling to the task or event at hand. There was also times where I didn't even notice the music in the background at all tuning it out. Which made me wonder how their soundtrack was so hit and miss I could never really wrap my head around it. I feel like the major points of the story the music fit in well supporting the mood while delivering the message it set out to send us.
All the music in between I honesty couldn't care less. None of the music was really terrible just most of it didn't really matter to the game. I feel the sound track aside all the ambient sound and voice acting (what little there actually is of it) is superb and immersed me more into the game.
Sound: 7/10
-----------------
Gameplay
So there is a common theme in my review which I'm sure you all have noticed. That theme being the story is the major strength of this game and I'm judging the other aspects of it based on how they support or elevate the story. Which brings me to my next category game play. Oh boy this game is hit and miss there are amazing moments to be had followed by head scratches and for game play this also holds true. The game play is honestly not very imaginative in this game and extremely straight forward.
There are two aspects to the game, running around talking to people and making decisions based of stats, skills and tidal abilities, then there's the combat. The first part is fun and has rewarding moments along with emotion and enlightenment. Though I feel that this ties more into the story with a mix of it being game play. The game play being you holding tab looking for things to interact with and get into the lore and story of the world. Which leads me to the second part of the game play which is more of the definition of the word and that's the combat.
Man oh man, I honestly don't know how to describe the combat for you I feel like the combat almost had no purpose. I mean it's not real time which that's okay but it's a turn based system without any real strategy or relevance. Abilities really didn't matter at least for me they didn't I was a glaive did not upgrade any abilities or used any at all for the entirety of the game. I put points into edge, stats pool, and effort I believe that's what it was called. Then I proceeded to click and auto attack on every enemy I went against till they died. Ciphers once again cool concept, it's a really powerful item that gives you stat boost or damages your foes or both but it can only be used once before its lost.
Unfortunately I used a cipher one time against one enemy throughout the entire game, even then I didn't have to I just was curious to see how they work. In the end all I did was stack artifacts that made me hit harder and sell all my ciphers I had for gear. Maybe this is a glaive thing and the other classes aren't so fortunate but by mid game my guy couldn't die and my auto attacks where taking 50 to 75% of enemies life pools a strike. To me I feel like the purpose of combat was to make the game last longer and nothing more, that's how bland and tedious it was for me as a glaive at least.
Gameplay: 7/10 (the aspects relative to the story, the combat id give a 4/10)
-----------------
Story
Last but not least by any stretch, the reason why I bought this game and I'm sure many others did the story.
Tides of numenera is carried by its excellent story telling, lore and connection you feel with the castoff and his allies. If by any chance you are 1/3 into the game and aren't feeling the story I advise you to stop playing the game. Why? because that's how much this game relies on its story to flourish. Without it, it's not even worth a steam summer sell for 75% off. Is the story perfect? No, but is it interesting fun and keeps you waiting for what happens next? Hell yes. *Slight spoilers* you are a cast off of a deity called the changing god who is in essence immortal. He achieves his immortality through transferring his consciousness from being to being improving himself from his previous life. Your role is one of these castoffs trying to figure out what is going on in this world.
The game has a lot of choice leading to numerous altercations and outcomes depending on how you act and treat your followers or the world around you. The voice acting is amazing but there is barely any which is unfortunate because I believe if the game had more of it, it would appeal to a larger audience. Warning if you do not like to read do not purchase this game it's basically a visual novel with combat being its mini game in between chapters. Overall this game is good but it has its share of flaws that are out shined by its interactive and amazing story telling. I would love to tell you more but I do not wish to spoil the main reason why you should play this game.
Story: 9/10
Closing statements
I had fun with tides of numenera I believe the game could have been a lot better though, There were a few moments in this game that where the best I have ever played in a crpg. That being said it was also inconsistent at times which lead to frustration, the combat is poor and needs to be revamped for future games. Also, some story telling which was the best and most brilliant in the game were flashbacks. To be able to play these flashbacks in real time would have been awesome instead we got a screen that we click on with nothing to show for it. Overall in the end I had a blast it was well worth the 26 hours I spent to complete it.
Overall: 8/10

I vacillated on whether to recommend this game or not.  It is not as good as Planescape: Torment, but as long you temper your expectations, it is an enjoyable experience.  However, it is somewhat overpriced right now.  I would wait until it is on sale for 20-30 USD before buying it.
The setting very much is that carnival of weirdness and peculiarity that one would expect from a successor to Planescape: Torment.  The Numenera setting is one of people trying to survive in the ashes of previous highly advanced civilizations; civilizations who built devices that appear magical to the explorers of this strange world.  This allows for devices that flagrantly taunt the laws of physics without the need for a sci-fi explanation as no one is alive who understands this technology.  While Numenera uses technology to recreate the setting that D&D used magic to simulate.  It lacks some of the coherence of the Planescape setting.  Within Sigil, belief had the power to alter reality and anything could be a doorway to another plane of existence, under those guidelines everything made sense.  There are fewer rules governing the Numenera setting.
The main plot passable but flawed.  You are the castoff of a human who has gained immortality by jumping from body to body through history.  Whenever he leaves a body a new personality inhabits that castoff body with some of the memories of the original.   This person is being chased by an immortal monster, and that monster is also chasing all the castoffs.  This monster is pursuing you because of something called the tides.  The problem is the tides (and the problem with the tides) are never well explained.  You essentially start the game being told you must repair a device that will stop this monster, and all your efforts in the game resolve around finding someone who can repair this device.  You never really question why you are doing all of this, beyond basic survival, until the last 10 minutes of the game.  Note that all the endings of the game are determined by your choices in final conversation.
The gameplay is not very good.  Much like Planescape: Torment, Tides of Numenera does allow you to talk your way through quests instead of fighting.  The problem is, while conversations are arguably the focus of the game.  They are not the main gameplay mechanic.  The gameplay is really focused on crises that can be resolved using stealth or combat.  Most of the crises consist of more than just beating the enemy and the early crises can be fun to play. As you progress the character mechanics and acquisition of items reduce the crises to trivialities.  The game features a very generous system of stat pools that can be used to purchase successes.  It is so generous that it trivializes the game.  Any conflict you encounter can be solved either using the consumables you acquired or spending some points from the pools that refresh whenever you rest.  The pools offer larger bonuses than skill levels, making skill choices redundant.  This also limits the character variety and reduces replayability.
Despite these flaws, there is joy to be had in exploring the world in this video game.  Some of the side quests are well done and the descriptions of the items and locations are interesting and entertaining.  The game clocks in at a respectable 20-30 hours, not great for an RPG you probably will not be replaying, but it is a memorable experience.

It felt a bit short and a bit hollow compared to the Torment of yore, but it is a true spiritual successor.  Lots and lots of text and dialogue, it was very well written.  There is usually more than one way to obtain whatever objective you have.  NPCs are complex and nuanced, each with their own motivation, personality, and attitude.
Very few required fights, and those that are forced are almost always objective oriented... you're trying to survive, escape or reach some goal rather than just kill the enemies.  It's a neat idea, and mostly successfullly pulled off - that said I would have liked to see more of it.  I also would have liked more opportunities to just pound some baddies.
The supporting PCs are all unique and very well thought out - you will be interested in your followers, their objectives, and what they have to say.
The leveling system felt a bit thin - most of the combat abilities weren't terribly useful in my "jack" (rogue type) playthrough.
The whole "tide" system felt really undeveloped - supposedly your behavior opened up options that you might not have had otherwise, but even after finishing the first playthrough I wasn't really sure whether it made any difference at all.
Overall, I was mildly disappointed, but the original set the bar very, very, high.  I still recommend the game on its own merits.

This game has raised the bar for me, with regards to representation. I've never before had the opportunity to play as a trans character, outside of web-only minigames. This is also the first time I've seen a canonically trans major non-player-character in a game, portrayed sympathetically. (And his story isn't all /about/ being trans either; it's just one detail in a fully-fledged character.)
I also appreciate that there's a fat character whose fatness is not the subject of derision, jokes, nor scrutiny. He's treated as attractive and strong and good. That's... unusual in media.
At least five of the dads are also of colour. I'm not in a position to speak expertly on the impact of the racial diversity in this game, being white, but it's another selling point that I don't wanna not mention either.
Overall my main complaint about this game is that it's relatively short; I'd love to see further expansion on the stories, maybe more dates, or more route options, in future. However, there's a good six to ten hours of gameplay in it, which combined with the emotional impact of finally seeing some folks like myself in a game, makes it well worth the money for me.
(My other complaint would be some quibbles about how Joseph's third date goes; but to detail those would be spoilers. I think there's some possible consent issues with not giving the player an "I don't want to do this right now" type option. I'll leave it at that.)
[ Edit to add: after reading some other reviews, I'll also agree that the Dadsona creator leaves you with a slightly odd-looking character. I'm hoping that this, too, gets a little more polish once the devs have a chance to address it. ]
Now I'm looking at other games and wondering, how can I go back to this, knowing what representation feels like?
So yeah TL;DR: this game raised the bar for me and was very much worth it.

I own a handful of challenging puzzle games that I (foolishly) play to relieve stress, only to have it backfire when I reach difficult levels. A good friend gifted me this game, and I was excited to it out. I was very satisfied with my gameplay experience.
If you like challenging puzzle games, uplifting/relaxing music (especially piano scores), and microbiology, then you will enjoy Splice.
The aesthetics are simple, yet offer a nice presentation with vibrant colors. All of the microbial pieces are the same shape, however, the shape you have to make varies slightly per stage. The music is wonderful - the piano pieces are relaxing and very pleasant to listen to.
The controls are very easy to learn and only require the mouse - you will utilize the left/right clicks and the scroll wheel. There is a basic tutorial to teach you how to play, and the learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your familiarity with puzzle games. The game has a very fair pace of gradually increasing the difficulty and adds new gameplay mechanics at appropriate intervals.
Gameplay consists of you taking pieces from a microbial and rearranging it to match a picture - the catch is you must do this within a set number of moves. "Angelic" stages signify the possibility of completing a level without using all of your allotted moves (this is indicated by an angelic portrait at the bottom left of the screen. These drive me crazy whenever I try to figure out the precise move you have to make. You can reset your level progress, or rewind/fast-forward time with the mouse scroll wheel.
As you progress through the stages, new mechanics are added to increase the difficulty. For example, one of the first new elements you will encounter is a "splitter" piece, which duplicates itself (including anything and everything attached below it) when you right-click. An "arrow" piece adds one more microbial piece beneath it when you right-click. Any right-click moves do not count as "action points," and you will actually have to do these first to solve a few of the puzzles. The latter levels add a very interesting mechanic -
Overall, the game is a very nice casual and relaxing puzzle game, and anyone interested in the genre will find enjoyment. Experienced and new puzzle enthusiasts should definitely give this game a try.
Recommend!

This game kept everything that made Arkham City amazing and added upon it. Here's a list of pros and cons that I've experienced during the game:
Pros:
1. The new detective vision allows far more interesting interactions with crime scenes and now actually requires effort to solve a case.
2. Fast travel is now available to compensate for the larger city
3. Superior story telling. This game tells a fantastic story of Batman's  beginnings and lets you see into the internal struggles of Joker. In terms of story and character presentation, Origins well surpassed its predecessor.
4. Much improved graphics including higher texture resolution, dynamic lighting and ambient occulsion.
5. Far more optimized than Arkham City for the PC, better performance overall
6. More gadgets provide more ways to terrorize your enemies
7. More complex city geometry with multiple layers
Cons:
1. Bugs. Even though bugs still exists, they are more or less small glitches that are less likely to be game breaking. Of the 20 hours of gameplay there have only been 1 time where a bug actually got me into trouble.
2. Factial animation. While most of the characters have impressive facial animations, for some reason a few characters just never got the same effort put in to them. Gordon and Alfred talks without ever moving a facial muscle, which feels quite creepy...
3. Somewhat shorter in length compares to Arkham City, less side quests and shorter main story.
4. Grapple lock feels less accurate than its predecessor, aiming of your grapple can be a serious issue when you are trying to do some fast swings.
Overall I am incredibly pleased with the game, if you still have doubts, pick it up after it goes on a steep sale, which is likely to happen soon due to the relatively low sales figures...

Arkham Origins is a slice of greasy pizza after a meal of medium-rare steak and wine. Sure, it's not outright
, but it leaves the pallet unsatisfied. The combat felt off in Origins and for the longest time I had trouble figuring out why. But during the halfway point, I think I figured it out: The baddie placement. In the previous games, lots of care had been taken in picking which baddies work in what amounts and when special enemies were needed. Here it seems like more of a copy-paste job, carelessly throwing in specials even if their abilities severely hinders the combat. It leads to a lot of frustration and eagerness to get out of combat, something the series hasn't had an issue with until now.
In terms of new content, Arkham Origins is kind of bare bones. You have a majority of your old weapons available to you very early and some new ones that, unfortunately, don't mean much in combat. Some of the items feel completely shoehorned in, such as the Sonic Batarang. Not only did it seemingly just appear in my inventory, but there is never any sort of need for it or tactical advantage for using it. So why is it here?
The story is fairly muddled. It starts off with Black Mask hiring 8 supervillanous hitmen to take you down on Christmas Eve. Why Christmas Eve? "Who cares" is the answer the game gives. The story actually rehashes some villains, such as Bane, the Riddler, the Penguin, and Deadshot. Unfortunately there isn't much to talk about when it comes to the plot without getting into spoilers. It's not exactly clear why Black Mask hired the assassins in the first place and by the end of the game it's even more confusing. Topping that off, the game ends seemingly out of nowhere, in what I thought was the beginning of the third act. It just sort of stops.
There are still a handful of graphical errors and strange Not to mention several game-stopping glitches I encountered in-game despite the titles having been out for 5 months.
I don't really think fans of the last two Arkham games will get much out of Arkham Origins, it feels like microwave leftovers. The only people I would recommend this to are die-hard fans of the games or Batman in-general, and even then I would recommend getting it at a low price.
Also can I mention that the game DOESN'T HAVE A ♥♥♥♥ING MOUSE SENSITIVY SETTING?

It's been more than a decade since Remedy's Max Payne first debuted on 2001. One would expect the game to "feel" quite old and "outdated" in many aspects, if played today, and rightfully so. But Max Payne was not exaty remembered for its graphics, which many players seem to use as a "litmus test" to choose a game.
Max Payne was known for its seemingly unique gameplay, especially for its implementation of Bullet Time, being one of the first games to implement it in-game, and of course, sorta layed the groundwork for the games in future who would go on to include it into their own games too. The shooting mechanisms can be wonky at times but never "gamebreaking".
Gameplay was just another famous features of Max Payne. However, it was mostly known for its beautiful, dark, yet exiting story that is narrated in such passion and feeling, it really grips you into the game, making you to actually "feel" for Payne's suffering. Max Payne's gritty story coupled with fantastic narration by the protagonist himself makes max Payne one of the best games of all time. Especially in the department of "Story Telling". The game has aged so well in that aspect, and can only be judged upon when played. When it comes to the current gen of games,  Only a few titles (let alone AAA titles) give their heart out in the "Story Telliing" aspect of the game.
I'd defenitely recommend Max Payne to anyone looking for a great narrative thats coupled with equally great gameplay.
And I'd defenitely reccomend anyone or everyone to buy the Max Payne Bundle that includes both 1 & 2, especially when on sale.

Starting off as a seemingly basic third person shooter,  Spec Ops: The Line twists itself into a horrific tale of  a Delta Force Operator, Captain Walker, as he battles not only his foes, but his mind. As you progress through the game, you'll notice the story striding away from the default "shoot em up" style games that it appears to be when you first start playing it. I'm a pretty casual guy and I rarely take games (or anything, for that matter) seriously. Only a handful of games like Fallout and other immersive RPG's will I really get in to. THIS is one of those games that surprisingly made that list. For those of you that are reading this in 2015 or later, I promise you the age of this game does not hinder it at all. The graphics are impressive and the gameplay is solid, for the most part.
There's no real way to describe this game other than by calling it a journey, this game was meant to be experienced, not played. The title has real meaning to it once you beat the game. All I will say is, as you experience the game, at a certain point along the way, you'll cross a line, and when you cross that line......you'll understand what everyone in this review section is talking about.

I wasn't sure how this one was gonna go:  it is either a tentative recommend or a just barely, spend a paragraph trying to sell you on the game anyway, ...unrecommend.   Ultimately, there is enough of a cool game here for me to keep putting time into it.
The games name is strange, don't worry about it.  Here's what jumps out:  Action RPG.  The game is an FPS action rpg.  It looks like an ASCII Minecraft, but has all the ARPG symptoms.
XP grind?  GODDAMN RIGHT SON.  Your skills increase as you use them.  Pick some pockets dawg, raise that stat.
Loot? Yo, the big guy over there wielding a sword with fangs that one shotted the NPC from your faction?  You take his life, you take his blade.
"... But clizzy, this dudes sword SUCKS BALLS dewd!"  Yeah, it happens.  But you can sell that piece in almost any area.  Items scale with the enemies, who scale with the zone.  You're in a level 9 zone, the level 9 enemies drop level 9♥♥♥♥♥♥that usually be sellin' for a pretty penny even when they are booty butter.  This is awesome because....
There's mad cool♥♥♥♥♥♥to loot in this game!  This is my favorite part:  your character can equip jet packs and grappling hooks that give you crazzzzzzzzy mobility.  You can fly into sky fortresses, or zip around the landscape with non-stop grapple shots.  Thing is, though, these ♥♥♥♥♥es also scale.  Level 1 hooks/packs can be used when holding 40 weight, no more.  Every level adds an additional 40 lbs.   It's cool zipping into a high level zone, on a mad hunt for the shopkeeper or drop zone with the clutch twink grappling hook/jet pack.  You have to get out alive too, because when you die you lose an item.  The game is sadistic, it will eliminate the item you hold most dear.
I suppose I wish the game felt more complete.  I've put some goodly time into it and I'm not sure if there is anything else to do but loot grind.  The building mechanic?  No idea what's going on there.  Completely arbitrary, in my experience.

There's a little bit of RNG involved with quest givers having to give you a specific reward to advance - it can get a little frustrating.   Hunting for the right people always devolved into loot grinding and murdering things.  This was really fun for a bit, and I'll probably sit down a few more times to see just deep the game goes, but it becomes nothing more than pure carrot-sticking.   Still hours of fun.

I would call ‘3079 – Block Action RPG,’ a ‘cult-classic’ even though it’s still fairly new.  The reason I say that is because I feel that you’re either going to love this game or hate it.  Personally, I could not get into it.  I restarted the game about 12 different times, each time seeing if I had ‘missed’ something or simply didn’t understand the concept.  However, even after 12 times, I continued to scratch my head – wondering about the many facets of this game.
I really loved the music, it does a great job driving-home the ‘futuristic’ vibe of the game.  I also love the ‘mechanics’ to the game.  You progressively get better at skills in the game by doing them – don’t like your terrible aim with that rifle, then keep shooting at things (all the things!).  I also noticed that the game included skills such as ‘mining’ and ‘stealing,’ which is awesome!
Though, I believe what ruined this game for me was the story and setting; I think that’s what made me restart the game so times, too.  The, seemingly, inconsistent size of the NPCs, the strange location of buildings (yes, I realize it’s a randomly generated world, but there needs to be some consistency for an RPG), and the way items are distributed to the player (randomly generated on the ground, just sitting there or sold by a vendor – very inconsistent).  I tried to discover the reason, but it didn’t appear to be laid out anywhere obvious to the player, no in-game ‘books’ to discover with clues, no conversation with NPCs to help get answers.  The world needs to be 'plausible,' (not to be confused with possible) and the developer has not achieved that.
I feel that a video game has the same mark that books, movies, and television bear – these outlets have a very small window of opportunity to grab their audience, if they miss that window it’s gone.  For me, ‘3079 – Block Action RPG’ missed that opportunity, and I really wish it hadn’t.

What can be said about Undertale that has't already been said.  This game is an instant classic, and will likely be referenced and used as a shining example of gaming acheivement for decades!  Choices TRULY matter.  The game learns who you are and how you play, and IT REMEMBERS IT FOREVER!!!  ....or at least until you delete the local data for the game.  But, still, it references things you did that you wouldn't think a game would keep track of.
It also actually really makes you care about the story and the characters.  I remember in the old days when I felt something when a character died in a game's story.  It felt like I had lost something, but it was meant to hapen.  Undertale makes you feel like you acheived something great when you do something good, and it makes you feel like a horrible human being when you do something wrong... like terrible.  Even when you know you are able to, and in some ways encouraged to (for completions sake) go the "bad" things, you still feel like garbage for doing it!
Finally, the music is phenominal!  I know some of it is sampled from other games (kind of...), but I don't care.  A game's music can make or break the experience.  Even if the music is great on its own, if it doesn't properly convey the mood or theme of the story or situation, it can completely emove the immersion you felt while playing.  Undertale has the best of both worlds:  I can listen to the soundtrack on its own AND it melds well with the mood of the game!
Overall, a must play for any gamer.  And  dare you not to feel something by the end of this game!

My first reaction to this game was crazy positive.  I'm an old-school RPG guy and it checks off all of my boxes.  Unfortunately, it's sitting on my hard drive unfinished and unplayed for months.
I just don't feel compelled to go back to it.  Why?  I don't mind text-walls but there's very little game-play outside of the dialogue boxes.  The writing is meant to be the big draw of the game, but it's wildly overwritten.  It aims for flavorful but ends up being obtuse, even pretentious.  The density of the text also makes re-starting feel like a slog.  And you will re-start.  Character choices, both in the beginning and at advancement, aren't meaningfully explained, and there's no respec option (to my knowledge). The infrequent combats feel more like puzzles than fights.  It's is the only respite from Torment's relentless purple prose, but it's easilly the most irritating part of the game.
While it's admirable that this game is trying to do something different, the end result just isn't fun.

I thoroughly enjoyed my first playthrough, and plan to do at least 2 complete others.
Beware, this is a text heavy game, and there is very little "action", so to speak. I personally loved it.
I liked talking or sneaking my way through crisis. I may have had to fight at some points, but it was due to my choices, I believe.
I liked the level up system. I loved that combat didn't really matter as far as XP is concerned, and that you don't have to grind to advance the story.
I liked every single companion you can recruit, their respective storylines, and their relationships with each other.
I enjoyed each and every interraction with NPCs, even though sometimes I felt limited in my choices, and more annoyingly, I coudn't act on the knowledge I gleaned from reading thoughts most of the time.
The story and universe were compelling and very interesting, if a bit short.
All that said, there are a few thing I didn't really like.
First is the feeling that my choices were deeply meaningful to my character and their companions, but not that much to the world at large, and most importantly, not that much to the end of the game.
Second is the difficulty. The game was much too easy. Most of the time you can't really fail, and even if you don't try to make a good combattant, you most likely end up being a monster. I honestly breezed through every crises but one, and even that one felt difficult because the others were so easy that a medium difficulty one seems tough.
Third is the length. The story was very very interesting, as stated above, but I think it could have benefitted from a longer development, or maybe branches. Because that was quite linear, which is a bit of a shame given the kind of game it is.
But other than that, I had some of the best time I had lately playing a game. There are a few bugs here and there, but they are mostly inconsequential or easily bypassed.
I must admit, 45€ is a bit much for what is there at the time of this review, but I know that more content is coming, and that it is included in the price. So I'm pretty sure it will be worth it sooner rather than later.
All in all, I would give this game a 8/10. Solid gameplay, marvelous world, wonderful NPCs and companions, possibility to never actually hit anyone would have made this a 9 or 10, but the shortness of the story and botched difficulty make it an 8.

**Note: This review is for SOLO gameplay. I believe co-op would be different.**
Hmm, playing the game actually felt like a chore. Even though I enjoyed BL1 and put a lot of hours into it (unknowingly), completing lots of side missions and kept upgrading my weapons, completing all DLCs etc, I feel that unless you TRULY LOVED the genre, playing either one of the two is sufficient.
I played the entire campaign solo. Even though the game is open for co-op play, I don't like how the game turned out extremely hard for solo players. Dark Souls was tough, but NEVER unfair, and I even enjoyed myself when constasntly dying to bosses and even laughed at how bad I was. Borderlands 2 felt different: it felt really unfair. You are usually swarmed with mobs such that you rely heavily on your special to actually put up a fight. Gameplay basically came down to 2 factors: your level and your weapon. The damage you do and the damage you take scales drastically with your level. I remember being stuck at a boss fight (Bloodwing) for 3 hours because I was so underleveled and got 1-shotted all the time, until I leveled up (from the mobs that spawn in the boss fight) and I defeated her in 1 attempt.
I was almost always underleveled throughout the campaign as I chose not to do most of the side missions. Most of them were really repetitive and usually involved traveling to a location and killing things/ collecting things/ a mixture of both. (I did more than 20 side missions for an achievement so I believe I didn't generalise.) After experiencing the likes of such mundane missions in BL1 I had no intention to grind yet again. Regretably, these missions also yield much more experience compared to say, those that you get from killing mobs as you progress through the campaign. Hence the being underleveled and the dying lots of times. However, even when my level was on par, I still get overwhelmed by endless mobs (especially the Hyperion loaders), and things like ION loaders setting up a force field when I was in FFYL (solo play, mind you) really got on my nerves.
*My Recommended Changes*
I think a gameplay element that could be implemented is the option to enable bots as teammates. This shouldn't be too overpowered since co-op with friends are allowed, even recommended anyway. While bots don't usually make the best game decisions, at the very least they would draw some enemy fire and that itself is already a welcoming change. Also, I feel that optional missions should stay optional, and the player should not feel forced to complete them to level. (Come on, of course I read reviews and googled etc when I felt the game was too harsh and the universal answer people gave was: do side missions to level up some.) As such, a second change could be the matching of campaign missions to the player's current level so one could actually progress smoothly. While concerns such as people rushing the game might arise, I feel that this is utimately a game and a player should have the right to choose how he wants to approach it, campaign only or a 100% run. Those are just my 2 cents.
As for comparisions to BL1, I felt that the graphics in BL2 were very much improved. While the inventory would require getting used to, everything was very smooth mechanically (unless you die repeatedly like me, then the dying-to-respawning animation can be a pain). The boss fights were very dynamic, bosses themselves memorable (magestic, even). However, it was kinda sad I had to resort to cheesy strats such as finding safe zones and snipe for 10 minutes straight till the boss dies. (Except for bloodwing which I actually had to move LOL.)
Would ONLY recommend if:
1) You truly enjoyed BL1 and are prepared for the similar side missions it offered;
2) You didn't play BL1 and are willing spend a long time on the title {more than 2x average gamelength}; or
3) You have friends to play co-op with.
6/10 solo play. Felt like a chore. Games shouldn't feel like a chore.

Splice is an unconventional puzzle game that has you rearranging cells (pieces) to form branches in order to recreate the  silhouette behind it. Similar to how you look at the box when assembling a picture puzzle. Only instead of pieces, you have long cells. Each end of these cells can have only one or two cells attached. Think of it like -- is one cell attached to another cell, while -< is one cell that has two cells attached to it. This is what makes your puzzle look like a an upside-down tree. The root cell cannot be moved. Every other cell can be clicked and dragged to reconnect onto another cell as long as it doesn't already have two cells attached. Its easy to do, but not as easy to explain.
Each puzzle is limited to how many splices (moves of cells) you can do, but there is no time limit. When you run out of splices, you need to restart or rewind the puzzle... even if you run out of splices as you finish the puzzle. The real downside is no replay value. The puzzles will always be the same.
Once you get a few puzzles in, the game will start throwing in three different types of special cells for you to master. That's where things get complicated. First up is what I'll call a dead cell marked with an X. Like every other cell you can move it, but when you click the root cell, it will remove the dead cell and everything after it. Next up is a pusher cell. When you click on the root cell, the next pusher cell down the line will push out, making a new cell attached to the pusher and turning the pusher cell into a normal cell.
The final special cell is the cloner cell, which will divide itself into two normal cells when you click the root cell. Everything following the cloner cell will be cloned as well. If there are two branches after the cloner, then there will be two exact copies. The cloner cell can be the only cell attached to the previous cell, because it splits in two. So it can only go at the end of the line. If you have multiple special cells and you click the root cell, the next special cell down the line will activate. So if you have a cloner cell 2nd in line on a left branch with a pusher cell on the right branch, that cloner cell will divide on the first click, the pusher will push out on the second.
When things get complicated with the special cells, the game can become trial and error. You'll end up memorizing what you did to get where you are and having to remember everything you did to fail the puzzle. By rolling the mouse wheel you can easily rewind time and try again from there. Its never frustrating because of the music and the atmosphere. There is a soothing, relaxing vibe in the game. You're looking at beautiful vivid colors while trying to solve a black tree of a puzzle. Soothing subtle piano plays to help keep out the real world from interrupting your puzzle. Even the menus fit the rich art style the game has. Nothing was able to break me out of the immersion.
The main game is divided into two halves. The first half is called Origin and its split up into 7 sequences for the main part of the game, each with 7 puzzles. These puzzles are fun, easy, but they do get challenging. Once you complete the Origin main game, the credits roll and the game unlocks 4 more sequences of 7 puzzles for the Epilogue half of the game. These puzzles are far more difficult.
For me, this was about 2 or so hours worth of 49 puzzles. They felt just challenging enough to get stumped on some of the later ones, but still overcome. The 28 after that were just too difficult for me, but that's me and not you. Perhaps if I enjoyed the game more I'd tough out the others. Replaying the game only went by faster. There's just no replay value once you're done. Splice could come out with puzzle packs for the the fans out there, its only 24 more puzzles until 101! I recommend the developer's other game Fractal much more than this.
If you're into puzzlers (like SpaceChem or the like), this one should be on your list.  Quite enjoyable, limited mechanics to consider and beautiful on many levels.

It took me a few runs through Heavy Bullets to understand what it wanted out of me. Those few runs were very, very short, brutal and frustrating, until I understood that this roguelike FPS had a depth to it that belied it's simplistic polygonal graphics and LSD-inspired color palette.
It took me those first few runs to realize that sprinting in guns blazing is not an approach that pays off here. Instead, you creep forward, peeking around corners to catch a glimpse of an enemy turret's weak spot, or one of those dastardly worms hiding almost in plain sight in the undergrowth.
You hear the bark of an imp that you know is coming screaming towards you at speed, but you haven't got a bead on which direction it's coming from yet. You spin, spot the imp that's right on top of you and squeeze off a single round, all in the blink of an eye. You know that there's a medbay a little ways back, but you also know that you're going to have to press onward to find the money to buy the heal you so desperately need.
Heavy Bullets is *tense*, and it rewards your patience, care and attention to detail. It puts finely calibrated constraints on  every aspect of the game, from your limited titular bullets (a mere six rounds) that you can pick back up off the ground where they fall, to the single-item inventory that has you wondering whether you should have left that armor pickup and taken the megabomb instead. The powerups available for purchase are similarly well balanced, with you never quite sure that you made the right choice. Should you have bought the life insurance that will carry forward some of your money into your next run, or gone hell-for-leather and stocked up on a bigger inventory and a pocketful of rockets?

Ok. So it looks like Minecraft in space, spawning a whole lot of U RIPD OFF MINECRAFT posts in the forums. It does look like minecraft. But it is nowhere near a rip off. Its not even remotely the same game. Now dont get me wrong, I love Minecraft and have owned it since late alpha. So another similar-looking game isnt bad in my book.
Now for the review.
As I said, it looks like Minecraft. Its a procedurally generated 3d block game, where the world/items are different every single time. So big 3d blocks with texures, prodecurally generated huge maps.
But thats where the similarities end. Its a space-RPG for starters. And all the quests and stuff are randomly generated, as far as the quest structure, it runs more like Daggerfall (without the horrid bugs). Ein Action-RPG, angesiedelt in der fernen Zukunft. Der Spieler strandet auf einem hart umkämpften Planeten, wo er den freundlichen Humoids in ihrem Krieg gegen die Neanders und böse Dämonen zur Seite steht, sowohl zu Lande, als auch in der Luft. Die auf Voxel basierende Grafik ist stark von Minecraft inspiriert und dementsprechend besteht die Landschaft aus Blöcken und ist extrem verpixelt. Ebenso können manche Blöcke zerstört und neue Blöcke oder auch Fahrstühle und bewaffnete Türme mit dem entsprechenden Werkzeug gesetzt werden, allerdings nur in begrenztem Maß, ist das Werkzeug aufgebraucht muss ein neues her. Das Spielprinzip erinnert stark an Titel wie Borderlands: Es gilt dutzende Items zu sammeln, darunter verschiedene Arten von Schilden, Medikits und Radars sowie diverse Arten von Waffen, wobei manche wie bei Borderlands durch zusätzliche Effekte entweder mehr Schaden austeilen oder dem Spieler z.B. durch schnellere Energieaufladung helfen. Auch das Levelsystem erinnert an Borderlands. Die Waffen verbrauchen keine Munition, sondern Energie. Je stärker die Waffe, desto mehr Energie wird pro Schuss verbraucht. Ist der Energiebalken leer, muss einen Moment gewartet werden, bis er sich ausreichend aufgeladen hat. Dem kann der Spieler durch das Sammeln und Aktivieren von Generatoren und Batterien entgegenkommen. Seine Aufträge erhält der Spieler von den sogenannten "Leaders" der Humoids, welche mit einem Stern markiert sind. Überschüssige Items können bei den mit einem Dollar-Zeichen markierten "Merchants" gegen Credits, die Spielwährung, verkauft werden. So findet man sich ratzfatz in einem absoluten Sammelwahn wieder, immer auf der Jagd nach noch besseren und schlagkräftigeren Items.
FAZIT: Man erhält hier viel Spaß für wenig Geld und Festplattenplatz. Für Fans von Minecraft und (vorallem!) Borderlands ist dieser Titel definitiv einen Blick wert! Vorallem aber auch, weil es durch sein Oldschool-Spielprinzip und die verpixelte Grafik an die guten alten Zeiten erinnert, als ein Spieler nicht nur kurz in Deckung gehen musste, um sich zu erholen.

I just finished this game and enjoyed it pretty much. It is a successor of Planescape: Torment in a way that it is an exploratory game. T:TON is about discovering the denizens of the sixth world, finding clever solutions to people's problems, using junk you found on the way to invent new solutions. It is fantastic, the quests are well thought-out, the game truly shines in this aspect, every quest has several solutions, you can find another one and another one way to get what you want. You can see the amount of love and care that was sunk into this game and it really makes a difference.
To add to this the designers managed to solve a problem as old as crpgs: How to avoid ruining the whole experience by saving/restoring. It is pretty hard to die, yet characters have three pools which they can use to solve different tasks which refresh every time they sleep. If you sleep a lot, you can solve every problem that can arise, with a little twist: Some quests change when you sleep, some goals become unattainable as time passes. This system is brilliant and most likely will become a new basic mechanic for crpgs.
The world itself is beautiful and exciting, however I feel it is a bit fragmented, some cohesion would have made it even better. Several companions can be hired, most of them are interesting, and have rich backstories. The story of the game is enjoyable, not as great as P:T's but still entertaining and iimmersive.
Considering everything I can only recommend this game to everyone.

I remember playing a bit of Planescape:Torment back in the day, but I don't really remember it that well.  So I came at Torment: Tides of Numenera from a fresh perspective, I also know that spiritual successor doesn't mean direct sequel.  So I wasn't expecting one.  I have to say that I was almost immediately immersed in this game.  The Numenera setting is a mind blowing, imagination inspiring setting that I have had such an amazing time in this game.
I'm about 30 or so hours in on my first play through, and I really don't want it to come to a close.  I'm also, for the first time in a while, feeling fairly conflicted about which paths to choose, because the consequences of my actions actually seem to carry weight.
The combat is simple, but can be challenging as well.  I'm playing a nano, and I've just reached tier 4, so I've got some pretty sweet abilities.  But I actually get more fun out of trying to avoid combat if I can.  My next playthrough will be on a Glaive (the warrior class) and we'll see how differently it plays from that angle.
This is quickly becoming one of my favorite cRPGs in recent times, easily eclipsing Tyranny (Tyranny was great, but really really left me wanting more), Pillars of Eternity was good too, but came off a tad generic.  Again, for me, the star of this game really is the setting of the Ninth World, and the ecclectic mix of characters, settings, and abilities you'll find there.  I highly recommend you give this game a try.  Once you make it through the first hour and half or so, you'll be hooked.

I backed this game on KS ... it was actually the reason I even got a Kickstarter account! I had extremely high hopes and that might be part of my problem with the game now.  Planescape was - for me - the best computer RPG ever. Memorable setting, characters, stories ... Torment tries to carry on that tradition and in my opinion fails.
It's not about the graphics, it's not about some of the strange design decisions (combat ... amongst other things). It's about writing. Writing made Planescape such a great game and Torment is lacking in writing. It tries to reach Planescape, but it fails. A lot of overblown dialogue, trying to sound meaningful, hiding the fact that it is not under big words and extravagance.
Memorable characters? Have not found many yet ...
The setting? I could get into Planescape because despite the world being strange, I could relate to it.
This one here? Too much ... trying too hard to be strange.
Interface feels clunky in many ways, too. Granted, old RPGs had that problem, too. But it does not have to be that way. Why should I live with "old" graphics, "old" interface ... etc? It's 2017 now...

Have you ever wondered, why ETS2 is one of the most played games on Steam? You should have, as there is no way getting around this wonderful simulator, at least not if you want to be a real PCGamer... but what makes that sim-game so special?
Euro Truck Simulator makes it easy for any new players to jump right in and is very suitable for beginners as the options allow for massive customization when it comes to how realistic the game shall be. Talking about beginners, you don't need to have the latest and greatest PC in order to enjoy the game, it even runs on a five year old Intel HD Graphics but trust me, if you're lucky enough to own a high-end graphics card/ a decent rig in general, you will be able to push the graphics to a level on which you might be able to forget that you are just playing a video game! Anyways, if you don't want to sleep, you don't have to, just remove the mark in front of the fatigue simulation and you are free to drive for how long you want! But if you're one of those players, who would give everything for realism, you will also be absolutely pleased by what ETS2 has to offer. Let it be the fuel consumption of your truck or the air brake system, the possibilities for realism fanatics are endless. At that point, I should also mention that the game has great support for various steering wheels and TrackIR to give you the best possible driving experience. It is also possible, to mod the heck out of your personal Euro Truck Simulator version, in order to make it your very own experience. For those of you that aren't very interested in modding, you can also purchase a wide array of DLC packages that will add new parts of Europe or some new tuning options. Some of the best DLC that I can recommend at this point are the Scandinavia DLC as an example for a map expansion and the Mighty Griffin DLC that makes the stock Scania trucks almost look as awesome as some of the modded ones do.
But does that mean that the game is flawless? No, it's not. Considering the AI drivers' behavior or some of the old parts of the map, there are some minor problems here and there but they definitely don't brake the game or make it unplayable. Just enjoy the game and listen to some of your music in the background, you will not regret it!
UPDATE: ETS2 is still one of the best games on the market! :D

An interesting little game with a very nice, if somewhat repetitive soundtrack.
There is nothing in the way of a tutorial, but the game does a pretty good job of introducing you to new concepts so it doesn't get confusing. It doesn't waste time with context or even a bare-bones story- just a pack of puzzles with some fun mechanics. It's short but remains challenging throughout. For what is is, I can't recommend paying full price for this, but if you can get it for under five dollars it's a few hours worth of enjoyment if you like puzzle games.

Overall, an enjoyable puzzle game. The graphics and overall visual style make it fun to interact with the puzzles and are just visually pleasing to watch. The way the mechanics are slowly introduced prevent it from being too frustrating.
What makes the puzzles especially engaging is how it plays as they become more complex. In some puzzle games, it just becomes an invitation to "brute force" a solution, which is not very fun and tends to be frustratingly boring. In this game, however, the puzzles each seem to have several "insights" that you can discover as you play around, which you can then use to develop a solution. The rewind mechanic makes this discovery process much easier and more pleasant - for example, if you find all of your splices used up but your result is really close to the end goal, you can rewind and keep trying different things to try to "fix" your splices until you get the answer. You can also take the approach of trying to discover useful properties about each puzzle as you experiment with different splices and exploit those properties to devise a solution.
So, not only are there multiple solutions - there's multiple, challenging and rewarding strategies you can take to discover those solutions without using brute force.
One downside is that the music seems to have only one track and is too short and played too often, however, which gets a bit annoying after awhile.
And despite beating the main game in 4 hours, I'm sure you can get a lot of additional play time out of the bonus levels (the "epilogue").

I took a sh-t on this game in my first review several years ago.
Seeing the curator recommendation below the very box where I'm typing this review, "a deliberately mundane shooter", reminds me of why I was so poisonous towards it in the first place: there's so much hype and expectation and unconvincing excuses surrounding this game that I had an impossible time approaching this game objectively.
But that still doesn't mean it was fair of me to look at it through such a filter. I recently reinstalled and gave it another go, no hype, no expectations, just letting the game be exactly what it is.
So, what is it? A mediocre shooter with a very good story and fantastic presentation, that is worth your time.
Seeing suggestions that "the developers made it boring on purpose" still makes my skin crawl and does a terrible disservice to the game. There's no way in hell that a developer has ever said "I'm having too much fun, dial it back, we don't want to distract people from the importance of our message". The fans helped bury this game with that kind of crap by forcing people to call them out, instead of letting the conversation be about what the game does right.
Now, gameplay isn't terrible, it performs competently as a 3PS despite an aching lack of variety. There's really not much to say about it, imagine if Gears of War had every weapon behave the same way, and there's like 3 types of enemies and they also don't really change things. I wouldn't go as far as calling it joyless, but it's never exciting.
What the game does do right is the presentation. There's a lot of care and detail that I took for granted on my first playthrough. Your squad, and your interactions with them, are great. The dialog got some genuine laughs but also works admirably in service of drama. There's a lot of unnecessary animations for humans in this game that make them look and behave believably, and it adds a lot of life.
The music rocks and strengthens everything it touches, be it a cutscene, a gunfight, or a menu.
The story has been praised to death, and I won't say it doesn't deserve the non-hyperbolic bits of it. Maybe books and movies consider it old hat, but it's largely unique for video games and it's done really well.
Graphics are nice, especially at 1440p. Everything is crisp, colorful, and worth admiring. The sand effects, be it in a storm, a breeze, or an avalanche, looks wonderful, and Dubai Proper looks awesome.
Overall, I recommend this game, and I especially recommend that you don't let anybody overinflate your expectations until they pop. It's not a life-changer, or especially fun, and it's especially not a damning indictment of modern AAA military shooters (oh my god shut the f-ck up), but it's still a very worthwhile piece of art that deserves your attention.

So I wasn't really expecting a lot out of this game. For those of you who don't know, the studio (rocksteady) that handled the first two Batman Arkham games wasn't involved in this one, causing many to cry foul and say "THIS ISN'T EXACTLY THE SAME SO I DON'T LIKE IT!!" I sort of let the negativity get to me, so it wasn't until I saw the game on super sale that I hesitantly went "Fine I guess." Now I am really glad that I did. The naysayers were correct in that it isn't as good as the last installment. Arkham City in my opinion was damn near perfect, and Arkham Origins does more than take one step back. But I am still incredibly engaged in the story and liking the game itself. It was a bit strange at first, as it is the prequel to the first two batman games. Everyone is just starting off in their new character roles, which might be appealing to some. In Batman Arkham City, the characters had been around long enough, that when the Joker spoke of "his biggest plan yet" you actually went 'oh s***, this is gonna get messy!" Because it is Joker in the early days, you don't get the same menacing feel. He's fresh off the press, and doesn't have a menacing track record yet. The game makes up for it however, by providing more explanation behind his origin story, and you even get to see him meet the lady who later becomes Harley Quinn.
As good as the game is, the one complaint I have is the combat. Arkham Asylum's combat was great, and Arkham City did a good job of maintaining the same feel while adding a few new tricks. However, to those who have played Arkham City (which I really strongly recommend) it feels lackluster. In Arkham City I took every chance I could get to engage in a brawl with some thugs. Now, if it is easy to do, I avoid them. The worst part of this is that the game still does it's best to be like "LOOK HOW AMAZING OUR COMBAT SYSTEM IS!" by throwing you into a bunch of encounters with goons.

I'll try to be as on point and brief as possible about my main gripes:
Skill system.
In conversations you often have the option to use intellect, speed and might to get whichever result you find most appealing.
This is a good thing. The problem occurs when your companions can help you with this, because the overall difficulty is below meaningless.
It's like it's designed to not let you fail. Even if you do fail one skillcheck, you'll be provided with a second chance or simply getting what you wanted either way by some other conversation option.
Add to this that you have more than enough chances to Rest and replenish your stat pools, or simply using "heal potions" for any given stat pool. The money to buy any of this is also very abundant.
Combat/Crisis:
The difficulty here depends a bit on how you build your character and choice of companions, but it's never come off as very challenging in any way.
The system itself feels sluggish and slow as I spend 99% of the time in a crisis looking at the enemy go through it's movement/attack animations.
Story:
Decent? I don't know.. I haven't finished the game, nor am I likely to.
I've been a fan of all the infinity engine games (IWD,BG,PS:T) since their first release and always loved a game rich on lore and dialogue/interaction.. but ToN is just disappointing and bland.
The writing is so try-hard that it's actually tedious and it feels like the writers sat down with the intention of writing something that is really just difficult to get through.
For all the fancy words, phrases and variety of vocabulary it transfers very little meaning.
I guess some like that though, to be swimming in a sea of words and phrases just to describe a wooden spoon.
Conclusion:
It just feels like a missed chance at making something great, it's mediocre at best.. and I wish I hadn't paid for it.

Admittedly I haven't got very far into TTON yet, but what I've seen so far hasn't impressed me a great deal.
I am a huge fan of Planescape Torment, though I've never claimed it to be a perfect game. PST suffered from an overabundance of trash fights, but made up for it by having some of the best video game writing I've ever seen.
As a successor to PST, TTON fails in many areas. Every character in PST, from party members to random NPCs on the streets of Sigil, were extremely memorable. In TTON, characters usually serve only as lore dispensers, lacking interesting personality or anything particuarly interesting to say.
The issue of lore dumpy, boring characters is compounded by generally poor writing. There is an overabundance of "purple prose", that is text excessively extravagant, that often feels like it was just added to increase the length of a lore dump. PST was also fond of extravagant description, but Chris Avellone managed to work within the setting so that the rich descriptions of the crazy planes immersed you in the setting, rather than frustrating you with another long lore dump.
The combat falls flat, much like its predecessor, though one improvement over PST is that there are far less "trash" fights, so in that at least, it is an improvement.  The combat is extremely slow, and the whole "one move and one combat action" system feels incredibly restricting. Divinity Original Sin had far better turn based combat than this (and most other recent TB games)
The stat system feels like a system that works in a P&P, but not a CRPG. You see all skill/stat checks regardless of your stat levels, and "spend" your stats to increase the chance of a successful attempt. This removes replayability, as all you need to do is save before a stat/skill check and reload until you pass, compared to say Fallout 1/2 and PST where extra options appeared based on your current stats. A super smart character gets no extra options over a dumb one, just an easier time passing the checks.
Overall, I am disappointed with this release. It might be salvageable, but it would take a lot of work.
