I've had my eye on this game for a while, being a very big fan of Torment. I bought it soon after its release and finished it just two days ago. Time for a small assessment.
This is the first hub of the game and by a long shot the most polished part of the game. It is fairly big with an adequate number of side quests and things to do. Truly, if the game had 2-3 more locations like Sagus Cliffs, we would be talking about a game much better than the present one.
Τhe game's side quests are in general interesting. They are sufficiently diverse and allow you to learn the world better. Better still, they almost always offer more than enough ways to resolve them.
The world of Numenera, without being Planescape, is nevertheless peculiar in a very interesting way. I would certainly like to see more games set in this world
From a gameplay perspective this is the game's highlight. I can't even remember how many times I've been annoyed with a cRPG because once a fight starts, 99% of the time the only way out is to slaughter everyone. Crisis resolves that. I've seen it referred as a combat system, but it's much more than just that. As the name suggests, it's a critical event management system. During a crisis you can do more than just fight, you can talk, interact with your environment etc, the goal is not to defeat your opponent, but to resolve the crisis. It's a shame the game doesn't have more of these crises and I would definitely want to see this system implemented in other such games.
In this game there are no alignments, there are though Tides. You can think of them as counters and each of them is affected by a different type of action. You love knowledge and learning? The Blue tide increases. You are charitable and gentle? The Gold tide increases. Etc. Your character starts balanced and depending on the sum of your actions you receive a dominant tide. This is a great idea. But when it comes to it's execution it leaves a few things to be desired, since it is rather unlikely to play such a game, in which you want to learn the story (and indeed you should) without the Blue tide becoming the dominant one. In the end the poor implementation didn't bother me much and it remains a positive because of the idea.
Unfortunately the 6 available companions generally disappoint. For me the most interesting one was Matkina, not because she is anything special, but because she is the only one that has an organic relationship with the story, has enough to say and can affect the ending. The rest are simply there. And they range from ok-ish, like Aligern, to downright terrible, like our resident homosexual Tybir. How terrible that last character is cannot be overstated. I'm not going to discuss the need for a "queer" character, we all know what kind of a SJW world we live in. I will say this though. You buffoons. You want to show to the world how ok it is to be gay. How it's nothing special, how it doesn't define one's personality etc. All this is good and fine, but you attempt to do that by giving the only gay companion in the game the side-quest about his love life? Are you that unhinged?
Unfortunately, even with my rather thorough and slow play style, the game ended in 30 hours. A duration that simply is unsatisfactory.
It seems that after Sagus Cliffs, money run out. The rest of the game's locations range from bad (Miel Avest), to indifferent (Necropolis), to simply unpolished (Bloom). The sum is unfortunately rather negative.
Of course in such a game, graphics are not a decisive factor. But then again I'm not saying we should be expecting another Witcher 3. Just something passable. Well nope. With the exception of a few nice backgrounds and companion portraits, everything else is a mess. From the character models, to every portrait that doesn't belong to a companion. In a crisis, when the game becomes turn-based and you can see at the top of the screen the portraits of everyone involved, this becomes particularly noticeable. Seriously they look as if they were created by an infant in paint, or at least by a graphic artist that recently lost his hands in an accident and had to finish them with his feet. Pity, Pillars of Eternity with less funding was much prettier.
What sound? Music=zero. And maybe 2-3 minutes of voiced dialogue total. This must be one of the most silent games I can remember playing lately.
Terrible UI, truly terrible. Clumsy, cluttered, unnecessary and ugly. And the same goes for the character development system. The whole focus there is in the combat system, but this game is not about combat. It's as if they designed this system for a different game.
And finally we reached the most serious flaw. The main story is weak. And in game like this, where the main story should have been its greatest strength, this is particularly disappointing. It doesn't have the necessary depth, it's not as personal as it should be to justify the title of Torment, it simply exists to exist. I can't say I hated it, with the exception of a certain twist that annoyed me a bit, in general it was just indifferent. As for the ending, indeed this can be chosen through a discussion right at the end and you can (with one exception I think) pick whatever ending you want. The game will simply comment whether your choice matches your conduct so far, by checking your dominant tide, but will let you go through with your choice nevertheless. I don't know if that's for the better or worse. Maybe indeed the ending should be locked based on your dominant tide, but with how unpolished the tide system is, it would be quite hard to see any ending other than the Blue one.
To sum things up, the game has potential, but in the end disappoints. For sure something went wrong during its development, I can't think of another explanation. Would I recommend it? It depends. If you get this game expecting another Torment simply forget about it. There is no relation and it's insulting that they are even using the name, or rather abusing it. If you get this game expecting a peculiar old-school game, the game will offer you a few good hours ending up somewhere on the average range. In other words yes, I do recommend this game, as long as one measures his expectations.
Here I should stress, that irrespective of the things I wrote above, if you backed this game on Kickstarter, then sucks to be you. You have every right to be furious.

I just finished my first playtrhough of the game and finished in around 34 hours of actual game play.  I did as nmany optional quests, maps, and more to explore the world, and I really enjoyed it.  I tried the game, aand after about an hour,I gave up and created a different character.  I saw that there were ways to avoid combat with dialogue and challenges, so I decided to embrace that and became a charming jack, with skills like persuasion and deception and then added perception for a talk-y character who gets out of things and can convience anyone of really anything.  And I would often go hours without combat.  Later when it was needed, I was able to slide my Jack heavy party into stealth ambushing, with a fun group of folks.  So I enjoyed the game.
Now mechanically, the game is limited to just three stats and classes, but the massive amount of skills and abilities helps out with that.  And combat is interesting, and you can stealth and flee, or try to find items to interact with to end teh encounter that way, so there's a lot of cleverness to that, but overall, the mechanics were about what you;d expect from these sorts of RPGs, from Wasteland  2 and Pillars to Baldur's Gate and Fallout.
Where the game really shines is the Ninth World.  It has a very bizarre, fleshed out, and detailed world, and better than the previous worlds.  It felt, in terms of flavor, like an odd cross between the original Planescape and the flavor of Sunless Sea.  In fact I found quite a large number of synergies in flavor from Torment: Tides of Numenera and Sunless Sea and Fallen London.  The flavor was sharp and totally on point, and the world was evocative.  It breathed.
So the result is a fun game, where you have a lot of options, and often I felt like prick becuase I;d choose something that kept my party together or my warrior...er...glaive...from heading off, and I had to be really antagonsitic about it too.  It had some nice moments where I didn't like myself.
Anyways, good game, with the expected amount of fun!

This game is probably the worst I've ever played. It seems that the devs really had no idea what they were doing.
Gameplay
The gameplay is medicore at best, and for a game who's selling point is gameplay, that's pretty bad. At worst, the gameplay is a broken mess. For example, there's something called "Second Wind" in which, if you kill an enemy in time, you don't die. That's a great idea. But, I can't tell you how many times I killed an enemy just as I got killed, and there were no enemies nearby to kill. No health packs that you can carry, so I'm basically screwed. Or, I'm in a boss fight, where it's only me and the boss, so what am I to do when I get knocked down? Also, I'd like to comment on how hard this game is. I'm not knocking it because it's hard, I'm knocking it because it's hard just by how badly it's designed. The only way to get adequate gear is to do the side quests. But the side quests are all monotonous fetch quests, so it can't keep my interest.
Graphics
Now, this game does not have bad graphics at all. If I didn't know any better, I'd say they spent all their time on graphics. The game looks nice. If you crouch and look at the ground, you start to see the pixels in the texture, but that's to be expected. The lighting and natural cloth movement is beautiful, it looks very nice. The art style is not really my taste, but other people like it. No one can knock this game for it's graphics. Hell, just the look of acid on the floor is amazing.
Story/Writing
Calling this games story a story is an insult to stories. This games story is so cookie cutter, it makes me want to scream. No, Handsome Jack is not a good villain, no, Pandora is not interesting, and no, the writing is not funny. Yes, I'll be the first to say it, since everyone else in this section seems to be kissing this games♥♥♥♥♥ The writing didn't make me even crack a smile. It's not funny at all. That is, unless you're in between the ages of 7-10 years old. Spongebob is legitimately way better written than this game.
Music/World
Pandora has to be one of the dullest worlds I've ever explored. There is so little going on, it hurts. A radio in the car would be nice, but no, that is not found. There's tons of different areas, like Tundra Area, Desert Area, and Urban Area. And the music is just as bad. It's like one guy got his banjo and recorded everything in an afternoon. It's bad. Very, very bad.
Summary
This game is not fun, it is not interesting, the only thing is has going for it is graphics, IF you like the art style. I give this game a 2/10, complete waste of money. I'm never buying another Gearbox game again, because this was an absolute MESS. And it makes me worry for the future of gaming when THIS has so many fans. Be sure to mark my review as Helpful if it swayed you, and with that, thank you for reading this

Splice is a pretty interesting puzzle game, in which you modify several strains of cells in order to solve the puzzle by forming the target strain. It has a very relaxing soundtrack, and the puzzles themselves are quite challenging; in some cases, they may be a little frustrating even. There were times I found the  solution by pure luck, and other times in which I stared at it for minutes without  knowing how to solve it.
It's still a good game, in my opinion, so I can recommend it.

Unfortunately, achievements and Steam Cloud features are broken on Linux, so I wouldn't recommend buying this game if that is your primary gaming platform. They appear to have been broken since the game's release in 2013 and the developers don't show any signs of moving to fix it.

This game serves as a testament to the indie gaming community's ability to constantly find new ways to draw me in and get me hooked on something worthwhile. Splice's immediate appeal is in it's visuals; minimalistic, smooth, and aesthetically pleasing. The relaxing and easy to listen to music make it even easier to get lost in the mind-flexing elegance of Splice. Successfully manipulating a strand or completing a sequence is often quite rewarding.
Splice is a well rounded and well made game. There is no aspect of the game that is really lacking, and at the same time there isn't anything that's unnecessary.
If you're looking for a good way to relax for a while, or something for your mind to chew on, Splice is well worth your time.

Splice is a puzzle game in which you reposition cells in order to line up with an outline and create a biochemical strand. Cells are constrained by various rules and special cells such as those which duplicate or delete themselves, and it's in thinking around these that the puzzles are formed. There is a lot of playing with perspectives and intentionally attempting to overwhelm the player to mask a simple solution, which fluctuates between satisfying challenging and infuriating, with little middle ground and wild inconsistency.
Ultimately Splice's saving grace is also its downfall, and the same as virtually every game by developer Cypher Prime I've yet played, as they opt for a significant amount of style to make up for a lack in substance. The presentation is immensely cinematic, making great use of shifting planes and colors as you move from level to level, all complimented by an absolutely gorgeous piano score. It's a beautifully artistic game, but unfortunately I never found the puzzles remotely as well constructed. On the contrary, by the end I was fuming over some of the more difficult ones, and was more than happy when I was finally finished. Much of Splice's design seems dependent on confusing the player, but after a point this becomes immensely frustrating, almost as if the developers are just seeing how far they can push you without any hints or direction before you finally crack and quit the game.
My feeling on Splice are very...convoluted. The presentation is remarkable, yet the gameplay noticeably lacking. The entire time I spent with it my feelings were a mixture of awe and anger, kept only in line by a few simpler puzzles and a handy guide. I can't fully recommend it, nor can I entirely reject it, so my suggestion would be to check out the demo and see if maybe it clicks for you. If nothing else you'll get to appreciate a bit of the excellent audio and visuals, which rise so far above everything else.

I took a sh-t on this game in my first review several years ago.
Seeing the curator recommendation below the very box where I'm typing this review, "a deliberately mundane shooter", reminds me of why I was so poisonous towards it in the first place: there's so much hype and expectation and unconvincing excuses surrounding this game that I had an impossible time approaching this game objectively.
But that still doesn't mean it was fair of me to look at it through such a filter. I recently reinstalled and gave it another go, no hype, no expectations, just letting the game be exactly what it is.
So, what is it? A mediocre shooter with a very good story and fantastic presentation, that is worth your time.
Seeing suggestions that "the developers made it boring on purpose" still makes my skin crawl and does a terrible disservice to the game. There's no way in hell that a developer has ever said "I'm having too much fun, dial it back, we don't want to distract people from the importance of our message". The fans helped bury this game with that kind of crap by forcing people to call them out, instead of letting the conversation be about what the game does right.
Now, gameplay isn't terrible, it performs competently as a 3PS despite an aching lack of variety. There's really not much to say about it, imagine if Gears of War had every weapon behave the same way, and there's like 3 types of enemies and they also don't really change things. I wouldn't go as far as calling it joyless, but it's never exciting.
What the game does do right is the presentation. There's a lot of care and detail that I took for granted on my first playthrough. Your squad, and your interactions with them, are great. The dialog got some genuine laughs but also works admirably in service of drama. There's a lot of unnecessary animations for humans in this game that make them look and behave believably, and it adds a lot of life.
The music rocks and strengthens everything it touches, be it a cutscene, a gunfight, or a menu.
The story has been praised to death, and I won't say it doesn't deserve the non-hyperbolic bits of it. Maybe books and movies consider it old hat, but it's largely unique for video games and it's done really well.
Graphics are nice, especially at 1440p. Everything is crisp, colorful, and worth admiring. The sand effects, be it in a storm, a breeze, or an avalanche, looks wonderful, and Dubai Proper looks awesome.
Overall, I recommend this game, and I especially recommend that you don't let anybody overinflate your expectations until they pop. It's not a life-changer, or especially fun, and it's especially not a damning indictment of modern AAA military shooters (oh my god shut the f-ck up), but it's still a very worthwhile piece of art that deserves your attention.

I'm ~27 hours into the game at this point and am close to the end and have been having an absolute blast playing it. I'd recommend this game at a $30 price point.
The Awesome - I loved the art, loved the story and the writing as a whole.  They did a great job creating worlds and characters that will stay with me for awhile.  The blend of sci-fi and fantasy was refreshing.  I thought Planescape was well served in these regards.
The Okay - I enjoyed the original game mechanics (spending of attribute resources to accomplish tasks and pass checks) but certainly felt they could have done a better job detailing character progression.  Every level/tier I gained was a surprise in regards to what skills and abilites would automatically be doled out.  I had already invested time, money and points into a number of them having no idea that I would get them for free a level later.
The Penny Pinching - The technical execution re: animation, models and combat polish was quite frankly amateur.  There's no excuse for not having matching character models and portraits, no NPC portraits during conversation and in-game armour for the main character only.  There's a ton of other shortcuts taken but I digress.  It's the little details like this that make a good game great.  It cheapened the experience and made you wonder what they spent all that money on.  The phyiscal game itself reminded me of a "hidden object" game in terms of production value.  Obviously not the games strong suit.
Ultimately it's a well written storybook with some beautiful backdrops and whimsical art.  The game itself leaves you with a sad sense of what might have been as it feels like they dropped a finely tuned engine (the writing) into a cheaply made car.  I hope they get a second chance to right the wrong because what matters most is certainly there.

I got banned from the Torment Steam Community Discussion board for posting this review there:
I grew up a huge fan of all the infinitiy engine games. I backed Pillars. I backed Torment. I thought the new golden age of cRPGs was upon us. It had to be, these games had record funding.
And they were incredibly poorly planned and managed. We saw some of these issues, much less significant, with Pillars - where ambitious stretch goal were delivered but hastily developed, not fully realized, insignificant to the grander scheme, and tacked on feeling - but it's even worse with Torment.
Much of the base game that was planned was cut. Entire stretch goals that we earned were cut. These cuts, while not only making the game significantly more shallow with significantly less replayability, are the antithesis of this RPG system. Go on, count how many companions shipped at launch, the laughable amount of focuses, literally no factions as we were promised, no crafting system. No orchestral sound track. Compare the stretch goals, which is literally what people were paying for, to the final delivered product, which is what we were given. Imagine yourself being Italian backer and being promised an Italian localization that wasn't delivered- Because that happened.
Kickstarter is allowing developers to deliver whatever they want. And that is something I'm never going to support again. If there would be a platform that binds the developers with a contract to fulfilll their promises and design targets, I would reconsider it but Tides, along with so many incredibly successful kickstarted games simply aren't delivering what they're promsing. What we paid for.
InExile has had zero transparency about the entire thing, and will only acknowledge it after the fans make it into a scandal. Zero accountability. I am sorry I backed Bards Tale 2 and now I understand why they kickstarted the next Wasteland before this launched and blew up in their faces. Who knows how many dollars from this sinking ship they put into those more marketable games?

This game is getting a thumbs-up from me, WITH qualifications. Also, since the game labels itself as a spiritual successor to Planescape:Torment, I will be making references to that masterpiece. Also, some SPOILERS
Before you decide if you want to get this game, you need to figure out if you love to read. Personally, I love reading, so this game is a few steps up for me. The prose is effective and appreciated. If reading is a chore for you, skip this game. I say skip it in that particular instance because the combat system is not sufficient to make this game stand on it's own. In fact, the game has no real challenge of its own due to a problem within its mechanics. See, for any skill check or combat check, you will use your pool of stat points as a finite resource. This could be a potentially interesting system, especially if you combine this fact with the notion that even failure on skill checks brings a reward (sometimes even a better reward). You would have a system where failure was as common as success, leading to an almost real-life scenario where people fail and live with the consequences.
Except the Edge mechanic burns this system to the ground.
As you level, you will eventually get Edge points for your stat pools. In essence, Edge gives you free points to spend on a task EVERY TIME you attempt a task using that stat pool, e.g., 3 Edge for intellect means 3 free points spent every time you attempt an intellect task or attack. This corresponds to a rough 45% increase for your chances for success. For free.
Then you specialize one character per stat pool, and you'll never fail a roll again. Ever. Taking the uncertainty out of the system was a mistake, particularly since combat does NOT have variety in its abilities.
In fact, Planescape:Torment had more combat options. Let that sink in; a game from 1999 had more combat options and variety than one released in The Year of Our Lord Two Thousand and Seventeen. Sigh.
And since we are on the subject of comparison, let's compare companions. PS:T's companions not only had more depth and backstory, but they all revolved around the theme of that game; "What can change the nature of a man?" T:TON's companions, while ranging from acceptable to pretty good, never achieve the success of its predecessor because they don't cleave to the theme of their own game: "What does one life matter?"
In fact, the game doesn't really deal with this theme either. If we saw, more directly, how the tidal manipulations of the other castoffs and the Last Castoff himself truly hurt the people around them, we could see the tension between hurting others by merely existing. However, it all rings false when I play my character like a paladin and improve the lives of almost everyone around me: Sagus Cliffs and most of its serious problems resolved, including the removal of the adversaries, who want to wipe out all life on Earth, yet I'm told at the end of the game, and not really before in any significant way, "sorry, your existence makes life miserable for anyone you come in contact with" I can't help but roll my eyes at the fact that my suspension of disbelief lies bleeding on the ground before me. Outside of this attempt using the titular tides to move the theme, there are no other appeals to "what does one life matter/"
Also, some really annoying sound effects tied to buffs can't be turned off. REALLY ANNOYING effects.
So why the heck am I giving this game a thumbs-up? Because the whole is greater than its parts. Any one system from this game held up to the light looks mediocre at best, but when put together with everything else, it... works, and I don't regret a single hour of the 22 I spent beating the game. It doesn't come close to topping Planescape:Torment, but it doesn't have to. This is a fairly well-written game that takes lots of risks; while those risks don't always pan out, I prefer developers to take risks and fail on occasion as opposed to playing it safe, Assassin's Creed style.
TL:DR If you like to read, give it a shot; not as good as PS:T but still good.

I backed this product for $35 (the all digital art level).  Watching the development process and seeing the writer's and artists ideas come to life was worth the price of admission. Getting a game out of it has felt like a bonus.
That said, this game may not be for everyone.
Strengths: Visuals are conceptually imaginative, subtle soundtrack, dynamic dialogue, descriptive prose which unleashes the imagination, character alignment has more to do with philosophy than arbitrary dichotomies, navigating the strange gameworld is convenient with mouse and keyboard.
Weaknesses: combat system is not very deep, long dialogue trees means fewer companions to choose from, voiced dialogue is limited, graphical detail is and visual customization are limited by the format.
IF you wanted a sequel to Planescape: Torment, then this game is for you.  IF you liked Baldur's Gate/Dragon Age/Wasteland 2/Pillars of Eternity but thought there should be less combat and more dialogue, then this game is for you.
IF you feel like lore skills are dump stats, then go play diablo.

In nearly all cases, even the minimal thought required for the puzzles still takes longer than simply systematically trying all solutions. Episode 2 does not show much improvement, so I'm refunding while still possible.
Abundant in the first episode are the 'riddle poles', where you have to order three sentence fragments, one of which has a dot. Most egregious is the musical puzzle shown at 33 seconds in the trailer. Put instrument on air hole, listen if sound is okay, place on other air hole if not. Repeat. The answer is literally bruteforcing.
Same with episode 2's lockpicking. I've had two of them so far, so I assume this is a recurring puzzle as well. There are four pins, which all need to be pressed, but in a certain order, which you don't know. Pressing pin 1 will eject pins 2,3 and 4, while pin 4 ejects nothing. You can figure out which pin is which, but just keep pressing pins from left to right, you will need at most 10 presses. Literally. Like, math.
The episodes were released in 2009, 2011, 2012. This does not excuse the terribad graphics. Gamecube Resident Evil looked better, and that´s 2003. The graphics are simply because the first episode was made with a team of three, in six months. Not much time for modeling your first game if you don´t know if it will start a franchise, I get it.
But update it when you make a bundle edition. This is just painful to watch. They made a new game in April, just lift the models from that one. At least fix spelling errors. Seperate.
The voice acting is abysmal. Think Inspector Gadget saying "wowzers". Now imagine everything being said in this half-cheery monotonous voice, whether it's a 'humorous' quip or "do X or I will shoot you".
The secrets found ingame give you codes, get them all and fill them on their website for concept art and backgrounds. But it does this by simply hyperlinking you to a different numbered page. Just go through their sitemap by incrementing this number to "unlock the secrets" as well.

Adam's Venture Chronicles follows the adventures of Adam Venture and Evelyn Appleby (yes, obviously named after Adam and Eve) across three episodes as they attempt to thwart the plans of the greedy Clairvaux company to steal from and/or destroy locations from Biblical history.  Their journey begins at the gates to the Garden of Eden and continues to King Solomon's temple and ancient locations in Jerusalem.
As far as adventure games go, this one is kind of bland.  You explore some ancient sites, crawl through some tunnels, and perform some minor platforming actions.  Instead of trying to be an Uncharted clone, the game clearly focuses on the puzzles.  You are constantly confronted with puzzles as the game progresses.  Puzzles types primarily include item collection, logic, math, and pattern recognition, though there are also a few others mixed in.  I feel many of the puzzles are unique to this game as I have not seen them in other puzzles games.  Most of the puzzles are mildly challenging.  Unfortunately, several of the puzzles repeat frequently with very minor adjustments to what you need to solve.
The game locales focus on Biblical events and locations.  These Biblical references tie into some of the puzzles, primarily in Episode 2, a bit in Episode 1, and not at all in Episode 3.  One puzzle requires you to order the names of King David's sons in the order they were born, which I imagine most people can't do without the aid of Google or a walkthrough.  The rest of the puzzles can be solved with little to no Bible knowledge.  Although Biblical references are present, they serve primarily to set the scene and background.  The game never tries to force Christianity upon the player.
The story is okay, but nothing special.  Voice acting is unexpectedly good for a B-class adventure game.  Adam's witticisms are very much akin to Guybrush Threepwood's and, although the comedy is a bit hit or miss, they provide quite a bit of comic relief that helps keep the story from becoming too bland.  Adam definitely made me chuckle more often than not.
Hidden throughout Episodes 1 and 2 are a number of chests that provide codes to redeem at
.  These chests are far too easy to find, and the Bonus content isn't really worth redeeming.  I appreciate the effort from Vertigo Games to include extra content even though the execution is lacking.
Mechanically, the game performs very well.  With few exceptions limited just to puzzles, the camera cannot be controlled by the player, yet I never found the camera restricting.  Movement controls are very basic.  Adam can walk or run, crouch and jump.  These work as you expect, though the jump mechanic is a little broken.  Anytime you try to jump on something you can't--like a wall--that object throws Adam backward.  Thankfully the jump mechanic is rarely needed, but it is quite comical to see Adam flying backward through the air.
Overall I enjoyed playing the game, even though I'd classify it as a lite adventure.  It doesn't offer anything new on the adventure side but it provides some decent puzzles and clever comedy.  I'd rate the game around 6.5/10.

SOLITUNE is a very passive, very brief experience with some colorful, well-done visuals with very little player interaction that ends up being mostly nonsense.
SOLITUNE is a very short (15 minutes total, you see almost every single envrionment you will experience in the game in the 1:00 minute trailer) surreal, relaxing experience with very minimalistic gameplay. You play as a "shepherd" entering a series of small rooms which have an NPC in them you're unable to talk to until you click on the right sequence of things throughout the environment, which then unlock a door for you that leads to the next room to do the same process. You do this about 7 times and then the game ends.
You walk around and click on things and random surreal moments happen, such as trees sprouting from behind you or binders stuck in trees that then shake loose and you click on them when they're on the ground to stack them next to a character, or clicking on some lights until they match the color displayed on a computer monitor in the same room. Aside from the color-matching sequence mentioned (or another where you match 3 icons to be the same on another set of computer monitors) the "puzzles" / sequences never have much logic to them beyond just happening to click on objects randomly until you've exhausted all options and the NPC then unlocks and says a few cryptic, wannabe profound lines to you and then you go to the next room to do the same thing. You do this about 7 times then after a brief scene the game just sits there forever (did my game freeze??) with a bunch of sheep lined up below you, crouched down, until you choose to exit the game.
The incessant bleating from the sheep as you progress from room to room after helping the NPCs (get it??? The sheep are the people you're helping!! *MINDBLOWN*) becomes very loud and grating as you explore the mostly calm environments. This game's art style and colorful visuals are its most appealing aspects. I did enjoy seeing what random, surreal moments would occur in the environments and I didn't expect this game to have complex gameplay, but even when taking those into consideration I feel like SOLITUNE was pretty to look at with not much else going for it.

Hold A to Do Things: The Game.
Alright, Jesus f*ck, I'll do an actual review. *clears throat* Mad Max is a game that has a lot of great qualities, but those great qualities get buried under a crushing weight of collectible ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and dickish game design, which is apparently common for sandbox games nowadays. Below are my thoughts:
First, the good. The car combat is pretty damn good, with ramming grills, tire grinders, rocket launchers, harpoons, flamethrowers, a shotgun, and more. It's fun to occasionally just buzz around, destroying enemy cars in various ways and trying to avoid getting destroyed yourself. It's let down, however, by the terrain. You'll notice that in the films, most car battles take place in flat, featureless desert. Because of this, the focus is on the cars' interactions, not their trying to stay on the same path. The game's world, on the other hand, is filled with hills, cliffs, ditches, and bumpy patches, so you can't trust that you won't crash horribly or go completely off course while taking your eyes off of the road to shoot at an enemy. This makes the car combat significantly less fun, which is a shame.
The melee combat is basically the same as that of the Arkham games, but with a few key differences. First of all, the animations for everything, especially the finishers, are hilariously over the top. It's like Max learned everything he knows about fighting from watching Arnold Schwarzenegger films and professional wrestling. If nothing else, you can get in brawls just to have a dumb chuckle at how Max decides to dispatch someone IN THE MIDDLE OF A REAL FIGHT with a SUPLEX, of all things, and then go after his friend with a headbutt and a leg-lock (although enemies not dead after one one finisher will be perfectly happy to stand on their broken legs and punch you with their shattered arms). Second, it's generally easier overall, which there's nothing wrong with if you want to make an easier game. Third, you have the option to dispatch any enemy bothering you at any time with a shotgun blast at the cost of one shell, which is hilariously abrupt. Fourth, you can use melee weapons and single-use knives, which adds a nice bit of variety. Fifth, it's pretty ♥♥♥♥♥ily programmed. Especially near the end of the game where the enemies start piling up, you can occasionally press a button and have Max not do the thing you just ordered him to do, which is ridiculous and frustrating. Finally, you can get attacked in the middle of finisher animations, which is just stupid. It's perfectly realistic to have someone hit you in the back while you're piledriving his friend, but in a game where you can't do anything about it it's the very epitome of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tty game design.
There are bases scattered around to liberate that are really interestingly designed, with catwalks, teetering structures, towers, ziplines, and lots of nooks and crannies that are fun to explore and seem like interesting places to live. At times, though, the various collectibles scattered throughout are so well-hidden that I had to consult walkthoughs to find all of them.
The car upgrades overall are really neat and varied, but they can be applied everywhere, instead of just the garage. Normally I wouldn't mind such convenience, but it wouldn't make that much of a difference in this case and it doesn't make sense if you can completely overhaul your car anywhere.
The game looks very good, especially the wasteland and the fire effects, but not as good as Just Cause 3. (But then, what does?)
You're allowed to run over random neutral NPCs, even questgivers, which is always fun.
The sound design's good.
The mocap's also good. There's a nice limping animation for when you take fall damage, and there's a dog in particular who looks and acts exactly like how you'd expect a dog to act, except for the fact that he seems perfectly content to sit in a confined box for the entire game.
There's judicious use of slo-mo throughout the game that adds a lot to car crashes and fight scenes.
The Cleanup Crew upgrade is really convenient, as it automatically collects Scrap (the game's currency) from car wrecks you just created, but I feel like it should also apply to Scrap drops from fallen Scarecrows and enemy troops.
Alright, that was all the good (although looking back, a lot of those were backhanded compliments and damning with fine praise), so here's the bad. Prepare for a lot of petty complaints.
The world is outwardly the same world as the Mad Max films, specifically the same general area as Fury Road. There are a few problems with this, though. First of all, the plot has some ties to Fury Road, but none of Fury Road's characters show up and that's not Tom Hardy we're playing as, so I'm not sure what the point is. Also, the main villain is Immortan Joe's (until now unmentioned) son, Scarabus Scrotus. He's another 7-foot-tall goliath, but he doesn't have any severe physical defects (at least at first) like Joe's other two sons, which completely undermines Joe's emotional conflict in Fury Road. More generally, the world is outwardly the same Mad Max world as ever, but it's lacking George Miller's deft touch and artistry. The cars are either basic hot rods or lumps of incoherent vehicle instead of machines with personality and theme, and the insane people just speak random pidgin English instead of the natural-seeming dialect of the films. Giant lumps of muscle like Humungus and Rictus Erectus were anomalies in the films, but they're just all over the place here. It's clearly someone trying very hard to be George Miller, and while I don't blame them for not having the guy on hand at all times and having to make do without him, it's still very noticeable in-game.
The story and characters are just kinda ♥♥♥♥♥♥. Max has a couple of nice moments (laughing at a guy who thinks a fiberglass helmet will protect him from headshots springs to mind), but most of the time he and everyone else are annoying, entitled, and stupid.
Fury Road's toxic masculinity overtones become just toxic masculinity...tones here. Scarabus Scrotus wears a spiny♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on a codpiece for some baffling reason, and lots of other minor villains have weird sexual backstories and fetishes that the game brings up constantly.
This driving game doesn't have handbrake turns for some baffling reason. They could even bind it to RB! Why isn't it there?
There's supposed to be some sort of survival element, with constant shortages of scrap, gasoline, water, and shelter, but resources are f*cking everywhere and you can quickly unlock the ability to get infinite ones every time you return to a garage, so I'm not sure what the point is. Scrap in particular is ridiculously abundant; by the end of the game I had about 15000 in reserve with nothing to spend it on.
There's two different upgrade systems for Max, but both are easy to fill out fairly early in the game (making you overleveled and overpowered for most of the rest of the time) and neither make sense, as this is another game with a protagonist already fully formed at the beginning with no real room for improvement.
The population density is absurdy high for the apocalypse.
This game has the worst jump button I have ever seen. It's unreliable, clunky, and only necessary for a handful of optional Scrap locations. If you don't need one, don't have one.
There are lots of other small problems, but overall, the game's main issue is that there's a ridiculous ♥♥♥♥ton of content for content's sake. Scrap, Scarecrows, Snipers, relics, bases, minefields (those are a chore), side missions; I felt compelled to do all of it, and got drawn into an endless pit of boring, repetitive collection. I started out thinking this game was OK, but over time those feelings dissolved into hatred of the endless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Any joys the game has are eventually consumed by the endless, meaningless
. Ugh.

I am a backer of this title and consider Planescape: Torment one of the greatest PC games of all time. It is with a heavy heart that I find myself writing a bad review for this game. The problems are numerous:
1. The story is dull and uninteresting. I find myself pushing forward thinking it must surely get better soon.
2. The characters are lacking in personality. Near the beginning of the game, you are introduced to two characters who eventually choose to split up and force you to choose which one to follow. It occurred to me at that point that I don't really care which I follow because the characters are so lacking in personality that it is impossible to distinguish one from the other without resorting to judging by looks and character class.
3. The writing is bad. I don't mean "writing" as in "the plot" (though that's not good either); I mean the dialogue and other text you read throughout the game. This is a game that relies heavily on the writing. The prose needed to be good; it isn't. The writing should be at least good enough that you don't stop to think about whether it's good or not. Instead, it is so bad that you wonder if it was written by amateurs.
4. This game feels less like a video game and more like a "Choose your own adventure" book. Quite often, things that deserve a cut-scene are merely described to you using that bland prose I complained about in #3 above. Why am I reading about a flash-back memory instead of seeing it as a cut-scene?
5. I'm bored. Yes, I'm barely getting started, but I don't recall ever being bored of a game this quickly, especially one I had been looking forward to and eagerly anticipating for several years.
Pretty much the only redeeming quality of this game is the setting. The setting is fantastic; I could imagine many great epic stories taking place in this world. Unfortunately, the story they tell in this title is just bland and boring.
Having said that, I have to admit that I have barely put any time into the game yet and its possible it will get good soon. If it does I will update this review. In the meantime though, I am bored and don't really feel like playing it.
If you do choose to get this game, just be aware of what you are getting into. This is not a classic RPG and doesn't actually resemble Planescape: Torment in any way. This is more along the lines of Sid Meyer's Sorcery! and other text driven games. You will spend most of your time reading descriptions of events that you are not actually seeing on screen and interacting with dialogue menus.

It's tough to give a recommendation for Arkham Origins. It has been plagued by bugs and glitches ever since it was released, and to this day a fair amount of these issues remain. About two weeks ago this game stopped working altogether, which had me trouble shooting my computer for a few days. The problem was caused by a few corrupted INI files that didn't happen to get deleted when uninstalling the game in Steam. The game has been running ever since.
However, even with the game working, I still find there is a siginificant amount of lag and stutter, especially when exploring the city; a serious flick in the nuts for people who have spent a lot of money on high-end hardware. It is extremely noticeable and distracting. Other than that I haven't encountered anything too aggravating so far when talking about pure bugs and glitches.
As for the game itself, Arkham Origins is actually pretty good. In no way is it as groundbreaking as Arkham Aslyum or Arkham City were, though. Arkham Origins feels more like an expansion on Arkham City than an entirely new game. The combat has not been updated or improved, in fact it feels a little more sluggish than in Arkham City, there are no new noteworthy gadgets and some parts of the map are right out of Arkham City. In terms of story, I think this game actually has the best in the series, although I won't get into it to prevent any spoilers. The voice acting isn't bad, either. While I do miss Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamil, both Roger Craig Smith and Troy Baker are great regardless.
The reason why I wouldn't recommend you get this game, is because WB Montreal really doesn't seem to give a f*** about their customers and their game. This company has no plans to fix Arkham Origins, yet has time and money to produce DLC. It is greedyness at its finest and a supreme example of why the game industry is hurting a bit right now. Unless WB Montreal fixes the game, stay away from this one and get Arkham Asylum and/or Arkham City instead, or wait for the recently announced Arkham Knight to be released in October. Although I get my enjoyment from this game, looking back now I wish I had listened to others and didn't fall for this one. It's time to take a stand against the industry and not have them bend us over and f*** us from behind. Out of pure principals, don't purchase anything from developers and publishers like this, as it will only make matters worse and worse. If you do decide to get Arkham Origins anyway, it is still good and worth playing, but I would at least wait for a price drop.

Ok, this game was a bit of a dissapointment for me unfortunately. The whole Arkham Origins kind of was. Love the Batman franchise though. And most of this would sort of be nitpicking, but it's the little things right?
1. Yes I know, he's a "hero". But still, the game taunts you by giving you all these lovely rooftops, and yet you cannot throw people off? Or at the least, hang them from the railings like he does in numerous torture scenes? I mean, the enemy, on the edge of a building, I kick him straight back and he just goes up in the air like he's too good to fall off!
2. If you are giving me the "counter" symbol, and I press the button, it was because I wanted to counter.
3. Gotham is a beautiful city right? I'd like to go to one of their lovely bars and knock a few drunk heads around or something.
4. I know I know, he's afraid of firearms. But still, it would be nice to be able to use say, a tranquilizer gun, or a at least shoot one of the thugs in the knee. I mean if you're allowed to beat them to a bloody pulp with their own skulls, a bullet to the knee sounds like a much nicer way to take someone down if you ask me.
5. The game just starts to become quite repetative quite quickly. The only real difference is WHERE you repeat it. And it's not just the Bat Man games. It's ALL superhero games. Go here, mash the button until conflict is resolved. Attempt stealth but hope to hell it doesn't glitch out on you.
6. Those ♥♥♥♥ing vent covers! I'm sick of having to mash the A button everytime I come across one of those. I mean seriously! What are they, trying to build up our thumb muscles or something? Just play the cutscene, and stop this useless crap.
7. Again, Gotham is a beautiful city. I'd love to be able to jump and run around it all over the place. 8. The Puzzles: Ok, I'll admit, that one where you have to do a whole bunch of forensics is fun. It makes me feel immersed in the whole "detective" role. The replayability is great, with several routes to take each adding its own challenge, perks and rewards.
You can play Neutral, which is how I would recommend playing the first time. You simply play the game and enjoy it.
You can play Pacifist, you cant kill a single enemy, staying at level 1 to the very end. This a great challenge and really fun.
You can play Genocide, you kill everything, no exceptions, I have yet to play this but I think it will be interesting.
The fighting system is unique, challenging and enjoyable. No repetitive spamming right click, no emotionless enemies.
Every NPC has its own dialogue and fight options, suiting everybodys prefered playstyle.
All in all, Undertale is easily in my top 5 games, the first genuinely fun experience ive had in a long time.

I’m writing this having not yet completed all routes. I have to say that overall, I’ve enjoyed this game for what it’s worth. I’m a sucker for dad-jokes, puns, and the like. The dialogue between characters was engaging, and I found myself playing despite my higher brain-power telling me that I was wasting my time.
I admire what the devs were trying to do with this game as well as the subject matter, but I think it suffers greatly from an inconsistent tone. Heavy♥♥♥♥♥♥happens, then the next dialogue or scene change completely disregards its existence (happened more than once when talking to Amanda and in Robert’s route, I noticed it most.)
Which is a glaring problem instead of a minor annoyance with just how short the game is. And for how short it is, there really isn’t a lot to be learned about the dads. Again, this is where the inconsistent tone plays a huge role. You’re supposed to be forming deep bonds with people, and there are times that the dialogue starts to tilt in that direction, but it’s immediately broken up and many of the endings (even good endings), while they made sense, didn’t fit in to the rest of the game’s light-hearted whimsical nature. Either commit to portraying an aspect realistically or go completely stylized. This game tries to do both and ends up doing neither.
The character customizer is also a bit disappointing. It doesn’t fit into the overall style of the game and left me trying to make a character that would fit in while trying to ignore the ridiculous options available. Which. Again. The tonal dissonance… It’s a thing, even here. It’s hard to take the serious talks seriously while you look like Goku with a rad beard. And if I didn’t want the funny options, I was still left with a character who looked too feminine for my tastes or, worse yet, like a poorly rendered background character (This wouldn’t have even been an issue had the rest of the game had characters stylized in the same way.)
Amanda is hit or miss. I liked her and thought her personality made sense in context with her dad’s. Was she often portrayed as the “cool” teen? Yes. But it was better than an extremely whiny one in my opinion. I also had no qualms with the dad’s character being unsocial and having to be forced to interact with others. I thought that this was one of the things the game did very well portraying and was able to poke fun at without going into cringe-territory (your mileage may vary.)
I don’t know if they ran out of time or money making it or what happened behind the scenes. I just wish it had been better because it has the potential to actually be pretty damn good. Which is why I want to list the pros.
Pros:
- dad jokes. all of the dad jokes.
- interesting character cliches (dad types)
- pontential for growth (this doesn’t follow through, however.)
- good dialogue and banter
- aside from the character creator, the rest of the art is pretty damn good
- the moments of serious tone ARE done well, they just aren’t integrated well
- great way to turn off your brain and relax a bit
Cons:
- inconsistant tone. already mentioned in detail above.
- character creation. also mentioned in detail above.
- extremely short routes that only give you glimpses into a character’s life without really delving too deep. (it seems like you end half-way through a story instead of it being a true ending.)
-not great replay value. due to there really only being normal/“good” endings…
-you get locked into a route early game and that will be your life for the next 30 minutes of the story. no chance for world expansion except for replaying to start another route.
-lack of chemistry between the characters. seriously. half the time i thought there was no good reason for the dads to be on the verge of romance which is probably the reason for some “good” endings being less than stellar. even the writers couldn’t justify romance coming true when the characters themselves don’t seem too keen on it.
Do the pros outweigh the cons? I don’t know. For me, I’d still say I recommend the game to anyone who knows what they’re getting themselves into and can appreciate the game for what it is. I’ll leisurely play the other routes I haven’t done yet to see how everything turns out. I don’t dislike the game, and I think it’s worth picking up if you like humor and don’t mind vague expositions. I think what bothers me most is that really, there could have been MORE done with this game- a few more dates added, more dialogue, more chemistry-building, more time spent fleshing things out. Even if the game had been purely comical and stylized as such, it would have been a better experience.

DDADDS is not a bad game by any means, but there's simply not enough content.  It's wholesome and cute and can cheer you up when you're in a bad mood, which is great, but it's also not what I look for in my visual novels.  The developers promised "Secretssssssss" and I got, well, no secrets.  The only compelling question, the only thing I was ever /curious/ about in any route was who Robert's kid was.  "Secretssssssss" feels like it's promising me a plot.  DDADDS is a purely romantic dating simulator, which is great in its own right, but the description did get my hopes up then let me down.
It also promises multiple endings per dad, but as far as I can tell there isn't anything very interesting about the bad ends as opposed to good ones; It seems to just boil down to 'well the romance sure did fail between us'.  That's really not another unique ending.  Not to mention that after playing a dating sim which offers you a /story mode/ after you romance every option in addition to its 10+ different endings, it really does feel anticlimatic to finish the, in essence, 7 endings of the game.
To nitpick a little bit, as glad as I am that Damien Bloodmarch is a trans man (as it's a unique form of fatherhood to be the one who carried the child which really helps carry the developers' statement that the game is primarily about caring for another person) the reveal makes me... not so glad.  It makes me concerned for his health, actually.  The reveal takes place when he discusses having a gothic wardrobe, including binders.  It's natural, yes, but... His voice and facial structure make it quite clear he's been on Hormone Replacement Therapy for a good while now, and if he can afford to turn his cul-de-sac home into a gothic mansion, he can afford top surgery.  HRT and Top Surgery go hand in hand; doing one without the other can lead to serious health complications, not to mention that binding daily for even just one year can cause serious physical damage.  Binding is really not the indicator of the trans man experience, and there are numerous ways it could have been revealed without making me worry about Damien.  Mary warning the player not to 'get him knocked up again', or Lucien reminding him that today's the day he needs to do his injection are just two examples I thought of.
In conclusion, a good game, but lacking.  No storyline.  Only one compelling plot point.  It's fun and wholesome dads, cute and with a good sense of humor too, but it really is fluff, which for me lacks the replayability I hope for from a 15$ game.  Buy it on sale or hope for free DLC later down the line, and enjoy a few hours of Dad-ing it up.

When I start playing a new game, I always take notes of my first impressions (I was a reviewer of pc games about a decade ago), it's like a habit now for me. And I've rarely been so impressed with the early game as I was with Mad Max.
The menu, the presentation and early game - very well done. The game world is unbelievably beautiful. It's freakin' gorgeous! Probably my most visually impressive 3rd person action game that I've ever played. Characters have good animations and are detailed. Controls are intuitive. Special effects and lighting is jaw-breaking. Weather effects <3, scenery <3 - everything is eye-gasmic. Day and night cycle makes the desert look so real and beautiful and ... sometimes lonely (in a good way).
This game is based all around the battle cars and combat between them. It's very satisfying to combat a full convoy of them. The cars look deadly and diverse. Cars sounds are very satisfying. Even the controls are pretty good! Nitro animations looks awesome + you can speed up your car with it and whack other cars of the cliffs and stuff.
I really like the hand-to-hand combat (It has some Shadow of Mordor vibe to it) and how the upgrade system works in Mad Max (too bad that you can get all the upgrades before or slightly after the midpoint. Of course, only if you do lots of side objectives, like I always do in these kind of games. And there are a lot of those little objectives or mini quests that you can participate in. (Just like in Batman or Far Cry, or Assassin's Creed games).
The random storms are awesome. You really feel like you are in the middle of a f*cking disaster! Lots of mini tornadoes, lightning and flying debris that can damage you greatly.
I really like how quickly you can descend the ladder. You just slide down and you're good to go. I hate when other games puts you in that unskippable animation and you sometimes have to waste 10 seconds of your precious life on the ladder.
I really like how quickly Max can get out of a burning car before it explodes. You are never stuck in silly scripted animations.
One thing that made me wonder - why Max can't jump high? He really despises jumping. I bet he couldn't even jump over his own shoes if they were lying somewhere on the ground. But then I realized. He looks like a ~35-40 year old man. He probably had to do a lot of jumping and running in his life so somehow he damaged his knees and he is just not able to do this sh|t anymore, so he said - f*uck it, I will not jump in my life anymore! Just like big NBA players in their late 30s. They can only run at a slow speed and can't even think about lifting off of the ground.
Oh and explosions. Explosions. Seriously, explosions. No other game has better looking explosions. Period.
This game has a little thingy called - capture mode. It literally makes you a photographer. if you want to be one - you can learn some basic things here: composition, depth of field, perspective and so on. Last 15 hours I was just hunting screenshots. Sometimes to make/take a perfect shot you need to invest dozens of minutes, but it's well worth it at the end. I've done like ~300 screenshots. I believe I could have done thousands of them If I would have used that mode from the very start. It's a great tool and I urge you to try it. (It's a bit buggy sometimes, but you will enjoy it anyway).
Since I mentioned bugs - this game is pretty bug-free. BUT. I was trying to 100% this game and hunt for all the achievements and then a bug happened. I completed a mission and as a reward I had to receive the ability to build a maggot farm in one of my strongholds, but the game doesn't allow that. I've searched the internet and this thing is STILL not fixed (sad, sad face). I was/am disappointed. A great game with such a -+ game-breaking bug. But this should only matter to those who like to hunt for achievements.
As a 3rd person action game - it has it all. And if you are one of those people that like to LIVE in the world, not just run through the main quest and be done with it - this game will provide you with lots and lots of fun hours.
On a side note - this is how Fallout 4 should have looked like (from a graphical standpoint).

For a game that has had fairly negative reviews by "professional game reviewers" I sure am having a lot of fun. The game starts out a little slow, but if you're a fan of vehicle to vehicle combat and customizing cars to be anything from a racer to a small tank you need to check this game out. I have heard a lot of complaints about this game usually from people who have not played it or people that are blind because this game is great.
Pros:
-Great car combat and the ability to customize your car. Eg. Harpooning an enemy inside of his vehicle and pulling him through the windshield.
-RPG elements that let Max himself become a better ♥♥♥ kicker
-The hand to hand combat system is not incredibly deep but it can be challenging at times and watching Mad Max pummel some one against a wall or cut them up with a well timed shiv is a lot more satisfying then any fighting game I've played...not a fan of Down,A,X,B,A,Y,X,Left,A to make your fighter spin and shoot a fire ball? Me neither.
-The story starts a little slow after the opening cinematic but it picks up and turns into a pretty epic story. Complete with a dream sequence with a talking dog head on a human body...
-I have a GTX750ti and I have all graphics options maxed out. No lag, No hitching, No Freezing.
-I have seen very few if any bugs so far.
Cons
-There is some repetitiveness and some grinding involved with the game but I feel the rewards and story are a pretty good pay off.
-The physics can get a bit wonky at times. Eg. I got hit by a car once and instead of getting knocked away I got shot straight up in the air spinning like I was caught in a tornado. Another time the same thing happened to my car when I hit a large rock that an enemy shoved me into.
-Darn Aussies their steering wheel is on the wrong side...
I am sure I have some other minor issues with the game but I have been having so much fun I can't remember what they were...all in all this is an excellent game that well polished and a lot of fun. If you like vehicle combat and at all are interested in Mad Max or post apocalyptic settings then this game is for you.

I was a late purchaser of this game, however as it seemed to have a unique way of implementing the lightsaber combat system I decided to give it a go.
I was not disappointed.
The lightsaber combat mechanics are some of the best I've ever used, which is saying something for a game that predates more modern games like Star Wars Battlefront (Original), Star Wars Battlefront II (Original) and other games with melee combat systems like Skyrim, which could have benefitted from taking a leaf from this game regarding the fluidity of combat. The original Battlefront games are the biggest issue however, as they should have had much better lightsaber combat systems considering they came after Jedi Academy.
The one let down in terms of combat mechanics for Jedi Academy however is the blaster mechanics, which leave something to be desired. While the blasters can be used alongside some of the more acrobatic moves the player can use, its considerable overkill as even on Master difficulty most basic enemies with blasters are easily slain. More work in this area to make blasters easier and less awkward to wield would have been appreciated.
Story is fun and engaging, although while there is not much choice in terms of dark and light side choice options, there are two endings to try out that are fun to do.
Overall, if you're looking for a bit of nostalgia and a decent lightsaber combat system, this is worth a go. I've had huge enjoyment out of this and I'll no doubt play it through a few more times in the future.

Max Payne is a fantastic third-person shooter, strategic and gritty, from the glory days of Remedy Entertainment. If you don't want to read on because you're lazy, just know that I highly recommend it.
Playing as the titular character Max Payne, an undercover cop who has lost everything and everyone in a series of tragic events, you're really put up against it as you're forced to fight hordes of gangsters, mercenaries, and more using your skills and reflexes. Emphasis on that last part- Max can only survive a few shots before going down like any other human being out there, so you're forced to watch your step all the time and use the slow-motion 'bullet time' to hit your enemies with precision before they can get a shot off at you. There's a wide variety of weapons to help you with that, from melee tools such as a baseball bat to dual handguns to assault rifles. Nothing that particularly stands out- well, unless you want to count the Jackhammer seeing as that's a very rare weapon in real life- but certainly a wide range that will let you fight with a variety of playstyles. Go in with the big guns and try to be tactical with your ammunition, or simply go mad with your handguns and dance around the bullets being fired at you.
The AI on this game is very advanced at times. Enemies have sophisticated behaviours, such as standing around and chatting, or patrolling down corridors. They can work very effectively as a team, advancing on you in numbers if they feel confident or retreating and firing from cover if you start to thin their ranks. Admittedly the boss enemies in this game seem to deviate little from the philosophy of 'Just run at Max because we're bullet sponges' but you're going to have some very good gunfights in this game and die plenty of times if you buy it. Save often or risk being taken back a fair bit when someone jumps around the corner and fires a shotgun at your face.
The atmosphere, dialogue and effects are all as good as the gameplay and combine to form an immersive environment that really makes you feel like you're venturing the cold hard streets of late nineties New York.  As you explore abandoned subway stations, derelict apartments, seedy underworld dens and more on your quest to help Max get revenge, you'll be stunned by the level of detail and attention. Max will make idle comments on various objects you stumble across. Gangsters will talk about all sorts of things and seem human at times. You'll find junkies quivering and mumbling to themselves down back alleys. The attention to detail is amazing.
Admittedly there's some drawbacks with this game, the biggest one being the shocking state of the port which I'm surprised Remedy hasn't hotfixed. Whilst on a functional level it works relatively fine- I'm getting silky smooth performance and no graphical glitches or crashes which is a rarity on a lot of old shooter games- there's a big problem where no music plays. I highly recommend getting the patch on the community hub that fixes this: it's relatively easy to install and solved all my problems. Another technical problem is the Windows 10 issues with this game- but since I'm still a Windows 7 boy (gulp) I can't speak much for that. But there's patches for that too- like any old PC game with a cult following people have patched the hell out of it. I think there's mods which spice things up as well, but I've only played this through vanilla.
Another aspect what annoys me are the platforming segments in this game, simply because Max jumps about as well as any other protagonist in a shooter game. There aren't that many of them, in fairness, but there's some obnoxious jumps and precise platform jumping (particularly in the despised 'dream sequences' that occur between each of the three parts of the game) that really require a lot of saving and loading because you're more than likely going to mess them up a lot. Thankfully, it's unlimited saves unlike something like Hitman.
But anyway, if you dare to try this game, you're going to have a fun time. Maybe it's not for everyone and it might be a bit hardcore for filthy casuals, but I really enjoy it.

Torment: Tides of Numenera, the successor to Planescap...wait, no.
Torment: Tides of Numenera, the spiritual♥♥♥♥♥♥..nope!
Torment: Tides of Numenera, the thematic successor? (What the heck does that even mean...?)
What is this game? Here's a better title:
Numenera: The Fluffy Tides Make You Fall Asleep (a poor attempt at Star Wars: The Force Awakens.)
Who's in torment? It certainly isn't the Last Castoff. The Tides may as well not even exist, or be referred to like something as gravity for that matter. They have no impact on game play, nor are they an ethical system, or what people think of you. Legacy is just another name for "extra screen at the ending."
So we're left with this idea: take the template from Planescape:Torment, look at it, then throw it away.
-Switch up the setting, since they can't get the license. (The setting is amazing by definition, not by opinion.)
-Create a boring protagonist who has the character of a blank RPG sheet -- minus the stats, since there are only 3.
-Forget everything from P:T that made the characters deep with their personal conflicts, faults, and philosophies, and forget putting tropes upside down on their heads in a fantasy D&D setting. Instead, create people who are simply there and have almost nothing to do with anyone (save maybe Matkina?)
-Get Chris Avellone to write the only entertaining character, Erritis, instead of putting him in charge.
--"Oh but if you give Rhin to X, she becomes tall and..."--zzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzz.
-Waste Mark Morgan's time and have him create over 40 pieces of forgettable pieces of music.
-Get, in some cases, highschool level artwork to have "meres" or memory experiences that change other castoff's memories or time or whatever (?), because that worked so well in Pillars of Eternity. So you can change your tidal affinity. Which does nothing.
-Re-invent "turn based combat" by providing dozens of weapons and armor -- armour that only you can wear -- but half the time during "Crises" you're going to be talking, or running through a group of enemies to solve the problem in a non-combat way. Essentially the strategy of running around like an armoured up A-Team truck, because a selling point will be to "go through the entire game without fighting." Thus, making combat for people who play Glaive, or of players who want to actually play a game, a chore. Thanks, endless amounts of teleporting Bloom--Predatory Echoes. (If I wanted to play a visual novel, I'd get one with sex, nudity and actual drama. Thanks, senpai.)
-Lie about in the marketing how Glaives can attack twice in a turn (note:provided your first turn killed an enemy, and you bothered to get the skill to attack again.)
-Get oddities from long sidequests that literally do nothing but clutter up your inventory
-Have a scrolling inventory of useless items -- 2 rows of 14 items at a time
-Pick up Cypher Sickness when completing a quest if you didn't choose a Jack. If you are a Jack, die.
-Bombard us with narrative fluff in an already padded out story of figuring out how to fix a Resonance Chamber, whatever that is, 95% of the time.
-Beat your daddy by telling him he doesn't exist, because he's actually an AI program. I'm not kidding.
People who were expecting Planescape: Torment? Get used to entire weird worlds of disppointment.
People who want drama and philosophy and conflict and layers of meaning and memorab-- look elsewhere.
Pros:
-I'd say the writing is on a level only slightly better than Pillars of Eternity. And Good Lord is there fluff; you'll be going through this text faster than any other Infinity Engine style game, choosing the option where you get to use your Effort.
-You can tell all your hipster friends you like narrative heavy games, because you're a smart video gamer.
"What does one life matter?" After 4 years and 5 million bucks of delayed, dropped content, I don't know, Colin.  If that's your response to "what can change the nature of a man", well, I guess we all knew what we were getting into beforehand.
Like Star Wars, The Force Awakens, this is a fan made game trying to use a winning formula, only worse: they didn't understand why the original worked.

Overall I liked it. It tries really hard live up to the "Torment" legacy and while it unfortunately falls short of this ambitious goal, it's still a enjoyable experience. It focuses heavily on the story element with combat being very infrequent to almost non existant depending on choises made. Where it falls short is mainly in it's companions and general difficulty. Where Planescape really made you work to achieve "good" results Numenera feels a bit more like an extended choose your own adventure, as long as you have the right skills nessesary most things solve themselves rather effortless, if an dialog option shows that it require the use of a skill it's almost univesally the "right/best" option.
The companions, while well written, are a bit unfortunately not well integrated into the story. You'll encounter them, learn their intriguing backstory and then drag them with you until you hit upon "their" sidequest, after which they are for the most part done narratively. I miss the interwoven and gradually exposition of the Planescape companions.
Still it's a good game in a nieche genre so I'd recommend it.
