An outstanding achievement, especially considering it was built within the framework of a crowdfunding budget. It is a worthy follow-up to Planescape: Torment both in terms of its writing and how it tackles themes of identity within a truly atypical landscape. Despite some of the familiar-looking fantasy trappings of some locations, Torment: Tides of Numemera constantly serves up reminders that you are not in Fantasy 101 Kansas anymore.
Tides of Numenera, like its predecessor, plants both feed firmly on the narrative side of the fence. Combats and dungeon crawls are of secondary concern. If you aren't fully prepared to engage with the narrative and the world-building, then this is not the game for you. If you love a good story-driven RPG, though, or if the narrative was always your favorite part of the Infinity Engine era and its successors like Pillars of Eternity and Tyranny, then take the plunge into the world of Torment: Tides of Numerea.

You open your eyes. You are falling through the sky. You are the new conscience, birthed when your creator left the body you now possess. Alone, abandoned in a world you don’t know, you ask yourself: who will I become? What will be my mark on the world?
Torment: Tides of Numenera is a narrative-focused, text heavy RPG. Even though it doesn’t continue the story of Planescape: Torment, ergo accessible to new players, it touches some of the same themes and builds on the formula of its antecessor. There is a lot of text. A LOT of text…
The game adopts and adapts the tabletop RPG setting of Numenera by Monte Cook that takes place on a future Earth in which countless civilizations have risen and fell, leaving behind pieces of technology. These are the Numenera, that constitute riddles to be solved or devices to be feared by the new inhabitants of the planet. This gives the writing a pretty long leash to explore whatever it wants, with each sci-fi/fantasy vignette providing an opportunity to make you question what you thing about identity, legacy, morality. What do you say to a hideous mutant that everybody hates for its appearance that is considering a pretty invasive equivalent of plastic surgery? Do you think it’s better to be truthful to what he is, potentially subjecting him to a lifetime of poverty and exclusion? Is it better for him to change completely? Does he have someone that loves him for what he is and should that have weight on his decision? Should you, a stranger, even get involved with his choice? This is only a 5 minute episode in a journey that has taken me close to 50 hours to complete.
You will walk on a transdimensional predator that also happens to be a city, meet an ancient warmonger condemn to an eternity of peace, a religious leader enslaved by the adoration of his followers, learn of an endless conflict between two sides who can rewind events to get different outcomes, and an alien creature that is fascinated by our mating habits. Some of your companions have some great depth. Continuing the cliché-braking of Fall-from-Grace from Planescape: Torment, Erritis is, at first glance, the heroic, reckless warrior, but with time (or the ability “Scan Thoughts”) you start to see there is something more to him and a interesting deconstruction of the Hero trope. Rhin, is a controversial companion. She is a child you can choose to take in, and once you choose to, you have to stick by that decision and keep her in the party or lose her forever. This worked well for me, because it made sense that a lost child, with a talent for hiding and who had been betrayed several times before, would not stick around once you had abandoned her. However, this is controversial because she isn’t the most useful in combat and some people feel frustrated by having to keep her in the party to see her storyline unfold. To me, she was a character I had to be a father-figure to, and would try to shield from harm, not because she was bad in combat, but because I didn’t want her getting hurt. Some call it emotional manipulation, I say I have no problem with a character that wants you to see her as more than a chess piece. There have also been some complaints about the use of less common words that, to me, English not being my first language, don’t seem prevalent enough to be distracting or unintelligible and, when they come up, add to some of the strangeness of the world.
Presentation could be better, with very little in terms of narration and voice-acting and the beauty of the 2D back-drops contrasts with the blurry character models. It is evident that you are supposed to do most of the work with your imagination, often too much, but if you have the habit of reading, you probably can get passed this hurdle.
The combat is relatively limited. Much of it can be avoid by having the right skills and choosing the right option in dialogue, but when you can’t or choose not to you enter a Crisis. A Crisis puts you in a turn-based battle with your party, where you can use your weapons, abilities, items do defeat your enemies. The way it stands out, however, is that in some cases you can resort to dialogue to make some opponents surrender or even turn to your side. Sometimes, even the order in which your foes fall have different consequences, although I can’t really tell to which extent with only one playthrough. These sequences were occasionally fiddly to interact with (sometimes not being clear if a character is blocking the way do something, for example) and buggy in some areas (namely in Anechoic Lazaret). That being said, I played in the first week and I’m sure there will be patches to fix a great deal of it.
You can see some crisis shine with their intricacies in a way where you wished there were more of them. One of them in The Bloom is a good example: when you enter one of the areas, you are put into a Crisis that hasn’t yet turned violent, but must decide in the time-span of a couple of turns which side of the battle to take or if you can even defuse the situation. It was a welcomed change of pace that I feel could have been integrated and adapted to other quests.
Having played Planescape: Torment for the first time in about a year or so, and still not having nostalgia settled in, playing Torment: Tides of Numenera felt very much like playing Planescape. Just as with latter, I couldn’t put it down for more than a day, always wishing to tie some loose thread or see what was waiting in that unexplored corner of the map. All this without bats and thugs coming out of nowhere for an arbitrary battle.
For those looking for a comparison, I still cannot decide if Torment is better than its antecessor. It would take second playthroughs (which I haven’t taken off the table) of both of them to say for sure. What I can say is that Torment: Tides of Numenera is an acquired taste, but a modern masterpiece in interactive narrative nevertheless. A little polish here and there and it can stand tall and proud in my top 5 (or even maybe 3) games of all time.
A true spiritual successor to PS:T, Numenera blends intuitive combat and skill mechanics with brilliant writing.

Where to begin. I backed this game on Kickstarter at the same time that I backed Pillars of Eternity (2012). PoE was released about three years later. Torment, meanwhile, was released two years after that. Given the millions of dollars it received from Kickstarter and the two extra years of development, I was expecting a game that not only matched its predecessor, Planescape: Torment, in depth and detail but exceeded it. Instead, I was left with a final product whose status as a worthy successor to Planescape was mostly illusory. The game also failed to measure up in most (but not all) ways to Pillars of Eternity and even some of the older but classic isometric RPGs such as Baldur's Gate.
But let's break it down. The first "act" of the game, which composes about ⅓ of the total game, really impressed me. Sagus Cliffs was designed with such detail that it blew Defiance Bay (PoE) out of the water. Where Defiance Bay's design felt oddly inauthentic and lifeless due to its bizarrely clean, overly-perfect, wide avenues and promenades, lack of population, and total lack of anything unique or interesting, Sagus Cliffs felt alive and like there was something neat around every corner. And that's a big achievement, I think that should not be overlooked. This ⅓ of the game had me thinking of Sigil from Planescape, Amn from Baldur's Gate II, or even some of the wacky but fascinating cities of Final Fantasy IX or VII. It felt like a homecoming in a way; back to the cities of the games I played as kid. The characters and party members also seemed pretty promising at this point, as there was a fair amount of dialogue and intrigue involving them.  I thought it would be fascinating to watch their characters develop (with perhaps a romance even?). I thought the city would be a neat place to return to late-game. I thought there would be further, late-game quests to do with the people and organizations I met early on that would yield powerful artifacts, abilities, and new insight into the lore and history of the Ninth World. I wanted to explore the area outside the city, and generally delve deeper into the story of it, it's inhabitants, and history later on. But none of it happens. Once I caught that airship out of the city I could never return, and all the quests I failed to complete would be forever lost, along with the most interesting part of the game. That was the first bad feeling I had.
Then, not long after my abrupt departure from Sagus Cliffs, I was met with my second disappointment: the second act. Where the first act arrived with detail, history, intriguing characters, stories, quests, items, beautiful scenery, the second act more or less just showed up. Or phoned it in, rather. It was essentially a glorified checkpoint with little to do or see that was actually interesting. A few things here and there advanced the stories of my party members, but they were mostly silent through this act, their personal dialogue trees exhausted, and their commentary on the overall story virtually nonexistent. Thankfully, this act was also pretty short and quick, aside from the agonizing combat, which I'll get to later. So I didn't focus too much on its flaws and foibles and eagerly moved on to act three.
Thankfully, the third act came close to matching the first in quality. There's a lot to do here, but mostly in terms of minor side quests that yield relatively underwhelming rewards. Did I like taking a portal to a space station? Sure. Did I get anything useful or interesting out of it? Was it tied to the rest of the story in any meaningful way? No, and aside from an inert ball I got to take with me that serves to tell me where I am at any given moment, I had nothing to show for the quest, which seemed exceedingly promising when it started. In addition, my party members hadn't seemed to recover from whatever torpor the second act placed on them. They remained mostly silent, aside from a few comments and quips here and there. I was able to complete a few more dialogue options, but they didn't really have anything interesting to say or do, and if they had anything for me to do it was relatively trivial and boring. Admittedly, I was happy with how Rhin's story played out in this act, but I can't say the same for the others. Despite the gorgeously rendered landscapes and artwork, and despite the fascinating setting, I was once again left wanting more. Once again, I left the setting of the third act without the ability to return. The game was pushing me in a relatively linear path. I was essentially playing a book, one that left you feeling like it wasn't quite finished yet. And after the third act, there was a quickly wrap up and conclusion that at least answered some of the outstanding questions, but did little else.
And that's the real problem with Torment: the world, the setting, and parts of the story, are fascinating. The game inside that setting is significantly less so. It's unpolished. Unfinished even. It gives you a taste of a fascinating, fantastical world, and then the curtain falls and you realize there's nothing more beyond that taste. I mean, some of the most interesting events of the game essentially happen in your imagination thanks to the whole Mere system. Not in the game, your imagination. You don't actually get to see them, and your ability to interact with them and control them is incredibly limited. I don't want to complain too much, because the art was beautiful and it's a neat idea for these types of isometric RPGs, but it just felt like certain events warranted more attention.
So what of the effect of your choices on the game? Pretty minimal. There are a few obvious ones that affect your companions, but pretty much everything else didn't matter. Even when certain characters died in the third act's final crisis, there they were in the concluding fourth act, still breathing and without so much as a mention of their death a mere minutes before.
The combat was pretty lackluster. I think some people prefer turn-based combat to the real time combat of PoE or Baldur's Gate, but I'm not one of them. It's just too slow. The whole system is painstakingly dragged out. I had issues with the combat in Shadowrun: Returns, but at least the combat there had more to it than being essentially just a game of numbers. What's more, there seems to be a lack of interesting abilities or opportunities to use them. I more or less used the same tactics in the beginning of the game as in the end of the game.
My equipment was virtually irrelevant too, aside from the damage and resistance modifiers on weapons and armor. I bought one set of armor the entire game, and couldn't really identify a moment where I received an item I was really impressed with. There is no lore or history to the items you find, and most of them are useless trinkets only good for selling.
Finally, the graphics. Wow. Ok, I've already said several times the backgrounds and scenery are mostly really well done and gorgeous. But the characters and some of the companion portraits? The actual moving pieces? Kind of horrible. Almost like they were designed with the same technology as Planescape: Torment back in 1999. What's more, most of the characters have very little detail. Really, there is only ONE character in the entire game whose level of detail impressed me, and she only shows up at the end of the third act, and is not the main character or a compassion. What a waste. Additionally, the voice acting may as well have been nonexistent, there was so little of it.
So what did it all leave me with? A question of where that $4.3 million in Kickstarter funds actually went. Apparently it created a 20 hour game with an admittedly fascinating world and gorgeous artwork, but with a very limited and linear story, underdeveloped characters, uninteresting combat, and relatively limited replayability, especially if you're someone who puts in the effort to turn over every rock and stone in an RPG.

If you're a fan of simulators and want to get the feeling of a cross-country road trip, there truly is no better game on the market that does it better than ETS2.
You start out with some lame headquarters, and you have to deliver cargo cross-country to earn more cash and gradually your business grows as you get your first truck, buy a new garage, and start hiring new drivers, all in a way that makes this game surprisingly replayable.
The environments are gorgeous and the diversity of trucks never lets up. Volvo trucks, Iveco trucks, MAN trucks - they're all here.
As you sit behind the wheel of your truck, you're free to control whatever you like on your truck - indicators, lights, wipers, retarders (on higher-end trucks).
Not to mention you can download your favourite music and put it in your Documents folder to listen to your favourite music while you're trekking across Europe. For me, that feature is absolutely gorgeous. And even if you don't want to, there are a plethora of European radio stations that you can listen to in the game - from Pop to Rock to Jazz to news by BBC, the diversity of music available with just a few clicks and button taps never gives up.
However, while I feel the driving experience is spot-on in most areas, rarely the AI can start doing some stupid things like swerving into the overtaking lane while you are overtaking them, therefore crashing into your truck and causing more damage. However, that is just a bee in an otherwise exquisite honey.
I would definitely recommend this game to people a fan of the genre. It may not be for everybody - but if you want a game like this one, ETS2 is one of the best for you. I never get tired of starting my Volvo and heading to collect my trailer to deliver it across Europe.

As has been noted by everyone else, the three Adam Venture games which was at one time sold individually have been grouped together to produce one long game named Adam Venture Chronicles (2015) created by a Dutch company which can be found here
It claims to be an online adventure similar to Allan Quatermaine and Indiana Jones and it does have that type of feel about it all. It was also created to be suitable for Christians and young children as it contains little to no violence or bloodshed in the entire adventure series. However let’s still look at each individually.
Chapter 1: The Search for the Lost Garden (2009 released)
The graphics in this particular instalment are quite cheesy. Granted the backdrops are often vibrant with countless eye catching sparkle and glimmering spectres everywhere your main character travels. Seriously diamonds, crystals and glitter fill the caverns like as if some sort of Mardigras parade had been through the whole cave system moments before you got there. Yet it still never takes the focus off the question why your character Adam Venture is wearing MC hammers pants? Couple this with the fact that when the game starts there is a lizard which seems to do a river dance in suspended air for some reason and you’re really waiting for the moment when the bass kicks in and that immortalised sentence ‘you can’t touch this’ and everyone starts to doing the signature hammer dance. Alas it never happens. But the game is so corny it could have and it would have gotten away with it. Trust me.
This part of the game will take you about 2 hrs - 4 hrs if you want all achievements. With the exception of the first puzzle, the rest aren’t that difficult. Half the puzzles are simply scripture columns which have been broken up into three parts and need to be placed in the correct order. However other puzzles and their requirements are more obscure when you first come across them and like me you’ll probably just start randomly clicking as you know there is a limited amount of combinations it could be.
Story is that you have discovered the location of the Garden of Eden. The big problem is, that many game developers who choose to do a religious themed game, because let’s face it, the target audience is huge, often these people have no idea what so ever, what they are in fact talking about and often just make a fool of themselves and their product to those that do.
Are you ready for this? The Garden of Eden is still around and so is the snake! In fact it wasn't really a snake to begin with, but more the smoke monster from the TV series 'Lost' and apparently the smoke monster was doing God's work all along and stopping people from getting to the 'Tree of Life' ?.... Completely lost me there... (Actually Gen 3:24 says that God posted a number of Cherubs and a flaming sword to protect the trees, not a smoke monster.)
But the biggest downer for me personally is that you never get there. You never do see the Garden of Eden. Which is a complete bummer. This disappointment could have been rectified if the bass kicked in at this moment and the snake started singing ‘you can’t touch this’ and all the archaeologists dropped their differences and started doing the running man dance as the caves came down. Golden opportunity lost forever…
Chapter 2: Solomon’s Secret (2011)
In this instalment (which will take you about 5 hrs) the developers seem to have zero care for actual history and take just as many liberties as the Star trek franchise does with science.
For those that don't know, King Solomon was a real king. In fact not only the richest king at the time, but is still the richest man who has even ever lived. In today's terms he was earning somewhere around 250 million a year. Just imagine all the Steam games you could get with that!
Anyway there has always been thoughts that there might be some hidden riches waiting to be unearthed in a hidden temple somewhere and here is what the games main story premise plays on. An evil corporation is digging up the temple mount. Oh dearie me who will save us all from dire calamity. Steps up to the plate Mr MC Hammer Pants/ Adam Venture.
This particular chapter of the game surprised me for two reasons.
1) I did not think this was possible, but they somehow have worked out how to make every back drop even more vibrant and blinding than the first episode. Seriously you nearly have to wear sunscreen just to play certain scenes outside.
2) The developers who must have learnt there history from a pop-up book, somehow made a even bigger blunder than the previous episode. Are you ready for this one???
King Solomon spends vast millions upon millions creating booby traps and puzzles that will do your head in, to hide not treasure, but to hide his writings. Because apparently to Solomon his wisdom was greater than his treasures. What’s wrong with this premise? Have you ever heard of the book of Ecclesiastes? No booby traps needed to read that book. Jeez.
Chapter 3: Revelations (2012)
First, this instalment has nothing to do with the book of Revelations in the Bible. Instead the title is in regards to the character discovery that a gamer will get to experience as he plays what begins as a prequel. The title also further hints to a secret agenda the evil Clairvaux Corporation has which gets revealed at the end of the game.
After the first two instalments of this game I was kind of expecting that I would go blind with this one by all the bright colours that would be radiating from my screens monitor. Kind of disappointed they toned it down a little and I won’t need that expensive eye laser surgery after all.
I also expected them to make a bigger blunder in this episode than what they made in the previous two. Something absurd like the four horsemen of the apocalypse would turn out to be a merry go round at Chernobyl or something like that, but as stated before this has nothing to do with the book of Revelation and what information they do subject us with is at least plausible.
It seems that those at Vertigo have improved over the years, and time and time again have reacted to feed back by looking at how they can make things better. I agree with a friend of mine and will be forever interested where they will send us next. Noah’s Ark? The disappearance of the Assyrian Army? The graves of the Nephilim? I’ll have to wait and see.
A final comment I would like to make is that I personally had some issues with one of the instalments thanks to a graphics card issue, but those at Vertigo were very quick and efficient in sorting out the issue. In an ever growing market where technical support is nearly extinct, I find that good customer service is just as golden to me as any game with top notch graphics and sound. Vertigo= Great customer service and for that I applaud you the most.

First, I will concede that this game is not without its faults. There are negative reviews here that present valid points: the game is rife with spelling and grammar errors, the "Build That Dad!" feature is quite limited in its customization options, and there are a few bugs here and there that are kind of annoying at times. Essentially, I am more than happy to support this game and still recommend it highly. The characters and dialogue are extremely well-written, hilarious, and even a bit sad at times. So many different types of people are represented in this game in such a refreshing manner, and while it isn't perfect, this is definitely a work which, at its heart, is pushing to take video games in a positive direction. I even appreciate how the game challenges typical dating simulator experiences, as well.
Again, we could all critique this game to oblivion, but I think it is more important to acknowledge and celebrate the time and love that was obviously poured into this game by its creators. It is a wonderful game and--after my initial playthrough--was already worth the $15.

It is somewhat reluctantly that I am giving Heavy Bullets this negative review.
A lot of the game is good: The art design is sweet, the music plays in well, the enemy types are just varied enough, and the sensitivity and gunfeel is spot on.  It's gimmick, the way you have to pick up and conserve bullets plays out really well and the game does a great job of making that fun.
But there are all these roguelike mechanics that just make me not enjoy my runs.  You can bank gold and an item for a future run.  You can only carry one item at a time, or two with a backpack.  The shops are randomised, so you aren't always able to buy what you want.  There are some certainties: the Medical shop will always have heals and the ammo shop will always have bullets, but you are in no way guaranteed a shot at the rarer upgrades such as the backpack or increased MaxHP.  That last one's a killer, especially when there's no way to practice against bosses.
Furthermore, while the level design is complex and fun to run around in, it doesn't always make much sense.  You find shops before you find enemies and hence have no money to spend.  There are doors that go to empty rooms.  Some levels will have three secrets in them, and in some runs I can go three or more levels without finding a secret.  Now, since you can only carry one or two items, missing out on a few extra choices isn't so bad, except for the fact that you can sell items for money.  I just feel that having a few failsafes built into the level generation would be a huge boon.  Other games in the genre ensure a secret in each level, or a locked shop, or an item, or something, but with Heavy Bullets the only consistancy are the banking machines.
Perhaps that's part of the game's design, part of it's theme:  You have to grind up to win.  You have to throw away lives failing in order to pay to win.
It's a decent enough game, but it's just so discouraging to play.

Heavy Bullets is an FPS/Rogue-lite in which you play a nameless, blank character in an exceedingly colorful nameless dungeon for no real reason who is armed with the game's hook: a revolver that shoots giant heavy bullets, which can be recollected for more uses though the revolver usually has a low ammo reserve so every shot matters. As you progress you fight various strange enemies who attack in either the most basic or most dastardly ways possible. The most basic enemy is an imp with huge teeth which just runs in straight lines to get to you and bite your face off. Imps won't dodge, won't curve paths, make loud noises to warn you, and won't stop chasing you except to rotate X amount of degrees when confronted with a corner; so they're boring, a nuisance instead of a threat, and lame. Another simple enemy is the turret. You encounter a number of laser shooting turrets which are either easy or hard based on how many other turrets are around, because they all fire fast and have to be hit in a specific location. If there's only one or two it's a bit of a cakewalk if you aim right. Otherwise they'll light you up if there's more. Conversely, there's also snakes which hide in the dense foliage, waiting for you to get close to leap out and posion you. Snakes are usually hidden well, quiet, and often manage to leave a lasting poison which I've had take off three hearts of health before (important note here is that you start with 3 hearts and I only ever maxed out at 5 hearts) so a cheap enemy is one of the biggest threats. Then there's my favorite of the game's many FU's. The living bomb bug. You get suicide rushed by small purple bugs that zoom at you like they're trying to win the ♥♥♥♥ing Indy 500 race so it can do a large AOE blast which does a full heart of damage and seems to stun you briefly. Remember, you only start with 3 hearts, slow movement for an FPS, and everything is overgrown and neon colors, so it's a HUGE THREAT. So, basically the enemy design sucks both for the player's survival, and for the player's lasting interest in playing at all, because they are so uninspired and have limited AI.
Continuing with gameplay feedback; there are a number of items in game to pickup, similar to say, The Binding of Isaac, where there's both "use" items and "passive" items. Unlike BoI however, you can only carry 1 or 2 items total in Heavy Bullets depending on whether or not you bought a backpack. There's a good variety in items, though most aren't as helpful as they should be. For instance, there's a "use" item called the Ritual Knife, which deals the player a heart of damage and used to give you as many coins as you would need to buy a heart on that floor, but now jips you a few coins. Another such neutered item is the "passive" Repelent, which claims to repel bugs and snakes, which would be so great if it actually did so. Instead the repelent only gives the player an extra secind before they attack. So, snakes and bomb bugs will still ruin your fun constantly anyway. The items that actually are good with no downside don't have a big payoff, so there's no full heal just minor, the antidote only cures poison for one instance of poison, and there's no lasting buffs- just ones that last a few seconds. So items play a smaller role than they typically do in this type of game.
As far as lasting thoughts, I felt like it was a game that would have been a gem had it been made in the 90's, as a lot of the ideas would have been fresher and more appreciable then. Rogue-lite's weren't really a trend back then, and the randomized dungeons would have been novel. The visuals are really basic, but 3d games usually were in the 90's. The music was not really very inspired, and should have played a lot more. Sound effects were quite bad. It's hard to get to like a big gun that makes a small "boof" noise, creatures sounded as robotic as the turrets, and everything sounded like it came through a bad chipset with a damaged speaker. I think the character was supposed to occasionally say things like "Oh yeah!" and "Whew!" but it sounded like the sound desginer(s?) burped and farted into a mic or attempted to go for 80's level synthization. All those sound issues would be easier to overlook in the 90's when it was harder and often expensive to get good sound in videogames, but here it's off-putting now.
Overall, a dissapointment on many fronts. I love FPS'es, Roguelites, and games with some style, but this let me down in every cateogory. Things just don't meld well in this game, and the existing content is rudimentary and unfun. 4/10.
If you want a good example of an FPS/Roguelite which delivered where this game failed, I suggest Eldritch or Ziggurat. Eldritch has more stealth, adventure, and horror elements complemented by immersive sound design. Ziggurat provides better FPS movement, more interesting items, weapons, enemies, and impressive visual flair.

Super fun gameplay that combines bullet-time with a "shoot-dodge" mechanic, allowing you to dive through the air in slow motion as bullets whiz past you. Every bullet is a physical object in the game world and reacts realistically with the environment around you, something that was quite amazing at the time. Although it all feels a little bit stiff when compared to modern games, it's still fantastic fun, elegant and "cinematic", and not many games have achieved that stylish John Woo type action in the way that Max Payne did.
This is a very moody and atmospheric game, with a clever art style and an intentionally tongue-in-cheek story. The writing is flowery and filled with metaphors, nailing (and in many ways parodying) a neo-noir style, and most of the story is relayed to you through graphic novel sequences at the start and end of each chapter. It's dark and depressing with a good dose of humour and cheese on top. It's mature, gripping, and not something you see much of in games, but it's not meant to be taken too seriously.
My main problem with Max Payne is the difficulty. The game is very difficult even on the easiest setting, and that would be okay, except it's not difficult in a very enjoyable way. You lose all your health extremely quickly, and enemies have pinpoint accuracy and telepathic knowledge of where you are in the map. The way enemies are placed in some rooms means that the only way to know where they are is to run inside, get shot and lose half your health so you can work out where the bullets are coming from. Often enemies will be standing right next to doors that you need to enter through, pointing their weapon at the door ready to shoot you the millisecond they see you. The best way to have a good experience with this game? Save-spamming. Quicksaving before every encounter. It's cheap, but so what? The game is cheap too, so fight fire with fire.
But apart from that, a little awkwardness in things such as the level design, and obviously the graphics; Max Payne has aged very well and it's still a very unique game, despite some aspects of it being copied a lot by other developers in subsequent years.

The bullit-time gunplay never gets old and for that reason alone it's worth recommending.
What did get old though is the game itself. Visually it did not age all that well and you'll need to track down both an unofficial widescreen patch and an unofficial soundpatch to run this thing on a modern (Windows 10) gaming machine. One would expect some official support from Rockstar for such a franchise but nope.
Also be prepared for some frustration as this is oldskool gaming where enemies can pop out of nowhere instagibbing you with a shotgunblast to the face before you even have time to react. You're going to have to memorize the enemy placement to get through a level. Thankfully there's a great quicksave and -load system preventing too much anger from building up.
Despite those negatives this is considered a classic and rightfully so. Play it if you haven't already!

I played Max Payne a long time ago; a couple of years after it came out and around the same time when the sequel was released. I recently read an article where someone said it wasn't worth revisiting, but I couldn't believe that.
It has aged a bit, and the gunplay lacks a certain immersive "umph", but it's still a fun game. It also wasn't as hard by today's standards. I did a fair bit of saving and loading, but still played through and beat it in three or four days of mostly casual gaming.
The story is generic "hard-boiled noir" stuff, but that's part of what makes it so much fun. The nods and inspiration of outside influences like "Twin Peaks" is fun and interesting, and the real-world locations are still fun to go shooting through. Max's attitude, voice, and metaphor-laden narrative is still great, and so are the graphic novel sections of the game.
So it's been outclassed by what came after, but the original is still a fun play. I would recommend it to anyone who likes shooters, or is a particular fan of Max Payne (I still haven't played the third one as of this review, but I will eventually). Also, Remedy fans who might be familiar only with "Alan Wake" or "Quantum Break" might want to dig into the company's history; they might discover that the original "Max Payne" is still a bit of a treat.

Firstly the class design is odd and takes a while to actually know how when you'll get new active abilities.  Most games offer new active abilities every level, and TON gives them every 5, in their hybrid system.
I was getting into the odd system during the game, and when I finally felt the system was going somewhere, I hit the level cap at for all but in name Level 4.
So the class design is very poor, as it simply doesn't have time to grow over the game as my second point is the game is way too short.
It may boast 1 million words, but frankly when a world is so small you wonder where the dev time has gone?
Add to that the confusion sometimes in conversation between multiple people on the screen, when you only get the name of the person talking, in a wall of text.  Simply we have come to expect character portraits of speaking characters in the game, and even the dev teams Wasteland 2 did it, so what where the artists actually doing?
So all in all, a disappointment.
- Class system not given time to develop (small cap)
- Small World
- No clear path for expansion (Story opens and closes fully)
And would not recommend only for the die hard CRPG fans like myself hungry for the next one to drop!

Welcome to T:TON, the show where everything's made up and the points don't matter. That's right, the points are just like a hat in an orgy.
My only gripe in this game is irrelevance of character building, and oh boy is it a big gripe.
You'll make a talky guy and you'll 250% all conversations and the companions faceroll all combat content.
You make a combat guy and you faceroll all combat content and 150% all conversations without breaking even a sweat.
If you have the foreknowledge to know what permanent stat boosts to hit in the beginning of the game you'll hit all the knowledge/perception/anamnesia checkpoint rolls flawlessly straight out of the gate even as an inept monkey without even his signature wrench.
Its... all... fluff! Like storyline to Diablo 3, T:TON treats character building decisions as the crusty cream over the doughnut. Wether or not its there, you're going to scarf down on that doughnut like it was made out of angel dust aint'cha?
I can understand that it gives everyone a chance to finish the game and enjoy it like a book.
But I wanted an choose-your-own-adventure novella with meaningful choises!
I wanted it to -hurt- that my character is a learned nano and every talky conversation with npcs would be like pulling a teeth in toothfairy cringefest watching a horribly socially inept parrot try to woo a lady. But nope, inability in conversation skills isnt even a hinderance! At the direst of moments just cram down some juice to boost your intellect straight up after dumping it in a check, no biggie! Waaaay enough intellect angel dust to just blow it all on conversation checks.
I wanted to feel like a big dumb brute as a strong glaive and mercilessly eviscrate all my foes for I would be unable to peacefully talk them down! Wellp... nope. I'm actually about equal to the bonafida learned nano despite the huge int malus. So the big dumb brute just forces his flowery words into everyones proverbial listen-box and walks off scott free.
Okay, but what about their unique skills, wont those make the game feel different when you're playing on other classes?
.... aaaahahahahahaha! Good effing luck! You can get the Jack's signature move by buying an item and using it to sweet talk another from a second guy right after you get to Sagus Cliffs.
Whoa, oh boy that really ought to make a Jack player feel dumb, but atleast he could give the item to an npc! How about the Nano's mindreading, surely thats atleast unique in so- nopenopenope.
You'll miss out on a bit of mindreading content in the beginning. Thats all there is. But sooner rather than later, you'll get Scan Thoughts from an item. Oops.
Well... then... surely there are some unique special abilities only the Last Castoff can learn that'll atleast make you feel special in combat?! ... not... really. What you can do, companions can do more than adequately and some even stupendously better.
The only -real- choise is how pretty do you want to paint yourself with pixels in wether you get enough armor use to wear heavy armor, or mill it out in light armor. And even then you can wear heavy armor just to spite everyone since its only -6 to str and dex plus a paltry -30 to esotery attacks. Nothing some appropriate edge cant overcome.
The only truly unique thing for your mc is anamnesia. Which I suppose everyone is going to max anyhow since whynot. And even then one point is enough to unlock all the hidden past reading content. Hnnnngh.

This "spiritual successor" to the RPG legend PlaneScape: Torment does its best to mimick its predecessor, but falls ever so short on a few important facets. Me saying this might be a bit hypocritical though, as I did not play PS:T back in the day, but I know of its premise and characters. As a huge fan of recent
RPG game renessance had to give it a go.
Playing TToN is like reading a novel most of the time, with some added loot management and interactive choices (and few consequences) added as a bonus. Now I'm into reading even huge♥♥♥♥♥long book series, so in that sense the game was not off-putting in itself, but while TToN has lots to say, it does not always just feel quite
. Its a longish game (clocked 51h) if you wade thru all the million point two words it has. Some parts of the storytelling is very interesting, some parts just feel its extra filling, lets say like fetch quests on some open world game!
The companions and NPCs are not often super interesting, and their interactions with you feel lacking. The "crisis" combat sections - around 15 fights in the whole game - are mostly cool, but too easy at least after the first few, and as an INT character its trivial to power thru all the discussion choices to get "best results" without fighting.
The game's systems feel a bit too simplified for yours truly's tastes. I hear many companions, a big city hub and things like crafting got dropped. The first area is superb (and takes 20h!), the ones after are tad 'meh'. I'd like TToN to have more voice acting, now its just first sentence of some important plot related discussions. There are also some technical issues and bugs; long discussions start to lag more and more, combat can get stuck (game breaking) and so forth. If there will be a Special Edition like Pillars and Divinity:Original Sin had, I could give it another go. It's not a bad game in any sense, but not a masterpiece either.

Pros:
- Well written. A story focused RPG that can't fulfill this criteria isn't worth playing, just as a roguelike with terrible gameplay mechanics wouldn't be worth anyone's time. So. The story is interesting, the story is personal and it carries the game from start to finish as it should.
- Good sidequests with multiple solutions. I can't stress how important this is.
- Reactive companions with their own opinions and comments.
Cons:
- Main plot lacks narrative focus and sometimes you lose sense of what you're supposed to be doing there until you remind yourself with the journal.
- NPCs, followers and even the game world itself can sometimes feel like it's missing character. Sure it's well written, a lot of it feels a little flat. The world itself seems *small* and very localized to a linear path, broken into small locations, rather than the more open exploration of Pillars of Eternity or Baldur's Gate II.
- Combat isn't that well thought out.
- Skill checks don't scale, so eventually you'll pass everything with ease.
Conclusion:
Looking at the list of cons you'd think I would not recommend the game, but I do. It's not a masterpiece, and perhaps that is why it is receiving so many negative reviews from old Planescape: Torment fans, but it is a decent and original RPG game well worth your time, despite its flaws.

The fact that Numenera is 1.2 million words is both its greatest strength and weakness. I struggle to think of games more generous in ideas, and also struggle to think of a game that needs more of a trim. It's easy to get a little bewildered by the strangeness of the world that lies in every interaction. It's easy to lose sight of the humanity among all of the ideas vying for attention.
I love it though, I really do. This is the kind of game where the world-threatening Cthulu space-cosm is relegated to the side-quest of some dingy bar. It's the kind of game where you're just some guy or gal looking out for their own hide, and getting to define what exactly "your own hide" is, while dragging some people along with you for the ride. It's the kind of game where a tesseractal cube tells you the secret of the universe - through inscrutable similies.
If you're interested in ideas and concepts more than execution, and like I bounced off of Tyranny and Divinity like as if it was made of cement rubber, I think you'll find a lot to enjoy here.
Just for gods sake ditch those losers at the start and find Rhin and Erritis. My advice.

Well, I have finished this game. I don't know how much time I spent into it, but if you don't grind (like I did in the first hours of the game) I guess you can finish this game in something like 10 hours or less.
It's not ugly. It's not that "buggy" (even if it may be sometimes).
BUT
This game is clearly not worth 20$. I bought it 3$ and still I have a bad taste in my mouth.
The reason is simple:
Warner is just kidding us. Basically, they took the last Batman Arkham engine, copy/paste it and then put the title "Mad Max" on it. The difference is that Batman was a decent game for two reasons: the story and the character.
But here:
- The story is ridiculous. They don't even try to be original. It has been the first game for a very long time in which I skipped all cut scenes because I just don't care. Seriously, nobody does. However, I precisely know what was the purpose of the story, because I think any 8-years old child could write it.
- The gameplay. Oh boy, the gameplay... It is oviously one of the most outrageous copies of Batman/Assassin's Creed/Shadow of Mordor (u name it...) without a slight pound of originality.
We all know it, and after let's say 5 minutes, you would have seen the complete gameplay that you will be facing during the rest of the game : press "X" to punch until a big "Y" appears on the head of a foe, then press "Y" and do it again until all ennemies are dead.
- The controls : well, I guess a random script was used to assign actions. I mean: "LT" to jump ? "RB" to roll ? "B" to shoot ? Come on guys, have you ever hold a controller in your hands ?
- The content : well, it's quite strange because it seems that they tried to do something interesting at some points. At least they tried.
There are 4 types of structures in this game: fortress (=sanctuary), camps u have to clean, towers u have to destroy and dumps where u can get metal to improve your car. That's it.
Some would call it content, I personnaly call this filling empty game with sh***y things.
But sometimes you feel like they tried, for instance the sort of stoves that u may find in the camps sometimes : obviously, it was made to be interacted with. I mean, they clearly get out of the rest of the decor. But no, in the release u can't use them while I imagine it was an element of "survival" where u should cook to stay alive (see my next point)
- The atmosphere : isn't Mad Max supposed to make u feel like ressources are precious ? I mean, come on, it is obviously the purpose of the movies: people taking control of ressources and making slaves of others that don't own them.
In this game you don't give a s**t: gas is never a problem, food neither, drink neither, ammo neither.
- The music is what we could call "forgettable". I just exited the game and still I do not remember one single music/theme of the game.
Roughly, don't buy this game unless you have 10 hours to loose, and what's more don't even dare buying it at 20$. Please.

There's something about Undertale... something one cannot ignore or forget. Indeed the community has been vocal about this particular title, putting John Lennon's immortal words of being bigger than Jesus to shame. Sorry John, Undertale now ranks above the lord. But just to put it back on solid ground: it is just a game with just a little out of hand fan base. Still an unforgettable experience mind you.
I will not go into much detail about what makes Undertale... Undertale, but a summation would boil it down to fantastic 8bit music, quirky lovable characters and the range of emotions it is capable of invoking in you. Gameplay consists of linear exploration of a 2D top down world, interacting with characters and battling it out (or not) in short bullet hell combat sequences. Writing is comedic most of the time, drawing influence from internet culture, but can be serious or more relaxed when there is call for it. The excellent background music fits each character interaction well and tonality of the situation and the character can be sensed from the music alone. Even before a new character says anything, the music playing will tell you their intentions. Visually the game may feel a little behind at times but you will be moving through the world at a steady pace, nothing will feel repetitive. The great thing about Undertale is that every interaction feels unique. You move to new locations with different climates portrayed in with different colors, meeting different characters with different traits, battling different ways and doing different things all while listening to different music. It doesn't get old. An impressive feat for an one man developer to achieve.
I'd recommend this game to anyone with just a little bit of an open mind. The music is great and you can expect internet culture referenced humor with a bit of an anime flair to it. Combat optional but bullet hell based. I did only one playthrough in six hours but apparently the more you do, the more you will love the game. I'd say ignore the fandom and judge the game for what it is. A high quality experience at an affordable price. And yes, expect the soundtrack to be making top ten lists for a while.

TL;DR: Archeology-themed puzzle adventure game provides fun and challenging mental puzzles for several hours with a moderate story and annoying main character.
The new owners of the Adam's Venture IP are swell people: they provided Chronicles to everyone who owns the original three games. It's a good thing: there's very little difference to the originals aside from requiring to play it in order. Is it a good game though? Let's find out.
You are put into the overconfident boots of Adam Venture, an archeologist whose personality will likely both annoy the hell out of you and keep the story light-toned as he can at least be ridiculous in fun ways.
Story begins as Adam and pals have supposedly found the lost location of the Garden of Eden. Flying there with the plane provided by the generous Clairvoux Corporation, you get trapped inside the maze of caves and have to solve logic puzzles and biblical phrase puzzles to proceed.
Yup, it's one of those Christian Games. Despite that, only the theme and ancient places are religious - the characters and the story are not and religion is not shoved down your throat. That said, knowing something about biblical stories might make the story more enjoyable because of the references. Text puzzles appear only in the first third (Garden of Eden) of the game though, and you can always guess the correct order of the phrases.
Most of the puzzles are different logic puzzles. There is mixing dynamite, solving labyrinths and elaborate locks. There is fixing machines, lockpicking and wiring electronics. Puzzles are very varied and they get more challenging along the way, which is great. The puzzles in the end can be seriously challenging - I used a couple of hours to solve one (number lock puzzle) in my original playthrough, needlessly devising multilinear equations for what turned out to be a relatively simple puzzle once I saw its logic.
I think only one puzzle (music puzzle in Garden of Eden) was illogical to me and that might be due to myself not knowing certain myth from the Bible. This was probably the only part where that might be kind of required, unless I simply missed a vital clue. I had to bruteforce it by trying every combination. In other parts the puzzles could be solved by thinking or simply trying enough combinations, iterating towards the right answer. Some knowledge of simple math and skills of pattern recognition make it easier and probably also more enjoyable.
From the trailer it looks like a 3D action adventure but fortunately it isn't one, because the shadow effects are weak. This remains an issue in Chronicles as it was in the Episodes. While it looks fine enough, the environment does not react correctly to the dynamic lightning like torches. This manifests so that Adam and all the characters cast dynamic shadows but the environmental objects like stones or stalagmites do not even though light illuminates them correctly. Specifically, Adam's shadow might be hanging on the ceiling like in mid-air, because the stone he's standing on does not cast a shadow.
This is fortunately a minor issue but it makes it difficult to find some secret areas and in the (thankfully few) platforming and swinging blades sections it's difficult to see the direction where you are supposed to jump towards or assess the blade's path. Also fortunately dying just respawns you back at the same section, so at least you lose nothing because of the death. Only if Evelyn is with you do you need to hear her scolding voice saying "Adam!" in that particular way that's akin to "Stop
fooling around!".
Like said, Adam is an annoying guy. He boasts that he's awesome and he sure does have a knack for alternative solutions (like a true adventure game character should). Evelyn, his companion character, shows that she has much more common sense and the contrast is actually pretty funny. Nevertheless, Adam belittles her all the time like a tool he is while at the same time hitting on her. I found this very annoying but satisfyingly enough he gets called for it.
Adam and Eve(lyn) is of course a play on the story of Genesis and it's used in the Garden of Eden as a joke. Myself, I found Garden of Eden (the first episode of the series) to be the weakest part of the game. After that it gets much more interesting as the deviousness of the Clairvoux Corporation begins to unfold.
My original playthrough of the Episodes lasted 10 hours altogether (it took only 6 hours for this replay). Of course, now there's an option to play any sub-chapter again after you have played it through to go for those elusive achievements. Controller support has been improved, though sometimes the pad buttons appear on the HUD instead of the keyboard keys.
It's a decent adventure game with some good, challenging puzzles and an okay story. The differences to the original Episodes are very small so if you've played them already, you can only play this for a rerun or the achievements. For the rest of you I can't recommend it for the full price but at 50% or 75% discount it's good enough a tale.

If you played the episodes separately when they were still available, there isn't really any difference between them and Chronicles apart some puzzles being graphically enhanced.
However, for those who never had the chance to play it before, here's what I think of Adam's Venture: Chronicles.
Adam Venture is a young man, a bit sexist (you have to understand that we're in the '20, meaning that in our modern society, some of us will be offended by that characteristic), having found the key to the Garden of Eden. Trying to impress his father's assistant, Evelyn Appleby, he doesn't know that he will live a real adventure, even making him reminiscing the two years earlier.
The main goal of the first chapters is to discover some tales from the Bible, after that, it's more centered on the fun and gameplay than the Bible. The story is a good little one, if only there wasn't a problem in the chronology: it seems that Adam discovered the location of the garden the same year he's stuck in, yet, the flashback shows that it was three years earlier.
Besides, the fact that Adam is a bit sexist: you can see that Evelyn is more mature than Adam. But I don't know if this side of him is his way to show that he cares a lot about her or if he's really like that. Also, Adam is the comical relief of the game: he's thinking that he's the best but in a theatrical manner.
The gameplay is simple as it's an adventure game: you solve puzzles mainly. They're not hard but also not so easy. I can't really say it's flawed but when you have weird camera angles, your job is harder than before.
The graphics would be called outdated in our world, yet, I love them. I largely prefer the atmosphere in the Eden story, more mysterious. But the others chapters are also very good - I liked less the flashback in France.
The soundtrack is also fitting to the game and the voice acting isn't as bad as you could expect. Maybe the Clairvaux chief is perhaps a little too much in his arrogance but it can still pass.
20 bucks is probably too much for the collection, as the episodes were known to often be in weekly sales at 1,24 euros. So, if I was you, I would wait for a good discount.
But I've enjoyed Adam Venture a lot so, I can only recommend it... if you can get past Adam's little sexist side.

Pretty damn enjoyable game, Arkham Origins is Warner Bros Games Montreal's first attempt at an Arkham Game and the first game in the series that hasn't been developed by Rocksteady, the game feels very familiar which has its strengths and weaknesses. The story begins during the early years of Bruce Wayne's career as the Dark Knight.
Gameplay - The combat is exactly the same as Arkham City but with some new moves and takedowns etc, this is both good and bad, this is Warner Bros Games Montreal first attempt at an Arkham game and I can't blame them for taking the safe route and not messing around with Rocksteady's rock solid combat system, it's the same crisp setup we're used to and it satisfies that craving for Hungry Jacks mega combo stunner deals.  However if you try to play this game within a short timeframe of Arkham City you're going to feel pretty bored, my best advice let this one sit for a few months till you're jazzy fresh for some gut punches, within a few hours I was hooked again and just couldn't stop throwing out some coward punches. Gadgets are largely unchaged, you're arsenal is the same with an extra 3 or so gadgets, the best being the shock gloves which allow you to rack up some crazy combo multipliers and the rocket hook thingy that attaches two muppets to each others ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
Story - The story is satisfactory enough to keep me going, the prequel route is usually pretty predictable, so there aren't really any suprises here, its just a nice opportunity to flesh out some of the other lesser known DC characters and build upon the ones we're already familiar with. The voice acting is rock solid as always, as much as I miss Mark Hamill, Troy Baker does a superb job for the Origins story, as well as Kevin Conroy's replacement for Batman, Roger Craig Smith. Most of the familiar faces are voiced by the same people as before such as the incredibly talented Nolan North (Penguin) and Tara Strong (Harley Quinn) two extremely talented VAs with arguably some of the most roles ever played, think of a game or cartoon and chances are one of these two were in it.
Audio - Punches sound like punches, kicks sound like kicks, not really much to rave about here, it does the job, the Gadget noises sound just the way you want them, with neat little clicks and clonks, but a lot of it is re-used assets from City.
Visuals - Man these Arkham games are getting quite spiffy, everything is sharp, textures, lighting, character design etc. The weather effects are great and the effects Batman leaves walking through snow and♥♥♥♥♥♥is pretty kewl. All the visuals come together in a nice package, there aren't any bad spots that I can think of that had a poor level of quality. Level design was superb, but the map was pretty much the Arkham City map with a completely new section.
Conclusion
PLAY IT IF YOU LIKE BATMAN
If you still aren't sick of the Arkham games yet pick this one up on sale or whatever, its a good timed playthrough at 25 hours ish for me, somebody who takes it fairly slow and picks up quite a few collectables and does challenges along the way, and it probably isn't as long as Arkham City, which is a good thing because I think this ship has finally run its course, I look forward to Rocksteady Studios return to the series in what I hope will be something completely new. On the other hand I look forward also to seeing what Warner Bros Montreal can do next now that they are a bit more comfortable.
EDIT: I remember reading about bugs around release but the game was 100% smooth sailing for me.

A fairly decent series of games to spend an afternoon on.
I bought these games a while ago and just today decided to give them a go. To my surprise, the original series of games has been taken off of the store page and placed back on as one complete game, “Adam’s Venture Chronicles”. Which Steam has kindly given me a copy of as well.
Seeing as I can’t review the separate episodes anymore, I’ll review them as a whole here. So despite my 5 minute playtime for Chronicles as of right now, I have played them! I will surely be saving Chronicles for if I ever want to revisit the trilogy. Which, isn’t entirely impossible.
With a total of 7.7 hours put into completing them separately, These games are fun and definitely the kind of game I was craving today, but I’m not going to hype it up too much.
The very first thing I noticed about these games was that you don’t control the camera. The camera pans and follows you. I got used to it very quickly and was actually surprised with how well it worked. But it made the games feel all the more linear. The game is linear as it is, but not even being able to look around kind of supresses the sense of exploration even more. I don’t particular find it a problem, I just thought it was worth mentioning.
As for the graphics in general, given how long ago the first episode came out (2009), I would say it looks pretty decent. It definitely has its moments.
The Puzzles are probably one of the most interesting parts to these games, they are interesting and fun to figure out, without being too mind bogglingly difficult. It’s always nice to see some new unfamiliar kinds of puzzles.
The characters are okay but nothing special. Admittedly the main character Adam did have me smiling a few times. The cocky, full of himself, almost arrogant, yet somehow still charming, character reminded me of the Deponia series’ “Rufus” in quite a few ways.
Despite me thinking the characters themselves were alright, the voice acting generally isn’t the best quality. A few scenes made me cringe a little, but then again others I quite enjoyed. Just something to be wary of.
In terms of story it’s definitely playable and has its interesting parts. It doesn’t bore you to death but it’s definitely nothing too in-depth or profound. As far as I can tell it’s based around Christianity. I know very little about religious kinds of things so maybe for someone who follows the faith, this actually might be more interesting/clever? Either way, I still enjoyed it.
In terms of achievements, this would definitely be an easy 100%. Fortunately for me, playing them all separately, I managed to get 3 perfect games out of it. Each episode’s achievements were pretty straight forward to get. The majority are progression achievements, although there are some in there you can easily miss, so watch out.
All in all, this game is nothing amazing but it’s definitely worth playing. Anyone that likes adventure/puzzle games might get something out of this. It has a Tomb Raider kind of feel to it, with less emphasis on the platforming elements.
TL;DR : Decent third-person adventure/puzzle game, it’s fun, challenging and can be completed 100% in under 8 hours. Despite it looking fairly old it definitely holds up. I’d say it’s worth a go.

I would refund it if I didn't spend the first two hours in it trying to get the game not to crash upon startup and at almost every loading screen.
I understand it is an early access game, but I've played few other early access games this poorly optimized and unplayable, and honestly after spending what was almost an entire week to get it to work so I could play with a friend that recommended it, it didn't feel worth it at all.
So lets get down to the two main points I have to talk about, performance and gameplay.
Peformance:
This is obviously my main issue with the game. Not only is it riddled with problems simply getting it to run, when you finally find a way over all of those hurdles through what honestly seems to be just pure esoteric sorcery nobody on any forum suffering from the same issues can understand or recreate properly, the game itself has a high chance to just run like pure garbage even on a powerful PC. I say chance because honestly there seems to be no clear answer on how to get it to run properly for everyone, for some it runs great on a god damn laptop that costs barely 500 dollars. For others, they might crash on start up or it might tank their desktop PC even if it's worth three times that. My own experience can play anecdote here, as can the experience of people all over the internet who suffer the same problems with the same or even more powerful builds, as can the experience of another friend who bought it alongside me and couldn't even play it at all while I could despite him having a tower that would blow mine out of the park.
The general answer you'll find if you run into any problems will probably be either "it works on my PC" or "just wait till they patch it", and you'll probably find these answers dating back since the game first came out many years ago. Well all these years later, despite numerous supposed "performance updates" and so on, they never patched all the holes and these people still aren't worth listening to.
Gameplay:
Gameplay in rust is interesting, assuming this is your first ever open world survival multiplayer early access game and it's still 2013. First you knock down trees, pretty original, right? Then you mine some stone, you make some tools, you build a hut and you upgrade and defend your hut while your armor/weapon progression slowly turns you into what can best be described as a side character from mad max. All the while you'll be trying to manage hunger, thirst and even battle the elements to a small degree by dressing appropriately. But that obviously isn't the only draw of this game, another draw is that it's multiplayer on top of it all, you can play with friends you can make enemies start little wars and enjoy some very basic PvP action. Unfortunately it takes a bit of time to fully experience this outside of naked rock/torch fights, and even then it usually devolves into that because nobody really wants to take too many important goodies out of their base on the chance they could lose them. I won't lie, I had some fun with the gameplay once I'd grown used to suffering the endless optimization flaws, but if people didn't enjoy these types of games there wouldn't be so many of them.
And thats part of the problem, there are so many of them, and the gameplay doesn't really compare superbly well to many of them. Content wise there may be more to do but that's because the game has been in development forever and even then you'll still run out of things to do inevitably if the PvP doesn't really interest you.
Sadly in the end I can't recommend it at all in it's current state and given how long it's been in the state it's in I don't believe I'll ever be able to in this lifetime. Another early access game that will never ever leave alpha I guess. Perhaps one of the trendsetters for this plague on steam.

A brutally punishing FPS with tight controls and precise shooting.
Despite the above being true, this game lacks. Almost every death is cheap with snakeworms poisoning you with barely any health left on level 7. If it isn't snakeworms, it's the ridiculously powerful turrets (especially the ones that fire ROCKETS at you).
The bosses are the worst part - they're always far too quick for you to even understand what's happening as both of the 2 bosses last usually less than 15 seconds. Unless you have the focus pills (single-use slow motion powerup), you'll systematically either die or come out of the fight with half a heart left.
Besides all that, it's nevertheless a good FPS.
Did I mention performance? It's all over the place - I've read reviews in which performance was perfect, and others that complained about low FPS, which I have to confirm. The game runs poorly on a GTX970 and i5-4690k @ 3.50Ghz, a PC able to play almost any game on ultra with a steady framerate. This includes stuff like MGSV, Far Cry 4, Crysis 3, and other generally demanding games.
The game doesn't look bad, but judging by the low amount of polygons and textures, there's really no excuse for it to dip down to 30-40FPS at random intervals.
If you find it on sale, buy it. Despite my review being mostly negative, there are a lot of positive aspects to the game - but also negatives.

Max Payne: a classic game from 2001, gets a new lease on life through Steam. I played the ever loving poop out of this game when it was released, and after seeing it here for a pittance, I decided to purchase it once more (my disk version, which I still have, doesn't work on Windows 10). I was not disappointed. This game is still fantastic 16 years later, and it has one of the best mechanics I've ever experienced in a game - bullet time. Great story, memorable characters, and fun gameplay make this a must-have game, in my opinion.
A few caveats, however: first, you will have to install the community-provided patch to get the sounds to work correctly. This is very easy to do, and it improves your experience significantly. Second, there are a few minor glitches in the Steam version. These can be worked around, but the frustration level was real.
Glitch one involves a chase involving Vince Gognitti - he falls between two buildings and cannot be harmed. Later, you can get caught in a death loop as he respawns during a cutscene, and his goons kill you instantly. To avoid this, just climb back up the stairs and the game should progress normally.
Glitch two involves the inability of Max to jump properly during the dream sequences. You can get around this by performing sideways shoot-dodge jumps, which should solve any issues.
Other than that, the game performed perfectly. It's a fun, smart, exciting ride, so pick it up if it interests you.

Torment has both a long history across iterations and rosy glasses syndrome for the predecessor.  Although Planescape:  Torment has been universally lauded in hindsight, it's initial release didn't do well enough for the notoriously money-hungry TSR at the time to greenlight a successor.  After decades we receive a new setting and original story by a new studio, some of whom worked on the original game.  I would like to say to every reviewer that spent 30 hours or less and declared it a feeble attempt that you didn't spend enough time with it.  Sure, you can gulp down a rare vintage French wine as easily as Mad Dog 20/20 and opine that you don't see the big deal and question why you had to wait a dozen years for the French bottle.  You can do that and you will be an idiot.  Torment:  Tides of Numenera grants instant nostalgia, but it isn't the same game.  You aren't playing a continuation of the Nameless One's adventures (that story concluded) and the setting and interactions are different.  Some people simply can't get past that.  I would not say that this is a gripping tale that needs to be debated in the halls of academia, but it is a well-crafted thought exercise that considers many of the finer points of philosophy, chief among them what constitutes self.  So, for those on the fence:  the vast number of negative reviews seem to be from people who either don't understand this type of reading heavy title ("this looked like a neat RPG, but I had to read") or desperately wanted Planescape:  Torment 2 ("why didn't I get Morte!").  Both types can be ignored.

I have spent almost a hundred hours in the Ninth World and still want to go back. This game is abolutely fantastic!
Torment: Tides of Numenera achieves a new level of storytelling and game design that I could only have dreamed of. The way everything you do binds into the theme of the game down to a mechanical level and how it blends classical turnbased combat with problem solving throught the brilliant crisis-system, to make strategizing more than just number crunshing. How a seemingly unimportant line of dialogue or a sporadic side-quest ties directly into the over arching story. How nothing is good or bad, right or wrong or even real or fiction. It -is- then therefore there are consequences. That is what made this game for me!
What really amazed me was how you become part of the world in a way that most other games just does not. You start out as an outsider but as you go through the game you learn about the world. Not by reading lore or having someone explain it to you, but through interacting with it and piecing it together.
This game is not perfect, though. This game would sorely have benefitted from a few more weeks in the oven, or perhaps even months, as there were a lot of bugs throughout the game. Most of them were purly visual or easily circumvented. But a few times the game crashed, locked itself on an enemys turn in combat or failed to execute an action or attack. Some of the interface was sometimes hard to understand. (For example the chance clalculator that would sometimes show me a base chance of 0%, a modifier of +75% and a total chance of 20% to succeed)
As for another thing that I don't really think they failed at, but rather I would just have loved to see more of, were the crices throughout the game. They were easily one of the more interesting parts where you simply could not rely on he dice rolls alone, but had to really ponder every move to not have the situation spin out of control. There is a huge (and I mean HUGE!) potential with this system to lend RPGs of all kind a new sense of intensity, even when the game pauses to let you think. This along with the games way of seamlessly connecting challenges of battle with the challenges outside of battle is the game's biggest mechanical strength. I makes every choice in battle/crises effect what will happen between as well, instead of just effecting the next battle, as most old CRPGs.
I hope this game gains the success it deserves, and I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys RPGs in any way, even though it's relatively steep pricetag. And most of all, I hope this is not the last time I get to visit the Ninth World in a video game!

What a fantastic game!
"Tides of Numenera" is a worthy successor to "Planescape Torment", my favorite game of all time. Although not as good as the original, ToN is a first-rate RPG just like they used to make them back in the days.
+ The atmosphere
I can not stress this enough. The atmosphere in this game is simply gorgeous. The game makers perfectly managed to recapture that special Planescape feeling. Exploring the streets of Sagus Cliffs felt just like exploring Sigil for the very first time so many years ago. And "The Bloom" is one of the most scenic areas that has ever been created in video game history in my opinion.
+ The Lore
Lots of philosophy, just the way you like it. There is so much stuff you can learn about this world and it's always told in an engaging and informative way.
+ The Story
Suspenseful story-telling, cool characters, it's all there. I've heard people complain about the ending of ToN, but I can't share that opinion at all. The ending (at least the one I chose) was a perfect conclusion to the story arc.
+- The Party
In my opinion the biggest "flaw" of the game. The NPCs are not nearly as interesting or fleshed-out as the ones in "Placescape Torment". No companion has the charme of Morte or the wits of Annah. They are likeable (most of them), but I wish there would have been more interaction and more depth to the characters.
+- The Universe
ToN takes places in the Ninth World, which is not related to the Planes you know from D&D at all. In the beginning this was a bit of a let-down for me, regarding how much story potential the Planes still seemed to contain. In the end though, I found this new universe really fascinating. It's thoroughly developed and I think you should give it a chance. Don't listen to people who say: "It's not the Planes so it's bad!"
+- The Game Mechanics
Not really a bad thing. I like the new mechanics, but boy does it take time to get used to them. The fights are turn-based and you now have ability points that you can spend in order to increase the chance of success of a certain action. It's closer to an actual Pen & Paper RPG.
+- The Length
It took me about 30 hours to complete the game including most side quests. Not too bad, but I think the game could have lasted just a bit longer.
Nothing really. The game has some small flaws, but nothing serious that would interfere with the game experience.
If you can get over the fact, that the new Torment is set in a different universe and you don't mind learning new game mechanics, I strongly suggest you buy this game. It might not be as amazing as the original Planescape, but it's a very strong second installment that manages to fill the foot-steps made by it's predecessor.
