First thing first: TToN is not an RPG. It's a story-driven adventure game and should be judged as such. Its progression type is actually that of a point-and-click game: you get a hub, you find the correct order to click things, you uncover the plot and then move to the next area.
This is all fine in my book, but should be kept in mind.
Sadly, the game has a bunch of glaring downsides:
Does this all make the game unworthy of playing? No. Unworthy of its price tag? Yeah, perhaps.
Trying to remember PST without nostalgia goggles, I'd actually say that TToN does a good job of capturing the spirit of the now-franchise. You get the sense of a huge and wondrous world with plots and events criss-crossing each other—and there you are, thrown in the thick of it, your head spinning from the weirdness that surrounds you. This feeling is strongly enhanced by the fact that the game
—meaning that most characters and situations you'll encounter will have unique models, scripts, and so on. The lack of junk content makes the world feel rich and true.
TToN actually builds upon PST's methods, trying little neat tricks to make everything seem... I wouldn't say "more natural", but rather "more engaging". You get dialogue options that are only available once. You get failure states more interesting than successes. You get hidden timers that make certain events change and unfold.
All these things are great improvements over PST.
Another thing that captures the spirit of the old game to a T is the soundtrack. Reserved, non-grandiose, yet full of genuine tingling sorrow, it seemed perfect.
Honorable mentions to some other elements of the game:
They're okay. The game features:
They're less original than in PST, but way more fully-realized. However, for some inexplicable reason they are also all human.
Now, like I said, I do recommend this game. For all its downsides, it's more than worth your time if you just want to immerse yourself in the Ninth World and play an adventure game of epic scale.
But—and there's no way to put in lightly—the main plot sucks.
I'm not talking about the writing, although I did find the major plot scenes to be among the less well-executed. But that, once again, would be forgivable... if the game didn't spend its second half to destroy the great premise of the first half.
You start as a person in a startling, but not unique, situation: you are a shell of a body, cast off by your creator who jumps vessels to stay immortal. You are not special in any existential way—however, you are technically the best candidate to oppose The Changing God/Sorrow, since each new body he makes is better than the previous ones, so you're the best among your brethren. Sounds like a great "fit for this story, but not The Chosen One" setup.
Basically, it's a mess of "Fahrenheit" proportions. In the third act, new entities get shoved down your throat one after the other, every new screen is a revelation that turns the plot on its head... leaving you confused and the game, robbed of focus.
With all its oddness and quirkiness, down below PST was a very simple, almost Hollywood-like story of redemption. The question it asked was Shakespearean in its simplicity:
And the bittersweet yet fulfilling answer was,
. It was a game about accepting death, plain and simple.
TToN's premise is actually at times more imaginative than that of PST... but what is it about? The ending devolves into a tangle of personal motivations, of
and
—but there's no central issue, no subject the game would explore and revolve around. It's just... abut people.
It's like a castoff: pretty and able to surpass its creator in certain areas, but ultimalety empty.
And that, my friends, is a bloody shame.

Torment is not a "bad" game - but it is not a "good" Inxile game either. The world building, storyline, characters and lore are all fantastic - at the very least the game has introduced more people to the Numenera universe, which is just a fun world. The problem (as I see it) is that I don't feel that the game systems of Numenera translate themselves that well to a computer based role-playing game.
In games of similar context (such as Planescape Torment which this is a spiritual successor to) I would argue that better concessions were made to make the game fun as well as interesting with a storyline. As it stands Torment is basically a choose your own adventure novel in electronic format, which isn't good enough for me.
Given the opportunity, I would purchase it again just to support Inxile and the hope that maybe they'll do another game in the Torment universe - its too rich a background not to explore, but I can't recommend that other people buy it.

I think it's a very interesting, and overall very good game. Would I recommend it? Yes, for sure. Alas, it isnt a game for just anyone.
tl;dr: If you like reading, and like slow pacing, and you are looking for something fresh and in some ways unique, with characters that have their own stories and are memorable (at least some of them), you liked Planescape Torment, and have enough time and have ability to focus, go ahead and get the game!
On the other hand - if you can't focus, prefer fast pacing, are action oriented, and you are more Pillars of Eternity type of RPG player, with more fighting, dungeon crawling, and you arent interested in companions at all, but progress and very visible main story is important for you - you may not enjoy Tides of Numenera.
What did I enjoy? What did I think was done right?
+ The world/setting is very good and pretty interesting. It does have that bit weird feeling to it, as Planescape Torment had.
+ Characters are very good. They aren't just a stat-sticks, that you drag along. They have their stories, their opinions, and the world reacts to them.
+The game is story driven, and the story is good.
+Quests are very interesting, because they can be solved in so many ways! And I don't mean: just one-or-two possible solutions. There's plenty!
+it's a game you can re-play and discover many new things on your next playthrough. I think it is worth re-playing and I am just about to do that.
+After you finish the game, and will look up the achievements that you can get, you're like: 'wow, is that really possible to do THAT? I need to try!' The game is flexible, and the more effort you will put into it, the more things you will discover.
+Combat system - it's new, and fresh. It is turn wise, and at first I wasn't convinced, because I hate turn system with a passion, but in this game, the turn system has it's merits. It isnt used only for combat. It's more narrative, you can even try to talk to your adversaries at times and try to get them to your side. It's different from just - go and kill everything that moves.
+You don't like fighting? You don't have to fight. At all. There are many ways to solve the problems, and fighting is only one of options.
What I think they could improve:
-No intro/movie at the begining - I couldn't care less for the cutscenes, but because there is no intro, you are plunged into a world you know nothing about, story you know nothing about, and you get all those seemingly random quests you just go and do, without really knowing why the heck are you here and what is your purpose.
- There is just too much of text! Wall of texts absolutely everywhere, make your attention go away quickly.
Overall I think that it's a very good game, and I am very happy it got released. They did cut some content, but what is left in the game is well made. At first, I was very confused and didn't like the game too much, because I had no idea what's going on, and it smelled too much like a weaker copy of Planescape Torment. But I gave it a fair chance, and I am very pleased that I did. The story isn't a copy-paste of Planescape, which I did dread for a time, it has many options and you can play as you like. So it's honestly a game to experience.
I am very pleased that I got it, that I didn't quit, and I am totally going to re-play. I consider the game Time well spent.

Damn I wanted to like TToN so much, I didn't though.
Pros:
+Beautifull landscape art
+Very interesting setting
+Rhin (companion)
Cons:
-Ugly character art, made worse by ugly or nonexistent character portraits
-Pointless character developement system:
*Combat skills feel pointless because there's so little combat, of which most is avoidable anyway
*All other skills feel pointless after few levels, because you end up automatically passing every single skill test with minimal effort / points used
-Simplistic, unengaging combat (Crisis)
-Uninteresting companion characters (most of them)
-Bugs. I've found two bugs in vendor screen taking all my money, one side quest I couldn't complete, and one crisis in main quest line I had to load/save a dozen times to get through because of a crucial companion being unable to use his skills due to an UI bug.
-Complete lack of anything that would make this an engaging computer game. It's more like a book with graphics you need to click on to read more, and couple of very simple puzzles to solve.
I suppose it all boils down to the writing though, and how you like it. I'm a constant reader, and I mainly read science fiction and historical novels from a lot of authors, all of which usually contain a lot of world building and lengthy descriptions, and I loved PST. In TToN I still got completely exhausted by the amount of text one has to wade through. Sure the world *is* interesting, and some of the quests are too. However, there's just so much text explaining just how interesting and clever and filled with hidden meaning and lost secrets everything is, even when said item, NPC or concept is pointless and never mentioned again, I can't be bothered to read it all. I got tired of it. I mean, there's pointless stuff you can collect and sell, and those all have lengthy descriptions. Every NPC has a wall of text to wade through, just so you can be sure that the NPC in question is a pointless sidenote that doesn't even have a named sidequests tied to it. I mean, it took me like five hours to finish my first quest in the game, because I felt like I had to talk to all of the NPC's in Sagus' Cliffs (several of them twice), to be sure I was making an educated decision. Five hours is two movies worth of writing, or half a book, without any kind of conclusion or advancement of the plot. After being exhausted by this sort of gameplay, where the "game" was actually just me clicking my character between NPC's and reading their comments for hours, I really couldn't believe it that the game then even took the graphics away, and made me do text adventures (most of which seemed totally disconnected from the story.)
I'm sorry about writing a review without finishing the game, but I suppose that speaks for itself. I'll maybe return to TToN in couple of months and try to struggle through it.

It's a game about egoism, shortsightedness and all-destroying anger which will bring nothing but suffering and death. The end is really bitter. It left me quite depressed after finishing the game... Which actually means - the game got me. And it's something, isn't it?

Well, I have finished this game. I don't know how much time I spent into it, but if you don't grind (like I did in the first hours of the game) I guess you can finish this game in something like 10 hours or less.
It's not ugly. It's not that "buggy" (even if it may be sometimes).
BUT
This game is clearly not worth 20$. I bought it 3$ and still I have a bad taste in my mouth.
The reason is simple:
Warner is just kidding us. Basically, they took the last Batman Arkham engine, copy/paste it and then put the title "Mad Max" on it. The difference is that Batman was a decent game for two reasons: the story and the character.
But here:
- The story is ridiculous. They don't even try to be original. It has been the first game for a very long time in which I skipped all cut scenes because I just don't care. Seriously, nobody does. However, I precisely know what was the purpose of the story, because I think any 8-years old child could write it.
- The gameplay. Oh boy, the gameplay... It is oviously one of the most outrageous copies of Batman/Assassin's Creed/Shadow of Mordor (u name it...) without a slight pound of originality.
We all know it, and after let's say 5 minutes, you would have seen the complete gameplay that you will be facing during the rest of the game : press "X" to punch until a big "Y" appears on the head of a foe, then press "Y" and do it again until all ennemies are dead.
- The controls : well, I guess a random script was used to assign actions. I mean: "LT" to jump ? "RB" to roll ? "B" to shoot ? Come on guys, have you ever hold a controller in your hands ?
- The content : well, it's quite strange because it seems that they tried to do something interesting at some points. At least they tried.
There are 4 types of structures in this game: fortress (=sanctuary), camps u have to clean, towers u have to destroy and dumps where u can get metal to improve your car. That's it.
Some would call it content, I personnaly call this filling empty game with sh***y things.
But sometimes you feel like they tried, for instance the sort of stoves that u may find in the camps sometimes : obviously, it was made to be interacted with. I mean, they clearly get out of the rest of the decor. But no, in the release u can't use them while I imagine it was an element of "survival" where u should cook to stay alive (see my next point)
- The atmosphere : isn't Mad Max supposed to make u feel like ressources are precious ? I mean, come on, it is obviously the purpose of the movies: people taking control of ressources and making slaves of others that don't own them.
In this game you don't give a s**t: gas is never a problem, food neither, drink neither, ammo neither.
- The music is what we could call "forgettable". I just exited the game and still I do not remember one single music/theme of the game.
Roughly, don't buy this game unless you have 10 hours to loose, and what's more don't even dare buying it at 20$. Please.

Ah... this old gem. I loved the living hell out of this game when I was a kid (until my mum banned me from playing it because it's technically an FPS and she doesn't like those).
Story: It's... more than a thing. It's no great, epic tale of darkness and light, right and wrong etcetera, but it serves it's purpose and is somewhat interesting. It's not the draw of the game though. It does throw some good old-fashioned nostalgia fuel in there on all three sets of levels, especially in the first set.
Music: it's Star Wars. A lot of the classic tunes are there. Not sure if there's any new music - a lot of it is unmemorable aside from those classics. But then again, it serves it's purpose, so no actual complaints.
Level design. Variable. Sometimes it's really good, sometimes it's not. Be aware that out of every five-level set, there's a horror-esque one with one or more giant monsters. It does let you skip one mission per set though, so if you don't like horror than that's cool, provided you are fine with not being quite as powerful at the end of the game.
Gameplay: D'you remember episode 1? Those angels Anikin was talking about? Well they made this game. It's not Devil May Cry, it's not Bayonetta, it's not the Force Unleashed. It is Jedi Knight: Jedi Academy and you will know it's name. It's a kendo-based sword combat system that is satisfiying, a power fantasy and balls-to-the-wall hard if you want it to be. Furthermore, it is easily the focus of the game. At the start, you'll mostly be fighting gun-toting mooks such as strormtroopers which if you've watched any anime, you should know how that ends. The second set of levels has more gimmicky levels which are a nice change of pace once/if you get the hang of it. The third set will pit you against more swordsmen than you can believe - ESPECIALLY the last level. And it kicks♥♥♥♥♥ since by that point you'll have a wealth of force powers, more moves and one of three fighting styles: single blade, the versitile and precise pic; it tends to have an advantage over two swords due to better aim; Jar'kai which is two blades -a  defensive and pretty style; it tends to have an advantage over saberstaff due to being able to block everything and saberstaff which short ranged, less precise and less defensive but aggressive and powerful as all hell once you get in range; it tends to have an advantage over single saber as they have issues weathering the storm of blades. Both the later weapons can switch into single-sword, but single sword has three styles to compensate - light (fast), medium and heavy (strong). Your cuts are based on the direction you move, so footwork is important. Click to swing. Right click to be risky and throw your sword (it comes back though unless you equip a different weapon mid fight. You can resummon it by attacking)
Do not, repeat, do not play this game for a first person shooter. The guns, with precisely one exception, are about as useful as a pea shooter except in certain circumstamces. This exception is the concussion rifle, which is basically a rocket launcher on steroids. With a splash damage and specific damage setting. The other guns are: a pistol that you will never use. A stormtrooper gun which upon using it you will understand why they never hit anything, and that question will be replaced with why they never use the rapid fire function. A Wookie Bowcaster which is stronger and more accurate than the others and has a slow shotgun charge up, but the lightsaber is still more useful. An EMP gun which is useful for precisely one level, and you have to pick it before it starts otherwise you can't get it in that level. A disintegrator sniper rifle, which is really satisfying but there aren't many chances to use it. A Machine gun that does WAAAY too little damage and has a grenade launcher. A shotgun. God mode for a few shots (the concussion rifle), provided you don't shoot yourself. And a normal rocket launcher that can at least home in on targets.
Multiplayer: haven't played, meaning to try.

So to start I'd like to say that I enjoyed this game immensley.  The jokes are beyond hilarious while the writing remains quite clever.  True, some of the dads in question received a great deal more attention than others, but overall what is here is good.  Unfortunately, there isn't all that much.  To play through one single storyline with one dad takes little to no time at all, with only three short dates before the game ends.  These dates are usually hilarious, sweet, endearing, and surprising, but the game could have definitely benefitted from having perhaps two or three more dates for each dad.
Customisation of your own character is incredibly lacking here, especially if one wants to create a reasonably life-like charater, but there is ample scope to create the most hilarious dad you can think which I believe was the main goal for the creators.  It is a bit jarring though for the dads to be so well-drawn and your own character to be a bit of a cartoon.
On to bugs, and I can't say I've noticed quite as many as other reviewers have, but if you decide that your dad was once married to a woman well... the game won't recognise that, instead defaulting to your former spouse being a man.  Also, there is no "good" ending for the Joseph storyline which may be a bug, but could perhaps be a design choice.
In all, I'd say this is a very good game, if perhaps an unfinished one.  If you're looking some laughs, however, this is the game for you.

Thumbs up with caveats. Overall it's wonderful to play a game that features normal guys romancing guys. I love the humor of the Dadsona and the relationship you can build with your daughter - one of the most realistic and awesome familial relationships I've seen featured in a VN. The little voice acting there is? I really like that as well. And I think most of the dads you date are cool dudes. Some of them have solidly won over my heart.
Are there issues? Yes. One of the endings is a massive letdown considering this is a fantasy dating sim, and might even be a broken route. There are misspellings and grammatical errors (not many but they do exist). Considering you're dating DADS, most with young children, I don't think there's enough interaction with the kids and their input on any potential relationships or your daughter and HER opinion on it. And there is the option to make your character a trans man but that really is suuuuper unclear, just appears to be a crop top on a male torso. That needs a lot of clarification and/or explanation. Is it worth $15? Debatable. I would prefer $10, but it's not an unreasonable price.
What I am indifferent on is the customization and minimal amount of voice acting. I can count on one hand the VNs that allow any customization /at all/. This isn't Elder Scrolls. Anyone expecting a million options needs a reality check. There's actually a respectable amount for a VN. True voice acting is also incredibly rare and I personally prefer minimal so that my imagination can work the smexy magic. The suggestions and phrases that were used seemed 100% fitting and worked perfectly for me. This is true personal preference and opinion - and some truth since I am a VN junkie.
With some expectations kept in check this is a lovely game and truly enjoyable... but I am looking forward to a patch or two in the near future.

Adam's Venture chronicles is a great and fun puzzling adventure game. It really challenged me to use my brain, which I quite often didn't actually do and ended up googling the answers instead.
The graphics are quite nice for an adventure game and I loved the characters personalities, they weren't as stereotypical as most games.
I'd recommend this game if you love puzzles and adventure, and if you love solving brain cracking riddles that made me swear like a sailor.

Lately it was decided to (finally) combine the 3 episodes of Adam's Venture to this very title, and that happened exactly when I was in the middle of playing episode 3. So, despite the short playtime - I did complete this game, and even reviewed the first two episodes (and those two probably just faded away). I'll take it as a chance to review the entire game and not each episode seperately.
While I don't find the game amazing, it does get better as you progress, and eventually it's an alright "action"-adventure game. It is rather casual, though, in almost every aspect. If that's your cup of tea then you might want to give it a chance.
Adam's Venture is supposedly an action-adventure game which seems like a childish version of games like Tomb Raider or Uncharted, definitely not as good, and seems a little like a 'wannabe'.
On the technical aspects the game swings from decent to nice quality. Again, nothing special or memorable unfortunately. It seemed to me like the graphics got better optimized in the third chapter somehow, as it ran smoothly on my machine with highest settings while the first one was faltering on medium, and my machine definitely has the recommended system requirements (this game does get old..)
The story is a cliche but actually a nice one. As I said, it's all very casual and so there's nothing too bombastic or complex. Acting is decent but not a major part of this game.
Gameplay is fairly simple, rather linear with numerous puzzles along the way, which start out ridicolously easy but on the third chapter become somewhat more challanging (and at times obscure and unclear).
When I reviewed the first and second episode I've written that this game is good for children, but somehow on the third episode the difficulty significantly rises and therefore I'm not too sure about that anymore.
Anyway, as I said, the game does get better from episode to episode, and for that reason alone I find it a little hard to review all the 3 episodes.
While the 1st one didn't leave such a good impression on me, the 3rd actually made me like this game much more.
Adam's Venture isn't terrific, but it's an OK piece of adventure. The rather boring first episode evolves and becomes mroe fun and bearable in the second and third ones.
It took me about 2-3 hours to complete each episdoes, which gives you in a whole a 6-9 hours experience for 20$, depending on your gameplay style.
That's a little steep for this game, and I'd say - get it on a sale like I did. If you're a die-hard fan of adventure games you'll enjoy it.
As a parent you could play it with your kid perhaps, and that might also be nice.
Really, that's a fine game. A little meehh but worth a try. I might even play it again one day.

I added this to my wishlist without knowing much about it. I honestly thought this was going to be a short walking simulator game like The Old City or Dear Esther. Imagine my surpirse when I booted this up for the first time. Completely caught of guard.
This is a fast paced game that chucks you in the deep end. All you have to do is get the edge of the screen. There will be giant Vines and Blades blocking your way and closing in on you as you play, so its no walk in the park. You dont really get time to stop and think what to do, you just have concentrate and keep moving. You have to survive for 100 levels with one life. If you die, its back to level one. This gets annoying but it would be pretty bland if you had checkpoints. Having one life keeps this intense and exciting.
Its simple so theres not much to love and not much to hate really. It is just a bit of fun. There are only two things that annoyed me. The hit boxes are unreliable and can screw you over. You can get abosered by the Vines and still live or you clip the tip of one of the spikes and die instantly. Its not too big a problem, but when you are on a good run and get killed by something that just barely touched you it can get quite infuriating. The other problem is the ending. This game doesnt try to have a story but it throws in an odd ending that doesnt really fit. It feels like its just there to try and make the game seem more meaningful.
However, these don't ruin the game by any means. Its still a fun and tense game that is alright for the 30p I paid for it. If you have some money in your Steam Wallet from selling cards and you want to get rid of it, buy this. You'll either love it or hate it.

This game... this game! You know when you're at the arcade and you give that claw machine a try? The claw dips down, finds a slight grip on the ear of some stuffed animal, and wow, you've actually picked it up! The game has that way of making you think you can do it and that's why you die a thousand times trying to complete one level. The game has that special something that makes you want to stay and keep on trying, when in other games you'd just give up. It looks hard but you know you can do it!!

Amazingly fun, amazingly difficult! Recommended ten times over!

Excellent game. Game has insane world building with no copy pasting at all and it's a heaven for exploration types like me. Lots of interesting places and backstory elements that flesh out the Mad Max universe like never before. Also has a very good (and dark) story with an insanely good ending.
Visually the game is stunning and runs at 60 fps on ultra  even on my 2013 pc. It really is a shinning example of good coding.
The game is even better on the sound department. Everything sounds insanely good from the vehicles, to the guns and punches. Performances are universally excellent also.
As for the negatives there are only a couple of them: The game was very easy for my taste. Water is abundant, fuel is never needed, (except if you are the driver type that like to side burn everything:P) and scrap becomes irrelevant after some point because of the camp income. The strongholds should really not refuel and re-ration the player. This fact alone makes the game very easy.
The second negative doesn't apply to all people but the game can be a bit grindy if you don't progress organically through it. What I mean by that is that anyone that tries to rush the main story must be ready for a few huge walls along the way (loewring threat, destroying camps etc). For anyone that takes the time to play the game as intented that's not a problem though.
Overall the game was very solid. I really don't know what the game press was smoking when reviewing this one tbh. This is easilly worth the 60 dollars they asked on release. It's better than the last Batman game and better than shadow of Mordor (maybe not for some people but it was for me). Sure it isn't Witcher 3 by any means but it's still a solid 8-8.5/10.

Mad Max was a fun open world action game. The thing that sets it apart is definitely the higher focus on cars, which was refreshing. They're more than just methods to go from A to B where you do things, you actually had car combat and could do a lot from your car. It also had a lot of upgrading and customization to it, which I appreciated. Better armor gives you higher defense, but does come at the cost of speed / handling. You get to make choices that suit your playstyle. The setting was neat as a desert isn't often used. I liked how much stuff there was to do in it, while still feeling like a desolate wasteland. That was well done.
That said, I do have some complaints about the game too.
- The minefield game is awful. First off you're forced to switch to the buggy, so you can't just do them as you come across them. The buggy also can't even fast-travel, so you have to drive around a lot more to get to all the minefields. Then the minefield itself is just a slow process of driving around at a snail's pace until a mine pop-up, getting out of your car, disarming it and watching a cutscene play and fade to black, before you repeat it two more times. All the while the dog barks constantly. Very annoying, and I didn't bother doing all of them.
- Fuel was an interesting idea, but executed poorly. There was always more than enough fuel that you never had to worry about your car running out. It only ever mattered for some of the vantage points. But that's where the real issue comes in: you can't see how much fuel is in a container while holding it. So you can carry this empty jerrycan all the way to the top of the vantage point only to THEN find out it's empty and have to go back and find another one. Just replace the water icon with a fuel one while carrying a jerrycan so I can see.
- For a game so focused on cars, the driving wasn't perfect. If you ever wanted to attack anything, your camera would focus on the target. This means that attacking something to the side (or behind) of you will make it so you can't see where you're going. I ended up driving into a few more walls than I would've liked due to this. Cars in general also felt like driving on ice at times, with very poor traction and slipping out like crazy for the most minor things. It gets better in your upgraded Magnum Opus, but it still gave me issues every now and then.
Overall a fun and good action game, but it definitely had some flaws that made me question the game design. I did get 43 hours out of it and it was mostly positive though, so I would recommend the game to others looking for an open world action game like Far Cry, that has a bit more focus on vehicles.

I really wish I could say I don't regret buying this. I want to support this game and love it but... there's too many issues. And for $15? Save your money. I don't think I'd buy it for more than $10.
Sure, this is their first game, but there mistakes are so sloppy and some don't even necessarily require being a AAA developer (Grammar) that they're ultimately unexcusable.
Lets start with the pros. 
- Gay dating sim that's positive and enjoyable with characters that aren't the exact same guy with different hair styles 
-Light, enjoyable dialogue, funny dialogue 
-I love amanda with all my heart 
-art is absolutely gorgeous and wonderful to look at 
-Lots of diversity in all aspects 
Here's the Cons. 
- Didn't feel like there was ... Enough. Three dates with a dad and that's it. That seems awful short, especially if you're really excited for one dad in particular. 
-BUGS. A LOT OF THEM. 
-Seems sloppy in some places. Like Mat's kid places a flower crown on his head but it takes several scenes for it to appear on his head. Mentions 'had fun at the bbq yesterday!" when what i did yesterday was go on a date someone.
-missing quality of life stuff. Like pressing esc to access a menu (closes the game which is kind of weird ? usually it brings up a menu.) There's literally only two options for music and 'streamer safe' stuff. 
-Feels more focused on Amanda than dating some Dads. Listen I love her, don't want to Not do dad things, but I came here to smorch some boys 
-Joseph route. You literally cannot get a good ending on him due to bugs. Given that they postponed the game 5 days to fix bugs this is a little ridiculous, given that its ... you know.... a whole ROUTE. Even if its not a bug, its extremely complicated to figure out (as no one has done it yet, or very few have) which is weird and convoluted given that all the other routes are pretty straightforward. If all the routes were complicated I wouldn't have a problem but its odd to make one character so complex. 
- Hugo's voice acting sounds like it was recorded in an empty room and echoed. 
-Within the routes, a lot of them were 1/2 other various events, and only 1/2 romance. Given that there's only 3 dates that's a little upsetting. 
-not all of the dads have 'happy' endings that feel satisfying to the player. It's so frustrating to get to the end only for them to dump you or something.
-dadsona model looks... off. All the characters looked fully shaded and colored, but the dadsona has only flat colors and almost no shading. The choices for your dadsona also don't match the art style of the rest of the game, so you look very out of place.
-I was surprised to see that Amanda is 18. She acts like she's 14-15.
-A lot of tropes that, when used well, are enjoyable, but feel stale here
-Voice acting is weird and awkward grunting
-minigames feel so out of place and badly done. Don't match the art style at all, they're weird, and get quickly repetitive and boring.
-Theres more I could say but I think you get the point.
TD;LR sloppy, rushed, takes weird turns a lot, doesn't feel like I'm really romancing much, too much Amanda and not enough gay, too expensive for something so full of mistakes.

If this is what Payne feels like, then I'm a self-proclaimed masochist.
The game itself is a third-person shooter that recounts a dark and dirty flashback of undercover DEA agent Max Payne. Within the first 20 minutes of the game, your wife, baby, and boss are dead. Seeing as how you don't have much left to live for, you go after the Mafia drug syndicate where you've been working as an undercover mole, exacting justice on the people you think are responsible for your family and friend's deaths.
The story elements are handled through a variety of means, presented through in-game cutscenes, conversations during gameplay, and narrated graphic novel-inspired panels that fit the game perfectly, and really add a lot of style and character to the game in the process.
A lot of the action in the game revolves around "bullet time," a slow-motion state where Max gains super-human reflexes. It's a non-stop thrill-ride the whole way through, and you never go for more than a few seconds without seeing a gangster who's ready to take you down.
To help you with kill those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s is Payne's impressive arsenal which includes close range weapons, pistols, shotguns, sub-machine guns, an assault rifle, a sniper rifle, and explosives.
Environments themselves react like you would expect them to react, further immersing you into the digital world. Almost everything in the world is interactive, meaning you can flush toilets, turn on sinks and showers, shoot cash registers and watch them explode in a shower of sparks, break glass, and even blow out speakers in elevators.

AO is a solid game despite the vitriol surrounding it. The story itself stands out as the best in the series, taking a page from the Nolan book both in terms of visuals (the bat suit is clearly a carbon copy of Bale’s in the Dark Knight), and in a preference for (relative) realism over mystical ninjas and shapeshifters. Still, the few game play innovations Arkham Origins manages to make are disappointing—namely the "I-win" shock gloves that sap all thought from combat and break any RP connection you have with old bats, and the remote claw which, while cool in concept, ends up giving the player three free stealth kills in every predator encounter. Since most stealth sections contain eight thugs max, this majorly undercuts the teeth-grinding challenge they ought to pose in the latter half of the game.
The world also feels empty. There are Riddler challenges to tackle but nowhere near as many as in Arkham City. Gone too are the citizens of Gotham, relegated to their homes by a dubious Christmas Eve curfew. This in particular robs the game of a potentially fantastic innovation—the interplay between Batman and the common citizen. Wouldn’t you love hurdle over a rooftop only to land next to an awed/terrified couple canoodling on the fire escape? How would they react? How would YOU react? Part of Batman’s mystique is the image he cuts in the non-criminal mind. In the next game I’d love to see that aspect explored.

TL:DR: Like it’s predecessor, Tides of Numenera is both deep and unique. If you’re expecting something more superficial and action-packed, move on.  If, however, you’re willing to play and read a captivating story that seemingly takes place across myriad volumes of sci-fi novelettes, play on!
Like Planescape: Torment, Tides of Numenera gives back what you bring in to it.  It is rich in story, and never lacking in intrigue.  The combat and graphics may not be what some people seem to have wanted, but if that's what you were looking for then you picked the wrong class of game. This is more of a tome of philosophy and diversity than your typical cRPG: it brings both familiar and alien perspective to life with a brilliantly creative writing style that is sure to captivate any willing imagination.  To that end, it is a perfect spiritual successor to PS:T.
When I think back to PS:T, I think of all amazing stories that seemingly random NPCs would have to share about their travels across the planes and how their lives were irrevocable altered--for better or worse.  I wonder about the relationship of the protagonist and the antagonist, about the circumstances of the very mufti-faceted reality that governed the story’s landscape, and what can really change the nature of man. It has been nearly two decades and those stories and philosophies still resonate with me to this day.  I can confidently say that after my first play-through, clocking in at nearly 48 hours, T:ToN will be apart of my future in much the same way, and in some ways, maybe even more so.
I’ve only played through once, but I know for certain that choices *do* matter in this game.  Not every NPC needs closure, and might not get it, so some choices my seem ‘empty’ because you don’t see your various cookie-cutter meta-moral status bars adjust.  You have to remember though, this game has stories within stories. And as I said, it gives back what you bring in. While it *may* not always find fruition in the game, I can well imagine the fate of someone who’s life I impacted, and how they may one-day tell their story to another pilgrim of the Ninth World (assuming of course, they are around to tell it) and I sure as hell would be quick to pick up a book that comes out related to *any* of the characters I came across in this game.  However, there are many quests, dialogue options, and interactions that I could have done *very* differently, or in a different sequence that would have made real changes to the story and future in a variety of ways.  Let’s just say I have *big* plans for experimentation on my second play-though.. admittedly I *will* need some time to let this play-through sink in before I dive in again.
I have read other reviewers claim that the game is too short, or warn that it cuts off in a manner similar to Tyranny, and nearly every negative review has something to say about combat To those issues I can only expound upon the aforementioned: my first play-though was almost 50 hours, and I definitely missed stuff. I didn’t find the ending to be abrupt at all. I thought each act had perfectly adequate pacing for both the story and character stat progression—I had to measure out my actions carefully in act one, but by the last act I was confident I could handle whatever came my way.. except maybe the weight of my own choices.  While I loved Tyranny’s emphasis on choice and dialogue, I would feel remiss to lump these two games into the same category, T:ToN is far more story-intensive, and you can see that story through to the end. Like PS:T this is not an item-based game.  If you’ve played any turn-based cRPGs before then you know the drill: you’re going to have to wait a bit during a ‘crisis.’ I really only actually fought in probably half of the crises, but considering the crises make up about .01% of the game, I think the combat was challenging enough to warrant the circumstances leading up to them, and rewarding no matter how they ultimately played out..
It is hard for me to review a game like this because, like a good book, it is really more of an intimate experience that begs lengthy discourse.  All I can really say is if you *do* decide to play this one, accept it for what it is--rather than how it’s *not* whatever else is out there--and really play it.  Get to *know* everyone, explore every nook and plunder every cranny.. interact with everything you can.. it will be worth it. Find out just how much you believe one life matters.

This is not your derivative of a derivative game. Seek elsewhere. It is about  immersing thyself into an intriguing and alluring lore and weaving the protagonist's path according to the narrative. Torment:ToN is far from being perfect, personally I believe the story is beyond the 10/10 scale. The game has only one predecessor, Planescape Torment, which is in a sense a cult-classic.
As for the price, it did not deter me. Speaking from the main stream's eye, then patiently wait for a price reduction.
I recommend it even with its short comings. YES you have to read more than three sentences and will need a pair of reading glasses - so whippersnappers beware. Old school veterans of the trade will appreciate ToN!

This game doesn't fail on a mechanical level, it's competent and offers a paint by numbers isometric RPG experience identical to the Baldur's Gate 1 + 2, Icewind Dale 1 + 2, Pillars of Eternity, and Tyranny. What it is not, is an adequate imitation of Planescape: Torment.
The superficials are there, with walls of text and colorful characters, and the sheer strangeness. But the strangeness is hollow, the intelligence behind the strangeness of Planescape is missing.
Party members have their one obligatory side quest that places their fate in the player's hands, but there is nothing about them to discover. A high intellect will not unlock any new conversations, change one's outlook on a character, or change the nature of the game.
There is no Circle of Zerthimon. There is a Bronze Sphere, but unlike the original, which carried with it untold lifetimes of experience, this one summons allies, and is bugged. The piles of strange items in the game will not have any use outside of being worth cash. The point I lost hope for the game getting better was when I sold off all the "Oddities" in my inventory because I needed cash to install Wolverine claws on my character.
The main character, from the model to the equipment is ugly. It looks like a default Poser model. During the beta, I thought it was a placeholder. The fact that it's made it into the final product is indicative of the standards that TToN set for itself.
The game is not broken, it will not induce rage or fury, it simply exists. We are all mortal however, and anyone who played  any two of the above mentioned games, or played Planescape: Torment, will find nothing new here, and will be ~20 hours of their life poorer.
Anyone who has not played previous Obsidian or InXile games will find an inoffensive experience, but is better off waiting for a sale.

The original Planescape Torment was one of my first introductions to RPGs in any form, and I actually played that game prior to ever playing tabletop D&D. It remains one of my favorite games of all time, and it (and the setting it introduced me to) has genuinely molded and continued to influence my taste in games, my style of running D&D, and the material I've since gone on to publish for various tabletop RPGs like Pathfinder and D&D.
Fair warning here. I was and am in many ways a Planescape superfan, even now that people occasionally pay me to write RPG material of my own. Understandably my expectations were high as all hell for what was billed as a spiritual successor to the original PS: Torment. Torment: ToN is its own game, with its own story to tell, and a completely different setting and system versus the original game, but pike it and call me a barmy but I absolutely adore this game.
My own writing has crawled to a snails pace since I got this installed. My sleep has suffered as a result of wanting to find out where the Last Castoff's story goes and the unfolding story of the world surrounding her (I played the female Castoff). The characters are deep and complex, the world rich and captivating, and the mysteries and open questions have me aching to replay the game with different choices in mind and a different set of companion characters in tow (except for Rhin, Rhin must be there for any play-through because she's awesome).
The setting and the writing are weird in the best possible way, and given that I cut my RPG teeth on Planescape... that's high praise from me.
My only complaints are that unless you stick with the same companions, any that you don't actively involve don't ever really increase in tier and end up being useless in any combat situations. The potential companions are so richly written that I feel robbed in some capacity for not being able to see their own individual stories unfold and develop all in one play-through. I also miss tieflings. Someone make a mod to change the Last Castoff model so I can play a Planescape style tiefling. That's my one wish.
tl/dr Torment: Tides of Numenera is brilliantly written and I consider it the best cRPG game since the original Planescape: Torment. It's there and nearly on par with the game that I consider the best of all time.
Play this game or the yugoloths will win (yes yes they'll win in the end anyway of course). But seriously, play this game.

I think this is a good game. Everything about the game aside, I really hope to see more of this type of model of game publishing happening in the near future - creators who "made it" giving back to help other creators acieve their dreams.
The game itself is fun and well written though it's really more of the "graphic novel" type game with some dialogue choices added here or there. It's also nice to see a queer-specific game out there that's mostly wholesome and doesn't rely on sex-appeal to move the game forward.
However, the important question: is DD:ADDS worth it's price tag? If you want to support the creators and the model of game development financing that's used? Sure, go ahead. If you're not into that "bigger picture" stuff, then maybe wait until it goes on sale or see if they release some free DLC in the future.

Best and most realistic truck simulator game out there!

If you're a fan of simulators and want to get the feeling of a cross-country road trip, there truly is no better game on the market that does it better than ETS2.
You start out with some lame headquarters, and you have to deliver cargo cross-country to earn more cash and gradually your business grows as you get your first truck, buy a new garage, and start hiring new drivers, all in a way that makes this game surprisingly replayable.
The environments are gorgeous and the diversity of trucks never lets up. Volvo trucks, Iveco trucks, MAN trucks - they're all here.
As you sit behind the wheel of your truck, you're free to control whatever you like on your truck - indicators, lights, wipers, retarders (on higher-end trucks).
Not to mention you can download your favourite music and put it in your Documents folder to listen to your favourite music while you're trekking across Europe. For me, that feature is absolutely gorgeous. And even if you don't want to, there are a plethora of European radio stations that you can listen to in the game - from Pop to Rock to Jazz to news by BBC, the diversity of music available with just a few clicks and button taps never gives up.
However, while I feel the driving experience is spot-on in most areas, rarely the AI can start doing some stupid things like swerving into the overtaking lane while you are overtaking them, therefore crashing into your truck and causing more damage. However, that is just a bee in an otherwise exquisite honey.
I would definitely recommend this game to people a fan of the genre. It may not be for everybody - but if you want a game like this one, ETS2 is one of the best for you. I never get tired of starting my Volvo and heading to collect my trailer to deliver it across Europe.

Max Payne is like a dark, noir novel made into a video game, and pays tribute to a lot literature and philosophy. Most of the dialogue (if not from the other characters) are from Max, and how he views the other characters and his surroundings. All of which use metaphors and makes you really think. Max Payne is about a rouge, snooty NY cop named... you know... and is set after six months after his wife and baby daughter were viciously murdered in cold blood. Since then, he's been with the DEA busting big-time drug dealers and looking for answers. But when his partner is killed, and he's left to take the rap, he goes out on his own taking out big names and going further and further down the rabbit hole. The gameplay is something you will have to get used to, and you have to use stagedy against the enemy with features like bullet time. One thing that kind of bothers me is how random the damage is at times, sometimes you'll get shot up-close with a shotgun and maybe have 90% of your health left while the next time you'll die instantly. Yeah, Max Payne isn't one of those games where you run in shooting. It requires more than that if you want to succeed. Anyway, Max Payne is a really great game and I highly recommend you guys getting it.

A brutal storyline that shows how dark and sadistic human nature can be if that separates survival from death, or just greed and comfort from sharing. Paired up with a relatively short but compared to today's standards completely normal playtime and the well known generic TPS gameplay, it's a masterpiece where you won't even notice that the gameplay feels like the 1000th same TPS, because the atmosphere and the narrative is what gets you hooked on Spec Ops: The Line until you finish it. With all it's horrors and misleading delusions, it could be among the best fictional war movies with a perspective that slowly blurs reality with losing your mind to all the terror happening around you, with you, with your loved ones up to and beyond a point where you can't make a difference of what really happens and what is a delusion, and who is responsibile for all the death and suffering shown in shockingly real instead of overdramatizing and coloring it like the rest 99% of games do. It really is a masterpiece of psychological themed games. It makes YOU, the real person do horrific things and question your own morality, MAKES you want to find a twisted way to justify your decisions and depending on your choices, it possibly makes you feel like a monster.
Other games tried it too but it was either too black and white or overly dramatized, almost cartoon-ish to keep the player reminded about this is fiction, and always gave a reason not to worry or feel like you are doing good in some way, even if that requires doing bad things.
You'll question yourself here eventually, where were the line you shouldn't have crossed, and how long ago.
And this is unprecedented in the gaming history.
Throw in all this to the postapocaliptic feeling of Dubai being swallowed by the desert, with the people there being isolated from the world and are starving to survive any way neccessary.
And the greatest thing is, that this isn't a selfish way of the developers to make their sick gore fantasy (partially) come to reality, everything you see is part of a greater puzzle, and once you see the whole picture it just blows your mind and leaves you in shock for minutes.
TL,DR: It's pure genius worth mentioning (and being recommended) among the top games, even looking back more than two decades in the genre.

What a game! I really enjoyed playing BAO: Gotham City is huge, the graphics are a blast, the story is cool, some of the boss fights are really epic, the soundrack is awesome, the batsuit is the coolest ever... in short, it's a really good game. Is it perfect? unfortunately no. There are a few bugs that should have been polished off long before launch, and considering that this game has been out for a while now, it's a shame  that  they are still present. Some bugs are combat related, which is quite frustrating. For example, sometime the batclaw will shoot in the wrong direction; your silent takedowns won't work even if they should; you grapple on a ledge and Batman automatically climbs over, so that a ledge takedown is impossible. Other bugs are game breaking, like the one that happens in the elevator after you meet Copperhead: the autosave will freeze before completion and your game is ruined, at that point you can only restart from the beginning! Things like these shouldn't happen in a game that belong to the prestigious Batman Arkham series, and is very disappointing that an official fix hasn't been released yet (I blame the new Montreal Studios who took over the franchise).
So, overall, for all the good things listed above this game should be a gem, especially if you are a fan of the Bat, but all the bugs make it very hard to list it among the best games ever. I would recommend it to all those who enjoyed the previous Arkham games, but only if you have the patience to tolerate a few bugs here and there. My final score is 8/10
Btw, if you are among those few unfortunate people who encounter the above-mentioned bug in the elevator you will have to Follow these steps:
1. Go to your steam folder, open the steamapps folder and go to common.
2. Then go to Batman Arkham Origins\SinglePlayer\BMGame\Config
3. Open file "BmEngine" with notepad
4. Locate " AllowD3D11=True" and change it to False, then locate " AllowD3D1o=false" and change it to True
Make also sure that you regularly backup your saved games (located in Steam/Userdata/92582524/209000) just in case you get that horrific bug, or after fixing the BmEngine file you will still have to restart the game from scratch.

Mad Max features a huge open world to explore. When starting the game for the first time I was pretty sure I'd be bored by the vast desert in no time. However, the regions of the game are beutifully arranged and drawn.
Despite the main story line there are the usual side missions that reward players with scrap (the currency in the game) or unlocks for bases or Max's car. The upgrade system works beautifully, with proper farming players are able to get ahead of the enemy to a certain extend without ever letting questing in the current region get too insignificant.
The game mechanics focus onto two fields, (mainly) melee combat on foot, and combat in the car. The first being somehow a simpler version of the contemporary Batman titles, the latter being insanely entertaining. Whether ramming cars, harpooning their drivers out of their seats, ripping off tires, or simply shooting rockets at badies - car combat is simply amazing.
The story is one-dimensional, the characters vivid - exactly what one desires for this kind of game. Bought it when it was on sale for 5 or 7.5€ which is a steal. Buy it!

Story
Left for dead after a lethal encounter with a group of warboys and their ruler Scabrous Scrotus, Max Rockatanksy must scavenge the Wasteland in search of tools and parts that place him one step closer on his path for revenge. Roar through a post apocalyptic world with an arsenal of weapons and vehicles, diminish threats in regions to gain trust with the wastelands neutral forces. Wonderful game that sticks true to the Mad Max tone despite being it's own story.

Gameplay
Exceeds expectations. Vehicular gameplay is where Mad Max shines brightest (who would have thought?), driving feels natural and handling reacts accordingly to each surface. Relentless enemies and open world exploration make each engagement unique to a degree and present different options for each encounter. On-foot controls are nothing to gossip over and the hand-to-hand fighting, while engaging, is casually easy. Game physics are surprisingly enjoyable and explosions/destruction are not only detailed, but impressive.
Enjoyable character, stronghold, and vehicle customization, RPG elements in terms of skills and abilities. However, while Scrap is an abundant item used for most upgrades, the pursuit of unlocking end-game/post-game items comes at the cost of some serious time devoted to 100%'ing each area.
Sound
Fantastic. A noticeable amount of time was put into making each object feel alive visually and aurally. Character dialogue stays true to the bizarre world of the Mad Max series and the voice acting is on par with the game's overall quality. Engines sound powerful, object destruction comes off as believable. From the scratching of metal to whipping winds, everything comes together masterfully to provide a full experience once paired with the beautiful graphics.

Graphics
Undeniably stunning. The idea that it's a game based off a movie probably paints a mediocre picture in your head but I assure you that this is the nothing like it. Detailed environments, objects, characters and vehicles. Polished visual effects and animations. To top it all off it runs great and consistently, not since MGSV have I played a game so well optimized. Mad Max takes it even once step further by featuring a customizable free-moving screenshot tool.
Replay Value
Mad Max offers a great deal of repay value as you are free to roam and scavenge any missing collectibles or parts after story completion. The size of the wasteland is quite large and while bases and camps can feel likes clones of one another there are certainly unique atmospheres and environments tucked away in each region. Vehicle/base customization and the longing for bigger, better, faster parts/equipment help bring you back into the action even after the story has run it's course.
Wrapping Up
With all that being said, my only gripe with the game is that after a decent amount of time has been spent unlocking regions and building up your arsenal, the chore of collecting materials grows heavier. Throw in a hidden blade and some hay bales and you'd swear you were playing Assassins Creed XVI: Wastelands, meaning that scavenging for scrap and collectibles over saturates the thrill of roaming in a dangerous world. With that in mind, it is still a fantastic game that I would recommend to fans of the Mad Max series or not. If gritty vehicular combat is your fancy or you're simply looking for a quality open world game, Mad Max has something to offer in a multitude of avenues.

While I enjoyed the game at first, I have to agree with other people about a few things.
-game feels short and incomplete. I've run into a fair share of glitches. Odd seeing as they delayed the game. Honestly, I would've preferred a longer delay if it made the game run smoother and longer.
- the character creator is REALLY lacking, and it's treated a lot more like a joke than an actual character creator. It makes the atmosphere right off the bat feel like a joke, and it honestly feels a little condescending. Which is a negative because the creators wanted this game to be good representation for lgbt+ people to enjoy.
-the "multiple" endings thing is not as great as you'd expect. There's a "good" end and a "bad" end for each dad, the bad end happens if you consistently pick blatant bad choices basically. It's painfully easy to get the good ends for the dads as long as you're mindful or y'know, just go back and choose a different dialogue option. There's nothing in between, or different types of good endings or bad endings. It's just one or the other.
-limited choices overall, I feel. Your dad has a very set personality and there's points in the stories that'll leave you begging to choose your dad to say something different.
-Once you get all the good endings for the dads, there's nothing really contributing to the replay factor unless you're truly curious about something or you want all the achievements. This is made even worse by the fact that it's so short.
-In my personal opinion, there's a very forced ending/lesson with one of the dads that's ultimately disappointing. Writers have confirmed that there's really not a way around this, and it honestly feels horribly handled and very sudden for the game. Also serves to contribute to the above complaint about the lack of versatile choices or endings.
-This might just be me who dislikes this, but what takes place on other dates hardly become relevant in other paths except for one scene that really doesn't impact anything nor explain much. By what I mean by this is that sometimes you encounter other characters on a certain date, and you learn information exclusive to that path. It seems like this'd be a perfect way to open up new endings or options in a different path depending on the order you do them in, but it doesn't. I find it personally aggravating.
-From what I've seen, the writers and developers aren't really understanding the fans as they should be, which I consider to be a negative if you care to get into that side. Especially because they made a point about valuing their fans.
EDIT: An article gave information that let down fans, and revealed their ignorance towards fan point of views despite claiming to be so mindful.
These are SPOILERS for Joseph's route so tread forward carefully, but they purposefully put a "romanceable" married man in the game and then expected fans to feel guilty over playing his route. They also refused to put any sort of versatility in the endings to Joseph, so you're trapped getting two "bad" ends and that's it. It's supposed to some sort of point, but for a game that they treated largely like a joke from beginning to end, I think it's a little weird they refused to break conventions.
Their point isn't helped by the fact that they make it obvious in game that his marriage isn't a happy one. You don't even do anything with Joseph until after he said he broke up with his wife, but this is somehow written as if it's infringing on a sacred, happy marriage. The first two "dates" aren't even romantic. You're hanging out with your neighbor. You're just spending time with your friend. Last time I checked, having fun and NOT flirting with a married man doesn't mean I'm trying to infiltrate his marriage. It'd make more sense if the romantic intention was more clear, but aside from this being a dating simulator, there's nothing in-game that really gives away you're seeking romance aside from clunky, forced internal dialogue by your dad. Things only get romantic until after Joseph said he left Mary.
You get multiple opportunities to learn more about his wife, what's true and not true about her, and even befriend her... but this leads to absolutely nothing? There's no point. None of the dates cross over except for one (and like I said, ultimately impacts nothing). There's no unique endings. He always gets back with her, which this is tossed in suddenly at the epilogue, leaving you disappointed and confused. There's no way for a poly relationship or for the both of them to realize it's not working out.
No, not everything works out in real life. Yes, things like this happen in real life. But I just think this showcases how uncreative and restrictive the game can be, and the flaws in storytelling and path taking. They force a narrative that your dad just wanted to get laid and ruin this marriage, and punish YOU for THEIR writing.

**Note: This review is for SOLO gameplay. I believe co-op would be different.**
Hmm, playing the game actually felt like a chore. Even though I enjoyed BL1 and put a lot of hours into it (unknowingly), completing lots of side missions and kept upgrading my weapons, completing all DLCs etc, I feel that unless you TRULY LOVED the genre, playing either one of the two is sufficient.
I played the entire campaign solo. Even though the game is open for co-op play, I don't like how the game turned out extremely hard for solo players. Dark Souls was tough, but NEVER unfair, and I even enjoyed myself when constasntly dying to bosses and even laughed at how bad I was. Borderlands 2 felt different: it felt really unfair. You are usually swarmed with mobs such that you rely heavily on your special to actually put up a fight. Gameplay basically came down to 2 factors: your level and your weapon. The damage you do and the damage you take scales drastically with your level. I remember being stuck at a boss fight (Bloodwing) for 3 hours because I was so underleveled and got 1-shotted all the time, until I leveled up (from the mobs that spawn in the boss fight) and I defeated her in 1 attempt.
I was almost always underleveled throughout the campaign as I chose not to do most of the side missions. Most of them were really repetitive and usually involved traveling to a location and killing things/ collecting things/ a mixture of both. (I did more than 20 side missions for an achievement so I believe I didn't generalise.) After experiencing the likes of such mundane missions in BL1 I had no intention to grind yet again. Regretably, these missions also yield much more experience compared to say, those that you get from killing mobs as you progress through the campaign. Hence the being underleveled and the dying lots of times. However, even when my level was on par, I still get overwhelmed by endless mobs (especially the Hyperion loaders), and things like ION loaders setting up a force field when I was in FFYL (solo play, mind you) really got on my nerves.
*My Recommended Changes*
I think a gameplay element that could be implemented is the option to enable bots as teammates. This shouldn't be too overpowered since co-op with friends are allowed, even recommended anyway. While bots don't usually make the best game decisions, at the very least they would draw some enemy fire and that itself is already a welcoming change. Also, I feel that optional missions should stay optional, and the player should not feel forced to complete them to level. (Come on, of course I read reviews and googled etc when I felt the game was too harsh and the universal answer people gave was: do side missions to level up some.) As such, a second change could be the matching of campaign missions to the player's current level so one could actually progress smoothly. While concerns such as people rushing the game might arise, I feel that this is utimately a game and a player should have the right to choose how he wants to approach it, campaign only or a 100% run. Those are just my 2 cents.
As for comparisions to BL1, I felt that the graphics in BL2 were very much improved. While the inventory would require getting used to, everything was very smooth mechanically (unless you die repeatedly like me, then the dying-to-respawning animation can be a pain). The boss fights were very dynamic, bosses themselves memorable (magestic, even). However, it was kinda sad I had to resort to cheesy strats such as finding safe zones and snipe for 10 minutes straight till the boss dies. (Except for bloodwing which I actually had to move LOL.)
Would ONLY recommend if:
1) You truly enjoyed BL1 and are prepared for the similar side missions it offered;
2) You didn't play BL1 and are willing spend a long time on the title {more than 2x average gamelength}; or
3) You have friends to play co-op with.
6/10 solo play. Felt like a chore. Games shouldn't feel like a chore.

Neat, short and sweet puzzle game.  The concept is interesting, the graphics and music are lovely, and once you've figured out what the goal is, the puzzles can be a little challenging.  My biggest complaint is that the game seems to short, and, as other have said, the bonus levels feel like where the real game begins, as most of the other levels are building up to one large puzzle, teaching you each step one at a time.  Other than the shortness, I really enjoyed playing through.  A good one to save for a sale day.
Recommended for:  casual puzzle gamers, especially those who want to try something a little outside the usual format.
Don't do it if:  you really want a brain-wracker of a puzzle (Splice's are usually pretty straightforward, once you figure out the basic moves), you need more than an hour or two of gameplay to justify paying for a game (as there's not yet a randomly generated puzzle feature, so once you've done all the puzzles there's not any ongoing challenge to come back to).

Splice is a puzzle game about manipulating genes; puzzles consist of moving individual cells into a predetermined pattern within a set number of moves. When first launched, the cells seem troublesome, erratic, and difficult to handle, but after a few sequences their patterns become obvious, allowing advanced assumptions and predictions to be made. While the puzzles start easy enough, the introduction of utility cells which can extend, duplicate, or destroy other cells slowly ramp up the difficulty. Later puzzles can be difficult, yet remain fair and can be overcome with enough thought and tenacity; this allows Splice to blissfully incorporate a nice balance of increasing difficulty without moving into the realm of the absurd or impossible.
Visually and audibly, Splice truly shines. Minimal graphics and a haunting soundtrack add a surreal quality to the puzzles. Even on the more difficult levels there is something soothing and beckoning about the looks and sounds being offered to the senses. For a puzzle game, it is difficult to imagine a style more inviting or enticing.
The only deterrents are those common to the genre; if you are not immediately struck by the puzzle type there will not be a sudden change in the gameplay. The puzzles are diverse and interesting, but never leave the general concept presented from the start. Length has also been mentioned as a negative, but with the epilogue, Splice totals just under 100 puzzles which seems more than reasonable. Other puzzle games have offered nearly limitless levels, but often those levels seem to sprout from random generation and not through individually, well thought out puzzles such as those found in Splice.

If a splitter and another node were siblings, that would result in three children after the split). The puzzles, on the other hand, can be quite fiendish.

I don't typically write reviews of any kind.  This game was recommended to me while still Early Access by my older brother, and for the price, I thought "Why not?"

I get the feeling that should they get pushed to the limits one day, these 'made up' crimes that their virtual selves committed might come true some day...
Anyway, the game is beautifully made and runs very smooth.  You don't find the typical AI glitches that come with automanaged workers like you do in other sims.  Every worker, every guard, every staff member does their job exactly how it should be done, telling me that each staff member assigned multiple tasks at once automatically prioritize said tasks so that they take care of that which is most important or pressing.
The replayability of this game alone convinces me to strongly recommend it to others.  If you have not had the chance to do so yet, go ahead.  You won't be sorry.  You'll do what I did, and that is peel back layer after layer of complexity from what seems so simple early on.  Only when you have peeled back the last layer do you truly create the prison your morbid, deranged heart desires.
10/10

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is one of, if not the best, truck simulator game out there right now. It focuses on the very core of Europe; allowing you to create and grow your own trucking business to your own liking across the motorways and roads that spread across the land, with your own customised vehicle with many upgrades and additions that make the game dynamic and gripping.
- Huge map to a decent scale of Europe, including many of its key cities and locations that allow you to discover new places, stores, recruitment centres etc. encouraging you to explore - giving you an aim.
- Levelling system of unlocking new parts of the game, upgrades for your truck, and a business is brilliant - you are constantly striving to grow bigger and better.
- Ability to create, manage & expand your own business which operates all around Europe with your own staff, trucks, and money.
- Weather is although decent and realistic, only offers minimal options - features like snow would be a brilliant addition.
- Roads are repetitive and plain; however updates are routinely being brought out to help tackle this (as well as DLCs available to open more diverse locations).
- For the average gamer it may be seen that to set up a business and to customise your truck to a satisfactory level may take more time than would be preferred.
The game is a must if you are a truck fanatic or generally wanting the simulated experience, it offers a realistic approach to trucking in the modern day world. You even have the option of playing multiplayer with thousands of other truckers (an unofficial mod, but trusted by all) which makes the game more diverse and interesting than it already is. Buy it, and you definitely won't regret it.

You play as Jaden Korr, an initiate into the Jedi order and the super cool kid in his class because he already has his lightsaber. After the ship you're a passenger on crashes and you fight your way to the academy, you and some loser called Rosh are assigned as students to Kyle Katan, the protagonist from all the other games. From there you embark on an adventure to figure out who was behind the attack on the academy and just how many people you can sword fight at once.
It's two, I can barely manage two. I'm not very good.
As stated before, you no longer play as Beard Man, but instead as Jaden, a character who's race, gender, and appearance you pick yourself. The options for character creation are limited, but it doesn't really matter outside of appearance since your name, voice, and back story are ultimately the same.
Unlike the previous game, Jedi Academy lets you pick your mission and load out before you embark. It's a little bit jarring compared to the previous game where the game flowed from planet to planet and mission to mission through the narrative. The levels are also a lot simpler this time around, with less opportunities to get lost. After each mission you get a single point to put into a force power of your choosing.
There are both light and dark side powers to choose from, but the only difference there seems to be between picking Light or Dark outside of the obvious is what Luke says to you after you do enough missions to advance the story. The change isn't unwelcome but I did prefer the more linear story telling in Jedi Outcast compared to the broken up missions in Jedi academy.
The gameplay is mostly the same, with a few changes that are mostly just cosmetic. Blaster bolts leave a noticeable black mark on Storm Trooper armor and your lightsaber leaves streaks of burn marks that no amount of Polysporin will fix.
You still have the same weapons from the last game with a few new additions. In blasters you get what is essentially a rail gun that kills most enemies in one hit if you can hit them, but lets get to the meaty bits, the space swords.
From Dark Forces II onward, Kyle used a single lightsaber, but since you are playing a customization character this time, you have more options. Jedi Academy came out in 2003 when the prequels were still coming out. So because of that, they gave you a few toys to play with. You can still use the normal singular space sword, but you can also use that double headed staff space sword, just like that goofy looking Satan guy from Episode 1
. Other than those two, you can also just grab a second space sword and be like that weird kid from that Kingdom Hearts YouTube video.
You know the one.
Each lightsaber style has it's own moves and special abilities. The single lightsaber can change between three styles, the dual lightsabers are fast and you can use one at a time, and the staff can...Kick...I think, I'm not sure I only used it a few times.
Like the last game I checked out the multiplayer, and not so surprising there's a rather large population this time around. Like Jedi Outcast, the dueling community took precedence over the other game modes, and is very much alive.
I sat around and hung out for a bit with a bunch of them while they fought one another or ganked someone that was trying to break up duels. While I was hanging out someone in the fat Reelo skin sneaking up behind me and wiggling his lightsaber in my butt. We had fun.

Yes but only if you can name the blue elephant that played the piano in Jabba's palace in Return of the Jedi.
In my opinion, Jedi Outcast had the stronger single player experience, it was a bit longer and better thought out. The last two levels of Jedi Academy were almost exhausting by just how long they were and how many Reborn you had to fight at once. Even then I had a few more hours in the Single player for Jedi Outcast than I did Jedi Academy.
But if you're looking for lasting value, the multiplayer in Jedi Academy is still going strong, so you can probably find people to play with throughout the day. I'd still say get both, you can get them really cheap during most sales.
