I'm going to recommend this game only because I loved it as a kid and it is practically the same thing as Jedi Outcast, except its not, in many bad ways. How can I say this in the nicest way? It pales in comparison to Jedi Outcast in two very critical areas, lightsaber fights and level design. Lightsaber combat is way overpowered. I mean seriously, if you opt to get duel sabers or two sided saber then you are basically cheating. Is it a fun little novelty to play around with, yeah. But you can pretty much one-hit any Sith with little to no skill at all, which makes combat incredibly god-aweful boring after a while. Luckily this can be avoided by just choosing to use a single saber set up. The "mission" implementation doesn't really add anything  cool to the game besides the fact that you can skip levels you don't like or get stuck on. I find that to be kind of cheating as well. On top of that, MOST of the levels are super boring and linear. What I mean is you can pretty much apply the same brutte-force speed slash method on all levels. The graphics are nice even today, though. You get a lightsaber immedeately when the game starts, which is one advantage of this game over Outcast. As many other people have complained about, the story is pretty crappy, even by today's standards, but hey I didn't play it for the story but for the lightsaber fun. Other than those things and a few other quirks, it is worth buying just as a sequel to Outcast, and the bright side is there is a more diverse set of force powers (arguably the most impressive and cool part about the game) that balances out the overpowered lightsaber combo moves. And don't get me wrong there are a few very impressive levels, like Tasper III (lava planet), the rancor levels (3), Vaders castle, a huge sprawling crypt-like sanctuary filled with dark jedi. I am picky, but only because I fell in love with Jedi Outcast first. I would say buy it if you like these types of games, but dont expect too much.

How to make the best Chicken Parmesean
Directions:
Preheat oven to 400 degrees.
Cut or pound chicken breasts to 1/2" thin.
Rinse chicken breasts in water.
Mix bread crumbs, flour and parmesean cheese in large bowl.
Coat both sides of chicken thouroughly in bread crumbs, flour, and parmesean cheese mixture.
Heat oil in skillet over medium heat.
When oil is hot, carefully place chicken breasts in and turn to brown on both sides.
Spread a thin layer of the marinara sauce on bottom of baking pan.
Drain browned chicken and place on baking pan in a single layer.
Pour remaining sauce over chicken.
Sprinkle italian spices, then some parmesean cheese on top.
Bake for 20 minutes or until sauce is bubbly and hot.
Take casserole out of oven and turn temperature to broil - 500 degrees. Remember to leave the oven door open a little bit when broiling.
Top entire casserole with the shredded mozzarella to entirely cover so there will be lots of gooey cheese.
Sprinkle top of mozzarella with oregano.
Put back into oven and broil just until mozzarella is light gold in some areas and bubbling. Watch very carefully as it melts very quickly and you don't want to burn it!
Take out and enjoy the aroma!
It will be extremely hot right out of the oven.
For each serving I put my chicken parmesean on top of cooked egg noodles and cover it with the sauce, then sprinkle on even more parmesean cheese.
Serve and get ready for the oohs and ahhs!

For a gameplay Yager offers you a railroad shooter with a bit of squad support. If you seek a glorious, challenging gunplay - look the other way, that's not about Spec Ops the Line. For some reason, the most of the action feels like you were shell-shocked from the start of the game. Shooting part not really engaging. Two big notes about AI:
1) your companions are not that bad, as you can expect, playing in games like Bureau: XCom Declassified or Battlefield3. They scoring kills, and it feels like in normal difficulty setting they can bend opposers almost without your support. If only they were not rushing forward before it's clear sometimes, I'd say they are a perfect team.
2) Quite opposite, behavior of your enemies usually is quite weak from the point of battle effectiveness. Even in the hardest difficulty setting where they shoot very precisely, and you dying alot being both outnumbered and outgunned... Still they a prey, and you are the hunter. You mow them, in dozens and hundreds.
Being quite a mundane FPS, Spec Ops the Line offers a rather spanning visual experience, though. Sights of Dubai, all those sand and weather features are gorgeous. Impression when you destroying something to let another portion of sand, symbolizing chaos, gets even more space over a once-a-great-city... Can't buy it with mastercard, obviously.
And music! Music part is fabulous. Maybe the best part of whole game.
Overall, an artwork, audio and visual feast, all of this combined - is what keeping your interest, where the rush for gunplay challenge leaving you.
But again, all of that - gunplay, visuals and one of a kind soundtrack - still just a cover for story with guaranteed catharsis in the end. For that Spec Ops the Line is taking such inordinanar reviews, like "take a PTSD in 6 hours. 10/10!" That game Will Be Remembered.
Story what starts like "Only the dead have seen the end of war", and goes with "I destroy therefore I endure". What we observe as happening with the protagonist, Erich Fromm called "splendid isolation". This philosopher was describing destructiveness as a defence mechanism to preserve a human integrity, which is offended by some unexpected trials. That mechanism is never working like you think it should. See the game for it.
Overall mark 7.5/10 killed Americans

An intricate and deep simulation with an engaging and thoughtful campaign built on top of it. It's more approachable and has a more gradual learning curve than other games of this nature, while still maintaining complexity. Despite that, it's probably going to require more patience to enjoy than most people (like me) can bear. Its key flaws are due to the complexity of the simulation and the user interaction with that simulation.
I kind of burned out on this game. Once I got to the final campaign mission, it really started to feel like a job or a chore. All I could  think about while I was playing is all the work I'm going to have to do to get my prison set up, starting from scratch. I'm going to have to figure out where all the rooms should go, what sizes they should be, and I'm going to have to keep on clicking and clicking and pulling up menus to keep on making progress. It really piles on the decision fatigue and, as I played, I just felt a constant reluctance to do what I know needed to be done because I didn't want to have to navigate through all the menus and options and make all the little small decisions needed to keep building.
The key example of this is building a new prison wing. You need to create the foundation, measure out all the cells, build the cell walls, put all of the crap into each individual cell (bed, toilet, and door for each), build the shower, put all the shower heads in, then run wire so that it can reach each cell, run pipe to the cell block, and run small pipes through all the toilets and all the shower heads. Each of these steps involves clicking through menus, deciding specifics like where things go, exactly how big things should be, and how they should connect. Sounds fun? Not to me. It may sound lame, but I'd honestly rather just wave my hand and say "this area is the prison area", and have things be taken care of for me.
The feeling I get with this game is the similar to the feeling of reluctance I get when I know I need to do my laundry.
So, I would not recommend this to most people. I'd only recommend it to you if you really are into this sort of game - management, simulation, and building. Otherwise, it's just going to demand too much patience from you in order to really engage with it. At that point, you'll probably be left wondering why you don't just play one of the many other games out there that provide more instant and constant enjoyment and stimulation. It sounds fun on paper (as do most simulations), but it just doesn't translate to consistently and instantly fun gameplay, and, for many people, that's all they are looking for in a game.

Your goal in this game is to splice, remove, relocate, and rearrange cells to a certain shape.  You are given a certain number of moves to create this shape.  Splice is a very enjoyable puzzle game based around doing certain moves in a certain order.  You are always able to rewind if you make a mistake via the mouse wheel, or fast forward if you decide that is the way to go.
Splice introduces complexity to the game slowly, and this is a good thing.  It starts out with moving cells, then splitting cells, and so on and so forth.  The game gives you enough levels to understand a new mechanic before it gives you another, while always slowly increasing the difficulty.
The later puzzles can truly be difficult, until suddenly, the bulb goes off and all seems clear to you.  This game will most definitely provide you several hours of playing with beautiful piano music playing in the background and its sexy graphics.

I finished the game 100% but in many sittings. Spice is a good puzzle game but it shines in the atmosphere and design which engrosses the player. Each puzzle is solved in a few steps but there are a few challenging puzzles at the end that required thinking and planning, not possible with only trial and error. Beautiful and well produced, the interface is minimal but Spice runs responsively and smoothly. Rules and strategies are introduced in the levels but that is about the first third of the whole game, which means the game is short.
Splice could have been improved by a slower, more punctuated pacing. The game really does need more levels, especially when the high difficulty puzzles showed how complex and cerebral the puzzles can be. It also would be greatly helped with a save feature that remembers your moves in previous attempts across sessions (the game only remembers which puzzles have been solved). For a future game the team should be more ambitious and open the game to user created content.
I recommend this game not only because of the relaxing atmosphere, but also the nature of game play. The limited number of moves allows for starting a puzzle in the middle of the day, relaxing in the atmosphere while easing into a new puzzle, but not being tied down when something comes up or running short on ideas. When I found it challenging, I went back to my day and came back to the game later afresh, and usually a new perspective would be my ticket to solving the puzzle. It is a nice parallel with how some decisions and obstacles can be tackled in the real world.

Max Payne comes with a few glitches that are hard to ignore. The sound patch is great, and I thank the person who made the fix. Something that isn't fixable though, is the dream sequences, specifically the beginning of the third act. If you try to jump normally, you'll get stuck in the ground and fall to your death. Instead, you have to jump sideways. It's not really a problem once you figured it out. With that said, on to the review.
The story is unique, especially at the time of release. There hasn't really been any other style of game like Max Payne.
I've beaten Max Payne on all of it's four difficulties. Unfortunately, the difficulty ramp is just too easy. I beat the game faster and faster the higher I went up due to knowing the tricks and patterns of the AI. Bullet time can be used to manipulate all of the bosses into dying before they can even attack. Even if you screw up, the save state feature makes it impossible to get stuck on any parts. The final difficulty only lets you save six times per chapter, but they come frequently enough to where it doesn't really matter until the final chapter of the last act. Even the speedrunning mode is too forgiving on the timing.
Difficulty aside, it's a blast to play. Finding the ways to exploit the AI is hilarious. Bullet time is an absolutely satisfying way to kill your enemies, albeit sometimes cheap against "bosses". You'll find yourself using a ton of weapons that all work well. This review comes from a fanboy of the series who was willing to overlook the flaws of this particular game:
I personally prefer this approach and look to the Arkham franchise. Might not be the same as Arkham City in some aspects but its a good game still, and decent when the bugs aren't causing too much trouble (there are still some bugs present in City that were brought over here which mildly annoyed me). Story-wise it still is engaging and excellent. The environment felt a bit emptier compared to City despite the larger map of Gotham, proving that bigger isn't always better. New gadgets were introduced albeit some reminiscent of Arkham City's gadgets with the exception of added features which were very much welcome such as the shock gloves. Side missions were short and sweet as they are supposed to be. Collecting Enigma's datapacks were more or less enjoyable since it didnt take as much effort compared to its predecessors. However, the riddles from the older games are greatly missed. Multiplayer is flawed but very entertaining (one should not expect something groundbreaking). It brings a new twist to the conventional modes of multiplayer shooters with Invisible Predator Online and Hunter Hunted. Playing as customisable elite thugs added a few elements which enhanced the overall experience, especially when playing as the Joker or Bane, who turn the tide of battle really quickly. Despite the good things about it, one pervasive issue which really ticked me off was how long it took for matches to start due to impatient players going in and out of servers and connection problems which are still rampant; which is a shame because the multiplayer is great when it works.
In conclusion Arkham Origins is a really flawed game but with some new elements which I personally preferred. Character development and function design may not have been as good (Deathstroke felt a bit too much like Robin from Arkham City), multiplayer was not as well developed as it should have been, but nonetheless enjoyable to play. Arkham Origins is a solid 8.5/10 if the person is willing to forgive it for its mistakes and flaws.

TL;DR: A good game which got bad reviews from magazines and sites, but shines in both gameplay and performance. Story kicks off a bit late, but doesn't bring the game down. Doesn't define the genre, but endures its good sides. Easily a solid 8/10.
Mad Max is a open world game which consists of both vehicle and no-vehicle gameplay. The game borrows it combat from Batman Arkham-series and falls a bit short in comparison, but to be fair, Max ain't Batman. Driving is made to be responsive and fun overall, though couple of frustrating moments with the car do exist, but they are pale in comparison with the overall feeling and functionality.
The game is not a survival game, and it doesn't try to be. You are not playing against time with hunger or thirst or so. Only thing which actually is limited by use is fuel, which is to be expected considering the world, but in my time of playing I never actually ran out of it, because there is plenty of it; no need for stress.
The desert theme might be a turn off for some. I expected so from my self, but the game area itself is filled with doings and things so there actually are not any boring bits or trips. Vehicle parts of traveling are made smart too; there are no too long trips to drive, and there are plenty of fast travel points too later in the game. Driving doesn't get boring.
Game performs extremely well on GTX 960 2GB and i5-2320 (3.00GHz) + 8 GB RAM. As a person who likes to tweak their games I was extremely satisfied with the settings from the start, and I didn't to bother to mess with them; the game just worked well and looked great straight from the start.
Most of the play time consists of doing side quests and optional objectives like looting and capturing camps. There is♥♥♥♥♥♥ton to do, and most of the activities reward the player in some way, like regular drops of scrap, which is used to upgrade stuff.
The story itself isn't too long. Story fades a bit into the background while doing side activities, but it really kicks up in couple of last missions and shows exactly why this franchise has its name. Overall the story could be considered more as a red line which ties everything together.
I didn't expect much, but got a lot. Bought this from the Winter Sale of 2016 and would recommend this to any, who enjoys open world type of games with great gameplay and entertaining story. After playing the game I can safely say I could have easily payed for more, and giving this game a proper positive review is something it certainly deserves, even though its published by WB Games. I hope this encourages some to buy it.

Unfortunately, I can't recommend this game.  While I love the general setting and theme, this is the definition of a mediocre open-world game.  Exploration, which should be thrilling, quickly becomes dull once you realize the landscapes and environments don't change much, the enemy camps are far too similar to each other, and the quests are largely monotonous.
Pros:
1.  Driving and upgrading your car is fun and makes the game feel a bit different from other open-world games.
2.  Periodically, the environment can be quite beautiful.
Cons:
1.  Repetitive gameplay that gets old fast.  If you're looking for 5-20 hours of fun, then go for it - but don't pay more than $20.
2.  Dull primary quest line that doesn't motivate you to see what will happen next.
3.  Boring combat - unless you've never played Batman/Mordor/etc.  This system is played out, folks.
4.  Missed opportunity to make car combat interesting.  Attacking convoys comes close, but again, is highly repetitive due to lack of variation in weapons/enemy design.  Why not go whole-hog and incorporate V8-style weapon systems that would make for a much more exciting sojourn in the wasteland?
5.  Annoying, unnecessary mini cut-scenes for so many basic actions (drinking water, eating food, going up in a balloon, etc.)
6.  Designers' lack of understanding of what makes a game fun.  Playing to upgrade "stuff" is tedious.
7.  Nothing innovative (e.g., Shadow of Mordor's nemesis system, etc.)

++ Good and immersive writing & setting, left me thinking about some of the characters.
+ Different from other recent RPG:s (such as Pillars of Eternity) in its emphasis on solving problems through dialogue, making the game feel fresh even for an RPG veteran
+ Failure can also result in interesting events
+ Combat sequences are not "filler", each encounter is different, and there is usually a non-combat solution available
+ Text adventures in the style of old "choose your own adventure" books bring some variety to the gameplay
+ No grinding for levels
+ A fairly good amount of content if you do all the sidequests you can find. Good for at least one playthrough, possibly more if you want to find everything.
- Some minor crashes in combat sequences
- Although combat scenarios are well done, the "flow" of combat could be better
- "Choose your own adventure" sections could have a wider variety of possible good endings, now there is often some optimal path to take and lots of ways to die, resulting in a need to reload
- Unless you develop an interest in the game world and its themes, there may even be too much text at some points to develop minor NPCs.
- A bit too many "lore dumps" from minor NPCs. Fortunately, the main story is not told just in text but also through gameplay and visually.
- Some areas are a bit too crammed with stuff visually, leading to a theme park aesthetic in e.g. the Valley of the Dead zone.
Overall a very solid 8/10.

I kickstarted this game free and clear the instant I found out about the campaign, waited four years to play it and I am mightily satisfied. The game is a thoughtful and well written RPG, and an excellent introduction to the unforgettable Ninth World Numenera setting.
Like everyone else I have some complaints, but if you like to read and you're not bothered too much by some clunky mechanics, your money won't go to waste. Now for the complaints.
The cypher system, a peerless tabletop system, is not particularly well suited to CRPG gameplay. The adaptations committed to make it playable strip away a lot of its tactical nuance. Its true that you can "avoid all combat" assuming that "abusing the hide button" is satisfying to you. The crisis system makes for very specific encounters, but there's really not many of them, so a lot of the time the game is a "running back and foreth simulator" which was fine with me, but I can see people getting impatient.
The art is amazing! The graphics are... not. I found the models for the characters to be quite low clarity. Its very difficult to get a good idea of what NPC faces are like, which makes it difficult to get attached to them. Some of them are meant to be horribly disfigured and you just... can't see them. Even the NPC portraits lack impact. There's also no text area where combat logs and chat transcripts are kept which seems like a tremendous oversight.
Overall I definitely recommend this game. I also recommend patience and circumspection while playing it.

The developers paid a lot of attention to the story and as you progress through the story the player and his teammates will evolve to reflect their experiences with not just changes to their looks but to the dialogue as well. Even common dialogue like "Reloading" will reflect their state of mind based on their tone of voice.
Despite it having a great story it is very short, being only 3-5 hours for the average gamer. However, I've found that I loved every second of it. I feel not a minute was wasted and none of it was stretched out to keep you playing. It's as long as it needs to be. I feel that even the collectibles were worth collecting since it helps explain what happened to everyone in Dubai.
The gameplay is roughly above average. I haven't found a bunch of problems with it save some issues with the cover mechanic which is mostly user error. I do feel some of the checkpoints are a bit too spaced apart which is punishing on the higher difficulties. The NPCs are very generic and lack in variety. Apart from the regular enemies, you only really have snipers and heavies. They aren't too unfair though and there is little artificial difficulty in this game so it's mostly your own skill you'll have to worry about. Your teammates AI, on the other hand, is a different story. You only have one button/key you can use to order them, which is simply "kill this guy". You don't have any advanced commands which would certainly be welcome considering they can and will rush out in front of enemies to kill them and you have little control on where they go and when they do, they will likely go down and if both of them go down you will have to rescue them.

The multiplayer, on the other hand, is terrible and not worth playing even once. It has a tacked-on feel and look to it, like it's simply there to be there. Objectively, this game is OK, at times even enjoyable. Not great, but I completed it, so it is engaging enough. Without the "help us to recreate a Planescape: Torment experience" I would give it a 70% rating and might have considered to get it in a steam sale. Yet, the story of this game is a different one, in every aspect a disappointing one.
When I heard that a group of creators of the original P:T wanted to revive the spirit that so many modern cRPGs have lost, I was excited. Games with character, games that challenge players instead of just catering them, games that depart from the average and breathe life into unknown worlds, are being replaced by endless sequels without ambition or spirit. So here they are, promising to take a giant and build something on his shoulders, with enough funding for that shiny new Ferrari and free of the shackles of pleasing publishers and the market of "casual gamers." I hold the developers in high regard for their experience and achievements in the past, but in my opinion they have completely lost track here. If they really think that Tides of Numenera is fulfilling their own ambitions to live up to the sublime immersion and storytelling that is P:T, then they have lost much sense over the years. The game is neither ambitioned or bold, it is bland and tries to scrape by with the least effort required. It is not polished or rich in content; it feels more like an unwanted step child locked into the cellar than a love child.
There are many thoughtful reviews out there that capture the good and bad to the game, I just want to add a few personal observations.
- Numenera is a great choice for a Planescape setting replacement, it enables similar storytelling elements to P:T. I feel that it was worth the 35$ of backing just to discover this gem of pen and paper gaming. However the game mechanics adaptation is not good, once you reach three or four edge points there is no challenge in any task. I hardly used any of the 26(?!) intellect pool points for any of the tasks in the later game, and you can solve anything with intellect. The fighting mechanics are also unbalanced, and there is no room for developing combat tactics, you simply don't need them (health feels too low, though).
- Seriously, where is the content?? I finished the game in 50 hours after reading every description and looking at every nook, but I was really expecting 200++ hours of gameplay. Only two major locations (which you cannot revisit)? About 10 fights in the whole game, 80% of which you can simply talk your way out of? Your "mind labyrinth" consists of four almost empty rooms connected by a bridge? 6 companions, half of them as dull as a rock? You can choose from exactly three character foci? You only have 3 item slots? Animations look horrible, only about 20 lines of text are narrated? The inventory implementation is buggy, I mean how hard can it be?  These are not design choices, it is simply laziness. Where did all the time go, where did all the money go? This game is 10~20% of P:T or BG2, and takes away the enjoyable parts without reason. Where other games have seven chapters, this feels like one and a half. When you are not inspired you should at least put some sweat in it.
- There was supposed to be some personal stronghold that you can furnish and develop. I was hoping for a De'Arnise Keep on steroids, and got ... nothing. Is the mind labyrinth supposed to be it? That would be just pathetic. Just take the your pocket dimension from Throne of Baal and add more adventure to it, but no.
- Fights. I can understand that people don't like random fights, and want to put some more meaning in them. However, I liked walking up to some random basher for XP and money in P:T, even when the combat mechanics were not great. I'm not even talking about the highly enjoyable fights in BG2. I did not expect this game to be Icewind Dale, but ... where is the combat? They are only a few completely scripted scenes you walk into with companions bumbling about, and with heavy-handed non-violent solutions that are always feel like the better choice. The turn-based system reduces the tactics to an absolute minimum, and most of the skills are useless or not required because of the unbalanced combat mechanics. I don't really care if the combat is turn-based or real-time, as long as it's enjoyable. Nothing was enjoyable here, so maybe the lack of fights is even a good thing.
- Where is the promised impact to the world? I was looking for some effect of my choices, but the color of the tidal emblem seems to be the only thing that is changing. I was hoping for a system similar to KotoR, where you can alter the outlook of your companions, but this time with effects on the whole world. I did not feel anything to that effect.
- The Meres are a great idea, but the execution is lackluster. The game hints that they can change the course of the story, even change other characters. However with a few exceptions there are no effects on the game world, and even then the effect are just dialogue options. I envisioned great replay value and interesting interactions between your choices, but got some inconsequential mini-stories that don't even yield XP. Still, whoever introduced this was up to something, way better potential than the similar narration element in Pillars of Eternity.
In conclusion, I cannot help but notice that the game started out great, with lush background art and high ambitions, with the first Mere showing that your choices can matter, only to reveal a shack cobbled together behind the facade. It feels like all developers suddenly lost interest in extending their ideas beyond the beta contents or even completing the game. I would be very interested to learn why this breakdown happened, but it seems they want to focus on PR babble of a "spiritual successor" of P:T that fulfills all promises. Just admit that the money was still not enough to deliver what you envisioned, or that the creative spirit has left you. Looking at the stretch goals and seeing what you made of them just makes me sad. At least I am motivated again to replay the Icewind Dales, Baldurs Gates, and of course Planescape: Torment.

I love RPGs in general and I have been looking forward to this game for several years. I regret that I didn't have the income to be able to back it when it was in its kickstarter phase as I would have loved to.  It claims to be a spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment and I think it delivers on that and then some. Here's my overall thoughts on the game.
This game grips you right from the start and makes you start asking questions. What is the Sorrow and why does it hate me? What is the Changing God trying to do? What do all these memories mean? You learn over the course of the game answers to these and many more questions in such a great setting. The Numenera world is the first one since Planescape itself that makes me want to take up tabletop RPGs again. It's that interesting. You never know what is around the next corner from a mirror that kills you to Total Recall style mutants to a psychic bar and everything in between.
I love how virtually everything in this game from the Crises to the quests themselves can be resolved in a multitude of ways that all feel meaningful. Failure isn't always bad necessarily as it often results in resolutions you never would have seen coming. When it comes to the skills and abilities, the developers have done more with less. There may not be a huge variety of abilities but there's enough that each choice you make feels meaningful and there are a wide enough variety of builds that even replaying as the same class doesn't mean you'll be the same castoff as before.
On a technical aspect, I really enjoy being able to effectively choose which input style you want to play with. Most games seem designed with keyboard/mouse or controller in mind and seem extremely clunky with using the "offhand" input. This game not so much.
I get that this game is centered around dialogue and story but the combat is at best mediocre and at worst strait up boring. There are a lot of bugs with the heavily scripted fights in the second half of the game that was relatively untested compared to Sagus Cliffs crises that we got in the early access. Even when your UI doesnt lock up from the knockdown bug, there are a lot of pathing and pacing problems that make you want to go grab a drink until your next turn. Several fights seem to take longer than they should due to respawns in fight that make you want to ignore the fight and just beeline to the objective.
There are also NUMEROUS bugs with the current release of the game. These vary from minor cosmetic things to the knockdown bug where you have to alt+f4 the game and restart to game saves being deleted entirely. I wish the developers had given early access the full game to test these kind of things out because I feel a lot of these bugs are going to hurt unless they're addressed soon.
For all it's greatness, this game has its fair share of mediocrity as well. I'm a big fan of game music and still listen to PS:T soundtrack to this day. This game soundtrack will not be something I listen to very often. It's not bad, it's just not great either. Nothing stands out other than the tidal noises and opening theme.
It also doesn't feel like any of the companions except Matkina seem especially memorable. Callistige is a pretty generic mage, Tybir is a pretty generic rogue, Aligern is a generic fighter (who happens to be a Nano, wtf?). Rhin is a complete waste of a slot until you get to tier 3 then she goes from zero to hero faster than a Disney film. I haven't used Erritis much but I didn't get anything more than a "nuttier than squirrel turds" vibe from him what little I used him. The banter is few and far between and generally unless prompted, once you talk to them the first time and ask everything, you won't need to talk to them anymore. I wish they had been more unique overall.
Overall I think this game generally delivers where it matters and most of the failures are easily remedied or ignored and I will continue playing it for a long time. I hope you all will too!

Pros:
* While I'm not personally familiar with the table-top implementation, the Numenera world is pretty captivating and unusual in its portrayal of life among magitech ruins. The very purposeful sci-fantasy is, to my knowledge, a bit of a neglected one in video games, and there's a lot of wonder to be had here.
* Not only is there very minimal combat (an exceptionally bold move given what most people think of as a defining element of CRPGs), but its implemented via a slightly abstracted 'Crisis' system that is used to cover non-violent but time critical scenarios as well, ranging from intervention in a rapidly degenerating diplomatic situation to conducting a heist. I am delighted to see an attempt to include and mechanize these more unusual sorts of situations that come up so often in table-top, but have been so often neglected in digital formats.
* The core mechanics work very well in the early game. The world appears to change a bit with each rest you take, and so there's some incentive to avoid the infamous Five Minute Adventuring Day, trying to push your limited daily Efforts as hard as they can go. The push-your-luck core mechanic works well here, and it was the most engaged I've ever been in CRPG gameplay outside of combat and story.
Cons:
* At the end of the day, the writing and main plot just didn't work for me. It felt frequently overwrought, extremely awkwardly paced, and I just failed to develop an emotional attachment to any of the characters or situations. I'm the target audience for very wordy games, and even I found myself pretty bored and just wanting to skim through a lot of it eventually. More than anything else, this is damning.
* While the early Sagus areas are fantastic, past this point it feels like the game got punched in the gut with the "ran out of money" effect harder than I've seen in any other CRPG. A lot of what's left feels like it was cobbled together from disjoint cut content. The second Hub area feels so much more by rote than the curiosity filled playground that was the first.
* The abstract Crisis system just isn't very *good*; the combat encounters, in particular, just feel awkward and obligatory more than they are tense, tactical, or fun. Half the time they don't even matter anyway, to the immortal protagonist; on several occasions I died, only to find myself waking up such that I'd somehow bypassed what the encounter was guarding!
* The dynamism of the game world due to resting ultimately proves to be very minimal, and sensations of urgency quickly recede. This is made all the more the case that as characters progress and specialize, the Edge mechanic ensures that they need invest less and less into tasks, where by the last third of the game even the most challenging tasks can be trivially accomplished at no cost whatsoever. My characters felt like they'd pretty much broken the entire system over their knee.
* Despite the above, the game is full of mechanical traps. The gameplay and story extremely heavily emphasize the intellectual and social, which makes the fighter-type character class a total misfire; they excel only at the *maybe* the 8-12 violent encounters throughout the game, and even the rogue-type is better for all other non-combat purposes. Within the classes, little thought seems to have gone into anything like balance, with some abilities clearly orders of magnitude more useful than others.
* The game's ending is, unfortunately, in the Ending-O-Tron format. Hardly a damning sin by itself, but I apparently chose the wrong answer, and rather than getting anything like an epilogue or denounement... I got a game over screen. Not even an achievement. As the final taste of the game, it left me sour that apparently they included the wrong answer as an option.
* I was a Kickstarter backer, and there was a lot of content slashed and stretch goals walked back. I work in software, I know how it goes and I understand how that happens, particularly with the marketing frenzy that are Kickstarters. What is significantly less cool to me is that these changes were announced to backers only a month prior to release, far far after such choices would have been committed to. Unfortunately, despite initially being greatly enamored with the game and even recommending it to friends, by the end the holes had begun to show in force. I wanted to love this game. I loved Planescape: Torment. I wasn't going in to this expecting it to BE Planescape: Torment, but I did hope to go in thinking it would be better than this. When I first found myself disliking parts of it, I thought it might be nostalgia, but upon careful consideration, it simply has a number of flaws I can't overlook.
My first major problem? It feels like it cut off about 2/3 of the game. We were just starting to see things tie together, but the game suddenly just outright explains everything to you and begins the trek to the endingtron 3000. Thanks, Tides, I was getting interested there for a moment.
Storywise, it's okay, if heavyhanded. I hate saying it's just okay: there are a few flashes of brilliance, where someone obviously took a lot of time and effort to craft something. But these are few and far between. There are only so many ways you can say, "Look at this thing that was made by an ancient civilization. You don't understand it. You can interact with it a few times. Move along now." That's a trick you can pull a few times, but if you're going to do it with every interaction, you need to at least do it in a different way. The underlying question is something strongly undercut by not seeing the outcomes of your choices.
Companions. There's
and there's everyone else. The others didn't engage me at all. Two are vaguely interesting conceptually, but so little is done with them that you might as well have had self-generated characters.
, on the other hand, is well done.
Mechanics: You'd best be here as a sightseer, because otherwise the game fails, hard. First, the good: the system itself seems interesting, something a better game could do a lot with. You can get past most of the game without combat, which is always nice when an RPG can accomplish. Combat is really a type of "crisis", which means that encounters works much the same way if you're sneaking through an area or swinging your sword.
The bad: the balance is all over the place. After the first two hours, if you carry a balanced party, you will never fail at anything. Actually, even if you carry an UNBALANCED party, you'll probably never fail. I ignored one of the stats altogether. There was one combat near the very beginning that I had problems with, after that, I don't think I failed a single thing. You're encouraged to get rid of your cyphers, but since they're mostly one-shot and you never know what you'll need, I don't think I ever used one.
There also didn't really feel like there were enough encounters. Maybe that's a function of the lack of difficulty, but there really felt like I should be in crisis mode more frequently, even when I wasn't in combat.
tl;dr: I'd pick it up on sale. I don't regret kickstarting it, but it's too short to pay full price. My biggest fear is that this will ensure there's never another game. The idea is that there's an underlying philosophical question you, as the player, are answering by playing the game. I think that's a good concept. The fantastical setting helps by ensuring that we're not grounded on our normal ethical compass. If you come across elves and orcs in a game, you have a good idea of who the good guys are. In Torment, not so much. It lets the game designer ask more complex questions without tipping their hands, and you can see that they're attempting it during Tides.
Planescape: Torment did a good job of this. This game tried, even succeeded at times, but the mechanics and story brought it down at the end.

Overall I'd say this game doesn't deserve all the hate it gets in reviews, at least from a gameplay perspective. Prison Architect puts the player in the place of a prison builder. This classic tycoon management games offers a unique and satisfactory experience to the player. Creating & managing your own prison is guaranteed to give you a pleasent gaming experience in Prison Architect. The crafty and charming graphics style adds a really nice touch to the game, along with the simplistic art style.
This title gives the player an easily navigatable interface in order for you to build your dream prison, along with in depth reports and charts regarding your inmates. Prison Architect follows the same principle as any other tycoon management game, yet places your camera over the top of your prison and let's you see all the action from this perspective. This game can be just as enjoyable watching your prison run day in day out as it is initially building it. Riots will break out, SWAT will be called, gangs will be formed, this is the ultimate prison builder. Fact.
The graphics follow a simplistic yet charming art style, while the sound quality used replicates the prison environment beautifully (not that I'd know). The aesthetic created via the graphics & sound is very satisfying, and this game will run on even the lowest end PC/laptop.
The game does offer a tutorial along with a rather minimalistic storyline, yet this is a sandbox, and is made to be a sandbox. The lack of a narrative of any kind is not really offputting in the slightest, because this game focuses on its gameplay and replayability, the storyline can easily be overlooked.
It's a tycoon. Play it to your hearts content, there's enough going on in Prison Architect to keep you hooked for months.
This game offers no multiplayer functions, however there is an active Steam Workshop.

I did enjoy this game quite a bit but it does fall short of other romance visual novels, especially for its price point.
Positives:
+The comedic dialogue is really well written and humorous

+DVP by PUP. I'm not a fan of punk rock but I'm glad they included that song in this game.
Negatives:
-The characters feel like stereotypes and have little depth past their stereotypes
-Diverse games like this tend to have really toxic fanbases. Avoid at all costs.
-The romantic writing style feels like a cheesy fanfiction
-$15 for a game you'll maybe get 10 hours in
-Doesn't do anything with the diversity other than it just being there. Feels like they were pandering...
-No real story depth. This is a clearly a dating sim and not a visual novel.
Overall, if you're looking for a laugh or two and some cheesy dad jokes then this might be the game for you. If you are looking for a well thought out, meaningful romantic visual novel with depth then you should take a hard pass on Dream Daddy.

Although Max Payne hasn’t withstood the test of time as long as Doomguy or Mario, there is a reverence associated with his games and his character that makes him The Godfather of modern video-games.
Perhaps the acclaim is something beyond its stylistically poetic, cynical visuals and audio effects inspired by the noir fiction genre and more due to the series being the first to take the cinematic effect of bullet-time from John Woo films and translate the concept into an entire game around its usage. Perhaps the game was in the right place and time after the success of The Matrix as well as the shift in video-games to focus more so on its narrative than its gameplay to garner a massive audience. Perhaps, simply, the character of Max, a deadbeat cop who lost all he had once believed about the American Dream, resonated with older audiences who grew up with games and felt the same Damocles of the times ever present on their minds.
Whatever the reasons for its success, Max Payne remains video-games’ original take on Hollywood action heroes as much as Agent 47 embodies video-games’ original take on 007. Everything about its gameplay, its style and its narrative all contribute in creating a classic in one medium born out of the influences and the gamification of another, and this is perhaps why with time the name and success of Max Payne will remain far longer than the absence of future titles.
At its core of gameplay, Max Payne is a third-person shooter with a lot of its design decisions based off its 3DRealms’ influence, Duke Nukem 3D. With DOOM-styled level environments that promote labyrinthine environments, admittedly more linear than in DN, mixed in with enemy encounters and with downtime to promote resource management along with the protagonist’s quips, the set-up for MP’s gameplay is rooted in as much FPS traditions as it is based on TPS games. This is perhaps why the gameplay remains as refined as it was back then because it was based on the tried and true methods.
Describing MP entirely as a throwback to other games in a new trench coat would be undermining how it blends its narrative elements with its gameplay.  For starters, the player’s role as an omnipresent audience better suits the design of its verbose elements to expand upon its expositions than occupying the first-person perspective. One-liners and monologues better suit MP as they’re paced with the level design to make the quiet-time reflective as the player catches their breath and stay engaged with the game, and the comic-book style cutscenes give the creators more liberty to tell its story beyond the limitations of its engine. These elements may entirely be skippable or ignored by the player’s actions, so the constant dialogue never impacts the player’s choice to ignore the story and focus on the gameplay.
Combat boils down to moment-to-moment encounters that utilize as much of the player’s mobility and positioning of the character to take advantage of each situation with as much risk as reward. Bullet-time allows players, whether on mouse and keyboard or controllers, to weave around bullets and plan shots with some time to consider where to aim as well as preplanning their next attack, and the way in which bullet-time is recharged through killing mooks adds a sense of thoughtfulness on when the player should or should not rely on this resource. When not in bullet-time, the player still has access to various mobility movements such as the dive or dodge-rolling, and learning how to anticipate enemy projectiles is imperative to survive such as getting close enough to shotgunners to avoid the spread when far away. Each battle, as a result, is a hectic mash-up of death-defying stunts the player improvises on the spot as well as coordinating the next ambush to take out as many enemies in one dive to duck behind cover to avoid damage from the rest of them.
As much as the gameplay itself is addictively simple and fun, if there weren’t moments of quiet-time as well as various narrative tricks such as level variety and unique moments that go beyond its emphasis of realism, the repetition of the combat would begin to overstay its welcome as well as show how broken the dynamic difficulty that punishes players the better they become.
Had no one told me about Max Payne’s dynamic difficulty that influences how much of an aim bonus/penalty or damage bonus/decrease enemies are given I would have assumed the game was inconsistent about its challenge. Consoles were given more variability with its difficulty settings that was probably due to account for analog aiming, yet on the PC the baseline of its difficulty is on its highest end and increased to situations that would be almost unwinnable to most players. This doesn’t even account the two stats-based difficulty modes and a speed running mode, New York Minute.
On paper, adjusting players’ sense of challenge works when it’s never explicitly known to the player as it makes the game feel more tailored to the player’s abilities and makes for a more enjoyable experience the better a player becomes. Knowing these systems exist often will open them up to exploit, such was the case in Resident Evil 4; however, not knowing these systems are in place when making constant failures can lead to many players wondering if they’re getting worse at the game when really the odds are turned up against them until the game reaches back to the baseline. Death in MP isn’t so much a punishment but a blessing to have the game ease up on the player.
This difficulty is also compounded by the fact that there are too many weapons in MP1 that become obsolete the farther you play, which often means ignoring the two variations of a shotgun, pistols, or the uzis in favor of the weapons that will get the job done. It wasn’t until Max Payne 3 that this problem was addressed by making all weapons viable by limiting the number of guns given to the player at all times, and Max Payne 1 goes to show that simply having more guns available isn’t always the best solution in keeping the gameplay from getting stale. These blunders are the only notable flaws with the game that makes it easier to accept once you know they exist.
If the movie adaptation of Max Payne was indicative of any one thing, aside from how different the tone and execution were from the noir style of the original, the box-office blunder proved that video-game characters are beloved because of the interplay of the player and the character. Movies cannot replicate the off-camera blunders that result in the player and Max overcoming the odds, nor can they capture the vividness and disturbing feeling of wandering in Max’s nightmares that are as alien to the player as to the character himself. Max Payne, a game that blends comic-book styles, cinematic elements and gameplay, is conglomeration of mediums into one experience that cannot be replicated without having the ability to play in his shoes.
As far as the future of Max Payne’s video-games, the future seems bleak that there will ever be a continuation of the franchise under Rockstar as it appeared Max Payne 3, a great game in its own right as well as a fitting end to the trilogy, was more of a tech-demo for the much larger success story of GTAV. Simply looking at the gameplay comparisons and the cemetery levels shows an obvious foundation from one game into the basis for another one, and if GTA Online is any indication of the future of Rockstar single player experiences appear to be a memory of the past.
If Max Payne’s adventures are done, then his legacy is one in which players can always relive the trials and tribulations of Max as the cynical, poetic action-hero who captures the disdain of life through his constant failures until his stubbornness gets him the girl.

The nostalgia goggles on this one are massive. "Max Payne" heralded an era of third-person shooters when it was released and it also held the distinction of being the platform of the original "The Matrix" games, before WB Games got off its♥♥♥♥♥and made "Enter the Matrix" and "Path of Neo" and that's largely because it was the game that popularized the "bullet time" mechanic.
The game itself is stylish and full of atmosphere. It's presented in a film-noir style, complete with protagonist narrating over dime novel-style cutscenes. The problem is that the gunplay hasn't aged well. The game becomes way too hard way too soon. It's not unbeatable, but it requires a lot of retries. Part of the issue, especially in high resolutions where everything shrinks, is that Max can't shoot for♥♥♥♥♥♥ whereas enemies are the genetic opposite of a Stormtrooper. Gunplay also relies on damage and body-part hit to calculate damage and good luck getting perfect headshots, which don't always instantly kill to begin with, even while using bullet time.
The implementation of the bullet time mechanic doesn't help as much as it should and it's a glorified slow-mo camera in this original game. This means that effectively (and seeing how little space there often is for moving and dodging), instead of dodging bullets you only get to see them hit you in slow-mo. The ordeal becomes even more ridiculous as the game progresses and you notice small annoyances; for example, enemies can deal massive damage hitting you using a pump-action shotgun from the other corner of the room, but it takes Max 2-3 shots sometimes using the same weapon to drop them. Consistency is also lacking and the arsenal underneath Max's stylish coat is more for fun and variety than actual strategic value.
The second game pretty much fixed all of the above and it's the better game for it. However, I would still recommend "Max Payne". For one thing, if it gets too frustrating, cheats are easy to enable. For another, the many mods, Matrix-themed or not, which were released for the game still exist and anything with such a wide variety of content from a strong modding community is worth a shot.
Just be warned that it will require patience to get through the game and you'll be excused if you decide to drop it half-way through. Also, get it on a sale, because 10 bucks for a game so old and with significant porting issues on some systems (reportedly), is an insanely high price-tag.
PS: I played the CD version of the game way back when I was still a tyke. The 3 hours Steam has logged aren't representative of my experience with the game.

Right off the bat I just want to say that I really like this game! As someone who never played any Max Payne game I'm glad that I introduced myself into the Max Payne Series.
Remedy Entertaintment really nailed the story of this game and it is one of the best storylines I've ever experienced from a video game. The game is set in New York film noir style and it really fits with the story line. The game tells the story using a graphic novel style panels with the characters speaking through voice over and speech bubbles. The characters are unique and memorable especially Max Payne himself.Throughout the game Max narrates the story to the player in cutscenes and during gameplays which gives the player clues on the story and how to progress. Overall the story, the setting, characters, and how the game tells the story in this game are pretty solid.
The gameplay is really unique compared to other shooters thanks to the bullet time and shootdodge mechanics. Every gun feels unique and has their own attributes that other guns don't have making no gun feels the same. Being able to carry every gun in the game really gives the player more strategies to face enemies, such as using a long ranged sniper rifle to pick the enemies form far away or take the advantage of the shootdodge and bullet time mechanic to bust into a room with a shotgun or dual-wield pistols. Even though Max narrates the game and "tells" the player on what to do there are some part of the game in which the player must pay attention in order to progress (or the player could just find a walkthrough in order to continue the game). Some objects in the game can be interacted with such as televisions and radios, sometimes they give more explanation to the situation like the news broadcasts and sometimes the can be a break to the shootout like the tv shows. In general the gameplay in this game is really good and it's satisfying to explore the level.
Despite all of the positive things I said above about this game there are still somethings that I don't like in the game such as the inability to carry more than 8 painkillers and the ineffectiveness of the lead pipe(since the baseball bat has longer reach). The enemies don't really flinch much and they just keep shooting even though the are shot in the chest(which makes no sense). Also, This game is also incompatible with newer hardware, if you have problems with this game because of your modern computer or laptop I suggest you check the internet for some patches
In Conclusion Max Payne is an amazing game both story-wise and gameplay-wise. If you find this game on a sale or you are searching for a series to play try this game out and experience the Max Payne Series, maybe you will find something that you really like!

TL;DR: A good game which got bad reviews from magazines and sites, but shines in both gameplay and performance. Story kicks off a bit late, but doesn't bring the game down. Doesn't define the genre, but endures its good sides. Easily a solid 8/10.
Mad Max is a open world game which consists of both vehicle and no-vehicle gameplay. The game borrows it combat from Batman Arkham-series and falls a bit short in comparison, but to be fair, Max ain't Batman. Driving is made to be responsive and fun overall, though couple of frustrating moments with the car do exist, but they are pale in comparison with the overall feeling and functionality.
The game is not a survival game, and it doesn't try to be. You are not playing against time with hunger or thirst or so. Only thing which actually is limited by use is fuel, which is to be expected considering the world, but in my time of playing I never actually ran out of it, because there is plenty of it; no need for stress.
The desert theme might be a turn off for some. I expected so from my self, but the game area itself is filled with doings and things so there actually are not any boring bits or trips. Vehicle parts of traveling are made smart too; there are no too long trips to drive, and there are plenty of fast travel points too later in the game. Driving doesn't get boring.
Game performs extremely well on GTX 960 2GB and i5-2320 (3.00GHz) + 8 GB RAM. As a person who likes to tweak their games I was extremely satisfied with the settings from the start, and I didn't to bother to mess with them; the game just worked well and looked great straight from the start.
Most of the play time consists of doing side quests and optional objectives like looting and capturing camps. There is♥♥♥♥♥♥ton to do, and most of the activities reward the player in some way, like regular drops of scrap, which is used to upgrade stuff.
The story itself isn't too long. Story fades a bit into the background while doing side activities, but it really kicks up in couple of last missions and shows exactly why this franchise has its name. Overall the story could be considered more as a red line which ties everything together.
I didn't expect much, but got a lot. Bought this from the Winter Sale of 2016 and would recommend this to any, who enjoys open world type of games with great gameplay and entertaining story. After playing the game I can safely say I could have easily payed for more, and giving this game a proper positive review is something it certainly deserves, even though its published by WB Games. I hope this encourages some to buy it.

Unfortunately, I can't recommend this game.  While I love the general setting and theme, this is the definition of a mediocre open-world game.  Exploration, which should be thrilling, quickly becomes dull once you realize the landscapes and environments don't change much, the enemy camps are far too similar to each other, and the quests are largely monotonous.
Pros:
1.  Driving and upgrading your car is fun and makes the game feel a bit different from other open-world games.
2.  Periodically, the environment can be quite beautiful.
Cons:
1.  Repetitive gameplay that gets old fast.  If you're looking for 5-20 hours of fun, then go for it - but don't pay more than $20.
2.  Dull primary quest line that doesn't motivate you to see what will happen next.
3.  Boring combat - unless you've never played Batman/Mordor/etc.  This system is played out, folks.
4.  Missed opportunity to make car combat interesting.  Attacking convoys comes close, but again, is highly repetitive due to lack of variation in weapons/enemy design.  Why not go whole-hog and incorporate V8-style weapon systems that would make for a much more exciting sojourn in the wasteland?
5.  Annoying, unnecessary mini cut-scenes for so many basic actions (drinking water, eating food, going up in a balloon, etc.)
6.  Designers' lack of understanding of what makes a game fun.  Playing to upgrade "stuff" is tedious.
7.  Nothing innovative (e.g., Shadow of Mordor's nemesis system, etc.)

This review comes from a fanboy of the series who was willing to overlook the flaws of this particular game:
I personally prefer this approach and look to the Arkham franchise. Might not be the same as Arkham City in some aspects but its a good game still, and decent when the bugs aren't causing too much trouble (there are still some bugs present in City that were brought over here which mildly annoyed me). Story-wise it still is engaging and excellent. The environment felt a bit emptier compared to City despite the larger map of Gotham, proving that bigger isn't always better. New gadgets were introduced albeit some reminiscent of Arkham City's gadgets with the exception of added features which were very much welcome such as the shock gloves. Side missions were short and sweet as they are supposed to be. Collecting Enigma's datapacks were more or less enjoyable since it didnt take as much effort compared to its predecessors. However, the riddles from the older games are greatly missed. Multiplayer is flawed but very entertaining (one should not expect something groundbreaking). It brings a new twist to the conventional modes of multiplayer shooters with Invisible Predator Online and Hunter Hunted. Playing as customisable elite thugs added a few elements which enhanced the overall experience, especially when playing as the Joker or Bane, who turn the tide of battle really quickly. Despite the good things about it, one pervasive issue which really ticked me off was how long it took for matches to start due to impatient players going in and out of servers and connection problems which are still rampant; which is a shame because the multiplayer is great when it works.
In conclusion Arkham Origins is a really flawed game but with some new elements which I personally preferred. Character development and function design may not have been as good (Deathstroke felt a bit too much like Robin from Arkham City), multiplayer was not as well developed as it should have been, but nonetheless enjoyable to play. Arkham Origins is a solid 8.5/10 if the person is willing to forgive it for its mistakes and flaws.

I found the setting to be fresh and fascinating. This isn't just a testament to the world of Numenera, but the excellent work of the writers and artists who made the essence of that world fill my screen.
While the settings were wildly different, all of it screamed Planescape and Baldur's Gate to me - in a way that Pillars of Eternity frequently did not. Torment's environments were perfectly foreign, which made my comfort in them even more surprising.
Benjamin has an essay on translation where he likens the task of translation to the construction of tangent circles -- Torment feels like that to me. Beautifully connected to, and reminiscent of, a game that I love, while complete on its own terms.
--
Mechanically, the game was sound. It felt like I had multiple avenues to resolve each of the vignettes that I participated in. I reloaded many times throughout my playthrough to experience some of the alternate ways of solving and creating problems.
I encountered a few annoyances, but no bugs. The combat was fine. There were a few times when I became frustrated while trying to activate an ability 'behind' someone, but the perspective made that impossible. Hopefully that will be patched out.
--
While I'll give the game some time to breathe now, I am planning on a second run where I push entirely different Tides to the forefront. My limited exploration of alternate paths satisfied my curiosity as to whether the game handled them effectively.
--

Spec Ops: The Line disguises itself as a typical 3rd person shooter while it is actually one of those thought provoking 'art' games. The shooting and gameplay is decent, however, where this game really shines is from story and story telling. Very generally, the story involves a soldier going into a warzone to help civilians but the events on the battlefield slowly wear him down.
Stuff I like about this game is the detail thats has been put into expressing the mindset of the character as the story progresses, from the lines he says when he gets shot, to the message on the loading screen. This is the only game I know that demoralises you with a loading screen message thats for sure. Other stuff I like is how the game is 'relatively' challenging, and the good graphics.
Stuff I don't like is mainly sometimes the gunfights felt slightly clunky, but that may have been because I rarely play 3rd person shooters. Also, the music didn't seem to make any impression on me cos I can't remember any.
Generally, I think its worth playing, especially if you like story driven games.

This game has problems, and it's certainly not perfect, but I really enjoy it and I think other people will too.
One of the things I especially like about this game is the way it punishes you for rampant violence. Pulling out a gun and shooting someone in broad daylight almost never ends well, simply because you can't survive more than a few gunshots in a row. That feels more realistic to me than being able to mow down countless civilians without consequence.
I also like that some objectives cannot be achieved without ingenuity or nonviolent methods. For example, in order to destroy the virus in Sapienza, you have to reach the lab (which is heavily guarded and has many keycard-locked access points) and find a way to destroy it without getting immediately spotted by the numerous guards (whether that be with a kill switch, manually, via stalactite, from a distance with a gun, or with a penetrating sniper rifle [though that can't be used until Sapienza has been mastered]). To reach the auction in Paris (almost certainly a necessity in order to kill Dalia Margolis), you have to find one of four specific and rare disguises, a secret invitation, or a hidden access route. I like the way the game makes you plan out your actions and try to learn people's habits. The always online component is annoying and sometimes buggy, and my computer isn't fully equipped to run the game at a good framerate, but I still think it's pretty great.

Are modern games too easy? Do you miss the controller-shattering days of Mega Man 2? Brother, have I got a game for you. SMB is a tough-as-nails platformer that masters the biggest rule of platforming: the mechanics are fair. There's no missed jump, no frustrating death that ever feels like the game cheated; no, every failure is on you, and could be avoided if you were just a liiittle bit better. This urge to improve is what drives this game, the desire to master the tough, yet fair, world of sentient meat blobs. The humor is a bit dark and a bit crude, and some of the art crosses the line into "gross," but everything that isn't the gameplay of this title is ancilliary. This game can technically be played without a controller, but shouldn't be.
Overall recommendation: if you like hard games, or platformers at all, then this is required playing. Not joking about the controller, though - it's practically required.

I've read one or two reviews which are critical of 'Jedi Academy' on the grounds that it is too similar to 'Jedi Outcast' and doesn't really bring anything new to the table. Whilst I do think that's a valid point, it certainly didn't detract from my experience of the game - an experience which I found immensely enjoyable. In 'Jedi Academy' you play Jaden Korr, who is canonically a human male but can be played as several well-known alien races like the Kel Dor (Plo Koon's race) and Rodian (Greedo's). On my playthrough I chose the Kel Dor, which I admit later regretting due to the fact that the voice sounded nothing like a Kel Dor voice. (Perhaps it's unfair to pick holes in a 14-year-old customisation system!) The rather superficial appearance of your character isn't the only thing you can customise, though. As you progress through 'Jedi Academy', you are introduced to different fighting styles, which culminates in the ability to choose your own lightsaber. If you thought this feature was good in 'Knights of the Old Republic', wait until you see what 'Jedi Academy' can offer. Overall, I'd say that whilst this game falls slightly behind 'Jedi Outcast' in one or two areas (e.g. a less memorable villain, a less challenging final level), it's a fantastic way to spend 10-15 hours (per playthrough, that is), and I'm almost certainly going to return to this game at some point in the future.

Let's be honest, if you're reading this, chances are you're bored and are only here to see what I'm whining about. If you're actually wondering whether or not you'll like this game then good news everyone! you probably will, just make sure you bring friends. That being said, if you don't like any other borderlands game then you won't like this one, it's just more of the same.
On to the review, the game takes place a few years after the first one, theres new vault hunters, you fight handsome jack, blah blah blah. The story at it's base is nothing to write home about. It's the characters and their wacky personalities we all love, especially when they're talking to each other, instead of just monologuing at you. I won't lie, Ashley Birch's Tiny Tina is really the only reason I was able to put 30 hours into this game. And I'll be fair, the variety of guns was fun at first, but like the previous game, it got old real fast.
The biggest issue I had with the game, is that it felt like a chore to do anything in it. All the missions are 'go here, shoot this' and 'go here, grab this' it was mindnumbingly dull. Then you have to run around an area opening all the lockers and chests to find hidden loot, which just adds to the teduim. The only reward for anything wasn't the chance at a cool new gun, but a hope that the characters would say something funny. That's it. If you've got friends to play with then it gets a bit better, but chances are your progress in the game won't match up perfectly, thus you or your buddy will end up replaying a couple of missions til everyone's caught up to each other.
Overall, I didn't like Borderlands 2, it felt like a huge grind all the way through with no improvements over the first game and the only highlights being when Tina said something funny or ridiculous. Chances are, however, that you'll like it, just like everyone else.

It's a wonderful game with loveable characters that have genuine personalities and believable lives that I just fell head over heels for. However there is one route (which is not bugged) that nearly ruined the game. The creators made this route to make us think about how we play dating sims and how we just expect to win every heart by saying the right things, but when I played it, all I got from it was a waste of time. Dating sims are fantasies where us average protags somehow win the hearts of every idealistic romantic interest, no matter how out of our league they are. To put in this end, in the way that they did, not only seems like a slap in the face to say "you should feel bad for wanting to have some impossible happiness" but it has also hurt those that identified with the dad in question due to the way it was handled.
With all that being said, all other routes were wonderful, I love the art and the characters so much. There were no other endings that bothered me. For these reason I struggle to reccomend the game on the basis that all the other routes are good, but the one nearly had me uninstalling the game.

This game was definitely a hidden gem. Especially at 20 dollars, the game is a steal. The story is very bare bones and it is what you'd expect from a Mad Max game, nothing super special there. As a matter of fact, there is nothing this game does that is particularly groundbreaking. That's not to say the game is bad. I just would not have recommended the game with a $59.99 price tag.
The game is just fun. The combat system is very similar to the Batman games, which I enjoy for mindlessly brutalizing guys as Mad Max. The game itself is gorgeous, and is very, VERY well optimized. It runs smoothly and looks great, even with some older video cards (I've heard people state they had cards around the geforce 760 and not had issues). The car chases and battle are enjoyable, and upgrading your vehicle and strongholds are fun without being tedious (at first). It's a well rounded, open world, action game based in the world of Mad Max, with you reprising that role. Everything about the world fits the theme, the voice acting was very well done, and the music was good. Again nothing spectacular there, just good, fitting where it needed to be. Sound design was very well done though. The roaring engines, the deafening sound of the shotgun blast, the griding of metal against metal in the car chases. It was all really well done. You can tell the developers put love into the design of the games world. From the different locations you will encounter, to the cars and people you will meet. The world feels very robust and not at all bland and copy pasted, like a lot of open world games in the style.
I only really have two drawbacks. The game gets repetitive, which is tough to avoid with games of this type. It eventually does feel tedious to do the random side stuff, but by that point I had done mostly everything and had nothing left stopping me from just completing everything story specific, and completing the game which is what I did. The other issue I have is how the last 30% of the game is where I experienced the only bugs. Dying from some weird glitch that shot a million feet into the air just to fall to my death (happened a handful of times), or getting stuck somewhere and having to exit and load from a saved point (happened once). They aren't prevalent, but they seem to exist later on (possibly from rushed development towards the end?).
Personally, I had an overall great time with the game and for the price, it was worth every penny.
Sidenote, I played briefly with a keyboard and mouse and then switched to a controller and ended up sticking with the controller. The controller definitely felt more natural as I believed it was designed moreso with a controller in mind. Therefor I can not say whether there were any issues playing with a keyboard and mouse.

Got this on sale for ~5 bucks.
I heard about the bad reviews for this game, mostly saying that it is just another open world game following the Ubisoft structure. While that is true to simply condense the experience to this game down to that is doing a disservice.
Mad Max perfectly captures the feeling of being max himself, starting from a bare frame to building a flame spewing war machine on wheels is fun and makes you feel real progression through the game world. The environment is beautiful and the designers did a great job to differentiate each environment and territory in the game. From dried up seas to craggy trenches all the way to highways, each area feels and looks different.
The combat is split between in car and on foot hand to hand. Growing up with Burnout 3 this combat is great, and nothing is more satisfying than taking out an entire group of enemy cars. On foot combat is Arkham style combat with little variation although you do have a shotgun that can be used sparingly to mix things up. The combat is best when you storm a hideout in vehicle and then move in and beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the scavs that inhabit it.
Story is very limited, I am about half way through the campaign and it is not really taking me in. Banter between you and a certain companion is great when it happens. Don't come in with any expectations.
Overall this game is one of the most underrated games of 2015, if you are looking for a game that near perfectly captures the Mad Max universe or loves cars then this is for you. If you are looking for an engrossing story, look somewhere else.

I have to admit, this is one of the best games I've ever played. It's a driving game, I loathe driving games but I really, really enjoyed the driving. It's tough, it's gritty and it's really immersive to ram and blow up vehicles from the first person perspective.
The combat is incredibly rewarding, I found myself wincing and smirking at the Fury Mode take downs, especially the one hit KOs.
The game is gorgeous, the look, the feel, the sound; all of it combine to be an incredibly immersive game which really paints the scene and setting of the Mad Max world. Storms are just mind blowing: visibility reduced to 10 feet, defeaned by the howling wind as lightning strikes all around you.
Even the story is decent, it captured the character of Mad Max perfectly. I would think back on something Max had done and question why he wasn't so helping or altruistic but that's when I would be reminded that he is just trying to survive. A tortured soul, conflicted by the need to give up and the will to survive.
In essence, this game is just...wow.
Until I got to the ending. God is the ending disappointing. I'm going into spoiler territory here so skip if you're still reading.
All I could say to myself about the ending was, 'Atleast it wasn't a QTE'.
So all in all, this game is great until you reach the ending. It's a good sandbox with actual fun missions and objectives, but the ending definitely ruined this for me. I'll still recommend it but man I am really disappointed. I picked it up for £5 which was most definitely worth it, but I would say wait for a sale on this one.
