From the gritty film noir type narration and atmosphere, to the well crafted characters, to the way it deftly moves between suspense, humour, tragedy and action, it's clear that Max Payne is a classic, plain and simple. At the time of its release, it innovated by giving Max access to "Bullet Time", which allows you to slow down the action to help you take down the mobsters and junkies that get in your way, all the while making you feel like an action hero. The game can be challenging, and bullet time is your way of evening the odds. This was one of Remedy's first great successes, and it has their style all over it, particularly with the way they use the background (ambient noise, enemy chatter, TV shows, etc.) as an aid to the storytelling, and as a way to inject humour here and there.
The game is obviously showing its age, being nearly 16 years old at the time of this writing. I needed to install a sound patch (as the game was designed for Windows 98 and doesn't play nice with modern machines). Also, if graphics are important to you, the visuals are obviously dated (Max's grimace, which was a meme before we called them memes, is particularly amusing), and the gunplay can feel a bit clunky compared to today's standards. These are small complaints though, and considering how cheap the game is (especially during a Steam sale), you owe it to yourself to experience this classic game.

So, before you buy, consider this is a game from 2001. The era when PC gaming was revolutionalizing and each new graphics card would become obsolete within the year. The year of Ghost Recon, Red Faction, Resident Evil 3 and Return to Castle Wolfenstein. Then consider that in 2001 -and probably 2002 as well- I only played this gem; Max Payne. (yeah, ok, and Comanche 4, which to be fair, is another genre and quite frankly another gem of gaming as well)
Before you buy, do make sure you remember what graphics looked like back then, google it, and accept that this game is old. Then buy it anyway. I bought it even though I already owned a copy long ago and finished it over 15 times. I just felt I needed to own a copy on steam as well, just to make sure I can keep on playing it again whenever I feel like it.
For me, this is the game from my youth I remember most fondly. It is the game I use to explain to non-gamers why I love gaming. As an intense and involved alternative to watching a movie or reading a book: a great and heartfelt story, cinematic and style-ish ways of telling that story and tense and simply way-over-the-top-cool slowmotion gunplay.
At the time, for me the game came out of nowhere and had me wow-ing at every cool slowmo-takedown or story-twist. To this day still, I believe it is unmatched in terms of atmosphere and attention to detail. And even though I can not imagine there is anyone who has not yet heard of or read about this game, if by an odd change you are that person: buy it. Buy it and play it just to experience what a blast gaming entertainment could be.
Be warned though, ever since 2001 I have been longing for that game to come along that would give me the 'Max Payne' exprerience once more. A longing that has only brought me back to this one, back to the night the Payne started.

Max Payne is one of my all time favorite games, and game series, for all the right reasons:
1) The story and titular character Max Payne is instantly quotable and memorable, but not for being bright or funny.  Rather his bleak, metaphorical narraration throughout, that perfectly paints the picture of a drear New York winter.  That being said, James McCaffrey does an amazing job as Max Payne's voice.
2) The gameplay is a very solid third person shooter with Bullet time and slow diving mechanics that are similar to that of the Matrix.  It added a new pace to shooter games at the time, and even now its a fun mechanic to use to kill foe after foe.
3) If you do enjoy this game, then I highly suggest the 2 sequels.  Max Payne 2 and 3 are wonderful games, just like this one.  2 follows after the events of 1(obviously) and 3 came out nearly a decade after the first two in the series.  Max Payne 3 happens to be on my Top 3 favorite games of all time, on some days.  That list is variable.
In conclusion, buy this game.  Or suffer the Gulag.

If the episodic format and essentially online-only nature of the game aren't deal-breakers for you, HITMAN is a great addition to the series. The levels released thus far have been huge and very open-ended, offering many, many ways to take out your targets. NPCs have tons of personality and there's an absurd amount of incidental dialogue and side-stories that require multiple playthroughs to fully uncover. Blood Money would be proud. It would be nice to have more VO variety (it's weird that almost every NPC in Paris and Italy sounds American) but that's a pretty negligible issue.
I actually think the episodic format works well for the series. It encourages replaying levels rather than just plowing through them and it's only through replaying the levels that you can fully appreciate their scope and detail. In addition, there are plenty of other incentives to replay levels like challenges, opportunities, unlocks, escalation contracts and user-generated contracts. I especially like the escalation contracts, as they add interesting conditions and obstacles that force you to approach objectives in different ways.
The biggest issue I have with the game is the lack of quality control for updates. The latest update as of this review introduced a pretty major bug where NPCs can die when you choke them out. There's also another bug where NPCs can see you through walls. Needless to say, these can be game-breaking in many situations. I'm sure these bugs will soon be addressed but they really shouldn't have made it through in the first place. Optimization could also use improvement, as performance often takes a significant hit for no apparent reason. This, too, will very likely be addressed eventually but for now, it's still an issue.

Promised to release separate episodes in consecutive calendar months.  We did not receive the 2nd episode until almost May, which still holds the company true to it's word.  But one can only play a single episode so many times before getting irritated at not being able to progress.
The game as a whole (so far) is awesome.  However, I do not recommend purchasing this game until it is complete.  Yes, it states that the game is released in episodes, but it feels like it's in beta with all of the bugs.  As a matter of fact, an update was released late Apr, that completely broke DX12.  I am able to play in DX11, but why should I have to downgrade what my computer is built to run at on a new game?
This release was an unfortunate mistake and I definitely won't be purchasing any more "early release episode" games in the future.

Would I recommend DDADDS? Hell yes. Though there are a few things you'll want to keep in mind before playing/buying. I broke it down into Pro-Cons.  Some of these could be deal breakers for folks.
Pros:
-Fantastic character writing. The game definitely is a subtle fond poke at Dating Sims, but has a lot of heart to it. You will not be disappointed with how each character is written here. They're all very fleshed out in a way that is kind of surprising for a dating sim. Those I've watched online (yo huniepop, im looking at you) are very one-note in the way they depict a character. Each character has so much life to them. I feel like a know a lot about these characters and just want to spend more time with them.
-Dates, all the dates are immensely fun and hilarious. Even if you don't pick the 'right' answer, you're still going to have a fun time. All of them are also genuinely different and tailored to fit the specific character. You aren't going taking all the characters to the same place each time. Every date is a different scenario for that character. Mini-golf for one dad, camping for another, etc. The dates aren't cookie cutter or purely to get in the object of your affection's pants.
-The art style is fantastic. Hands down this was my initial draw to the game before I heard the premise. Both sealed the deal for me enjoying this game. The character portraits are very charming as well as expressive. Not to mention the fact there are a variety of emotions for each character portrait, a rarity given how a lot of dating sims function. Even without the music going on in the background or the sound bites from characters, you'll be able to tell how a character is feeling from their expression. The entire UI design is incredibly nice and fits together nicely. A lot of attention went to keeping a cohesive look for the game as a whole, this much is obvious when you play through it. Even the loading screens are really cute.
-Tying in to the art style: The setting of Maple Bay is very realized. The background art is so, so lovely. It's a nice soft contrast to the more bright character portraits. You can tell a lot of work went into the backgrounds.
-Dad tips are wonderful. They loop over a few times but make me laugh.
Cons:
-Weird audio mixing issues/audio issues over all. There isn't any music on the loading screens unless a track was playing in the previous scene. Some audio clips are strangely louder than others.  Not to mention loop strangely in certain areas. This can be really distracting.  Examples: the 3rd Craig date, the background forest clip used is immensely short and obviously loops/collides into itself when the file finishes. Hugo's dialogue reactions are jarringly loud, he blares over other sound cues on occasion. I'm hoping this will be fixed in the future. I wish they had voiced a bit more dialogue over all, opposed to having a handful of sound bites. Some grunts/gasps/thoughtful sounds can overlap at times. Multiple characters in one scene together can make that a bit weirder.
-The Build That Dad feature is very sparse. There are a handful of preset outfits, body types, noses, and hair. I'm hoping in the future the dev team will do an update to expand things further. Right now you're not going to get exactly what you like, but get kind of close to it.
-Each Dad has three dates max to romance them. All in all if you focus on just one character to date the game will be very short. I doubt this will be updated, but if there had been four/five dates it would have felt more well rounded. Right now a lot of the relationship building between the MC and the Dads is hand-waved in text-boxes as the third date starts. This can be kind of a mood killer if you're invested in a particular character. I want to see more of each character honestly. Especially of the MC's daughter Amanda interacting with the other dad's kid(s).
-Bugs, hoo boy, this game needed more polish time. I wish they had held off announcing this game by a few more months to do a bit more polishing over all. Whilst I haven't encountered these bugs myself- I can tell you the game will bork up on occasion. A few friends and folks on tumblr have encountered this problem pretty hard. A character portrait will get stuck on screen if you save at the wrong time. You'll be stuck with that character on screen for a few scenes and need to reload or quit to resolve the issue.
-Plotline writing could use some tweaking/further editing. It's very small issues at best. Stuff a third or fourth read through would catch. Example:  >MC narrates 'we're loading up my car' >narration two text boxes later 'we got into other character's car'. Along with loose plot threads regarding Amanda's social life. I won't go into detail on that due to spoilers.
Over all I definitely suggest giving DDADDS a look. The game at best needs a bit more polish for its rougher edges, but is clearly something worth your time if the premise and humor click with you. The game will definitely make you laugh more than once and get shockingly real at times in a genuine kind of way. It's a game made by a pretty small team who definitely care deeply about the final product. The passion shows even with the rough edges present. Give it a shot if you think it would be up your alley.

I was intrigued by this game early on, back when they announced it would be happening and was relatively eager to try it out once the release date came around.
Anyway, I checked out the reviews first just to reassure myself before dropping $15 on it, and was taken aback by some of the negative reviews. It made me rethink the idea of buying it, but in the end my curiosity and growing love for the dads (via people on twitter sharing cute anecdotes) won out.
I absolutely 100% am in love with this game. It was DARLING. I fell in love with every single dad, even the ones I wasn't sure about (like Joseph, Brian, Robert, etc.) The humor was cute, and my daughter, Amanda? The absolute light of my life. Some of the mini-games were a bit difficult, but for the most part a fun way to keep things varied--and to make sure a good ending with the dad of your choice wasn't TOO easy lol.
I noticed some people had issue with how short the game was, but I didn't feel the way at all! True, three dates isn't exactly a whole relationship but I thought the development of each of the dads was so sweet. I loved helping all of them so much. And having a side story with Amanda was great too--after all, it's not just you dating dads, it's you as a DAD, dating dads.
Some people were irritated that the "voice acting" was just the grunting, but I'm not sure. what people expected? I figured there wasn't going to be explicit talking in the game when the Dream Daddy twitter account posted a video of the game grumps recording their grunts. But I loved it! Especially Craig.
Anyway, I only had a few, very small issues. First, the mini-games. There was almost no direction on (most of) them on what you were supposed to be doing so I just had to wing it--but I supposed that's what my dadsona was doing too so? Also, a few of the mini-games were surprisingly difficult. I almost couldn't get past the one in Mat's first date--it took me SEVERAL tries.
Overall, the game was great. I loved the art, the music (the theme? MY JAM), the characters' individuality, the inclusion/representation of LGBT folks and specifically mlm, the humor, the DAD JOKES. It was so much fun getting to date all the dads. I've recently fallen into the pit of dating sims, and this is easily my absolute favorite.(even if Joseph's end deserved more happiness)

From its appearance to its mechanics, Heavy Bullets is not a complex game, but it is an elegant one. Tight corridors, blind corners, a limited eight-round chamber with retrievable bullets and fast, aggressive enemies and turrets. You usually learn lessons the hard way, but the smart design ensures you come across each problem one at a time; at the same time this design encourages careful, precise play over guns-blazing tactics. 10 hours in, I still don't know exactly what's going to be around each corner, but I do know that usually the best option is to keep my eyes and ears open, aim true, reload often, and shoot sparingly. The feeling of learning the game is highly rewarding.
Heavy Bullets punishes mistakes hard, but it does well to alleviate frustrations with some neat twists. The ability to save money across playthroughs ensures that each inevitable failed attempt doesn't have to feel like a waste. Keycards, vendors and items, each as randomised as the rest of the levels, encourage different tactics and using whatever's on hand to your advantage.
As of this date, there is one significant negative holding the game back. Many users including myself have experienced regular yet unpredictable microstutters during gameplay. In a game so tightly based around reaction time and precision, it can be positively maddening to drop hearts or even die from losing a much-needed split-second to the game's lag. While the game is by no means unplayable or unbeatable when played this way, several users have refused to play the game until this issue is resolved, and considering the type of game this is, I can't entirely blame them.
Other than that, once the initial hurdles are overcome you'll find the game isn't particularly long, and I don't see myself returning to it once I beat this final level at last. The graphics are simple but clear and easy to look at, and it looks smooth enough at 60fps, the aforementioned stutters notwithstanding. The audio is punchy and fitting with the style of the game, if not particularly catchy. As I've said, it's a simple game, but it delivers a tighter experience than so many games much more complex than it. Overall, a highly respectable diversion.

Heavy Bullets, a permadeath FPS in which after every shot, you have to pick up your bullets to shoot them again. Your low count of bulets makes the game thrilling and difficult whilst still being very fun

I realized, I play Heavy Bullets in the same way as I play Receiver. They are as alike as they are different. You have a gun, you have bullets. You load your gun one bullet at a time. You shoot turrets that stand still and take potshots at you, or you shoot things that rush you. Both are rules-lite, systems-lite. I keep coming back to both of them.
However, Heavy Bullets is bright, and simple, and teeming with life, where Receiver is monotone in color, byzantine in keybindings, and thematically devoid of life. Heavy Bullets has an end but not much story. Receiver has little more than it's story, but there isn't really an end to the gameplay.
And I love them both for all of those reasons.
I have a feeling Receiver is the game I'll return to in the long run, not strictly the better game, but there it is.
But Heavy Bullets: "A+++ wuld shoot again!!!!"

With the "dearth" of First Person Shooters available on the market Heavy Bullets provides a fresh example that you don't need overly complex systems in place to be fun. In a move completely opposite to Borderlands billions of guns, Heavy Bullets has one, your trusty 6 shot revolver. Each time you fire a shot, you must then recover that bullet in order to be able to reload it and fire it again unless you are carrying more than just the 6 bullets your start each run with. This creates some interesting situations where you'll be aiming across the room and weighing up whether you're confident of hitting your target; missing may mean having to run across the room with no way of attacking enemies.
Heavy Bullets features an ever familiar roguelike formula of randomized dungeons as you work your way through 8 levels with increasing varied enemies; at the end of levels 4 and 8 you will fight a fixed boss. Each enemy requires a different strategy in order to tackle them effectively but all drop when hit with one bullet to their weak spot (The only exceptions being the bosses and one enemy). Enemies are varied enough but if you take a methodical pace you can deal with them fairly easily, as long as you're accurate with your shots. I would personally recommend using keyboard and mouse for this game, I tried using a wired Xbox 360 controller but could never find a setting I was truly happy with.
In addition to your gun there are a number of items in the world to help (or sometimes hinder) your progress. Each play through I'd race for a backpack which allows you to store an additional item as well as the one you have equipped, The only thing that is persistent between playthroughs is a bank balance which you can use to save money for purchasing items and upgrades, the bank can also be used to store an item for future playthroughs and purchasing discounts, life insurance and a last will. If you die with the last will in your possession all money on your person is deposited to the bank.
The duration of a playthrough will depend a lot on your play style; I tended to edge around corners slowly picking off enemies one by one and found playthroughs to be between 40 minutes and an hour but it is possible to complete a run in less than 10 minutes (according to the leaderboards!). The reward for dispatching the final boss is a fresh $5000 in your bank, Whilst I mention the bosses, I felt the final boss was a bit two easy once you figure out how to take him out and would clear the room of other enemies before finishing it off. The level 4 boss was a bit more tricky, but eventually you develop the skill to take it out with relatively little damage received.
Overall, Heavy Bullets feels like a fresh take on a huge genre and felt very different to what one would expect of a FPS. It's psychedelic colour scheme and upbeat music make it feel like a strange trip and aside from minor disappointment with the boss encounters its up there in terms of a single player FPS/roguelike experience.

The side quests are nice and interesting and I think they're interwoven with the main plot yet the primary quest doesn't pull me in, or perhaps it hasn't yet. It feels like the primary quest is there just to give the game progress. It's so uninteresting. After just finishing Tales of Berseria and having experienced a game story that makes you get in an eternal "one more save point" spiral just to see what happens next this one feels pointless in comparison.
Again, 12 hours in and I still don't get why I should be searching for the McGuffin. The main character, the Last Castoff, is so mediocre. According to what I've seen already there are thousands, maybe millions, of castoffs. Aside from being "the last" what the heck makes the main character special? Why does it seem like the main character compelled to do the things she's doing when the other castoffs are just taking their sweet time living (or dying) normally. The answer cannot be "because she's the main character" because that's just silly.
Overall it's not a bad game. Graphics are nice, sounds are fine, gameplay is good, etc. It's just that the main story didn't get enough attention from the developers. It's like everything else has been done lovingly but the main plot was just slapped in at the last minute to tie everything together.
Maybe my opinion will change once I progress further but right now I'm dissappointed. I do not know how much the game will be improved by the developers (like some enhanced edition or something) but right now I cannot recommend this game. InXile marketed this game as the spriritual successor to Planescape: Torment and it shows that they really tried hard to emulate it but unfortunately they missed the mark in the story department.
On a different note I would love a modern remake of Planescape: Torment.

I guess it's just not for me. Obviously others like it but if you're looking for a good and memorable story don't bother with this.

Wasn't expecting much after watching/reading reviews. I felt Arkham City was already a step back from Asylum, so Arkham Origins being an Akrham City 1.5 didn't seem appealing.
However, I have to say that this game is actually very good. The narrative is a lot more straightforward and fluid (no City-esque villians appearing just to tick '[insert baddie]' boxes); the combat is the same, but there's enough new spice to maintain its depth (to be fair, it envitably becomes repetitive in all Arkham titles); boss battles are absolutely amazing and totally improved; the map is broken into segments to help alleviate the overwhelming feeling of side-quests and Riddler extras (associated with Arkham City); and, my personal favourite, Batman's suit looks superb.
There are, of course, genuine issues over this game in terms of its PC porting (e.g. bugs and graphical issues) but thus far I have ran into no game-breaking or illusion-breaking issues. The multiplayer is, as expected, completely throwaway, however. Other than that, this is a solid game, but one I would not expect to pay more than £20 for, maximum. Diminishing returns apply if you've hammered the first two games, so asking for full-price seems unfeasible. Wait for a sale.

If the episodic format and essentially online-only nature of the game aren't deal-breakers for you, HITMAN is a great addition to the series. The levels released thus far have been huge and very open-ended, offering many, many ways to take out your targets. NPCs have tons of personality and there's an absurd amount of incidental dialogue and side-stories that require multiple playthroughs to fully uncover. Blood Money would be proud. It would be nice to have more VO variety (it's weird that almost every NPC in Paris and Italy sounds American) but that's a pretty negligible issue.
I actually think the episodic format works well for the series. It encourages replaying levels rather than just plowing through them and it's only through replaying the levels that you can fully appreciate their scope and detail. In addition, there are plenty of other incentives to replay levels like challenges, opportunities, unlocks, escalation contracts and user-generated contracts. I especially like the escalation contracts, as they add interesting conditions and obstacles that force you to approach objectives in different ways.
The biggest issue I have with the game is the lack of quality control for updates. The latest update as of this review introduced a pretty major bug where NPCs can die when you choke them out. There's also another bug where NPCs can see you through walls. Needless to say, these can be game-breaking in many situations. I'm sure these bugs will soon be addressed but they really shouldn't have made it through in the first place. Optimization could also use improvement, as performance often takes a significant hit for no apparent reason. This, too, will very likely be addressed eventually but for now, it's still an issue.

As a fan of the Hitman Franchise, I have to say, this IS the most disappointing Hitman game to date.  Why they chose to release the game in episodes is the main problem.  Calling it an early beta would have been more forgiving.
I loved playing all of the Hitman games.  Playstyles from person to person differ, some may choose to kill each and every persone they come across, some may choose to role play thouroughly and disguise themselves to get around different obstacles.  This still holds true to the game, but releasing the game with just one "episode" is just not enough.  The game was released early March, episode one.  Promised to release separate episodes in consecutive calendar months.  We did not receive the 2nd episode until almost May, which still holds the company true to it's word.  But one can only play a single episode so many times before getting irritated at not being able to progress.
The game as a whole (so far) is awesome.  However, I do not recommend purchasing this game until it is complete.  Yes, it states that the game is released in episodes, but it feels like it's in beta with all of the bugs.  As a matter of fact, an update was released late Apr, that completely broke DX12.  I am able to play in DX11, but why should I have to downgrade what my computer is built to run at on a new game?
This release was an unfortunate mistake and I definitely won't be purchasing any more "early release episode" games in the future.

This is basically the Hitman game I wanted since the first one. Large clockwork environments, tons of ways to complete objectives and you feel really badass when everything goes smoothly. There are still some weird AI quirks and the odd bug here and there but if you like stealth games this is about as good as it gets.
To address the elephant in the room, yes this game is being released episodically. The starter pack contains two tutorial levels (which are as intricate as full levels in past games) and the first real mission set in a very large Paris environment. The first piece of DLC is set in Sapienza, Italy which is even bigger and more intricate than Paris. There will be 5 more episodes presumably containing one level each that will roll out over the rest of the year. I personally really enjoy this approach and look forward to the new content each month. You could wait till the end of the year when all the episodes are out and have a great Hitman experience but I'm enjoying this episodic approach. This is such a strong Hitman game at its core that I kinda hope we see additional content roll out next year too.

I'll start by saying that the first Hitman game I played was Absolution.  I thought it was great.  I loved the creative kills and stealth.  I went back and bought Blood Money on Steam, and honestly, I found it boring.   The controls were terrible, the kills were just decent, and I didn't get the hype.  I ended up returning the game.
Then I decided to give the new Hitman a try.  I love it, it's very fun.  Yes, the episodic thing is annoying, but really, it isn't as bad as I thought it would be.  I would say you definitely need at least the first DLC to make it worthwhile, as the Intro is a bit short.
I'm just going to buy each DLC as they come out, that way, if there's one that gets bad reviews, I just won't get it.
As far as gameplay, it's a freeroaming stealth game.  You do things how you want to.  Maybe you want to poison your target, or maybe stage an accident, or maybe you just want to go in guns blazing.  The choice is yours.  This one has a lot more freedom than Absolution, and the online aspect makes the game even deeper.
It's a great game for killing time...and people.

-The game might be too much for some, it's not all fun gunning down enemies, you have to deal with the consequences of your actions (in a more realistic manner than most games) as well.

I was very positively surprised by this game.
The story starts out in Dubai, where most of the population have been evacuated due to heavy sandstorms. Your team is sent on a recon mission, and when discovering dead American soldiers, you continue further in to the city to investigate and look for survivors.
The basic mechanics of the game are those found in most third person cover based shooters. Most of the time you're behind cover, returning fire at any enemies present. You also have grenades at your disposal, and you can issue simple commands to your squad members (target certain enemies, and in some situations order one of them to throw a flashbang).
The game mechanics themselves are good enough to make the game worth it, but as the game unfolds, you discover that there is more to it than most other modern action games. You are faced with some difficult choices, and have to live with the consequences of your actions in the game.
The choices are few and far between, and don't really change the storyline, this is not a role playing game, it's more of a cinematic experience (the player is even credited as a "special guest star" in the credits) where you take control over the action. The level design is quite linear, but this isn't necessarily a bad thing.
I don't want to reveal too much about the story, but when you in other games kill hundreds of enemy soldiers and don't think much of it, this game makes you think about what you're doing. You experience the trauma through the main protagonist, and chances are, you won't feel great about what you've done after playing through the game.
Excellent graphics, solid game mechanics, and a story that makes you stop and think. I would definitely recommend Spec Ops: The line.

I am absolutely in love with this game.
What I love about it is that it's not just a "let's see how we can get to a sex scene with each character" kind of game. Each dad has their own quirks and even their own problems and issues that they're dealing with. You help them through those issues as much as you "date" them (dating, btw, is more about hanging out and being a friend and less about smooching, which feels more organic when it's a bunch of guys you don't know.)
I also love that it's as much about dads dating dads as it is about just BEING A DAD. You're helping your daughter through problems. Other dads are helping their kids through problems. Everyone grows and changes.
I haven't dated all the dads yet, but so far I'm in love with every one of them. None of them are pigeonholed into some kind of stereotype. They're just PEOPLE.
Examples. No one brings up sexuality in conversation. Being gay (or in a lot of guys cases, bi) isn't something to just DISCUSS. Being bay or bi isn't better or worse than being straight. It's just. . .  a THING. Just like being straight is. No one questions it. No one's worried about it. It's just THERE. It feels like a future we can hope for, where people are just accepted for who they are without question.
As a Christian, I also like the way they handled Joseph. He's a Christian, but he's not a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ And he's not a perfect person either. He's just. . . a GUY. He makes mistakes, he recognizes that he makes mistakes, and he moves on from them. He forgives others while struggling to forgive himself. He makes choices and that affects a lot of things. He's got personal problems and he works through them.
For that matter too, the whole idea of church was well handled too. Joseph invited people and they came or didn't. It wasn't a big freakin' thing depending on their answers. Joseph invited people to church activities, but he didn't PUSH anyone. Being Christian was important in his life, but he could take a joke about it. He let it guide his actions, but he still messed up, as we all do. He never acted holier-than-thou.
Honestly I could write similar analysis on pretty much every character. All of them were so well developed.
Robert was a fun character to play around with, despite having some serious issues. The game didn't stray from that, and while we hope Robert was aiming for a better life for himself in the end, it wasn't a magic fix.
Damien was trying to prove he was something he wasn't, and your whole story is about him discovering who he really is and how to cope with that. He grew as a person.
Mat had a tragic thing happen in his past, like your avatar, and together you guys worked through things and brought him to a better place in his life.
All the dads are like this. It's a fun, calming, smile-inducing game, and I promise you will not stop grinning as you play through it. Highly recommended.

Visual Novels don't seem to be too popular when it comes to video games. Sadly, people just don't like to read, and it's unfortunate considering how talented the people at Game Grump's are for putting together this little gem. I know that this game won't tailor to everyone, but for those willing to give Dream Daddy a try, it will warm your heart in so many more ways than one.
When it comes to customization in Dream Daddy, you pretty much have free regin over how you want your Daddy to look. From facial features and body type to a small selection of clothing, and even personality traits, there's plenty to mix and match. You can even customize the circumstances of how you had your daughter Amanda (adoption vs biological birth).
The dialogue and characters in Dream Daddy are where the game shines the best. I just love the conversations between Amanda and the MC, especially the good conversations where you can be your Amanda's friend and father and balance out the relationship. The game definitely gives me a lot of insight on how I can aspire to be a good father one day.
As for the Daddies, they are all great characters as well! I'm still working through all the endings but my favorite so far is Robert's ending. Prepared to have tissues ready because it's going to get emotional! There's a trick to unlocking his good ending and I'm very happy that you can save scumb your way through choices if you make bad ones. SAVE OFTEN!
I found the mini-games to not be necessary but fun and polished nontheless. The soundtrack in this game was also memorable and relaxing to listen to.
For those of you on the fence with this game for whatever reason, just keep an open mind. The dialogue Is light, kind hearted, and oftentimes very humorous in a lot of ways. I also really like that the game deconstructs the stereotype that all gay men are feminine or not "regular guys", when it couldn't be more false.
Overall, I'm really happy to have given Dream Daddy a try. The story is short, but playing through all the romances and getting perfect endings for each one well definitely take you some time. So short, but good replay value. I'm really happy to see and financially support games that support the LGBT... movement.

Alright so, it took me awhile to think about how I was going to talk about this game. First thing is that by no means is this game "bad". But as someone who is a bisexual man, I don't know if I can really say that the game was "astonishing" or as "revolutionary" as some reviews have been claiming.
I think the best way to describe this game is as "cute". The art style is wonderful and the general dialogue and humor is absolutely top notch. Where the writing at times falls short is in the relationships themselves. I have to say that by far the best relationship, in terms of writing, in the game is with your own daughter: Amanda. While this isn't necessarily a negative thing, I certainly expected the writing of the romantic relationships to be on par. Which they were not.
The main problem that Dream Daddy runs into is its insistence on letting actions speak louder than words. Often times a route will end with you cuddling with your chosen love interest, without any mention of you two ever speaking about your relationship or whether or not you're actually dating. By writing the relationships in this way, it comes off as almost fanfiction-esque and makes it appear as though the target audience for the game was one that was happy to read things into the actions of men, that is the target audience was women. While I know this most likely wasn't the writers intent, it certainly comes off as rather weak and boring in terms of an ending. As a queer man, I expected the couples to at the least discuss their relationship to some extent, which they never do.
Another problem is the lack of uniqueness in the routes themselves, which primarily has to do with how short each of the routes are. You only go on three dates with each prospect, and these dates while unique often felt rushed in ordere to get the protag with their love interest. In most routes it felt as though the relationship between you and your love interest's children was stodgy, if not completely rushed at worst.
Ultimately, Dream Daddy is by no means a bad or poorly developed game. It screams of potential and you can see that the team making it really tried. However, this potential ultimately feels somewhat wasted by lackluster endings combined with vague writing in terms of defining a mlm relationship. Get it if you want, but if you're looking for better mlm dating sims, there are definetly several others out there that do a much better, more hear felt job at writing and creating mlm relationships in media.

"All flavor, no meat" is the best way to describe Torment 2 :ToN.
I should point out that I am one of the original backers from 4 years ago and loved the Original Planescape Torment - having played it a dozen times at least. The original Torment was reviewed by the New York Times which felt that it should be elevated to the status of literature due to the depth, beauty and originality of the writing - and I completely agree - the writing was that good.
... tions.html
Not so much the sequel, Torment 2 - Tides of Numenera. I am not sure where to begin with all the problems this game has.
1) Poor NPC introduction and character development. During this game I really reached a point of not really caring at all about my fellow companions. Mainly because there wasn't really anything compelling to care about. If you look at the original game, each companion is introduced to you from a space that matches who they are. Morte you meet in the beginning after you awaken in the dusties mortuary. Fall-from-Grace in the Brothel Of Slaking Intellectual Lusts, Anna-From the Shadows you meet in the Beggar Kings domain surrounded by shadows and thieves, Nordrom is found in a tainted Modron construct and so on... They are all incredible well-voiced and have distinct opinions and personalities as well as extensive backstories that you have to dig out. They also are linked to you through a unified theme - that of being broken and/or creatures that defy their own nature. In ToN I felt the companions were just kind of there - not much to the backstory nor are they all that important.
2) Way too much flavor without substance. There was just an exhaustive amount of shallow flavor interactions with this game that didn't have a whole lot to do with the main story. Although this feels like more a result of the universe - the Numenera - which is everywhere. The whole point of the Numenera is you never find out who made any of it or what its original purpose is/was - which can be fun in small doses but this game is lousy with that sort of thing. It just becomes one exhausting and unfulfilling interaction after another - wondering if this strange thing is important (usually not).
3) Show don't tell - this has been said many times and it is spot on. This just doesn't feel like an RPG - more of a story we are being told and we have to click the screen a bunch to get to the next part. I lost count of the number of times the writing devolved into telling us what we should be experiencing and what we should know instead of showing us what is there to see and letting us figure it out. The original Planescape has been called literature - and I agree - it definitely hits that bar. ToN is barely bad storytelling - and at the juvenile level at best.
The excuse I keep hearing from people is - "Well the original had a lot of writing - maybe you just don't like that" and my response is "Please shut up if you can't tell the difference between good writing and bad"
4) The combat is terrible, boring and confusing. It actually ends up being a blessing that combat is so rare in this game (although it shouldn't be if the game was well made), because it is really unsatisfying. Thankfully mostly you can skip it.
5) It is derivative in the worst kinds of ways. It felt like they just copy pasted aspects of the story from the original and pasted them onto this story. The overall feeling is a story that feels pieced-together and does not flow organically.
So basically there is a lot more but it comes down to this -it's pretty clear that the real genius behind Planescape Torment was not present on this project. I am done with Brian Fargo and InExile Entertainment. Wasteland 2 was just as weak and tedious story-wise as this title and its clear they don't have the writing chops to offer anything worthy of the titles and legacies they are pilfering.
This game will not do well. I hope you guys felt it was worth it to waste your resources on porting instead of making sure you had a solid product with great writing.

Finished playthrough at around 55 hours.
Although it fell short of its ultimate potential, Torment: Tides of Numenera is still an excellent RPG set in an unforgettable world. Seamlessly blending fantasy and science fiction, the setting and writing are by far its strongest points. That being said, the game is almost entirely dialogue. If you don't like reading - and I mean REALLY reading - this game is definitely not for you. The combat is few and far-between, and is mostly avoidable entirely except in a few plot instances.
Now, I was not a Kickstarter backer, so I can't comment on what they did not include in the game, what they said they would, etc. I'm just going to review what made it to the final product.
PROS:
- Amazing writing, memorable characters, fun companions (the first two you encounter are honestly the most boring), a treasure trove of lore and exploration.
- Fast and easy leveling and skill system (a little TOO easy, some might say...)
- Death is an important part of the game - you'll actually gain bonuses by exploring things in the Labyrinth inside your head whenever you kick the bucket. Finding new methods of suicide is always fun.
CONS:
- Combat sucks. There, I said it. You can easily overpower almost any enemy from an early point in the game, even without using cyphers. The combat itself is painfully slow, and just plain boring.
- Your character becomes far too powerful too quickly. I played a Nano, and after selecting the stealth trait tree, all I had to do in combat is hide for the crit/damage bonus and then and cast Maelstrom. Boom, combat over. Skill check? I've got 3-4 Edge in whatever. Instant success. I never even really used any ciphers except the perma-boost ones.
- The Tides don't do much of anything. It has a tiny effect on people's first impressions (I only noticed this 2, maybe 3 times in the entire game). They're supposed to be what makes castoffs so special, but aside from the rare Surge opportunity, they're utterly pointless.
- Little to no replayability once you know all the twists and turns of the plot. The most meaningful choice in the game happens...yep, at the very end. Just reload your final save if you want to change the world.
All things considered, it's worth the money. Just don't expect a genre-breaking epic saga like the old Infinity games and you'll have a good time.

Torment: Tides of Numenera is a overall neat Science Fantasy RPG, a lackluster spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment in some regards, and a better one in others. Mind you, I find the pseudo-intellectuality, inherently, stronger in the PnP RPG Planescape setting than the Numenera one, even if the creativity is stronger in the former ... Christianity is Platonism for the people...
Thematically I think that they nailed Abandonment--it's beautifully woven into the setting, the narrative and the overall ambience-- and to a lesser degree Mystery where I am a bit mixed, whereas Legacy especially in the form of the ending is lacking and lackluster. Which brings me to philosophy, this speaks of high culture, even if the Planescape setting and Planescape: Torment of course was a mix of pop culture and high culture, and so is obviously Numenera and this game. Regardless I don't know if the developers  ran out of time or had unrealistic ambitions, or I had unrealistic expectations...
Do the new companions live up to their heritage? No sadly not though I still find them fairly interesting. For my first play-through I had Callistege, Rhin and Matkina along with me. Also they seemed to be bugged so I had no inter-party banter between them :/. But on a strictly conceptual level I didn't find them as compelling as say Morte, Fall-From-Grace or Dak'kon - some of the more fleshed out companions from Planescape: Torment. The emotional journey I went through with them seemed impactless concerning their predicaments, though it probably would have helped quite a bit with party banter. As their comments on quests and NPCs were interesting and helped developing them. The companions partially had it easier in Planescape: Torment, in virtue of the fact that The Nameless One / The Player-Character had a history with, some of, them before the game began, making the player more emotionally invested in them. I didn't really care about any of the three companions from Numenera when the game was done, though there was some cool things no doubt and potential for greatness! Another minus is the bland and deliberately limited Voice Acting, I'd wish they'd use resources on other parts of the game when it wasn't of better quality.
Combat is sadly lackluster while it was a noble ideal to get rid of filler encounters, the mandatory combat /Crisis encounters weren't interesting in my combat-avoiding-Playthrough. It strikes me as a bit peculiar to use this many resources on this aspect of the game without using enough to make combat truly compelling. The occasional bugs in one mandatory fight made it especially tedious to go through several times.
Overall I think the game is a glorious and worthy spiritual successor even if it's a bit bland and lacking in certain aspects, it's shining in others even if it never quite reaches or surpass its predecessor concerning its artistic and narrative vision - though it's most likely stronger in the choice and consequence department for instance.
Hope that InXile Entertainment will be more upfront, transparent and honest with their backers in the future or I'll lose trust in them.

I want to like this. I want to recommend it. But I can't.
At its core, a Torment game should be a visual novel.
Except the writing in this game is terrible. There's no details, save when you  use Anamnesis, but even then it's vague.
They should have taken a page from Shadowrun: delve into the writing. Don't just tell me about the world, show me it in words that grasp the entire human vocabulary.
And the world. InXile's representation of Monte Cook's world manages to take the exotic, the alien, and the innately fascinating, and turn it into something mundane.
This is science fantasy. This is Clake's Third Law.
Distilled, pureed, and rendered homogenous.
Instead we're left with a lackluster swipe at fame, an attempt to emulate the greatness of Planescape torment without understanding what made it special.
As an early backer, I'm disappointed.
As a fan of Planescape: Torment, I'm saddened.
As a person whom yearns for the days of old-style CRPGs, this title solidifies the fact that we're not going back. It is no longer possible to do so.

Well, now that Steam supports proper reviews rather than just the limited recommendations, I think its high time I wrote a game review.
Batman: Arkham Origins gets a lot of hate, and there is some truth to what people say. Cited by many as a buggy mess and a blatant rehash, at first glance you may not be interested in the game at all. However, I would say that the negativity surrounding the game is blown way out of proportion.
Arkham Origins takes place before Arkham Asylum. Bruce Wayne is just in his second year of being Batman, and in the beginning of the game he learns that the crime lord Black Mask has hired eight assassins to try to kill him. The player must take to the streets of Gotham as the Dark Knight himself for another adventure set in the Arkham universe.
The story in the game is absolutely top-notch. The writers have proven that they can craft an engaging, gripping Batman story, even better than the past Arkham games. Players will get to see a more human side of a less experienced Bruce, as well as one of the greatest depictions of the Joker and Bane in anything Batman related. The voice acting only makes it better - while some may shy away from the idea of new voice actors for their beloved childhood heroes and villains, Roger Craig Smith and Troy Baker both really nail their performances as Batman and the Joker, respectively. As someone who grew up with the animated series, I can honestly tell you that I have no problem with them keeping this cast forever if they must.
The gameplay is where the negativity begins to appear. Virtually everything about the gameplay is identical to Arkham City - with a few changes here and there. With only one real new gadget, one can understand how this game would be labelled a rehash. However, more of the same in an Arkham game isn't really a bad thing. The combat is still fluid and fun, and the new enemy types really spice up the gameplay - the game has become a bit more challenging, forcing you to do more than just build up massive combos.
As for the bugs, the game's initial release was quite a mess - some of the sidequests weren't even able to be completed. These bugs have, for the most part, all been patched out, so you won't be hopping into a glitchy, messed up game.
All-in-all, Arkham Origins is a fantastic addition to your library - if not a bit similar to its predecessors. With tons of content and the same fun gameplay we all know and love, its great for anyone who wants another Batman game. If you're looking for innovation and change, this game may not be your cup of tea, but if what you want is another epic story in the city of Gotham, this game is sure to deliver.

Batman : Arkham Origins is definitely a game worth buying if you love quick combat, detective games or both, and if you're a Batman fan.  The number and variety of villains you encounter is huge and even as someone who isn't a huge Batman fan I never felt like I was struggling to keep up with who was who.  I also really like the different boss battles when fighting different assassins or the open world content you have to complete in order to stop another villain from, say, blowing something up.  Another great thing about this game is the amount of gadgets that you acquire throughout the game, it's really fun to use them all in different scenarios even though it can take you a while to realise which one you're suppose to be using.  The final aspect of the game I really enjoyed is the detective missions, like for example the Lacey Towers mission, piecing all the evidence together is really fun to do even though the game does do a lot of it for you.
Now on to the graphics.  Overall they're pretty good, the game looks good and the attention to detail is pretty extensive, I particularly liked the way Batman's costume changes throughout the game gaining bullet holes in the cape or scratches after fighting a large crocodile/human. The only thing I don't understand is why the cutscenes look so misty, like the quality of the graphics was suddenly switched to medium/low.
Now even though overall I'm enjoying the game and keep wanting to go back and play it I have discovered quite a few flaws to the game.
First of all the gameplay is pretty terrible, it's really hard to get Batman to do what you intended during fights or when jumping off rooftops, the response time isn't always very good, highlighting events on the map is almost impossible, the auto targeting system is also pretty bad, and I won't even go into the issues when trying to remain unseen or "in stealth mode".
Secondly, I don't understand why when having to examine a crime scene the computer does pretty much all of it for you, yet during simple missions I get stuck because of something I wasn't told I could do earlier in the game or the path I have to take to get somewhere isn't clearly explained.  The number of times I had to look up how to do something of this genre was extremely frustrating.   All I want is a tip to pop up every now and again just to nudge me in the right direction.
And finally, this is something that annoyed me personally, I don't know if others will feel this way, but the voice acting for some of the vilains is over-exagerated and made my face screw up.
At this point I'm sort of 50/50, some aspects are great but all the frustrating issues really balance it out.  If I could go back in time I probably wouldn't buy the game.  But for people who are huge Batman fans or people who are just really good at these types of games then I would suggest buying it.

This game reminds me of Spacechem, only it doesn't feel like homework.
Splice is a game made by the creators of Spacechem. It is an experimental puzzle game where you are given a limited number of "splices" to re-arrange the composition of a cell. You do this to try and match the predetermined shape given to you.
...Yeah, that sounds complicated as hell now that I think about it. But it is a complex game. Each level is a puzzle that needs to be solved. Its an interesting puzzle game, but the presentation is what I think makes the game. The music is great, creating a peaceful and calming atmosphere. The graphics, while simple, are very pretty, with cells moving in an organically smooth way when moved.
Its a small little puzzle game, but I found myself enjoying it much more than I thought I would. Give it a go.

Splice is a relatively short puzzle game involving strands of DNA. Your job is to change the DNA (by splicing it) in a variety of different ways in order to match the pattern you are given. There are seven main chapters and four epilogue chapters, with seven levels each. The ambient-like music is beautiful, and the game is nice both if you want a mental challenge and something to relax with.

They say the game's nothing new. It's not innovative. And apparently that's bad. When you follow up from a game that is already quite perfect, what is there left to do to improve it? Add multiplayer apparently. I haven't tried it yet.
Anyways, back to the game. It's great. It's fantastic. It's like its predecessors. Once again, it's not new, gameplay-wise. But is this really a bad thing? The game isn't bad. The story is great. Better than the previous iterations, and boss battles actually don't feel so terribly like boss battles. They're not easy, but they don't feel forced either. Did I mention the story is great?
There are a couple bugs that make the game nigh unplayable - I encountered one that hindered some side-quest progress, but it didn't last long - but everything else is just as it should be.
This is a worthy addition to the Batman Arkham Series.

Splice is a deceptively simple puzzle game.  You manipulate microbes to match a pattern given to you for each level.  Some microbes have special abilities to split, expand, or remove themselves which add a lot of complexity to the later levels.
The game has a very soothing style, with a nicely designed minimalist interface and calming piano music.  It'll help keep you calm when you reach the absolutely maddening levels near the end.  There are also some challenges built in in the form of "angelic" solutions, meaning you finished a level using less than the allotted number of splices and those can be just as maddening.
Overall, quite a fun game though frustrating at parts.  I guess that's the status quo for puzzle games.

Dream Daddy: A Dad Dating Simulators is a game from the minds of the Game Grumps.
Take a classic dating simulator like Hatoful Boyfriend, pump it full of bad (good) puns, self-satirising jabs at older generations struggling to understand the concepts of the likes of memes and social media, and you end up with Dream Daddy.
In it, you have seven different daddies you can fu....uh, date. While you do indeed have sex with them, there is no actual nudity nor any lewd noises, you just go to bed with them and then it cuts to the next morning.
There are three dates with each daddy, but the third one will result in the game being completed so if you intend to do all the daddies (like I did) then either make a save when you first get the chance to date them, or do the first two dates with each of them, make a manual save there and then do the third dates. Of course, this is only if you wish to see what each daddy's storyline is like.
Being a visual novel, there is unsurprisingly a large amount of text to read through, multiple choice responses included, usually involving some sort of pun or dad joke. Yes, the game is filled with dad jokes, what the heck would you expect with so many DILFs....uh, dads around?
Mat was my first choice of which daddy to date, in fact he's the very first one you can meet if you opt to go for coffee during the first few minutes of the game. Within the first minute of meeting him, he's throwing band-related puns at you left and right, asking you which one sounds best for his menu items. The first date with him contains of the several minigames in this, in this one you're placed at the music venue you go to but have to dodge other crowdmembers to get to Mat, all while the band plays incredibly loudly, but damn I enjoyed the track.
Speaking of music, the title track is just superb.
Other minigames you can play include pirate themed minigolf (yes it involves pirate talk) which was a blast, another one where you catch fish and my favourite, which has you flailing your hands around while you "play" a piano at a one-man solo comeback concert for your ska band Skammunist Manifesto, the song being a ska pun based Star Trek one.
Overall, its a short game, really short. I did the first three dates and got the ending within an hour, the others took me another two hours or so, thanks to liberal use of the fast forward button for previously viewed scenes.
Whether you like visual novels or not, Dream Daddy is a wonderful little treasure to experience, but maybe a few more extra daddies would have been a nice addition to help extend the overall playtime.

This game is meant to challenge you. Don't savescum for best options. Accept that you'll make mistakes. Burn through your limited resources. But talk to -everyone-. So many people have a story. So many of them might have some hidden secret for you.

Being a long time fan of the Hotline Miami series, I thought I would try this game out. My friends recommended it to me, and at first, I thought it would just be a simple fps dungeon-like game. Without a doubt, heavy bullets is probably the most stylistic "rogue-lite" (I refuse to call it a roguelike) on the market right now. Does that make it a good game?
In Heavy Bullets, you're basically playing a person whose goal is to do something about the security system, but honestly the story pretty much ends there. Other than some really strange flavour text that pops up whenever you start up the game, there's nothing else to the story other than you're going around shooting spiders and turrets.
The "music" (more like sound) and graphics are beautiful. I have heard some people complain about the colour palette, and while I sort of agree at some parts mainly I think it's pretty to look at and the sound fits perfectly. There's usually no soundtrack in the background unless you beat a level or walk up to a vending machine, which even then is only glitchy ambience instead of actual full on audio tracks. When you're almost dead, a intense drum beat starts playing which amps up the tenseness (is that a word?) of the game.
That's where my positives mainly end. While graphics and sound are a big part of this game, the other is the gameplay- which unfortunately is not spectacular. The picking up bullets mechanic is at first, very interesting and fun until you realize that you're either going to be stuck at basically swimming in bullets, or no bullets at all and no way to proceed (which is amplified even more by another thing that we'll get to later).
But what's wrong with the mechanic? Isn't the point that you get punished for bad aim, and that you have to risk your life to go grab more? That is all fine and dandy- until you realize that it forces the game to become a slow, methodical almost stealthing game rather than the fast "shoot or be killed" shooter that the game's movement speed and controls hint towards it wanting to be. Moving fast and shooting fast FEELS good, but you get punished for it so harshly by the enemy design and the nature of dropping bullets that you are forced to camp behind pillars and take your shots slowly- something that would work better for another game, but for the twitchy controls of Heavy Bullets it just feels like it bogs the game down to unplayable levels.
In turn, this all creates a loop of camping and inching to preserve bullets and then running out of bullets because you're camping, making you have to camp harder and be even more careful as you try and make a sneak attempt to the bullet you dropped, probably ending up in your death unless you got a bunch of health to camp with or bullet magnet+ to grab it from afar. Overall, I don't think that this mechanic is pulled off well mainly because the dangers that are presented to you are too high to make the game that fun "run-n-gun" game it wants to be so much.
Other problems I have are more nitpick and personal preference- I honestly feel like the banking system kind of encourages grinding and money grubbing more than actually enjoying the game the first times through; although you don't have to play the game like this, and there's even an achievement for ignoring it altogether. I feel like also some of the items are death sentences, I've never used running shoes without me running into a snake and killing myself and bombs seem like they're kind of on the useless side of weaponry even though you get a lot which ends up balancing them out somewhat.
So, do I recommend it? Well, if it's on sale as it currently is for 2 dollars, I'd recommend it just for the graphical and audial experience, but otherwise I'd say no. The trailer of popular LPers screaming at snakes attacking them is basically all this game boils down to- being killed by hidden things as you camp in corners trying to hold onto your bullets.
Heavy Bullets is an extremely pretty game game that adds a few innovative features, but squanders them by wanting to be both a slow stealth-like game and a fast run-n-gun, making your twitch based controls and movement basically useless as you inch around levels hoping a snake or turret doesn't kill you around a corner as you camp behind pillars. Get on sale for the graphics/audio, avoid on non-sale price because the gameplay is kind of bad.

Such a great game, with the story, atmosphere, and gunplay. But in all honesty, it's hard to recommend the game in it's current state, because if you have any of the recent versions of Windows and you are interested in getting this game, be prepared to put some work into it to enjoy it.
First things first, the sound is messed up, and you will need to get a third party sound patch in order to fix it. Without it, cutscenes with have no sound and shooting weapons sounds like the gunshot audio is played 10x over. It's pretty easy to fix, and there are a couple of tutorials on how to set it up. Big thanks to Darkje for the patch, search for him/her on steam and find his/her tutorial and you'll be set.
Second, if you have a generally decent computer, it's going to run the game at a higher frame rate than intended, which results in Max clinging to the ground during his shoot-dodge (he doesn't leap in the air like he's supposed to), Max magnetizes to walls during his nightmares and not jumping properly a certain parts of said nightmares, and cutscenes not executing the way they were intended. Granted, all of these issues do not make the game unplayable, in fact, I had beaten the game with those issues still present on my playthrough. But if you want a try to fix those problems, you could force V-sync to be on through your drivers control panel, which didn't work for me (Nvidia), but could work for others. Another option is to get third party software that could limit your frame rate manually to a desired amount, I guess it would depend on your computer specs on which one that's available that you should get. There are a few other options available, but these two were the most recommended solutions that I found.
With that aside the game is great experience. The story is good, with the narration done by Max being very atmospheric, and the comic-esc paneling cutscenes being a great touch. Gunplay is very smooth and satisfying, with every encounter ending with you feeling like a total badass.
There really isn't much to say about this game that hasn't been said already, it is truly a great game that should be experienced, but the game is not optimised for up-to-date hardware, and that really hurts it. But if you have the time to fix the sound issues and the frame rate, you got a real gem of a game in your library.

The enemies are tougher, faster, and harder to beat than the previous Arkham games, and Batman doesn't react and move as fast as the previous iterations. It makes for a difficult and harrowing experience at times.
The puzzles are lot easier, and one thing I really miss from the previous games were the riddles. It was fun trying to seek out the and find the objects or items that the riddler was alluding to. The puzzle aspects of Origins were pretty hollow, and it ended up being more of a chore than it should have been.
Many people have complained about the plot being more about :spoilers: The Joker than the assassins :spoilersover:
which I didn't find to be that irritating. It was interesting to find how the relationships Batman had with many enemies in his gallery were established in the Arkham universe. "Our previous warden died or something like that, so now you're in charge. What? Need a tutorial? Sure, here's how you build a house, build utilities, hire people, designate rooms, execute people etc.. What? Oh, the rest of the stuff? Don't worry about that, you'll learn the meaning and the use of it just seconds after you fu*k something up!"
So... It's a prison builder. You would think that there would be nothing really to do, other than boss around the inmates, but you are wrong. IVSoftware has made it really, REALLY detailed. And they make you care about your prisoners, especially if you have less ~50 prisoners. This game allows you to manage prisons in the way YOU want, with YOUR political or ethical standarts. And that is what a sandbox should be: the ability to express your creations the way you want and not be forced to do otherwise.
Has great mod support and a growing community to make sure, that, even if you somehow get bored, you will be able to find something new to try out. But that is also a negative. After 8-12 hours I have done everything: completed the campaign, built a functioning prison with 300+ prisoners, played the "Escape" mode (which is a LOT of fun at first, but after like your third or fourth prison, each new prison becomes a speedrun on "How fast can I break the shower heads and toilets, stirl up a riot, grab a shotgun and run out". But, as it's only found in the "Extras" section, I believe, that this bare-bone mode is not finished yet, despite the game being released). All that's left is to find those meaningless photos and notes, in which I can't figure out the handwriting.
All and all, this is a great sandbox and the price is fairly cheap for a game, that gives content for atleast a day, plus mods, plus replayability with different playing styles. I rate the game with an 8/10- a MUST try-out, with a potential of stealing tens or even hundreads of hours, depending on your taste.

I like "Heavy Bullets" for the following reasons: It is as simple as it HAS to be. The game is not filled with tons of random items just so the developer can say in the trailers that the game has 100+ items from which half do the same thing anyway and the other half is totally useless. Still, there are 1 or 2 useless items in this game and maybe some more items or at least character upgrades would make it more rewarding. With Character upgrades btw I mean that there are items in the game which permanently increase something from your character, for example you can reload more bullets at once or you can run faster.
The second reason I like this game is that exploration is worth it and will be rewarded. The levels are designed like mazes, kinda like in Doom, but everything is on the same height. There are also secrets, but they are very rare and I think there is only type of secret (maybe I simply didnt found other types).
The third reason is the enemy design. Every level you get one or two new enemy types to fight and every enemy has a distinct role, look and is defeated with a different tactic. Most enemys die in 1 hit and thats a nice thing because first it makes you feel powerful, second this is a game which rewards quick reaction and reflex (like Counter-Strike). Also when enemys die they kinda explode which is nice hit feedback.
And the last reason is the presentation of the game which is very cool and consistent. Obviously the game looks "bad" because technically its very low quality, but it knows how to present itself. I really like the main menu. Also sound-design is good in the sense that everything has a distinct sound. For example coins and bullets you can collect dont just stay on the ground, they sometimes bounce a little and make a sound so you always know that there is something you forgot to pick up.
The only reason I said that this is only worth at sale price is because it is very short, it depends on your skill. I played a little over 2 hours and beat the final boss. I know many people probably think the Bank is a good design choice, but in my opinion its just a cheat, so at some point everyone will finish this game. This could easily be fixed by limiting the amount available of an item at one vending machine, but you can currently just upgrade carry+ and then take tons of red potions and silver hearts with you. I paid 1,5€ on a Sale for this game and for that price it was a very solid experience and made me write a review even if this game is already old.
What I can definitly say is that the developer of this game (which I believe is a single person?) is definitly a good game designer and I wish him the best of luck.

My issue with this game is as follows:
1. Combat. Seriously, forget the turn based part of it, where the heck is it?  XP through kills = pretty much non existant. I can't say how the whole game is, but I'm pretty far into it, I've been in 4? 5? fights, and only 1 gave me any symblance of XP (You might say, well that's good cause it means you don't have to choose combat as an option! But I ---wanted--- to fight. I designed a glaive character, went out of my way to go into battle, and did everything I could to annoy people. Heck I ran into three thugs that were all "Hand over the girl or else!" I picked or else, and it just throws me a dialogue "You did 20 damage fight ende dinstantly." Like what?! WHERE IS MY BATTLE?! What happened to the axe wielding scar covered madman slaughtering innocents in the street that I played as on PST?)
2. The illusion of choice, isn't as well casted as the previous PST (in the previous one I did playthroughs with 2 or 3 fights, and playthroughs with everyone in every town dead that you could kill. Lots of variety!). Each decision I make seems rather "flat" ? In a good choice RPG, decisions will keep piling up on top of each other, each quest you complete, each choice you make in dialogue, it all stacks up. This one? Not so much. There were a few quests that required some chaining behaviors, but mostly their "choice" system was just the occassional 'oh you could have gotten +1 str if you played it this way. Too bad, suckah!' Combined with the fact you don't really get a lot of fights, this can feel a lot like reading a book and having to roll dice every now and then to see if you're getting all the pages or an angry troll is going to rip a few out before you can read them and much less like you're shaping the RPG with your choices.
3.  The plot is slow and drags into errand boy in several sections, and the characters were interesting, but I didn't get to feel I connected to any of them. I wanted more out of my Main Char Side Char relationships, I wanted to feel like my scruffy gang of 3 was really impacted by my existence. I didn't get that at all.
Things that I really enjoyed about the game:
1. It wasn't a good hit for me, but I did like the skill point system stretch they did with effort. It was interesting and forced me to think about a lot of decisions I normally wouldn't have had to .
2. The artwork was, as it was in the previous game, really good. The landscapes were constantly changing so much so that even in the same town I could feel the differences between area one and area two.
3. The character backgrounds were interesting, which made point 3 of the cons that much more frustrating.
Now these are all just personal opinions, and I would only not recommend the game because there are a lot better RPGs out there that do what T: ToN tried to do in terms of execution, but better, and they're cheaper. If you've played every RPG on the market though, consider my thumbs down a thumbs up.
