Buckle up, as I'm about to tell you a tale of one of the greatest games of all time:
Jedi Knight - Jedi Academy is among the first games I ever played all the way back on my first PC when it came out. I remember dad coming home with the case and although some may call this game flawed story-wise and in its mission structure not exactly holding up all these years later, I fondly remember my first hour almost as if it was yesterday. The graphics were a huge step-up from the games I had played until then and I was amazed at witnessing that Star Wars intro I had grown to love so fondly in a game I had heard nothing about but praise from my friends. Immediately after the first cutscene, I was thrown in with a lightsaber in hand and it felt great! I couldn't wait to cut through some stormtroopers, even though I had no idea what the story was about, but that's what it was like back then. Not understanding English back in those days, I was all about the action. And boy, what a game to make you feel like a true jedi this turned out to be. Now that I'm older and have replayed it for about the 20th time (with a new pack of mods, but we'll get into that later), I can appreciate the complexity of the lightsaber combat even more than when I was a kid. Force management, and multiple ways to replay the game with an assortment of different force powers each time. Not to changing into two lightsabers or a dual lightsaber in the 3rd arc of the game, or keeping your trusty single saber from the start, now fully capable to handle any situation with all the saber styles at your disposal. That's what made this game feel like a joy to play, from start to finish, every single time I've replayed it so far (except for the mission where you collect parts for your ship which is a drag).
Let's get into the meat, that is the lightsaber combat. Like I said, Jedi Academy was my first Star Wars game on the PC and although I played Outcast and Dark Forces 1/2 later, I never managed to appreciate them as much as this one when I was younger. Now I see Outcast for the amazing cinematic story it provides with the right twists and a progression system that forces you to adapt to the situation, which I honestly prefer over Academy's skill points between missions. Though one thing Academy's got over Outcast where it counts is its last arc where it's all about fast duels with a multitude of bad guys and their cultist supporters with annoyingly strong force powers. Outcast never had that. Its level design and story may have been better, but Academy's combat shines in comparison. This is how you refine a system you developed in your last iteration and make it the spotlight of your game. Everything post-Vjun in this game is pure action and I love it every time I get to that part. The missions up to it feel like child's play when you actually think about it, but that's just how great the pacing is too. It doesn't make you feel to powerful right off the beginning, yet by the end, you don't feel overwhelmingly powerful either. Also, the music... John Williams' tracks from the movies. Could've used a few original pieces of work but, not complaining as this is what defines classic Star Wars.
The game has aged pretty well and is well-worth your $10 of investment for the ~6-7 hours of entertainment it should provide in a single run. However, let's address the elephant in the room. Yes, Disney now own Star Wars, and hence LucasArts is no more. That however benefited these older titles. Both Jedi Outcast and Academy have their source codes released to the public for personal use, which has given us some of the most amazing modifications that a game can have, keeping it still alive in the modding community to this day. I'm talking about the Serenity Engine, the Evolution of Combat. Among the most advanced mods for this game, bringing in a whole new feel to the long-time classic, in the form of manual parrying, new combat styles and animations, as well as reworked and rebalanced combat system. If you're not into trying new stuff, you may like some of the many mods at disposal all around the internet. I'd suggest into looking through moddb and most importantly
(the definitive JK mods site since the filefront shutdown) to find some long-time favorites and fan-made side stories, or just expand your game with a few brand new models, animations or sabers. Some of my personal recommendations are Vengeance of the Sith (a really well-made mod that follows Mara Jade through the Jedi Knight universe with great pacing, difficulty and constant action in your face, and this came out in 2004!), Jedi Outcast Academy (JOA is a mod that ports the entire Jedi Outcast story into Academy's newer engine and allows you to switch between the two games on the fly. Really great if you have Outcast in your library and would rather play it with slightly better visuals and the new moves that JA brought to the formula. Though you need to OWN Jedi Outcast), the aforementioned Evolution of Combat (which is also getting a new version pretty soon), Movie Battles 2 and Movie Duels are Multiplayer and Singleplayer modifications, one of which is heavily-focused on teamwork and coordination, and is likely the most active among the Online community, and the other allows you to replay your favorite battles from the movies, and too many other mods to list.
Bottom point is, after playing through all of the games through my life, multiple times in fact, I can say for sure that this was a heck of a way to end the series! Amazing combat, great pacing, lovely modding community and an online component that's still active to this day. Don't trust the hours I have on Steam. This is a game that I keep coming back to on a yearly basis to replay or mess around in for a few days, which eventually grows into weeks, months, and wouldn't you know it, I haven't had this gem off my HDD ever since I installed my OS back in 2013. Truly a masterpiece, worth your $10. If you're into this sort of games and would like a more story-driven experience, get Outcast. And if you're feeling like you wanna try them both, go for it! So many things to say about this game.  It's more-or-less Arkham City 1.5, but with a lot more problems than I remember.  The objectives, gameplay, free-roaming, story-telling style, combat, and graphical style are more-or-less the same from Arkham City.  The graphical fidelity did get a nice boost.
But, that's it.  The story, although interesting felt unfulfilled.  None of the villians were fully explored, many of the encounters were dejavu from AC.  The build-up of a story with Black Mask and Deathstroke is ultimately unfulfilled; without spoiling anything.
Most upsetting though is the combat.
- The super-fluidity of AC is gone; and how upsetting.  Batman no longer can counter mid-punch, or mid-takedown, or mid-grapple etc; so be prepared to lose your multiplyer a lot & by no fault of your own.
- The electric gloves break the point of countering when they're activated
- Enemies now can counter from off-screen, leading to unexpected hits
- Batman's no longer can counter any enemy on the field; so you have to guess which enemies he'll be able to counter & which he won't
- multi-enemy counters seem to have nearly vanished
- enemies constantly need countering hugely wrecking the fluidity
Ultimately, its not that the game is bad.  Its just that WB Montreal, in inheriting a beautiful franchise from Rocksteady gets a pass on this one.  It does everything AC did, nothing more, with a couple bugs that won't be fixed.  Its worth a play through & a couple challenge maps; but not the love you'd give AC or AS.

Arkham Asylum came as a breath of fresh air in a genre combination that had left a long trail of mediocre at best games, even when coupled with some of the biggest licenses in the world. Arkham City expanded on that with an open world and a ton more things to do. Can Arkham Origins, the third game in the series, a prequel made by a different developer, keep the same high quality and still make the franchise feel fresh?
The answer is, thankfully, yes. Though Rocksteady didn't work on this entry in one of the best new franchises in years, WB Montreal has hit it out of the park and convinced me that even if Rocksteady has moved on, WBM's hands are more than capable.
The game starts out long before the events of Arkham Asylum, and you play as a Batman who's nowhere near as confident. He has no allies aside from Alfred, the criminals of Gotham City still aren't quite sure he's more than a myth or urban legend, and the police force will stop at nothing to take him down. On Christmas Eve, Batman discovers that someone has hired eight assassins to kill him, with a $50 million reward to the one who manages to take him down.
The story takes place across Christmas Eve night and a couple hours into the very early morning of Christmas, and it's wonderfully well told, which is good because the story was the most worrying thing to me, since I figured the gameplay looked nearly identical to the past two games.
The gameplay isn't just a cut and paste of the prior entries, though, with a handful of new gadgets, takedowns, and combat moves thrown in to keep things fresh. Obviously there are some gameplay continuity quirks, since why would Batman have lost some gadgets between now and then, but for the most part you'll forget about those kinds of things as you fight quite a few new enemy types, the best bosses in the series, and use your detective skills to solve crimes with some cool new crime-rewind/fast-forward stuff. It's all very fun and I have no real gameplay complaints, though those expecting radical departures from the series' formulas will be disappointed.
The non-story stuff is at its best in this entry as well, with cases to solve, criminals to catch, and an enjoyable random crime system to mix things up.
The only real downsides to AO are negligible. The multiplayer mode is both dead and somewhat pointless, though it could be fun if you could find some games and play with friends. The other issue is that the game, unlike Asylum and City, could use a couple more passes of polish. There are quite a few bugs in this entry, mostly with mission triggers not occurring or enemies becoming unable to be interrogated. Sometimes while rewinding a crime you will become stuck in the ground until it finishes,  things like that. I didn't run into any of the gamebreaking bugs some people have, but I guess your mileage may vary.
All in all I had a blast with B:AO and I look forward to what both Batman developers have up their sleeves.

You could pay all the salary you're ever going to earn in your entire life, and you'd STILL be able to get a whole lot of bang for your buck with Prison Architect. And I'm not even sure if that's an exaggeration.

I got this game on sale not expecting much. It's a licensed game and truth be told, I don't know what persuaded me to buy it. Critics bashed it, making it seem like it was just another cheap licensed game to make a quick buck off of. The critics are mad (and probably only watched Fury Road). This game is a kind of hidden gem.
If you've watched any of the Mel Gibson Mad Max movies or even the more recent Fury Road, don't think and just grab it. Knowing the game now, I feel like $20 is a very reasonable price for it, let alone the $6 I paid for it. I'd give it 4/5 stars.
The story in this game serves as an alternate prequel from the comic book version to Mad Max Fury Road. It happens before Fury Road and explains who the little girl in Max's flashbacks is. However, the story in this game goes even further back. Way back, when Scabrous Scrotus (yes, his schtick IS that) beat Max and left him for dead. That's when Max meets up with Chumbucket, a mechanic (or "blackfinger"). From then on, their purpose becomes to tune up the Magnum Opus, a car you will tune up and upgrade throughout the game, and make it all the way to Gastown. On the way, they meet several camps who will helped Max if and only if Max helps them.
So, gameplay-wise... Imagine Grand Theft Auto on a wasteland. Unlike GTA, you only have a shotgun and your fists on foot. Unlike GTA, you car can be equipped with a grappling hook, "thunderpoons," and side flames. Also, you can ram your car into other cars, which is fun. Actually, explosions become kinda common if you go after convoys or fight other cars. So, driving is fun. Fighting on foot is fun too, with your standard fisticuffs fighting and shotgun blasts. You can also do shiv executions and as you progress, you will be able to do other moves too. You can also counter attack, which is actually more fun than it should be. Fighting on foot does have a weakness- closed quarters, where the camera starts to go a little weird can sometimes hide enemies and their cues. It's a mild annoyance. A targeting system might've been useful.
There are camps to take down and plenty of places to loot. Although loot usually only the takes on the form of "scraps," a sort of currency with which to upgrade Max and the Magnum Opus, there are other things to loot, like car bodies and parts for the different friendly settlements. It kept me distracted for a while, for certain. There are also "Death Runs" which are just races. I didn't very much enjoy these and thankfully only one is actually mandatory (but maybe I'm just a bad driver).
All in all, I really enjoyed this game. Its story is relevant to the broader Mad Max mythology, so any Mad Max fan should have fun with it (or, I guess, look up a Let's Play if you don't want to play it). Fallout fans might enjoy it too, for the setting and easier to understand loot (it's dumbed down, but it's fun- I actually described it as Fallout 4 but dumber to a friend). Fist of the North Star fans might like to pretend that Max is Kenshiro due to his sudden combat prowess (which I feel isn't quite as prevalent in the movies, hah).
I'm actually looking forward to a sequel! A sequel that, I hope, builds on this game and doesn't end up mediocre.

If you are a fan of the HITMAN series this is going to be a tough installment to love.  The episodic nature hurts the overall game play.  Having said that let me explain.  As you are getting ready for an episode you start getting psyched up to go through and eliminate your target(s).  While you are in the episode things are great.  The gameplay is good and the environment is immersive.  Nearly all of the situations you find yourself in are believable and most of the time you can find a way to work with stealth, or not so subtly if you prefer.  Now the downside, after you finish the mission you're done.  Granted there are some extra challenges that help with replayability and help you improve your skills, but your immersion in the character and the world is broken at that point.  When the next episode gets released you get to ride the same rollercoaster.  I think this is going to be great when all of the episodes are out.  Then the backstory will make more sense and becoming 47 will feel more natural by having the ability to run through several missions at a time.
This new Hitman is a masterpiece.  Each level is like a whole novel, rendered in 4 dimensions.  They all tell a story, develop characters, and provide many interesting ways to kill them.

Tides of Numenera is NOT as good as Planescape: Torment. But if you liked Planescape and manage somehow to curb your sky high expectations, you will have quite a bit of fun here.
- What I like the most about Tides is exploring the weird of the Ninth World, to the point that the side adventures often overshadow the main plot for me. I think it's a great adaptation of Monte Cook's setting in a video game, and hopefuly not the last.
- With a few caveats, I like the way P&P mechanics translated into the video game, although I thing it could have probably been more faithful to P&P version without too much additional complexity. For example, the rest system in table top where first few rests are essentially free (although they do not restore all resources), and only the fourth requires a night's sleep, would have worked very well in a video game.
- I like Cyphers. While in other games I find myself hoarding one shot magic items, I had no such issues with Cyphers and used one or two in almost every crisis - and never felt like I was wasting them. There is enough variety so they don't feel too generic, and effect is usually strong enough not to feel useless.
- The main premise of the game - an incredibly powerful near-immortal being that sheds used bodies is interesting enough to keep me hooked.
- I also very much appreciate that this game does not attempt to please everyone and pull punches with "all opinions are equal" BS.
This is far from perfect game of course, and there are quite a few things that I wish were done differently.
- Some things are too obviously cut from final release. There is a little bit of Tides, a little bit of Meres, but both of these elements feel underutilized and tangential. I kinda wish developers would just drop one completely in favour of thoroughly developing the other.
- While PS:T was frequently criticized for large amount of pointless "trash mob" fights, Numenera has the opposite issue - crises are so few and far between that I can hardly make use of my new abilities before I gain yet another level. Of course if they were more frequnet, the snail pace of turn based combat would be the killer.
- Companions feel completely inconsequential. Remember the first companion you get in PS:T? Morte was both a huge motivator for the main plotline, a floating setting encyclopaedia that provided exposition for the unfamiliar elements of the setting, and a comic relief. First companions you meet in Numenera are a bickering couple who have no relation to main character whatsoever. Almost every party member in PS:T had a stake in your story. Morte was Nameless One's best friend and owed him a huge debt. Hannah was hopelessly in love with him. Dak'kon owed Nameless his life. Ignus was Nameless' apprentice. Vhailor was Nameless' eternal nemesis. In Numenera, companions feel like random people who just tag along because reasons.
In fact, companion development is probably the biggest disappointment for me in Numenera. The quality of companion writing is surprisingly inconsistent with the rest of the game - I often find more interested in NPCs than in permanent party members. Definite room for improvement there, especially considering the "other" homage to old school RPGs, "Pillars of Eternity" did companions much, much better.
Overall, I absolutely recommend this game, it's a solid 8/10 in its genre. Just make sure you don't go in expecting another Planescape: Torment.

I picked up Heavy Bullets during the roguelike sale for $2, and I suggest that everyone should, even at full price. It's another one of the "fps roguelikes" that seem ever so popular these days, with a very retro feel.
The first thing about the game that I noticed was extraordinary was the quality in audio and visual feedback: coins and bullets jingle on the floor, enemies clearly alert you through sounds when they're around corners, and worms scare you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ as your screen shakes and a loud bassy sound drops when they attack from behind.
Although "retro", it manages to keep the player very immersed in the game, both with sound and mechanics, which is something games like Spelunky and Isaac tend to fade from doing as you get better and better at them. This may be good or bad, depending on how much immersion you're looking for from a roguelike.
Mechanics are very in-depth, with magnets for coins and bullets, homing bombs, and even the ability to invest in a discount on all other items, a "last will" that saves your items and consumables on death for your next run, and a "life insurance" investment that lets you keep money on death for your next run.
Finally, as far as performance, it runs great; maxxed, including FXAA, I get about 100 on a GT 640 / AMD FX-6100, which is a rather budget setup. There should be very few FPS issues, likely even on laptops.
Overall, it's a very different experience from your average roguelike, and I love it.  If you enjoyed Paranautical Activity, Receiver, or Fancy Skulls, give this game a shot.

EDIT: Revised significantly.
I backed the Kickstarter campaign early on, and have been looking forward to Torment: Tides of Numenara for years. And, having played it for several hours, I have to say I'm quite disappointed.
Generally speaking, the game designers seem to have neglected game mechanics to concentrate on narrative. That would have been a credible tradeoff -- but frankly, the storytelling isn't very good.
After nine hours of play, I realized that I don't care about the protagonist or his predicament, I don't care about the antagonist, and I don't care about the protagonist's companions. Each has a narrative; none has a personality.
If you've played table-top role-playing games much, or online role-playing, you're likely to have met an enthusiastic but inexperienced player who has written out an elaborate back story, and then reads it out at the first opportunity. But no matter how well-written that backstory is in itself, it's a static element, and not an interaction that builds a relation between characters in a dynamic story. The NPCs in the game are like this: all static backstory, with little interactivity.
The game opens with a classic setup: the protagonist has no memory, and is in a crisis. This is a classic precisely because it forges a bond between player and character, based on their common interest in getting answers to the obvious questions. But, that crisis is quickly resolved, and immediately after, you get the basic answers to your questions, and several strong hints that completing the main quest really isn't in your best interests at all. All the virtues of this classic storytelling opening are quickly abandoned, and you're left with only an arbitrary main quest that the protagonist has no real motivation to pursue.
It doesn't seem to get any better after that. Everything confirms that initial impression; nothing hints at an alternate interpretation. The companions are flat and dull, and offer no additional motivation.
In general, the writing feels like a compilation of creative writing class exercises with no organic connection between them.
It concerns me that whether TTON is remembered as a success or a failure, it will be regarded as such for the wrong reason. Many reviewers, professional or amateur, seem to accept the idea that TTON is about elevating writing over gameplay, so that if it's a failure, it's because players want only hack-and-slash power fantasies, and if it's a success, it's because this is the kind of writing we like. But in my opinion, it's a failure, precisely because it fails in its primary emphasis, as an interactive story.
The real tragedy is that many of us supported this project because we saw an opportunity to send the game industry a message that we want intelligent, mature interactive stories, and we were willing to provide all the resources needed to make them. That opportunity was squandered.

What I am mainly confused about is how the character has... no... actual job... I get the concept of how after three dates, you have to commit to one ~daddy~. however, that is the point where you start develop the feelings for the guy and you start to fall for him, thus entering the extended plot line. I'm still not grooving to the fact that Joseph wanted to f*** on the DL because he wanted to keep the image up of him and Mary. If people already know Mary as a barfly, then why even care. What's it in... Beta? Alpha?
It certainly isn't release, because stating so would be an insult to other actual releases...
The Hitman series, a way for many of us to get our fill of strategically planned and surgically performed assassinations, or of cold blooded mass murder once we got tired of the same old routine...
These games might not have been everyone's cup of tea (there's a genre for everyone), but their quality was undeniable. I'll spare you the retrospective, because that would be a waste of time: They were awesome, for the most part... *cough*
*cough*
This Hitman(tm), or Hitman 2016 or... Dammit, Googling it is going to be so much fun!
Anyways, Hitman. A chance at a reboot, after the 180° turn of the
Absolution (we all have our opinion here).
A chance to bring the series back to it's former glory, a reference, or THE reference of Stealth games, hell a genre of it's own!
Hit or miss? As much as I would like to give this one the benefit of the doubt (it is after all highly unfinished), I simply can't.
Fact of the matter is, this is sold not as an "Early Access title", but rather as an "Episodic game". Make no mistake, this nomenclature is nothing but a fancy new way of saying "Early Access", a pretext to advertize a game as "complete, with a twist".
Having to wait for each episode does not bother me, no. It is weird, but acceptable. No, what bothers me is how it is sold with no mention of it being unpolished and unfinished. It really feels like playing a Beta?!
Frequent disconnects (because yes, you have to log in...), mild bugs, not so good performance, a feeling of general lack of polish...
And this, is but the tip of the iceberg.
My main gripe: Where Blood Money allowed you to explore all possible outcomes, this one feels like nothing more but an on-demand murder gallery.
Press F1, out comes your menu. From here, you have access to anything and everything a map has to offer. Available assassinations, opportunities, discoveries, you name it...
After that, all you have to do is pick up item
, or speak to NPC
to trigger event
, where
inevitably happens. Super, scripted.
Obviously, it is the player's choice to disregard this entirely or go with it, but you'll have to admit it's hard to resist the urge. Locking that info up, encouraging you to unlock it would've probably been smarter.
Last but not least, a general lack of new features.
While the game is FAR better than the previous title, it fails to provide much appreciated innovations, things to spice up and improve the experience, and not make it just an "HD Hitman".
One example: Hidden and Dangerous 2. Now this game is some 13 years old, a real gem (you should definitely try it out if you get the chance). Such an old game had an ingenious feature, shoot an enemy, and their uniform is rendered unusable. No, if you wish to suit up, you have to somehow incapacitate the nazis...
This small, yet so great detail makes all the difference.
Yet Hitman clings to the past, hoping to extract more of that ol' nostalgia juice. Sure, we do crave for some nostalgia, but with a 2016 taste, if you please.
All in all, I sincerely hope this review will become nothing more but a snapshot of how the game was on this date.
There is room for improvement, I will not deny that there is ongoing progress, but I can in no way recommend the purchase of this not even half-finished game.

If you liked Baldur's Gate, BG2, Planescape: Torment, Fallout 1,2 or Tyranny then you will most likly enjoy this game, It is well written and nailbiting fun, however the combat system and Effort system can be a bit annoying in the start but as you level up and learn more about it, it will infact become quite fun.
One flaw in the combat however is the lack of delay turn, especially with aoe abilities that will harm your companions. But this flaw is the only one That bugged me.
Another flaw if you will is the lack of re-training your self and your companions so i suggest you focus on reading about the companions and what roles they are suited for and what Edge and pool points you should focus on.
My first playthrough had Ali, Mata and Rhin. I myself was a Nano.
Ali is easy he works as a close quarter fighter with some spells, making might pool and edge a priority and you wont go wrong, but since he isnt a Glaive his survivability comes from spells and health potion items. But I found him a more likable character than the other melee characters and this is why i kept him around.
Mata is another castoff, meaning if she dies in combat he gets back up without any lasting penalties, she is also a rogue with some spell abilities that are very nice. Focus on Speed pool and Edge and you will be fine. Her teleport and damage ability that uses speed is amazing since it only use a move action and places her easily behind opponents and can do untold damage by teleport followed by a weapon strike. Which is why Speed edge and pool is important, she will also aid you greatly with speed releated tasks due to this.
Rhin is perhaps the most overpowered companion you can have, but at the same time the weakest by far. She is only a child but her tier 3 ability is amazing and will at this point become a powerhouse of doom. Focusing on Intelligence pool and Edge in the start might crippel you a bit, but in the end game it will pay off. Mainly because her tier 3 ability has 3 uses per day at the cost of 4 intelligence points, the effect is that you do not use up a Cypher. She can also equip a lot of cyphers and this makes her insanly powerful, as a healer and a damage dealer depending on what cyphers you use, but since she is limited to 3 uses per day it is best saved for hard fights. For instance, you have a Cypher you find really early in the game that restores all might, speed and intelligence points you have called the Third man, using this item uses it up, but if rhin activates the ability first she can use it again and again, effectivly being a massive might, speed, intelligence potion that heals all party members near her. Other Cyphers include self ressurect with all pool points restored, aoe heals that heal for a lot and with the proper skills Rhin heals for quite a bit extra, but there are also Cyphers for dealing damage or crowd control and in short, she can infact cause untold damage this way, but only 3 times per day. To make up for her lack of overall health and combat ability a good shield and intelligence based weapon will be needed (or if you divide Speed and intelligence edge/pool evenly she can use dexterity weapon or intelligence weapons) Best to have her at ranged because of her low health points.
The story is very well written and with several endings and variations in the epilogue makes it a very replayable game, the main endings can be explored in a single playthrough however, similar to mass effect 3. Door no 1,2,3 (and 4,5,6 in this game)

The writers are focusing on world-building, yet they don’t seem to comprehend that no matter how intricate their imaginary world becomes, it will appear meaningless if the story is poorly executed. A setting-rich, nuanced, intriguing, and sometimes profound RPG that's more of an interactive codex than a video game proper. It's a mishmash of mostly unrelated stories interwoven with setting as the common thread, and most--or perhaps  exclusively--rewarding to the sort of gamer who is comfortable with experiencing those stories by proxy and through dialogue. There's choice, but you often lack freedom. There's exploration that involves little actual travel. The game knows what it is, but what it is isn't for everyone, and whether or not you'll enjoy it comes down to how inclined you are to meet it on its own terms.

Max Payne is a prime example of a game that actually shows the capabilities of the medium as a storytelling device. It has characters you care for, good (if a bit hammy) voice acting and an excellent presentation to boot. The story is tight and feels just like a noir flick. It's cheesy at times for sure but it's all tongue-in-cheek and tiptoes between this more silly tone and the genuinely gripping more serious parts that delve into the psyche of Max as a character.

The gameplay is also excellent with the, at the time very innovative, use of the bullet time mechanic. This doesn't make Max some sort of superhero but is rather an extension of the gunplay and will require careful planning as well as fast reflexes as you die from just a handful of bullets. It can be a tricky game at times but it always feels rewarding when you beat a particularly difficult section. However, the later parts of the game has a couple of cheap enemy placements which does bring down the end product a bit.

Despite this, Max Payne is one of the better third-person shooters I can think of and is overall a must-play.

Spec Ops The Line was an emotional experience with a mixture of realism and superb shooting and physics. After your first encounter in the beginning of the game you begin to question your motives and this game demonstrates the horror and cruelty of war. The cinematic scenes display the astounding quality Spec Ops possesses. The graphics and use of overall detail and color are expressed nicely also. The concept of war does appear overused but this game approaches it on a different perspective. Spec Ops has a great portion of emotional detail and sorrowful tone. You can reflect on every action you commited by the end, with the assistance of a great soundtrack and memorable plot twists. The shooting is enjoyable and you must rely on your surroundings and movement to survive. Throughout the storyline the gameplay becomes more stern, the intensity increases, the character development drastically changes and the missions become slightly more difficult. I'm certain that this will never be one of my favorite games but the way the gameplay expresses the emotional downfall of one individual provides enough reasoning to easily purchase it. I highly recommend this to anyone who enjoys a spiritual plot and pleasurable shooting. 7.9/10

This game has a lot of similarity to Just Cause 3 which makes sense because it’s by the same developer. The big focus of both games Is taking over this massive open world map. I think it’s a good game that I played in the background while doing side content just like I did with Just Cause 3, (listening to YouTube videos or podcasts and commentaries while playing) because if I didn’t the game would have ended being a very repetitive and tedious experience. It still is of course very repetitive but doing something else at the same time kind of helps you get through it much easier. In Just Cause 3 I felt compelled to take over every part of the map and do all the side missions, but in Mad Max after about a dozen hours of side missions and taking over the map I got sick of it and just started focusing on the main story. I think the problem is the side content doesn’t have the gameplay to back it up to make you keep doing it like Just Cause does. The gameplay in Just Cause 3 has a lot of variety with the weapons, vehicles, wingsuit, more open world freedom, variety in the visuals and the grappling hook but the gameplay overall in Mad Max is pretty basic with the dumbed down arkham combat and the decent but repetitive  car combat. Also just some of the objectives that you have to do to clean out an area of the map is very tedious like taking out snipers, scarecrows and minefields, it’s just not fun to do. Taking over camps also gets old after a while. So in my opinion the side content in Mad Max is a complete failure, but that leaves the main missions, story and characters. Even though it’s a very basic story just like the movies it works well, the first half is very slow with barely any plot progression but the effective climax makes up for it. I really like Max as a character, I think he is well represented in this game and the supporting cast of characters do their job just fine. I did have fun playing through the main missions and that was what made this worth playing. It was just annoying at times when you have to do some boring side content to keep progressing through the story. I did like this game more than Just Cause 3 because I did enjoy leveling up max and upgrading the car and I prefer main story over side content, the two games are opposite in that regard. Just Cause 3 has fun side content but boring and uninspired main missions while Mad Max has fun main missions and boring side content.

Early Access done right. One of very few examples of such a phenomenon. From the communications the devs had with the community through both written and video updates, to the constant patching of the game which added significant changes and additions at an incredibly effective pace.
Truly, this game deserves your attention even if you're not interested in its gameplay mechanics or ideas. Simply because we ought to support this kind of transparent, respectful and talented videogame development. We need to show the rest of the industry that hard work and good communication is in the end rewarded.
Oh yeah, and the game itself is of course really good. It's like a more complex and more free-form version of Theme Hospital, chock full of intentional and unintentional humor. It's virtually replayable ad infinitum due to the smart integration of really complex systems and mechanics that are still simple enough to get a basic grasp on quickly.
And then you add the solid Steam Workshop integration that's already been out for months and months, molding into a vast web of minor tweaks and major total convention mods to further extend your playtime. Like the mod that lets you take control of a prisoner, and use the game's own mechanics to try and break out of your own (or someone else's) prison! How genius is that?!
You could pay all the salary you're ever going to earn in your entire life, and you'd STILL be able to get a whole lot of bang for your buck with Prison Architect. And I'm not even sure if that's an exaggeration.

I kept having this nagging suspicion that the game should have been twice as long. The pacing of content was tedious at times. The first city had dozens of quests, and thats basically why the ending areas probably felt lackluster. Whole areas were created with minimal quests, and almost no interaction between your decisions and the order of completion.
This turned into a storyline where any single one of the quests could have been taken out, and you'd never of missed it.
Even the core storyline felt discombobulated, all the way up to the end. Sure it had a "loss of memory" trope attached to it, but you could very easily see where it was all heading, even if your character avatar couldn't.
In the end, the return of Isometric RPGs is a _great_ thing. This particularly isometric RPG, however, was not.
I'd recommend a Pillars of Eternity or Tyrant over this title, any day of the week. Thats a shame too. I really ended up loving the universe they'd created, even if you were given only tiny glimpses of it, with limited ability to interact with it. The concept of this universe would have been better suited with an open world experience, and not constrained by the likes of an Isometric RPG. Worse, it seems as if they've set this up for a sequel or "DLC" content, with little if any point, story-wise, to return to this game.
The big bad evil isn't a bad evil. The actual evil is dead.
Buy it if you like really like RPGs; But only if you already own Pillars of Eternity or Tyrant.

What's it in... Beta? Alpha?
It certainly isn't release, because stating so would be an insult to other actual releases...
The Hitman series, a way for many of us to get our fill of strategically planned and surgically performed assassinations, or of cold blooded mass murder once we got tired of the same old routine...
These games might not have been everyone's cup of tea (there's a genre for everyone), but their quality was undeniable. I'll spare you the retrospective, because that would be a waste of time: They were awesome, for the most part... *cough*
*cough*
This Hitman(tm), or Hitman 2016 or... Dammit, Googling it is going to be so much fun!
Anyways, Hitman. A chance at a reboot, after the 180° turn of the
Absolution (we all have our opinion here).
A chance to bring the series back to it's former glory, a reference, or THE reference of Stealth games, hell a genre of it's own!
Hit or miss? As much as I would like to give this one the benefit of the doubt (it is after all highly unfinished), I simply can't.
Fact of the matter is, this is sold not as an "Early Access title", but rather as an "Episodic game". Make no mistake, this nomenclature is nothing but a fancy new way of saying "Early Access", a pretext to advertize a game as "complete, with a twist".
Having to wait for each episode does not bother me, no. It is weird, but acceptable. No, what bothers me is how it is sold with no mention of it being unpolished and unfinished. It really feels like playing a Beta?!
Frequent disconnects (because yes, you have to log in...), mild bugs, not so good performance, a feeling of general lack of polish...
And this, is but the tip of the iceberg.
My main gripe: Where Blood Money allowed you to explore all possible outcomes, this one feels like nothing more but an on-demand murder gallery.
Press F1, out comes your menu. From here, you have access to anything and everything a map has to offer. Available assassinations, opportunities, discoveries, you name it...
After that, all you have to do is pick up item
, or speak to NPC
to trigger event
, where
inevitably happens. Super, scripted.
Obviously, it is the player's choice to disregard this entirely or go with it, but you'll have to admit it's hard to resist the urge. Locking that info up, encouraging you to unlock it would've probably been smarter.
Last but not least, a general lack of new features.
While the game is FAR better than the previous title, it fails to provide much appreciated innovations, things to spice up and improve the experience, and not make it just an "HD Hitman".
One example: Hidden and Dangerous 2. Now this game is some 13 years old, a real gem (you should definitely try it out if you get the chance). Such an old game had an ingenious feature, shoot an enemy, and their uniform is rendered unusable. No, if you wish to suit up, you have to somehow incapacitate the nazis...
This small, yet so great detail makes all the difference.
Yet Hitman clings to the past, hoping to extract more of that ol' nostalgia juice. Sure, we do crave for some nostalgia, but with a 2016 taste, if you please.
All in all, I sincerely hope this review will become nothing more but a snapshot of how the game was on this date.
There is room for improvement, I will not deny that there is ongoing progress, but I can in no way recommend the purchase of this not even half-finished game.

At first I was very cynical toward the casualisation of this game. It introduced new concepts to the stealth genre that would only serve to further handhold. Specifically the 'Opportunities'.
Instead of being diligent and eavesdropping on NPCs to see if you can pick up on hints to devise a plan, the game will HIGHLIGHT the conversations and then give you precise directions on how to do your mission based on those, which is a total kick in the teeth. Now, you CAN turn this highlighting off, but in a score-based game its a total pisstake, don't you think?
That aside, there is a lot to do in a mission zone. Episode 2 gave us Italy and, oh my gosh, this is a HUGE and detailed (if a bit static) level. HUUUUGE. And its all used! You have no reason to go to specific parts of the map, but if you do they're all lived in! Theres a hippie with a sea-shell decorated room. Theres a street performer, theres a cafe, theres an icecream shop, a beach with sunbathers. Heck, theres even a road leading out of town where a car accident just took place.
THIS is where the game excels, you have to admit that there is a certain giddiness when a game you play has high attention to detail. In the mission, you will often hear NPCs talk about one of the targets deceased mother, who was old and frail. Lo and behold, if you look around the house, it LOOKS like it once catered to a disabled woman: The stairs has a chair lift, her bathroom had disabled facilities, her bed has a bell, and its all decorated to show her tastes.
Infact, if you look around town, you'll see that not only can you go into almost every apartment room, but you can even tell who lives there! They will never go to their rooms during their scripted cycles, but you can deduce where they live based on their personalities and how the room matches it!
For goodness sake, theres even the room that Agent 47 most likely lived in just before embarking on the mission!!
My point being is that IF they were to simply reuse this map, it would be completely fine! Without changing any assets, they could move around NPCs, change the context, and it would make totally justified.
The joy of the completion-ism of the game is that the game will demand that you assassinate the target in certain ways, and you have to discover how exactly to do that. I do believe that they could afford to be more cryptic, like we know that you can use a cannibis joint because the game tells you. How cool would it be if a player randomly stumbled upon the joint, made a post on the forums about it, and then someone else found a use for it?
I do take issue with the escalation missions. Escalations are when you do a shorter mission, and then you do it again four more times with extra rules. Its an incredibly lame way to increase play time because for about 95% of these they dont change how you play the mission in anyway. I play a mission for 10 minutes killing the target, then hiding the body. And then in the next level it says "Okay, now this time, kill the target, and hide the body". DUDE I JUST DID THAT!!
What they should really do is give you the option to tackle the Level 5 mission from the get go, and if you do it then it auto-completes the previous four.

This is not a good game, actually.
This is a wannabe Settlers remix of german-style RTS mechanics with a few notable UI/UX choices and one relatively new naval trade mechanic. Given these ingridients one may mix a pretty good game for the fans of economic RTS with indirect control, but Dawn of Discovery fails to deliver anything but its shallowness of gameplay.
There are a few primary resources here, as you could expect from a decent german-style RTS. But the number of said resources is, well, as low as if you're playing your usual RTS: there are only about three or four of them. Secondary resources are, too, low in numbers, but what is worse - they're used in a very few combinations. All the resource chains are started and terminated almost immediately.
Buildings are not being built - they just appear.
Roads look like they've been added only to satisfy the economic-based strategy guidelines. You make roads only between a groups of buildings, but if you have a building cluster somewhere else - just forget it, you won't need a road to connect your clusters.
Economy in this game just works. As long as you have a basic buildings set, your economy will grow. After a while your peasants become citizen and will ask for more advanced products. You click a few times, build a few linen factories, and that's all - keep yourself busy with staring at sea or whatever until next time. The reason I am so frustrated with this is that it takes all the best from Settlers and turns it to a meaningless crap.
Your people don't even go anywhere - they just pointlessly roam in the living cluster doing nothing. All you have to do is to make their number grow to unlock new building chains. Compare this roaming to the Settlers - or as I am already full with Settlers' comparisons, compare it to Skylines, where every citizen walks somewhere because he has a reason: to work, to get resources, to home, to work again. Installing this game you think you'll have to maintain a complex logistic system, roads, passways - but no, you just point and click to make another building appear.
Finally, the supply chain clusters. See, if you have a building A which makes primary resource A, and you have a building B which uses resource A to produce secondary resource B, you obviously should consider a supply line between them. In case of Settlers you have a central hub, where resource A is put before taken to the B building, so you just maintain the lines between A, B and hub clean and unobstructed. In case of Factorio you build an effective supply line to bring the A resource, buffer it and feed to B building. What do you make in Anno? Nothing. You just put a piece of road around those buildings, and here you go. If the secondary resource B is, say, electricity, you don't even have to build a road to anywhere else. What? Electric poles? Nah, forget it, everyone knows electricity is magic.
That makes your supply chains look like clusters - you have a mine up in the hills, next thing on the road is your melting factory, and next thing is your tool makery building. All up in the hills, and no traffic except a worker mule which takes fresh made tools down to market.
Let's now talk about what's good in this game. I liked the naval trade mechanic: you can manually deliver your goods for trading with other islands and then, later, you can build ships, make trade routes for them and assign which goods are to be transferred and in which quantities. This is actually a cool idea for a strategy game - I've wanted this for Civs and for Settlers for a long time now. But in DoD (and Anno 2070) its just useless because there are no additional systems to support it. You just mark some surplus of your goods as "for sell", make a trading route and that's all. This system reminds me of a train mechanic in Factorio: goods, routes and vessels. But in Factorio you have to build a sustainable supply system to make this work, and here, in Anno, its just plug-n-play.
After all, I hope that these series someday will be a decent Settlers-inspired strategy to play, with its own smart design choices.

Dawn of Discovery is an Ubisoft game which of course comes with it's own set of problems, such as multiplayer locked behind verification servers that don't exist.  That said, the single player version of both this and the associated expansion have enough content to keep you playing for a while.  The idea of the game being multiplayer in the first place is somewhat just for kicks, as regardless of single or multiplayer, your goal will basically be to generate the largest economy in the shortest amount of time.
(While there is a military/navalcomponent, those components of the game are severely watered down compared to other titles.  The important thing is that you set up an economy chain good enough to just have more units, which are more or less identical to one another.)
The campaign itself is short and the meat of the game is entirely the randomized games, which you can add complexity to in a variety of ways.  With mods you can add a lot of extra content to the game (just look in the community section!)
Overall, It's an ubisoft game that works outside of multiplayer, and a great game in the resource management space alongside such contenders as Dwarf Fortress or a A game of Dwarves.

Star Wars – Jedi Knight: Jedi Academy is shares most of the traits of an early 2000s action/adventure game: Tough as nails at any difficulty (with higher level sith enemies easily able to one kit kill), Checkpoints few and far between (roughly 10 – 15 minutes of game-play apart, quick save bound to an easily accessible key recommended), and, nearly no hand holding through the levels (if you want to complete that level, you better be prepared to do a lot of  exploring). If anything, Jedi Academy is a fantastic bit of nostalgia and a throwback to when video games made you work if you wanted to win. The levels are fantastic in scale, some huge open areas that are more impressive than some levels in modern games. Single player is pretty much the only way to go at the moment as multiplayer is non-existent unless you can find 10+ players to lobby with. Single player usually lasts about 8 – 9 hours (7 if you try and run past some of the harder enemies as I did…). Jedi Academy is well worth the $10 (usually $2 when it’s on sale) and a solid 9/10.

Despite my hours on Steam, I've owned this game for years and years on disc. 10-12 years, at least. And I've played it throughout. At the time of this review I have about 8 hours on Steam? But on disc I have hundreds upon hundreds, if not thousands accumulated over the years.
I can say without a doubt that the Jedi Knight series is most likely the best entry into Star Wars video games there is. There is simply no other game that blends lightsaber and/or blaster combat with such immersive use of The Force so perfectly. They even have decent stories to go along with them! There's just so much at your disposal to use.
The variety of locations/planets you go to is fantastic, a large majority of them have, as far as I'm aware, never been seen in Star Wars media otherwise beyond literature, or perhaps some comics. They are very imaginative portrayals that remain true to the typical original trilogy style. Music puts the original trilogy's music to great use.
As I said, the story isn't half bad. The voice acting could be better for some characters, but it's not horrendous, just a little funny. Kyle Katarn, however, comes off just as well as he always has, and he features rather prominently in some areas, and is easily Jedi Knight's greatest character (given he was the protagonist for most of it.)
There's plenty of opportunity for blasters vs. blasters and lightsaber vs. blasters, and later in the game there is a -lot- of lightsaber vs. lightsaber combat, with a choice of a doublesaber, dual lightsabers or single saber proficiency being open to you eventually!
Modding? MB2. Very fun multiplayer total conversion mod. Somewhat like Counterstrike for Star Wars (I say somewhat, it's an incredibly reductionist comparison but it's the best I could do.) Plenty of other maps and mods for single and multiplayer, however. Including single player campaigns. Maps, skins and gameplay mods multiplayer are rife to suit all you can think of. Fun maps, environmental/immersion focused, even roleplaying maps. There's simply no end to the modding content available for this game.
TLDR; Best Star Wars gameplay since its release in 2003. If you want a better story, play KOTOR or SWTOR. Want a prettier game? Play The Force Unleashed. But Jedi Knight has always been excellent for gameplay and level design that's fun and intuitive. For a 2003 game, anyway. Amazing modability with a modding community that's still somewhat breathing.

Great game but not without issues.
- Not had issues with crashing until near the endgame. Mysteriously, game has suddenly began crashing randomly. Did not experience any crashes with the game up until this point. Before anyone comments about updating this and updating that, again... the game never crashed up until a couple of days ago. Had it been a driver update issue or Window's update issue then it would have appeared long before 100+ hours of gameplay.
- One of the reasons I have always disliked driving games is that the physics are completely unrealistic. One minute, the vehicle seems to drive and react as one would expect IRL but then suddenly you're unable to control the vehicle and it simply does what it wants. I'll be able to take a corner without issue and then I am spinning out of control after a similar maneuver elsewhere without any variation to the roadway.
-
Apparently the SURVEY CREW perk doesn't display all of the minefields... ended up that there were a couple of minefields not found/destroyed. Threats reduced to zero now. Quite the annoyance!!
- Another point of annoyance is that upon selecting a destination, the mapped route takes you to an area that disallows you access to the actual destination. One destination in particular is the area that allows you to transit from Gutgash's territory [Chalkies] into Pink Eye's territory [Wailing Wind] on the extreme Western section of the map. There is a steel barrier gate that is only able to be opened from Pink Eye's territory but selecting that destinations routes you to the Gutgash side of the gate. There are several other misguided map routings throughout the course of the game but I'll not list them all as I'm sure that others have found this out as well.
- As noted by others, the game does get a bit repetitive.
- Maxing out your legend comes way too soon in the game. I was able to do so by about mid-game. There should be more levels or it should take longer to do so.
- One of the biggest disappointments in the game is the lack of ability to modify all of the vehicles to your own desire. There are some pretty awesome vehicles in the game but they are made mostly useless by this fact. You can only use Chum Bucket's buggy with the dog but you are essentially weaponless other than the shotgun. As well, driving other vehicles lacks the ability to be repaired during use since Chum Bucket is only available in the Magnum Opus or the Archangels vehicles. On a side note, regarding the Magnum Opus, I find it that there seems to be no real performance difference to the functional characteristics of the vehicle upon obtaining/installing the V8... kind of sad.
Sadly, once the main storyline is completed, thus ends the game. There is nothing left to enjoy since there are essential no more adversaries to attack. No wanton destruction afterwards.
All in all, I still recommend the game and only really wish for a fix to the mysterious crashing issue. Other than the weird crashing issue, the game is quite fun to play. I was able to complete it nonetheless.

While this game is by no means a masterpiece, if you are tired of generic, unimpactful shooters that have all the depth of a poorly written soap opera, then you should, by all means, buy it.  It leaves a huge impact on you from the first few decisions you make.  After one section that I cannot elaborate upon because of massive spoilers, I became physically ill watching the fruits of my actions; I've played several shooters before, and this is one of the first that really made me think, "Wow...I really am a horrible person for doing this", even though that particular part of the game forces you do make that specific action.  It is a military shooter that is highly critical of the military and of war in general, which is quite the oddity in video games in general.  Unfortunately, the singleplayer and its message are undermined by the tacked-on multiplayer, which 2K apparently insisted on.  Don't blame Yager for this, however; 2K had another developer, Darkside Game Studios, make the multiplayer.  It was completely out of Yager's hands.  That said, I have not played it, so I cannot comment on the quality of the multiplayer.  Anyway...the story is, overall, quite good.  It suffers from a bit of the normal ridiculousness that many modern AAA games have in them, but aside from that, I don't remember any problems in the story.  The gunplay is smooth, or at least what I can remember of it.  I'm planning on replaying it in the near future, so I'll update this part of the review when I get to it.  It can be said, though, that ultimately, the gameplay doesn't matter that much, except for a few main points, like using the mortar while assaulting The Gate and making one of the many choices in the campaign.  The main draw of this game is the story, without a doubt.
If you try the demo before playing the full game, please note that it's incredibly misleading.  It does not show what the game is really about, and to be fair, it was intended to be that way.  It was most likely designed to lure in CoD and other typical shooter fans; it does not showcase even a bit of the game's true essence.
I never had any problems with crashes or bugs (except for getting physically stuck in a few areas and having to restart at checkpoints), and it runs quite well on my GTX 770 and i5-4670K.  I felt no need to remap the controls, but that will obviously vary depending on your preferred setup.  As I didn't have a 360 controller when I played this game, I cannot comment on the controller support.  The graphics, while not mindblowing, are quite good on the highest settings, and I do not recall encountering any framerate issues.  All in all, it is quite a good PC port, in my experience.
TL;DR: If you like singleplayer games with intense stories and want a new shooter experience that will leave you hating yourself and questioning your own morality, pick this game up.  It's not one you'll forget about anytime soon.

Dream Daddy: A Dad Dating Simulator is exactly what the title says it is.
You're a dad that can bang other dads, which is as ridiculous, hilarious and fun as you might expect. There are plenty of puns and dad jokes for the whole family to enjoy.
What there is not enough of, however, is story. 7 hours of game time for a visual novel might seem like a lot, but keep in mind how many routes there are. With 7 hours of game play, I have completed 4 good routes of the dads, and 1 bad dad route (aka the awful knife dad route where you sleep with him on the first night and proceed to waste your game thinking that's how you romance him).
The reason for this is because once you complete the story once, the replay value is not very high. After your first playthrough, you skip the entire story just to go on three semi-okay dates with the dad of your choice. Unless you want to be an absolute butt to your daughter and get her bad ending, there's nothing new in her story depending on what dad you prefer. I think it would have been nice if she was struggling to decide on what college she wanted to go to, as they all focused on various things, eg. sport, art, science etc. and as her father we could encourage her to do one or the other and then see how her character developed from that.
Another problem is the art style. It is fantastic when it comes to the characters and the backgrounds. But let's be honest, your dad actually looks like he was ripped from Deviantart. I struggle to see why the character creator was drawn in such a less appealing way than the rest of the art. It's not like the creator is extensive - it's very limited.
Voice acting was also promised, which is a complete lie. Strange grunts and the out-of-context "dude!" every now and then doesn't count as voice acting. The game would have been better off without it.
All in all, it's a fun game. You'll play once for the main story, and then every other replay will be to just see what happens in the other dates. For all of the above faults, it's still enjoyable and I still recommend it, but I honestly would not recommend for $15.00. Try getting it as cheap as possible, as I've played better games for free. Would honestly recommend for $5.00.

I thought I'd like Heavy Bullets, because I like FPS and Roguelikes.
Sadly I don't.
The premise of the game, to have to pick up your bullets after firing them, seems novel until you realize that we've had this mechanic dozens of times with bows and arrows.
The real issue with the game is that deaths feel really cheap.
There are turrets that have a glowing box that you need to shoot to take them out and they fire fast projectiles at you as soon as they see you and they track you through walls. This means that you need to move at max speed to pinpoint the spot and then pre-shoot after peeking from a wall. The game does have quick movement, but there are snakes hidden in the brushes that bite you if you come close, so you shan't move fast. Conflicting signals.
After seeing a turret, it shoots at you within half a second, which means you'll lose HP even if you instantly shoot it.
Having snakes wait around 90° corners feels cheap (they rarely make a sound).
There's a "Repellent" item that supposedly repels snakes, but it just makes them more aggressive.
You start with 3 grenades and besides the bullets, it's the only item that doesn't occupy "the" item slot, so you'd assume that they're a core part of the game. Most of the game plays quickly, but the grenades fly slowly and the throw distance is abysmal (am I playing a T-Rex?).
Most items use up that one item slot so you end up leaving lots of items behind.
Technically the game has no excuse why it doesn't run at a constant 120fps. There's hardly any geometry to render.
Bullets and coins on the floor make sounds and jump around, which makes it easy to pinpoint them and is useful early on, but it becomes a nuisance later when there are dozens of coins on the ground, which mask enemies in their noise.
The environment has no variety at all, which makes backtracking to a vending machine very confusing, as you can easily get lost in the repetitive rooms.
There are banks where you can drop off your gold so that you can use it in a future run. It feels like they're excusing the unfair difficulty by giving you a way to grind currency.

I love this game.  I LOVE this game.  It's a first-person shooter, if you're into that sort of thing, with a semi permi-death thing going on.  It's rogue-like, and it has some gnarly colors (a good thing).  The soundtrack is sparse and electric, but pumping at times, which is surprisingly effective--it's quiet at times, but then it rolls up from the background almost like it knows things are going to get rough.
The enemies are a mix of almost trivially easy and ridiculously hard, though you won't see the hard ones for a handful of levels.  Everything except the bosses dies with one hit, which is good, but you're still going to have trouble, especially when confronted by groups, or when you have to hit a weak point.
You're forced to rely on items and upgrades, which is a pretty neat system, except that you'll lose them if you die, in all but a handful of circumstances; that could be a dealbreaker for some, and a challenge for others.  To say more would be giving away too much.
If I had to find flaws with the game, there are two big ones:
- It gets annoying pretty quick when you die over and over on the same boss, which can be hard enough to the point where your beating it is largely luck.  Should you actually beat it, and die later, you're stuck starting from the very beginning.  It's a near rage-quit.  In the same vein, sometimes your items will save from one game to the next (the result of an item), but sometimes they won't, despite having that item.
- The bigger problem for me is the frame drops.  It's not a terribly demanding game, and I have a decent system, yet, whenever I play (and I always have Steam's frame rate counter running), there are multiple times where the game will drop from 60 FPS (you can change this in the settings) to ~52 or 53 FPS.  It seems slight, but when you're playing a twitchy game like this, and the frame drop causes you to get snagged by an enemy, (and it happens ALL THE TIME, enemy on the screen or not), it's enough to really♥♥♥♥♥♥you off.  I've tried all the different permutations in the settings:  FPS caps on/off, shadows/vsync on/off, FXAA on/off...you name it, I've messed with it.  No change.  It's always just enough of a drop to screw you.
All in all, I give it a 7.5/10.  Worth the price, absolutely.  Fix the frame drops, and I'd give it a 9/10.

Heavy Bullets is a Rogue-Like FPS where you have one objective: Get to the end of the security mainframe to stop machines and creatures from killing the clients of your company, and yourself.
It's a very simple game. You are armed only with a Revolver, and you need to survive the 8 levels of the hunting grounds where various creatures and machines lie about to kill you. Your revolver can kill everything in one hit, and is 100% dead accurate. There's no bullet time travel, it instantly hits whatever you point at. You only have 6 bullets though, so you need to pick your bullet back up, and reload it back into your gun (Which is also instant with a press of the R key.)  Enemies will stop at nothing to chase you once they have you in your line of sight, but they drop coins which you can use to buy various items.
Many items and stations exist to help you along the way. Lots of items are hidden throughout the floors, or locked away in doors that require keycards (Which you get from killing certain enemies), so you should do some searching around the area, you might find something good. You have items that bring up passive effects such as taking one hit without losing health, resistance to explosions, or a backpack for additional storage; or they can be weapon items such as mega bombs, mines, or rockets. Other items are handy tools. Speaking of storage, you can only hold one item at a time, so you need to make your choices carefully when you have to pick from 2 or more items, unless you have the backpack, then you can hold two items.
There are 3 stations: Banks are the most important ones. You can store your earned money into the bank for future use when you die, you can also store items in the bank for another run. You can withdrawl money from whatever you stored, and you can buy a last will, or life insurance which'll transfer a percentage of your money on-hand to the bank when you die. There is also the Medbay station for healing items, and Bullets (And Stuff) for weapons and other weird little items.
This game is permadeath, so if you die, you're sent all the way back to the beginning, but there is the Bank station to help you out on your next run. It kinda brings a thought of "should I store money in here now for better runs next time, or                    withdrawl some money from my current bank so I can have more help on this run?" Same thing does for storing items, too. It's a bit of decision making when you think about it, so be smart about what you do.
It's not an easy game, either. Everything (Besides immobile turrets) charge directly at you, and aren't afraid to get in your face. You need to make your shots carefully because you only have so many bullets before you have to reload, so accuracy is a must for surviving large encounters. That means don't freak out; keep a cool head. Making it all the way to level 8 and beating the boss will be quite the challenge.
Overall, Heavy Bullets is a pretty unique rogue-like with it's fast paced nature of your insta-kill revolver, the metroidvania vibes of searching for items, and the strategic thinking of the bank and what items to bring with you. I think you'll find quite a bit of enjoyment out of it, and it's cheap too. It's something to try out sometime.

Back in June 2014 is when I first purchased and devoted my life to the legacy version known as Rust (Alpha).
I may not have as many hours as some others who have posted here, but let me tell you why.
I loved the Legacy version of this game, it ran fine on my old 'gaming laptop' with 8gb of ram and a 720m, fine, with 60fps most of the time and little to NO drops at all.
When Legacy stopped being updated and they moved to the 'new and improved' version of rust, I was sceptical but optimistic. Turns out the newer version of rust didn't run on my old reliable laptop, and so I stopped playing for a few months until it was better optimized. Skip forward 3-4 months, and it still didn't run above 30(ish) fps.
I then played it again for a few days, just to get a feel for the new version, and when I found my lack of fps a struggle when fighting, I opted to quit rust until I had a better computer.
Skip another 2-3 months, and I had just finished a custom computer with a gtx 770, i5-4690k, and 16gb ram.
Beauty, I thought, I'll be able to run rust easy with this, and they'll have optimized it more in the time I've been gone!
Wrong.
Even my new computer struggled to run rust at a steady framerate. I tweaked the settings and barely managed to get my fps to hover around 60. Which was fine, I put a fair few hours into rust during this period, was active on mainly one server, and actively waited for wipe day and updates like a kid on Christmas.
But it seemed with every new feature implemented, the devs drew further away from optimizing their game.
And although there was always talk about performance increases and fixes in devblogs, I never saw an immediate improvement in the game's performance, a game that has been in early access for over 3 years and has seen no 'massive' improvements in optimization. Which is one of the core features that simply turns me off rust everytime I try to get back into it.
Which is why I cannot recommend this game.
EVen now with a GTX 1070, there is constant stuttering during gunfights, massive lag spikes for no reason at all, and random drops that make it nearly impossible to play this game sometimes. And I just cannot understand why they insist on adding paid cosmetics into a game, that has barely had any massive performance enhances since it's change to the new version.
I have not played rust for a long time, and I doubt I will until some sort of progression is added, and stability gets a major overhaul. Unfortunately that's just how it is with early access games, but I look forward to playing rust when it is optimized, and I feel the same excitement I felt during Legacy.
I miss legacy :')

Old school gamers who loved classic 90's RPG games such as Baulder's Gate, Icewind Dale, and of course Planescape:Torment will love what this game has to offer.  Rich and immersive story telling that forces you to slow down and take your time to read the dialog and put things together to figure out the optimal solution to quest lines.
The game lets you tread a path that mostly stays clear of combat situations if you desire allowing you take an intelligent approach over fighting.  Killing NPC's doesn't net you XP so your focus can remain on character and story, yet even if you choose a more brutish approach over compassion or intelligence you will find an interesting and fulfilling game to play.
If a good game is a series of interesting choices than Torment is exactly that, a series of interesting choices leading to interesting consequences.  Despite its relatively short 35 hour play time its rich, compelling, and satisfying to play.

Overall I am very disapointed in the game.
I haven't been able to even finish the game, because of a game breaking bug, where my all of my save files load with the game zoomed in and you are unable to move the character.  This happened twice.  I restarted after the first time, but not the second.
There was a massive amount of content that was paid for by kickstarter backers (which I was one of) that was cut from the game.
The combat is mediocre.  The overall story and world are interesting, but the actual dialog seems lackluster.  The setting/background/visuals are amazing.  The music is well done and is enjoyable.  The character models and animations not so much.  The voice acting is terrible and seems random when it comes in.  Important characters you'd think would have their dialog voiced only sometimes have one line.
I do not recommend this game.  It has tons of bugs, a lot of them that break the game, making it unplayable.  Tons of cut content, mediocre gameplay, and lack luster dialog, along with a $45 price, make this game not worth buying.  If the developers fix the terrible bugs and the game goes on sale for a third of the price, then it might be okay to pick up.

So - another game from the anointed messiahs of old-school CRPG development, and this one is supposedly the 'spiritual sequel' to the hallowed
, no less!
On its own merits,
is good game. I backed it on Kickstarter at the lowest level (which was about £10-£15 if I remember right), and for that price I got great value for money and lots of enjoyment. I think I would wait for a sale rather than pay the release price though.
The world is a weird and wonderful one, with lots of nooks and crannies to investigate, colourful characters to meet, and bizarre hightech powers and weapons to wield. Most of the inhabitants of the city of Sagus (where most of the game takes place) are ignorant of the technology behind all this, so all the fancypants electro-swords and brain-cooking zapper pistols are often seen as magic. The result is a pleasing steampunk scifi sort of vibe.
Combat is unfortunately a rather dull, clunky, turn-based affair - but thankfully as I broke from my usual habit of playing a tanky sword and shield guy and went for a silver-tongued brainiac nano (the game's wizardish class) I often found that fights could be ended early (or more often avoided completely) thanks to my gifts of the gab. This also made my psychic powers stronger so the occasional fight I did get into wasn't too hard with some help.
Companions are an amusing and varied mix of archetypes, if a bit shallow,
with good flavour voice acting on a small amount of their and other NPCs' conversations, which add a little richness to what is otherwise large amounts of silent text. Lots of reading to do in this game which I enjoyed - descriptions and speech are well-written but brief enough so as not to interfere with moving things along.
Graphics are decent enough and quite pretty in places, although characters' faces do tend to look a bit like clothes mannequins.
Overall the story and setting were engrossing enough to have me playing enthusiastically until the credits rolled.
This game isn't being judged entirely on its own merits. Instead of just being called
, this game is called
. And that's the main reason lots of nostalgic people like me funded this game (and a real can of worms).
What struck me most about the original was the main character - the Nameless One. Gravel voice, scars and tattoos, ghoulish looks. He begins as a fairly cliched amnesiac

I get that in Numenera the Last Castoff is intentionally a blank slate so that the choices players make shapes his character, but what was so clever about Planescape was that the Nameless one could be a fully rounded prewritten character by the end of the game, whilst still being shaped by the player's choices. And these choices still made sense within the larger context of the Nameless' character
The Castoff on the other hand, is a non-character. Voice acting has a generic hero sound, and he has no experiences because he was literally someone else just before the game begins.
The supporting cast of NPCs in Planescape was likewise so much more memorable than Numenera. Morte, Annah, Fall-from-Grace, Dak'kon, Ignus. That weird cube-man who had Homer Simpson's voice. The Lady of Pain, Deionarra, the Night Hag, the Silent King. That hive-mind of super-intelligent rats! I haven't played that game in years and I can still remember them all. I think the only character I will remember in any detail from Numenera is Rhin. Plus perhaps the Changing God only for his name, and the BigBad Sorrow
Planescape had a grimy, grim, at times nightmarish atmosphere. Numenera approaches this later in the game
, but never manages to reach those heights before or after.
"What can change the nature of a man?" - the thought-provoking question and motif that appears throughout the game and is relevant to so many of its facets, and to its main character in so many ways. There is no simple answer to it.
Numenera's limp counterpart is "What does one life matter?" - the answer being "it matters loads, because you are the Chosen One who must defeat the Big Bad."
