It's not very good.
This has been one of the most anticipated Kickstarter games of all time, what with it's prestigious legacy, and it falls short.
To be brief and fair, I'll not compare it to it's spiritual predecessor overmuch, and will instead judge it on it's own merits as it's own game.
Torment: Tides of Numenera feels like a game that was in the oven for so long that it was held in stasis, while an entire generation of new, great cRPGs (the Divinities, Tyranny, Pillars of Eternity...) came and went. It's been in developement for four years, and yet it still feels like a rough draft that pales in comparison to what other luminaries of the genre accomplished with less.  It's on the short side for a cRPG, but I'll not hold it against Torment: I rather like shorter cRPGs, as Tyranny showed.
The biggest problem I have with this game is how rough the interface and controls are. Movement is somewhat floaty and imprecise, interactable objects and characters can be tricky to click on, character icons can overlap and block environmental interactables, there is no fast movement/exploration option, the UI feels slow and clunky to resolve... It lacks polish is most every regard.
One of the best ways to explain that lack of polish is in the sound design. There are many effects in the game without any accompanying sound effect, making for a weird feeling of incompleteness. The sound desgin that there -is- is actually quite bad, with many zones being hampered by repetitive, grating, loud and annoying sound effects. Coupled with the lackluster and sporadic voice-acting, after a while I just started playing without sound.
Many people have complained that there is very little combat - and they're right. I can't remember participating in much more than a dozen combat encounters overall, but I won't chalk that up as a negative. One of the few innovations Torment brings to the table is the introduction of the Crisis System, a sort of turn-based gameplay that is mostly used for combat, but also for some interesting non-combat interactions, even in the -midst- of combat. Through the Crisis Sistem, you can interact with objects and other people even while in combat, which makes for an interesting, if not very refined experience.
I had no problems at all with the very low number of combats throughout the game, especially because combat itself is not very enjoyable, what with that cardinal sin of 3D RPGs - slow and clunky animations.
Torment utilizes Monte Cook's Numenera System and scenario. This is an entirely subjective point on my part, but I have never enjoyed Numenera, and this game has not changed my opinion. The mechanics of it are quite weird, and they exacerbate the particular mania of many a player.
Specifically, especially in the lower levels (or 'Tiers'), you have to burn your attribute points in order to increase your chance to succeed at any particular task. Early on in game, you fail at most everything, missing all your attacks (I had a pitiable performance in the very first combat encounter in the game whereupon I missed all of my attacks for so many turns that combat ended, the boss literally taking pity on me and leaving) and must trade even your slightest chances to succeed later to have an ever slighter chance to succeed now. This curves rather awkardly - later on in the game once you've stacked enough Stats Pools and Edge, you steamroll through any and every test and check. There is not happy middle ground. In the end, it's pointless, because you can just savescum to succeed in most every check - and I'd argue that this system encourages you to.
In addition, there are Cyphers, which are items that produce powerful, reliable effects - but are consumable, each Cypher having only one use, with very few exceptions.
Having to burn your own Stat Pools to have a bigger chance to succeed, and almost all your powerful attacks being one-offs, feeds into that particular gamer paranoia of not wanting to use up your limited items or resources for the fear of needing them later. I know I'm not alone in this, and I finished the game whilst hardly using any Cyphers at all or burning Stat Pools beyond my Edge.
Finally, there's the Numenera world itself - the Ninth World to be exact. It's a literal mishmash of random sci-fi and fantasy elements from dozens of different sources, what with the debris from different worlds and realities piling up in a giant junkyard reality, with nobody knowing anything about how anything works and just cobbling everything together from alien junk. The aesthetic is all over the place, from wooden shields to pilot jackets to H.R. Geiger walls to future guns. There is no consistent design, everything seems equally plausible, there are no real rules. It's hard to be invested in such a scatterbrained world.
The story is- fine. Functional. The companions aren't bad, but they feel like holdovers from the Planescape Torment era. Nowadays we're used to much better written and relatable companions, from Obsidian to Bioware. It's just not good enough for the present age.
In short, Torment: Tides of Numenera is a middling cRPG at best, unworthy of your hype, or your money. Avoid it unless on sale.

Summary: If the concept of the game draws you, you'l almost certainly enjoy it. If it doesnt, stay far and far away! Torment is a great game that is absolutely not for everyone.
Pros:
- One of the best stories and writing I've ever seen.
- Plays with new ideas and concepts all the time.
- A game where violence is rarely ever the only option.
- When it happens, combat is very challenging.
Cons:
- A very short game for it's genre with very few zones. Only 3 main zones and 1 "mini-zone".
- Companions seem interesting, but have very little to offer or say except one.
- Character creation is non-existant, you can decide the gender and that's it.
Review: Torment is, for me, an amazing game, one of the best I've played this year that absolutely blew my mind away. If you like the setting and like long reams of well-written dialogue, this game is absolutely for you. But if you are looking for a more traditional RPG, it is absolutely not, because Torment is *not* that kind of game.
The game's zones are very rich and fleshed out (sometimes literally). Every NPC has a story to tell and each and every one is worth listening to and fascinating reading. The story is rich and will keep you interested all throughout. Even when the main quest falls into obscurity, the sidequests make up for it, and then some. There are always multiple ways to resolve a quest, and the game's writing and the situations it thrusts you in can leave you on the verge of tears sometimes. I know it did for me.
I was disappointed by the lack of zones - Why only 3? And the game's length was very short. By the time you finished the story many things are left unanswered.
As always, the lack of possible romance options is a pity. For games that put so much emphasis on the player's ability to choose, it's oddly restrictive in this manner. I can sell a young girl to a slave trader, but I can't choose to kiss someone I like?
There's not much more to say. Cons aside, if you read some reviews and read the concept and feel it's for you, it probably is!
On the other hand, if you're a little put off by the game's unusual theme and design, it probably isn't.
This is one of those games where you can go with your gut.

PS:T was the game I used as proof to skeptics for years that video games can be literature. That, if someone wanted to, they could make a game with the same level of depth and nuance as well-crafted novel.  This is what I was hoping to find in T:ToN. Short version: If you came for an interactive novel with interspersed RPG elements that plays like a Baldur's Gate-era CRPG, you'll like this. If you wanted something more...fighty, wait for Pillars of Eternity II.
It's fairly important to my opinion of this game that I didn't particularly care about things that, in many other games, I would. Specfically, balanced combat, interesting character / gear progresion (in a combat sense). The damage types were opaque and if there was a way to find out which damage types worked better against which enemies, I never found it. If you're avoiding combat you'll rarely fight enemies of the same type more than once, so trial-and-error isn't a good approach. Inventory system is annoying, made worse by me being something of a hoarder. It would have been helped substantially by having either sorting options or, at least, more than a couple rows visible at a time. Plus, remembering to take everything from each of your companions before dismissing them was a needless irritant. So, from a mechanical standpoint, this was a decent, although very flawed, game.
But none of that was why I was here. I was here for the interactive novel, in a well-crafted world that unraveled as you played it. It wasn't PT:T, and for me I don't think anything could be. But they *tried* to make it that, and very, very few have even made the attempt. The writing, overall, is solid, although I found it somewhat more disjointed than PT:T was in terms of sidequests and how they fit into what was happening around them. Some of them just sort of felt plopped into the world, even though in isolation they were, on the whole, well-crafted and interesting.
I found the companions, on the whole, the weakest point of what I hoped to see in the game. They're less interesting than their PT:T counterparts and generally less compelling, although I'll need to devote some time to thinking about it to determine exactly why that is. Rhin was hands-down the most interesting (even outside of the interesting gameplay options of having combat with a character who simply couldn't fight), Tibyr and Erritis were somewhat interesting, but the rest...eh. And when compared to Morte, Annah, and Dak'kon they're just...flat.Most importantly, you have far fewer opportunities for conflict and progression with most of them. Maybe this is just memory but it felt like a much longer journey to getting Dak'kon to not hate you, or to wheadle the truth out of Morte. Here, you'll hit one or two places / events critical to that character, talk to them, do one quest, done. They have less to say and feel less part of the world than did their PT:T counterparts.
I'll need to play it again to know whether this is an illusion or the truth, but it definitely felt like I had some choices that would affect events down the line. I'm curious how different the game would be if you can't persuade anyone of anything and just bash your way through problems. I'll have to try it before I can say if there's any substantive narrative variation, something very few games (I'm looking at you, Dragon Age II) do well.
The story isn't as compelling, the voice acting isn't of the same quality, The Changing God and the Sorrow have *nothing* on Ravel or the Trancsendant One, but even for all that, it's worth playing, and even good. Saying it's not quite up to what is, to my mind, one of the best CRPGs ever made, but that it's a solid imitation, is actually fairly high praise. It's not quite as good as I hoped it would be, but it was a taste of a type of game no one's *really* attempted since. If you loved PT:T for the same reasons I did, you'll probably like this. It won't make you love it the same way, but you'll enjoy it.

I would like to recommend this game, but in its current state I simply can't.
I've played it thoroughly. I really tried to like it. But given the amount of time and money inXile had for the development it leaves me with mixed feelings.
I'll revise this review over time as gain more insight.
What follows are not 100% dispassionate observations, but mostly my personal opinions.
What I liked in the end:
+ Choices, many different choices: Morally difficult choices. Even though some of the choices you make might be just an illusion of freedom since the outcome will be the same, you still choose your own path.
+ Character with unique abilities.
+ Very good overall writing: Solid story. The plot... see below.
+ Soundtrack: It's varied. It contains Armenian duduk piece (which I personally like).
+ Stable game: At least in my case I have had only a single crash in over 70 hours of playing. The experiences of other players may differ.
Here what I didn't like:
- Annoying bugs: The game doesn't accept certain or all inputs after an loading screen and so forth. On my first play-through, close to the end of the game, the loading screen got stuck at 49% when I tried to enter one of the fathoms where my party members were trapped. I had to reload older savegames and tried many variations of entering and leaving zones until being able to get through to the Oasis Fathom.
- The general plot of the game is very derivative: If you played the original Planescape: Torment, you'll probably notice far too many parallels. You can smell the plot twists, if you want to call it that, from a mile a way due to blatant foreshadowing. Although the story and the writing itself isn't bad.
- The combat system is awkward: I'm not sure how the tabletop handles these things, but in the computerized version it simply lacks tactics. The concept of the combat is solid, but I feel the environments in which the combat happens could have been designed better in many cases. The developers should have taken a closer look at Divinity: Original Sin, a game that does excellent turn based combat (although with its own balance issues)
- Balancing: Nanos are way too strong compared to other classes. Especially when you go down a path where you avoid combat when possible, where you probably invest a lot into intellect and intellect edge, the Nano becomes far too devastating with its offensive spells in the few forced combat situations.
Especially when you have a nano heavy group, many of the cyphers become pretty much useless. Unless you have Rhin in your group, get her to tier 3 and make use of her Cypher Adept ability, which kind of turns here into a 2nd Callistege or Nano Last Castoff in destruction capabilities, it's often better to just sell most of them. For the money you get from selling your cyphers, you can buy plenty of 'sleep' in order to refill your pools and hitpoints.
If you're playing a Glaive of Jack they're more useful.
- Graphics can be crude: In many areas if you don't zoom out as far as possible game game is not a pretty sight. Although some areas have beautiful renderings.
Sure, graphics are not such an important factor for a game that lives off a textual narrative, but since the game insists on zooming in all the way every time you die and come back from the labyrinth or the first time you load a safe after you started the game, it's still another one of those (fixable) little annoyances.
Maybe in a couple of months, when things get patches and perhaps the community adds additional content (some of which was cut and original ones) I could recommend the game. But not like this.

TL:DR. BUY THIS. This is the North American release of Anno 1404, a much desired sequel to my favourite Anno 1503 (1503 AD here). It's a perfect economic, city-building, and progression simulator with series-specific quirks that make it unique and unimitable.
If you have ever been a fan of the old American release of Anno 1503 (it was called 1503 AD here), this is exactly what you might be craving. Released in Europe as Anno 1404, this title serves as a modest remake/sequel game that really replaces the old game (that's why I say remake). Everything here is exactly how you want a real Anno game to be.
The newer ones (2070 and 2205) cannot capture the true feeling Anno 1503 used to give me all the time, but this one? Well, I played a random game with easier opponents and swiftly lost almost all my money even though it said I had positive growth and change in finances. I was lost, confused, and wasted 4 straight hours of building on 4 islands simultaneously because each had a different resource I needed. Ultimately, my failure to understand the trading mechanics, the financial mechanics, the building mechanics, the war mechanics, and the general development progression of the game left me stranded and lost...
Well, same time tomorrow!
To be utterly fair, this might be one of the smartest games I have. I love games like Port Royale 2, where the whole point to to develop a strong economy, but I'm very big on conglomeration, or making it all myself. I believe the strategy is to make only what you have to and slowly trade for the rest, but my ten-year-old-at-heart-self continually sees the building and just makes it. I love games like this and will happily burn an afternoon sitting at my computer for it.
This was a much-needed treat because 1503 AD was one of my favourite games from my youth. If any of the comparisons I made or descriptions I give can assist you, then this was time worth spent writing this. Usually these contain a rant or a joke, but this is a geniune thank-you to the team that made these games. You all rocked my childhood, now, my adulthood can make more sense. Thank you.

Also known as Anno 1404, the game makes it's mark as an absolutely gorgeous city builder. A stunning entry in the genre.
This game is markedly different from the followers of Sim City. It focuses on the details and needs of a very class based populace as you grow and attract more and more wealthy and powerful individuals. The peasants are happy with just some fish and cider and a chapel, but a Noble has much more extensive needs like steak, fur, books, reading glasses, beer, jail, candles, and a church. The needs of the peasants and citizens are simple enough, but the desires of the patricians and nobles require an extensive amount of land and resources that you might not have. Which gets us to the second part of the game, trading.
The Annos takes place in Islands. The map is large, but you will quickly run out of land on your main island and will have to start looking to other islands to get new resources and expand your production. These resources are sent to a warehouse in that island, you will need to ship them if you want your population to use them. To help is a very easy to use strategic map which will let you build a trade route to pick up and deposit from locations. The trade routes will get sufficiently complex as you run out of land you have to keep track of more and more resources for more and more people. Additionally, you will have transform raw materials to usable consumables as well, so building a good layout is important.
All of this to achieve your final goal: to create a metropolis so that you can build a Cathedral or a Mosque.
There IS an army, but it's very abstracted out and really has a boardgame feel than anything. It's something that could defintely be improved, do not play the game if you are expecting/wanting battles.
The only thing that I am not sure about the game is that you are supposed to build two cities. But I only ever had the attention or care for one. If you are going to do it, I would highly recommend getting the Venice expansion so that one of you can build a Occidental city and other the Oriental. I have spent 40+ hours in the expansion, so don't let the number of hours played fool you.

Cautious lack of recommendation, I'm sure there's still content to discover, but so far I'm a bit disappointed by how thin this nevertheless very interesting FPS/rogue-like feels. It succeeds as far as atmosphere goes, especially on a sound design level. It's retro chip-tune design feels threatening in an almost abstract sense, with some hidden monsters in the grass only being given away by the little blip noises they make, though of course you also have sounds to signal uncollected items and jaunty tunes to tell you a kiosk to make purchases is nearby. It's a really terrific use of sound design to fill in the visual holes.
Gameplay wise, the hook is gripping. Instead of collecting masses of bullets like most FPS's, you have to make due with a limited number of bullets that can be recovered after battle, and only one kind of gun. You can also collect bombs, but run out of both and you're basically done for. The problem I have is that there's really only one strategy for each fight; run out, listen for enemies, run back, wait for them to follow you around a corner, dispatch them, then poke your head back out and deal with turrets carefully. It's possibly an inherent flaw with smushing rogue-likes and FPS's together, since the former is based on randomization and making due with what you have and the latter is much more dependent on strong level design. I feel a lot of those flaws could be compensated for with stronger RPG elements, but leveling up is so far not that involved. You can buy or acquire more bullets, upgrade health, purchases a backpack to carry more than just one item, and of course find items that make you run faster, heal, or give you a melee attack. But in a game called "Heavy Bullets" there's no way to upgrade your gun or your bullets. Certainly I'm sure a lot of this has to do with the game's creator being a single individual, but I wonder if scaling down to a top-down shooter or even just making it a survival arena shooter and focusing on the gunplay wouldn't have made for a better game.
In any case this is by no means a bad game, so give it a try yourself, and I'll keep chipping at it to see if there's more depth than is immediately apparent.

I typically don't write reviews for games but, in an economy where money is tight and purchases matter, I felt I needed to review this one.  Here's the summary: don't buy this game.
The storylines for most of the dads are lighthearted and cute.  It truly is a heartwarming game.  However, that's where the positivity ends.  The routes are short, only taking around four hours to complete if you do the whole game and around 1-2 if you only do the dates.  The content is lacking as you only get three dates with each dad and this is hardly enough to build a true connection with them.  It feels like the route ends just as you are falling in love with the dad.
Not only is story content lacking, the mechanics are abysmal.  There are bugs, unachievable endings, typos, continuity errors, and unplayable games.  The games are perhaps one of the worst parts.  One of the main advertisement points for this game were the minigames during certain routes.  However, in game, you are thrown into one with no instructions, no way to tell if you are playing the minigame correctly, and honestly come out of it with massive frustration.  For content coming from so-called game developers, the minigames aren't just irritating, they're a complete joke.
Perhaps it would be better, too, if the developers had acknowledged the game's several flaws and made statements about what the bugs are and how they're going to fix them.  Nope. Nothing.  The game devs haven't said a word about the magnanimous amount of issues with the game and frustrations of their customers.
So the low down is this... I can't and won't recommend this game.  It is almost laughable that the price is $15.  Maybe... MAYBE... if it were less than $5 I would recommend but my advice is to use your money to buy a better dating sim game.

Well that was a hell of a ride.
Just wish I hadn't had quite as much of it spoiled beforehand.
Pros:
The story.
Mechanics subtely reinforce the story. (Executing a downed enemy yields precious ammo and grenades.)
Decent challenge.
Cons:
Not good for people who can't read between the lines.
The controls are pretty wonky and tend to not work so well all the time. (I'm looking at you, vaulting and shooting over cover detection. And cover detection. And moving in cover without standing back up for no reason.)
Also controls: All popups show what buttons to hit for a controller, which really isn't helpful while playing with a mouse and keyboard.
Still controls: Sometimes the keyboard key for is isn't the same as the controller bound key. (B skips cutscenes. B is melee/vault. E is bound to melee/vault. Enter skips cutscenes. Wut?)
Controls again: Very different things are bound to the same key. (One key for sprint, take cover, jump off a ledge, and use a turret. Makes it easy to confuse the game with what you're trying to do.)
This game was very fun to play through, but it felt that the better I got at it, the more the clunky controls got in my way, leading to a number of deaths by standing up while trying to move in cover, melee attacking a wall I want to vault over, or clicking away to try to blindfire over cover when the game decides I can't blindfire from that spot.
But I got through it. I didn't come for airtight controls, I came for the story. And boy did it deliver. Though, the blow was softened considerably since I had been spoiled about just what the game was really trying to get at before I started.
Would definitely recommend this game to others, just don't read spoilers beforehand.

Hello everyone :D Throughout my years of playing many of the Hitman series, I have always become addicted by the vareity of strategies and playing fields in open world locations that Hitman known to offer me in the past. This one is especailly is a great imiprovement over previous generations of hitman games. Although HItman may not be perfect, the game developers did a great job in expanding the physical space of each mission, and giving us even more intereactions with our environment. Small improvements of course will be game graphic and fluid movement of our player character, but beyond that, the strategies and the locations are what makes Hitman really fun to play and replay as well.  For the first 2 locations in the game that i have played so far, as soon as i am placed into these missions esepcially for the first time, I become completely and happily lost from the immense freedom and chaos that I felt in these locations. The numerous interactions especially those intended to take down our taraget that we have in our environment are desgned with so much creativity andi imitation of life-like experience in the real world. For example, although there are only certain beverages that the targets will drink, so you can poison them, this hitman games has made it possible to poison almost every drink that we come across. We can pretty much flood any sink as a distraction as well. Although some interactions aren't necessarily useful. The options are always there to make the Hitman world very realistc to our everyday life. The reactions of NPC (Non-playable Characters) aren't perfect, but from my experience, I feel like I am being dropped into a real world as agent 47 and trying to blend in with the people around me as I commit a murder with a vareity of improvised weapon that are invisible to average people. With so much details and complexity in a reflelction of our everyday world, the game guides me through these opportunity that pops up with waypoints, which makes life a little easier in this huge open-world stealth game. This game just takes a lot of planning and patience to get through successfully, but it makes you engage mentally as I try to plan my assasination through and physically as my heart trembled and my eyes glanced quickly from one corner and person to the next one. The also cool thing about this game is that although it is not designed as a shooter game, you still have that option available with a variety of weapons at your disposal as you playthrough the game long enough. The only think that I could think of for improvements are just to improve interactions and environment just a little, but that's not a big deal for me because I say it is good enough already. Other than that, the Hitman team did a great job in their work !!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!:D

A very "Torment" experience. Combat is much better than in the original Planescape: Torment (where it was adapted from dungeo-crawling AD&D 2 and never felt right). Texts are plentiful. Locations are exotic.
The companions, probably, not as good as ones in PT, but then again, I only ever really like Morte and his jokes. The game is shorter than PT, but this might be actually good, because this kind of games wears you down a little with lack of diversity in activities (a lot of reading, and a bit of fighting).
All in all, this is a good game, probably deserving of "Best writing" award for 2017, though probably not "Game of the Year". It is also an experiment in moving the gameplay balance away from combat toward dialogues and other interactions with NPCs. As an experiment, it is not enirely successful, but not a complete failure either. It's an opposite or Action RPG, where there is so much combat that it tires you out quickly. Here, sometimes you wish for talking to stop and fighting to start.

I will commend this game on the premise and story. While not a particularly original plot, it is told well and at a good pace. This Batman is younger and more angry, and it was interesting seeing people react to him as a new figure in the city of Gotham. These things alone made the game worth playing. Even the item collecting seemed a bit more grounded, which made that more entertaining as well.
However, one is left with the sense that the game simply did not get enough playtesting, or not enough time to react to the results of playtesting. There are minor glitches here and there, but the most glaring oversight is in the combat.
Batman is no longer able to consistently interrupt his own attack animations. This most commonly manifests itself when trying to counter an attack that begins after you've already started attacking someone else. You'll find yourself getting hit a lot more. More difficulty is fine, but not allowing the player to respond to threats as they happen generally makes the combat feel unfair. This seemingly small change makes much of the gameplay less satisfying than in previous iterations, but is rendered moot about 2/3 into the game when you get a new upgrade that makes the combat fairly easy.
Batman Arkham Origins is not a bad game, but given its predecessors and its potential, it is a disappointing one.

I only have one problem with this game:
You know that one level in every RPG? The one where you enter the "dreamscape" or the extra-planar pocket, the memory realm or go "inside the computer?" That one level that's full of a bunch of random nonesense, with all kinds of crazy art, and literally every single NPC you meet says stuff like, "I'm the one who sees, but is unseen," or "this is the nexus of all places, where anything is possible, all futures exist... or is it? Maybe, maybe not. Is it reality? What is reality? If a tree falls in the forest..." You know, *that* chapter of the game that makes no sense but you can tell the developers thought they were being philosophical, edgy, and avant garde?
EVERY SINGLE PART OF THIS GAME IS *THAT* PART.
Every map is full of crazy nonsense. Every single character, from your companions and major antagonists to lowly shopkeepers and random street NPCs, is a red herring enigma rubik's cube that vomits a never-ending stream of sphinx riddles at you if you so much as introduce yourself. "I'm the last of the first, doomed to walk the ever-dream of the nightmare labyrinth for all eternity. Want to buy some weapons or armor?" The item descriptions go even further: "This thing is unlike anything you've ever seen. It defies classification. It's made from something you don't recognize and it does something wildly unpredictable. You have no idea what this is or what it's for. It's worth 120 space bucks."
All that being said, I'm recommending this game for every other part they got right. The art is amazing, the sound and voice acting are great, the game system is clever, and I never encountered a single bug.

Torment:ToN currently holds a score of 84 on Steam, which is why I'm writing this review.
That's far too low.
The reasons for this title to have a score lower than approx. 92 (which is about what I'd give it) are as follows:
Torment:ToN was not designed to appeal to mainstream gamers. It was Kickstarted by people for whom the original Planescape:Torment was one of the best gaming experiences they'd ever had. People buying it on Steam without having had experience with PC games from the 1990s are unlikely to get something they expect.
Torment:ToN won't be playable for people who don't read much, or who read slowly, or who need plenty of hand-holding to figure out what to do. It's true the game has a fantastic journal which notes new information for you and keeps track of what you're working on, but players who grew up with the flashing 'X' on their mini-map and an arrow pointing in the direction of the goal are likely to get overwhelmed.
Game critics have called the Crisis combat system poor -- I don't understand this, personally. I enjoy the combat system enough to want to see it return in other games. It's streamlined, sensible, and challenging when it should be.
Other critics have said the game should have been longer. I'm just out of the first area and I'm already planning my second playthrough. I expect to get many hours of gameplay out of Torment.
Note also that this game is not priced at triple-A cost. It's about forty dollars now and I've already got sixty hours of gameplay on it.
People say the character models are wonky. I don't understand what people want. I think the graphics are beautiful.
In my opinion, the majority of people giving Torment a thumbs-down *must* be the sorts of players for whom it was never intended: children, poor readers, gamers who don't like an intellectual challenge, gamers who depend on iMac-easy tutorials, gamers who need to be told exactly where to go...
I think this paints a pretty clear picture.
If you love great interactive fiction and the ability to twist your story 1,000 ways, stunningly creative settings, and truly inventive puzzles, this is a game you're going to like.
If you're really, really into first-person shooters, you should probably move along.
Bravo, InExile. This is easily your best work of art to date.
Last note: there are many scorching, damning reviews on T:ToN. Most (all that I've seen) are by players with as few as five or as many as thirty hours in. As I wrote, I have sixty hours and just left the first area. Subtracting a few hours for when I left it paused, let's assume I spent thirty-five hours on that beginning section. What this means is either I'm a terrible reader, or these negative reviewers aren't playing/reading much of the game. Often these bad reviews mention that the game is boring to them. Clearly, if you skim through a book, it's going to be boring. By all means, take bad reviews into account, but note the played hours, too. It's simply not possible to *get* Torment without putting in time.

The most difficult decision before writing this review is wether I would recommend it or not.
Not recommending it would probably gather me more votes but that's easy way out.
If you are considering buying this game and expecting a "traditional" rpg with character options, interesting combat and encounters like Baldur's Gate I&II, Neverwinter Nights, Divinity series or Dragon Age: Origin you'll probably be disappointed. You might be pleasantly surprised by the setting though.
It calls itself the spiritual successor of Planescape Torment, a beloved, text-heavy old rpg which is a lesser known but much loved game in the genre.
In nearly every conversation I've had with another gamer who said he liked rpg's I've probably said: “Yeah, that's cool, but have you ever played Planescape Torment?” If he/she said “yes offcourse!” and I was drunk I probably hugged him or her.
I should stop asking that question …
If you enjoyed Planescape Torment you've probably backed this game so this review is rather pointless but you like reading wall's of text, clicking a button afterwards and influencing the world around you so, be my guest, and keep on reading.
I honestly don't know. It might be if you like exploring locations, talking to npc's, reading item descriptions and diving, head-on, into a world you haven't seen before.
The one thing I can assure you that you have never played a game like this one before.
Wether that's a good or bad thing is up in the air though. Like everything in life, the game is a mixed bag. Sometimes it shines and sometimes it stinks. Currently (06/03/2017) the game still has several annoying bugs, combat is repetitive, cumbersome and will test your patience.
It delivers on the text heavy style of its spiritual predecessor but unfortunately the story, although well told, isn't as good. Where Planescape left the downtrodden path of most rpg's where you're the focal point of the world who has to save the town/country/the world/planes of existence/ reality itself from a certain evil and his macguffin. Planescape told a personal story of a man trying to find the bane of his own existence, Tides manages to rehash the standard rpg story from the get go.
You're a castoff, on the run from or towards, depending on your point of view, of a big evil who threatens you and every one of your kind and the key to all this is, you guessed it, a certain macguffin that you need to repair.
Thankfully the creators, for the most part, told this story in a interesting setting and  there are several memorable gems in the dialogues with npc's and companions
In a world without Planescape this game would have blown me away, in a world with Planescape it only rattled my cage. It was an interesting ride and if you, someday, want to play something that's more different then most rpg's then atleast put this game in your wish list.

The combat system (if you're lucky to see it) seems to be based on Pillars of Eternity, and slightly simplified. I understand combat is not the main attraction in any Torment game, but still something more could have been done.
On the positive side, combat events are originally named as "crisis" as you can have non-violent solutions to them. Also the characters are interesting, the world is original, if a bit dark and gloomy, and the usage of stats to solve issues is quite interesting as well.
I wouldn't recommend TToN it at full price and I wouldn't recommend it if you're expecting a RPG, but otherwise, it's a pleasant adventure game with some (very small) hints of RPG.
Edit: Somewhere halfway the game, a choice I picked while chatting with a NPC, killed me instantly. This is unacceptable on a RPG and barely acceptable on an adventure. The game has just too many bad design choices, so I'm changing the review to "Not Recommended"

Mad Max is around a 40 hour octane-fueled love letter to the film franchise.  It excels at the Mad Max elements - but not so much the video game ones.  I thought the films were alright, and so the game is alright.  If you don't care at all about the movies, the game probably isn't going to cut it for you unless you're a car guy in one sense or another.
The story begins with you fighting some warlord dirtbag named Scrotus (yes, it's a stupid name) in a cutscene, during which you lost your car and took a beating.  You stumble across a mechanically-inclined hunchback named Chumbucket who in his automotive-religious fervor is building a dream machine called the Magnum Opus, which he wants you to drive as his "Saint". However, Max isn't happy with a V6, and must overcome a series of tasks to acquire a V8 engine instead.
At least that's the initial plotline.  Yeah, no, not kidding.  There are a few characters thrown in at the last second that you're supposed to care about (Max does, somehow), but the game simply does not commit the necessary time for them to be effective.  Max confronts his inner demons via some mystical desert dweller every time he wants to upgrade his base attributes, resulting in interesting conversations.  There is a small selection of functional side quests that will help round out the experience.  Finally, Chum has many anecdotes about the places you will go and the people you will meet.  The whole experience is a little bare bones for a video game, but quintessentially Mad Max.
Something I do criticize the story for, though, is all of the end-game events are tied up by a single boss who, by that point of the game, you are absolutely kicking the sh*t out of.  But, you'll somehow get beaten, and thrown down a hole anyway, because plot device.  All of the ways the plot resolves itself afterwards hinge on this one fight that there was no way you'd lose, but you do anyway.  Bad form, Avalanche Studios.
The framework for this open-world game is that it's divided into multiple regions with four strongholds.  Each stronghold is a destitute, spiteful pit of human suffering until you start doing projects for them.  Things like water collectors, armories, scrap crews, and so forth.  Each one has a tangible benefit for Max as it will refill his ammo, health, or gas every time he visits, alongside other perks.  I should mention that building these projects negates a great deal of atmosphere about the game.  No more finding fuel, or bullets, or water, which should be one of the most immersive things about a post-apocalyptic game.  The sub-regions within a stronghold's territory are overrun with Scrotus-controlled facilities.  Eliminating them nets you routine shipments of scrap, and occasionally project parts.  Personally, I found this part of the game asinine.  If you murder every war boy in an oil refinery, wouldn't you want control of the pump?  Shouldn't there be some sort of resource system for that?  But no, every place you go you simply blow everything the f*ck up, after which allies move in and start dismantling the place (in theory) to send you your precious scrap.  Lazy.  I will say though that since most of the game is a fairly bland desert, they spent a LOT of time meticulously crafting every actual structure to make sure it's different from every other.  This effort was immediately noticed and appreciated, though more than once it was profoundly annoying not to have the ability to jump.
The stronghold leaders help the immersion, but aren't likeable at all.  It is essentially you that turns each stronghold from a hovel where people go to die into something like a proper tribal home.  These people owe you everything, and although you'll hear passing comments of gratitude, you don't get a god*amn thing for it.  If you yank down every scarecrow, build every project, kill every sniper, take over every camp, destroy every convoy, and clear every minefield to reduce a territory's threat to zero, you will will unlock car upgrades, and increase passive scrap income, but that's it.  Everything in the game is very heavily gated with mandatory busywork, and since you can fast travel, it's only worth it to build all the projects in one stronghold.  There was a stunning lack of a sense of reward about the game.
Scrap is everything.  Outside of achievement tokens to upgrade Max's base attributes, scrap is the currency for any and all upgrades.  There are many sources of this element of the game, and most of them are a waste of time.  Rare scrap pallets, the occasional passing scrap truck, and taking over camps are the only viable means for this resource.  The game even has the ability to gather scrap for you when you're not playing, as long as you have an internet connection.  How much you need will depend on the upgrades you're looking to unlock, but in the end if you're maxing out everything, you're going to need probably over 10,000.  Compare that to the average 5 scrap you get from blowing up a vehicle, and you'll quickly lose patience for the game's heavy padding.
So, what about the cars?  The car is the linchpin of the whole game, as it should be for this title.  There are at least five upgrades in ten categories for the Magnum, and the same in eight categories for Max himself.  Having said this, however, there was very little creativity spent on the upgrades themselves.  The looks will always change, but every upgrade to the right in any category is better than its predecessor, almost without exception.  It's just numbers.  You can scale back on some things to increase others, like defense vs. speed, but most categories present no reason to have anything but the best, which narrows down "optimal builds" far more than it should for a game that is essentially about car customization.  There are also 32 other vehicles to collect in the game, acquired by finding them and driving them to any stronghold, but although they have a great variety, you cannot alter any car except the Magnum.
Car combat ranges from slightly thrilling, to annoying as hell.  By the end you'll have a harpoon, explosive javelin, ramming bar, and side flamethrowers to get it done, each with their own upgrades.  Explosions are spectacular.  Quests where you must drive a vehicle other than the Magnum will generally give you a sh*t car that drives like a boat so you can get mobbed by enemies.  Later in the game, blowing up cars becomes a chore as they are heavily armored.  Something always works, and I give the game credit for making you vary your strategies, but as vehicles started to take longer to destroy, I found myself skipping combat as a nuisance with very little payoff.  Convoys regenerate, so if the target gets a little far, he'll get all his health back, and two escorts if they all died.  Regular enemies also patrol these routes and will join the bedlam.
Ground combat is meat and potatoes.  Max is a street brawler of the Arkham variety, and while the game's combat has a great sense of impact, it is at the same time limited and repetitive, outside of the laughable but fun wrestling moves he breaks out now and then during fury mode when he hits much harder and regenerates health for each kill.  The counter-system to the game is annoying, and half of the time you cannot cancel an animation to execute one.  This means a lot of cheap shots from the back while you're beating someone down.  Rolling out of the way, however, seems to be 100% guaranteed, but it breaks the combo.  Bosses or Top Dogs are almost all identical, and there aren't enough enemy types to make it interesting otherwise.  The only way the game attempts to scale the difficulty higher is to throw ever increasing numbers and ever bigger crowds of these dimwits at you.
Overall, the game is average - for a game.  I doubt there will ever be Mad Max 2 because in spite of minor gripes, this one had everything it was supposed to.

This game really is wonderful. It explores some of the intricate parts of being a homosexual man, being a father, being a guy, and the human condition. I also have to applaud the writing of this game. The script is really amazing for a game that is, ultimately, very simplistic in style and gameplay. The word "gay" is actually never used once anywhere. There are no outright mentions or even questions from any character at any time about your Dadsona's (or any other character's) sexuality. It takes place in a universe in which there is no taboo or political aspects of sexuality, which is actually very refreshing and makes the game that much smoother. Plus, the puns and overall humor and allusions to pop culture are excellent and in no way shoehorned into the game in a desperate attempt to make it more relatable.
Additionally, I have to commend the use of the player's daughter being ethnically ambiguous, but clearly not caucasian. Once again there is no troublesome questioning or mentions of why your daughter's skin may or may not match your own. This little detail also doesn't end up creating a plot hole, because the biological mother (should you choose your Dadsona to have had a heterosexual relationship originally) is shown being non-caucasian as well.
Now, as for some not-so-great aspects...the game certainly isn't perfect. My main qualm was with the way the universal scenes (scenes that appear no matter which path you choose for your Dadsona) connect to the datable dad-specific scenes. A lot of times there would be continuity errors that would make the following scene confusing or incorrect. One example: depending on your choice of path with the initial encounter with the character of Robert, your Dadsona may or may not have time to shower the next morning. Regardless of whether or not you've chosen the path in which the game describes your Dadsona having time to shower before running out of the house, the next scene has your Dadsona saying he feels kind of gross because he "didn't have time to shower or brush [his] teeth." Boom; continuity error that causes a discrepancy in the linking of the specific to the universal scenes.
Next, there are rampant spelling mistakes in the text. Even some of the best console games (Kingdom Hearts, for example) have the occasional mistake when the copyist entered the original script into the game's coding, but unfortunately Dream Daddy has more than a few. One of the "Dad Tips" on the loading screen has not only a missing word, but a formatting mistake in the sentence which creates a weird spacing gap between words. There are also several off-screen character names that are misspelled due to their infrequency, the most notable name being "Colin" who is mentioned in a universal scene at your daughter's school, but also several more times in Hugo's dad-specific scenes where it is sometimes spelled as "Collin."
Finally, the only other complaint I have with Dream Daddy is the mini-games that appear on the third date with your chosen Dream Daddy are completely bogus and have little to no instructions at all. A fishing game that follows the most basic formula of a match three style game doesn't even mention that you have to click and drag instead of just clicking on the fish to make matches. This lowers your overall score because the mini-game is timed. Next, the aggressive shift in art styles from one mini-game to another is just bizarre. The penguin mini-game, which also has no instructions at all, has sprites that look like clip art from Windows 95, and not in a purposeful ironic way. The radio mini-game is incredibly frustrating because all you get is a crude modeling of the inner workings of a transistor radio, a few wires, and a bunch of crap for comedic effect. The only instruction you get is "Fix that radio!" You've gotta just mess around and hope for the best. The clearly most frustrating mini-game is the piano game. There are no instructions other than to "Tickle those ivories!" and "Please sing along." I get that the game is supposed to be crappy on purpose because your Dadsona has no idea what he's doing, but there should be some hint that there's no real way to play the game instead of sitting there wondering what you're doing wrong. The Dream Daddy timeline that the piano game exists in is by far the most difficult to get the "good ending" on, so it gives the player the impression that they're making a mistake during the mini-game.
All in all, Dream Daddy is a super fun, hilarious, and heartfelt game that is simple to play and fun to progress through by figuring out what to say and do on the dates with these 7 Dads who are, in a phrase, way too damn sexy for illustrations. Each Dream Daddy follows a not-too-aggressive stereotype which ends up being flipped on its head in the most creative ways. There's some cursing and sexual content (no nudity, though) which make the game slightly edgy and more realistic, especially getting to see some of the Dads without their shirts, and without their original costumes shown on the title screen and during your initial meetings with them.
I absolutely recommend this game to anyone with that "contemporary" SNL-style sense of humor, gay or straight, regardless of gender. It's hilarious, wholesome, sexy, clever, and devastatingly heartfelt in all the right ways.

I'll start off by saying, This game gets -far- too much flak. Is it as good as City or Asylum? No. Is it a step down for the series? Yes. Is it a step back? No. It's not, but it's not a step forward either. The game is essentially Arkham City all over again, the same combat mechanics, and a few gadgets that can make things insanely simple. Notably, the Remote Claw, which allows you to hang thugs up from the rafters, at range.
Did it have a horribly glitchy release? Definitely. And there's no excuse for that, patches or not. The bugs should've been ironed out. I myself, was lucky enough to not encounter any on my first playthrough. The mechanics are much the same as City, though it's a common complaint that thugs can hit you, even if you're countering someone else. As I would politely put it, "Well... yeah?"
It's not a new thing. It happens in City. You try countering someone, and expecting it to stop the path of a giant hammer in City, see what happens. Takedowns are a different story in both games, but it leads me to my greatest issue with Origins. The Dark Knight System. As you play the game, you will be continually graded on your performace, complete with marks, and awarded EXP accordingly. However, the Dark Knight System seems to reward grandstanding more than efficentcy.
The Combat -is- somewhat harder, enemies are faster, and will corner you, and attempt to dogpile you with a flurry of hits, if you don't think tactically. Origins is the first Arkham Game where i've actively started using Gadgets in combat, from a few quick batarangs to a glue grenade or my standard Batclaw.
The new Batman voice seems.. fitting, though it's jarring to not have Conroy at the helm. This younger Batman is meant to be more aggressive, and he definitely sounds it. On the other end of the spectrum, Joker is -close- to hamill's voice, but it's different enough to seem -very- off. Joker always seems like he's rehearsed his lines, and while it's true for the voice actor, it's something Hamill never dealt with. Joker's voice and actions, always seemed to be completely in tune.
The boss battles are an improvement over City, a couple of them can be nightmarishly hard on Hard New Game +, for example, Copperhead. A common complaint is that the boss Deathstroke is too difficult. After careful examination of the fight, i've managed to deduce why people claim this. They're too busy looking for a Win button. Deathstroke is -insanely- simple, on any and every difficulty. I got the achievement for beating him without a scratch on Hard New Game +, and i'd of gotten it on hard, if I hadn't been having a conversation while I played.
The game is harder, slightly. The story however... for me, is a disappointment. It felt as though they were -afraid- to change anything up, and after a particular point in the game, to do with a bank, I was left annoyed at the story. The Deathstroke DLC is quite fun, Deathstroke himself handles well, and hits hard. It's fun to play, and makes me wish for a Deathstroke game.
This game isn't City, or Asylum. It's the worst of the franchise. But when a franchise is -this- good overall, even the least of it, is pretty damn good. If you beat City, and wished it was longer, or just wanted another story with the same general mechanics, this is for you. It's not big on innovation, but not all games need to be. We'll get that from Rocksteady. If you're not a fan, i'd either go back to Asylum and City, or wait for Rocksteady to release their next.

What is the definition of a blockbuster game? Well, some would say that either of the games from the Arkham series are exactly that. What Arkham Origins is, however...is not much different from what the other two games were. So much of the story was in the shadows until now, when Origins was made to be a prequel to the other two monumental games. What Arkham Origins isn't however…an overhyped or underwhelming game, in fact...it has much more content than what Arkham Asylum had. I personally always wanted to see what all happened before the first game, because there was quite a bit of backstory between Batman and the villains that lead up to the first game. Here is my experience and thoughts of Batman: Arkham Origins.
Gameplay: What some people complain about is that the game is more or less the same than Arkham City. This would seem like it is a little bit of a problem, but Arkham City is an amazing game. Having the same concept for the gameplay is more good than bad. Combat is what Arkham has always been, a beat-em-up system with combos similar to how Devil May Cry is. Every new mechanic added to the game, while not making it counterproductive to what the premise of the game or story is.
Sound: Everything seems to be up to par with using the old sounds, with all the new sounds being clean and precise. Not much has been changed or improved, but how can you improve on something that was already perfect? There were little problems with sound cutting out or not triggering, but it was more of with one cutscene that you will see whenever you use the fast travel points that are in the city.
Graphics: Arkham Origins is a demanding game, like how Asylum and City were when they came out. I am currently using a GTX 760, and it was running the temp close to 80 C yet still able to run on max at 60+ FPS in 1920x1080. What the game gives is a masterpiece molded together into a beautiful but dark game. PhysX is used to more of an effect than most other games with smaller objects like dollar bills, toilet paper thrown around and even steam that reacts to your movements.
Story: Everything that was culminated in the Arkham story is all shown at it's start, with quite a few of the villains that were talked about in the story were actually battled for the first time. It does feel like the general story that Batman does have, but it's a timeless classic and does deserve to be told in the ways that it is done nowadays. Batman has a massive $50 million bounty put onto his head by an unknown person, with every villain and mercenary gunning for your head. It gives you a sense of doubt that you can handle everything that is thrown at you, with many story elements around every corner.
Multiplayer: This part of the game I have yet to be able to get into due to poor Steam integration and lack of dedicated servers. In the year 2014, there are and will be games that are going to use Peer-2-Peer as a main source for online server hosting. Though this does make me sad, because from what I have seen in videos of people being able to play the multiplayer with others, it does also make me hope that others will attempt to play it more.
Overall, it's an amazing game and well worth buying if you plan on playing the other games. Playing this one first before Asylum and City is a great way to be introduced to the story and characters since it is in fact the beginning of the Batman in the Arkham storyline. The few bugs and glitches that I did encounter were somewhat annoying, but nothing major happened throughout the several hours I spent playing through this game. Definitely worth the money that I spent on the game, and will be willing to play the game again, as it does have quite a bit of extra content both during the story and after it is over.

Back in June 2014 is when I first purchased and devoted my life to the legacy version known as Rust (Alpha).
I may not have as many hours as some others who have posted here, but let me tell you why.
I loved the Legacy version of this game, it ran fine on my old 'gaming laptop' with 8gb of ram and a 720m, fine, with 60fps most of the time and little to NO drops at all.
When Legacy stopped being updated and they moved to the 'new and improved' version of rust, I was sceptical but optimistic. Turns out the newer version of rust didn't run on my old reliable laptop, and so I stopped playing for a few months until it was better optimized. Skip forward 3-4 months, and it still didn't run above 30(ish) fps.
I then played it again for a few days, just to get a feel for the new version, and when I found my lack of fps a struggle when fighting, I opted to quit rust until I had a better computer.
Skip another 2-3 months, and I had just finished a custom computer with a gtx 770, i5-4690k, and 16gb ram.
Beauty, I thought, I'll be able to run rust easy with this, and they'll have optimized it more in the time I've been gone!
Wrong.
Even my new computer struggled to run rust at a steady framerate. I tweaked the settings and barely managed to get my fps to hover around 60. Which was fine, I put a fair few hours into rust during this period, was active on mainly one server, and actively waited for wipe day and updates like a kid on Christmas.
But it seemed with every new feature implemented, the devs drew further away from optimizing their game.
And although there was always talk about performance increases and fixes in devblogs, I never saw an immediate improvement in the game's performance, a game that has been in early access for over 3 years and has seen no 'massive' improvements in optimization. Which is one of the core features that simply turns me off rust everytime I try to get back into it.
Which is why I cannot recommend this game.
EVen now with a GTX 1070, there is constant stuttering during gunfights, massive lag spikes for no reason at all, and random drops that make it nearly impossible to play this game sometimes. And I just cannot understand why they insist on adding paid cosmetics into a game, that has barely had any massive performance enhances since it's change to the new version.
I have not played rust for a long time, and I doubt I will until some sort of progression is added, and stability gets a major overhaul. Unfortunately that's just how it is with early access games, but I look forward to playing rust when it is optimized, and I feel the same excitement I felt during Legacy.

This Game is fantastic.
When it came out I was naturally suspicious. A good prison simulator? Heresy! I've played the ludicrously bad "Prison Tycoon" series and have come to expect a total mess out of any attempt to make a game that simulates a high sec prison. As any gamer knows, AI can only be so good; which limits how tricky the guards and inmates can be.
And yes, this games AI isin't perfect. But unlike most other simulators you are able to make up for your guards weaknesses by directly shaping how your prison operates. Every single room and corridor you build directly changes how your inmates and guards act, because this is a game of subtle changes bringing huge consequences. Inmates can find contraband in several different ways, but most reliably from rooms. Failing to place enough guard patrols will allow them to gather a surplus of tools to dig with.
Architect really is the name of the game. Building rooms too small, not enough of them, or not having enough of specific items can greatly change how your inmate population behaves. Mixing populations usually leads to fights, some inmates hate others and must be segregated, legendary criminals may end up in your institution, etc. A glaring mistake can enable mass escapes, riots, or worse.
The other thing I like about PA is it can be as easy or hard as you want it to be. You can turn off fail conditions, or even enable infinite money. So those that want to play the game without having to play it a specific way can do so.
With release came Escape Mode. You play a new inmate in the prison and obviously must escape. You could dig out, fight your way out, etc. What bothers me about the new mode is that digging and fighting are what the mode revolves around, the player does not actually use cash, contraband, or facilities; just being assigned a cell. I'm sure within a few updates the mode will include more of the games systems, but for now it's fairly dull especially since you will understand where the weak points in your defenses are... and the prison won't replace anything permenantly damages (AKA: Fires are OP since the AI won't replace destroyed areas)
Buy this game. This is a simulation game every strategy fan should have; and we should support the games it inspires.

JiXXR REVIEW:
Max Payne is one of those classic games that you have to play to really understand why there was so much love from one side, and hate from the other. Let me just say "Bullet Time".
The Matrix just hit theatres 2 years prior to the release of Max Payne. At this time, the slow motion bullet time effects that have now been soooo overdone that they are now seen as a movie trope or cheesy, were state of the art. They were new and exciting. So playing through this game at release was a whole new experience. You could watch the slow motion dives and bullets flying through the air for hours and still be amazed every time it happened. I don't know about you, but I was pretty excited. There were people who loved slow motion and people I know who despised it. That is what made this game a hit for some people and a "meh" for others.
The Bullet Time effects are now an overdone trope and so play through this understanding that it was a groundbreaking thing at the time. Appreciate it for what it was 20 years ago.
The seedy New York city setting also caught my interest. It is a dark game. Not dark in the literal sense, but more in a "Your family was murdered and you're going insane from guilt" kind of dark. On top of all of that the story is told in a graphic novel style similar to what you would see in Sin City (or something like that).
As far as visuals, expect something dated. The facial expressions on characters as they fire their guns make me giggle every time. Having your enemies show emotion rather than just be static textures over a poly frame was a fresh change, but it is so cheesy now that it hurts. You have to laugh at it.
I would recommend this game if it's on sale or you are just bored. Play through it again if this isn't your first time around. It's still fun and I love nostalgia.

Heavy Bullets stands out like a neon buoy in a sea of generic rogue-likes. The garish art style may seem gimmicky, but in fact perfectly complements the vivid, nightmarish tension of hunting in The Highlands. In fact, the bizarre color palette and unusual enemy shapes serve an important purpose - to reset your perception and your ability to discern friend from foe. An experienced FPS player may welcome this departure from artisic norms as a means to retrain their reflexes, and those who love fast-paced FPS combat will find Heavy Bullets' frenzied bursts of action to be quite satisfying. The reusable ammo system adds a layer of skill and strategic depth while avoiding RNG-based ammo generation issues. Even sound is a critical element in the game, as different SFX help you predict enemy movements.
Sadly, Heavy Bullets suffers from highly repetitive level generation. At least half of the items in the game are fairly useless, and the same can be said for many of the upgrades and extra weaponry. Although not inherently bad, the player's bullets are not projectiles in the traditional sense - should your reticle center on an enemy's weak point, they will die the moment you squeeze the trigger, regardless of distance or movement. Additionally, enemy aggro relies heavily on line-of-sight, making it easy to pick off enemies one-by-one in most rooms. These atypical mechanics add to the quirkiness of the game, and feel very appropriate amongst the other design choices.
Heavy Bullets is best-suited for roguelike fans, who will love the tension and atmosphere that it offers; however, it is possible that those who pick this game up for other reasons may find its permadeath and repetition a bit more of a grind than they can bear.

Mad Max is around a 40 hour octane-fueled love letter to the film franchise.  It excels at the Mad Max elements - but not so much the video game ones.  I thought the films were alright, and so the game is alright.  If you don't care at all about the movies, the game probably isn't going to cut it for you unless you're a car guy in one sense or another.
The story begins with you fighting some warlord dirtbag named Scrotus (yes, it's a stupid name) in a cutscene, during which you lost your car and took a beating.  You stumble across a mechanically-inclined hunchback named Chumbucket who in his automotive-religious fervor is building a dream machine called the Magnum Opus, which he wants you to drive as his "Saint". However, Max isn't happy with a V6, and must overcome a series of tasks to acquire a V8 engine instead.
At least that's the initial plotline.  Yeah, no, not kidding.  There are a few characters thrown in at the last second that you're supposed to care about (Max does, somehow), but the game simply does not commit the necessary time for them to be effective.  Max confronts his inner demons via some mystical desert dweller every time he wants to upgrade his base attributes, resulting in interesting conversations.  There is a small selection of functional side quests that will help round out the experience.  Finally, Chum has many anecdotes about the places you will go and the people you will meet.  The whole experience is a little bare bones for a video game, but quintessentially Mad Max.
Something I do criticize the story for, though, is all of the end-game events are tied up by a single boss who, by that point of the game, you are absolutely kicking the sh*t out of.  But, you'll somehow get beaten, and thrown down a hole anyway, because plot device.  All of the ways the plot resolves itself afterwards hinge on this one fight that there was no way you'd lose, but you do anyway.  Bad form, Avalanche Studios.
The framework for this open-world game is that it's divided into multiple regions with four strongholds.  Each stronghold is a destitute, spiteful pit of human suffering until you start doing projects for them.  Things like water collectors, armories, scrap crews, and so forth.  Each one has a tangible benefit for Max as it will refill his ammo, health, or gas every time he visits, alongside other perks.  I should mention that building these projects negates a great deal of atmosphere about the game.  No more finding fuel, or bullets, or water, which should be one of the most immersive things about a post-apocalyptic game.  The sub-regions within a stronghold's territory are overrun with Scrotus-controlled facilities.  Eliminating them nets you routine shipments of scrap, and occasionally project parts.  Personally, I found this part of the game asinine.  If you murder every war boy in an oil refinery, wouldn't you want control of the pump?  Shouldn't there be some sort of resource system for that?  But no, every place you go you simply blow everything the f*ck up, after which allies move in and start dismantling the place (in theory) to send you your precious scrap.  Lazy.  I will say though that since most of the game is a fairly bland desert, they spent a LOT of time meticulously crafting every actual structure to make sure it's different from every other.  This effort was immediately noticed and appreciated, though more than once it was profoundly annoying not to have the ability to jump.
The stronghold leaders help the immersion, but aren't likeable at all.  It is essentially you that turns each stronghold from a hovel where people go to die into something like a proper tribal home.  These people owe you everything, and although you'll hear passing comments of gratitude, you don't get a god*amn thing for it.  If you yank down every scarecrow, build every project, kill every sniper, take over every camp, destroy every convoy, and clear every minefield to reduce a territory's threat to zero, you will will unlock car upgrades, and increase passive scrap income, but that's it.  Everything in the game is very heavily gated with mandatory busywork, and since you can fast travel, it's only worth it to build all the projects in one stronghold.  There was a stunning lack of a sense of reward about the game.
Scrap is everything.  Outside of achievement tokens to upgrade Max's base attributes, scrap is the currency for any and all upgrades.  There are many sources of this element of the game, and most of them are a waste of time.  Rare scrap pallets, the occasional passing scrap truck, and taking over camps are the only viable means for this resource.  The game even has the ability to gather scrap for you when you're not playing, as long as you have an internet connection.  How much you need will depend on the upgrades you're looking to unlock, but in the end if you're maxing out everything, you're going to need probably over 10,000.  Compare that to the average 5 scrap you get from blowing up a vehicle, and you'll quickly lose patience for the game's heavy padding.
So, what about the cars?  The car is the linchpin of the whole game, as it should be for this title.  There are at least five upgrades in ten categories for the Magnum, and the same in eight categories for Max himself.  Having said this, however, there was very little creativity spent on the upgrades themselves.  The looks will always change, but every upgrade to the right in any category is better than its predecessor, almost without exception.  It's just numbers.  You can scale back on some things to increase others, like defense vs. speed, but most categories present no reason to have anything but the best, which narrows down "optimal builds" far more than it should for a game that is essentially about car customization.  There are also 32 other vehicles to collect in the game, acquired by finding them and driving them to any stronghold, but although they have a great variety, you cannot alter any car except the Magnum.
Car combat ranges from slightly thrilling, to annoying as hell.  By the end you'll have a harpoon, explosive javelin, ramming bar, and side flamethrowers to get it done, each with their own upgrades.  Explosions are spectacular.  Quests where you must drive a vehicle other than the Magnum will generally give you a sh*t car that drives like a boat so you can get mobbed by enemies.  Later in the game, blowing up cars becomes a chore as they are heavily armored.  Something always works, and I give the game credit for making you vary your strategies, but as vehicles started to take longer to destroy, I found myself skipping combat as a nuisance with very little payoff.  Convoys regenerate, so if the target gets a little far, he'll get all his health back, and two escorts if they all died.  Regular enemies also patrol these routes and will join the bedlam.
Ground combat is meat and potatoes.  Max is a street brawler of the Arkham variety, and while the game's combat has a great sense of impact, it is at the same time limited and repetitive, outside of the laughable but fun wrestling moves he breaks out now and then during fury mode when he hits much harder and regenerates health for each kill.  The counter-system to the game is annoying, and half of the time you cannot cancel an animation to execute one.  This means a lot of cheap shots from the back while you're beating someone down.  Rolling out of the way, however, seems to be 100% guaranteed, but it breaks the combo.  Bosses or Top Dogs are almost all identical, and there aren't enough enemy types to make it interesting otherwise.  The only way the game attempts to scale the difficulty higher is to throw ever increasing numbers and ever bigger crowds of these dimwits at you.
Overall, the game is average - for a game.  I doubt there will ever be Mad Max 2 because in spite of minor gripes, this one had everything it was supposed to.
