This game is a fraud and I would recommend against buying it.
I go back a long time with Planescape: Torment, so I was ecstatic when I learned about the kickstarter for Tides. Naturally, I became a backer of this game during the kickstarter and eagerly waited to start playing it. Having finished the first playthrough, I am sorely disappointed. Before I explain why, I'd like to point out that this game is extremely text-heavy and players who aren't prepared to spend about 80% of their time reading should avoid it regardless of the reviews being positive or negative.
My main source of frustration is the fact that the devs cut the content that had been promised in the Kickstarter project. I understand that this isn't rare regarding crowdfunding, but it is a scummy, dishonest business policy and borderline fraud which would prevent me from recommending this game even were it good, and it isn't.
To give credit where credit is due, the game mechanics are pretty solid. From character development to the item system,  Tides of Numenera is a streamlined, yet complex RPG. There are some improvements that could have been made, but the game is very satisfactory from a game mechanics perspective. Still, Planescape: Torment's best and most important attribute was the story, and Tides is pretty weak in that regard. Firstly, the game is very short. My playthrough was pretty thorough, yet I was finished about 30 hours in. For a game which spent so long a period in development and whose Kickstarter was considered a major success, I consider anything less than 50 hours a disappointment, and I was hoping for something like The Witcher 3, where you could easily spend 100 hours.
*the rest of the review contains spoilers*
Leaving behind game mechanics, I will comment on the story from the perspective of the plot, setting and the underlying philosophy.
The setting is bizarre and interesting and has a proper tormentesque vibe. It is based on a tabletop roleplaying game by Monte Cook, and I will gladly take the game up if I ever return to pen and paper gaming. At times the game was a tad too bizarre for my taste, but this isn't a major minus and many people will probably like it. The plot is a good fit for the general style of the game and the setting. Although it is nothing near to being spectacular, the small amount of story this game has is pretty good.
What makes the game intrinsically bad is the superficial philosophy behind it, despite several neat touches, such as the Lascar side-quests symbolizing religion. The primary question, "What does one life matter?", is tied to the primary story in a very loose way. One problem is the fact that this question is very wide, especially in comparison to the question posed by Planescape: Torment, "What can change the nature of a man?" PsT's question was interwoven in the storyline and by the time Ravel asks for your answer you have had plenty of time to seedifferent perspectives on this problem. In Numenera, the question feels forced. If we ignore wild interpretations and the places where such a wide question is inherently linked to the standard fantasy themes, it is hard to see how it relates to the primary story beyond the two times it is directly asked. Even when it is inherent in some problem which often appears in fantasy games, it doesn't seem to be significantly more developed than usual. What I felt was the main philosophical point of the story is a rather lame bioconservative eulogy of death. In very short and simple terms, The Changing God is fighting to prolong his life and The Sorrow tells you that prologing one's life inherently harms other people, so it should be stopped. I don't think that there is an ending which is further from this philosophy than the one I chose, and in my ending The Sorrow and the Last Castoff agreed not to kill any castoffs at that time, but The Sorrow forbade the creation of any further castoffs and also promised to slaughter them later on. This kind of ending is highly unsatisfying, especially as I wasn't very interested in the internal castoff-changing god issues since I perceived The Sorrow as the primary enemy. Although I could say that I am a quite radical transhuanist on the issue of death, I would be more than interested to see a nuanced bioconservative argument in this sort of a game. The problem is that the argumentation present in Numenera is quite flimsy and reductible to saying that simply living is harming other people. Even this argumentation lies on a very symbolic reading of the Tides, but without it I would be hard pressed to find one developed central philosophical argument in the entire game. In that respect, the philosophy of the game is quite under-developed even if my interpretation is lacking. Of course, I am open to the possibility that I missed something, but I feel that the philosophical background of the game is simply bad. The solid but short story and mecahincs don't compensate for this deficit in my books.
tldr; Regardless of the story, I wouldn't recommend Tides of Numenera because of the dishonest business practice regarding its Kickstarter project. The setting is great and the story and mechanics of the game are reasonably sound, although the story is very short. That being said, this game is highly entertaining, to the point where instead it's a the best lightsaber sim game to that it's G-Mod: Star Wars edition, yet TBH I think the mechanics here are far more fun and easier to manipulate than in source.

Of all Star Wars games, this still has the best lightsaber mechanics. Legit, you can keep fighting new sith or jedi, and you won't get bored because there are so many ways your lightsaber works here, and so many moves you can use to kick your enemy's♥♥♥♥♥ Mixed in with some awesome force mechanics, you actually can feel like a God if you put your moves right. So yeah, this game is freaking great. I don't know what else to say and my review is all over the place, but that fits with the context of this game.

Who didn’t play games similar to 3 Coins at School when you were going to school? I know I did and there were plenty of different variances of those types of games that my peers and I loved to play. Therefore when I saw that the game was released onto Steam I was immediately interested in seeing if I could rekindle some of my favorite school year memories. I wasn’t expecting anything but that opportunity.
Let’s get the technical issues out of the way first before I can get to the meat and potatoes point of my review. The game works as intended. The graphics aren’t pretty and I would have liked to see them improved upon but if they are nothing else they are serviceable. The game play mechanics work though I would have liked a better tutorial than just rules so that players could learn the game a little faster – though it has to be said that it is simple. I found it impossible to find a multiplayer game which isn’t surprising and there is no local multiplayer option. But why would you really need a local option because if you wanted to play all you’d need to do is get a few coins.
So my problem with the game…. Playing against the computer opponent is a relatively boring experience. It’s a time waster and not in a good way. It’s impossible to rekindle the memories of playing these types of games with friends at school because when all is said and done you’re not necessarily playing because you love the game, you’re playing because you love spending time with friends. You’re playing to spend the six to eight hours a day that you need to be at school in the most social ways possible. You probably even played these types of games because you were bored and you played mind numbing games to get those hours done with.
A game like this without playing with active people who you can laugh and talk with just isn’t a fulfilling experience. That is no disrespect to the devs at 89AM Studio and I appreciate their efforts in trying but ultimately they developed a sadly unnecessary game.

This Game is fantastic.
When it came out I was naturally suspicious. A good prison simulator? Heresy! I've played the ludicrously bad "Prison Tycoon" series and have come to expect a total mess out of any attempt to make a game that simulates a high sec prison. As any gamer knows, AI can only be so good; which limits how tricky the guards and inmates can be.
And yes, this games AI isin't perfect. But unlike most other simulators you are able to make up for your guards weaknesses by directly shaping how your prison operates. Every single room and corridor you build directly changes how your inmates and guards act, because this is a game of subtle changes bringing huge consequences. Inmates can find contraband in several different ways, but most reliably from rooms. Failing to place enough guard patrols will allow them to gather a surplus of tools to dig with.
Architect really is the name of the game. Building rooms too small, not enough of them, or not having enough of specific items can greatly change how your inmate population behaves. Mixing populations usually leads to fights, some inmates hate others and must be segregated, legendary criminals may end up in your institution, etc. A glaring mistake can enable mass escapes, riots, or worse.
The other thing I like about PA is it can be as easy or hard as you want it to be. You can turn off fail conditions, or even enable infinite money. So those that want to play the game without having to play it a specific way can do so.
With release came Escape Mode. You play a new inmate in the prison and obviously must escape. You could dig out, fight your way out, etc. What bothers me about the new mode is that digging and fighting are what the mode revolves around, the player does not actually use cash, contraband, or facilities; just being assigned a cell. I'm sure within a few updates the mode will include more of the games systems, but for now it's fairly dull especially since you will understand where the weak points in your defenses are... and the prison won't replace anything permenantly damages (AKA: Fires are OP since the AI won't replace destroyed areas)
Buy this game. This is a simulation game every strategy fan should have; and we should support the games it inspires.

Having only 3 in-game dates would be fine if those dates were more fleshed out and exciting. I found myself getting emotionally attached to all the adult characters and Amanda, some more than others, but an attachment nonetheless. The other dads' children were hit and miss, and even after playing out all available endings, I still feel like the other children were accessories and didn't really leave a lasting impact (except River, who by default was always there attached to Craig).
All endings basically tie into a single ending with dialogue changes, meaning I would click the skip button until I reached the specific "altered" dialogue. That perhaps was the most disappointing aspect of the game. I would've rather waited several more months for the game to be feel fully completed than to have a singular "one size fits all" type of ending, but I digress. Having the ending center around Amanda can say a lot about your dadsona, so it's kind of forgivable, however, I expected more from such a hyped game. The dating sim genre tends to allow for more creativity.
I abused the save function a lot, saving before every dialogue option to ensure I chose the one which would entice the reaction I wanted. Not sure yet if that's a good or bad thing, but it does make the dialogue choosing in this game of little consequence. Instead of having to deal with a decision I made, I could instantly reverse it. However, without this option, the game could be seen as a tedious chore, again because of the repetition of the game. You'll find yourself using the skip button a lot in your achievement and ending hunting.
While the dadsona seemed cartoonish in comparison to the other dads, I found it endearing and quite charming to have this caricature as the player. It just felt right, and it made the other dads all falling for your character much more entertaining. I love character customization, so this of course would never be a feature I'd criticize.
As a final comment, the game still has some bugs and pathway glitches littered about. From dialogue mistakes (such as choosing Amanda's other parental figure as being a mother but constantly having them referred to as Amanda's second dad) to bugs causing Joseph's twins to overlay a specific scene in Craig's second date... Not to mention just the general bugs saving in the middle of a date or other dialogue causes (an example would be the few times the character sprites would be enclosed in boxes, such as being in Robert's car or driving Damien around, and saving + loading the screen will cause the sprites to disappear off screen... as well as the hearts + eggplants + black spots overlays upon choosing dialogue being off-centre and completely to the side of the screen). I'm not surprised, as even games which have been released for weeks can require debugging, but these issues combined with several others pointed out start to amass into a singular central issue:
The game could have used more time in development. It feels incomplete, and hollow at times, in comparison to other dating sims I've played (such as Hatoful Boyfriend, Huniepop, etc.). The game has no distinguishing feature that makes it unique in comparison to other dating sims, such as a specific puzzle game (speaking of which, the golf mini game is broken and needs attention) or central plot twist.
Although I've griped about this game, there are some things that absolutely cannot be overlooked. The game is fun, colorful, comedic, and clearly a passion project. I did not mind the voice acting, as many other games incorporate this style (such as Fire Emblem). The score was pleasant and oddly enough I did not find myself tiring of it even upon hearing certain tracks numerous times in a row. The dates were enjoyable and the minigames were well spread throughout the character paths and dates (ultimately making Brian's route the most fun). LGBT + POC representation in a non-fetishy way is always appreciated. I expect my time played to only increase as I continue experimenting with the dialogue options as I await fixes, changes, and possibly additions. I definitely still recommend this game where it is currently at for those on the fence or not 100% sure about it yet.

Personally, this is my first time ever playing a legitimate dating-sim and from what I see for a first time game "Dream Daddy" is a wonderful twist on the idea of a same-sex love game. In its entirety, the game's mechanics are simple and easy to follow, and I found myself laughing alot due to the wackiness of the various plot twists that came with each decision I made.
Moreoever, the level of detail and care that went into developing the core dynamics between the father and the daughter to me felt the best I'd ever seen in a story-driven game ("Dream Daddy" being the dating-sim I've ever played from start to finish).
Of course there were some weak points as well.
For starters, as an incredibly picky person when its comes to games with character customizaton, I'm very critical at times because I like to design every aspect of my player character down to the last molecule; from their height and weight, to their hair color and eye color, to how they interact with people, to how they sleep at night--even their fashion sense is important to me, and I feel like while the "Build-a-Daddy" system is good for the engine the game plays on, the lack of any real depth to how I want my "Daddy" to be feels very shallow because my character already has memories and thoughts I feel are unnecessary or don't fit into the type of person I was hoping to create.
As an idea to throw out, I'd suggest adding an "Environmental Reactionary Background System" or ERBS*--*coined the term already so nobody can use it lol XD--in which players are given near aboslute control over their Daddies by being able to create entirely new content, fashions, styles, etc. allowing players to add a fresh persepctive to each individual Daddy they use. Another point for the ERBS would be allowing players the freedom to create their character backgrounds or "Daddy Times" (for example, your Daddy could be divorced and had adopted you child prior to),  and as a result, the game will automatically generate an environment in which the Daddy is like a real person. In this everything should be customizable, even the wife/husband, and even the children (don't get me wrong, Amanda is cool, but what if I wanna have a cute Asian as an adopted child?).
To do this, I firmly believe players should be able to type their character backgrounds as well as visually create them in character slots, 10 slots in total, giving them the ability to create over 100+ different daddies, and over 1000+ different families either married, separated, single, windowed, divorced, etc., with at least 4 children slots (8 if separated or divorced), all of which can be individually customized by the player.
In short, if I want to, I want to be able to make a Daddy who has 3 children (the fourth died stillborn and the wife died in labor) and as a result the game would essentially revolve around my Daddy trying to piece his life back together as his kids are getting older and out of control and his grief keeps him from moving on and finding love in the arms of another... a Daddy.
Then, the biggest point for ERBS would be the shifting of dynamics between the player and the NPCs, simulating real world/life events and having the player choose how to approach them (for example, if you caught Amanda smoking kush, or stealing money out of your wallet, you could respond a number of ways that would increase or decrease your relationship with her, but you could later change that dynamic by coming back with another action or so).
Another thing I found lacking was the dynamic between the player's Daddy and initial 7 daddies you could choose from.
Personally, I think that while the initial 7 are good starters for players to get accustomed to, I can honestly see the interest fading away with time, and I highly suggest adding more daddies to date, and, if not, at least adding more NPCs for the player to interact with that help to expand the game's lore and story more, as well as providing more information about the daddies the player's currently trying to date. As I said before, I loved the originality of the game, and I saw that in how each daddy is uinque and in-tuned to their respective environments, however I also feel that just the player should be allowed to create their own stories, and as such I firmly believe that the NPCs should very much be taken out of their comfort zones, giving more depth to the Daddies, so that the player is given more of a reason to fall in love with them... or even hate them. I want to make decisions or say things that make the game respond to my choices so I can see how EVERYTHING plays outs.
Plus, going back to my point on player customization, it would make the game even more amazing if the users could create clothes, hairs, accessories, etc., and share them together. Playing created Daddies and/or created families would incredible taste and flavor to each playthrough and giving players the ability to create complex/complicated relationships, love triangles, hate quarrels, lusts, revenge, etc. and improving the game's QTEs with more preparation could be help immensely. Even allowing players to record individual playthroughs and save their favorites in the gallery, or maybe even add screens that actively show the player's Daddy participating in the action the text outlines (like IDK, actually kissing their date, or selling food at a bake sale?) would keep the fire going and interest in the game alive.
Overall, "Dream Daddy" is a mainstay in my Steam Library, but I feel that the game needs more player input to be that type of game that most people can just go back over and over again.

Wanna feel a real "oooh shhhiiiiit" moment when you realize what really caused the several preceding "oh fuuuuck" moments? Wanna feel like a badass then feel dirty afterwards for enjoying being so badass? Read Heart of Darkness or seen Apocalypse Now and thought to yourself "gee that looks like a wonderfully fun time"?
Spec Ops may not be the most perfect shooter - the cover can get kind of clunky and the few rail shooter segments are weak, but most of the firefights are tense and challenging and exciting and the weapons are satisfying - but what it really offers is an engrossing examination of madness and how strength confronts - or fails to confront - trauma and horror. It's like an English paper in a video game. Or a video game you could write an English paper about.
Or it's an exercise in irony to have an FPS game take every opportunity to say "oooh look at that, you monster. That's the sixth head you've exploded in as many minutes. Ohh did you really have to turn that guy's head into chunky gazpacho? He was already down. Your teammates told you to stop but noooooo. Isn't war terrible? Now go blow up that convoy if you want to progress".
Or, you know, it's just a fun, easily digestible shooter (finished it inside of 9 hours total) with a good, if somewhat predictable (up until the end and the options you're given) story. If it's on sale at all, go for it. Definitely go for it if you like philosophizing about games as art and the torture of the human condition in the face of our illusory and unstable understanding of what it means to choose.

With the game's price dropped now, I think it's worthy of a review now.
I got the game as a deluxe edition (in a deal which costs HALF of the full price!) which gives me Nuketown Zombies, Nuketown 2025 MP map, the soundtrack, and a free copy of World at War. I'll explain that later.
The SP [POTENTIAL SPOILERS]:
The story kind of picks off where Black Ops 1 left. Except, we're actually in the second cold war. At first I thought, why is BO2 even a thing? BO already has a non-cliffhanger ending, so I don't know what to expect for this. Apparently, I forgot some details, that later explains why the events in BO2 happens. The game still introduces flashbacks, but it also introduces to present-time missions too. I got slight problems with the timeline keep changing back and forth, but it does explain the story well.
This is the first CoD that introduces you to non-linear storyline. Which means that every decision you make has a difference. There are 4 potential endings that you can find, which adds replayability.
Last, but not least, the campaign gameplay. It is the best campaign of all CoD history gameplay-wise, period. Instead of getting fixed weapons, you can customize your loadout to your liking, even to perks. This adds freedom to players, even though at the end you will still have to throw out your weapons if you ran out of ammo. But that's not all - if you think you're just doing mindless killing, think again - you are now actually scored/evaluated at the end of every missions. The amount of people you kill (extra points for headshots) do actually count. This adds yet another replay value, you always want to get the highest score of all your friends. Well, it ends up you killing more, but at least it's a lot more meaningful unlike others. You also have challenges to do (10 per mission) to unlock stuff in campaign, adding yet another replay value. Then, you can replay the whole story with the currently unlocked weapons for a different experience, yet another replay value added.
Black Ops II has the most replay value of all CoD, following with CoD4 with their cheats.
The MP:
MP in CoD is the most important selling point for CoD, and BO2, while dying on the PC, still has a playable MP to a certain degree. I can't really say it's the best MP, but it did introduce some mechanics that later CoD games replicate, for example the ever-popular Pick 10 system, in which you can fill up 10 slots with items that you want. This has some flaws, sure (for example, a 6-perk no attachment R870 is OP AF), but most importantly you have more freedom and adds a more specific niche to your classes.
The guns in MP are well balanced, and while some guns are pretty bad, they're actually good in a degree. Guns in this game actually have a specific role that it can fit, for example, the R870 I mentioned is very overpowered in CQC, but useless at very long range. The MP7 is similar - very deadly at close range, but good luck hitting people at med-long range.
The ZM:
Treyarch is iconic with its zombie mode which started way back from World at War (aka CoD5). Sadly, the earlier maps in this installment leaves something to be desired. TranZit is way too big for most people, including me. Die Rise is too confusing to navigate. Nuketown Zombies is great and all, but didn't really live up to the hype. Later DLCs do add good ZM maps, though. Mob of the Dead, Buried, and Origins are all great.
The Bonuses:
If you get this in a deal, then you're very lucky! The extra maps are very great, also you get a free copy of WaW, which is
due to zombie modding being trending in the last couple of years. I suggest you get the Deluxe Edition just for WaW and the extra others.
Overall:
Black Ops II deserves a
in my book. Few last CoDs have been quite disappointing for me, but Black Ops II returned big-time. This game still doesn't pass CoD4 or MW2, but it is money well spent (especially with the deal!)
If you feel like getting this, I suggest you get it in a deal, but if you REALLY need it now, go get it!

It's a little too Planescape Torment, than inspired by Planescape Torment, imo. How much yearning one has for nostalgia vs wanting something new will weigh heavily on how much you enjoy the game.
I haven't finished yet, but that's largely because I keep taking large breaks. Why do I keep taking breaks? Because the game crashes often enough to be annoying. So far, the crashes fall into the following categories:
1) Everything appears alright, but you're no longer able to interact with anything. Alt-tabbing out and back in and out again and you'll find the Torment Window is now unresponsive. Must kill the process and restart.
2) Audio starts to stutter, then the game crashes to desktop.
3) Audio starts to stutter, then the game causes Windows to crash to the BSOD with a kernal error.
#2 has been the most common crash.
Sometimes the last manual/auto save was right before a crash. Sometimes not. I find myself quite lethargic when it isn't, knowing I have to repeat everything between my last save and the crash. Hence the breaks. I suspect that says something about how I feel about the game, though I do enjoy the story.
Anyway, if games like Planescape Torment, the BG series, Pillars of Eternity, etc, are your cup of tea, this is more of the same. The effort system is the game's unique twist to the tried and true formula (though I swear I've seen it before in other games, I just can't remember what games exactly), and your best bet is to ensure you and your Companions all master a different stat, and maybe double up on either Speed or Intelligence (3 stats, 4 party members-including yourself).
So far, it doesn't appear you can change the armor for your Companions, which makes them increasingly fragile as the game has progressed so far, so even though I'm not playing a front line fighter, I still...play a front line fighter, because I have much better defenses than any of my Companions.
One Companion I'm keeping is basically useless, but I'm hoping there's some traditional RPGness to this Companion where if I stick with it for the long haul, there'll be a reward of some sort. Though, as a developer, I would definitely enjoy skewing convetions on that front.
Outside of the crashes, there are a few other bugs I've encountered:
1) One of the early quests didn't trigger completion. After searching the internet, it's obvious it should have triggered to another step and then completed, but it didn't. Sadly, the NPC thought it had, and no longer exists. It went undone, then was forcibly removed as I progressed to the next area.
2) Buff icons sometimes vanish while still being in effect, but will sometimes come back after zoning. You can still see the effects if you hover over a character icon when this occurs.
3) Lots of minor pathing issues where you or your Companions get stuck on an object on the map or a person. Clicking around the stuck point has, so far, caused them to repath and get unstuck.
Lastly, there's an ommision I always find very puzzling whenever it is omitted by a developer: A complete lack of Windowed, Borderless mode. I have never understood the point of a Windowed mode set to the monitor's resolution that isn't borderless, as such a Window never fits correctly. Considering one can write a few lines in Autohotkey to make a window borderless, it just doesn't seem like such a mammoth undertaking for a developer to make this a graphical option, and I am completely bewildered how anyone who's played more than a few hours of games on a PC doesn't consider this a basic function for a PC game. Certainly, the developers pertrude the aura of gamers, which makes this lack incredibly puzzling.
In conclusion, the game probably needs an in-depth bug pass. It definitely could use voice acting (I'm sure it was beyond their budget, but I'd probably have made that the very first stretch goal; it's all about priorities). It's too much of the same old same old for me to get too blubbery about it, but I am not hating it. I just find it a little exhausting, due to the combination of sameness and crashes.
If you know another game that's very similar to Planescape Torment, BG 2, etc, is going to wow and amaze you, then I heartily recommend it. If you're looking for something with similar written depth as Planescape Torment, but in a fresh and different package...well, this isn't really it (the second part).
I do wish Steam gave you the option for a neutral thumb, but for now, I'll go with a thumb down, just to potentially move the aggregate needle enough that perhaps the technical issues might get a patch or two in response.

Sadly I am joining the ranks of users dissatisfied with this game.  I gave it a good 8 hours but when I realized that I was forcing myself to continue playing in the hopes it would improve I decided it was not worth my time.  I'm sure there's a great story here, but I don't want to have to slog through text block after text block to uncover it.  I like playing my games, being involved in them moreso than just selecting another dialogue option.
I believe the lack of combat gameplay really hurt this game - in other CRPGs the combat/dungeon crawling provides a break from the text and allows the player to experience the world.  This is very lacking in this game.  There is very little combat at all and the existing combat is all staged - it feels less interactive and more like an alternate form of dialogue.
I guess that's my overall impression of the game: it's a videogame that feels like its designed to be read and not played.
There are so many ways a videogame can be used to show something, immerse the players, but this feels like someone telling me a story as opposed to showing/letting me experience it.
The introduction has you falling to your (believed) death - but, instead of having a quick cinematic showing you falling from a great height and crashing to the ground, there is a 10 minute narration about the fall, oh look there's a forest over there, oh were you being chased by something? oh wait is that the ground....wait for it....still narrating...finally, you hit the ground.  And the graphic display for this?  A black screen with white streaks that I think are supposed to be wind.
Each character you meet has blocks of descriptor but I have yet to encounter a single character portrait concept art.  There is a section of the dialogue box that looks designed to hold a portrait but it remains a blank grey canvas.  Even when you speak to your companions there is no close up portrait of them.
3 million plus words is not a selling point!  It's a sign that a better editor was needed.

9/10
Overall: An excellent example of Inifinity-engine style storytelling in the mold of Planescape: Torment. One of the biggest strengths of TTON is that it is without the excess weight of some elements that (while fun) don't contribute to this particular kind of narrative RPG; specifically, excess grinding and extra-story combat. On the downside, of course, some people will miss those things, and some will be further disappointed at the fact that this really is a specific story with a lot of beautiful text (ala PS:T), and not a free-form RPG like Baldur's Gate, where you can build a character of your choosing. However, the limited choices when it comes to character creation are still quite robust, and I didn't feel like the story was missing anything for not having, for example, more than three Focus paths to choose from.
Major Pros:
-Tight narrative that allows for MUCH more reactivity than I expected, making choices that felt thematically or logically correct actually have impacts (sometimes extremely significant impacts) to gameplay. Unlike BG/BGII or even PS:T, for example, sometimes a quest item is actually as useful as the person who asks you to retrieve it claims it to be...
-Interesting characters with personal motivations beyond "You seem trustworthy; allow me to join YOUR noble quest!"
-An interesting character with personal motivation that is EXACTLY: "You seem trustworthy; allow me to join YOUR noble quest!"
Minor Pros:
-Beautiful music and art
-Background item descriptions blend into interactivity and actual bonuses/powers; be sure to examine all the Oddities carefully.
Major Cons:
-The final act was so tight that I'm willing to bet anyone who doesn't play a heavy-Intellect/Lore/etc character, AND strive for finishing side-quests, will feel like it is lacking. The major narrative is strong and well-implemented, but I think it would be easy for someone playing a different kind of character to miss some things I found and enjoyed (though, I suppose, I could be wrong, depending on the usefulness of Smashing/Quick Fingers/etc as skills to find other ways around problems).
Minor Cons:
-Voice acting didn't hold up to the music and art; I was OK with it, but some characters were much weaker than others in this regard.
-I was surprised there are only 4 character tiers (sort of the equivalent of levels, or level-brackets) in the game, as I was assuming it would have the baseline 6 from the tabletop game. I was certainly not under-powered at the end, but when I stopped advancing, I had to go and check to see if that was a bug.

Too much text, not enough gameplay. They say good dialogue is what made Planescape great. They're not wrong, but what they didn't understand is that what kept the original from being a true masterpiece was the lack of decent combat gameplay. I remember playing it and by the end thinking "man, what a great story, great characters and intriguing world... now if only it had the combat gameplay mechnanics of Baldur's Gate, it would have been the best". Instead of correcting this, they made it worse. I can't play this 10 minutes without getting bored and rushing through dialogues and without the dialogues, there's nothing left. Show, don't tell. I find it ironic that whenever you ask a character a second time to repeat the trivial information he spent so long to describe he manages to summarize it in a few sentences only. These summary, more often than not, should have been the first and only answer.
The fact that you can't engage in combat with anyone also diminishes the impression of freedom and choice of action and reinforces the impression that you're really just a spectactor here, and the game just wants you to go about speaking to people and solve their fetch quests. Whatever your choices in Baldur's Gate, you knew you could always attack the npcs. Here? The game really just wants you to listen to its lore...
I don't recommend it. This is for hipsters stuck on nostalgia saying that PT was about something else than gameplay. PT was great but it's never been the classic game than Baldur's Gate was. It could have been so much better with a better combat mechanic and simply MORE COMBATS.
I understand PT strived to be the ANTI Baldur's Gate, and had its heart in the right place by having you focus in stats like charisma, intelligence and wisdom instead, but it went overboard with it, as it ends up way less balanced than BG and having little replay value. Fights is what give replay value to these games. Fights can go in so many directions, although less so in turn based combats, but that's another issue (at this point I'm just desperate for anything else than listening to NPCs narrating a fantasy's short story, so I'll take turn based, even with its obvious flaws). Dialogues options, on the other hand, is just a matter of reloading and finding out what happens if I click on one answer instead of the other. They are "nice to have", but they're not the meat of these video games.
Unfortunatly they chose poorly in this sequel by focusing even LESS on gameplay. I guess it costs less to produce. 50$ for this is ridiculous. It's worth 15$ at the most. Will not be purchasing from InXile again.

Boring and disappointing.
I can deal with the repetitive combat. It's isometric RPG, and while some games can still pull that through, that's quite a high bar to not recommend this on.
I can forgive the stale and forgettable companions. Creating a Bioware class side kick is difficult, something even the best RPGs fail to do. I'm not asking for another Minsc or HK-47. After all these years I've waited for something akin to Morte, Nordom, Vhailor, Dakkon, and Grace to resurge (no, I didn't like Annah, and Ignus was a filthy traitor), not finding any of character even close to likeable is disappointing. But this is not Black Isle's baby. It's just a self proclaimed 'Spiritual successor'.
I would have at least contended with something akin to Pillars of Eternity. Pillars was okay. Felt more like Ice WInd Dale than Baldur's Gate or Planescape Torment.
But then I reached (to spare you spoilers) a mid point crucial moment, and met a mentor like person who supposed to 'teach' you things, I felt the heavy heavy heavy hand of the writers imposing their point of view on you.
It's not necessarily 'poor writing' but it isn't good for gaming, especially this sort of gaming, where player agency is paramount.
You are presented with a fantastical world, and I've gobbled up all the text. I've read through every minutiae of description on baubles that you sold off as junk, just because they spiked the imagination. But after all that, if what you are faced with is some pedantic idiot spewing pseudo philosophical gibberish in their proclaimed role as the Obi-Wan Kenobi, then screw this game.
It's not RPG; it's not even Choose your own adventure. It's just the writers masturbating to their own writing; it shares its genealogy with the worst of Eurotrash, High minded, looking down on the player, force feeding mindless philosophy. It's not Planescape Torment. It's a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor imitation, and I regret backing this during kickstarter.

Trying to follow up PlaneScape: Torment - in my opinion the best RPG story ever told is ambitious. Tides of Numenera comes really, really close, which for me is enough. Especially considering how rare games like this are.
The atmosphere, mystery and above all uniqueness of the setting are great on their own right and when comparing it to PlaneScape I only like the latter slightly more because of personal preferences.
The lack of actual or forced combat where you hit things with a weapon is impressive - the game even calls them "Crisis" encounters and there's often a way to do something other than killing all the enemies to get through it.
The companions and places you visit are interesting, but left me wanting for more (which is often a good sign). It didn't feel like I got to know any of the companions well enough beyond their main backstory. The first big hub of Sagus Cliffs wasn't as interesting for me as Sigil or the other, weirder places you get to visit later in Tides and I wanted more of that.
The variety of meaningful choices and reactivity to them was probably the best out of any RPG I've played. Despite having hard-fought and "ideal" solutions to problems that probably wouldn't have any consequences later I was more torn than I ever have been between the all the other options. All because of how well written the game is and how many intriguing choices the game had for me.
The story of Tides manages to invoke similar deep philosophical concepts to the original Torment while not retreading the same ground. The plot, while slow to get going had some interesting twists and an overall satisfying conclusion.
Overall I haven't played anything as compelling as this since the original Torment.

A great game. I think it is more "Tormenty" than Planescape Torment itself.
The setting is very fresh and interesting. I think it is now my favorite setting. There is much to explore in this game. There is a lot of text to read - but it is interesting text (not boring walls of text as in Pillars of Eternity). Quests are interesting, have multiple solutions and influence one another. There are no fetch/kill quests. The characters you interact with are very memorable - each of them has a background, backstory. There is a lot of hidden "tastes". It is worth talking to absolutely everyone, play with every oddity in your equipment. You may always discover something new.
What some people may not like is the amount of combat encounters. These are almost non-existent. The game is more about the exploration than combat. Many of these can be avoided as well. So this contributes to the perceived shortness of the game - it took me just above 30 hours on my first playthrough. But seeing as almost none of it is combat, I think there is quite a lot of content. But I personally think some more dungeon crawling could be fun. Having said that, the encounters there are are actuallu quite interesting - killing the enemy is not always the only solution. Also you may utilize environment in the fight.
So I think this is not a game for everyone, but if you want something fresh this is definetely worth trying. If you want more classical cRPG experience, this may not be for you.

This game is a physical embodiment of the word 'adventure' and really makes you feel like you exist inside Star Wars.

The player customisation, different lightsaber styles, and a range of force powers makes you feel like this is YOUR story.
- Three different lightsaber options: Single blade (with three different fighting styles), Dual blades, and Double blade
- Five saber crystal colours: Blue, Green, Orange (I replaced with a black crystal mod), Purple, and Gold/Yellow
- Five different species to play as all with customisable outfits, although Human is the only one playable in both genders
- Force powers like push & pull, heal, jumping, lightning, mind trick, life drain, speed/slow-mo, and more
I've played through it twice now (with a purple double blade and a green single blade) and plan to play it a third (with black and gold dual blades)
I haven't tried Multiplayer with other people yet, but I promise you after the singleplayer you'll find yourself craving for endless lightsaber battles. Multiplayer is where you'll want to go to set yourself up against dozens of AI opponents with changable skins.
My only downside is its length. I would have liked it to be a tad longer but it has the replayability there.
A must-have for Star Wars fans.

I am not the kind of player who dates everyone, I already had my interests on Damien and that was all I was interested in seeing, and that short amount of gameplay with such limited options, being boxed in as such a simple father that it was not relatable by any means, and limited conversation pieces (only 3-4), this game should be fleshed out much more before it could be worth the $15 cost.
Yes, GameGrumps and friends are good people and I can tell (really, the art and effects are gorgeous and the mini-games are a blast) that they tried really hard to make this work, but I think this is a prime example that a year's worth of making does not mean you will get even a month's play out of it.

I came into this reluctantly. I’ve tried a fair number of dating sims, and I’ve only like two of them. I tend to find them pretty tedious, so I was pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed DD.
The artwork is lovely and the storylines are endearing and often funny. I liked being able to customize my dad (just remember to go for a neutral expression unless you want to see you character grinning happily while your date talks about his deceased spouse).
When delving into more serious topics, DD handles them in a very sympathetic way without weighing the game down with too much pathos. I found the Hugo, Brian, and Damien branches particularly delightful. I was surprised by how much the game made me care about the children and some of the dad-kid stories were my favorite parts of the game. The environments are warm and make you want to come back to chill with your dad dates and their adorable offspring.
It’s a lovely, friendly, cute experience that makes for a nice respite from stressful daily living.
A few complaints:
- Hugo’s voice acting was not great. It sounded like they went into a random echo-y dorm room and recorded a guy’s half-a**ed responses. And that’s a shame because the writing on his arc is fantastic. I ended up taking my headphones out so I wouldn’t be distracted by the VA.
- There are a few bugs to be worked out. The background music drops out if you load a save during the game and I got the creepy twins bug, which was hilarious but distracting.
- I wish it were longer.
These complaints are pretty minor and don’t detract from an overall great experience.
If anything about DD intrigues you, you should check it out. It’s not a erotic game and it doesn’t involve much skill, but if you like to get to know interesting characters, I think you’ll appreciate it. If the idea of wooing the Game Grumps doesn’t appeal to you (I get it), don’t worry, their voices aren’t really noticable.
I hope the devs decide to make more of this game, but even if they don’t, I look forward to whatever they’re working on next.

Tentative thumbs up from me - I'm having a ton of fun with this thing, but if you're going to enjoy it highly depends on your priorities. If you like your games technically solid and with intricate game mechanics, you might want to wait for a sale or pass on this entirely. If you're just here for goofy puns and ador(k)able and memorable characters and generally just want to have a good time, you'll definitely get all of that here.
Good Things:
Most of the art is fantastic, the 'voice acting' (varying noises, some dialogue snippets) is not all that exciting but... y'know, it works. I kinda like it.
The characters are all amazing. I love all of them. Every single one. Not just the dads. Everyone. Yes, even That One.
A lot of things in this game made me feel genuine Emotions(TM) - and usually very pleasant ones. It's adorable and occasionally a bit corny and full of awesome bad puns and I love it - most of the routes are also genuinely sweet and heartwarming. Bonus: The Player Character is my favorite kind of protagonist: dorky and painfully awkward but also really funny and actually oddly relatable.
Bad Things:
Unity. Visual Novel. WHYYYYY. I mean, I'm sure it's a novel (ha!) idea that affords one a large degree of freedom, but (apart from the relatively meh minigames), this game had nothing that Ren'Py or something similar couldn't have handled just as well... while also giving the devs a template for auto-skip and save options that are not a pain to use. Because yep, auto-skip and savefiles kind of suck in this game.
Also, the player character graphics are... slightly awkward. Can I haz some pupils for my terrifyingly blank eyes, plz? Some very basic animation for the PC (smiling and not smiling, mostly) would have made more of the options a great deal more useful, too.
Neutral Things:
Relatively short, relatively basic. 15$ is a tad expensive for what it is, but I chose not to wait for a sale because I was too dang curious about this game. Note that my expectations were actually exceeded for once. Anyway, waiting for a sale might be prudent if you're not super eager to get this game.

With the game's price dropped now, I think it's worthy of a review now.
I got the game as a deluxe edition (in a deal which costs HALF of the full price!) which gives me Nuketown Zombies, Nuketown 2025 MP map, the soundtrack, and a free copy of World at War. I'll explain that later.
The SP [POTENTIAL SPOILERS]:
The story kind of picks off where Black Ops 1 left. Except, we're actually in the second cold war. At first I thought, why is BO2 even a thing? BO already has a non-cliffhanger ending, so I don't know what to expect for this. Apparently, I forgot some details, that later explains why the events in BO2 happens. The game still introduces flashbacks, but it also introduces to present-time missions too. I got slight problems with the timeline keep changing back and forth, but it does explain the story well.
This is the first CoD that introduces you to non-linear storyline. Which means that every decision you make has a difference. There are 4 potential endings that you can find, which adds replayability.
Last, but not least, the campaign gameplay. It is the best campaign of all CoD history gameplay-wise, period. Instead of getting fixed weapons, you can customize your loadout to your liking, even to perks. This adds freedom to players, even though at the end you will still have to throw out your weapons if you ran out of ammo. But that's not all - if you think you're just doing mindless killing, think again - you are now actually scored/evaluated at the end of every missions. The amount of people you kill (extra points for headshots) do actually count. This adds yet another replay value, you always want to get the highest score of all your friends. Well, it ends up you killing more, but at least it's a lot more meaningful unlike others. You also have challenges to do (10 per mission) to unlock stuff in campaign, adding yet another replay value. Then, you can replay the whole story with the currently unlocked weapons for a different experience, yet another replay value added.
Black Ops II has the most replay value of all CoD, following with CoD4 with their cheats.
The MP:
MP in CoD is the most important selling point for CoD, and BO2, while dying on the PC, still has a playable MP to a certain degree. I can't really say it's the best MP, but it did introduce some mechanics that later CoD games replicate, for example the ever-popular Pick 10 system, in which you can fill up 10 slots with items that you want. This has some flaws, sure (for example, a 6-perk no attachment R870 is OP AF), but most importantly you have more freedom and adds a more specific niche to your classes.
The guns in MP are well balanced, and while some guns are pretty bad, they're actually good in a degree. Guns in this game actually have a specific role that it can fit, for example, the R870 I mentioned is very overpowered in CQC, but useless at very long range. The MP7 is similar - very deadly at close range, but good luck hitting people at med-long range.
The ZM:
Treyarch is iconic with its zombie mode which started way back from World at War (aka CoD5). Sadly, the earlier maps in this installment leaves something to be desired. TranZit is way too big for most people, including me. Die Rise is too confusing to navigate. Nuketown Zombies is great and all, but didn't really live up to the hype. Later DLCs do add good ZM maps, though. Mob of the Dead, Buried, and Origins are all great.
The Bonuses:
If you get this in a deal, then you're very lucky! The extra maps are very great, also you get a free copy of WaW, which is
due to zombie modding being trending in the last couple of years. I suggest you get the Deluxe Edition just for WaW and the extra others.
Overall:
Black Ops II deserves a
in my book. Few last CoDs have been quite disappointing for me, but Black Ops II returned big-time. This game still doesn't pass CoD4 or MW2, but it is money well spent (especially with the deal!)
If you feel like getting this, I suggest you get it in a deal, but if you REALLY need it now, go get it!

Tides of Numenera is great game if you like to read, you don't even have to fight 99% of time. This is the main resemblance to Planescape and good job done.

Bored already.
Uses Cook's horridly insipid Cypher RPG-Lite character system, which does not translate into a CRPG well at all and should be reserved for in-person casual role-playing sessions among gaming dilettentes.
Oh, there's a morality system? I thought it was telling me the color of my parachute.

Addendum: I don't know why people are hating on this game so badly, honestly. Maybe somebody can it explain to me. This is one of the very few times where I think professional critics get it right. I think this might have to do with the backer community feeling like they were underpromised, and maybe they were. I was not a big part of the community so I don't know. I didn't mind the delay of the game and while I am not happy about them wasting resources porting the game to consoles (I think the publisher footed the bill on this one) in the end if the company uses the profits gained to make future CRPGs like this one I will not complain.
IN SUMMARY: this game gives me the Torment feels.
The setting is weird. The characters are interesting and believable, in my opinion. The game is very epic and the world gives you a sense of history.
I enjoyed the writing, although it can get a little obtuse or flowery at times.
If you are impatient or don't like reading, this game is not for you.
If you love weird science fantasy and pseudo-philosophical characters, you will like this game.
The combat is passable, and clearly not the focus anyways.
Everything about it feels right. I wish it was longer, of course, but for what it is it is a real treat.
The world is responsive to your decisions, although I definitely wish it + the main story were much moreso. There was one quest where sleeping at an inn meant that innocent and endearing characters died, which floored me when I later discovered their grizzly remains. Failure often reslts in very interesting consequences, some good some bad.
The whole thing clearly has a ton of thought put into it.
The OG Torment was also bashed on release, but in my book this game will stand the tests of time. I love it and am very glad that I got to back it. Would back again, will back sequal.
Haters gonna hate. Whatever.
Please, inExile, make more.

This is a tough one. tl;dr I *would* recommend the game, but it comes with a few caveats in particular: don't buy it at the present price. they're having a laugh.
The details.
The bad
1. As a backer I was *really* disappointed with the difference between what was proposed in the kickstarter campaign and what actually ended up in the final product. I tried to keep an open mind when playing but it still did leave a sour taste.
2. The companions are mostly... kinda uninspired. In PS:T you could choose 5 companions out of 7 and I always stuggled deciding who not to take in my party. Here you could choose 3 out of 6, so you think it would be harder, but I had no such trouble - especially since you can't have Aligern and Callistege in a party together so that rules out a bunch of party combinations.
3. The character models are kinda... bad. In particular I often found the Last Castoff's running annimation pretty goofy looking.
4. A lot of the character options seemed pretty cosmetic (backed up by some videos I've watched). Tides, foci, descriptors... just don't seem to have very much impact on how the game actually plays out.
5. The UI felt incomplete to the point where I tried to avoid using it.
6. It's simply not as good as PS:T although it's not a bad effort.
7. It felt like there was a real lack of item progression in the game, and the effects that the various damage types did were never very clear to me. I think I changed my gear like... twice.
8. The price, IMO it's well not worth what they are currently asking for it ($74.95NZD at the time of writing).
The good
----------
1. The Mark Morgan music is on point again. Like that guy is fantastic.
2. The world is well imagined, I loved following through asking about everything and seeing the backstory piece together during the game.
3. The companion Rhin is great, whoever wrote her (kidding I know it was Patrick Rothfuss) is a champion.
4. The level backgrounds were bautiful.
5. Did I say I really liked the Numenera setting? I hope they or other groups write games set using the system in the future.
Now I know there's more bad than good but I honestly felt the good passed the bad in terms of my overall enjoyment of the game. However if you haven't played Wasteland II or Pillars of Eternity definitely go and play those first because they are both better games. If they haven't satisfied your itch then I would definitely say give Tides of Numenera a go after those, and the price coming down a tad.

I played the original Torment back in the day multiple times over multiple years. I was a diehard fan of the game, delving into several of the nooks and crannies of that wonderful universe.
I can't speak to anyone else, but I love this game.
The Numenera setting does a great job of keeping the weirdness and mystique of the Planescape univserse. I greatly enjoyed the writing, the worldbuilding, and the storytelling.
One of the things I liked most about this game was how easily you could go through it with little to no combat. Even the fights that were there could be approached in a way that involved fleeing/problem solving with no actual fighting. I really dug that.
I will say, however, that this is a wordy game, somewhere between a Choose Your Own Adventure game like Sorcery and the new age iso-RPGs like Pillars. This combination was practlically geared for me, but it might not be for you.
Also, the mechanics in some circumstances can be quirky, though not overbearingly so. I would have liked the ability to save while in a conversation or a "Mere" (a choose your own adventure style diversion that occur occasionally in the game). I personally like the turn based mechanics they introduced into the system, and likewise really like the streamlined Numenera system for skills that they use, but it may not be some people's cup of tea.
That said, I'd say this compares to the original Torment, which had its own quirks in converting the Infinity engine used in Baldur's gate to work in a much more character focused game. They both have a few areas that could use refiniement, but the other parts of the game more than make up for it.
I truly hope this game does well, I think it deserves to do so. I much prefer this character heavy type game over InXile's (still good) squad-based Wasteland series. I hope they make more games in this world, and continue to refine this particular system.
I heartily recomend this to anyone who enjoyed the first Torment game.

I really wanted to like this game, and was really excited to play it but honestly for me it was a huge let down.
There are some bugs in the system that really took me out of the experience. For example at the beginning you have to choose if you had a wife or husband previously. I chose wife but time and time again they were refered to as 'dad' or 'your father', just a small thing but quite irritating when I was given a choice. I also had some really weird stuff with Robert's route at the end where he got mad at me for trying to sleep with him, and I did nothing of the kind. It's like the games branches aren't working properly (another example is my character asking him about Val, and in that route he never told me about her...) It just takes you out of the experience and leaves you quite confused. You think this kind of thing would have been ironed out in testing.
The entire game became quite formulaic to me as just one wrong answer can give you a bad mark and apparently a bad ending, so I took to saving before every answer to make sure I got hearts for it. Going back and loading and saving for answers that seem really inconsiquential is a silly way to play a game like this but I really didn't want to have to skip through all the scenes again and again to get the good ending because of one wrong answer.
My main gripe however is that the game just feels...hollow. I really applaud the game for its inclusion, but the vast majority of the characters are really tropey and without any depth. The dates with them are super short and seem to go nowhere exciting. Honestly...I think the plots are really dull. They just do not DO anything. To have a characters entire story be 'I secretly like a sport that millions love worldwide' is not really the heartwrenching, romantic plot you expect from a dating sim. There is no build up to these romances, they come out of nowhere almost every time and feel forced and unnatural. There are so many things that are mentioned that seem important then never come up again, and a lot of the routes are very similar. In fact they ALL end on the exact same ending which kind of makes it feel like the whole thing was pointless to begin with. I'm not expecting Shakespeare or anything, but i've played dating sims which have made me tremble with anticipation and cry with sadness for way less money. (Tbh I wish they put that 'secret ending' in, because at least that sounds exciting, and all the hints for it are in the game.)
It's like they couldn't decide where they wanted this game to go or be  - funny, serious, sexy?? So instead it's a mishmash of all those things and all of them fail. Some of the dialogue is funny but it's not sidesplittingly funny as the situations don't give rise to anything that could be. Some of the scenes seem like they might be sexy then they cut to black. Moments feel like they might be serious and finally going somewhere, but then they're over in a click. It just feels rushed, unfinished and wholly unsatisfying. I can't even say it's TERRBLE cause it doesnt do anything extreme enough to be terrible, it's just dull dull dull, and in a way, I think that's far worse. :/

So, looking at the rest of the store page, there are a lot of bad reviews regarding the episodic content system and the wait between episodes, not to mention the lukewarm introduction in the form of the Paris Fashion Show, however, this review is based on content up to Sapienza.
TL;DR:
+ Graphically stunning
+ Hours of replayability
+ Living, breathing gamespace (Sapienza) with a real feeling of a busy town centre.
+ Vibrant storytelling without clumsy narrative.
+ Freedom to explore the game level with interpolated linearity. (Sapienza)
+ Encourages the player to re-approach the scenario with a different method or style.
- Episodic content is bad for those looking for a solid game to play.
- Disappointing introductory mission in terms of freedom/structure. (Paris)
- Benchmarks poorly on older systems. Recommend a GTX 950 + with sufficient memory.
- A few bugs here and there, which seem to occasionally get patched, mostly physics bugs.
- Have to play through the mission completing challenges in order to obtain certain features always afforded in earlier games (such as the TAC SMG (silenced)).
I've been playing the HITMAN series for 6 years, ever since my friend introduced me to Blood Money (I went back and played all the previous games too), and I get a lot of joy out of replaying missions, and exploring all the possibilities for the mission - without a doubt in my mind, this latest HITMAN game has proven to have the most intricate level of detail and possibilities to progress through the mission, and find entertainment in trying to repeat the process with different methods.
Paris was disappointing, in the same way that one would open the box for a toy, only to find it was smaller than you thought it would be, and that a lot of the parts don't move. With such detail put into the map, it felt like such a shame that you couldn't really take the time to explore it in peace and appreciate the gamespace the studio have created.
Sapienza has taken the game a few steps in the right direction - the way the game should have went from the start - 47 starts in the heart of the bustling town, reading a newspaper on a bench, looking across at the front gates to a large mansion complex. Unlike Paris, there is nothing to force you onwards into the objective - you can wander the streets, listen to the residents, learn the thoughts of the people in this small town. The story-telling in Sapienza is possibly the best self-contained plot in the entirety of the series and paints 47's mission in a different light - a relative hero, in the face of a horrific threat to humanity. A stroll down the winding streets can lead you to the marina, a high steepled church, cliffside cafes and more, and as you look around this well painted canvas, you begin to see opportunities - the vantage point from the church, the sewer access of the marina, the back passages of the cafes and beyond. There are many, many more secrets to see and opportunities to find, the challenges to complete, and of course, the obligatory gun rampage playthroughs. This will consume countless hours for me.
Then there is the matter of the maps still to come - if they have this same level of freedom to explore from the beginning and less linearity, then the only things that can really go wrong are the story-telling, and map design. I am looking forward to the next episode.
On the matter of episodes, as an MMO player, I think the episodic content for this game is fantastic. In a single session, if I play through a mission once, that is maybe an hour or so, plus the escalations, and custom contracts, which I'll play over a few days, and then probably revisit the game a few times during the month. In the rest of the time, I play other games, and will come back to HITMAN for a break every couple of days for an hour to break up the monotony of MMO grinding - this is great for me. For people who bought the game thinking they would get one straight 10-hour blitz, there was sure to be disappointment, but for those of you still looking to purchase the game, please check out some video reviews of Sapienza before making your decision, as the introduction package is merely that, and it does not show the potential of this game.

Having now completed what must be about 80% of the story, it seems like my initial concerns were well-founded.
In a nutshell, this is a very nice rough draft.
Where to begin? Let's start with the choices. Most of the time, they feel inconsequential. Granted, characters die, NPCs can be killed or made friends, but never did I feel like the death of a party member (I lost one person) or letting Qorro live changed anything momentous.
Skills and abilities didn't seem to matter much mostly because there are only about a dozen fights through the whole game. The advancement system seems very compelling, and I was excited to progress. But then I never got a chance to use my new talents.
Balance seems off, too. Either I found myself overwhelmed with up to a dozen foes with twice my hit points, or I was just talking my way through everything. I like that enemies could be spoken to during a crisis, but that only happened twice, maybe three times. The worst part about being outnumbered wasn't the frustration of difficulty, but how slow and repetetive the battles got. I'm looking at you, corpuscular maws.
Plus the game feels short, the pacing is tedious (if well-narrated), the voice acting is confusingly sporadic, crisis instructions were vague at best, and most of the game is the script to a cut scene that budget didn't allow to be rendered.
It's got great ideas. It has a fun world and character advancement system. It just doesn't do anything with them that makes any of it exciting. Had I spent $15, I wouldn't complain (or replay). At $45, I have to warn others to wait for a discount or a better option from another developer.

Recommend with reservations. I am glad I bought it, but I would read some reviews first if I was on the fence, as it might not be exactly what you are expecting.
Pros:
- A well done story and interesting locales and writing.
- Something different.
- Nice to see a different RPG ruleset (even if not faithfully implemented)
Cons:
-I really wanted to see a computer version of the Pen and Paper rules of Numenera.
Unfortunately, this is not that faithful of an adaptation. They added hitpoints, rather than having the damage taken from  your stat pools. This seems like something that could have easily been kept, simply by balancing the game differently (or even keeping everything the same, and altering the pool totals a little)- I don't see why this really needed to be changed.
Some other things, like the decision to not interrupt combat for pool spends on defense (in real rules players roll and spend points when attacking and defending) I can understand..but I still think it could have worked.
-I'm ok with it being a dialogue heavy game, I just wish there were more opportunities to actually use all of the abilities you accrue in the game. Let's face it, despite being a game about "exploration" and "discovery" and only offering XP for discoveries and solving problems, not kills--the pen and paper rules are very tilted torwards a combat focused game. Most of the Focii and abilities are combat related. The same with this PC game, but there just isn't enough combat to justify any of it. Also, most of the cyphers in the game are combat items, but you'll never find a reason to use them.
-Game is way too easy and linear, I feel like some kind of wilderness area connecting the three main hubs of the game should have been included. As it is now, you are railroaded through a few small areas where the goal of a quest is often only 50 feet or so away from the various quest givers.  Also, spending points is never reallly something to worry about. I've never had a test in the game where there wasn't someone available in my party with enough points to ensure success on any challenge (even without abusing the local inn to regain points.)
-I played this as someone who is very familiar with the source material. I'm not sure if I would have enjoyed it as much if I wasn't familiar with all of the lore namedropping that the game employs. Not sure how all of the lingo from such a unique setting works when it's not always explained.
------I know there are a lot of cons here, I just think this could have been something so much greater. I probably won't feel the need to play it more than once. yet...still was enjoyable the first time.
------Caves of Qud, despite being an altogether different setting, is probably what I'll return to when I feel like playing something Numenera-ish in the future. Check it out if you want to scavenge the remains of long lost civilizations in a science-fantasy type setting.

The gameplay is quite simple, one of the white block must touch one of the lower beams to beat the level. If one white block falls off the screen, the level is restarted. To clear a level you need to use the physics and the black blocks which you can destroy by clicking on it.
There are mostly two ways to win every level :
The puzzle one in which you use the right combination of blocks
The quick reflex one in which you act fast making the right choices
Despite its simple gameplay the game tends to be a little challenging by adding news blocks, beams and even boulders. (about 9 different objects)
Each block have their unique abilities: White for not moving on its own, Black for being destructible and Red for getting rid of it. Yes, you need to dispose of every red block in order to finish the level.
The only mixed part of this game in addition to not having any save file is the 3D feature in a 2D puzzle game. This will make some parts funny and a little more challenging as every collision may move a white block next to the edge. Only one level was kind of insane because a white block almost always fall off the screen regardless to what you did. This level was quite short so after many tries, I finally beat it.
Finally, the final level is quite challenging.

I can't really recommend this game. I mean, the concept is not really bad; it's a simple physics puzzle game in which you have to get the white coloured blocks to touch a platform, and there are other coloured blocks with their own properties; it even introduces you to the new blocks slowly, so that you can learn their properties without a tutorial. In that regard, the game does a good job. However, I'd say the execution is rather poor. Sure, it's entertaining enough, for the half hour it lasts (yes, it's that short), but it has some issues. The main issue is that while it gives an impression that the gameplay is contained to a 2D plane, the blocks can actually move in a third dimension, leading them to sometimes fall off the platform when they technically shouldn't. Another issue I encountered is that the physics seem to be a bit random at times and, in fact, I'll admit I couldn't beat the last level; not because I didn't know how to solve it, but because the physics wouldn't work the way they should. One more thing, it doesn't save your progress; while it's not much of an issue given its short length, it's still an issue.
In short: don't get this game; there are better alternatives out there.

Since it really only took 30 minutes, this game is a very short game; though it justifies the shortness with the cheap price tag. The game provides you a very gradual learning curve for the different blocks and by the end you are competent enough to finish the game without trouble. The music was not too bad, and the game itself played out pretty smooth. There was only one part where I found a bug, but I was easily able to solve the puzzle in another way.

As far as local-multiplayer arena games go this game is OK. It definitely works and has everything you'd expect from a game like this but beyond that...
The game-play is solid. characters move how you'd expect them to, the shotguns are satisfying to use and the power-ups all do things. (to be honest we never fully grasped the power-ups)
As far as my groups sessions went the deeper levels of play essentially revolved around gambling with shotgun distance. the close you are to the opponent when you fire the more of your pellets will pierce your opponents flesh. However the closer you get the more danger you are in as well. Making use of your shield and the recovery time between shots is the most important aspect to winning. You can also run out of ammo so playing it 'safe' means running out of bullets more often and having to expose yourself to pickup more.
Art and music are fine and befitting of the theme although I must admit that the background, characters, and stages blend a little too much at times which did lead to my death. Bullets especially can be hard to see in certain spots.
Everything works and the game flow is certainly there but the game just seems to be missing its 'thing'; nothing about the game stands out as being unique to only this game. All the characters are exactly the same meaning the only thing that changes the game are the stages themselves. there are quite a few modes but it still doesn't help this game from feeling like just another local arena game. I also think pretty much every hype moment will be experienced within a couple plays. Around our tenth game we weren't really surprised by anything that happened.
I'd say if you get it on sale or in a bundle its worth a shot but there are plenty of more innovative arena games out there.

Story wise, the game is great.  Unfortunately it had an abortion of a leveling system tacked on to it, and implimented pretty poorly.  The same dozen or so guns show up over and over again, with random stats depending on their level, and this determines difficulty.  A great gun will drop, and make the difficulty trivial for a little bit, but if nothing new drops the difficulty quickly compounds.  Shields suffer from this too, but you generally don't notice until something one-shots you.
The level design itself is very good looking, but there are no shortage of invisible walls.  The levels also turn into a series of unavoidable ambushes, because the monsters spawn in after you start shooting the bait.  I guess it makes it easier on memory or something, not having a ton of monsters wandering around when you don't need them, but it makes every fight very predictable and tedious.  The game is also a terrible offender for paid DLC, a trend gamers everywhere need to oppose.
So yeah, if the leveling system were removed and all the items normalized, and if the designers learned to make fights more diverse than dropping psycho's on top of you, game would be amazing.  As it is, with all the paid content, not even sure if the game is complete.

Torment: Tides of Numenera is a spiritual successor to the original Planescape Torment game. In this case, spiritual successor means that it follows the same sort of weird setting, wordy, and philosophical story that the original had. It is not otherwise connected in characters, story or gameplay, so you don't have to have played the original to enjoy this.
While there are plenty of fairly pretty (but not cutting edge) on-screen graphics thrown around, the game relies heavily on text to get its message across. If you don't enjoy reading through a lot of text, you probably won't enjoy the game.
Combat (which can usually be avoided if you talk your way out of it) is in the game, and can be hit-and-miss. If you've got the right party setup or you figure out the best way to use any environmental tools provided in the combat area, it can be pretty fun. If you have a couple of members who aren't good fighters, it can be far less enjoyable. It does get easier (and more enjoyable) as you level things like the ingame 'edges'. Combat is turn-based, not real-time-with-pause like Baldurs Gate or Pillars of Eternity, so it can run a bit slower than fighting in those systems. There also isn't really any trash-mobs to fight - all fights are usually important to a storyline, and so there's a limited amount. If you enjoy regular combat in your rpgs, this game is probably not going to excite you.
The story takes a bit of time to get into as you get familiar with all of the terminology and the weirdness being thrown at you, but does seem to click after a couple of hours and become fairly absorbing,
One thing it does do well, much like the original Torment game, is transport you to an unfamiliar rpg world that doesn't play to the usual rules of orcs and dragons. It's wordy, to the point where some may consider it too wordy, but if you enjoy a highly descriptive game then you should find something to enjoy here. Overall, while it has its flaws it does seem to be a fairly good spiritual successor to Planescape Torment. I don't regret putting money into the kickstarter for it all those years ago.
