Disclaimer: I do NOT reccomend the game at its current pricing. Furthermore, after much thought, I do not reccomened it for what it claims to be. This is no Planescape: Torment and it is not a worthy successor. Nevertheless, there is something worth the time it takes to play, even if it is deeply flawed. Below is my first formal attempt at a review, which I have tried to do indepth and professionally as possible.
At the conclusion, there will be a numerical score with a breakdown for my reasoning behind it.
---
Background
---
I backed this game for a sum of forty dollars the week it was announced. I discovered the kickstarter just as I was finishing Planescape: Torment, the last of the great CRPG classics that I was cleaning out of my backlogue. Starting with Baldurs Gate, I have gone through that entire series, the Neverwinters, the Icewind Dales, Arcanum, and had also played entirety of the newer roleplaying games of both high and low prominence, such as Mass Effect, Dragon Age, Jade Empire, Inquisitor, Knights of the Old Republic, and was also following the development of Wasteland 2, Pillars of Eternity, Age of Decadence, and so on and so forth.
I was one of the cautiously surprised wave surfers of the "age of incline" or the "new golden age of RPGs." And Planescape: Torment had just become the crown jewel and the capstone of that period of my life before the new era began.
Should a developer or InXile affiliate read this, I have a personal note. This was my first Kickstarter I ever participated in, and I was very hesitant to lay down that much (or any) money for any project. While my tier was low as far as backers go, it was a lot of money for me, considering that I was funding my own education at the time and came from a poor background. So I placed a lot of value in this game. During the years it took for T:TON to be developed, I went through multiple rough patches where suicide seemed to be the answer. Yet thought that persisted in my mind when I came close to doing something drastic was that I would never see the return on this monetary investment, and I didn't want to die after wasting thirty five ♥♥♥♥ing bucks. So yeah. I'm not claiming T:TON saved my life. It didn't. I had other reasons or pulling through in the end, but it was one of many minor things that kept me going.
---
Development, Production, and Publishing
---
Hype was generated through regular Kickstart updates and YouTube videos with lofty promises, but I have always been a pessimist and I decided early to not buy in. Many did, however, and ended up donating even more.
In the months to come, major cuts of important goals were promsied, but never mentioned. These were things that people donated for with expectation of their deliverance. It would have been forgivable if they had been straightforward and transparant about it, but they were not. A backer had to discover it and confront them before it was admitted.
An apology is owed to the backers. This is a shameful incident. Luckily, they managed to salavage (from whatever unknown difficulty and strife was responsible for these cuts) a decent game that delivers an excellent story.
They acceped a publishing contract with Techland  who, if I have the story correct, was responsible for the decision to port it to XBox-One and PS4, and footed the bill for the ports. The game was promised to be optimized for PC. In the end, it was not.
Of note, the Italians were also screwed over and never got a translation, as they were promised.
In the end, the hype:delivery ratio would make Todd Howard proud.

It seems there are two polar opposites in the reviews. I say both the positive AND negative reviews are correct.
Gameplaywise this is one of the best Hitman games yet. it's a true return to the sandbox like levels of Blood Money. and the game allows you to turn off all, some or none of the handholding gameplay mechanics making it a true and challenging experience for those that want it. The feature that sticks out the most is the oppurtinities.
Think of Oppurtunities as a list of about 10 or so different preset ways to kill a target. These oppurtunities are started by something like:
e.g. you overhear two waitors talk about the prefered cocktail that youor target drinks
Depending on what you want to play you can have the game set waypoints to take you through the oppurtunity.
e.g. Marking waitor disguise, then rat poison
And so on until you kill the target.
However you can turn this all off and explore the maps with practically no HUD and come across the oppurtunities and have to find the waypoints yourself.
The other big plus of this game is the maps. There are only three maps so far with one being released per month.
This is where the controversy lies. The maps are brilliant so far. each one better than the last. Particularally with Episode 2 the map feels natural. it doesn't feel like a sandbox, it feels like an actual world where you have to work your way to kill the target.
BUT why couldn't they have just waited.Before the announcement of this game we haven't really been asking for a Hitman game. Squenix could have waited and released a game with 12+ maps and tonnes of content for a standard AAA price and no-one would have complained.
Basically for what there is there is a LOT to do. But there are only a few maps, with more planned each month.
If you want your Hitman fix get the full experience now and if the episodes are as good as Episode 2, you will likely have the best Hitman game ever and you will be more than satisfied.
If you aren't really too desperate for Hitman you could wait until all the episodes are released and probably get the game for a lower price.
OR if you have some disposable income get the intro pack and see if the game is to your liking. If it is get the upgrade pack. If it isn't don't

This latest iteration of HITMAN feels like a must-have for fans of the series, and I would recommend it to anyone else who enjoys stealth games. There's a lot of variety here in the current levels, and the gameplay is deep and engaging.
I've played every HITMAN game, and Blood Money has always been the high point of the series for me. I enjoyed the increased narrative in Absolution, but they really lost out when it came to gameplay. However, HITMAN is the best of both. The levels are large and very 'sandboxy', with lots of approaches and methods open to the player.
I've really enjoyed my time with the game so far, and I'd highly recommend it to any fan of the series, or anyone looking for an interesting and varied stealth game experience.
As for the episodic nature, I personally am fine with it. The levels so far are really large and take about 2 - 4 hours to get a first decent 'basic' playthrough done, and completing the mission in a variety of ways unlocks new equipment, starting locations, drop-off caches, etc that enable you to try and plan the 'perfect' hit. Having the updates drop on a regular basis keeps the content interesting and frequent enough that it is enjoyable.
Season One's content is now available in it's entirety.
Two smaller levels designed as 'simulations', to teach you the basics and get you up to speed. Even so, these missions are fairly roomy (especially the second one), and give you lots to play with.
The first mission proper, this sees 47 attending a fashion show to eliminate two high profile targets. The mansion is expansive, with service staff working hard behind the scenes and in the basement areas, the fashion show on the first floor, and a secret auction taking place on the top floor. This level really starts to showcase the scale of the HITMAN levels and your options within them.
Off to Italy in this mission, where we have another two targets to eliminate in a grand manor, and a deadly secret to destroy in a hidden lab underground. The level is even more expansive than the Paris mission, including a large chunk of the town of Sapienza to wander, a morgue and church, shopping area, pier, sewers, the manor is divided into several large buildings including an observatory, plus the ruins of a castle at the back of the manor. The lab area requires a keycard to enter (or the use of noisy explosives), there are a multitude of 'zones' that you can access with different disguises (kitchen staff, gardeners, security, lab scientists, priests...). This feels like, so far, the best mission a HITMAN game has had.
For me Marrakesh is the low-point of this season of HITMAN. The level isn't awful, and there's plenty to do, but for me the level loses major points in terms of structure. You begin in the middle of a maze of streets. At one end of this maze is one target located within a Swedish consulate, and at the other end is your other target hiding out in a derelict school. There's little to do in the streets imbetween each end of the level (although a few opportunities are present), and these areas basically exist just to pad out and provide a little flavour. Whilst other missions feel like they offer a wide variety of ways into each location and a lot of opportunities, Marrakesh felt limited and repetitive. You need to rely on just a couple of entrances to each location at either end of the level only, and once inside the play area is relatively restricted, even once disguised. Visually interesting and varied, but a major disappointment to me in terms of sandbox play.
Off to Bangkok, to the Himmapan Hotel, a glorious little sandbox. You arrive, and can check in as 'Mr Rieper', an alias of 47's. The hotel comprises of two multi-floor buildings divided by an atrium. One of these buildings is open as usual, whilst the other is closed to the public due to pesticide spraying on the lower floors and a pop group have temporarily converted the upper suites into a recording area. Most of the suites here require a security keycard to access, so some sneakiness is required to obtain them, or to bypass them entirely. The two targets each occupy a different side of the hotel, although opportunities can pull them out of their 'native' environment. This level is visually spectacular and you really feel like the hotel is a working building with each group of NPC's going about their duty (hotel cleaning and desk staff, security, cooks, gardeners, etc). This level is an absolute highlight.
Here we see an increase in difficulty, as there are four targets this time spread across a militia-occupied Colorado farm. There is no 'civilian' area here and 47 must hide at all times or assume a military disguise. The areas of the farm are distinct and interesting, with portions being used for training drills, target practice, bomb creation and testing, and a farmhouse with a hostage held down below. The targets are each interesting and memorable, some with great narrative elements, and there are a couple of ways to get to them each through the opportunities (alongside the many ways you could improvise dealing with them). I had a great time wandering this map and experimenting with how to quietly and effectively deal with each target. A wonderful sandbox to play in, with a bit of care.
Season One's finale takes us to a private medical hospital located in the snowy mountains of Japan. Due to the secretive and restrictive nature of the facility, you must make do without any equipment when starting out (at least initially), which really helps increase the difficulty of this mission. Additionally, patients rooms are access via RFID tags within the gowns each patient wears, providing opportunities to subdue and access other areas. The medical facility is striking in design and visuals, and the glimpses of snowy mountainside exteriors and the zen garden area really compliment the stark, clean interiors.
Oh, and that skybox really is gorgeous, one hell of a view and beautiful paper lanterns drift by, a great touch.
Somehow Hokkaido feels a bit smaller, more personal than the missions that came before, but it is still an interesting finale for Season One, and it is a fitting and enjoyable challenge.
Two bonus episodes were released in summer, one for Sapienza and the other for Marrakesh. Each cuts out a small portion of the level, sets it at night and blocks off the exits, making a smaller sandbox area for a new narrative to play out. Sapienza sees a film crew recording a sci-fi blockbuster in the town square and 47 is hired to take out the director, whilst Marrakesh sees the action focus around the under-utilised markets area.
Whilst it's interesting to see these locations reworked for nighttime and with some fairly major overhauling of the levels, I didn't find the bonus episodes particularly engaging as they are so much smaller than the original levels. As a bonus they are fine, but nothing I'd rush to experience over the core experience, I found many of the vanilla levels 'escalation' missions (content that uses the existing levels but has new targets, conditions and complications) far more engaging.
Season Two of HITMAN has been announced. It will launch from the same game client, adding another series of new levels and challenges to the game, allowing all current unlocked content to be utilised. I will update the review as-and-when it arrives.

Whether you're wanting to play this game for the jokes and parody, or if you're really interested in dating some dads, this game works out either way. Tons of jokes and references, very funny the whole way through. Charming and interesting characters and story. I was originally leery of the game since it's first and foremost a parody of romance visual novels, and I legit just wanted to date some dads, but I can assure you that no matter which of the two experiences you're looking for, you can enjoy either (or both!) with no problem.
You can date a mustache teacher so this is already better than every other game on Steam. But I was pleasantly surprised with the quality and content of the game. I laughed a lot and couldn't stop talking about it with my friends, and I fell in love with some dads in the process.
A single playthrough without skipping dialogue and stuff probably takes 1-2 hours depending on how much content you see (you can skip a lot of stuff by just choosing to eat or sleep instead of interacting with people).  I spent my first playthrough "role-playing" things I'd really choose IRL, and then after that it took me three playthroughs to clear Hugo's scenario properly. Before playing, I wasn't sure if I was going to really even bother with all the stories and characters, but now I want to see every last scene and line of dialogue in the game for myself.
Also, if you're an actual fan of the romance simulation genre, this game is definitely not one despite the subtitle -- it's just a visual novel with a romance theme.
There are a couple of downsides, but in my opinioin they are minimal and don't take away from the enjoyment of the game (though fixing/adding them would improve the game vastly):
Firstly, the script needs proofreading. Like, badly needs it. Fortunately there's not a lot of really jarring stuff, but if you're a literal reader like me, you'll have to reread things several times or just be taken out of the experience because of the abysmal punctuation (missing commas everywhere, apostrophes where they shouldn't be, periods instead of question marks, etc.) and inconsistencies (is it DadBook or Dadbook? Who knows, they stylize it as both. And DADBOOK, too!) and just cringe-worthy elementary school errors like not capitalizing the word "English."
Secondly, there are no CG stills or special scenes, other than a single prize image for each dad upon completion of their scenario. Everything else is told completely through portraits and bottom-screen text. So if you're hoping for a gallery of cute scenes, you're not going to find it. This was a bit of a disappointment since that kind of thing is a staple in the genre, but I understand the burden of creating all that artwork, plus the game is tons of fun without them. It's short and varied enough, and with minigames, that you don't really need these rewards throughout the game as a break anyway. But I still would have loved to have seen a cool illustration for each date, maybe by getting the S rank or something.
Lastly, the voices are not so great. They have some funny lines (took me like a dozen times of hearing it to finally get the "goosebumps" one lol) and the voices are just little small clips here and there, so they don't hurt the game experience; I just wish they were better, and honestly I would like to imagine Hugo with a sexy voice (I thought the kid doing his voice was just some kind of weird "announcer" at the end of the date, like a game narrator... took me forever to realize it was even supposed to be Hugo because the voice was so unfitting). Being said, Joseph's "hmmm" sounds make my knees weak. So it's not all bad. Just... I really love Hugo, OK? XD I want him to be PERFECT.
Anyway,  I don't think any of those three things are worth avoiding the game. Great humor, great characters, charming and cute stories, tons of cheese, and of course a harem of hot dads. If you like any of those things, you'll probably enjoy the game. Also props to the devs for making the cast diverse and the character creation inclusive.
ALSO VERY MANY BONUS POINTS FOR USING THE PROPER NAMES FOR THE MUSTACHES. I can't tell you how much admiration I have for that!
Anyawy, I usually like to 100% a game before reviewing it so I can write the review based on the full experience, but I just really loved this game so much that I felt like I had to write a review for it now. I've only played Hugo's route in full (and like, 4 times LOL) and then barely waded into a couple of the other dads. With what I've seen so far, I can't imagine the rest of the game being bad. If somehow my opinion chagnes later, I'll just update the review.

Don't let my time played fool you (currently sitting at 29 hours), because I played for thousands of hours before acquiring it on Steam. This game was very much my life, my source of satisfaction and very much needed escapism, for the most formative years of my life.
I nominated Jedi Academy for the "Test of Time" Award because, as of November 2016, there still isn't a game that comes anywhere close to the complexity, depth, spectacle and accessibility of its lightsaber combat. There's a good reason that people spent years learning the intricacies of a single lightsaber loadout, let alone the other two (two sabers, and dual-ended) and the three styles (Fast, Medium, Strong) of each. This game is astonishing because of how fantastic its combat remains.
I mean, it's also got everything else going for it - enjoyable, memorable maps; distinct, unique Force powers; a delightfully cheesy campaign with surprising twists and turns; a great rhythm and sense of pacing; thousands upon thousands of mods...
To me, this is as good as Star Wars games get when it comes to the action genres. There hasn't been anything like it since then. It's very much a product of its time, with the freeform multiplayer, open singleplayer levels, a vaguely Quake-esque undercurrent tinting the game's combat and flow, and more. But looking beyond the sentimental attachment I have to it, Jedi Academy remains the epitome of third person melee combat, and as such, it fully deserves the "Test of Time" Award.

Spec Ops: the Line is far from great. The timing of its release was great, though, and did a lot to cement its relevance. I mean, when COD and its clones dominated the market, they were just itching to be brought down a few notches. And this game definitely chipped away at their image.
Spec Ops is a re-imaginging of Heart of Darkness, a novella by Joseph Conrad. It's central premise is that man, for all of his ability to do great things, is capable of terrible evil, no matter how advanced or civilized he or his contemporaries may consider himself. Spec Ops captures this beautifully by having you commit atrocities as you traverse soaring skyscrapers.
But the gameplay is bad, and the game itself is a slog. Heart of Darkness was a well written book, and the movie it inspired, Apocalypse Now, was well filmed. They were both technical and artistic achievements, the finest forms of their media.
This game is just an emotional achievement that falls short of its predecessors. When people forget about jingoistic FPSes this game will lose relevance because it completely relies on it its story, little else, and that story has been told in better ways. And I guarentee a better game will come out, with just as good timing and similar themes. I still recommend it, but it's really not that well done; it's simply a well-timed reminder of the horror people are capable of.

Well, I recently played and finished this game, and I must say it hasn't aged well. The things the developers tried to do with this game are similar to many other games that do them better.
The story is weirdly heavy-handed and disjointed, with your two supporting characters inconsistently swapping roles of being your conscience or urging you to brutality. There's a "twist" at the end, which either doesn't make sense or is just trivial. For "moral choices" and emotional gut-punch storylines in gaming, Walking Dead or Papers Please do a much better job.
Combat is jannnnkkkkyyyyyy as heck. For FPS games, there's a lot of getting surrounded by enemy mobs and getting pounded, while your AI companions stand around not killing things. I must have reloaded some battles dozens of times while getting just the right kills in the right order (or having my AI buddies do so by accident), in order to advance. A far cry from Gears of War, Call of Duty, or Far Cry. Figuring out which object provide cover or can be vaulted over is also super confusing.
The desert setting of a ruined Dubai is unique and gorgeous, and is probably the best part of the game. If someone wanted to make a Dune FPS with this team, it would probably look fantastic.
Some critics praised this game as a bold step in morally dark storytelling in shooters. I'd say some of that praise is exaggerated, and there are certainly enough other games that do it better.

SUMMARY
Great premise, awful execution. Do not buy.
There are way too many things wrong with the game at this stage. I don't understand how inXile spent $4M+ and several years at this, yet managed to produce something that feels so incredibly rushed, and has one of the worst implementation of the first ~2 hours of gameplay of all RPGs I've played.
If you're looking for a good CRPG buy Tyranny instead.
FIRST IMPRESSIONS
Start a new game, there's some voice acted intro text, and then all you see is greyscale hexes and black. You look at it for a moment and wonder if the game broke, until you realize there's a pretty gray character lying on the hexes too and that you can move. The game describes this pure black thing next to you - that on your screen looks like a deep hole with no detail at all distinguishable - as a bowl of sorts. The game describes how you can see the details of the bowl as a light source moves around. None of this you can see on your screen, just see a static black thing that sorta has a shape that could be a bowl, but it has no depth to it at all, just pure black. 5 minutes in the game looks rather dull and really unimpressive.
You run around a bit in this very linear bit going through dialog trees where you're supposed to make "choices". The dialog is phrased as if you knew what you were supposed to be doing, and then you're given several options to choose from. Many of these options refer to game mechanics there is no way for you to understand at this point, and you just get frustrated and think the game could just as well throw dice as there is no way for you to even make an educated guess as to what happens from the options or how you're supposed to choose.
Then it turns out these "choises" you made was the character creation, and the game just keeps dumping more and more references to game mechanics without providing any explanation to them. One option gives you "+15% willpower", but you have literally no way to figure out what "willpower" does. You have options to be, among other things, "Clever" or "Intelligent", each comes with bonuses suitable for a character of the type I wanted to build, but additionally really unintuitive negative points. It also feels like the game is misleading or lying to you about some effects, as I think I've heard it mention effects that then don't get shown in the details once you try to look at them. Tell me, do you want to be Clever, or Strong-willed? I have no idea, as there's no way to know what these mean in-game when you make the decisions.
At worst the game throws ~5 consecutive tutorial "Did you know" -dialogs at you so you already forgot what the first one said before you even get to the last one or get to use any of this information.
GAMEPLAY ISSUES
There's an ability to read people's thoughts or something. You get some rare insight into what people think mid-dialog, but after getting about 20 such insights the game gave me exactly 0 options to use the info.
Lots of dialog and flavor text is shown mid-game in popup texts that pop up and vanish without any interaction from you. Unlike in other similar games there's no combat log or anything where you could go back to check what that text said. You can use a pause key, sometimes, but never when you'd really need it as during scripted sequences the pause key does nothing. Why would you implement a "pause" key that doesn't pause the game?
All initial items for you and the first few party members are "only usable by X".
Dialog options seem to arbitrarily vanish after activating them once, there doesn't seem to be any logic as to which options just change to "tell me that thing again" -type things, and which ones just vanish.
It's possible to accidentally pick up items that give you a penalty if you have too many of them. You cannot drop them, you can only sell them, or swap them in the party, or use them, if you can. If you can't use them, don't have any empty slots in your party, and nobody to sell them to, you get a penalty and there's apparently no way around it except loading the game before you picked it up.
The game incorrectly refers to the ground as "Earth", when they are clearly not on our planet.
After the couple of hours the game has mentioned cyphers, tides, esoteries, etc. which I still don't understand the slightest bit.
Party members seem to follow you with an annoying delay instead of in formations. This probably leads to unfortunate combat setups.
UI/UX ISSUES
Camera feels somehow wrong by default, it feels a little less annoying when disabling the autofollow.
A blue dot is a bonus, two blue dots is more bonus, two red dots is a penalty. These are shown with some unclear text explanations, much before the game explains what these really mean.
Applying attribute points is done in a screen where you have two arrows on the left and right of a number for the attribute, clicking the arrows changes the value, which changes the amount of space the number takes and moves the buttons from right under your mouse cursor, when you're trying to click them. Similar issues are all over.
I'm playing on full HD resolution, with "full" anti-aliasing, yet there is not a single edge that doesn't look jagged. The inventory management screen has rough edges everywhere on the UI, your character is rendered with clear rough edges, as are all the items, and much of the text.
There are some really random obviously wrongly positioned effects sometimes hovered *almost* on top of your character portrait that don't seem to make any sense and then just go away when there's a scene transition.
In the inventory screen there are two places where your weapon is shown, right-clicking on one shows "details", right-clicking on the other does nothing. Why? Who knows. I sure don't.
Right-clicking on things sometimes opens this "detailed" view, which describes stats and shows flavor text on items. However, this is quite unclearly structured and it still often fails to tell you what is going on, and doesn't clearly indicate with graphical design e.g. what part is flavor text. You can't further hover over/click on unclear concepts to find out more about them.
Dialog trees look very boring compared to e.g. Tyranny. The colors are dull, there's nothing to hover over, there seems to be no extra information other than just the text for you to say and what the other people respond with.
FINAL NOTES
I was super excited to try the game out finally after all this time, and now I'm really heavily disappointed.
I helped kickstart this years ago, I spent $135 (+S&H) thinking I'd help inXile create something amazing. In the first ~2 hours of gameplay I hated almost every moment, though I saw that under the incredibly rough surface there is probably something worth looking at. However, as the game simply pisses me off constantly, I don't want to play any more of it until inXile fixes at least some of these issues.
Did inXile do exactly 0 internal testing before releasing this? Did nobody complain about these issues? How, after multiple years of development, can the first moments of the game be so incredibly weak?
After playing games like Pillars of Eternity and Tyranny, this game feels like garbage in way too many areas. The devs should play Tyranny, and then play their game from scratch, and then fix all the things they find were clearly better in Tyranny.
Most of these issues should not be big things to fix, add information here and there, a few tooltips, fix a few UI decisions (fixed width vs. variable width, etc.), and so on, if inXile had any interest in it. However, with what I heard about some big quest-line issues with Wasteland 2 (which I also kickstarted) never being fixed, I doubt inXile has huge interest in fixing these issues.
Unless inXile fixes these issues and they're sorry for messing up, I don't think I'll ever be able to support their kickstarters again, or buy their games for over $10.

Much like its predecessor, Anno 1701, Dawn of Discovery is an addictive, fairly slow-paced, real-time resource management strategy game.  The premise of the game is that you need to fulfil the demands of your population. You harvest resources to build houses; you build houses to increase your population and secure taxes; as your population increases, their demands for other resources increase; and as you fulfil those demands, you garner greater taxes and unlock the rest of the tech tree. It's hard for me to recommend this game over Anno 1701, this plays more like an expansion than a sequel (they both use the same engine), but I can assure you you can sink many hours into this game.

I don’t think there’s a hard limit on how long a game needs to be, but there are definitely games out there that are too short. Sometimes they’re like Detention, games so good that the scant two hours you get with it simply aren’t enough. Sometimes they’re like Shadowrun Returns, games that end right when it feels like they should be getting started. And then there are games like ENKI, games that don’t have enough content and try to hide that fact with little tricks. It’s not even that bad of a trick, really, it’s just that nothing in the game is put together well enough to earn it a pass.
I’m not real concerned about spoilers for a short puzzle game, but if you are turn back now. You’ve been unceremoniously thrown into a pit to await some terrible fate, because your killer has wandered off for exactly thirty minutes. In that time you need to find a way out of said pit and further out of peril, but a mess of locks and codes and hidden doors are going to make that tricky. If you’re diligent you might also learn a bit about why the hell you’ve been taken in the first place, and maybe even find some alternative solutions to your conundrum.
First of all, yes, this game is thirty minutes long. The timer starts the moment you gain control, and if it runs out you very much die. There’s a 99% chance your first attempt at the game is going to end like that, because the puzzles and items needed for them are not going to be very apparent from the start. Every time you die you start over with elements of the puzzles randomized, so you can learn what you need to do but not memorize exactly how to do it. I died on my first run but on the second, I was able to escape after a mere fifteen minutes.
That’s really the main caveat of ENKI, that it is extremely short by any metric. It’s also less of a puzzle game and more of one single, expansive puzzle of “how do I open this door”. All of your scampering around and scrounging for keys and medallions is in service of opening the one door that leads to freedom. Once you poke a bit deeper into the collectibles and puzzle out some symbolism there is an alternate ending that’s a bit more involved, but ultimately the goal is the same and it all fits neatly into a half-hour block. I personally didn’t mind the time limit itself but I am certain there are folks out there prepared to be outraged at having their progress reset every thirty minutes, and I can’t say I blame them in the least.
It wasn’t the time limit that grated on me, but the randomization element. To keep ENKI from being purely brute-forced, aspects of the puzzles are randomized every time you play. The puzzles themselves, like a safe with a symbol keypad and an incomplete crucifix, are always the same, but the items you need are in different places and the codes are changed up. I understand the need to keep subsequent runs fresh but this is the lowest-effort method possible, and leads to situations where you know exactly what to do and what you need, but not where to find it. It adds no depth at all to the puzzle, just the padding of finding the key or crest to continue.
I can level the same criticism at the horror element, and honestly I hesitate to call this one a horror title at all. The concept of being imprisoned by a serial killer and racing against the clock is certainly terrifying, but that tension is never more than implied by the time limit. You will never at any point be in any danger aside from the ever-ticking timer, no matter how hard the game tries to convince you otherwise. Indeed, the only reason I still call it horror is because ENKI is loaded with brainless jumpscares like gas pipes leaking and doors slamming. What potential there is for the atmosphere is utterly wasted, leaving you to fit the pieces of the puzzle together with aggravating hisses and snaps in your ears.
I’m not mad at ENKI, I’m just disappointed. The hook is good, the graphics are crisp (if a little dark), and the open-ended exploration and collectible-based endings are solid foundations for a puzzle game. But instead of building a grand house of horrors upon that foundation, we get a one-room shack with a flickering light bulb. The random element does little more than frustrate, and without that subsequent runs are just retracing steps until you do everything quick enough (which isn’t much of a challenge in the first place). The final nail in this coffin was when it crashed ten minutes into my third run, wiping out my progress towards a specific ending I wanted. If ENKI can’t even let me play it the way it’s supposed to be played, I don’t see how I could ever recommend it.

Before you take a person's recommendation or not it's important to know what kind of games they like.
I love horror games. Enki is a good horror game. At least, by my definition of what makes a good horror game.
There is no combat whatsoever, which I believe aids in the "helplessness" of the situation. Should anything attack me there is nothing I can do except die. Though nothing did attack me while playing Enki that didn't stop me from worrying that something would.
Which brings me to my next marker of a good horror game: fear. Enki is probably not going to give you nightmares or make you run to turn on all the lights. What it did was fill me with the anxious kind of fear that for some reason is appealing. The atmosphere is simple but tense. Being locked in a basement with too many rooms, hallways and doorways means that I'm constantly worried about what I might find.
Tension is one of the most valuable parts of a horror game. The more you play and nothing "big" happens the more tension builds and the more primed to freak out you are. That's where jump scares can be great. Eventually the tension has to be relieved. A big shock followed by a rush of relief, and usually laughter, is a satisfying way to relieve tension. A lot of games overuse jump scares, Enki did not.
Enki was a very enjoyable horror experience for me. It was more about atmosphere, tension and exploration than anything. The puzzles were easy and I could have enjoyed a bit of difficulty there . Most of the difficulty came from trying to find all the damn items that spawn randomly.
One thing I will note is that it is a very dark game. I cranked the gamma all the way up for my first playthrough and like this the lighting was just right. However, when replaying it at a later date I was not able to adjust the lighting to an acceptable level. With the gamma levels all the way up it wasn't even bright enough to play. I tried playing with my screen settings but I still couldn't get it to a playable level. I'll note that when I originally played it I had my comp hooked up to my big screen tv so it is something that can be fixed depending on screens or options.

So there IS a lot of problems with this game. In particular depending on why you like CRPGs you might hate this. I did not back this on Kickstarter, so can't speak to that. I can say that it feels like a complete game.
However, I loved it.
If you like tactical combat, and that is what draws you to CRPS, avoid this. The combat is "eh" (mainly because I feel like everything is so slow). Depending on how you play, there also is not a lot of it.
For example, you can talk or think your way around most combat. I think I only had 5 or 6 combats in my playthrough, and they were "crisis" where the victory was not "kill everyone" (or at least the only victory), but instead had alternate win conditions.
Honestly, I found it super refreshing. You don't often see that in a game.
It has an interesting world with an interesting plot. Some of the interactions were really good. One of the party members is up there as favorite party member in any game.
Time wise you can probably get through the main quest pretty quickly. However, playing through and exploring and taking your time will probably give you 30-40 hours.
HOWEVER,
The game does kinda look not so great. If you zoom in the graphics actually look much better (not the character models though. They are aweful). But I like to play more zoomed out, and it just does not look great.
I would have also loved to have character portriates while talking to NPCs.
I did not run into a lot of bugs, at least until the end. I experienced some loading problems that made it hard to complete the game.
TL;DR
If you like character development and exploration, don't mind a lack of combat, and don't mind reading, I highly recomend this game.

Overall...I have to say I'm very disappointed. Numenera is definitely not the game it was promised to be.
The Good:
Music and sounds - Weird, bizzare and mysterious, just like the 9th World itself.
Location design - Incredible, weird, curious, mysterious, "numenerish".
The Bad:
Main Plot - "What does one life matter?", in the end the game doesn't really answer that question.
Side quests - They are just there, forgettable and in the end it's all about the % roll on persuasion.
Linear Structure - There is no open world. Game is divided on hubs, every hub has a few locations to visit, but at one point you'll be asked "Are you sure you want to continue?", and then every single quest from that hub will become "Failed", there is no going back.
Compaions - VERY boring, uninspired, weak compared to the Main Hero, small choice to begin with and the most interesting one (The Toy) was cut out of the final version of the game. They don't have very interesting backgrounds and sometimes simply join you "just because". They don't have much to say, and when they finally say something it's not very interesting.
Skills and Spells - Not much to choose from, very boring and bare-bones compared to the "Corebook Numenera" skills.
Turn-based Combat - Sluggish, boring, completely NON-tactical. It was a huge mistake to make a pool on Kickstarter asking if people want turn-based or real-time. It was a bad choice, real-time would be much more tactical and interesting.
False-advertisement Polish Dubbing - People were promised to hear the legends of the polish RPG dubbing, and we hear them indeed, for about 3 minutes. And that's it. Read the rest of it.
In the end I'd say there are way better cRPGs out there. Numenera sadly feels solid only in some aspects but very weak in the others (more important ones). cRPGs should be all about you, your companions, relationships, friendships and adventures together. About tactical combat and overcoming the odds with clever use of your skills. Dialogues with your companions should make you feel something (like in Baldur's Gate where you could be betrayed in the most important moment as well as fall in love in someone who was near-irredeemable evil and change their heart).
5/10, very expensive, very lacking in the core aspects of cRPGs, painfully boring combat, good soundtrack with emotional music but nowhere near as many emotions were put into the dialogues.

It seems there are two polar opposites in the reviews. I say both the positive AND negative reviews are correct.
Gameplaywise this is one of the best Hitman games yet. it's a true return to the sandbox like levels of Blood Money. and the game allows you to turn off all, some or none of the handholding gameplay mechanics making it a true and challenging experience for those that want it. The feature that sticks out the most is the oppurtinities.
Think of Oppurtunities as a list of about 10 or so different preset ways to kill a target. These oppurtunities are started by something like:
e.g. you overhear two waitors talk about the prefered cocktail that youor target drinks
Depending on what you want to play you can have the game set waypoints to take you through the oppurtunity.
e.g. Marking waitor disguise, then rat poison
And so on until you kill the target.
However you can turn this all off and explore the maps with practically no HUD and come across the oppurtunities and have to find the waypoints yourself.
The other big plus of this game is the maps. There are only three maps so far with one being released per month.
This is where the controversy lies. The maps are brilliant so far. each one better than the last. Particularally with Episode 2 the map feels natural. it doesn't feel like a sandbox, it feels like an actual world where you have to work your way to kill the target.
BUT why couldn't they have just waited.Before the announcement of this game we haven't really been asking for a Hitman game. Squenix could have waited and released a game with 12+ maps and tonnes of content for a standard AAA price and no-one would have complained.
Basically for what there is there is a LOT to do. But there are only a few maps, with more planned each month.
If you want your Hitman fix get the full experience now and if the episodes are as good as Episode 2, you will likely have the best Hitman game ever and you will be more than satisfied.
If you aren't really too desperate for Hitman you could wait until all the episodes are released and probably get the game for a lower price.
OR if you have some disposable income get the intro pack and see if the game is to your liking. If it is get the upgrade pack. If it isn't don't

This latest iteration of HITMAN feels like a must-have for fans of the series, and I would recommend it to anyone else who enjoys stealth games. There's a lot of variety here in the current levels, and the gameplay is deep and engaging.
I've played every HITMAN game, and Blood Money has always been the high point of the series for me. I enjoyed the increased narrative in Absolution, but they really lost out when it came to gameplay. However, HITMAN is the best of both. The levels are large and very 'sandboxy', with lots of approaches and methods open to the player.
I've really enjoyed my time with the game so far, and I'd highly recommend it to any fan of the series, or anyone looking for an interesting and varied stealth game experience.
As for the episodic nature, I personally am fine with it. The levels so far are really large and take about 2 - 4 hours to get a first decent 'basic' playthrough done, and completing the mission in a variety of ways unlocks new equipment, starting locations, drop-off caches, etc that enable you to try and plan the 'perfect' hit. Having the updates drop on a regular basis keeps the content interesting and frequent enough that it is enjoyable.
Season One's content is now available in it's entirety.
Two smaller levels designed as 'simulations', to teach you the basics and get you up to speed. Even so, these missions are fairly roomy (especially the second one), and give you lots to play with.
The first mission proper, this sees 47 attending a fashion show to eliminate two high profile targets. The mansion is expansive, with service staff working hard behind the scenes and in the basement areas, the fashion show on the first floor, and a secret auction taking place on the top floor. This level really starts to showcase the scale of the HITMAN levels and your options within them.
Off to Italy in this mission, where we have another two targets to eliminate in a grand manor, and a deadly secret to destroy in a hidden lab underground. The level is even more expansive than the Paris mission, including a large chunk of the town of Sapienza to wander, a morgue and church, shopping area, pier, sewers, the manor is divided into several large buildings including an observatory, plus the ruins of a castle at the back of the manor. The lab area requires a keycard to enter (or the use of noisy explosives), there are a multitude of 'zones' that you can access with different disguises (kitchen staff, gardeners, security, lab scientists, priests...). This feels like, so far, the best mission a HITMAN game has had.
For me Marrakesh is the low-point of this season of HITMAN. The level isn't awful, and there's plenty to do, but for me the level loses major points in terms of structure. You begin in the middle of a maze of streets. At one end of this maze is one target located within a Swedish consulate, and at the other end is your other target hiding out in a derelict school. There's little to do in the streets imbetween each end of the level (although a few opportunities are present), and these areas basically exist just to pad out and provide a little flavour. Whilst other missions feel like they offer a wide variety of ways into each location and a lot of opportunities, Marrakesh felt limited and repetitive. You need to rely on just a couple of entrances to each location at either end of the level only, and once inside the play area is relatively restricted, even once disguised. Visually interesting and varied, but a major disappointment to me in terms of sandbox play.
Off to Bangkok, to the Himmapan Hotel, a glorious little sandbox. You arrive, and can check in as 'Mr Rieper', an alias of 47's. The hotel comprises of two multi-floor buildings divided by an atrium. One of these buildings is open as usual, whilst the other is closed to the public due to pesticide spraying on the lower floors and a pop group have temporarily converted the upper suites into a recording area. Most of the suites here require a security keycard to access, so some sneakiness is required to obtain them, or to bypass them entirely. The two targets each occupy a different side of the hotel, although opportunities can pull them out of their 'native' environment. This level is visually spectacular and you really feel like the hotel is a working building with each group of NPC's going about their duty (hotel cleaning and desk staff, security, cooks, gardeners, etc). This level is an absolute highlight.
Here we see an increase in difficulty, as there are four targets this time spread across a militia-occupied Colorado farm. There is no 'civilian' area here and 47 must hide at all times or assume a military disguise. The areas of the farm are distinct and interesting, with portions being used for training drills, target practice, bomb creation and testing, and a farmhouse with a hostage held down below. The targets are each interesting and memorable, some with great narrative elements, and there are a couple of ways to get to them each through the opportunities (alongside the many ways you could improvise dealing with them). I had a great time wandering this map and experimenting with how to quietly and effectively deal with each target. A wonderful sandbox to play in, with a bit of care.
Season One's finale takes us to a private medical hospital located in the snowy mountains of Japan. Due to the secretive and restrictive nature of the facility, you must make do without any equipment when starting out (at least initially), which really helps increase the difficulty of this mission. Additionally, patients rooms are access via RFID tags within the gowns each patient wears, providing opportunities to subdue and access other areas. The medical facility is striking in design and visuals, and the glimpses of snowy mountainside exteriors and the zen garden area really compliment the stark, clean interiors.
Oh, and that skybox really is gorgeous, one hell of a view and beautiful paper lanterns drift by, a great touch.
Somehow Hokkaido feels a bit smaller, more personal than the missions that came before, but it is still an interesting finale for Season One, and it is a fitting and enjoyable challenge.
Two bonus episodes were released in summer, one for Sapienza and the other for Marrakesh. Each cuts out a small portion of the level, sets it at night and blocks off the exits, making a smaller sandbox area for a new narrative to play out. Sapienza sees a film crew recording a sci-fi blockbuster in the town square and 47 is hired to take out the director, whilst Marrakesh sees the action focus around the under-utilised markets area.
Whilst it's interesting to see these locations reworked for nighttime and with some fairly major overhauling of the levels, I didn't find the bonus episodes particularly engaging as they are so much smaller than the original levels. As a bonus they are fine, but nothing I'd rush to experience over the core experience, I found many of the vanilla levels 'escalation' missions (content that uses the existing levels but has new targets, conditions and complications) far more engaging.

Max looked around.  How had he arrived at this place?  He didn't know.  He'd never imagined such a place could exist.  All about him were chattering voices, clamouring to have their opinion heard.  "This is great.  Highly recommended", "How anyone could find enjoyment in this I will never know", "Double Like, Two thumbs up!"...
None of the voices were really saying anything, and often the remarks didn't justify the rating.  Max was feeling a strange urge build up inside himself, an urge to to voice his own opinion on these opinions.  "Awful, just awful.", "ajskldjfalskdjf", "11/10  Would arrest again."...  The voices were building now, building in intensity, volume and number.  He looked and his hand was reaching forward, of its own accord.  Shaking as he strained to bring it under control.  It was reaching for one of the opinions.  It's not actually a helpful review, he told himself.  You're not supposed to click the Yes button.  It is what the Funny button is there for.  He felt his finger reaching down, he strained harder, it was no good.  His finger pressed the button.
Max shot bolt upright in fright.  His sweat soaked vest, grey and grimey, was almost the same colour as the sheets in this dank motel.  It had all been a dream.  His hand wiped the sweat from his brow, tomorrow his investigation would continue and this dream would fade from memory.  He grabbed the bottle of painkillers from the bed-side table.  Next to it he noticed a white square.  He tried to focus his bleary eyes on what is said.   "How would you rate your stay"...
The above would not be out of place in the world of Max Payne, if it weren't for the poor writing that is.  Madness descends as Max is caught up in an undercover investigation gone bad.  It has certainly aged from way back when I first played the demo, but I only bought and completed the game a few years ago and still very much enjoyed it. Spec Ops: The Line does for games what Heart of Darkness did for books and Apocalypse Now did for films. I do not write a lot of reviews, but this one deserves it for being a great game, showing war from a unique view in modern gaming.
This is a game that really shines on it's story and narrative. It pulls no punches and unflinchingly shows you every aspect of war that most other games brush over. This game provokes emotional responses that other games try to avoid and involves the player with the decisions faced in conflict situations, and sometimes those choices are not good, or have no good answer at all, but you are still forced to make the hard decision.
It starts off drawing you in as another 3rd person cover shooter, but changes as the game progresses so that you are less interested in the action and more interested in the story, which is masterfully done. It reveals just enough as you are going through so when you get to the end, you remember all those hints that were tugging at the corners of your mind, and catch yourself saying, 'I knew it!' On a replay, there are a lot of those subtle hints that you see that you miss on the first play, and it has been very well written that way. (Think Sixth Sense for this). The twist at the end is pretty clever and makes this game stand out from a lot, but it is not completely unexpected.
The action set pieces are done well in the desert city environment and this comes into play in the game a lot, though it can feel a little bit forced sometimes. The whole 'My Squad vs the World' gets a bit tiring towards the end, as you take on just about every living person in the city with a gun. As I said above though, the importance of the action at that point should have faded away.
Positives:
Negatives:
Conclusion:
A well crafted and engaging piece of work. Worth the effort you put into it as you walk away from it with more than just the simple amusement. If you want just a piece of gung-ho action, avoid it, but if you want more from games, dont hesitate, buy it, and enjoy.

It is a compelling game, and I've had some fun with it, but ultimately there is a better experience to be found with this game's competitors.
Heavy Bullets has decent enemy variety, and I like the art style. The shooting and re-usable bullets mechanics are not great in my experience, I would have preferred more variety. The bombs that you can throw are very hard to hit anything with and generally seem useless, so you're just going to be sticking with the revolver for the majority of the game. Items might be interesting, but I have no idea what any of it does. Some are self-explanatory, but what does a golden skull do? I just played a run through with one, and I have no idea what it did, if anything, because the game makes no attempt to tell you. I don't need to be spoon fed, but at the same time I do need information if I am to understand what stuff does. So I picked up some repellant, what does it repell? You can't test it by hanging around the various enemies, because you will end up getting yourself killed, and the game doesn't tell you one way or another.
The ease at which you can get screwed over by the game is not balanced with enjoyable game play, in my opinion. Stressful, tense game play is welcome, but there aren't any "♥♥♥♥ yeah" moments, no moments of "that thing I just did was awesome" to balance it out. There are also technical issues, if you are considering buying this game check the forums before you do. Currently (and for a while now) there is a bug causing really bad frame skips that can really screw you over if you happen to be trying to shoot something at the time. The aiming reticule is also not locked to the centre of the screen so it jiggles, and for some users wanders quite far from the centre making it hard to be accurate.
It's not a bad game by any stretch of the imagination, and maybe on sale it's worth a look but I can't recommend it in all honesty.

A short and sweet, cheap and cheerful puzzle game about blocks, where the aim is to click on black blocks to remove them in such a way as to make red blocks fall off the play area while keeping white ones safe and sound on terra firma. As the stages progress, new block types/colours are introduced to effect play in different ways, such as green ones that explode, yellow ones that bounce, or blue ones that grow, to name a few.
The arrangement of the levels are fairly clever and interesting, and while most are straightforward enough that you'll likely figure them out merely at first glance, some are ever so slightly more complex and will require a little trial and error, which is thankfully pretty painless since you can restart instantly at any point.
It's not without its issues as the music isn't all that great and also restarts with each new attempt, and the physics seems a little weird as repeating the same moves won't always necessarily produce the same results. Sometimes the blocks also have a nasty habit of falling backwards or forwards in three-dimensional space, rather than just along the two-dimensional plane along which the gameplay operates, but, again, thanks to the quick restarts, even when you fail, be it through your own fault or the game's, it's hard to say you ever really feel like you're being robbed of progress.
Arguably the worst issue of all, though, is the lack of a save feature, which means it'll have to be completed in a single sitting. But to be completely honest, if I hadn't read the user comments I never would have even realised it, since it's so short and doesn't have all that many stages or real reason to replay it once you're finished.
I'm sure some will debate the price, and maybe there's grounds to say it should be a free browser game, or that at best it should only ever be bought on sale, but either way, while I know it's all relative, 99c is hardly going to break the bank and I doubt anyone would genuinely feel robbed by the game one way or another. Buy it at full price, on sale, in a bundle, or not at all, it's up to you, but for me at least, I can say I had fun during my brief time with it.

So I've been an avid player of the Hitman series, dating back to the first one. I've devoured each and every Hitman game since then, played each of them a multitude of times and returned frequently over the course of years if only to return to a few handpicked favourite levels of mine. Like the the Hotel in Contracts or the casino in Blood Money and while we're on the topic; Blood Money's by far my favourite game of the series.
The level design, non-linear approach and responsive, intricate mechanics, having a base of operations, the newspaper reports that served as summaries of your past work, all of that made Blood Money an excellent game. A couple of years later, blending out the forgetable Absolution, which had more likeliness to a weaker iteration of the Splinter Cell franchise, I thought we'd finally get a worthy sucessor to Blood Money.
Alas, I was in for a surprise. The new game's again subpar to older Hitman games, in almost every aspect. I mean, thankfully I can't pull a sniperrifle out of my pocket anymore (Absolution anyone?), but other than that we've basically went one step forth and two steps back.
Naturally the graphics are better, however the animations are not. Aiming down the sights of your gun looks weird and it's even worse once you crouch and the professional holds the pistol like a ♥♥♥♥ing scrub. It just looks completely unappealing and I simply cannot comprehend how they ended up with worse animations than in Hitman's predecessors. Instead of holding larger rifles in his off-hand, they're now awkwardly slung over 47's shoulder on an invisible string.
Gunplay feels unintuitive and unrewarding, granted Hitman never had the greatest, but I remember spending a ♥♥♥♥ton of time just trying to get off the perfect series of shots when confronted with a target and its bodyguards and when in doubt, I finished one by one off after critically wounding them; another feature that's gone amiss. Also, remember how older games allowed you to shoot through doors? Yeah, that's gone too.
The new game's level design is pretty neat, to be fair, and paired with better core mechanics it'd most likely make for a great Hitman game. But not as it is, not when the game feels much weaker than its predecessors and more like a beta for a potentially promising Hitman game somewhere down the road.
To summarize;
+ level design is fantastic
+ graphics are much better
+ wide variety of options to complete mission objectives
+ proper disguise feature reinstated (to a certain extent. hell, you could put on a disguise and practically sprint through to your target and shoot it - nobody would blink an eye at you.)
- core animations are partially worse than in its predecessors
- former, much liked core mechanics missing (being able to wound, store a weapon in a suitcase etc)
- gunplay is absolutely boring
- killing melee animations are stale, unrewarding and furthermore very repetitive
- AI is literally braindead (kill a main target, e.g. the boss of an organisation, everyone's back to business as usual within 5 minutes)
- additional, former core assassin weapon arsenal has to be earned through a redudant online xp rewarding based component
All in all I'm very disappointed with the new game and uncertain how IO went from building onto their franchise, to stripping so many things away over the course of the last couple of installments.

Set in the dark, gruesome basement of a serial killer, ENKI is a horror title that is solely based around solving puzzles. You will have 30 minutes to figure out your escape route, and find all of the items that you need in order to do so. The game boasts a high replayability factor due to randomly generated item placement and multiple endings that depend on how much you've learned about your captor, his previous victims, and his occult interests.
The set up for Enki is fairly decent, the basement that you're locked in is creepy and has a very obvious Satanic vibe to it. There are books on demons, alchemy, and sorcery scattered throughout the area, along with cryptic symbols and notes. You have 30 minutes to gain your freedom, and to do so you must solve easy puzzles; most of them simply involve finding keys, but some require you to find other items such as sharp nails, fuses, and large circular tokens. If you happen to find the certain key that unlocks the cellar prior to the end of 30 minutes, you will have made your escape; if you fail, you will ultimately die. It's a simple concept with a simple execution, but the random item placement does make the experience different every time. Once you know what you're looking for and where it goes, the game gets a lot easier.
While the store page does talk about multiple endings, there are five, the only difference is the headline of the newspaper at the end; escaping with mild knowledge, all knowledge, no knowledge, and two deaths. There are fifteen total "collectibles", for lack of a better term, to find in order to piece together who the killer is; five drivers licenses for previous victims, five demonic books, and five pages about the murderer himself. This does add a bit more to the story, but not very much. More in-depth endings would've been welcomed.
The last time I reviewed ENKI, I completely crucified it for its abysmal optimization. Since then, the developers released an update that fixed that. I'm happy to say that on my 6700k/GTX 1080 rig, I ran at a flawless 60FPS with full graphic settings, at a 1080p resolution. I cannot say with certainty that this patch will help lower end systems, or AMD builds; my last rig was AMD and ran this game so poorly that I never got out of the 25 FPS zone, even on low settings, and my hardware was current at the time.
After a total re-evaluation, I'm happy to say that I can recommend ENKI now. Being able to actually see what you're doing in a fluid framerate really helps things, and the developer has even seemed to fix the random crashes that used to occur and totally ruin your run. The only real improvements here could be having the timer pause when you're reading documents or when the game is paused. Other than that, ENKI is a great little escape room title and escaping from the clutches of a serial killer in a timed environment does make for a rather intense gaming experience. It's sure to appeal to puzzle enthusiasts, as well as horror thrill-seekers.

My very first boxed PC game was Baldurs Gate. Then over the years I played every great Crpg. Fallout, Icewind Dale, Planescape Torment, Arcanum, Pillars of Eternity and the most recent Tyranny. I have played and replayed these games and IM happy to say that Torment: Tides of Numenera is amongst the best of them.
The Story is deep as the worlds lore. You have to leave some of your preconceptions behind and embrace the alien nature and laws of this world. Where aliens, otherworldly beings and mutants walk under the red Sun. If you are afraid of walls of text and lore then this game will not be for you. If you enjoy reading and learning about a brand new world you will adore Numenera.
Gameplay is the weak point of the title. Combat can be fun and engaging, with varied party setups, builds and interesting weapons and items but the way its system works can be a drag slowing the pace greatly. I have to admire a game where I can end a combat scenario without killing a single enemy, where I can avoid combat altogether. During my entire playthrough I didn't even have 10 battles. There are some technical bugs, but nothing game breaking. (Lets not forget that Planescape Torments combat wasn't great...).
As a last word Rhin is now atop one of my favorite npc's of all time. (If you think she is weak I can only laugh at you.)
Cheers

Full disclosure: I backed this sucker on Kickstarter three years or so ago at an amount that puts me in the game under another name ($150+).
I feel like I should correct a few misconceptions about this game.
First, it isn't an action game--if you want tactical combat, or just a lot of combat period, this is NOT your game. This game is designed so that fighting is a distant second option to other methods for resolving conflict. There are very few necessary fights, and most moments of conflict are obviously intended to be resolved via other methods, including lying your face off or doing favors for NPCs.
Second, it isn't a 'quick' game--if you dislike reading, or just want something that you can sit down, play for a few hours and not have to think about, remember, or otherwise engage in contemplation, this is NOT your game. This game is designed to be intensely story-rich, which requires a certain amount of effort from players. And in fact, this game almost predominantly balanced toward story and environment, over almost all other concerns. The story itself is extremely rich, thought provoking, and intricate, and in order to fully experience and enjoy it, players are going to have to do a ton of reading, thinking, and remembering. Think of it as a particular style of game, where on the one end we have games that are primarily about reflexes and short term memory, and on the other end we have games that are about long term memory and contemplation.
Third, as a creative effort, it simply cannot be exactly as predicted for backers--stick with me here. This is something people generally wouldn't know, unless they work in a creative industry, but whenever you engage in a creative effort, there is always a degree to which the result will deviate from your original direction. The more artists you have working on something, in a general way, the more divergence you will tend to have. This game was the child of around twenty established and/or well known fantasy and science fiction authors, who tackled stories, characters, and ideas. As such, it was pretty much going to deviate. I've been following the development for three or so years now and been active on the backer's forum, suggesting story ideas, approaches, and soundtrack ideas, all of which are yet another source of deviation. The result is not exactly what they promised us. Instead, we got something really, really interesting that has many of the promised characteristics, and in several cases even more than was promised us. I'd be first up, yelling about those discrepancies if it wasn't PAINFULLY obvious that the game's writers, artists, directors, and coders worked their butts off getting us a product that is incredibly polished, if slightly different than promised. They very obviously used my money, and the money of other backers well, and if it took a long time... well.... * shrug * they delivered.
Fourth, this is a direct heritor of PlaneScape: Torment. That was a request made so repeatedly on the backer's forums that I would have been surprised if it hadn't been. If you played the original game, this isn't set in the same universe, but the UI, the way characters react, the way scenery is pieced together, and the way you're expected to interact with the game is going to be very, very familiar. It's a top down, heavily story driven, philosophical, often bizarre little masterpiece, and this game, like its predecessor, is going to be a cult favorite. I'm just hoping it has enough success to encourage the publisher to do more like this.
Fifth, and finally, not a few of the changes are a direct result of requests on the backer forums. My suggestions all made it into the final product, as well as a good chunk of the ideas I saw others contributing. If it is changed from their promise, that is at least partially due to the feedback of backers over the years the game was in development.
Right, having said all this, I feel like I should be somewhat critical of the game.
.....Hmmm.
Uh, let's see. The combat is clunky, but I'm fairly sure that's intentional, since you aren't supposed to fight most of the time. The story can be a little bit obtuse, but if you read things closely, that shouldn't present a problem most of the time.  The top down view in a complex environment can be somewhat overwhelming, but holding down tab will highlight everything you can interact with in the environment (as in PlaneScape: Torment). The game script is, no♥♥♥♥♥♥ reams long, and you'll have to get comfortable with reading for tone and implication to really get the most out of it. The puzzles, for the most part, are set at knowledge you'd get in high school art or physics, but I feel like that's not a terribly high bar. The price is high, but not nearly as high as AAA developer games.
Yeah, you know what? I don't really have a lot of bad things to say about the game. Just be aware, if you buy it, that you're going to need to think alot, read alot, and explore alot, and you should be fine.

It's quite tense, atmospheric, and it feels good to play skillfully. Unfortunately, it has just enough problems that I wouldn't recommend it to someone.
First of all, the entire gameplay through each of the levels is quite fun. It reminds of more of the type of shooting you would do in counterstrike as opposed to quake. It's all about peeking corners and out-reacting the enemies. Pretty much everything you can shoot gets destroyed in one hit, which makes the combat more satisfying and fast-paced.
Sometimes, an enemy will notice you before you notice it and utter a cry, giving you a warning and a bit of time to respond to it before it gets the drop on you. Those sort of situations are definitely fun because you actually know what you could've done differently if you take damage. It keeps you on your toes, too, because you're always trying to listen carefully for enemy cries. I think it adds to the tense atmosphere in a good way.
Other times, however, you won't be able to get the enemies without completely leaving the corner and you'll have to strafe around the room trying to dodge the turrets and other enemies. The turrets' turning and shooting behavior is very unpredictable which makes these sort of forced situations very frustrating because there doesn't seem to really be a reliable strategy for dodging them. Furthermore, I found it very difficult to shoot while strafing in this game - it seemed like the game was always stuttering a lot when I was trying to do this, which is frustrating.
Also problematic, for a game that's all about aiming and shooting and lightning fast reflexes, it absolutely should not be having occasional lag/stuttering. Unfortunately, it has that and it seems to have it right when enemies are attacking me or coming into vision. It's not very freuqent, but it's enough to be annoying and mess up my concentration or ability to track what is going on enough to start taking damage. I am not alone in having this problem, so don't assume you're not going to have this issue either.
Finally, the biggest issue that makes me not want to recommend the game is the difficulty spikes. Specifically, I'm talking about the level 4 and final bosses. The level 4 boss is ridiculously challenging and doesn't at all fit with the methodical, patient playstyle of the rest of the game. Going in blind, you're almost certainly going to just die in a few seconds. Further compounding this issue is that, once you die, you don't get to quickly try again to see how you could've improved (which would be a very satisfying game loop IMO). You have to then carefully plod your way back through the first four levels. I found myself getting impatient because I just wanted to have another go at the boss, and I would end up dying before reaching it because the game really requires a patient, methodical playstyle. This is, of course, highly frustrating, and it feels like the game is just trying to waste my time. It's like, I've already demonstrated I can handle the first stages, just let me go back to where I was at the edge of my abilities, where games are most engaging, dammit!
The final boss is even worse in this regard. It's absolutely overwhelming when you first encounter it - there's so many enemies, new elements, sounds, etc... that it's just impossible to make sense of it your first time. And you have to play through eight stages again to even get to try to understand the boss after you inevitably die. While you're playing through the stages, you're not really getting better against the boss either because you play through the stages with such a different playstyle than you would need to use against the boss.
Overall, the game is intense, atmospheric, twitchy, and responsive (compared to the bullet-sponge type FPS gameplay in similar titles). If you like the sort of FPS gameplay in counter strike and are looking to spend a lot of time on mastering something like that, you may like this game. But if you're someone like me who just wants to have a fun gameplay experience, you probably will find this game more frustrating than fun because so much of your play time will be spent doing things that you already feel you've mastered.

Heavy Bullets. Where to start? At first, I'd like to say that this game is nothing for people who expect to finish the game within the first or second run. Death is permanent in this game and one of the essentials in the whole gaming concept itself. Once you're dead, you have to start the whole game again. However, the effects of death can be overcome by thinking of a clever strategy and planning in advance.
But what is this game even about? You start with a normal revolver filled with six heavy bullets and three bombs at the first level. The main mechanic of this game implies that you have to pick the bullets up in order to keep your revolver full to the brim. However, as you wander through the maze-like generated world, you encounter many sorts of enemies with their own and unique weak spots which you have to find out in order to make up your own way of beating the game. The game gets progressively harder and you'll be facing boss enemies at the fourth and the eigth level. Of course, you cannot beat them without proper preparation. That's when shops come in handy. You gain money by killing enemies, items by purchasing or finding them throughout the whole game (they can be both, passive or active) and special perks by upgrading your skills. With the right combination, you'll be able to finish even the worst enemies off.
This makes the game amazingly challenging. If it seems like you can't get past a level, you have to try harder. Don't stop until you have successfully beaten the stage. If you do stop however, then you're in bad luck because you may never get past said stage. The game forces you to play extended sessions which makes you come back for more. Furthermore, I do have the feeling like the game is adjusting to your style of playing since the more you play this game, the harder the earlier stages get. (If someone could verify said assumption, that'd be great.)
This is not just a FPS game where you are supposed to kill every enemy in sight. It's quite the opposite once the gears are running. With every death the game teaches you about the things you did wrong. Being in a tricky situation doesn't mean that the game's random generation is trying to outsmart your tactics, but you may want to think about a new strategy then.
The art style is very simplistic but still neat to look at which adds a bit of friskiness throughout the whole game itself. One thing I greatly acknowledge is the game's soundtrack. Although the game makes you think that you're in a serious situation considering that your inventory space is limited and you have to make choices wisely, the music emitted from the medbays, bullet shops and banks knocks you out of the skies and shows you that you may need a second to recover and think about how you're going to progress. It's not all about guns and bombs, you know?
However, there are a few minor bugs in this game which will (hopefully) soon get patched, but influence your way of playing heavily at some points. Sometimes, enemies recognize and attack you although you're not in plain sight (or/and if it's not declared in their attacking scheme), but hidden behind a wall. Sometimes, the game seems to lag out for a few frames periodically which can delay your actions significantly. However, like I said, those are minor bugs and will eventually get removed some time. They are no reason to consider not buying the game.
After all, I'd like to say that Heavy Bullets is a nice and refreshing twist for everyone who wants to take on a new challenge. The key to success is to never give up no matter how impossible a certain situation may seem. Everyone who thinks that this game is about blindly killing enemies is out of position. The game requires good reactions and a strategy to fulfill. If that sounds like your cup of tea, then this game is made for you.

The controls are super responsive and the shooting feels meaty and weighty. It's as twitch and skill based a shooter as you will find.
